## Page 6

Preface
This conference marks the 9th International Symposium on Superalloy 718 and
Derivatives. The legacy which started in 1989 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, con-
tinues to provide a rich forum for a combination of industrial and academic tech-
nical papers, presentations, and posters on highly relevant, high-temperature,
superalloy materials. The strength of this series is in its breadth of technical,
geographic, demographic, and application coverage. Over the years, it has provided
an event for all those interested in high-temperature materials and reaches well
beyond the simple exchange of technical ﬁndings. It is regularly a reunion for the
many who work together solving development and production challenges at a
distance from one another through ever-increasing electronic-enabled
collaborations.
This 2018 proceedings volume consists of 72 papers; topic coverage includes the
traditional subjects of casting, forging, and mechanical properties as well as topics
on microstructure, joining, and novel processing. In the most recent two confer-
ences, the advent of novel processing technologies including additive manufac-
turing has begun to open new avenues of investigation in what is a very dynamic
ﬁeld of engineering and science. Across the range of technology areas, the use of
advanced characterization and modeling continues to make signi ﬁcant advances in
the ﬁeld. Contributions in this year ’s conference have spanned a wide swath of the
industrialized world from Canada to South Korea and from the USA to Japan;
60% of papers come from outside the USA. Authors represent academic institutions
(44%), laboratories (17%), and companies (36%). Although from a great diversity
of areas and backgrounds, many gather to discuss knowns and unknowns and to
forge ahead with enriching the understanding of metallurgy and application of these
materials.

Part I
Superalloy 718 & Derivatives: Keynotes

## Page 19

Age Hardenable Nickel-Based Alloy
Developments and Research for New
High Temperature Power Cycles
John P. Shingledecker and John A. Siefert
Abstract Advanced Ultrasupercritical (A-USC) steam Rankine cycles and
Supercritical Carbon Dioxide (sCO 2) Brayton cycles are under intensive develop-
ment to enable low carbon generation of electricity. These high-ef ﬁciency power
cycles, aimed at fossil and in some cases renewable energy, require higher tem-
peratures and pressures compared to traditional steam cycles for pressuring
retaining components such as tubing, piping, heat exchangers, and turbine casings.
Extensive research and development to produce and characterize age-hardenable
nickel-based alloys containing Al, Ti, and Nb in judicious amounts have allowed
designers to now consider supercritical ﬂuid temperatures up to ∼760 °C which is
much greater than today ’s supercritical steam technology based on steel metallurgy
up to ∼610 °C. This paper will focus on the alloys developed around the world to
enable these advanced power cycles, and a discussion on their key properties:
long-term creep strength (100,000 h+), fabricability, and weldability/weld perfor-
mance. Most of these alloys contain less than 25% gamma prime, such as alloy
740H, 263, and 282, due to the need for heavy section weldability, unique to these
applications. While welding processes have now been developed for many of these
alloys using a variety of ﬁller metals and processes, key research questions remain
on the applicability of processes to ﬁeld power plant erection, the potential for
cracking to occur during service, and the long-term weld creep and creep-fatigue
performance.
Keywords Steam boilers
⋅ Steam turbines ⋅ Inconel® alloy® 740H

Introduction to Advanced Energy Systems Requiring
Nickel-Based Alloys
National and Global Trends
In 2015, the electricity produced from coal and natural gas in the U.S. was
approximately equal at 34% each, representing 68% of the total electricity generated
with the remaining major sources being nuclear at 20% and all renewables (hydro,
wind, solar, biomass, etc.) at 12%. In 2016, for the ﬁrst time in the history of the U.
S., electricity produced from natural gas exceeded that of coal generation 36 to 31%
as shown in Fig. 1 [1]. Globally coal and natural gas continue to be the predominate
fuels for the production of energy [ 2]. While future projection for the exact mix of
fossil fuels remain uncertain both nationally and globally, the world is projected to
need more electricity with fossil fuels being a major source of new generation [ 3].
In the US, the need for electricity continues to increase. As illustrated in Fig. 2,
which shows the historical use of electricity as a percentage of the total energy use
in the U.S., efﬁcient electriﬁcation for residential, commercial, and industrial sectors
has steadily increased for over 50 years as electri ﬁcation is recognized as a key
element of the future energy in the U.S. [ 4]. The need for environmentally
responsible electricity through signi ﬁcant reductions in the emission of CO
2 cou-
pled with these national and global drivers for continued use of fossil fuels
necessitates the need for highly ef ﬁcient and transformational fossil energy systems
in the future. Various roadmaps, such as the Coal Utilization Research Council
Fig. 1 Historical and projected U.S. electricity generation mix reported by U.S. Energy
Information Administration including the reference case scenario (left) and a scenario without
adoption of the Clean Power Plan (right) [ 1]
4 J. P. Shingledecker and J. A. Siefert

## Page 21

(CURC)-EPRI roadmap [ 5] and the International Energy Agency (IEA) High
Efﬁciency Low Emission (HELE) roadmap [ 2, 3] have identi ﬁed technology
pathways ﬁrst based on maximizing the ef ﬁciency of today ’s technologies and then
adopting new transformational technologies. EPRI ’s Integrated Energy Network
(IEN) is a vision for the future in which all energy sources are more ef ﬁciently
integrated through (a) producing cleaner energy, (b) using cleaning energy through
efﬁciency and electri ﬁcation, and (c) integrating energy resources [ 2]. A key aspect
of the IEN is the production of cleaner energy through the introduction of new
transformational fossil power systems which will lead to cost-effective low carbon
fossil generation (likely with carbon capture and storage).
Fossil Power Generation Technologies
Two major technologies identi ﬁed in the previously mentioned roadmaps are
Advanced Ultrasupercritical (A-USC) steam cycles and Supercritical CO 2 (sCO2)
power cycles. These concepts are explored in this paper because, as will be shown,
they share many similar structural materials needs and these cycles are required to
fully enable future transformational systems, such as an oxygen- ﬁred boiler
(oxy-combustion) with carbon capture and an A-USC steam cycle.
Today’s pulverized coal- ﬁred (PC) power plants operate at ultrasupercritical
(USC) conditions with steam temperatures up to ∼610 °C. A-USC conditions
generally refer to a steam cycle with steam temperatures of 700 °C and higher. The
world-wide development of A-USC technology started initially around 1998 with a
variety of European Projects [ 6]. In 2001, the U.S. Department of Energy in

conjunction with the Ohio Coal Development Of ﬁce (OCDO) and cost share from
all the major U.S. boiler and turbine original equipment manufacturers (Alstom,
B&W, Foster Wheel, Riley Power, GE, Siemens), the Energy Industries of Ohio
(EIO), and the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) with support from Oak
Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) and the National Energy Technology Labo-
ratory (NETL) Albany Research Center (ARC) and managed for DOE by NETL,
began an ambitious pre-competitive research and development project that would
lead to higher ef ﬁciency coal- ﬁred power plants with reduced CO
2 emissions [ 7].
Figure 3 is a summary of pulverized coal- ﬁred plant ef ﬁciency (HHV) and emis-
sions reduction, as a function of steam temperature for various U.S. based modeling
studies (solid symbols) with some current reported plant ef ﬁciency data (open
symbols). There is considerable variation due to local conditions (cooling water
temperature, fuel type, speci ﬁc design considerations such as size and utilization of
waste heat, etc.). However, when compared to the U.S. Fleet averages of 32.3 –
32.5% HHV, A-USC conditions are expected to raise ef ﬁciency up to 12.5 HHV%
which corresponds to a 35% reduction in CO
2 emissions. Even when compared to
today’s state-of-the-art USC unit operating at 600 °C (for US Conditions), A-USC
offers a CO 2 reduction of ∼13%. While an A-USC powerplant has yet to be built,
numerous economic studies have shown that in the reduction in operating costs
from fuel usage (increase in ef ﬁciency) for A-USC does not offset the increased
capital cost of the plant, until carbon capture and storage is considered. A-USC
becomes economically attractive for carbon reduction, as studies show it is more
cost effective to not produce CO
2 in comparison to producing it and then capturing
it through carbon capture and storage (CCS). In other regions of the world with
more expensive fuel costs or lower labor costs, A-USC may be economically
attractive without carbon constraints [ 9, 10].
Brayton power cycles with supercritical CO
2 (sCO2) as the working ﬂuid are
undergoing intense development for a range of power systems including fossil
energy, nuclear power, shipboard propulsion, geothermal energy extraction, and
solar thermal power cycles [ 11]. Principle advantages of the sCO
2 cycle due to the
physical properties of CO 2 include compact turbo-machinery, high ef ﬁciency, and

the ability to reject heat at higher temperatures when compared to traditional steam
Rankine cycles. These advantages may lead to lower capital costs and higher
efﬁciencies for future power systems [ 12]. Two general types of systems are being
investigated as depicted in Fig. 4. Indirect cycles with a closed loop of sCO
2 are
being considered for a range of application as the ‘heat-source’ could be coal,
natural gas, molten salt, waste heat, etc. To achieve high cycle ef ﬁciencies, ﬂuid
temperatures of 700 °C and pressures approaching 300 bar are being considered.
Current commercial offerings are only available at smaller sizes <10 MW and
lower temperatures [ 13]. A more transformational cycle is the direct cycle (right of
Fig. 4) which involves direct combustion of natural gas (or gasi ﬁed coal) and
oxygen into a high pressure sCO
2 system. The only byproducts of this approach are
high pressure ‘sequestration ready ’ CO2 and water. A pilot plant testing this
technology is currently under construction, and to achieve high ef ﬁciency the
selected ﬂuid temperature is >700 °C [ 13]. Some of the challenges of the sCO 2
system in comparison to a steam Rankine cycle are a narrow heat addition window,
the need for extensive recuperation of heat, much higher working ﬂuid recirculation
volume, and sensitivity to pressure drop. Many small-scale pilot demonstrations are
being investigated to develop these concepts for future power plant applications.

Both A-USC and sCO 2 power cycles require materials to withstand high temper-
atures > 700 °C and pressures > 300 bar for long times. In most cases, the materials
for piping, tubing, valves, and heat exchangers are pressure boundary materials and

there are a range of other properties which are critical for application to A-USC and

2 components including formability, weldability, corrosion resistance,
short-term strength, ductility, creep-fatigue performance, weld performance, and
manufacturability often in very large section thicknesses. Piping, header, and casing
components may require wall thicknesses approaching 100 mm, and there is a need

Conventional nickel-based alloys such as Waspalloy and Nimonic 105 which

bolting, but these alloys are not code approved nor do they have the weldability and

prime. Similarly, alloys strengthened by gamma double prime such as 718 which
have good processing characteristics lose their long-term creep strength above 650
°C, are not code approved, and won ’t meet creep and tensile strength requirements.
Therefore, the main nickel-based alloys of interest to A-USC and sCO
2, shown in
Fig. 5 (nominal compositions in Table 1), are either solid solution strengthened
with basic temperature capability for approximately 700 °C or gamma prime
strengthened with higher capability to about 760 °C. While Table 1 is not an
exhaustive list of materials, the material identi ﬁed have seen the most study pre-
dominately by the US and EU for A-USC applications. Currently, the
highest-strength code approved alloy is Inconel
® Alloy 740H ® which has been
successfully welded and fabricated into components up to about 80 mm in thick-
ness. This is a signi ﬁcant technological achievement (along with similar studies and
successes on alloys 617, 263, 230, and Haynes 282) in the processing of
age-hardenable nickel-based alloys. Table 2 describes some of the research done on
various components made with these alloys; more detailed alloy speci ﬁc informa-
tion and results from major government led developments is summarized in Ref.
[8]. In addition to large section thickness and similar concerns for A-USC steam
Rankine systems, sCO
2 Brayton cycles present additional unique nickel-based
materials challenges. One challenge is the need for very large pipe diameters due to
high recirculation requirements compared to steam; such pipe sizes can only be
fabricated through forming and welding. A second consideration is the need to
develop processing and performance data for compact heat exchangers with these
materials. Compact heat-exchangers are currently made using specialized methods
and designs based on combinations of etching, diffusion bonding, brazing, small
tubes, ﬁns, and wire meshes which will need to be developed for these nickel-based
alloys [ 14].
A number of recent conferences [ 11, 22] and summary reports/papers are now
available with extensive detail into the laboratory investigations, processing studies,
fabrication trials, corrosion performance, and long-term creep behavior of A-USC
alloys for boilers [ 23], turbines [ 24], and in-plant studies/component demonstration
activities [15, 25]. As stated previously, the development of welding procedures for
thick sections on age-hardenable materials including forgings, extrusions, and
castings represents a signi ﬁcant technological advancement. Figure 6 shows just
three examples of the progress made in welding large nickel-based components.

Weldability and Weld Performance
Based on the successful welds made around the globe for A-USC materials, a
comprehensive review was conducted by Siefert and colleagues on the funda-
mentals, weldability, and weld performance of A-USC nickel-based alloys [ 26, 27].
The major ﬁndings and recommendations for the materials listed in Table 1 are
highlighted in the following sections, but the reader is encouraged to review ref-
erences [ 26, 27] for a more thorough treatment of the subject matter.
Weldability
Nickel-based alloys considered for A-USC and sCO 2 applications may be sus-
ceptible to a range of potential weldability issues including: solidi ﬁcation cracking,
heat affected zone (HAZ) liquation cracking, ductility dip cracking (DDC), and
strain age cracking (SAC) which is also known as stress relaxation cracking.
Quantitative ranking of candidate materials for each potential mechanism is prob-
lematic because the number of variables which need to be considered include:
welding process, shielding gas (if applicable), weld metal composition, base metal
composition, grain size, heat-treatment, degree of constraint, sample size/thickness,

Fusion Zone Solidi ﬁcation Cracking
Solidiﬁcation cracking, which occurs in the fusion zone of weldments, is of concern
for the candidate alloys. Speci ﬁcally, many studies have shown that the potential for
solidiﬁcation cracking is sensitive to a host of compositional factors even within the

speciﬁcation range for the alloys. For alloys 617 and 230, the level of Boron (B) has
been found to have a major effect. Figure 7 shows the data gathered for
trans-varestraint testing in which a high B heat (0.004 wt%) of 617 exhibited a
higher tendency to solidi ﬁcation cracking (as measured by crack length) compared
to alloys 263 and 740. HR6 W, a laves phase strengthened Ni-Fe-Cr alloy with 6 –
8 wt%W and candidate A-USC temperatures <700 °C was included in this study as
well. Figure 8 shows results for testing on Haynes 230 where B free heats exhibited
fewer cracks compared to heats with 0.004 –0.006 wt% B. In general B is added to
improve high-temperature creep behavior and microstructural stability in
nickel-based alloys, but care must be taken to ensure weldability challenges are
minimized. In the case of Haynes 230 for example, matching ﬁller metals are
essentially free from B to reduce concerns over solidi ﬁcation cracking.
Liquation Cracking
Nickel-based alloys typically exhibit a wide melting and solidi ﬁcation range
depending on alloying additions. In general, the wider the solidi ﬁcation range
combined with speci ﬁc alloying elements can lead to HAZ cracking in areas of the
base metal near welds which may undergo partial melting during welding cycles.
Liquation cracking was ﬁrst identi ﬁed in alloy 740 during microstructural exami-
nations of thick section welding trials including base metal HAZ cracking as well as
weld metal cracking. Figure 9 shows the ‘Nil Ductility Range ’(NDR) for a host of
740 and modi ﬁed 740 compositions along with other nickel-based alloys [ 30].
Based on these results and other similar studies including computational thermo-
dynamics to help understand how alloying elements segregated and created
low-melting point locations in the material, an optimized 740H composition with
reduced B, Si, and Nb was produced. Multiple welding trials (see Fig. 6) have
shown this composition to be resistant to liquation cracking. Figure 9 also shows

Strain Age and Stress Relaxation Cracking
Strain age cracking (SAC) and stress relaxation cracking are often interchanged, but
generally SAC refers to cracking which occurs during post weld heat-treatment or
high-temperature service. The fundamental basis for SAC is that rapid precipitation
in the alloys during high-temperature exposure (PWHT or service) causes an
increase in strength and decrease in material ductility. If this change happens before
residual stresses from welding are able to relax (from the high temperature exposure
during PWHT or service), the material may crack to relieve the stresses. Thus, it is a
very complex mechanism which depends on level of residual stress, precipitation
kinetics, and material behavior all of which are affected by time, temperature,
composition, and component plus weld geometry. SAC is one reason many
nickel-based alloys are considered ‘unweldable’ or have very poor or limited
weldability in only thin sections (low residual stresses). Classically, this suscepti-
bility is measured by the amount (volume fraction) and rate of gamma prime
precipitation which is related to the amount of Al and Ti as shown in Fig. 10. This
ﬁgure helps show why for A-USC and sCO
2 applications, the alloy being inves-
tigated have <25% gamma prime. In practice, this ﬁgure does not take into account
the kinetics of gamma prime and other hardening addition formation (such as
carbides), changes in ductility with time and aging, nor does it address other
alloying elements such as Nb which contributes to gamma prime and gamma
double prime strengthening. The simplicity of Fig. 10 is misleading. Many labo-
ratory studies have reached different conclusions on the ranking and susceptibility
of A-USC alloys to SAC. In some cases, the age hardenable alloys appeared worse
than the solid solution alloys, but in other cases the reverse was observed. In
practical application, SAC (relaxation cracking) was reported to be widespread in
alloy 617 components in the EU Comtes700 [ 15]. Studies on 617 show that PWHT,
pre-strain/stress, composition, grain size, and the speci ﬁc temperatures of applica-
tion will radically change the alloy ’s susceptibility to this failure mechanism. Such
studies and an industry agreed upon testing approach has not been established for
the other alloys under consideration but, some work is currently ongoing to develop
a more global approach to the problem [ 33].

Summary on Weldability
Most of the published weldability studies and the susceptibility to cracking on
A-USC nickel-based alloys focus on alloy 617 and 740H. Clear conclusions from
this research have shown the practical importance of specifying the 740H com-
position to reduce the tendency for liquation cracking and the need for many 617
components to be given a PWHT to combat SAC. For alloys such as 230, 263, and
282, there is need for additional studies to vet the alloys performance for solidi ﬁ-
cation cracking, liquation cracking (both HAZ and weld metal), and SAC. In
general, all candidate materials are inherently susceptible to solidi ﬁcation cracking
and liquation cracking. SAC or relaxation cracking is also a concern, but the
complexity of the problem, lack of understanding of residual stresses, and lack of a
standardized test method provides a challenge to the research community to further
the science, perhaps through a combination of available computational methods to
address fundamental material chemistry and precipitation kinetics, experimentation
to validate models, and ﬁeld testing to con ﬁrm. Finally, there is virtually no data on
these alloys in the cast state. Alloy 282 is considered a key candidate for turbine
casing and valve body castings, but no weldability studies (beyond very limited
demonstration articles) have been conducted to assess how chemical inhomogeneity
and large grain size/dendritic spacing effects weldability.
Weld Performance
High-temperature creep performance (strength and ductility) is a critical criterion
for these future transformational power systems, and experience has shown that
welds are often the ‘weakest link’in the system. To that end, weldability (the ability
to make a sound weld without cracking and exhibiting room temperature tensile
properties nearly equivalent to the base metal) must also consider weld performance
for these alloys. Based on the comprehensive review of the available creep-rupture
data on weldments and weld metal for 617, 230, 263, 740/740H, and 282 [ 27],
major de ﬁciencies in data, reporting, and understanding were identi ﬁed. Only 617
(and variants) and 740H have appreciable reported cross-weld creep-rupture data-
bases (over 80 data points for each alloy were gathered), but even for these alloys
basic information such as specimen size, welding details, PWHT and failure
location are inconsistently reported (if reported at all). To plot disparate datasets,
the Larson Miller Parameter (LMP) using a universal constant of 20 was used to
show general trends in the data in comparison to base metal behavior. Figure 11 is a
plot of the 617 data for matching ﬁller metals segmented by welding process. What
is clear is a vast scatter depending in part on the welding process. For CCA617,
non-ﬂux welding processes (GTAW for example) generally show improved creep
life over ﬂuxed (SMAW and SAW) processes. It should also be noted that a few of
the data points extend to >30,000 h but many are short-term tests of <1,000 h.
Limited studies (optical microscopy) have been conducted on some samples [ 27],
Age Hardenable Nickel-Based Alloy Developments and Research … 17

## Page 34

but even with the long-term test data, there is an extreme lack of detailed metal-
lurgical work on the weldments to understand the underlying metallurgical factors
effecting weld performance.
Codes and standards often use weld strength reduction factors (WSRFs) as a
convenient way to represent the behavior of welds. There is not standardized
approach to the calculation or application of WSRFs (which also does not account
for sample size and the complexity of creep-failure mechanisms). Never-the-less,
various WSRFs for 617 have been reported from the available data which generally
show WSRFs of 0.8 –1.0 (meaning 80 –100% of the base metal strength) in
cross-weld creep. The use of an alloy 617 WSRF is complicated by the choice of
baseline non-welded data, which are the solid and dotted lines in Fig. 11, where
most data points for GTAW welds are observed failing above the average 617
baseline but below the modi ﬁed CCA617 average strength; the choice of 617 or
CCA617 baseline effects the calculation and application of a WSRF.
Alloy 740/740H rupture data are plotted in Fig. 12 for matching and
non-matching consumable welds (no autogenous welds have been evaluated in
creep). Limited rupture times beyond 10,000 h are included in this dataset, but most
of the data are for relatively short times. For 740H, the matching ﬁller metals in the
welded and aged condition do not perform as well (generally) in comparison to
alternative ﬁller metal 282 and 263. Only one detailed microstructural study has
been undertaken to understand how the formation of precipitate coarsened zones in
740H weld metal lead to degradation in creep resistance of the weldment (failure
locations was in the weld metal) [ 34], and the improvement in behavior using 282
and 263 ﬁller metals has not been studied in detail. Additionally, only 740H welds
with weld metal failures have been investigated so the mechanism of failure for
cross-weld HAZ failures is unknown at this time. Furthermore, solution annealing
appears to improve the performance of the 740H weld metal, but for the limited

dataset investigated did not fully restore the creep strength to base metal levels. For
WSRFs, the ASME B&PV code case (CC2702) uses a conservative 0.7 factor for
application to seam welds due in part to the uncertainty surrounding the data (this is
plotted as mean — 30% in Fig. 12).
Much more limited creep-rupture datasets are available on alloys 230, 282, and
263. In general, alloy 230 shows some reduction (WSRF of 0.8) due, speculatively,
to the elimination of B in the weld metal. The data show better performance for 282
and 263, but most are short-term creep without supporting failure information
(ductility and failure location). Thus, there is a large data gap for application of
these alloys. It should be noted that such WSRF values for all the nickel-based
alloys (0.7 –1.0) are similar to values reported and utilized in USC powerplant
steels, such as Grade 91 and 92.
In conclusion, there is a scarcity of weld performance data for many of the alloys
being considered for A-USC and sCO
2 application. Furthermore, new joining
methods for small channel heat-exchangers such as brazing and diffusion bonding,
have not been evaluated for performance at high temperature conditions. In cases
where data do exist, critical information including weld metal chemistry, failure
location, and ductility are rarely reported, making the development of WSRFs
problematic. Surprisingly there is an extreme lack of detailed microstructural
characterization despite the fact that metallurgically complex weldments are loca-
tions where long-term damage often initiates. One ﬁnal note is that in the future,
power plant cycling is expected. No work (in the public domain) to the authors
knowledge has been done to look at weld cyclic behavior (fatigue and creep-
fatigue) to compliment the cyclic data on the base metals.

## Page 36

Summary and Conclusions
Nickel-based alloys including age-hardenable materials such as 263, 740H, and 282
are critical to enabling the next generation of transformational fossil power systems
incorporating A-USC steam Rankine cycles and sCO 2 Brayton cycles. A large body
of fundamental materials R&D has been completed including signi ﬁcant laboratory
research and shop fabrication studies. Limited ﬁeld testing supports continued
evaluations through ongoing work in pilot scale testing. Major strides have been
made to fabricate and weld these materials, but a critical review of weldability and
weld performance shows much more research is needed to fully understand
weldability, weld performance, and weldment microstructural evolution to help
deﬁne design limits to ensure successful component durability.

Superalloy 718: Evolution of the Alloy
from High to Low Temperature
Application
Shailesh Patel, John deBarbadillo and Stephen Coryell
Abstract Alloy 718 (UNS N07718) was the culmination of a research project
started in the mid-1950s to develop a stronger pipe alloy for coal- ﬁred power plants.
It was never used for that application, but it was quickly adopted for aircraft turbine
engines because of its very high strength, thermal stability, formability and weld-
ability compared to the γʹ-strengthened alloys available in the 1960s. Alloy 718
derives its unique combination of strength and fabricability from a coherent ordered
tetragonal phase γʺ and the slow diffusion rate of its main constituent, niobium.
Very early in its commercial life, alloy 718 was recognized as having attributes for
both ambient and cryogenic temperature uses as well. Impact toughness, aqueous
corrosion resistance, and non-ferromagnetic properties were important attributes.
Alloy 718 replaced established age-hardened iron/nickel-base alloys such as A-286,
K-500 and X-750 as well as martensitic steels in a wide range of components in the
space launch, oil and gas, marine, nuclear and superconducting magnet industries.
As the applications became more specialized, so did the heat treatments and mi-
crostructures to accentuate speci ﬁc properties. A common thread through these low
temperature applications has been hydrogen embrittlement and a substantial body
of literature documents our increasing awareness of its role in service performance.
In recent decades, new alloys based on alloy 718 and the γʺ strengthening phase
have been introduced, especially for oil and gas production equipment. This paper
describes the early development of alloy 718 for these important applications, along
with alloy, microstructure and heat-treatment evolution and current status.

Introduction
Eiselstein and Tillack in their keynote paper for the second Superalloy 718 Con-
ference described the unusual origin of the alloy we now know as 718 [ 1]. The
initial development work took place at Huntington Alloy Products Division which
was a subsidiary of The International Nickel Company (Inco Inc.). Surprisingly, it
was not intended to be age-hardened, nor for use in an aircraft engine. Eiselstein
began his work in the 1950s with the goal of developing an alloy for use in the main
steam lines of supercritical steam power plants. This work was inspired by the
Philadelphia Electric Co. Eddystone Unit 1 power station (now an ASME land-
mark) that was designed to operate at 1135 °F (613 °C) and 5000 psi (34.5 MPa). In
this paper the reported units will be presented ﬁrst. The designed conditions were
beyond material capability at that time eventually resulting in derating of the plant
[2]. A power plant employing these operating conditions was not replicated in the
US until the John W. Turk plant was commissioned in 2012. Ironically, Eiselstein ’s
“unsuccessful” project enabled the development of the two largest volume nickel
base alloys: 625 and 718. The initial project goals included creep strength, weld-
ability and ability to fabricate tube, pipe and ﬁttings. Eiselstein explored a com-
bination of molybdenum and niobium in a nickel-chromium matrix in hope of
obtaining a strong solid solution strengthening response. Neither element had been
known at the time to produce age-hardening. Consequently, it was a surprise that
niobium, in the amount of 4 –6% within a narrow range of nickel, could produce
intense hardening during exposure at 1250 –1350 °F (677 –732 °C). This effect is
illustrated in Figs. 1 and 2 that are redrawn with the original data points from
Eiselstein’s 1965 paper that described the alloy development [ 3]. Note the large

The realization that the strengthening effect persisted to 700 °C (1292 °F) where
it greatly exceeded that of alloys such as 80A, A-286, X-750, and Waspaloy that
were strengthened with aluminum and titanium sent his project off in a different
direction. The quali ﬁcation and initial use of alloy 718 in aero-engines was
described in earlier Superalloy 718 Conferences by Barker of GE Aircraft [ 4] and
Paulonis and Shirra of Pratt and Whitney [ 5]. No reference was made in the 1958
patent of potential low-temperature applications for the alloy apart from an
emphasis on its high ambient-temperature strength. The patent disclosure also
included the comments “the corrosion resistance of the alloy is good ” and “the alloy
is non-magnetic ” [6]. The commercial development of 718 focused on turbine
engine applications, especially casings, ducts and nozzles where its superior
formability and weldability were exploited. Eiselstein turned his attention to the
project that resulted in the development of the “matrix stiffened alloy ”.B y
increasing chromium to 22% and molybdenum to 9% with lower niobium, he
obtained an alloy with exceptional balance of strength, formability and aqueous
corrosion resistance. Designated alloy 625, it was commercially introduced in 1964
[1]. An examination of internal Inco reports showed that a broad spectrum of testing
of alloy 718 was performed in the early 1960s in advance of a technical bulletin that
was published in 1968 [ 7]. It should be noted that alloy 718, per Inco policy at the
time, was licensed widely to nickel alloy producers, thus facilitating process

Alloy 718 Strengthening Mechanism
Due to its remarkable low-temperature strength, ductility and weldability compared
to that of other age hardened nickel-base alloys, alloy 718 was considered for a
wide range of applications outside the aero-engine ﬁeld. The strengthening
advantage of γʺ over γʹ is illustrated in Fig. 3 where room temperature yield
strength is plotted as a function of calculated second phase volume fraction for
various nickel-base alloys (yield strength data from Inco compendium of superalloy
properties [ 8], γʹ/γʺ phase volume percent calculated using JMatPro). Of course
many other strengthening mechanisms are operative, but the γʹ/γʺ differential is
clear. The structure and strengthening mechanism of γʹ were beginning to be
deﬁned at the time alloy 718 was conceived. Indeed, Eiselstein initially believed
that his age-hardening phase was the FCC ordered γʹ(L1
2) but with a formula
Ni3Nb instead of Ni 3(Ti,Al). That is probably because the overaged samples ini-
tially used for particle extraction and x-ray analysis had converted to γʹ in pro-
cessing. It was also believed that this phase was the precursor to the acicular
orthorhombic phase that was readily visible after aging at higher temperatures and
is now designated δ. Cometto (as cited by Wagner and Hall [ 9]) ﬁrst suggested that
γʺ was actually a distinct (DO
22) BCT phase. It was later observed by Raymond
[10] and con ﬁrmed by Kotval [ 11]. The latter author showed that the precipitates
are disk-shaped with the c-axis of the unit cell perpendicular to the plane of the disk
and oriented in the (100), (010) and (001) directions of the γ matrix. In a subsequent
detailed study of alloy 718 microstructure, Paulonis, Oblak and Duvall began to
unravel the complex nature of precipitation in the alloy [ 12]. The unit cell of the γʺ
phase is shown in Fig. 4. Figure 5 is a transmission electron micrograph showing
the complex oriented precipitate structure. These authors showed that both spherical
γʹ and disc shaped γʺ coexisted with γʺ being predominant. They also were the ﬁrst
to designate the phase as γʺ.
While the microstructural constituents of alloy 718 had been de ﬁned by 1970,
there was a continuing debate about why γʺ should be a more effective strengthener
than γʹ. Decker and Mihalisin had previously discussed the importance of antiphase
boundary hardening arising from cutting of ordered γʹ precipitates [ 15], but this
mechanism did not seem adequate to explain the additional strengthening of γʺ. The
question was ﬁnally settled by Oblak, Paulonis and Duvall who showed that
coherency strengthening was the predominant mechanism acting in alloy 718 [ 16].
Ultimately, this explained the cryogenic temperature potency of this mechanism.
More recent work has de ﬁned the γʺ strengthening in quantitative terms and de ﬁned
additional mechanisms including deformation twinning in the γʺ particles and
matrix which may be operative at low temperatures [ 17, 18].
26 S. Patel et al.

## Page 43

The early work on alloy 718 included a wide range of heat treatment conditions,
with no preference being de ﬁned in the patent [ 6]. Later, two distinct commercial
treatments emerged: Treatment A (sub-delta solvus anneal at 1750 °F (954 °C)
combined with a two-step age at 1325 °F (718 °C) and 1150 °F (621 °C) for a total
time of about 18 h) or Treatment B (super delta solvus anneal at or above 1900 °F
(1038 °C) followed by the two step age as in Treatment A) [ 3]. The tensile
properties of the two were similar, but Treatment A provided much better
notch-rupture ductility and better fatigue properties. This treatment, combined with
sub-solvus forging processes, evolved into today ’s aero heat treatment. Treatment B
provided better impact and low temperature notch tensile strength. This treatment
was adopted and subsequently modi ﬁed for many low temperature applications of
alloy 718.

Cryogenic Properties of Alloy 718
The ﬁrst alloy 718 aircraft engine applications in 1963 were for the GE J-93 Engine
for the XB-70 [ 3] and the P & W J-58 engine for the SR-71 Blackbird [ 4], that were
unique surveillance aircraft designed with NASA technical input. NASA was also
at that time engaged in materials characterization for liquid fuel rocket engines for
the Apollo Space Program. Alloy 718 was initially considered for components in
the H
2/O2 turbine (a high-temperature application) and it was realized that the alloy
also had desirable properties for handling high-pressure cryogenic ﬂuids. In an
interesting study reported by Eiselstein, yield and tensile strength and tensile
elongation were all signi ﬁcantly higher at-320 °F ( −196 °C) than at ambient
temperature for alloy 718 in a wide range of material conditions; as shown in Fig. 6
[3]. Work by NASA, Aerojet-General, Rocketdyne and others beginning in 1959
showed that alloy 718 possessed a unique combination of high yield strength,
ductility and impact toughness along with good corrosion resistance compared to
previously used alloys such as A-286 and cryogenic grades of austenitic steels [ 19].
Heat-treatment B was preferred for cryogenic applications; however, age hardening
treatments varied from those recommended by Eiselstein [ 9]. The relationship of
cryogenic tensile properties to annealing temperature is shown in Fig. 7 [20].
Ultimately, 1950 °F (1066 °C) became the preferred annealing temperature for
cryogenic applications.

powered the second and upper stages of Saturn 1B and Saturn V launch vehicles
(John R. Halchak, Rocketdyne, personal communication). The ﬁrst test ﬂight of the
J-2 engine was in 1966. An external view of the J-2 engine is shown in Fig. 8.
Alloy 718 use was expanded in later modi ﬁcations of the J-2 and the much larger
M-1 engine that was never built but continued to advance the technology [ 20, 21].
The role of alloy 718 continued to expand in the early 1970s as Rocketdyne started
to design the Space Shuttle Main Engine. Jewett and Halchak reported at the 1991
Superalloy 718 Conference that the space shuttle engine comprised 51% by weight
alloy 718 and approximately 1500 separate parts [ 22]. This paper presents detailed
drawings identifying speci ﬁc alloy 718 components. These include high pressure
turbo-pumps, tubing, valves, injectors, manifolds and nozzles. A cutaway drawing
of the turbo-pumps is shown in Fig. 9. Other liquid fuel rocket engines, such as the
gigantic Saturn ﬁrst stage booster F-1 engine and many more recent engines, use a
hydrocarbon fuel with liquid oxygen. Substantial amounts of alloy 718 are also
used in these engines.

Superconducting Magnet Systems
Aircraft and rocket engines are complementary applications where technical
cross-fertilization would be expected, but the relationship to high- ﬁeld
electro-magnets is not obvious. The connection again seems to be through
NASA, where intensive research on superconducting magnets with ﬁeld strength as
high as 20 T was underway beginning in the 1950s. NASA was interested is these
magnets for applications such as electric propulsion, magneto-hydrodynamic power
generation, thermonuclear propulsion, and space radiation shielding [ 23]. While
alloy 718 is not superconductive, it is non-magnetic with phase stability at cryo-
genic temperatures and no ductile-brittle transition. Its high strength and toughness
are desirable for structural components including bolts to contain the high stresses
generated by powerful magnetic ﬁelds. This makes it a logical choice for structural
components versus high-strength steel. High- ﬁeld superconducting magnets are
unique and often massive structures that were used initially for particle and plasma
physics experiments at Argonne National Lab. Since then, scores of “cyclotrons”
have been constructed throughout the world. These include the largest, the Large
Hadron Collider at CERN in Europe and the Long Baseline Neutrino Facility
(LBNF) at Argonne National Lab in USA. Each one contains multiple magnets.
Superconducting magnets are also used directly for high- ﬁeld magnet experiments.
An example is the 45 T hybrid magnet at the Florida State University National High
Magnetic Field Lab shown in Fig. 10.

## Page 48

While direct commercial use of alloy 718 in superconducting magnets has been
negligible (MRI’s for example do not require 718), the International Thermonuclear
Energy Reactor project (ITER) would propel alloy 718 into the world of advanced
power generation systems. ITER is an international consortium, of which the US is
a member, with the objective of demonstrating the viability of contained nuclear
fusion for generation of electricity. The project, based on the Tokomak concept
using a toroidal con ﬁned plasma, has been underway for 35 years. The selection of
alloy 718 with a modi ﬁed heat Treatment A was described in an early Superalloy
718 conference [ 24]. An enormous demonstration facility, now under construction
in Cadarache in southern France, is scheduled for ﬁrst plasma ignition in 2025. The
purpose of this facility is to demonstrate the positive production of electric power.
Alloy 718 is used in many sub-systems in this plant such as bolting, structural
supports for the magnet system, ﬁrst wall blanket and vacuum vessel, and bellows
for the plasma divertor [ 25–27]. Low dose irradiation induced stress relaxation is
one of the material concerns. Heat treatment A is preferred for this application. An
artist’s cutaway drawing of the ITER is shown in Fig. 11.
Aqueous Corrosion
As mentioned previously, Inco had conducted a broad screening investigation of the
properties of alloy 718 including resistance to general corrosion in a wide range of
aqueous and chemical media. When compared with alloy steel of similar strength
level, alloy 718 shows excellent resistance to corrosion in many environments. Of
course, some nickel-base alloys have superior resistance in speci ﬁc environments,
Fig. 10 36 T hybrid magnet at National High Magnetic Field Lab at Florida State University.

## Page 49

but none had the ambient temperature strength of alloy 718. Alloys such as 625 and
C-276 can be cold worked to comparable strength, but fabricated components have
geometry, size, and joining limitations. Consequently, alloy 718 began to be
speciﬁed for applications where high-strength and moderate corrosion resistance
was needed. Components such as fasteners, pump shafts, latches, brackets, springs,
valve stems and impellors were candidates. This opened potential applications in
nuclear reactors, marine structures, gas transmission, and, by far the biggest of all,
oil and gas drilling and production. One important category of environment is
aqueous solutions containing halide salts (seawater and many oil and gas envi-
ronments). While the general corrosion rate of alloy 718 in these environments is
minimal, localized corrosion leading to premature fracture is a much more
important measure of the alloy ’s suitability for service. Figure 12 shows the critical
pitting and crevice temperatures for a selected group of Fe/Ni-Cr-Mo alloys (James
R. Crum, Special Metals, unpublished data). Alloy 718 has suf ﬁcient resistance to
allow use in moderately corrosive media such as seawater. Figure 13 shows time to
failure of alloy 718 and other alloys in boiling MgCl
2, a common screening test for
stress corrosion cracking in chloride environments with the classic “Copson curve”
superimposed [ 28, 29]. Stress corrosion cracking is an important issue for many
components and applications. While the MgCl 2 ranking does not apply to all
environments, it illustrates a general bene ﬁt for higher nickel. Application speci ﬁc
stress corrosion behavior is discussed later for bolting, nuclear and oil ﬁeld uses of
alloy 718.
Alloy 718 is used in some large forged components that are used in corrosive
environments. One application shown as a cutaway drawing in Fig. 14 is for
impellors and other structural components for natural gas transmission pumping
stations. Hundreds of these stations exist throughout the world, generally consisting
of a small gas turbine operating off the pipeline gas that drives a compressor. While

Nuclear Power
As with superconducting magnets, alloy 718 appears to have a NASA connection to
the nuclear industry. The NERVA (Nuclear Engine for Rocket Vehicle Application)
propulsion system was under development for the Mars Rover project beginning in
1963 with Westinghouse and Aerojet as developers [ 31]. While the NERVA project
itself was terminated in 1973, alloy 718 was used extensively for both high and low
temperature components in the various prototype systems. The use of the alloy was
eventually extended to Westinghouse commercial reactors. Initially the alloy was
used with treatment A, but following a failure of a pressure vessel, an extensive
evaluation of the effect of heat treatment on fracture toughness of welded alloy 718
was initiated. Aerojet proposed a supersolvus heat treatment followed by furnace
cooling to the aging temperature and a conventional age cycle [ 32]. This approach
was further developed in a series of studies by Mills [ 33]. While the environment in
the reactor core is relatively hot 290 –315 °C (554 –599 °F), the alloy is in contact
with high-pressure water where stress-corrosion cracking is a possibility. EPRI
engaged a series of studies that explored the effect of chemistry, heat treatment and
microstructure on SCC resistance of alloy 718 [ 34]. This work showed that
stress-corrosion cracks often followed γ/δ boundaries and that resistance was
improved through the elimination of grain boundary delta phase. This work ulti-
mately resulted in a Babcock and Wilcox patent in 1991 for a heat treatment similar
to that originally proposed by Aerojet, which is a variant of heat treatment B [ 35].
In practice both heat treatments are used commercially. Nuclear grades of alloy 718
have a restricted level of cobalt (0.05% or lower) that makes their composition
distinct.
While there are a number of alloy 718 components used in reactors, one of the
more interesting is the structural assembly that holds the fuel and moderator rods
rigid in the highly dynamic water conditions in the reactor core. Stress corrosion
cracking and fatigue fracture are the principal concerns. Clips and springs are
manufactured from heavy gauge alloy 718 sheet and are usually used with heat
treatment A with a higher temperature aging treatment. A typical fuel assembly
module is shown in Fig. 16. Each module, or “egg crate ”, as they are sometimes
called, contains hundreds of springs holding an array of zircaloy tubes containing
the uranium fuel pellets.
Springs and Fasteners
Alloy 718 does not possess the tensile and shear strength of the ultra-high strength
steels such as 300 M and H-11, but its better corrosion resistance eliminates the
disadvantages of cadmium plating for galvanic protection. Accordingly, alloy 718
has been used in a wide range of critical applications. Alloy 718 fasteners were
initially used in the solution annealed and aged condition with a maximum tensile
36 S. Patel et al.

## Page 53

strength of 180 ksi (1241 MPa), super-solvus solution anneal being preferred for
notch toughness. As suggested earlier, these fasteners were applied for cryogenic
applications in rockets, magnets, nuclear reactors and certain marine and industrial
applications, as well as for high temperature use in aircraft engines. More recently,
alloy 718 has become widely used in airframe structures as well. Thousands of
these fasteners in an amazing array of shapes and functions are used in the assembly
of modern aircraft. Historically, high-strength martensitic steels were used, with
H-11 being a preferred material because of its excellent fatigue properties. How-
ever, H-11 is subject to stress-corrosion cracking, especially in marine environ-
ments and highly pre-stressed parts. A number of more corrosion resistant alloy
alternatives exist, but 718 was chosen over alloys such as PH13-8Mo due to its
superior stress-corrosion and hydrogen embrittlement resistance. While annealed
and aged alloy 718 does not have the tensile strength of martensitic steel, it was
shown by Heacox that higher strength could be achieved in alloy 718 by cold
drawing and direct aging [ 36]. The amount of reduction by cold drawing or rolling
is relatively small (10 –25%) due to the high work hardening rate of 718. The
development of alloy 718 for bolting was described in an earlier Superalloy 718
Conference by Thomas Roach [ 37]. No speci ﬁc composition restrictions are nor-
mally applied. Heat treatment B is generally used with some variations in aging
time and temperature due to the small size of the parts. This led to the quali ﬁcation
and application of 220 ksi (1517 MPa) tensile strength grade of 718 for airframe
fasteners in the 1980s that have fatigue resistance equivalent to H-11. Typically, a
coating is required when 718 is used to fasten aluminum to prevent galvanic
corrosion. Fasteners with tensile strength as high as 260 ksi (1793 MPa) have been
used in selected applications; however, the ductility is low and additional cold work
during fabrication can result in premature failure. An additional complication is the

Airframe fasteners come in a wide variety of con ﬁgurations beyond the traditional
bolt, nut, and rivet forms including up to 5-piece assemblies. Some examples are
shown in Fig. 17.
Novel Parts Fabricated by Superplastic Forming
Alloy 718 is used in many applications in sheet form and it is generally amenable to
all standard forming operations including hydroforming and spinforming. Super-
plastic forming (SPF) is a process that has been successfully used to make complex
sheet metal parts with recurved contours. Superplasticity was a popular topic in the
1960s and was applied initially to γʹ strengthened alloys for powder consolidation,
but it remained otherwise a metallurgical curiosity for fabrication of superalloy
parts. Rocketdyne began to explore superplastic forming of alloy 718 in the 1970s.
While conventionally processed (treatment A) 718 sheet could not sustain SPF
much ﬁner grain could be achieved through cold rolling and controlled annealing.
Chandler, Ghosh and Mahoney ﬁrst demonstrated this process for alloy 718 [ 39].
The role of grain size on the ﬂow stress-strain rate relationship is shown in Fig. 18
(actual grain size was not reported). The technology was reviewed in a prior alloy
718 Conference by Mahoney [ 40]. At the same time Inco Alloys International (the
successor to Huntington Alloys), working with various industry and university
partners, developed the technology for producing an SPF grade of alloy 718 sheet

[41]. This alloy called 718SPF (UNS N07719) has a narrower range of C, N, S and

at 1750 °F (954 °C) followed by hot isostatic pressing (HIP) at a similar temper-
ature and a conventional ageing treatment. An example of a prototype part pro-
duced by Rohr Inc. is shown in Fig. 19. Use of the process has been limited by tool
wear and reduced strength due in part to porosity generated by creep cavitation
during the forming operation.
Oil and Gas
It is unclear when alloy 718 was ﬁrst used in the oil and gas industry. Initially,
tempered martensitic alloy steels such as AISI 4340 were used for components
where high-strength was required. Age-hardened nickel-base alloys such as K-500
and X-750 were used where severe corrosive conditions were present. Alloy 718
provided an excellent alternative by virtue of its higher strength and availability
from distributors. The aerospace composition and heat-treatment was used initially
evolving over time to the unique composition and heat treatment used today. The
consumption of this “oil ﬁeld” grade had grown to rival that of “aero grade ”.
Detailed reviews of the origin, properties and microstructure of oil ﬁeld grade alloy
718 have been presented in proceedings of prior Superalloy 718 conferences
[42–46].
Alloy 718 was ﬁrst used in the 1970s for fasteners, valve gates, seats, stems, and
springs; applications that involve brief exposure to corrosive conditions. Later

applications included drill tools that are subject to some corrosion and higher

measurement-while-drilling (MWD) tools in which sophisticated electronic
instruments are contained in a strong, non-magnetic alloy tube (Fig. 20). These are
prototypical oil ﬁeld components in that they are cylindrical and elongated to allow
them to ﬁt into a well bore. Traditionally these parts have been machined from
forged and heat-treated bar.
In the late 1970s alloy 718 began to be considered for use in critical well
completion equipment. Components such as sub-surface safety valves (shuts off
ﬂow at the top of the well), side-pocket mandrels (injects inhibitors), packer and
seal assemblies (controls and directs ﬂow at the foot of the well into the collection
pipe) and hangers (supports the production tubing string at the well head) must be
able to withstand continuous operation in corrosive ﬂuids under sustained pressures
at temperatures as high as 450 °F (232 °C). Service failure of one of these com-
ponents could result in the loss of the drill string and possibly a spill or explosion
and release of deadly H
2S. Completion components are designed to ﬁt into the well
casing and allow passage of the production ﬂuid. They may be mechanically
attached or physically part of the well string. They can be very complex, containing
surface controlled hydraulic or electrically actuated devices to regulate ﬂow or
inject inhibitors. Oil tool manufacturers offer proprietary component designs tai-
lored for speci ﬁc ﬁeld requirements that conform to the general con ﬁguration
illustrated in Fig. 21 for a sub-surface safety valve.

These safety-critical pressure-containing and/or load-bearing components
experience long-term exposure to corrosive media during the production phase of
the well. Bhavsar [ 44] has described the development of the oil- ﬁeld heat treatment
for alloy 718 that is now expressed in API 6ACRA [ 47]. Annealing Treatment B is
preferred for microstructural homogeneity and fracture toughness and to minimize δ
phase content. The aging treatment was signi ﬁcantly altered to comply with NACE
standard MR-0175/ISO-15156-3 [ 48] that governs quali ﬁcation of materials for
sour oil and gas service. At the time, a maximum hardness of RC 35 was speci ﬁed
(later raised to RC 40). The conventional alloy 718 aging treatment typically
produces a hardness of RC40-45. Under- and over-aging treatments were investi-
gated, with the latter being selected for reproducibility [ 44]. Currently a range of
1425−1475 °F (774 –802 °C) is speci ﬁed. This limits the usable yield strength to
about 140 ksi (965 MPa) although alternate heat treatments that provide higher

## Page 58

strength are being considered. Analysis of service failures and laboratory simulation
showed that stress-corrosion resistance could be optimized if δ phase and carbides
could be minimized. This led to the de ﬁnition of today ’s controlled chemistry and
microstructure.
The composition of oil ﬁeld alloy 718 has evolved to support the microstructure
requirements and also to enhance toughness. Niobium is now restricted to maxi-
mum 5.20% to minimize δ precipitates and carbon is limited to 0.045% to limit
formation of continuous grain boundary carbides. Phosphorus is restricted to less
than 0.010% to improve toughness. Individual alloy producers have identi ﬁed
enhanced microstructure control with even tighter limits on certain elements. As a
result the oil ﬁeld and aerospace alloys have become distinct grades within the UNS
deﬁnition of alloy 718.
Although alloy 718 has served successfully for many years, its limitations have
inspired a search for alternatives. Users have continued to seek materials with
higher yield strength and corrosion resistance for service in increasingly harsh
environments. The preferred approach exploits the strength/toughness capability of
γʺ in an inherently more corrosion resistant matrix. Unfortunately, the alloy stability
range for γʺ is restricted as initially postulated by Quist et al. [ 49]. They determined
that the DO
22 structure is stable within an electron/atom range of 2.5 –2.62 and a
lattice misﬁt value of ∼1%. In practical terms those conditions are favored within a
relatively narrow range of iron and chromium. Burke and Miller also showed that γʺ
typically has a ratio of 4:1 Nb:Ti with virtually no aluminum [ 50]. The addition of
Al appears to stabilize γʹ at the expense of γʺ which lowers yield strength.

Accordingly, the new alloys contain higher levels of chromium and molybdenum
and sometimes copper for corrosion resistance, some iron and very low aluminum.
The initial approach of nickel alloy producers was to enhance the strength of an
alloy 625 base. Three “age-hardened 625 derivative alloys ” were eventually qual-
iﬁed for oil ﬁeld use. Alloys 725 (N07725) [ 51] and 625 Plus ® (trademark of
Carpenter Technology) (N07716) [ 52] are very similar. They rely on a Ti addition
to produce γ′/γ″ precipitation while minimizing solidi ﬁcation segregation. These
alloys have outstanding corrosion resistance and strength approaching that of alloy
718. The third alloy, N07626, that uses increased Nb for strength, is more prone to
form intergranular δ and is not in common use. These alloys are considered the gold
standard for use in the most severe environments, but these alloys are considered
too expensive for general use.
Recently, a new family of alloys with better stress-corrosion resistance than alloy
718 and higher strength than alloy 725 has been introduced. The alloy design
features lower Ni, Nb and Al to generate a stronger γ″ aging response and increased
Cr and Cu for improved stress-corrosion cracking resistance. Alloy 945
® (N09945)
was introduced in 2008 [ 53]. It was designed for use in the 125 –140 ksi (862 –
965 MPa) yield strength range. Later the strength was increased to 140 –160 ksi
(965–1103 MPa) by a small increase in Ni and Nb [ 54]. The higher strength version
is called alloy 945X ® (UNS N09946) (945 and 945X are trademarks of Special
Metals). Both alloys are quali ﬁed to NACE MR0175/ISO 15156-3 level V and VI.
The key to success of these alloys is their resistance to formation of δ. More
recently, a similar alloy that is designated 955 (UNS N09955) with higher
molybdenum content has been introduced [ 55]. Figure 22 shows the conditions of

## Page 60

Hydrogen Embrittlement
The discussion of hydrogen embrittlement (HE) of alloy 718 was saved for last in
this paper despite its potential in ﬂuence in virtually every low-temperature appli-
cation, in part because it has not yet driven a change in use, alloy composition or
heat treatment. Concern for unpredicted delayed hydrogen cracking continues to
drive research, and if the future holds a more hydrogen fueled economy, additional
responses may be required. While alloy 718 is relatively resistant to the ingress of
hydrogen from the environment, under certain conditions a dramatic loss of duc-
tility can occur. In applications such as airframes, rocket engines, nuclear power
and oil and gas, the consequences of a hydrogen induced failure could be catas-
trophic. The greatest negative effect is seen near room temperature as shown in
Fig. 23 [56]. Much of the early investigation of hydrogen effects in metals was done
in conjunction with the liquid fueled rocket program [ 56–58]. This work showed
that the degree of embrittlement increased with dissolved hydrogen content
(Fig. 24), and the yield stress of the alloy. However, even solution annealed alloy
718 experiences a loss of ductility and intergranular fracture when suf ﬁcient dis-
solved hydrogen is present. The literature of the 1960s and 1970s was largely
phenomenological and related to issues involved with containment of high pressure
hydrogen. A deeper understanding of the mechanisms of hydrogen embrittlement
began to emerge in the late 1980s in the work of Birnbaum, Altstetter and others
[59–61]. The mechanism is complex and involves multiple interacting variables.
One view is that hydrogen embrittlement of alloy 718 is associated with enhanced
localized plasticity on active slip planes combined with void formation ahead of an
Fig. 23 Effect of H 2 on the
ratio of tensile ductility in
hydrogen and air [ 56]
44 S. Patel et al.

## Page 61

advancing crack tip. Microstructure is an important variable with grain boundary
particles such as carbides and δ-phase being hydrogen trapping sites, as well as
preferred fracture paths.
In recent years, service failures in offshore oil wells have renewed the interest in
hydrogen embrittlement of alloy 718 and other age hardened oil ﬁeld alloys [ 62,
63]. The continuing work is proceeding along multiple fronts: (1) Identi ﬁcation of a
repeatable test that will unambiguously rank materials according to their hydrogen
embrittlement resistance in speci ﬁc environments, (2) Better de ﬁnition and control
of the environmental conditions affecting ingress of hydrogen in manufacturing and
service and (3) Identi ﬁcation and control of microstructural features that enhance
hydrogen cracking resistance. None of these issues are easily solved, hence a robust
engineering discourse is underway.
Concluding Remarks
Alloy 718 has proven to be one of the most remarkable alloy inventions and it is the
most widely used nickel-base alloy. It is particularly impressive in its versatility,
ﬁnding use at moderately high, ambient and cryogenic temperatures over a wide
range of environmental conditions. As a generic, widely available and thoroughly
characterized alloy it is one of the ﬁrst choices for designers. As the prototype for γʺ
strengthening, it will continue to inspire alloy developers. This paper intentionally
did not address potential additive manufacturing applications for alloy 718. The
alloy has been the subject of many additive demonstrations that have shown that it

Alloy 718: Laser Powder Bed Additive
Manufacturing for Turbine Applications
R. Kelkar, A. Andreaco, E. Ott and J. Groh
Abstract Alloy 718 has been utilized successfully in both static and rotating turbo
machinery applications for four decades. The combination of high strength, fatigue
capability, rupture strength, corrosion and creep resistance at temperatures through
650 °C are key attributes of this alloy. Conventional manufacturing routes include
cast, wrought, sheet, joining and fabrication by welding and brazing, powder
metallurgical processing and metal injection molding. Recent investigation of
aerospace materials like Alloy 718 produced by additive manufacturing technology
has provided an opportunity for disruptive component manufacturing methods,
geometries, and component capabilities which expand design space for complex
applications. At GE Aviation (GEA), development of laser powder bed direct metal
laser melting (subsequently referred to as DMLM) Alloy 718 was a natural choice
following the successful commercial application of DMLM CoCrMo in GE Avi-
ation and Safran ’s LEAP platform fuel tip component and the GE90 T25 sensor
part. GEA ’s DMLM 718 development started with demonstrator military applica-
tions, and now has expanded to include multiple commercial engine applications
across the size range of the GEA product line. The additive (laser) process
development for Alloy 718 involved a combination of laser processing parameter
investigation and heat treatment development to produce both acceptable build
geometry and metallurgical microstructures. Initial developments started with 20
μm build layer thickness, and expanded to 50 μm thicknesses for improved build
productivity. From the onset, the materials engineering focus was on isotropic, ﬁne
grain, pore free and fully developed microstructures for Alloy 718 by heat treat
design. Mechanical characterization included consideration of build direction,
machine type, machine to machine variation and processing gas effects. This paper
will discuss various metallurgical challenges and related, microstructure &
mechanical characterization of DMLM Alloy 718.

Introduction
Alloy 718 has been developed [ 1] and used extensively since 1960s, with an initial
focus on the aerospace industry. To date, it remains one of the most complex
superalloys from a microstructural development perspective (gamma, gamma
prime, gamma double-prime, delta, carbides and other minor phases etc.). The
average usage of Alloy 718 in a typical aircraft engine is about 34% by weight for
modern turbine engines [ 2]. One of the major features of the alloy is its ability to
maintain higher strength capability within its serviceable temperature range of up to
650 °C, making it an important alloy for major structural parts as well as latter
stages of the compressor in gas turbines. It is the most ubiquitous alloy incorporated
in GE Aviation (GEA) products, with applications including critical rotating parts,
airfoils, fasteners, supporting structures and pressure vessels. Generally, Alloy 718
is a workable and weldable alloy available in wrought, and cast forms [ 3]. This
alloy is also very popular in its powder form in the gas turbine industry with main
usage in repair and disk manufacturing. Alloy 718 was ﬁrst introduced into a
production application for portions of the J93 (XB-90 Bomber engine) turbine
frame that were welded to wrought Alloy 722 rings. The next application Alloy 718
led to signi ﬁcant production outlet; the GE1 development core evolved to GE ’s
successful, long running TF39/CF6-6/LM2500 family [ 4].
Additive manufacturing is a layer by layer build process using powder to build
up a part geometry. In DMLM, a laser is used as a heat source, and metal powder is
used as a feedstock/raw material. Additive manufacturing technology is revolu-
tionizing the industry with the advantages of quick prototyping, material ef ﬁciency,
part consolidation, unique designs, lower inventory cost, reduced post-processing,
and lower component weight. GEA introduced the DMLM technology, initially in
the CoCrMo alloy with the LEAP fuel nozzle and the GE90 T25 sensor. GEA has
many more parts in the pipeline and under development using this technology.
Since it is an emerging and growing part production technology, it requires process
and product development and comparison to previously developed, well-known
materials and manufacturing routes, including Alloy 718. A major advantage of this
technology is more “design freedom.”Limitations, on the other hand, often include
as-built surface ﬁnish which may impact fatigue behavior, thin wall structural
capability, machine costs and limited geometry due to current DMLM machine
dimension limitations. Since Alloy 718 is so widely used in gas turbines, it is
critical to establish robust DMLM process technology with this alloy to completely
take advantage of this new process. GEA initiated development with this alloy
using DMLM since 2011 to generate microstructures which yield an acceptable
balance of physical and mechanical properties. GEA ’s development engine pro-
gram, Advanced Turboprop (ATP) will have three structural parts using DMLM
54 R. Kelkar et al.

## Page 69

Alloy 718. Those three parts include the exhaust case, C-sump and propeller gear
box (PGB) housing, which are shown in Fig. 1.
GEA has made a substantial investment to understand and use DMLM pro-
cessing by developing and characterizing the connection to microstructure and
properties. This paper outlines experimental procedures, feedstock, DMLM pro-
cess, and heat treat details. Heat treat details include optimization of key processing
steps. Utilizing of those developed process parameters, mechanical test bars were
produced. Mechanical test results include dynamic modulus, tensile strengths and
ductility, strain-control low cycle fatigue (LCF), and cyclic crack growth. This
paper also covers micrographs for fully heat-treated bars.
Initial development of DMLM Alloy 718 by GEA utilized 20 μm layer thick-
ness, which subsequently evolved to the 50 μm layer thickness in support of higher
productivity. The micrographs and properties shown in this paper are representative
of the 50 μm parameter sets.
Materials and Processing
Powder
Powder is an important factor in ﬂuencing successful part build. As a minimum,
powder chemistry and particle size distribution (PSD) are controlled in typical raw
material speci ﬁcations. PSD impacts powder-bed packing density and the powder
ﬂow characteristics during DMLM operation. One important consideration in
processing of materials based on powder is that with a higher surface area asso-
ciated with ﬁne particles, the particle surfaces and bulk of the powder are sub-
stantially more susceptible to contamination. Contamination may affect bulk
chemistry local chemistry, and potentially degrade mechanical properties including
fatigue life. Like other powder metallurgy materials, it is important to mitigate
Fig. 1 GEA’s Advanced Turboprop (ATP) engine DMLM 718 components: a Exhaust case, b C
sump, c PGB housing
Alloy 718: Laser Powder Bed Additive Manufacturing … 55

## Page 70

contamination through processing and material controls. Many commercially-
available powders may have variation in PSD and morphology but may meet
powder speci ﬁcation limits. Cleanliness controls for better properties and ﬁxed
processes needed for consistent product, led to development of an internal GEA
“powder manufacturing process speci ﬁcation”, in addition to a speci ﬁcation which
controls powder attributes (chemistry & PSD) for Alloy 718. GEA ’s powder
manufacturing speci ﬁcation covers controls for each powder manufacturing steps
including contamination control and uses both PSD and additional characterization
methods to control and validate contamination mitigation. Figure 2 shows typical
gas atomized powder under SEM. The initial 20 μm parameter set was developed
based on 45/15 μm powder size whereas 50 μm parameter set was developed based
on 53/15 μm powder size. The speci ﬁcation requires gas atomization for the powder
production process.
Powder Reuse
Powder reuse is another key factor for establishing a cost-effective business case for
many components. Powder reuse may be affected by a number of factors. Some of
those are alloy speci ﬁc, machine con ﬁguration speci ﬁc, and site or procedure
dependent. Risks associated with reuse are bulk composition shifts, contamination
from handling/laser exposure, and PSD change. Quali ﬁcation of reuse processes
and incorporation of any changes to an already validated reuse process should
consider risks associated with both the effect on the DMLM process and risks
associated with the resulting material and its capability. Strict control on powder
reuse processing is needed particularly in the aerospace ﬁeld to control the anomaly
density which may have negative impact on the life of the part [ 5].
Fig. 2 SEM micrographs of typical Alloy 718 powder
56 R. Kelkar et al.

## Page 71

DMLM Machine and Parameters
As the DMLM technology matures, the demand for larger parts and similarly larger
machines to make them is growing. For laser-based powder-bed technologies like
DMLM, important parameters in the process include power input, spot size, scan
speed, and hatch spacing. Scaling-up these parameters needs to be better understood
to obtain structurally sound, durable large components. Gas ﬂow during the process
is also a key factor [ 6] and may affect properties. If one changes either machine or
parameter set, it can have impact on original properties. The goal should be to meet
original data set by statistical means to avoid generating many property curves. Key
elements of robust DMLM part manufacture include, laser calibration,
microstructural and mechanical property checks, machine cleaning procedures, and
powder handling practices among many other practices.
Heat Treatment
Heat treatment is important to set the ﬁnal microstructure, which impacts me-
chanical properties. General heat treatment for GEA DMLM includes, stress relief,
hot isostatic press (HIP), and alloy speci ﬁc solution and age (if required). GEA has
included HIP in the standard process for Alloy 718 to control and minimize
non-interconnected porosity. Porosity may have negative impact on part ductility
and low cycle fatigue (LCF) properties [ 7]. Since the stress relief and HIP are
additional heat treatments steps compared to conventional manufacturing processes
for wrought Alloy 718, it is important to consider the effect of these heat treatments
on the evolution of the microstructure with a focus on avoiding grain growth in
setting the key metallurgical phases in the microstructure. The following section
further deﬁnes the heat treat steps selected for the DMLM Alloy 718 used by GEA.
Heat Treatment and Microstructure Development for DMLM
Alloy 718
As stated earlier, the heat treat for DMLM 718 includes stress relief, HIP, solution
and aging steps. The purpose of the stress relief is to minimize thermal strains
incurred during the DMLM process, which in turn reduces distortion during
post-processing. Stress relief may also be utilized to start recrystallization of the
as-printed grain structure, which typically consists of small weld pools of varying
orientation. HIP is subsequently used to close non-surface connected porosity.
Finally, solution and age treatments generate generally equiaxed grains and develop
the precipitate size and morphology in the microstructure. Common precipitates
include delta, gamma prime and gamma double prime.
Alloy 718: Laser Powder Bed Additive Manufacturing … 57

## Page 72

The goal of the heat treat development on Alloy 718 was to obtain strain free,
pore free, equiaxed, ﬁner grains and balanced (in terms of phases) microstructure
without detrimental metallurgical anomalies in the material. Each step of heat treat
optimization is described with more details in the following paragraphs.
Stress Relief
DMLM produces high thermal gradients layer-by-layer that generate a high degree
of localized residual stresses throughout the part. Generally, in the as-printed
DMLM condition, it is not possible to remove the part from the build platform
without distortion. A stress relief step is necessary to equalize the stress gradients
caused by processing thermal gradients to allow removal of the part from the build
platform. To quantify and understand the residual stress in the part, as-printed
coupons were stress relieved at various temperatures between 800 and 1100 °C
(1472 and 2012 °F) with the same hold time. Subsequently X-ray diffraction (XRD)
was performed to quantify the residual strains. Figure 3 summarizes the results.
Results shows that there is an order of magnitude difference in residual matrix
strains detected by XRD at most of the tested temperatures compared with
as-printed coupon. Based on these results, the lowest temperature was selected as an
adequate stress relief temperature.
Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP)
HIP is employed to close non-surface connected porosity that may lead to fatigue
debit or poorer tensile performance. During the GEA heat treatment development
