## Page 73

for DMLM 718, two additional metallurgical effects were observed related to the
HIP process: ﬁrst surface oxidation and second partial recrystallization. Improve-
ment in the mechanical properties from the HIP process has also been attributed to
the dissolution of undesirable Laves and delta phase as well as pore closure [ 8].
To evaluate effect of HIP parameters on porosity closure, special porous bars
were produced using non-optimal DMLM parameters at 20 μm layer thickness. The
porosity level produced was around 7 –8%. It is believed that this level of porosity is
near the threshold where signi ﬁcant amounts of surface connectivity for the
embedded pores may begin to be observed. Those samples were HIP heat treated
using various temperatures and pressures as shown in Fig. 4 to understand trends in
pore closure capability. Then metallography was performed to evaluate the porosity
level change and porosity was quanti ﬁed using image analysis. Figure 4 summa-
rizes the results of this experiment. Low HIP temperatures with low pressure or low
temperature with high HIP pressure conditions were found to be more susceptible to
retained porosity while those at higher temperatures resulted in signi ﬁcant pore
closure.
The HIP process may also lead to surface oxidation on the DMLM parts. It was
observed that higher temperatures were more susceptible compared to lower tem-
peratures. Depending on the HIP parameters chosen, there may be an impact on the
cost and capability as well. Use of standard HIP cycles is advantageous in both cost
and availability and are therefore a priority in selecting cycles of interest.
Fig. 4 Effect of HIP parameters on porosity
Alloy 718: Laser Powder Bed Additive Manufacturing … 59

## Page 74

Commercially, for high HIP pressures there are limited numbers of furnaces
available for high temperature cycles. HIP optimization was carried out based on
the porosity, oxidation control and cost/capacity. Figure 5 shows the optimal pro-
cessing window using 20 μm DMLM parameter set. Further HIP optimization
concluded that the best commercial solution is intermediate temperature +83 °C
(150 °F) at low pressure for the DMLM 20 μm parameter set.
Solution and Age Heat Treatments
Solution heat treatment plays a key role in setting the fraction and morphology of
delta phase as it relates to the delta solvus temperature. Ideally it is desirable to have
discrete delta phase along the grain boundaries. If delta phase is continuous then it
may impact notch sensitivity and, in absence of delta phase on the grain boundaries,
it may impact the strength of the material. To get the right balance, the typical
solution temperature is 14 –28 °C (25 –50 °F) below delta solvus temperature.
Niobium content has a strong in ﬂuence on the delta solvus temperature. To
understand and cross check the effect of bulk niobium content on delta solvus,
historical powder chemistries were collected from two major powder suppliers
spanning 16 years and 54 lots. Thermo-Calc was used to predict the delta solvus
temperature for the heat history evaluated. The 2015 Thermo-Calc TTNi8 database
was used. Figure 5 shows a compilation of predictions for delta solvus temperature
as a function of niobium content (Fig. 6).
Based on this exercise it was concluded that the predicted delta solvus range is 997–
1032 °C (1827–1890 °F) based on the historical powder data. And hence the solution
temperature needs to be below that range for a consistent result. Finally, standard age
temperatures were used to complete the heat treat cycles (718 °C/1325 °F
and 621 °C/1150 °F for 8 h each).

In additive manufacturing, like any other processes, it is important to correlate
coupon quality and microstructural development to the actual part microstructure.
Figure 8 compares the grain structures for a test bar with a thick and thin area of an

DMLM 718 Mechanical Behavior
Gas turbine engine hardware processed with novel methods requires thorough
characterization of physical and mechanical properties. Based on the ﬁnal part
requirements, suf ﬁcient data is generated to capture the variation by statistical
means to generate the property curves for component design usage. For property
generation, gas atomized powders were used from two powder vendors, for
machined and as-printed surfaces in horizontal and vertical build directions. Current
heat treat of the bars and parts include: stress relief + HIP + solution at 982 °C
(1800 °F)/1 h in vacuum + age 1 at 718 °C (1325 °F)/8 h in protective atmo-
sphere + age 2 at 612 °C (1150 °F)/8 h in protective atmosphere. Generally, the
as-printed condition may give a debit of 10 –40% in LCF life compared with the low
stress ground surface condition for the same alloy, making it a limiting condition.
Hence during the characterization of the material both the machined and as-printed
property curves were generated. Figure 10 shows a fractured fatigue bar showing
typical side walls of as-printed surface. In general, the surface attributes are
expected to adversely affect the fatigue properties.
Dynamic Modulus
Figure 11 shows the dynamic modulus data tested per ASTM E1876. Data repre-
sents both the build (vertical) and horizontal directions and demonstrates no dif-
ference in the behavior, which provides evidence of isotropy of the material and
structure from a modulus perspective. The modulus for both conditions appears to
decrease linearly with temperature from 90 to 650 °C (200 to 1200 °F). Trend of the
data is similar to other forms of Alloy 718.

Tensile Properties
Figure 12 shows the 0.2% yield strength, ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and the
percentage of elongation behavior with temperature. Room temperature data was
generated per ASTM E8 and elevated temperature with ASTM E21. Each over plot
provides a comparison between the machined DMLM versus the machined cast
(with no HIP step) and forged Alloy 718. As shown, the DMLM yield strength is
nominally 10% lower than wrought material behavior, but 50% higher than the cast
material at room temperature. Similarly, UTS for DMLM approaches the wrought
curve, and is 60% higher than cast UTS. Ductility of DMLM 718 is similar to
wrought, and almost two times higher than the cast ductility. The better properties
for the DMLM 718 compared to cast 718 include the HIP step and the ﬁner,
equiaxed grain structure.

stress. Machined DMLM 718 has higher capability than as-printed, which may be

Conclusions
(1) In the as-printed condition, DMLM 718 exhibits a columnar/highly directional
microstructure.
(2) Investigation of stress relief condition indicates signi ﬁcant relaxation of
build-related residual stresses at temperatures in the range of typical solution
heat treatment temperatures.
(3) Investigation of the effect of HIP temperature and pressure highlights the need
to balance processing conditions to minimize non-surface connected porosity
while considering the potential for formation of thin oxide ﬁlms at higher
temperatures.

## Page 82

(4) After application of solution and age heat treatment typical of Alloy 718, the
microstructure shows the expected equiaxed grain structure with delta phase
precipitated primarily along grain boundaries. Fine scale precipitation of
strengthening precipitates is evident by the tensile properties achieved.
(5) Tensile testing of the DMLM 718 material shows capability about 10% lower
than wrought but signi ﬁcantly higher than cast. LCF capability is better than
cast Alloy 718.
(6) Crack growth evaluation indicates that growth rates are similar to that of similar
grain sized wrought materials.
(7) The DMLM process may successfully be used to produce Alloy 718 with
improved capability versus castings and with properties near those of wrought
structural forms.

Progress in the Processing
and Understanding of Alloy 718
Fabricated Through Powder Bed
Additive Manufacturing Processes
Michael M. Kirka, Alex Plotkowski, Peeyush Nandwana, Anil Chaudhary,
Suresh S. Babu and Ryan R. Dehoﬀ
Abstract This paper reviews currently available information on the processing and
understanding of Alloy 718 fabricated through powder bed additive manufacturing
processes, speciﬁcally selective laser melting, electron beam melting, and binder
jet additive manufacturing. In each instance, the microstructures formed exhibit
attributes unique to the process used. Through post-processing, these materials are
capable of achieving property behaviors similar to that of the long utilized wrought
material. While AM processes are complex, computational modeling has been suc-
cessfully applied to capture the heat and mass transfer, microstructure evolution, and
constitutive response of the material.

Introduction
The nickel-iron-base (Ni-base) superalloy Alloy 718 has been in use for over 60 years,
and is one of the most studied and remains the most widely utilized Ni-base superal-
loy owing to its excellent corrosion resistance and creep strength in the intermediate
temperature regime (650–700
◦C) [1]. Alloy 718 derives it strength from a combi-
nation of solid-solution strengthening elements and precipitation strengthening via
DO
22 𝛾′′ and L12 𝛾′′ precipitates. Unlike modern cast Ni-base superalloys and mod-
iﬁed derivatives, Alloy 718 is comprised of 20% volume fraction𝛾′′ at peak volume
fraction, with the𝛾′′ being metastable, and decomposing into theDOa 𝛿 with thermal
exposure [2].
With the increasing maturity of additive manufacturing, there has been an
increased emphasis placed on understanding the materials these processes produce,
as AM is increasingly being looked at for production purposes. While, AM will never
replace casting and forgings, AM oﬀers advantages not capable by traditional tech-
niques. Key amongst these advantages is design complexity and manufacturing cost
savings. For processing of high temperature materials via AM, Alloy 718 has become
a prime focus due to its legacy status, widespread usage, and high degree of weld-
ability. Demonstrating the potential of AM as a manufacturing process, Honeywell
fabricated a heat duct belonging to the HTF7000 engine from Alloy 718, utilizing
electron beam melting (EBM), which without changes to the design brought about
a 2x cost reduction over that of the traditionally fabricated heat duct [ 3]. Currently
the heat ducts are fabricated from rolled Alloy 718.
The intent of this paper is to summarize available information on the metallur-
gical processing and mechanical behavior of Alloy 718 fabricated through powder
bed additive manufacturing processes. Speciﬁcally discussed are the topics of pow-
der feedstocks, microstructure formation, mechanical behavior, and computational
modeling tools as a means to predict the process-structure-property relationships.
These discussions provide an insight into the entire spectrum of AM powder bed
research.
Additive Process Characteristics
Regardless of the speciﬁc process, all metal powder bed processes, require a thermal
source to allow for consolidation of the powder feedstock into a usable component
whether through solid-solid or liquid-solid phase transformations. Among the AM
processes seeing tremendous growth for processing Alloy 718 are selective laser
melting (SLM), electron beam melting, and binder jetting additive manufacturing

## Page 85

Progress in the Processing and Understanding of Alloy 718 . . . 71
(BJAM). Below the basic characteristics and operations of the processes are sum-
marized.
Selective Laser Melting
SLM is a two step process that involves the raking of a new layer of powder and
selectively melting areas with a laser beam. Typical layer thicknesses in SLM are
in the range of 20–40 µm, with builds normally occurring in an inert environment
of either argon or nitrogen. The movement of the laser beam across the powder bed
is accomplished through high frequency motions of mechanical mirrors. However,
the laser beam can only move at rates up to 3 m/s due to mechanical limitations. In
SLM, powder size distributions fall into the 15–45µm range, this being to maintain
surface ﬁnish quality and ensure proper fusion of the new layer onto the previous
with low energy density lasers. Additionally, SLM builds normally occur at room
temperature, although many commercial systems do have the ability of heating the
powder bed via resistive heaters to several hundred degrees Celsius.
Electron Beam Melting
EBM is a three step process, raking of a new layer of powder, pre-heating the pow-
der bed, and melting. Unlike SLM, the EBM process for Ni-base superalloys occurs
at temperatures in excess of 700 ◦C for the duration of the build. Heat is supplied
through scanning the diﬀuse electron beam across the powder bed surface to lightly
sinter the powder particles together. Aside from providing the heat to keep the pow-
der bed hot, the pre-heating/sintering step is necessary for avoiding over-excitation
(electrical charging) of the powder particles and large-scale removal of the parti-
cles from the powder bed, in a phenomenon known as smoking. During melting, the
electron beam is focused and near instantaneously deﬂected by the electromagnetic
coils, with beam velocities during melting as high as 10 m/s while maintaining a high
beam energy. An added beneﬁt of these beam speeds is the ability to locally control
solidiﬁcation conditions within the build area. Throughout the build process, a con-
trolled vacuum environment is maintained at a pressure of2−4 × 10
−3 mBar. Layer
thicknesses used in EBM are typically in the range of 50–150 µm, with thicker lay-
ers being to used to further enhance the speed of the process. Additionally, powder
ranges used in the process are typically in the range of 40–140 µm.

## Page 86

72 M. M. Kirka et al.
Binder Jet Additive Manufacturing
Unlike the laser and electron beam processes, binder jet additive manufacturing is a
process that relies on a combination of solid-state and liquid phase sintering mech-
anisms for material consolidation that occurs after building of the object. BJAM
occurs through a three step process for green body fabrication, powder raking, selec-
tive deposition of a polymeric binder, and then curing of the binder by an infrared
heater to bind the powders into the required geometry in a layer-by-layer fashion to
form a green body. Typically, the resultant densities of the green body are in the 45–
55% range. Further, the processes occur in open atmosphere and utilize feedstock
distributions of the order of 1–150 µm. Once the part is removed from the powder
bed, the green body is placed in a furnace to fully cure the binder, and then subse-
quently to burnout the binder prior to sintering the powder particles together. During
this processes, fully dense material can be achieved. It is important to note, since the
BJAM process does not involve fusion, the packing density of the powder bed greatly
inﬂuences the green body density.
Powder Feedstocks
Powder feedstocks are broadly classiﬁed based on their method of fabrication. Some
broader classiﬁcations are gas atomized (GA), plasma rotating electrode process
(PREP), plasma wire atomized (PWA), electrode induction melting gas atomized
(EIGA) and plasma atomized (PA). Gas atomized powders can be further classiﬁed
on the basis of gas used in the atomization process with nitrogen atomized and argon
atomized being two examples. The powders are further classiﬁed based on their mor-
phology and size distribution such as spherical or angular. In all fusion based additive
manufacturing processes the powders are typically spherical and can be fabricated
from any of the above mentioned production technologies. It is a common belief
that the gas porosity in the powders translates to porosity in the ﬁnal part [4]. Thus,
there has been an emphasis on using PREP powders to minimize porosity. However,
a recent study in Ti-6Al-4V has shown that this may not always be the case and that
the porosity is sensitive to process parameters [5].
Aside from feedstock type, powder recyclability is of interest, as in theory pow-
der feedstocks can be reused until depleted. However, in practicality the reuse of
feedstocks inﬂuences measurable properties such as morphology, apparent density,
ﬂowability, and powder chemistry. To date, only Ardila et al. [6] for SLM and Nand-
wana et al. [ 7] for EBM have reported on the recyclability of Alloy 718 powder
feedstocks for additive manufacturing. Ardila et al. [6] observed that with increasing
reuse times, the average powder size tends to increase, possibly due to some ejecta
(Balling of powder particles and ejection from the melt pool) being larger in aver-
age size but smaller that the screen size employed to sieve the powders. Similarly,
Nandwana et al. [ 7] observed the same occurrence with powder size distribution,

## Page 87

with the addition that chemistry of Alloy 718 powder feedstocks did not undergo
statistically signiﬁcant changes with six runs and over 267 h of cumulative exposure
in the EBM process.
Microstructure Formation in Additive Processes
Microstructure formation in Alloy 718 and the associated inﬂuence of
post-processing in relation to mechanical performance has been throughly studied
for material fabricated through casting and forgings [1]. Further, the understanding
of the process-structure-property relationships have become highly optimized for
a given application [ 8]. However, in the context of additive processes, a complete
understanding of the inﬂuence of AM process parameters coupled with the complex
phase transformations in Alloy 718 is still being established as available literature
does not provide full parameter sets and build conditions to make the necessary cor-
relations.
The typical microstructural attributes of Alloy 718 fabricated through SLM are
illustrated in Fig. 1a (adopted from Zhang et al. [ 9]) showing the retention of melt
pool boundaries which are deﬁned by elemental segregation associated with the
high solidiﬁcation rates similar to those observed in welding [ 10]. On the precip-
itate length scale, the retained melt tracks are comprised of ﬁne columnar grains and
dendrites oriented parallel to the build direction, Laves in the interdendritic regions
and carbides as shown in Fig. 1b. Due to the low pre-heat temperatures and high
thermal gradients, the cooling rates found in SLM are generally too high to allow for
precipitation of the𝛾
′′ and𝛾′ strengthening phases, or the decomposition of𝛾′′ → 𝛿.
Microstructure formation in EBM processed material is highly build and process
history-speciﬁc, with the process giving rise to a spatially dependent microstruc-
ture due to the generally high build temperatures (700–1000◦C). From macroscopic
and microstructural characteristics, the spatial dependence can be divided into three
distinct regions as illustrated in Fig. 2 [11]:
∙ Region 1: The last layers of the build solidify in a dendritic manner with a change
in the primary growth direction occurring within the last two layers. Within the
dendritic cores𝛾′′ has precipitated, while carbides and Laves phase occur as solid-
iﬁcation products within the interdendritic regions.
∙ Region 2: An intermediate transition zone which is characterized by a diﬀuse
dendritic structure largely lacking secondary dendrite arms and the interdendritic
Laves phase observed in Region 1. In place of the interdendritic Laves, networks
of ﬁne 𝛿 needles have precipitated.
∙ Region 3: Bulk grain structure consisting of columnar grains lacking characteris-
tics of dendritic segregation due to elemental homogenization occurring as a result
of the high build temperatures. Additionally, networks of𝛿 with both globular and
small needle-like𝛿 morphologies are reported to precipitate.

Additionally, Nandwana et al. [12] and Strondl et al. [ 13] in their studies on EBM
of Alloy 718 have shown that alternative morphologies of 𝛿 can form aside from
those shown in Fig.3a, b. These diﬀerent𝛿 morphologies can be associated with the
bulk temperature of the build and relate to similar observations made for wrought
Alloy 718 as illustrated by the time-temperature-transformation (TTT) diagram for
wrought Alloy 718 in Fig. 3c[ 14].
Stated previously, BJAM is a non-fusion based process, and the material requires
sintering to achieve full density. Turker et al. [ 15] explored the eﬀects of sintering
temperature and layer thickness on the densiﬁcation behavior of Alloy 718 fabri-
cated via binder jetting. They reported that samples fabricated with 125 µml a y e r
thickness and sintered at 1300
◦C resulted in roughly 99% densiﬁcation whereas the
extent of densiﬁcation reduced if the layer thickness was varied. Nandwana et al.
[16] conducted sintering studies to address the inﬂuence of powder size distribu-
tion and chemistry. In their work they found that supersolidus liquid phase sinter-
ing (>1290
◦C) is required to sinter Alloy 718 to full density. Fine powders (7 µm)
form a microstructure rich in carbides while coarser (70 µm) powders form 𝛿 and
Laves phases between grains during sintering (Fig. 4). This diﬀerence was rational-
ized based on the binder per unit surface area (carbon) being higher for ﬁner pow-
ders. The higher binder potentially leaves higher carbon after binder burnout thus
terminating the solidiﬁcation reaction in carbides while carbon lean samples would
result in formation of Laves phase and 𝛿. Additionally, it was noted that ﬁner pow-
ders resulted in ﬁne equiaxed grains (<25 µm) whereas the coarser powders resulted
in coarse grains (100 µm) with remnants of liquid channels in between.

To homogenize the microstructure and precipitate an ideal Alloy 718 microstruc-
ture, solution treatment and aging (STA) is a necessity, with hot isostatic pressing
(HIP) being an additional step to heal porosity retained within the material. Com-
mon throughout the reported literature is the application of AMS 5662, the stan-
dard heat-treatments for wrought Alloy 718, with a few studies applying alternative
post-processing conditions, amongst them [10, 17]. Due to residual stresses in SLM
fabricated Alloy 718, solutioning is reported to result in recrystallization of the as-
fabricated grain structure [18–20]. Additionally, Laves phase is also reported to be
retained within the post-processed microstructure. In the case of EBM material, the
columnar grain structure is stable and retained after post-processing, this is due to
the high build temperatures which relaxes the stress during the build [18]. Addition-
ally, Kirka et al. have shown the ability to homogenize and disperse the spatially
dependent microstructure through solutioning [21]. Interestingly though, Nandwana
et al. [ 12] reported grain growth of EBM Alloy 718 which initially comprised of
large needle𝛿. This suggests that the initial build temperature inﬂuences the stabil-
ity of the columnar grain structure. However, full conﬁrmation on grain growth vs
recrystallization mechanisms in EBM 718 required additional study [12].

Mechanical Properties
The process-structure-property relationships associated with the various possible
microstructures that can occur in forged and cast Alloy 718 have long been estab-
lished, such that post-processing treatments have become highly optimized for the
speciﬁc component service conditions [ 8]. In the context of AM, the literature is
largely incoherent in reporting the microstructure attributes of the material in the as-
fabricated and post-processed states, i.e. texture and precipitate volume fraction and
size make-up. While lacking detailed characterization, a picture of the mechanical
performance can be drawn to provide indication on the performance of AM material
in relation to currently utilized industry standards.
Tensile Behavior
The bulk of the published literature for powder bed additive manufacturing processes
is concerned with the tensile behavior of Alloy 718 at room temperature in both the
as-fabricated [9, 10, 17, 20, 22–25] and post-processed states [ 9, 10, 13, 17, 20,
22–26], with a handful of studies investigating the behavior of the material at tem-
peratures of relevance, i.e. 650
◦C[ 21, 24, 27]. Considering all reported values for
yield strength, ultimate strength, and ductility for as-fabricated Alloy 718 material,
considerable variation in reported values are observed, being in the ranges of 570–
1000 MPa, 900–1200 MPa, and 5–27% respectively.
Largely lacking𝛾′′ strengthening precipitates, SLM material in the as-fabricated
condition has been reported to exhibit strength levels at or near wrought material
at room temperature. Aydinoz et al. [ 23] considered this observation and reasoned
the high strength values and low ductility were the result of Laves phase and sub-
micron sized cell structures exhibiting ill-deﬁned boundaries. Additionally, it has
been reported that an anisotropy exists in the as-fabricated material with reference to
the build direction, this is largely attributed to the grain anisotropy [10]. In their work,
Kuo et al. [24] tested SLM material given STA and observed a retained anisotropy in
the ductility of the material at 650 ◦C vertical and transverse to the build direction.
Ultimately, the presence of interdendritic 𝛿 precipitates with incoherent interfaces
aligned parallel to the build direction were cited as the cause.
Material processed by EBM in the as-built state can similarly exhibit proper-
ties comparable to wrought material along the build direction [ 21, 25], however,
this is due to the continuous precipitation and aging of the 𝛾′′ strengthening phase
in the bulk structure during the build process. In relation to the spatially depen-
dent microstructure discussed previously, the transverse tensile properties exhibit an
analogous behavior, with the tensile response varying as a function of build height
(Fig. 5a). The spatial dependence is most sensitive when the material is tested trans-
verse to the build direction, where the full eﬀects of the under-, peak-, and over-aged
microstructures are observed in the yield behavior as a function of build height. This

Fatigue
Studies on the fatigue life behavior of AM Alloy 718 have been conducted for both
SLM [23, 28–30] and EBM [ 31]. Overall, in both instances, AM Alloy 718 was
found to preform similar to that of wrought Alloy 718. While the topic of this review
concerns powder bed AM processes, it should be noted that two additional stud-

ies concerning the fatigue behavior of Alloy 718 fabricated through directed energy
deposition exist [32, 33].
In their work, Gribbin et al. [ 28] considered the inﬂuence of material state and
post-processing on the LCF performance of SLM fabricated Alloy 718 at room
temperature. Under low strain amplitudes, as-fabricated material was observed to
perform similar to wrought Alloy 718, however at high strain amplitudes, process
induced porosity was found to negatively inﬂuence the material’s life with a 10×
debit. Additionally, Gribbin et al. [28] reported that recrystallization associated with
post-processing aversely impacted the strain-life behavior of the material, however,
the life results can be viewed to fall within the life scatter band of the wrought mate-
rial, leaving open the beneﬁt of HIP on material behavior.
Investigated by Kirka et al. [31] was the inﬂuence of texture on the LCF behavior
of HIP+STA Alloy 718 fabricated through EBM at 650
◦C. The reported strain-
life curves are shown in Fig. 7, columnar material aligned with the build direc-
tion resulted in a 10× increase in life on average over that of the wrought behavior
reported by Brinkman and Korth [34] and Koul et al. [35]. In comparison, columnar
grained material transverse to the build direction and equiaxed material fabricated
from non-standard scan strategies all performed similar to one another and within
the scatter of wrought Alloy 718. Overall, crack growth in columnar grain mate-
rial aligned with the build direction occurred from the surface, with transgranular
growth happening when the columnar grains were fatigued transversely. Addition-
ally, equiaxed EBM material was reported to fail in a manner through a combination
of link-up of cracks emanating from debonded/cracked carbides and voids forming
at grain boundaries and twins.

Creep
Of the properties of AM Alloy 718, creep performance is by far the most limited
in terms of data. Overall, three studies have been reported for the creep behavior of
Alloy 718 [13, 36, 37].
Kuo et al. [36] observed that heat-treated SLM material failed prematurely com-
pared to wrought Alloy 718 and attributed this to the precipitation of 𝛿 within the
interdendritic regions associated with the Nb segregation aligned parallel to the build
direction. Within wrought Alloy 718,𝛿 precipitates uniformly throughout the struc-
ture preventing a similar inﬂuence on the creep life [17]. Further, Kuo et al. observed
the preferential alignment of the𝛿 inﬂuenced the orientation sensitive creep-life, with
material taken transverse to the build direction declining severely. However, not dis-
cussed by Kuo et al. [36] is the potential impact of process induced porosity on the
performance of the material. Strondl et al. [13] reported on the performance of EBM
processed Alloy 718 under creep conditions at 800
◦C in the heat-treated state. When
crept in tension, the EBM material was reported to fail prior to reaching secondary
creep. Strondl et al. [ 13] attributed this to the presence of porosity in the material
that occurred during the building process.
More recently, Shassere et al. [37] considered the eﬀect of texture on creep defor-
mation of HIP+STA Alloy 718 fabricated through EBM. Similar creep lifetimes
were reported for the EBM materials compared to wrought Alloy 718 as illustrated
in Fig. 8. The behavior of Alloy 718 agreed with longstanding observations that
columnar materials with grains oriented parallel to the stress axis have superior creep

properties. Further, Shassere et al. [ 37] reported that the role of the 𝛿 phase in the
creep rupture ductility is equivalent in both EBM 718 and conventionally processed
material. Voids and cracking were observed along grain boundaries in equiaxed
and columnar material with a transverse orientation to the build direction, with the
columnar longitudinal material being an exception, which only contained voids. The
grain boundaries transverse to the tensile load were reported to contain the maxi-

samples, around the grain boundary 𝛿 phase.
Modeling of AM Alloy 718
To aid in understanding the development and prediction of microstructures and prop-
erties of AM materials, computational techniques have proven to be a useful tools
to gain insight into the inﬂuence of AM processing conditions. However, detailed
modeling of AM processes is a signiﬁcant challenge, requiring several key compo-
nents across a wide range of time and length scales. First, the heat transfer and ﬂuid
mechanics that occur during melting and re-solidiﬁcation in a given AM process
must be predicted. The resulting thermal history subsequently impacts the liquid-
solid and solid-solid phase transformations as well as macro-scale thermal stress
development. Micro-scale models must use this information to predict the character-
istics of the material microstructure, including grain morphology, size, and aspect
ratio, precipitate volume fraction and size, and the accumulation of plastic strain.
Lastly, constitutive models must be developed to translate these microstructure char-
acteristics into mechanical property predictions. As a consequence of the complex

## Page 96

82 M. M. Kirka et al.
multi-scale nature of the process characteristics and material structure development,
no single model is capable of predicting all of the relevant phenomena in reason-
able computation times. Instead, these models may be broadly broken down into
those predicting heat and mass transfer, microstructure development, and constitu-
tive properties, and then coupled across length scales to make meaningful predictions
[38–40].
Microstructure Evolution
For simple cases, some aspects of Alloy 718 microstructure, such as grain size, may
be empirically related to a small number of processing parameters (usually power and
velocity), such as shown by Thompson [41]. However, this approach is limiting in its
applicability across processes or for complex geometries and scan strategies (Fig.9).
Alternatively, the evolution of alloy microstructure in additive manufacturing shares
many similarities to that in casting, welding, and rapid solidiﬁcation, and there-
fore, researchers may leverage many decades of literature from these ﬁelds [42–46].
For example, Raghavan et al. [47] and Plotkowski et al. [48] applied the columnar-
to-equiaxed transition theory developed by Hunt et al. [ 49] and later extended by
Gaumann et al. [50] to understand the nucleation of equiaxed grains in electron beam
melting (EBM) as a function of the process parameters and their eﬀect on the ther-
mal gradient (G) and isotherm velocity (R) at the solidiﬁcation interface. Recently,
Raghavan et al. [51] have applied a similar approach to predict the primary dendrite
arm spacing in Alloy 718 in EBM using theories developed by Kurz and Fisher [52]
and Trivedi [53]. Other researchers have shown that the crystallographic texture of
Fig. 9 Modeling for additive manufacturing of IN718 covers a variety of length and time scales
depending on the relevant physical phenomena under consider. For each type of model application,

## Page 97

Progress in the Processing and Understanding of Alloy 718 . . . 83
columnar grains in Alloy 718 under various processing conditions may be related to
the directions of the thermal gradients during solidiﬁcation. This eﬀect was origi-
nally demonstrated by Dinda et al. [54] for directed energy deposition and related to
calculated melt pool shapes by Helmer et al. [55] for electron beam melting, and by
Wei et al. [56].
Solid state precipitation behavior may be predicted using the phenomenological
simultaneous transformation kinetics (STK) approach based on the classic Johnson-
Mehl-Avrami-Kolmogorov (JMAK) equation. This type of model has been success-
fully applied to understand 𝛾′ and 𝛾′′ precipitation in AM processing of Alloy 718
[38, 57]. These models show that cooling rates in laser processing of Alloy 718 are
high enough to prevent any precipitation without the aid of a subsequent heat treat-
ment [38], in good agreement with experiments results. Lindgren et al. coupled a
precipitation model to a heat transfer model showing diﬀerences in precipitate dis-
tribution for a slower gas tungsten arc welding repair process [40].
Numerical models that explicitly predict microstructure development have also
been applied to additive manufacturing of Alloy 718. The phase-ﬁeld approach has
been applied to AM conditions by Kundin et al. [58] and Acharya et al. [59]t op r e -
dict dendritic solidiﬁcation. In the former case, a multi-component formulation was
used, but was limited to predicting only the primary spacing of a small number of
dendrites. The latter work applied phase-ﬁeld models to simulate melt-pool geome-
tries by simplifying to two-dimensions and approximating Alloy 718 as a sudobi-
nary alloy. Longer length scale solidiﬁcation microstructures have been simulated
using the cellular automata (CA) technique. Rai et al. [ 60] used a two-dimensional
CA model to predict the competition of columnar grains growing epitaxially from
powder particles and previously solidiﬁed layers in EBM processing. Similarly, Pan-
wisawas et al. [39] used a CA model to estimate the inﬂuence of layer thickness on
crystallographic texture development in SLM of Alloy 718.
Heat and Mass Transfer
The thermal history of any point is highly dependent on material properties, heat
source information, geometry, and scan pattern. A variety of models have been
developed for predicting heat and mass transfer in additive manufacturing based on
these process characteristics, largely leveraging techniques developed in the past for
welding research. A wide range of physical phenomena are relevant to modeling
heat and mass transfer in AM, including heat conduction, the evolution of latent
heat, Marangoni driven convection within the melt pool, elemental vaporization
and recoil pressure, radiation, and complex boundary conditions that depend on the
speciﬁc process under consideration. Consequently, modeling approaches used by
researchers for Alloy 718 are generally selected for the problem at hand based on the
required length scale and computational expense, with corresponding trade-oﬀs in
the set of model assumptions and simpliﬁcations, and resulting simulation ﬁdelity.

## Page 98

84 M. M. Kirka et al.
Short length-scale models intended to resolve the details of the melt pool char-
acteristics are generally based on CFD type simulation frameworks. For example,
Panwisawas et al. [39, 61, 62] have developed a powder-scale heat and mass trans-
fer model using the OpenFOAM open-source CFD framework that is capable of
prediction heat transfer, solidiﬁcation, ﬂuid mechanics, and free-surface deforma-
tion behavior. The model uses standard ﬁnite-volume CFD techniques to discretize
the governing equations for conservation of energy, mass and momentum, and the
volume-of-ﬂuid (VOF) approach to track the evolution of the free surface. They
applied this model to selective laser melting of Alloy 718 to understand the inﬂu-
ence of the powder layer thickness on the surface topology of solidiﬁed single tracks
[39]. Other models, such as those based on the Lattice-Boltzmann technique [ 55,
63], have also been developed to track free-surface deformation.
While including much of the relevant physical phenomena related to heat and
mass transfer, models that consider free-surface deformation tend to be computation-
ally expensive, limiting the scale of the simulation domain. Other CFD type models
make additional assumptions (e.g. a ﬂat liquid surface coincident with the top domain
boundary, or neglecting ﬂuid ﬂow eﬀects) to reduce the computation time. Raghavan
et al. [47, 51] simulated heat conduction in single spot-melts in electron beam addi-
tive manufacturing of Alloy 718 to extract solidiﬁcation conditions as a function of
process parameters and relate them to phenomenological models for equiaxed grain
nucleation, grain size, and primary dendrite arm spacing. Plotkowski et al. [48]u s e d
a semi-analytical heat conduction model to predict solidiﬁcation conditions on the
scale of an entire layer in EBM processing of Alloy 718 to understand the relation-
ship between scan strategy and equiaxed grain nucleation. The ﬁnite element method
(FEM) has also been used to simulate heat conduction, often in conjunction with a
thermo-mechanical model to predict residual stresses. These models use techniques
taken from research in computational weld mechanics and range from those that
explicitly consider the path of the beam over one or several layers, generally for sim-
ple geometries like thin walls [40], to simpliﬁed heat sources that lump many layers
together to predict stresses over entire components [64]. These approaches have also
become popular in recent commercial software packages.
Constitutive Modeling
While a microstructure state is highly dependent on the path taken to that state, con-
stitutive equations are framed in a phenomenological manner such that the inherent
prior history is captured by the initial conditions of the state variables. To date, much
of the focus of computational modeling has been towards the process understanding
and not the mechanical response of AM materials. Utilizing a low ﬁdelity approach,
Chaudhary and Babu [38] captured the tensile response of as-fabricated SLM Alloy
718 using a Ramberg-Osgood formulation, while using the relations presented by
Ahmadi et al. [ 65] for determining the theoretical yield strength of the AM Alloy
718 strengthening mechanism. More recently, Ghorbanpour et al. [66] implemented

## Page 99

Progress in the Processing and Understanding of Alloy 718 . . . 85
a crystal plasticity model for SLM processed Alloy 718 for capturing the cyclic and
creep behavior of SLM Alloy 718. While not yet applied to AM Alloy 718 material,
the constitutive model proposed by Chaboche et al. [67] for wrought Alloy 718 could
also be readily applicable.
Conclusions
Reviewed in this paper are reported eﬀorts in developing the processing science
and structure-property-relationships for Alloy 718 fabricated through powder bed
AM processes to date. While many AM processes exist, each process is uniquely
suited for diﬀerent Alloy 718 applications. Each powder bed process, whether it
be SLM, EBM, or BJAM results in their own unique microstructures in the as-
fabricated state: SLM-𝛾 matrix containing interdenritic Laves phase and carbides,
EBM-Microstructure comprising of a spatially dependent precipitate structure sen-
sitive to build history, BJAM-Equiaxed structure with intergranular solidiﬁcation
products sensitive to powder size. In all instances, the as-fabricated tensile, fatigue,
and creep properties are inﬂuenced by these non-ideal microstructures. When sub-
jected to post-processing, particularly HIP, the dynamic properties of Alloy 718
become similar to that of wrought Alloy 718. With the large number of process vari-
ables, and complex boundary conditions encountered in AM processes, established
modeling techniques have been shown with great validity the ability to model the
fabrication of the material from the initial liquid to solid phase transformation up
through the constitutive response of the material.

Impact of Powder Variability
on the Microstructure and Mechanical
Behavior of Selective Laser Melted
Alloy 718
Chantal K. Sudbrack, Bradley A. Lerch, Timothy M. Smith, Ivan
E. Locci, David L. Ellis, Aaron C. Thompson and Benjamin Richards
Abstract Powder-bed additive manufacturing processes use ﬁne powders to build
parts layer-by-layer. Alloy 718 powder feedstocks for selective laser melting (SLM)
additive manufacturing are produced commercially by both gas and rotary
atomization and are available typically in the 10 –45 or 15 –45 µm size ranges.
A comprehensive investigation was conducted to understand the impact of powder
variability on the microstructure and mechanical behavior of SLM 718 heat treated
to Aerospace Material Speci ﬁcation (AMS) 5664. This study included sixteen
virgin powders and three once-recycled powders within the 10 –45 and 15 –45 µm
size ranges that were obtained from seven direct source suppliers and one reseller.
Although alike as highly regular spheroids, these powders showed distinct differ-
ences in composition (especially Al, C and N contents), particle size distributions,
and powder features such as degree of agglomeration, fusion and surface roughness.
Compositional differences expectedly had the strongest impact on microstructure.
High N and C contents formed TiN-nitrides and/or (Ti, Nb, Mo)-C carbides on the
grain boundaries, prevented recrystallization during heat treatment, and resulted in
retained (001)-scalloped shaped grains that ranged from 19 to 41 µm in average
size. In the absence of this particle pinning, the average grain size of the heat treated
SLM 718 ranged from 51 to 90 µm. Room temperature tensile and high cycle
fatigue (HCF) testing compared as-fabricated (AF) and low stress ground (LSG)

displayed the lowest tensile properties. A SLM 718 build fabricated from a powder
with eight times lower C content showed statistically better tensile properties
presumably due to enhanced coarsening of δ-Ni
3Nb precipitates. The specimens
from once-recycled powders had slightly higher tensile strengths and slightly higher

tionally manufactured 718 data, while AF lives exhibited a knock-down due to
surface roughness. The fatigue lives of AF specimens were statistically equivalent
across powder lots except for one and failures typically initiated at stress concen-
trators associated with SLM surface asperities. Fatigue testing of low stress ground
specimens result in both transgranular and within facet crack initiations. More than
half of the cracks initiated from these facets for the machined condition; however,
these facets appeared to be within grains that were larger-than-average in size.
A nitrogen-atomized powder with ﬁne prior particles of TiN-nitrides and M(Ti, Nb,
Mo)C carbides from atomization on powder surfaces resulted in the best fatigue
performance with segregation of these particles to the SLM 718 grain boundaries
leading to higher resistance to early-stage crack propagation. Typically the
ﬁne-grained builds with minor phases along the grain boundaries did not perform
well in fatigue, whereas a larger-grain build with lower carbon content and coarser
δ-Ni
3Nb precipitates showed the next best HCF response. Further details of the
build microstructure and its impact on tensile and fatigue behavior was considered.

Introduction
For three decades, Aerojet Rocketdyne RS-25, a liquid-fuel cryogenic engine,
propelled the Space Shuttle. Now, four of the RS-25 engines will power the core
stage for NASA ’s Space Launch System (SLS), a heavy-lift launch vehicle to
support deep space exploration. Alloy 718 comprises more than half of the weight
of a single RS-25 engine with more than 1,500 individual parts in use in hydrogen,
oxygen, and hydrogen-rich steam at temperatures ranging from −253 to 760 °C [ 1].
In an effort to reduce parts, eliminate welds and increase affordability, additive
manufactured Alloy 718 is being considered by NASA for a couple dozen SLS
engine components that are in limited production, with a speci ﬁc focus on selective
laser melted (SLM) Alloy 718.
Commercially viable Ni-based superalloys are highly alloyed with a rich mi-
crostructure. Conventional cast and wrought Alloy 718 are strengthened with
coherent, intermetallic precipitates of metastable γʺ(DO
22)-Ni3Nb phase and with a
small volume fraction γʹ(L12)-Ni3(Ti, Al) phase, which are uniformly distributed in
90 C. K. Sudbrack et al.

## Page 105

the matrix and the distribution re ﬁned during the aging heat treatments [ 2]. The
orthorhombic δ-Ni3Nb precipitates are incoherent with the matrix and may nucleate
at the grain boundaries or grow as platelets on the (111)-planes within grains [ 3].
Primary coarse Nb-rich MC-carbides, often irregular in shape, may form in Alloy
718 during solidi ﬁcation and high temperature solutioning (>1000 °C) and are
often distributed non-uniformly within the grains, grain boundaries and incoherent
sections of twin boundaries. The secondary MC-carbides (and to a much lesser
extent M
23C6-carbides) may form along the grain boundaries during prolonged
aging above 700 °C and may lead to a continuous carbide ﬁlm that promotes
intergranular fracture [ 4]. TiN nitrides may also form during solidi ﬁcation in the
interdendritic regions; both the primary carbides and TiN nitrides are generally
considered stable phases and will not change with thermal treatment at lower
temperatures [ 3].
Alloy 718 and its derivatives have found wide use in high-temperature aerospace
applications, due to a combination of good mechanical properties, environmental
resistance, and workability at moderate cost [ 5]. Their modest content of refractory
elements and intermetallic precipitate produces alloys that are weldable, which makes
them promising candidates for selective laser melting (SLM) fabrication and has
warranted a number of recent studies on SLM 718 [ 6–10]. To meet the full potential
for aerospace applications, quali ﬁcation and certi ﬁcation efforts are necessary [ 11];
NASA has released a standard [ 12] that considers material property development,
metallurgical and part process control, and inspection for space ﬂight hardware.
This investigation is an industry survey of 718 powders that are readily available
commercially and aims to understand the impact of powder variability on build
quality and performance of SLM 718. The investigation includes sixteen powder
lots from eight suppliers that are produced by gas atomization or rotary atomization
in argon or nitrogen. The survey results will help guide feedstock controls for future
updates to the NASA standard [ 12], which might include quantities like percentage
of ﬁnes, chemistry requirements, and/or defect tolerances. This paper focuses on
select variables evaluated, including powder chemistry, particle size distributions of
the powders, SLM grain and microstructure, and then discusses the relationship of
these variables to the room temperature tensile properties and failure mechanisms
observed for the room temperature high cycle fatigue behavior for the as-fabricated
surface and low stress ground surface conditions. The full investigation [ 13] also
discusses the static ﬂow, rheological response, more details of the powder and build
microstructure characterization and ﬂammability testing, and includes a
multi-variant correlation analysis using principal component analysis.
Experimental Methods
Sixteen powder lots of Alloy 718 were produced either by gas atomization or
rotary atomization in argon or nitrogen using industrial-scale equipment by seven
commercial direct-source producers and one third party reseller (supplier A).
Impact of Powder Variability on the Microstructure … 91

## Page 106

After atomization, powders were screened to achieve various powder cuts requested
and particle ﬁnes were removed using standard supplier practices. Typical shipping
procedures were that screened powders were sealed under an inert environment and
shipped in multiple plastic canisters containing 2.27 or 4.54 kg of powder. Once
received by NASA, powders from a single lot were combined and transferred to
two larger aluminum canisters in a glovebox under a nitrogen atmosphere for
storage and to minimize plastic particulates (contaminants) from original packag-
ing. To obtain well-blended and representative samples, the powders were tumbled
for at least an hour prior to sampling for chemical analysis, microscopy, metal-
lography, particle size analysis, morphology analysis, ﬂow testing, rheology testing
and reserve powder.
Powder chemistry was measured using an average of two analyses by a LECO
CS-444-LS C/S determinator, a LECO TC-436 N/O determinator, and a Varian
Vista Pro ICP atomic emission spectrometer for boron and the metallic elements.
Loose powder and metallographically prepared cross-sections of powder were
imaged with a Nikon Eclipse MA200 optical microscope and a Hitachi S-4700 ﬁeld
emission scanning electron microscope (SEM). The Malvern Morphologi G3SE
system was used to image the silhouettes of a minimum 20,000 individual powder
particles per scan using transmitted illumination, automated optical image collec-
tion, scan area with 25 mm diameter, and a minimum feature size of 30 pixels
(0.88 µm). Particles with a solidity value (particle area divided by convex hull area)
of less than 0.9 were excluded from the analyzed Morphologi distributions, which
combined data from two separate scans. Circular-equivalent diameters were plotted
on a log-scale to obtain the number-basis particle size distributions (PSDs).
Build sets from each powder lot were produced on a Concept Laser M1 SLM
machine at NASA Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) equipped with a
custom-built small-volume build box (100 mm × 100 mm × 80 mm) using
30 µm layer thickness and customized parameters that are similar to Concept
Laser’s recommended parameters for Alloy 718. A cross-hatching scan strategy
was applied, where the scanning direction was altered by 90° between consecutive
layers and contours applied to the perimeter to heal porosity associated with turning
points. An aerial schematic to scale of the build layout is shown in Fig. 1a. Each
build set included ﬁve net-shaped mechanical test bars for the as-fabricated
(AF) surface condition, 4 near-net shaped mechanical test bars for the low stress
ground (LSG) surface condition, a full-height coupon for the green-state condition
(i.e., as-processed by SLM), and another full-height coupon for the fully
heat-treated condition, all of which were built with a taper for easy snap-off from
the stainless steel build plate. The diameters of the near-net shaped bars were
0.762 mm wider than the net shaped bars for grinding to net shape. The custom
build volume required 2 –3 powder re ﬁlls during fabrication, which led to re ﬁll lines
on test bars and coupons (Fig. 1b, c). Approximately 20 kg of powder completed a
single build set without powder reuse.
The green-state test bars and one coupon were hot isostatic pressed (HIP) at a
hold temperature above 1100 °C for several hours in batches. During HIP,
each specimen from a build set was wrapped with stainless steel foil to getter

Each test bar was photographed prior to testing to document its condition and
after testing to record failure location. Tensile tests were conducted on one test bar
per condition at room temperature ( ∼22 °C) under strain control at a strain rate of
3.3 × 10
−4 s−1 until 2% strain. The test then continued without unloading in stroke
control at an equivalent displacement rate until failure. High cycle fatigue
(HCF) tests were conducted on three test bars per condition in load control at a
frequency of 20 Hz. Tests were run at 22 °C using a sinusoidal waveform at a load
ratio, R
σ,o f −1. Tests were conducted at stress levels expected to give sample
failure in one million cycles. The required stress amplitudes were determined to be
about 271 MPa for the AF bars and about 464 MPa for the LSG bars. Test bars
were cycled until they broke into two pieces, or interrupted upon achieving
approximately ten million cycles. Two test bars (C1-3-2 and C1-3-8) were inter-
rupted and were subsequently re-tested at a higher stress level until failure. The
fracture surface of each test bar was photographed optically to document the crack
initiation sites and then the failure modes were evaluated more carefully using SEM
to determine failure initiation sites and modes using JEOL 6100, JEOL 840, or
Hitachi S-4700 microscopes typically operated at 15 –20 kV. The front of the fa-
tigue test rig relative to the fracture surfaces was oriented at 6 o ’clock position in
the SEM images.
Evaluation of Alloy 718 Powders
Table 1 lists the 16 powder lots evaluated for this investigation, which were pro-
duced to composition speci ﬁcation for AMS 5664 by gas atomization (GA) or
rotary atomization in either a nitrogen or argon atmosphere. The powder lot
identiﬁcations (ID) referenced throughout this paper refer to the eight powders
suppliers as A-H with the ﬁrst, second, third, fourth lots supplied 1, 2, 3 and 4.
Fourteen of the 16 powders were acquired in powder cuts common to SLM with
about half in the wider 10 –45 µm range, the other half in the narrow 15 –45 µm
range and with two additional ones in an undersized cut, G1(0 –22), and an over-
sized cut, G4(45 –90), from supplier G.
Powders from all suppliers except from supplier E met AMS 5664 composition
and are within narrow weight percent compositional ranges of 0.35 –0.51 Al, 0 –
0.039 C, 18.1 –19.2 Cr, 18.0 –19.2 Fe, 2.9 –3.1 Mo, 4.8 –5.2 Nb, 0.8 –1.0 Ti, balance
Ni and trace impurities. The E1 powder is outside the acceptable AMS 5664 ranges
for Al, Cr, Fe content with a composition of Ni-0.09 Al-0.096 C-17.72 Cr-21.49
Fe-2.93 Mo-4.86 Nb-0.91 Ti wt%, while E2 powder meets AMS 5664; however, it
has higher contents of Al and C than the powders from the other seven suppliers.
The variation in Al, Cr, C and N contents when signi ﬁcant (Table 1)i nﬂuences the
γʹ-precipitates, carbides and nitrides as discussed in more detail below. The G series
powders show statistically equivalent compositions, which gives an opportunity to
separate composition from size effects.

In addition to composition differences, the Alloy 718 powders evaluated show

powders in Fig. 2 highlights the differences in surface roughness, satellites, fusion,
and size ranges. All the powders exhibit fairly smooth and spheroidal-shaped
particles, demonstrating that the powders are distinct and the powder suppliers had
varying success in particle ﬁne screening as quanti ﬁable in the number-basis PSDs

Selective Laser Melted Builds and Microstructure
SLM fabrication was employed to fabricate eighteen build sets from 15 different
718 powders (Table 2). Most powders from this investigation were procured
off-the-shelf in 22 kg amounts; second lots in larger quantities of >500 kg, were
procured from suppliers D, E, and F, which allows the impact of a single powder
reuse to be assessed for SLM Alloy 718. To study once-recycled reuse, the powder
in both the build and over ﬂow chambers were removed, sieved with a 100 µm
sieve, and returned to the dose chamber with no additional mixing. The
once-recycled build sets are identi ﬁed as D2-R, E2-R and F2-R. There were
challenges in SLM fabrication for the off-nominal powder cuts evaluated. The G1
powder lot with 0 –22 µm particles clumped and spread poorly; the attempt at SLM
fabrication was not successful. The G4 powder lot with 45 –90 µm particles did
build, but the test bars and specimens exhibited poor interlayer bonding, which led
to compromised mechanical integrity not discussed further here. For the G3 build
set, a test bar was lost and another compromised due to a build fault during normal
operation on the trailing side of the build plate.
SLM full-height coupons, as shown in Fig. 1b, and the mechanical test bars
appear shiny after fabrication and are golden in color after heat treatment due to a
modest amount of oxidation during the HIP treatment. SLM build sets were fab-
ricated successfully with a custom, small-volume machine con ﬁguration, which
unlike the regular con ﬁguration, required 2 powder re ﬁlls of the piston, leading to a
restart layer across the build set for each re ﬁll (e.g., prominent lines on coupons in
Fig. 1b). In addition to the 2 re ﬁlls, about half of the powders triggered one or more
piston failures with the H1 powder triggering ﬁve failures during its build set,
possibly due to its high ﬁne content. These planned and unplanned restarts were
mitigated by following the MSFC-suggested restart procedure of adding a thin ﬂux
coat of powder (about ½ of a layer thickness) and performing 3 full layer melts to

Post-processing heat treatment in SLM 718 aims to reduce the high residual
stresses (see [ 14]) and grain texture [ 10] associated with fabrication, as well as
reﬁning the microstructure for mechanical performance. Post-processing heat
treatment may also be bene ﬁcial by minimizing undesirable Laves phases through
solutioning [9] and eliminating large pores with the HIP treatment that may lead to
fatigue debits. Due to reasonable build parameters, the as-processed SLM 718
exhibits a modest level of micron-sized pores throughout most of the green-state
builds, less than 0.3% and 12.2 µm average pore diameter (Table 2). Notably higher
levels of porosity (>0.75%) are observed for two of the three build sets from the
powders sets that are once-recycled. The porosity is reduced with HIP to man-
ageable levels with most fully heat-treated builds exhibiting less than 0.02%
porosity with an average pore diameter of less than 4.5 µm.
Prolonged HIP treatment of as-processed SLM 718 above 1100 °C leads to
recrystallization of textured grains in SLM 718 [ 9]. Fourteen of the 18 build sets
post heat-treatment exhibit equiaxed grains with little to no texture (Fig. 4a) that
can be attributed to recrystallization during HIP; the powders associated with all of
these builds were atomized in argon. Excluding the G4 set, which exhibited
irregular build quality, the mean linear intercept grain sizes ranged from 51 to
90 µm for these fully heat-treated builds (Table 2). In contrast, the build sets that
are fabricated from the three powder lots atomized in nitrogen show scalloped
(001)-texture grains characteristic of as-processed SLM 718 (Fig. 4b). The H1 build
set, which is from a powder lot atomized in argon, is partially recrystallized with
some texture (Fig. 4c) and shows some areas with the scalloped grain structure.
A closer examination below establishes that the retained grain structure after heat
treatment is due to particle pinning of the grain boundaries (GBs) by highly stable
minor phases during the high temperature heat treatment.
Two populations, “large” and “small”, of titanium-based nitrides are observed
after full heat treatment for the SLM build sets as quanti ﬁed in Table 2. The “large”
nitride population is comprised of faceted particles with 7 –8 µm average diameters
that are sparsely distributed in three builds sets: E2, E2-R and H1 powder lots.
Figure 5 shows, for the E2 lot, that similarly-sized TiN particles are present in the
powder, the green-state coupon and the fully heat-treated coupon. The large nitrides
precipitate during the gas atomization and continue to be stable over the localized,
rapid melting of the SLM powder-bed and the post processing heat treatment. The
nitrogen content for N-atomized E2 powder is very high at 2770 wt% ppm (Table 1),
about double the content of the two other N-atomized powders at 1395 and 1220 wt
% ppm for C1 and E1 lots, respectively. Large nitrides are found at 0.13% volume
fraction (V
f) for both the ﬁrst and second once-recycled build sets of the E2 powder,
but not for the C1 or E1 build sets, which contain fairly high N contents. The build
fabricated from the H1 powder with a N content of 562 wt% ppm also shows
sporadically large nitrides that are similarly in size, but ten times less frequent,
V
f = 0.013%, than the E2 and E2-R builds. The second nitride population, or
“small” nitrides consists of spheroidal particles that range in average diameter from

80 to 141 nm and that are 50 –100 times smaller than the large nitrides. These small
nitrides are distributed uniformly throughout all the builds sets, including the B1
powder which contained only 25 wt% ppm of N. As the nitrogen content of the
powders increases, the mean diameter and V
f of the nitrides also increases (Table 2).
The series of images in Fig. 6 shows the differences in minor phase distributions
between builds and helps elucidate the role of the Ti-based nitrides and carbides in
pinning GBs after post processing the C1, E1, E2 and H1 build sets. The small
spheroidal particles that image with dark contrast are the small TiN nitrides that
tend to distribute uniformly in most builds, while the brightly imaged particles are
refractory-based carbides and Nb-rich δ-precipitates. Like in the majority of lots
atomized in argon, the GBs in the B1 build are mostly free of nitrides and carbides
allowing the as-processed grains to recrystallize. The platelet particles imaged along
the B1 GB are δ-Ni
3Nb precipitates that nucleate heterogeneously, and are present
along some GBs for the various SLM 718 investigated here, despite the fast air cool
equivalent from the solutioning heat treatment that aims to help suppress δ-for-
mation. The bright spot on the right edge of the EDS maps in Fig. 6b is a typical
0.5 µm MC-carbide present intergranularly and intragranularly in all builds. Typical
to this type of carbide, the MC-carbide that is mapped is enriched in Nb, Ti, and
Mo, but not Cr. In contrast to all other SLM 718 builds evaluated, the heat-treated
GBs in C1 are ornamented with a ﬁne dispersion of Ti-based nitrides and carbides,
which are less than several hundred nanometers in diameter (Fig. 6). As shown in
the EDS maps of GB area for a C1 build (Fig. 6b), the ﬁne nitrides along the GBs
are enriched in Ti only (dark-contrast), whereas the ﬁne GB carbides (light-contrast)
are mostly enriched in Ti but also contain some Nb and Mo. The enrichment in Ti
and Nb within the carbides suggests that they are likely carbides with the MC
structure. Both the ﬁne nitrides and carbides are attributed to prior particles that
form on powder surface during the gas atomization in nitrogen. During the
development of powder metallurgy, nitrogen-atomized Alloy 625 in the 1980s,
such prior particles, identi ﬁed as titanium MC-carbides and nitrides, were found to

a similar number density of nitrides at the GBs as in the bulk in contrast to the GB

surfaces from the E series with SEM. The GBs in the heat-treated builds appear
instead to be decorated with closely-spaced, ﬁlm-like carbides that vary in size from
100 nm to a couple microns (Fig. 6a), indicating these carbides are mainly
responsible for GB pinning in the E series builds. In contrast to E series powders,
the H1 powder has a much more modest C content (215 wt% ppm) and moderate N
content (562 wt% ppm). The fully heat treated H1 builds exhibit areas which are
ﬁne-grained and other areas that are coarse-grained, such as the areas labelled as 1
and 2 in Fig. 6a, respectively. The GBs within the coarse grained areas are similar
to those in the large-grained SLM builds; that is, GBs with occasional δ-needles and
carbides yet mostly free of minor phases. The GBs in the ﬁne grained areas appear
to sometimes image brightly, which may be related to GB segregation of refractory
elements. Sometimes the areas contain narrow ( ∼50 nm width) ﬁlm-like phases
along the GBs, which are not well resolved with the EDS maps in SEM. Further
investigation that includes higher resolution GB analysis with TEM is needed to
resolve the mechanism that leads to the bimodal grain distribution. It is plausible
that the bimodal distribution may be associated with transport of the lighter ﬁnes
(∼75%) to the outer edge of the melt pool, which may alter the composition of these
edge areas from surface absorbants and segregants and contribute to differences in
GB chemistry.

Mechanical Testing Results
Table 3 summarizes the room temperature tensile properties for each powder lot
tested in the as-fabricated (AF) and low stress ground (LSG) surface condition in
rank order by ultimate tensile strength (UTS). The strengths for a given powder lot
are ranked in a similar position regardless of whether they are AF or LSG samples,
indicating that surface ﬁnish is not a factor in the strength of these builds. Test bars
fabricated from the recycled powders have slightly higher strengths by 5 –10 MPa
and slightly higher ductilities by 0.9 –1.9% than those made from their virgin
equivalents. While these differences are small, neither the strength nor ductility are
degraded and seem to improve by ﬁrst powder recycling for SLM 718. For the AF
surface condition, the various powder lots fall within a statistical group with a mean
UTS of 1310 ± 40 MPa. This group is bound by the G2 powder lot on the upper
end and by the H1 powder lot on the lower end. Only two lots are outside of the
standard deviation, where the response for B1 and E1 powder lots are the strongest
(1383 MPa) and weakest (1233 MPa), respectively. A similar response is observed
for the LSG condition, but the mean UTS is slightly higher at 1365 ± 29 MPa. The
main group is bound by the G3 powder lot on the upper end and by the C1 powder
lot on the lower end. Again, the B1 powder lot displays the strongest response

The outlier responses in B1 and E1 build strength may be explained by differ-
ences in 718 powder composition (Table 1) and carbide distributions (Table 2), and
the resulting effect on the γʺ(Ni
3Nb) and γʹ(Ni3Al, Ti) distributions as primary
particle strengtheners. In addition to solid solution strengthening, Nb partitions
strongly to the MC-carbides and γʺ-precipitates in Alloy 718. The B1 powder lot
contains 4.5 to 10 times less C leading to 4 to 50 times lower V
f of carbides
compared to the group. The much lower carbide V f of 0.002% leads to a higher
supersaturation of Nb in solution to form γʺ(Ni3Nb)-precipitates; accordingly, the
γʺ(Ni3Nb)-precipitates from heat-treated B1 build set are coarser at similar number
densities to the rest of builds, which contributes to the higher strength. In contrast,
the E1 powder contains 2 –4.5 times more C leading to 2.5 –28 times higher V
f of
carbides, and a lower number density of γʺ(Ni3Nb)-precipitates, contributing to its
lower strength. The E1 powder also contains signi ﬁcantly less Al at 0.09 wt%
(0.2–0.8 wt% is required by AMS 5664) than the other powders, which typical
contained ∼0.4 wt% Al. The Al de ﬁciency in E1 powder leads to fewer γʹ(Ni3Al,
Ti)-precipitates to strengthen the E1 build. The next four build sets with the lowest
strengths (AF UTS of 1265 –1285 MPa and LSG UTS of 1333 –1342 MPa) are
from the C1, H1, and E2 virgin and once-recycled powders, which includes the
builds with the highest N contents due to their atomization in N. This result is
somewhat surprising as the re ﬁned grain sizes of this group (19 –41 µm compared to
51–90 µm mean linear intercept) and narrow grain widths in loading is expected to
lead to strengthening. Further work is needed to understand the mechanism that
contribute to the weaker response of this ﬁne-grained group with a high nitrogen
concentration. It may relate to less strengthening due to fewer γʹ(Ni
3Al,Ti)-pre-
cipitates forming with less Ti available after partitioning to nitrides during solidi-
ﬁcation. It may relate to a degradation in GB strength due to increased
concentration of minor phases at the GBs. As noted above, the H1 test bars are
unique due to their atypical surface condition, which may also be responsible for its
weaker response.
As shown in Table 3, the 0.2% yield strength, UTS, elongation to failure and
reduction in area meets or exceeds the minimums given by AMS 5664 for solution
and aged bars, except for the AF condition for the E1 and E2 powder lots. The E2-R
powder lot barely meets the requirements with the slight bump in strength that is
observed with ﬁrst recycling. An average over all samples shows an elastic modulus
of 186 GPa. For each property within Table 3, the SLM materials tested in the AF
condition are slightly lower than the materials from the LSG condition. Strengths
and stiffness differ by 4% and ductility varies by a wider margin. The lower values
in strength and stiffness may be a result of overestimating the cross-sectional area of
the AF test bars due to the rough surfaces with fused particles. The lower ductility
for the AF tests is presumed to be a result of the surface defects associated with the
AF surface condition.

were run at room temperature for the AF and LSG surface conditions for all powder
lots. Three tests were run for each surface condition per lot with an extra test for the

bar charts and individual tests as markers that also indicate the crack initiation
mechanism identi ﬁed from the fracture surfaces. The maximum stress to achieve
about million cycle average for the LSG test bars is 464 MPa. The LSG testing
results are in reasonable agreement with cast wrought 718 with AMS 5664 heat
treat from the literature [ 13], indicating consistent material properties and SLM
fabrication is reasonable to process for Alloy 718. The roughness of the AF surface
led to a ∼40% knock down in maximum stress to 271 MPa for the AF condition to
achieve the similar million cycle average. It is worth noting that the restart pro-
cedure used is effective at retaining material integrity, as only two of the 102 test
results are excluded (AF G2-1, LSG A3-8) because the bars failed at poorly
bounded layers (major lack of fusion) at a restart layer. The gauge, radius and grips
of the test bars are single-build SLM 718. Tests bars A2-1 and G3-5 with the AF
surfaces broke in the grip section and show fatigue lives consistent with the other
two tests from these build sets; all other test bars failed in the gauge section.
The room temperature HCF behavior for the AF surface condition are fairly
consistent across powder lots except for the H1 powder lot (Fig. 8). The AF tests
show fatigue lives that span from 0.6 –1.8 million cycles for most tests (Fig. 8a),
which overlap statistically on cumulative probability plots for all powder lots except
for the H1 powder lot. The mean life of test bars fabricated from the second-use the
D2, E2, F2 are statistically equivalent to, though in most case lower than, the mean
life of the ﬁrst-use powder samples. This suggests that for SLM 718 the ﬁrst recycle
does not substantially degrade the room temperature HCF lives. The H1 bars tested
in the AF condition represent an obvious outlier with fatigue lives lasting well
above 2 million cycles for all three tests and this is examined further below. The
scatter by powder lot between the lowest and highest values in fatigue lives for AF

Failure sites are identi ﬁed from the fracture surfaces with SEM for each test bar
to better understand the failure modes (Fig. 8). The fatigue failures of the AF bars
initiate overwhelming, 48 of 49 non-grip failures, at facet failures within grains,
which fail in crystallographic manner due to concentrated slip at a cleavage plane.
Figure 9 shows the four types of facet failures observed: (a) surface facet; (b) sur-
face facet with additional crystallographic steps; (c) near-surface facet (within
∼200 µm); (d) internal facet. The failure site for the E2-R-1 test bar is a 50 µm
nitride near the surface instead of a facet (Fig. 9e). The additional crystallographic
steps with some facet failures, such as shown in Fig. 9b, are observed for one or
two tests in every powder lot that was fully recrystallized (A, B, D, F, G series).
These recrystallized conditions produce larger grains with fewer minor phases at the
GBs that presumably have poorer resistance to crack growth than GBs reinforced
with minor phases. The steps may result from persistent slip bands associated with
strain localization during Stage I crack propagation under these conditions (see
review by Jiang [ 17]). Notably, 90% of the tests failed at the surface (30 tests) or
within a few grains from the surface (14 tests) with only 5 tests initiating at internal
facets for the AF condition. The failure sites for the AF condition are sometimes in
the vicinity of a surface step, cusp or depression as shown for representative
cross-sectional images of secondary crack (Fig. 10). With the longitudinal ridges
(Fig. 7a, b), the inherent rough surface and fused particles, all the test bars have a
high number of stress concentrators and stress gradients that decay from the surface.
The statistically equivalent fatigue lives across powder lots implies that these stress
concentrators, which are common to all test bars, have a greater in ﬂuence on fatigue
life in the AF condition than variations in powder attributes, composition or build
microstructure. Cracks tend to propagate transgranularly after initiation (Fig. 10).
For the AF surface condition, the H1 lot showed signi ﬁcantly better fatigue lives
than the all other powder lots (Fig. 8a). Cracks initiated from facets just as dis-
cussed above. For example, the AF H1-5 fracture surface shows a deep surface
depression initiating failure at three closely spaced facets (Fig. 11a), where the

The fatigue tests of the LSG surface condition result in more variation than
occurred in the AF surface condition, Fig. 8b. The cycles-to-failure mean value
ranged from 0.29 to 6.86 million cycles for the LSG condition, but only 0.71 –1.46
million cycles for the AF condition excluding H1. For the LSG condition, there is
also a slightly larger range in individual fatigue lives from 0.4 to 2.0 million cycles
for most tests. The C1 is a clear outlier as the best performer with 2 runouts and test
bar that failed at 3,540,392 cycles, which is well above this range. For the B1 and H1

f = 5,500,000 cycles and at 3,540,392 cycles, respectively. The mean

million cycles are distinctly higher and lower than the group that excludes outlier C1.
Compared to the AF tests, there is a larger degree of scatter between the highest and
lowest values by lot for the LSG tests with only one powder lot with scatter less than
1.5, with four lots with scatter between 2 and 3 and ﬁve lots with scatter above 3.
Additional tests are required to better establish the mean fatigue lives and trends.
Like for AF testing, recycling once does not appear to degrade substantially the
fatigue lives; the virgin E2 tests on average are three times lower than the mean for
the ﬁrst recycled equivalent, which may be related to the larger scatter.
Moreover, the crack initiation mechanisms for the LSG surface condition also
show more variation than the AF surface condition, Figs. 8b and 12. Similar to the
AF tests, the highest percentage of the failure initiations are surface or near-surface
facets, but only 63% for the LSG tests compared to 90% for the AF tests. The
number of failures initiated at internal facets is nearly double with 9 internal facet
failures for the LSG condition compared to 5 for the AF condition. With the rough
surface removed, the facet failures appear to initiate at larger than average grains, as
shown in Fig. 12. These internal, sub-surface, and surface failures occurred at
grains that are about double the mean grain size of 92, 63, 41 µm for the respective
powder lots F1, G2 and H1. In contrast to the AF failures, transgranular initiations
(Fig. 12d) compete with facet failures in the ﬁner grained LSG test bars from the
C1, H1, E1, E2-R powder lots with 10 tests recorded. Within the C1 powder lot, the
two run-out tests failed ultimately from sub-surface facets, while the test that
reached 3,540,382 cycles failed transgranularly. Grain boundary resistance in
adjacent grains surrounding the failed facet grain is important to initial propagation
during Stage I crack propagation. The superior fatigue lives for the C1 LSG

Summary and Conclusions
An investigation of the impact of powder variability on microstructure, room
temperature tensile and HCF behavior was performed on material produced by
selective laser melting (SLM) of Alloy 718. The sixteen commercially available
powder lots were produced either by gas atomization or rotary atomization in argon
or nitrogen (Table 1), were heat treated per AMS 5664, and made into uniform
gauge test bars. The following summary and conclusions were observed:
 All these “off-the-shelf” Alloy 718 powders were spheroidal and highly regular
in shape. The differences in powder production practices, however, did lead to
variation in average diameters, particle size distribution widths and modalities,
percentage of particle ﬁnes, fusion between particles, and degree to which the
powders were agglomerated (Figs. 2, 3, and Table 1). The powders with higher
quantity of ﬁnes and agglomeration were more prone to unplanned stops during
SLM fabrication. These fabrication dif ﬁculties led to layer discontinuities that
were likely due to differences in spreading behavior of the powders (Fig. 1).
