Introduction
After an extensive research and development activity, a new precipitation hardened
(PH) Ni-base alloy has been developed to ful ﬁl the recent stringent requirements of
the oil and gas industry. The new alloy is commercially designated as AF955 and
produced at strength levels of 827 MPa (120 ksi) 0.2% offset minimum yield
strength (MYS) and 965 MPa (140 ksi) MYS with very good ductility and
toughness, low susceptibility to hydrogen embrittlement and with microstructure in
compliance with the requirements of API 6ACRA speci ﬁcation [1] for PH Ni-alloys
like UNS N07716, N07725, N09925 and N09935. The 827 MPa (120 ksi) level is
designated as Grade 3 and the 965 MPa (140 ksi) is designated as Grade 3HS. The
AF955 exhibits good corrosion resistance and has been accepted for inclusion in
NACE MR0175/ISO 15156 to be used for any equipment or component within the
environmental limits of NACE Level VII [ 2]. These properties make alloy AF955 a
very promising material for widespread applications from oil and gas drilling and
production equipment to downhole applications, power generation, chemical ap-
plications and many others. Details of the manufacturing process and properties are
presented and discussed in this paper.
Experimental
AF955 Melting Practice and Manufacture
Table 1 reports the average chemical composition of this alloy.
The alloy is produced by the following manufacturing steps:
• Raw materials are melted in an electric arc furnace (EAF) followed by melt
reﬁning via the Argon-Oxygen Decarburization (AOD); alternatively, raw
materials are melted and re ﬁned by vacuum induction melting (VIM) process;
• Material is poured into round molds, stripped from the molds and re-melted by
consumable-electrode Vacuum Arc Re-melting (VAR) process.
Wrought products are obtained by the following main manufacturing steps:
• VAR ingot homogenization consisting of a controlled temperature process to
remove primary segregation;

• Primary conversion of the VAR ingot to intermediate bloom followed by bloom
forging to a round bar by computer-controlled forging to obtain uniform
reduction from center to surface;
• Heat treatment using furnaces calibrated and surveyed to aerospace require-
ments of Aerospace Material Speci ﬁcation (AMS) 2750E [ 3].
AF955 Characterization
Mechanical Properties
Mechanical properties were evaluated in the longitudinal direction at mid-radius of
bar prolongations. Mechanical testing consisted of room temperature tensile testing
according to ASTM Standard E8/E8M [ 4], hardness to ASTM E18 [ 5] and Charpy
V-Notch impact according to ASTM E23 [ 6].
Microstructure Characterization
Microstructure characterization was performed on specimens removed from dif-
ferent locations over the cross-section of bar prolongations. The average grain size
was determined according to ASTM E112 [ 7] and ASTM E1181 [ 8]. Secondary
phases were assessed by light optical microscopy and scanning electron microscopy
(SEM) with energy-dispersive X-ray spectrometry (EDS). Strengthening phases
were characterized by Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) on specimens
prepared by ion milling.
Stress Corrosion Cracking Resistance
Both Grade 3 and Grade 3HS were tested for stress corrosion cracking resistance by
the NACE TM0177 Standard C-Ring Test Method (Method C) in the conditions of
Table 2 [9].
For each grade, one 152.4 mm (6 in.) diameter bar, one 203.2 mm (8 in.)
diameter bar and one 254 mm (10 in.) diameter bar were manufactured by the
EAF + AOD + VAR melt route from three different heats and tested at SSC
Level II, GHSC Level III and SCC Level VII.
In addition, one 254 mm (10 in.) diameter bar of AF955 Gr. 3 and one 254 mm
(10 in.) diameter bar of AF955 Gr. 3HS manufactured by VIM + VAR melt route
were tested at SCC Level VII for 6 months.

Furthermore, one each 203.2 mm (8 in.) diameter bar of Gr. 3 and Gr. 3HS were
manufactured by the EAF + AOD + VAR melt route and tested at SCC Level
VII + S
0 for 1 month.
Each stress corrosion test was performed on triplicate C-ring specimens at 100%
of yield strength at the test temperature. C-ring specimens were machined in the
transverse orientation with the apex at the mid-radius location of a bar prolongation.
The nominal C-ring dimensions are given in Table 3.
Details of the test procedure are given elsewhere [ 10, 11].
After environmental exposure, each C-ring was cleaned, re-weighed to deter-
mine any weight change, examined by visual inspection at 20X magni ﬁcation and
photographed. After exposure and cleaning, all C-rings were sectioned in the cir-
cumferential direction at the apex for further examination by optical microscope of
the area subjected to the maximum deformation.
Hydrogen Embrittlement Susceptibility
Assessment was to a recently developed test procedure [ 12] comparing results of
Slow Strain Rate Tensile (SSRT) tests at 40 °C and 10
−6 s−1. on NACE TM0198
sub-size specimens [ 13] under cathodic polarization (CP) to obtain a hydrogen
charging environment with SSRT tests on the same specimens in air. CP was
obtained by a 0.5 M sulfuric acid solution with 5 mA/cm
2 of applied current density.
Elongation to failure ratio (EFR) is determined as the CP to air ratio of the
aforementioned average values. A precipitation hardened alloy is de ﬁned as sus-
ceptible to hydrogen embrittlement if the EFR is less than or equal to 45% and the
fracture surface is signi ﬁcantly intergranular.

The 120 ksi MYS grade also exhibits a transverse toughness of at least 15 J

Microstructure Characterization
The microstructure alloy has been engineered with focus on exceeding the industry
requirements in API 6ACRA speci ﬁcation [ 1]. It consists of an austenitic matrix
with equiaxed grain structure and unimodal grain size distribution as de ﬁned by
ASTM E1181. The average grain size is ASTM E112 No. 3 or ﬁner up to 254 mm
(10 in.) bar diameter, No. 2 or ﬁner for larger bar diameters. As a result of precise
thermo-mechanical processing, no duplex grain sizes, randomly or topologically
distributed as de ﬁned by ASTM E1181, are present. The microstructure is free of
Laves, acicular delta phases or continuous grain boundary precipitates as shown in
Figs. 3 and 4.
Precipitates consisting of M
23C6 and M 6C carbides are present at grain
boundaries with titanium nitrides and niobium carbides scattered in the matrix.
Further investigation was performed by Transmission Electron Microscopy
(TEM). In 120 ksi MYS (Gr. 3), the strengthening precipitates consist of ﬁne,
disc-shaped γ″ phase with 2:1 aspect ratio, about 15 nm mean long axis and about
7 nm short axis. In 140 ksi MYS (Gr. 3HS), the strengthening precipitates consist
of ﬁne, disc-shaped γ″ phase of the same sizes as in Gr. 3 with the addition of ﬁne,
spherical γ′ phase of about 14 nm mean diameter. Figure 5 shows TEM micro-
graphs of Gr. 3 and Gr. 3HS.

To further assess the stress corrosion resistance, both Gr. 3 and 3HS were tested
in a more severe condition than NACE Level VII by increasing the temperature
(260 vs. 205 °C of NACE Level VII) and adding 1 g/L of free elemental sulfur.
These environmental conditions were selected to compare with alloy 716 which is
immune to this environment and also to simulate conditions which could be
encountered in future exploration. Both 120 ksi MYS and 140 ksi MYS grades
passed the test [ 11] with no failure after one month of exposure (Fig. 8). No cracks
or other relevant defects were subsequently observed on the cleaned surface of the
tested specimens.
Microscopy of the area subjected to the maximum deformation also showed no
cracks or other relevant defects up to 200X magni ﬁcation (Fig. 9).
Other precipitation hardened Ni-alloys like 718 and 935 showed readily
observable SCC and signi ﬁcant weight loss [ 15], while Alloy 716 also passed the
test.
Susceptibility to Hydrogen Embrittlement
Alloy AF955-120 ksi MYS showed 45% elongation to failure ratio (EFR) with
mainly ductile fracture except for a few zones located at the periphery showing
brittle transgranular fracture and facets (Fig. 10). AF955-140 ksi MYS produced
33% EFR with ductile fracture at the center and intergranular brittle fracture at the
fracture perimeter (Fig. 11).

## Page 215

Conclusions
AF955 has been designed and manufactured in two strength levels, 120 ksi MYS
and 140 ksi MYS up to 495.3 mm (19.5 in.) bar diameter. Both grades have a
microstructure meeting the requirements of API 6ACRA speci ﬁcation for precipi-
tation hardened Ni-alloys like 716, 725, 925, and 935, and features toughness
greater all other PH nickel alloys in the respective yield strength class.
Alloy AF955 has excellent corrosion resistance with SCC resistance up to
NACE/ISO Level VII at 260 °C (500 °F) and in the presence of free sulfur. Based
on these results, the alloy AF955 has been accepted for inclusion in NACE
MR0175/ISO 15156-3 for usage in any equipment or component up to NACE
Level VII environment.
AF955 susceptibility to hydrogen embrittlement is much lower than Alloy 716
and similar to that of 718.
The combination of properties makes AF955 alloy a potential solution for
widespread applications ranging from oil and gas drilling and production equipment
to downhole applications, power generation, chemical applications and many
others.

Hydrogen In ﬂuence on Crack
Propagation and Stress-Strain Evolution
of Alloy 718
Sergey Kolesov, Robert Badrak and Aleksey Shakhmatov
Abstract Nickel base alloys such as 718 are used for many applications in the
drilling, completion and production segments in the Oil and Gas Industry. The alloy
selection is based on high strength levels while exhibiting resistance to embrittle-
ment and environmental cracking. Hydrogen embrittlement can be a limiting factor
to applications and this investigation was undertaken to better understand the
mechanisms and characteristics of hydrogen in 718. Saluted hydrogen into metal
could be presented in different conditions: diffuse-active and trapped by different
defects and structure elements. Fatigue was used in current work as a tool for (1) the
generation of structure defects and (2) hydrogen effects on crack growth. The
following items were studied: (1) hydrogen solubility into different versions of 718
alloy; (2) effects of increased surface and volume defects density on hydrogen
solubility; (3) hydrogen effects on stress-strain evolution; and (4) effects of hy-
drogen at different locations within the structure on crack growth rate. The speci ﬁcs
of each type of hydrogen location within the structure on crack propagation
including diffusion-active and trapped by different defects and structure elements
were discovered and presented.

ment and environmental cracking. Hydrogen embrittlement can be a limiting factor
to applications and this investigation was undertaken to better understand the
mechanisms and characteristics of hydrogen in 718 and its effect on properties.
Saluted hydrogen into metal could be presented in different conditions:
diffuse-active and trapped by different defects and structure elements with different
trapping energies. Energy dependence of trapped hydrogen was published by dif-
ferent authors [ 1–4] for steels. Table 1 presents the list of different hydrogen traps
with corresponding activation and binding energy.
It possible to extrapolate that the general dependence is the same for nickel base
alloys with respect to shifting in trapping energy. It is well known that contact with
sour (H
2S containing) environment causes the hydrogen penetration into metal and
the resultant potential for embrittlement. It is also well known that galvanic couples
and cathodic protection also causes hydrogen penetration with the potential for
embrittlement. The subject of this initial study was the better understanding of
hydrogen presence and its distribution in initial/as-received condition and its change
as a result of exposure with sour environments.
Experimental Details and Results
The materials used in this study were production heats of UNS N07718 with
slightly different compositional details and operational history. The materials with
the key variations are summarized in Table 2.
The initial as-received hydrogen amount was measured by vacuum extraction at
800 °C on the three versions of 718 alloy. The dislocation density was determined
via Williamson method [ 6, 7].

Discussion
Initial Amount of Hydrogen
The initial as-received hydrogen amount was practically the same for all tested
versions of 718 alloy as shown in Table 3. The results agreed with dislocation
density determined via Williamson method. All materials for this study had vari-
ations in operation history that made it dif ﬁcult to afﬁrm that manufacturing process
was the sole root of the measured difference. The differences were most likely a
combination of operation and manufacturing speci ﬁcs.
As presented in Fig. 1 the hydrogen amount is practically the same for two
temperature intervals including 200 –300 and 600 –800 °C for all tested versions of
718 alloy. The visible difference could be seen for temperature interval 400 –
500 °C. Based on dislocation density calculations this temperature interval could be
associated to the hydrogen trapped by dislocations and dislocation structures. The
lower S and P contents in Modi ﬁed 1 material that results in a corresponding lower
amount of nonmetallic inclusions did not dramatically have an effect on the hy-
drogen amount. This can be observed by examining the small differences at 800 °C
temperature. The hydrogen trapped at 800 °C represents that hydrogen trapped with
the highest energy.
Hydrogen Cathodic Charging
As presented on Figs. 2, 3 and 4 the low energy trapped hydrogen (extracted at
200–300 °C) could be due mainly to the hydrogen added to metal during cathodic
charging. There was no signi ﬁcant cathodic charging effect on hydrogen distribu-
tion at higher energy.
Stress-strain change was measured by X-ray technique and the results presented
in Tables 4 and 5. The measured effects on micro and sub-micro levels caused by
low energy hydrogen were due to adding mainly this type of hydrogen resulting
from cathodic charging (see Figs. 2, 3 and 4). Therewith the stress-strain condition
changes were found to be signi ﬁcantly bigger on grain/micro level in comparison
with atomic (sub-micro) level. The general tendency of stress-strain sate change for
different versions of 718 alloy was in the line with the trend for calculated

## Page 224

dislocation density and difference in hydrogen extracted at 400 –500 °C (see
Table 2 and Fig. 1). There are two possible explanations of bigger effects on grain
scale level: (1) electrochemically added hydrogen localizes in grain boundaries
only. In this case it is understandable that there is a large increase in micro-strain
and small changes of stress-strain state on sub-micro level. This trend corresponds
to the literature data presented in Table 1 with lowest hydrogen activation energy
for grain boundaries. (2) The hydrogen could be concentrated into the same
structure elements (like dislocations or dislocation structures, matrix etc.) but with
different trapping energy due to hydrogen presence in different states like ion, atom
or molecule. It could be assumed due to visible change on micro-strains in results of
cathodic charging (Tables 4 and 5) but lack of effects on hydrogen distribution for
high energy extraction (400 °C and above region on Figs. 2, 3 and 4). The changes
in the value of micro-strains measured at depth 5 and 30 microns allow making an
assumption that main amount of charged hydrogen accumulated at a depth no more
than 5 microns from the surface.
Hydrogen presence into metal would be expected to signi ﬁcantly reduce the
fatigue by, perhaps, 30% and this is represented by comparing the measured
micro-strain values as resulting from hydrogen charging (Tables 4 and 5) with
micro-strain changes under fatigue (Fig. 6).
However the expected decrease in fatigue life as a result of hydrogen cathodic
charging was not detected. The results of comparison fatigue tests of charged and
uncharged 718 alloys at the same testing conditions (Table 6) were within exper-
imental error the same. This could be explained in two ways: (1) cathodically
charged hydrogen presence was in the condition where large diffusion activities and

In another words, the hydrogen was no longer present in suf ﬁcient quantities during
the fatigue tests. The applied energy of fatigue hastened the diffusion of hydrogen
under these conditions; (2) hydrogen saturated overlay is too small (4 –5 microns)
for getting signi ﬁcant effects on general fatigue life. Fatigue crack could be initiated

The fatigue tests at hydrogen charging during fatigue testing and testing of

2S saturated environment during
3 months are in the progress and will be presented on conference.
Conclusions
Hydrogen total amount in as received conditions is practically the same for all
tested versions of 718 alloy.
Low energy hydrogen only could be added as a result of cathodic charging.
Added hydrogen by cathodic charging could cause the stress-strain state change
and potentially reduce the fatigue life of materials. However it was not detected due
to very small hydrogen saturated overlay or due to very big diffusion activities of
added hydrogen.
There may be additional conclusions that will be presented at the conference
after completion of planned tests in autoclave and with constant charging during
tests.

## Page 227

Isothermal Oxidation Behavior
of EBM-Additive Manufactured
Alloy 718
Esmaeil Sadeghimeresht, Paria Karimi, Pimin Zhang, Ru Peng,
Joel Andersson, Lars Pejryd and Shrikant Joshi
Abstract Oxidation of Alloy 718 manufactured by electron beam melting
(EBM) process has been undertaken in ambient air at 650, 700, and 800 °C for up to
168 h. At 800 °C, a continuous external chromia oxide enriched in (Cr, Ti, Mn, Ni)
and an internal oxide that was branched structure of alumina formed, whereas at
650 and 700 °C, a continuous, thin and protective chromia layer was detected. The
oxidation kinetics of the exposed EBM Alloy 718 followed the parabolic rate law
with an effective activation energy of ∼248 ± 22 kJ/mol in good agreement with
values in the literature for conventionally processed chromia-forming Ni-based
superalloys. The oxide scale formed on the surface perpendicular to the build
direction was slightly thicker, and more adherent compared to the scale formed on
the surface along the build direction, attributed to the varied grain texture in the two
directions of the EBM-manufactured specimens. The increased oxygen diffusion
and high Cr depletion found on the surface along the build direction were attributed
to the ﬁne grains and formation of vacancies/voids along this grain orientation.

Introduction
Additive manufacturing (AM), also known as 3D printing or rapid prototyping, has
shown an enormous potential to substantially shift manufacturing concept, espe-
cially for high performance components with geometrically complex designs such

## Page 228

as superalloy turbine parts [ 1]. The technology has recently raised an upsurge of
research interest on Alloy 718 as a frequently used material in aero- and land-based
gas turbine engines [ 2, 3].
The electron beam melting (EBM) process is an AM technique that employs an
intense high-energy electron beam to melt metal powders layer by layer to produce
dense parts [ 4]. The working principle in the EBM process differs from the other
commonly used powder-bed fusion AM techniques like selective laser melting
(SLM). First, whereas a focused electron beam is used in EBM, a laser beam is used
in SLM as the source of energy to melt the powder. Second, an electron beam of
great quality requires a relatively high vacuum (around 10
−3 Pa), while the laser is
much less affected by the atmosphere and works with an inert gas (Ar or N 2). Third,
the high scanning rate of the electron beam is able to preheat and sinter the powder,
however there is no need for such preheating in SLM. The rapid melting (up to
∼105 K/s) and high solidi ﬁcation rate (up to ∼107 K/s) in EBM may lead to
formation of metastable phases, e.g., γ״in Alloy 718 [ 5]. The stability of such
phases is essential in Alloy 718, where high temperature strength and oxidation
performance need to be simultaneously addressed [ 6].
Alloy 718 used for turbine discs typically experiences operating temperatures of
maximum ∼650–700 °C, in which a continuous and dense layer of chromia pro-
tects the alloy against further oxidation [ 7]. However, the level of protection may be
affected by many factors, including the alloy ’s Cr content and inhibition of Cr
diffusion towards the formed oxide scale due to the alloy ’s grain size or crystal-
lographic orientation [ 8–10]. The preferential oxidation of the scale-forming ele-
ments may facilitate formation of a protective oxide layer in the favored grain
orientations [ 11]. Thus, control of size and growth of the grains could help to
improve the oxidation performance of the materials. The EBM process due to
epitaxy is able to develop columnar structures along the build direction that facil-
itates elemental diffusion, in particular Cr, and accordingly alter the oxidation
resistance in the preferred grain orientations [ 4, 12].
Previous research on Alloy 718 fabricated by EBM (referred to as EBM 718
hereafter) has mainly focused on investigations of microstructures and mechanical
properties [ 13, 14]. The oxidation behavior of the EBM 718 was scarcely studied
[15], however it is still unclear whether the chromia layer thickens commensurate
with directional growth or whether the complex microstructure produces a notable
difference in morphology and/or the growth rate of the chromia layer in the EBM
718. The aim of the present work was to assess these differences through a detailed
metallography of oxidized specimens of EBM 718 and compare to wrought Alloy
718 (referred to as wrought 718 hereafter). The isothermal oxidation tests were
performed in ambient air at 650, 700, and 800 °C up to 168 h. The weight change
was precisely measured to study the oxidation kinetics. Phase constitution within
the oxide scales was determined by an X-ray energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS).
Surface morphologies of the scales were characterized using a scanning electron
microscope (SEM) and the effect of grain orientation on the oxidation behavior was
studied using an electron backscatter diffractometer (EBSD).

Materials and Experimental Procedures
As-Received Materials (Powder and Wrought 718)
Plasma-atomized Alloy 718 powder supplied by Arcam (Mölndal, Sweden) was
used with spherical morphology as shown in Fig. 1. The powder was mixed with
recycled (up to 10 times) powders in order to reduce the cost of the AM parts [ 16].
The new powder (Fig. 1b) showed a uniform microstructure with similar chemical
composition to that of wrought 718, whereas the presence of a Ni-poor secondary
phase could be seen in the recycled powder particle (Fig. 1c). As the recycled
powder was exposed in high temperature ( ∼850–900 °C) into the build chamber for
several times, emergence of the δ phase which forms in a temperature range of
∼870–1010 °C was expected [ 17]. The sieve analysis in Fig. 1d showed that 99 wt
% of the powder had a particle size range of 45 –126 µm with the remainder
<28 µm.
Rectangular coupons (2 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm) were cut from the
as-received sheet of wrought 718. The nominal composition of the powder and
as-received wrought 718 are shown in Table 1.

Electron Beam Melting (EBM) Process
An Arcam A2X EBM machine (Arcam, Mölndal, Sweden) with an acceleration
voltage of 60 kV was used to produce rectangular specimens ( ∼20 mm × 50
mm × 3 mm thick), see Fig. 2. Process parameters proposed by Arcam for Alloy
718 was used together with an operating temperature of ∼1023 °C and a layer
thickness of 75 μm. A vacuum of 0.2 Pa was used during operation together with a
small amount of He in the build chamber. The EBM process parameters used are
given in Table 2. The specimens were cut to size ( ∼10 mm × 10 mm × 3 mm)
and all the surfaces were wet ground using SiC paper up to 2500 grit and polished
with a 0.02 µm silica suspension to produce a smooth surface ( R
a < 0.1 µm). All
edges and corners were chamfered to reduce stress concentrators and polished to
similar surface ﬁnish as the bulk sample. The ﬁnal dimensions of coupons after this
preparation were measured using a micrometer. Following this, the specimens were
cleaned in ethanol and dried.
Oxidation Tests
The isothermal oxidation exposures of EBM and wrought 718 were conducted in a
box furnace. The specimens were placed in separate alumina crucibles and inserted
into the furnace at respective soak temperature. The tests were performed in
ambient air at different temperatures of 650, 700, and 800 °C with time intervals of
24, 96 and 168 h. Empty alumina crucibles were prepared at the scheduled test

Characterization of Pre- and Post-exposure Samples
The surface morphology and the cross-section of the scale formed on the surface
were examined using a FEI QUANTA-200 FEG (FEI, Oregon, USA) scanning
electron microscope (SEM) equipped with SDD (silicon drift detector)-based X-ray
energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS).
Grain orientation of the specimen surface was measured using a Hitachi SEM
(SU70, Tokyo, Japan) equipped with electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) sys-
tem at a voltage of 20 kV. The EBSD maps have been recorded with a step size of
2 μm. After the oxidation test, crystallographic texture of the oxidized sample was
characterized by EBSD to identify the relationship between the grain orientation
and oxide growth. To compare the results of orientation measurements before and

after oxidation, all parameters used for the EBSD measurements were kept the
same. HKL Channel 5 software (Oxford instrument, Abingdon, the UK) was used
to visualize the EBSD maps.
The phases present on the surface of the exposed samples were identi ﬁed with a
Siemens grazing incidence X-ray diffractometer (D5000, Bruker-AXS, Karlsruhe,
Germany). The instrument was set using Cu K
α (1.1542 °A) in the theta range of
25° ≤ 2θ ≤ 80° with an incident angle of 1°, the step size of 0.04 and dwell time of 5
s. The phase identi ﬁcation program Diffrac plus Evaluation (EVA) with reference
pattern data sheets from the International Centre for Diffraction Data (ICDD) Powder
Diffraction File (PDF-2) database was used for data analysis and interpretation.
A schematic of the as-built sample and the areas of interest for oxidation study
are shown in Fig. 3. Particular attention was paid to the oxides formed on the
surface perpendicular to the build direction (Zone A) and surface along the build
direction (Zone B) in order to evaluate the effect of the grain texture on the oxi-
dation performance of the EBM 718 specimens.

## Page 234

While the microstructure of wrought 718 was free of δ and Laves phase when
examined by SEM, grain boundaries were mostly decorated by MC-type carbides.
The microstructure of the EBM 718 sample consisted of columnar grains perpen-
dicular to the solidi ﬁed layers, see the optical microscopy image in Fig. 4b. In this
sample, the average length and width of the grains were measured and found to be
∼1–3 mm and ∼50–100 µm, respectively. Similar to ﬁndings by other researchers
[19], strings of precipitates (mostly attributed to carbides) parallel to the elongated
grains were uniformly distributed in interdendritic regions within the grains
(Fig. 4b). The precipitates were smaller than 1 µm in size, therefore too small to be
quantitatively characterized by EDS. Hence, this analysis presumably include
background signals from the matrix and neighboring particles. These precipitates
were rich in Nb (based on the EDS analysis, not reported here), attributed to the
presence of the carbides, based on the morphology of the particles which were
cubic/spherical shape as reported in the literature [ 20]. The other common Nb-rich
phase in form of plate-shape precipitates (corresponding to δ-phase rich in Nb) was
also observed in both intergranular and intragranular areas (Fig. 4b).
The pores found in the EBM 718 sample were arranged in strings parallel to the
build direction (Fig. 4b). The chain of round shape pores at region perpendicular to
the layers was appeared to form in interdendritic areas. The dominant mechanism
that induces such shrinkage pores is the residual stresses caused during the rapid
solidiﬁcation. The shrinkage pores form during cool-down phase of the molten top
layers which is hindered by the underlying previously processed layers [ 20, 21]. The
precipitates formed in rows were also in line with the pores, and perpendicular to the
layers (Fig. 4). Carbides in Alloy 718 prefer to precipitate in the interdendritic
regions which are rich in Nb and correspond to the last stage of solidi ﬁcation [22].

Weight Change of the Exposed Samples
A comparison of the progressive weight change of wrought and EBM 718 at
temperatures ranging from 650 to 800 °C are shown in Fig. 5a. This ﬁgure shows
the data of weight gain per unit area ( Δw in mg/cm 2) as function of time (hour).
This ﬁgure con ﬁrmed no spallation or evaporation occurred during the course of
exposure for any of the specimens tested, as no sudden drop was observed in the
weight change graph. In all the exposure temperatures and time intervals, the
wrought specimens performed slightly better than the EBM 718 specimens.
The mass gain of all oxidized specimens generally followed an identical trend,
i.e., increased rapidly in the ﬁrst stage and then continuously decreased in its rate as
the exposure time increased. This results from the rapid formation and growth of a

as a function of (t in second) according to Eq. ( 1) to obtain the values of kp, which
are given in Table 3. The kp values increased about three times by increasing the

specimens (∼800 times). The kp values increased about 1300 times for the exposed
wrought 718 at 800 °C compared to 650 °C.
The calculated parabolic rate constants of the EBM 718 samples fall within the
range of 3.3 × 10 −9 to 2.8 × 10 −7 mg2/cm4s, typically reported for Cr 2O3 formers
[24]. It should be also noted that the parabolic rate for Cr 2O3 scale growth may vary
depending on temperature and alloy composition.
The kp values are shown as a function of the inverse of the temperature (1/T) in
the Arrhenius plot of Fig. 5c to measure the activation energy of the oxidation
reaction. The experimental activation energy values for the oxidation of Alloy 718
in air at the temperatures ranging from 650 to 800 °C are shown in Table 4.I t
should be noted that although the term “activation energy ” was used here, this was
not meticulously correct since more than one alloying element was being oxidized
and a single activated event was not being investigated. However, it was a practical
approach of describing the temperature dependence of the reaction kinetics.
The value for the activation energy found in this study (Q ≈ 248 kJ/mol in a
temperature range of 650 –800 °C) was comparable statistically to values obtained
for chromia-forming Ni-based superalloys from the earlier studies: Q ≈ 286 kJ/mol
for RR1000 [ 24], Q ≈ 250 kJ/mol for Udimet 720 [ 25], Q ≈ 270 kJ/mol for

different temperatures. The phases formed on both samples in each temperature

were almost similar and showed several diffraction peaks corresponding to several
elements constituting the Alloy 718, which were more or less oxidized, especially
Cr, Ti, Al, Ni and Mn.
The X-ray detected strong diffraction peaks corresponding to the γ matrix phase
at the temperatures of 650 and 700 °C where the oxide scale might be thinner, so
the signals from the background could be anticipated.
At 800 °C, the peaks of Cr
2O3 developed, and the γ matrix peaks disappeared.
Due to complex chemical compositions of Alloy 718 and diffusivity of chromia, a
small amount of other alloying elements like Ti, Mn, Al, Nb, and Ni enriched the
Cr
2O3 scale. TiO 2 was not identi ﬁed on the surface of the exposed samples in this
study, however in some other studies, high content of Ti in the alloy composition
(Such as in ME3 [ 26]) led to formation of TiO
2 grains within the chromia scale.
The XRD results showed that while the outward diffusion of alloying elements,
e.g., Cr, Ti, Al, and Mn appeared to be suf ﬁciently high, the rate determining step
was related to the diffusion of Cr through Cr 2O3 layer which clearly seen to be
affected by of the alloying elements like Ti [ 24].
The ability of chromia to dissolve the alloying elements like Ti in the oxidized
state has been already shown [ 28]. It was reported that Ti incorporates as Ti 4+,a s
this has minimal effect on the chromia lattice spacing, even at high solute levels
[28], in consistent with the XRD results in the present study.
Cross Sections of the Exposed Samples
Figures 7, 8, and 9 show the back-scattered cross-sectional images of the EBM 718
specimens after 168 h of air oxidation at 650, 700, and 800 °C. It can be seen that
as the temperature increased, the thickness of the formed oxide increased. At 650
and 700 °C, a continuous and very thin oxide scale formed on the surface (Figs. 7
and 8). Figure 10 shows that although the oxide formed on EBM 718 at 800 °C was
thick ( ∼2 µm), it was still uniform and continuous. More information on the
structure of the formed oxide scale may be drawn from the EDS elemental map-
pings of the cross-sections (Figs. 7, 8 and 9).
In Fig. 9, formation of δ-phase (Ni
3Nb), with a length of ∼5 µm and a thickness
of ∼100 nm, was con ﬁrmed with SEM and EDS analysis, present in the alloy near
the specimen surface after oxidation at 800 °C. However, in the wrought alloy
(Fig. 10), the δ-phase formed more extensively throughout the alloy on both grain
boundaries and grain interiors. Both wrought and EBM 718 specimens exposed at
800 °C showed the presence of Laves (rich in Mo and Nb) phase. To emphasize
these differences, Fig. 11 shows etched images (using 10 wt% oxalic acid) of
wrought and EBM 718 after 168 h at 800 °C. At this high temperature, the δ-phase
precipitation in the wrought alloy was similar to the distribution in the EBM 718.
While it was bene ﬁcial to accelerate oxidation testing by increasing the test tem-
perature, it showed a strong negative effect on the microstructure of Alloy 718.
Therefore, higher working temperature than 700 °C was recommended to be
230 E. Sadeghimeresht et al.

## Page 239

avoided in practice. No sign of the Laves or δ phase was observed at 650 and
700 °C.
The oxide scales that formed on the EBM 718 at 800 °C consisted of a con-
tinuous external chromia scale- enriched in Ti, Ni and Mn and an internal oxide that
was branched structure of alumina. The small level of Al in the chemical compo-
sition of the as-built Alloy 718 was not suf ﬁcient for outward diffusion and par-
ticipation in the external oxide [ 29]. The high contribution of alloying elements in
the outer oxide scale like Ti might be due to their content as well as high diffusion
coefﬁcients rather than other elements like Al and Nb [ 8]. The element with the
largest in ﬂuence on the oxidation rate is Ti by a factor of ∼4 because of the
Wagner–Hauffe impurity effect [ 30]. Based on the theory, the addition of higher
valent cations (Ti) to an n-type oxide (Cr
2O3) leads to a decrease in the ionic defect
concentration whereas, the electron concentration is increased. This results in

be more rather than the oxide formed on Zone A containing the coarser grains, as
seen in Fig. 13. The limited number of the diffusion paths (only columnar grains)
perpendicular to the build direction slowed down the oxygen diffusion. Although
the oxide scale formed on Zone B was slightly thinner, the high Cr depletion might
endanger the specimen from this direction after a longer exposure.
Figure 14 shows that the exposure at 800 °C did not signi ﬁcantly affect the
specimen’s grain orientation. The grains were coarse and columnar in the build
direction (001), but ﬁne near the side edge (Zone B), as expected and also reported
before in the literature [ 34].

The effect of grain orientation on the oxidation performance was already
investigated in many materials [ 19, 35–37]. It was already showed that (001) faces
oxidize faster than other faces such as (111) in oxidation of Ni [ 38]. It was sug-
gested that oxides on the (001) face produce higher concentration of high-angle
grain boundaries, which were considered as short-circuit diffusion paths for metal
ions, thus accelerated oxidation process. It was also illustrated that oxide islands
were favorably formed on (001) faces, while islands formed on the other planes,
e.g., (111) were barely observed [ 39]. Furthermore, the size and area of oxide
islands that cover (001) planes were larger than on other planes. These were
reported to be associated with different atomic densities with different binding
energies of individual crystal faces [ 19]. The oxidation rates of grains with different
orientations were also related to the atomic densities of planes. Therefore, for face
centered cubic (fcc) materials, the oxidation resistance should be reasonably in the
order as (111) > (110) > (001). Surface free energy of planes also tends to
decrease for higher atomic density, which may result in better resistance properties
in severe service environment. However, in this study, while the oxide was thinner
on the side edge (Zone B), the oxide scale formed on the surface perpendicular to

the build direction (Zone A) was denser and more protective, see Fig. 12. Here,

The weight change measurement study in Fig. 5 showed that as the oxidation
process prolonged to the stage that the sample surface was covered by a continuous
oxide scale, the growth of oxidation scale was ruled by the diffusion-controlled
oxidation behavior (according to the parabolic growth behavior). The diffusion
process was normally proceeded by means of the outward diffusion of metal ele-
ments like Ti and Mn and inward penetration of oxygen along the grain boundaries
owing to short-circuit diffusion that accelerated the diffusion process compared with
diffusion within crystal lattice [ 40]. It seemed that the diffusion of alloying elements
especially Cr was faster in Zone B with the ﬁner grains rather than Zone A with the
oriented grains. The slow diffusion of the alloying elements along the build
direction favored formation of dense and protective chromia scale on the surface.
The oxide morphology seems to be also orientation dependent. A rather dense,
compact, adherent, and uniform oxide was formed on the surface perpendicular to
the build direction (001); loose and non-compact oxide was formed on the side
edge, as could be seen in Figs. 12, and 13. It might be also attributed to the high
coherency of the formed oxide grains to the columnar grains in the build direction.
As a result, some gaps or voids might form between the oxide formed on the side
edges and the bulk, due to the less coherency of the oxide with the ﬁne grains.
These gaps or voids, therefore, directly introduced the oxidation environment to
contact with the substrate grains, which accelerated their oxidation rate.

Conclusions
An air oxidation study has been conducted on the EBM 718 over the temperature
range of 650 –800 °C for times up to 168 h. The oxidation behavior of the alloy
was compared to a wrought 718. The main ﬁndings of the work are itemized as

## Page 246

(1) The EBM processing had little effect on the oxidation behavior at 650 and
700 °C compared to wrought 718. However, at 800 °C, the specimen mass gain
was higher on the EBM 718 specimen and this difference was attributed to
crystallographic grain orientation and grain boundaries.
(2) The weight gain kinetics were essentially parabolic with an effective activation
energy of ∼248 kJ/mole, similar to the values found for other chromia-forming
superalloys in the literature. The slight increase of oxidation rate in the EBM
718 in the present study was attributed to increased ionic transport caused by
doping of the chromia layer by other alloying elements such as Ti and the
consequent creation of vacancies beneath the outer layer.
(3) A continuous external chromia oxide enriched in Cr, Ti, Mn, and Ni and an
internal oxide that was branched structure of alumina formed at 800 °C,
whereas at lower temperature of 650 and 700 °C, a continuous and very thin
chromia scale was only detected. The oxidation process was con ﬁrmed to be
controlled by the outward diffusion of oxide forming elements and inward
penetration of oxygen along the grain boundaries.
(4) The increased oxygen diffusion and high Cr depletion/consumption on the side
edge were attributed to the ﬁne grains and formation of vacancies/voids along
this grain orientation.
(5) In the light of the present study, the corrosion resistance showed high grain
orientation dependency in the as-built parts. It means that during manufactur-
ing, the corrosion behavior of the aimed surface must be considered during
design of the part and support structures.

## Page 250

A Computational Model
of the Electroslag Remelting
(ESR) Process and Its Application
to an Industrial Process for a Large
Diameter Superalloy Ingot
Kanchan M. Kelkar and Corey J. O ’Connell
Abstract This paper presents a comprehensive computational model for the
prediction of the transient Electroslag Remelting (ESR) process for cylindrical
ingots based on a two-dimensional axisymmetric analysis. The model analyzes the
behavior of the slag and growing ingot during the entire ESR process involving a
hot-slag start with an initial transient, near-steady melting, hot-topping and sub-
sequent solidiﬁcation of the slag and ingot after melting ends. The results of model
application to an industrial ESR process for a 1.12 m diameter nickel-iron-
chromium superalloy and its validation are presented. They demonstrate the com-
prehensive capabilities of the model in predicting the behavior of the ingot and slag
during the entire process and properties of the ﬁnal ingot produced. Such analysis
provides signi ﬁcant bene ﬁts for the optimization of existing process schedules and
design of new processes for different alloys and ingot sizes.
Keywords Electroslag remelting
⋅ Computational analysis ⋅ Experimental
validation
Introduction
The Electroslag Remelting process (ESR) is used for the production of many
high-performance nickel-base alloys, cobalt-base alloys, and specialty steels.
Figure 1 shows a schematic diagram of the ESR process that uses a stationary
crucible containing the slag and ingot. The process typically involves the passing of
an Alternating Current (AC) from a consumable electrode to a water-cooled copper

## Page 251

crucible to create resistive heating in the slag that melts the electrode. The resulting
molten droplets formed at the electrode surface pass through the molten slag and
build up in the crucible to form the ingot. Thus, the ESR process involves complex
interactions among the electromagnetic, ﬂow, and thermal processes. These phe-
nomena control the transfer of heat to the crucible and, in turn, the ingot solidi ﬁ-
cation process which has a direct impact on ingot quality. Therefore, the
solidiﬁcation behavior of an ESR ingot is dependent upon many factors such as slag
composition, amount of slag, electrode-ingot area ratio, applied current and voltage,
and the resulting melting rate of the electrode.
Electroslag remelting is used in the manufacture of critical components used in
aerospace, marine, and nuclear applications which require ingots of high quality.
The ESR process behavior governs the structure and chemical homogeneity of the
ingot and is therefore of great importance to both the ingot producers and end-users
of the ﬁnal product. The conventional approach to developing relationships
Fig. 1 Schematic diagram of the electroslag remelting (ESR) process (Courtesy of ATI Specialty
Materials)
244 K. M. Kelkar and C. J. O ’Connell

## Page 252

between the ESR process parameters and ingot solidi ﬁcation structure is through
mechanical sectioning and characterization of the ingot. This is an inef ﬁcient and
also costly method to the ESR ingot producer since the ingot product is sacri ﬁced.
The trial-and-error approach is also inadequate for capturing the effects of various
process variations on process performance. Mathematical modeling offers a
physics-based and cost-effective approach for developing a fundamental under-
standing of the underlying phenomena that govern the process performance which
can then be used to predict the effect of various process variables on the quality of
the ingot.
Computational analysis of ESR processes has been an area of active research and
there have been several signi ﬁcant advancements in recent years. These studies
involve computational analysis at various levels such as analysis of only the
electromagnetic phenomena or a coupled analysis of all phenomena, analysis of a
single region (slag or ingot) or both regions (slag and ingot together), steady-state or
transient behavior, and 2-D or 3-D analysis. Only brief highlights of some of the
relevant studies are discussed here. Analytical models for the prediction of elec-
tromagnetic phenomena in cylindrical ingots for ESR and Vacuum Arc Remelting
(VAR) processes, and for rectangular slabs are presented by Patel [ 1] and Patel and
O’Connell [ 2], respectively. Analysis of ﬂow and heat transfer in the slag region is
presented by Dilawari and Szekely [ 3] and Jardy et al. [ 4]. A coupled analysis of the
slag and ingot regions for steady conditions has been presented by Choudhury and
Szekely [ 5], and more recently by Kelkar et al. [ 6]. Kharicha et al. [ 7] have pre-
sented studies involving axisymmetric 2-D analysis that are focused on various
aspects of the ESR process such as the in ﬂuence of the slag-pool interface on ingot
solidiﬁcation, conduction of current through the slag skin into the crucible [ 8] and
its effect of the quality of the ingot surface [ 9], and melting of the electrode [ 10].
Models for transient analysis of the ESR process that address ingot growth are
presented along with capabilities for the prediction of the slag skin thickness,
electrode melt rate, and chemical segregation by Weber et al. [ 11], Yanke et al.
[12], and Fezi et al. [ 13], and Kelkar et al. [ 14]. Very recently, several studies have
also been presented for a 3-D analysis of the ESR process. Examples of these
include a 3-D analysis of the slag region for predicting the formation of droplets at
the electrode surface and their motion through the slag by Kharicha et al. [ 15]. This
study also reports occurrence of strong three-dimensional ﬂow within the slag.
A 3-D model for the ESR process that considers both the slag and ingot regions
have been presented by Karimi-Sibaki et al. [ 16] and Wang and Li [ 17]. It is
important to note that while 3-D analysis can provide details about ﬂow behavior
that cannot be analyzed through axisymmetric models, the corresponding compu-
tational times are very high (of the order of few weeks) making such analysis
impractical for routine use in process design. More importantly, the study by
Karimi-Sibaki et al. [ 16] found that that the difference in the predicted pool pro ﬁle
between the 3-D and 2-D axisymmetric approaches was negligible so that 2-D
axisymmetric calculation was suf ﬁcient for capturing the melt pool pro ﬁle. This
observation is con ﬁrmed in the study by O ’Connell et al. [ 18] which demonstrates
that the pool shapes predicted using the 2-D axisymmetric model of Kelkar [ 14] and
A Computational Model of the Electroslag Remelting (ESR) … 245

## Page 253

its extension to 2-D Cartesian analysis for slabs agree well with the measured pool
shapes in industrial-scale ESR processes.
The objective of this study is to present an ef ﬁcient and comprehensive com-
putational model for the analysis of transient ESR processes that can be used
routinely by process engineers. The sections below describe the mathematical
formulations of the physical phenomena underlying the ESR process and their
computational solution. Following this, the details of the application of this model,
as incorporated in the software program MeltFlow-ESR
TM [19], to the production
of a 1.12 m diameter ingot of a nickel-iron-chromium superalloy are discussed.
Finally, a comparison of the predicted and observed ingot pool pro ﬁles is presented.
Mathematical Formulation
Assumptions
The computational model is developed using an axisymmetric domain as shown in
Fig. 2. It includes the slag and ingot regions in a uni ﬁed manner. A frame of
reference attached to the electrode-slag interface is utilized so as to enable accurate
treatment of the electromagnetic, thermal, and ﬂuid dynamic interactions between
the slag and metal regions. The computational domain expands downward at the
instantaneous casting velocity of the ingot to accommodate ingot growth. Analysis
is performed for a prescribed melt schedule involving transient variations of the
total Root Mean Square (RMS) current and its frequency, power or slag resistivity,
and melt rate. A hot-slag start is assumed with the volume of the molten slag
remaining constant during the melting process. Calculations are continued for a
sufﬁcient time after the end of melting so as to determine solidi ﬁcation of the
molten slag and metal pool. This allows for the determination of the thermal history
of the ﬁnal ingot during the entire solidi ﬁcation process. The model assumes that
the nominal densities of the molten and solidi ﬁed states of the metal and slag are
identical and does not consider solidi ﬁcation shrinkage in the bulk of the slag and
ingot. Note, however, that the effect of ingot shrinkage on heat transfer due to loss
of contact with the crucible is accurately analyzed. The temperature-dependence of
all other properties of the metal and slag is rigorously addressed.
Electromagnetics
Since practical ESR systems use Alternating Current in electrically conducting
media, magnetic ﬁeld diffusion is the primary electromagnetic phenomenon. Also,
the time scale for electromagnetic phenomena is orders of magnitude smaller than
those for the ﬂow and thermal phenomena. Therefore, electromagnetic ﬁelds in the
246 K. M. Kelkar and C. J. O ’Connell

## Page 254

transient ESR process are determined by solving the magnetoquasistatic form of
Maxwell’s equations for the periodic steady-state at the instantaneous RMS current,
frequency, and ingot length to predict the distribution of the magnetic ﬁeld in the
slag and growing ingot. The exposed portion of the top surface of the slag and also
the circumferential surface of the ingot are electrically insulated. Since the electrical
conductivity of the electrode is large relative to the slag, current enters into the slag
from the electrode in the direction normal to the slag-electrode interface. Its radial
variation at this interface is determined by the model for the prescribed total
instantaneous current. Finally, the current density and the resulting Lorentz force
and Joule heating distributions needed in the analysis of the ﬂow and temperature
ﬁelds in the slag and ingot are determined from the calculated distribution of the
induced magnetic ﬁeld.

A Computational Model of the Electroslag Remelting (ESR) … 247

## Page 255

Fluid Motion
The unsteady macro-level ﬂow in the molten slag and metal pools is driven by the
buoyancy and Lorentz forces and is governed by the unsteady Navier-Stokes
equations. Use of the two-equation k- ε turbulence model allows for determination
of the spatially non-uniform mixing in the molten pools so that the pool behavior
can be analyzed for a wide range of ingot sizes and processing conditions. The
molten metal pool evolves continuously during the melting process due to the
time-varying melt schedule and changing ingot length. Also, the molten metal and
slag pools solidify after the end of melting. As a result, the ﬂow and temperature
ﬁelds are coupled not only through the buoyancy force but also through phase
change in the ingot and slag during and after melting.
The interaction of the ﬂow ﬁelds across the slag-metal interface is automatically
addressed through the use of the uni ﬁed computational domain. The velocity in the
mushy regions of the ingot and slag (after melting) below an assumed immobi-
lization liquid fraction is set to the instantaneous velocity of the corresponding solid
region (Bertram et al. [ 20]). Thus, the solidi ﬁed portion of the ingot moves at the
instantaneous casting velocity while melting is ongoing and it is stationary after the
end of melting. The ﬂow in the molten pools is subject to no-slip boundary con-
ditions on all other solid boundaries.
Heat Transfer and Phase Change
The temperature ﬁeld within the slag and metal pools is determined by ﬂuid motion
and turbulent diffusion. Furthermore, heat transfer in the slag occurs also by radi-
ation since the molten slag is semi-transparent. In the present study, this radiative
heat transfer is analyzed using the Rosseland approximation (Siegel and Howell
[21]) which involves a diffusion treatment of radiation using a temperature-
dependent radiative conductivity. In the solid ingot region, the temperature ﬁeld is
determined by the local solid velocity and conduction. Solidi ﬁcation behavior of the
slag during and after melting is analyzed in the following manner so as obtain
computational efﬁciency in the transient analysis:
 During melting, the molten slag bulk is enclosed in a layer of slag skin formed
on the crucible surface. Since the slag skin is thin, it is assumed to have a
negligible volume so that it lies at the radial boundary of the computational
domain.
 After melting ends, the bulk slag solidi ﬁes. The computational technique tran-
sitions smoothly from “thin slag-skin ” to the “bulk-slag solidi ﬁcation”.
Solidiﬁcation of the metal (during and after melting) and the slag (after melting)
is analyzed using the enthalpy-porosity technique (Brent et al. [ 22]) with a speci ﬁed
248 K. M. Kelkar and C. J. O ’Connell

## Page 256

variation of the solid fraction with temperature for the slag and alloy. The following
heat loss conditions are used at various boundaries of the computational domain.
 Top Surface of the Slag — Heat loss at the slag-electrode interface is calculated
from a global heat balance on the electrode for the instantaneous melt rate. The
molten metal droplets formed at the slag-electrode interface are assumed to fall
through the slag under thermal equilibrium conditions and appear in the metal
pool below the slag-metal interface. The exposed surface of the slag loses heat
by radiation and convection to the environment.
 Slag-Crucible Interface During Melting — The thickness of the slag skin formed
at the slag-crucible interface varies in the axial direction depending on the local
rate of heat transfer from the bulk slag to the crucible. Due to the uneven outer
surface of the slag skin, heat transfer to the inside surface of crucible occurs by
conduction across the slag skin and radiation from its exposed surface. The
calculation of the overall thermal resistance for transfer of heat from the slag to
cooling water also considers the thermal conduction across the crucible thick-
ness and forced convection heat transfer coef ﬁcient between the crucible outer
surface and cooling water as described by Yu [ 23].
 Ingot-Crucible Interface During Melting — During the melting process, ingot
grows into the slag skin that is formed just above molten metal surface so that
the thickness of the slag skin on the ingot surface also varies in the axial
direction. Presence of the slag skin increases the resistance for heat transfer from
the ingot to the crucible. Additionally, the shrinkage of the ingot away from the
crucible as it solidi ﬁes creates a gradual loss of contact between the outer
surface of the slag skin and the inside surface of the crucible. The effect of ingot
shrinkage on heat transfer between the ingot and crucible is determined using
the method of Bertram et al. [ 20]. Thus, at each axial location of the ingot, the
computational model calculates the rate of heat transfer to the crucible by
conduction through the skin thickness where the ingot has not separated from
the crucible and radiation from surface of the slag skin where ingot has shrunk
away.
 Heat Loss from Bottom Ingot Surface — Heat loss from the bottom surface of the
ingot to the crucible is calculated using an empirically prescribed heat transfer
coefﬁcient that is representative of the metal-to-metal contact created by the
weight of the ingot.
 Heat Loss After End of Melting — Since the bulk slag solidi ﬁes after the end of
melting, it also gradually shrinks away from the crucible. Therefore, heat loss
from the slag and the ingot to the crucible is calculated using the method used
for determining the heat loss from the ingot surface during melting in presence
of shrinkage as described above. In addition, the entire top surface of the slag
now loses heat by radiation to the environment since the electrode is no longer
present.
A Computational Model of the Electroslag Remelting (ESR) … 249

## Page 257

Thermal History and Defect Formation Probability
The structure of the cast ingot is determined by its thermal history during the
solidiﬁcation process. Due to the unsteady behavior of the ESR system during and
after melting, the thermal history at any point in the solidi ﬁed ingot depends on both
its axial and radial locations. The computational method uses a specially developed
Lagrangian formulation for determining the thermal history of each elemental
volume from the calculated transient temperature ﬁeld in the growing ingot. The
thermal history calculation is very comprehensive and includes determination the
local solidi ﬁcation time, and the cooling rate, temperature gradient, isotherm angle
and velocity of solidi ﬁcation at various temperatures within the solidi ﬁcation range
of the alloy.
Since the objective of remelting processes is to produce ingots that are free of
defects, a computational model for ESR would ideally incorporate an approach for
predicting the conditions under which a defect may form during the solidi ﬁcation
process. In the case of superalloys, the ability to predict a channel-like defect or
“freckle” would be useful for assessing the quality of the ingot. Calculating the
degree of microsegregation by solving the species transport equations in the
interdendritic region from ﬁrst principles would result in a model that is compu-
tationally infeasible for routine use by process engineers. Therefore, the compu-
tational model in this study utilizes the method proposed by Auburtin et al. [ 24] for
an efﬁcient quanti ﬁcation of the probability of freckle formation through the Ray-
leigh number criterion for thermosolutal convection in the interdendritic region. In
this method, alloy-speci ﬁc correlations are used at each location in the solidi ﬁed
ingot for relating the thermal history parameters to the corresponding metallurgical
structure parameters which, in turn, are used in the calculation of the interdendritic
Rayleigh number.
Computational Solution
The equations governing the electromagnetic, ﬂow, and thermal phenomena are
solved using the framework of the control volume method (Patankar [ 25]).
Important aspects of this basic computational method and its enhancements for
addressing the unique features of the transient ESR process that have been incor-
porated in the computational model are described below.
 Discretization of the Governing Equations — The axisymmetric domain is divi-
ded into control volumes. Discretization equations are constructed by integrating
the respective governing equations so that exact conservation of each physical
quantity is preserved. An implicit time-stepping technique is used for dis-
cretizing the unsteady terms. Multiple iterations are performed to obtain a
converged solution within each time step to address the nonlinearity in the
equations and coupling among ﬂow and temperature ﬁelds.
250 K. M. Kelkar and C. J. O ’Connell

## Page 258

 Ingot Growth — Growth of the ingot results in gradually uncovering control
volumes in the computational grid. As a result, within each time step during the
transient calculation, the row of control volumes in the active portion of the
computational domain expands downward at the instantaneous casting velocity.
Therefore, integral forms of the governing equations are utilized for constructing
the discretization equations for the expanding control volumes. In addition, the
computational solution is limited to the control volumes that contain the slag
and the formed ingot at that time instant so as to achieve computational
efﬁciency.
 AC Electromagnetics — Due to the use of AC power, the discretization and
solution of the equation for magnetic diffusion and the subsequent calculations
for current density, Lorentz force, and Joule heating utilize complex variables.
 Thermal History and Rayleigh Number-Based Defect Formation Probability — A
special Lagrangian technique has been developed for the determination of the
thermal history of the ingot. It utilizes the transient temperature ﬁeld calculated
in the reference frame attached to the top surface of the slag for a precise
determination of the temporal variation of the temperature of each elemental
metal volume in the growing ingot as it cools from the liquidus to the solidus
temperature. A comprehensive thermal history at each solidi ﬁed elemental metal
volume is determined and then utilized for determining the probability of defect
formation in the entire solidi ﬁed ingot.
The computational method described above has been incorporated in the com-
mercial software program MeltFlow-ESR [ 19]. Application of the model for the
analysis of an industrial ESR process for a nickel-iron-chromium superalloy ingot is
discussed in the sections below.
Application of the Computational Model for an Industrial
ESR Process
Experimental and Computational Methods
An electrode of a nickel-iron-chromium superalloy was prepared by vacuum
induction melting and subsequently electroslag remelted to a 1.12 m diameter ingot
at Special Metals Corporation. The ESR process involved the use of an initial slag
charge of 295 kg with a continual addition of slag in an attempt to maintain a
relatively consistent slag cap layer throughout the duration of remelting. The
composition of the slag employed was nominally 30 CaF
2–28 CaO-7 MgO-28
Al2O3–7 TiO2 (wt%). A selection of the furnace signal transients are shown in Fig. 3
in which the absolute values have been suppressed. During the ESR process, two
signiﬁcant melt rate excursions occurred which were attributed to cracks in the
electrode. After the ingot had cooled suf ﬁciently in the static crucible arrangement,
A Computational Model of the Electroslag Remelting (ESR) … 251

## Page 259

the ingot was sectioned along a longitudinal plane and plates containing the cen-
terline were extracted at the top and bottom of the ingot. The surface of the plates
were then ground and chemically etched to reveal the solidi ﬁcation structure.
The industrial ESR process was then analyzed using the commercial software
package MeltFlow-ESR. The temperature-dependence of material properties,
including the variation of fraction solid with temperature, of the slag and metal were
incorporated in the analysis. Due to space constraints, only their representative
values are listed in the Table 1. Properties of the slag correspond to data from
Special Metals Corporation and reported values from prior studies (e.g., Mills and
Keene [ 26]). Properties of the alloy were taken from sources internal to Special
Metals Corporation. A computational grid of 250 (axial) × 55 (radial) control
volumes was used for the analysis. Calculations were made for the entire ESR
production process which included the durations for melting of the electrode and
subsequent cooling of the slag and ingot after the end of melting when the electrode
had been removed. This analysis required a total of 22 h on a PC with a 2.67 GHz
Intel processor.

Results and Discussion
The computational model provides detailed information about the distributions of
the electromagnetic, ﬂow, temperature, and liquid fraction in the slag and ingot
during and after the end of melting. In the sections below, results of the analysis are
discussed in terms of the overall process behavior and detailed ﬁeld variations.
Overall Process Behavior
The behavior of the overall process can be evaluated by observing the evolution of
the molten slag and metal volumes and also the slag skin thickness as shown in
Fig. 4. Early in the melting process, the molten metal pool increases sharply with
time as the ingot grows and then begins to approach a plateau. The calculations
suggest that a steady-state condition was not reached. Notice that the size of the
metal pool ﬂuctuates during the melt rate excursions as a result of the change in the
electromagnetic and thermal conditions. The thickness of the slag skin formed at the
slag-metal interface also responds to the change in the ingot length and melting
power. In the very early stages, the temperature of the slag is colder mostly due to
higher heat loss through the ingot bottom leading to a thick slag skin. After the
ingot is sufﬁciently long, this thickness depends only on the melting conditions and
reaches a relatively stable value. A signature does appear in the slag skin thickness
during the melt rate excursions. As the melt schedule transitions to the hot top, the
lower power input results in a dramatic increase in the skin thickness. After the end
of melting, the slag and metal solidify rapidly. The molten metal, however, takes
longer to solidify due its larger volume and the inadequacy of the hot top cycle in
shrinking the metal pool prior to power off.

## Page 261

Electromagnetic, Flow and Temperature Fields
Figures 5, 6, and 7 show the electromagnetic, ﬂow and temperature ﬁelds in the
ingot. The electromagnetic ﬁelds show that the Joule heating is concentrated in the
slag and the current is nearly uniformly distributed over the cross-section due to its
low electrical conductivity. Conversely, due to the high electrical conductivity of
the ingot, the current distribution in the ingot shows the “skin effect ” where the
current ﬂow is concentrated in the outer radius. The Lorentz force is perpendicular
to the current density and is, therefore, mainly oriented inward radially.
At the beginning of melting, the volume of the molten metal is small and the
pool contour is ﬂat. This can be explained by the short ingot length and the
signiﬁcant heat loss ﬂux through the bottom of the ingot. Near the end of melting,
the metal pool reaches nearly a steady volume corresponding to a centerline depth
of 0.34 m for the 0.98 liquid fraction contour. Unlike the metal pool, the slag shows
strong mixing with velocities at least an order of magnitude larger than those in the
molten metal pool. After the end of melting, the comparatively large metal volume
requires more time to completely solidify than the slag. The slag temperature falls
below its liquidus temperature relatively quickly, within 30 min after the furnace
power was turned off. After 60 min of cooling, the bulk of the slag has more or less
solidiﬁed whereas a signi ﬁcant volume of the metal is still liquid.

Thermal History and Probability of Defect Formation
Figure 8 shows the ﬁeld variations of the local solidi ﬁcation time and Rayleigh
number for assessing the probability of freckle formation in the solidi ﬁed ingot. As
mentioned previously, the cooling rate is high at the ingot bottom due to the high
rate of heat transfer to the crucible bottom face in the very initial stages of the
process. Therefore, the local solidi ﬁcation time is very low in the bottom portion of
the ingot. As the ingot length increases and the melting conditions stabilize, the
transfer of heat occurs primarily in the radial direction. As a result, the local
solidiﬁcation time is high in the center and decreases radially outward. Due to the
melt rate excursions, the local solidi ﬁcation time follows the ﬂuctuation in the
thermal behavior. Relatively high solidi ﬁcation times are seen at the ingot center-
line during the excursions. After the end of melting, the metal pool shrinks rapidly
from the side but not as fast at the top due to the insulating effect of the slag volume.
As a result, the rate of cooling is lower at the ingot top.
The probability of freckle formation increases with an in increase in magnitude
of the interdendritic Rayleigh number. In the regions of the ingot where the cooling
rate is high, namely the bottom and outer radius, the dendrites are spaced closely
together and freckle formation is less likely due to a lower permeability. At the
ingot centerline, the average spacing between the dendrites is larger due to lower
cooling rates. The gravity-driven ﬂow is parallel to the primary dendrites for which

the permeability is lower relative to that for secondary dendrites. Typically, the
probability of freckle formation is observed to be highest in the mid-radius region
due to a combination of a relatively large spacing between the dendrites and the
direction of the ﬂow (as effected by pool angle) that involves a component along the
secondary dendrites. However, in the case of a larger ingot diameter and a shallow
pool, it is observed that the Rayleigh number is highest more toward the centerline.
As expected, the disturbance in the solidi ﬁcation conditions caused by the melt rate
excursions resulted in a larger probability of defect formation. After the end of
melting, the angle of the liquid metal pool contour increases due to a larger pro-
portion of cooling in the radial direction. Eventually, as was shown in Fig. 7, the
directionality in solidi ﬁcation is lost as additional cooling begins to occur from the
ingot top-down. Therefore, the high Rayleigh number observed at the ingot top is
believed to be purely a computational output of the form of the Rayleigh number
employed which was derived through the study of more traditional unidirectional
solidiﬁcation conditions involving a columnar dendrite structure.
Model Validation
A comparison of the predicted liquid metal pool contour at 0.98 liquid fraction (red
color) and the etched ingot plates is shown in Figs. 9 and 10. Overall, the com-
putational model reproduces the observed process transients with good agreement.

In the initial stages of the remelting process, the liquid metal pool shape is extre-
mely ﬂat and shallow. These predictions follow the directionality of the dendritic
structure. As the ingot length increases, a curvature to solidi ﬁcation front at the
outer edge develops due to a decrease in the effect of heat extraction from the
bottom, as shown in Fig. 9. The model predictions for the top 0.5 m of ingot are
shown in Fig. 10. The calculated pool shapes match well to the direction perpen-
dicular to the primary dendrite arms. In this region, the pool has deepened slightly
but there is still little curvature to the pool contour. The difference between the pool
depths at the edge and the ingot center is close to 0.1 m or approximately 9% of the
ingot diameter. It is interesting to note the porosity seen at the top of the ingot near
the centerline. This agrees well with the predictions of the model regarding the
inadequacy of the hop top cycle employed, where a signi ﬁcant volume of molten
metal remained at the end of melting. In addition to the previous validation efforts
using MeltFlow-ESR, these comparisons illustrate the utility of the model in pre-
dicting the transient melt conditions of an ESR process for a larger ingot diameter.
Summary and Conclusions
A comprehensive and ef ﬁcient computational model for the analysis of electro-
magnetics, ﬂow, and heat transfer in the transient ESR process for axisymmetric
conditions is presented. The model accounts for the period during melting and also
after the end of melting through the treatment of slag and ingot solidi ﬁcation. The
spatially-dependent thermal history of the entire ingot is determined from the cal-
culated transient temperature ﬁeld and tracked for subsequent calculations and

analyses. The implementation of an interdendritic Rayleigh number allows for the
prediction of the probability of freckle formation in the ingot. The model described
in this work was applied to the analysis of an industrial ESR process for a 1.12 m
diameter ingot of nickel-iron-chromium superalloy. A selection of ﬁeld variations
for the current density, volumetric heating, molten pool ﬂow, liquid fraction,
temperature, local solidi ﬁcation time, and interdendritic Rayleigh number at various
time instants during the process were used to evaluate the behavior of the ESR
process. The predicted liquid metal pool pro ﬁles compared well with the solidi ﬁ-
cation features contained in the centerline plates of the ﬁnal ingot. The computa-
tional model within the commercial software package MeltFlow-ESR
TM offers a
cost-effective method for reducing the traditional trial-and-error approach for pro-
cess design and for the production of ingots of high metallurgical quality.

Effect of Homogenization Temperature
on Microstructures of IN718C Alloy
with Different Solidi ﬁcation Cooling
Rates
Xiaofei Yuan, Fanguo Meng, Qiang Zeng, Wei Li, Shengguo Kong,
Jiantao Wu, Ping Yan and Juntao Li
Abstract In order to reduce the porosity and improve the performance stability of
IN718C alloy castings, hot isostatic pressing (HIP) process are usually conducted.
Due to the different solidi ﬁcation conditions, the segregation and microstructure
present various features in different positions of castings, especially for castings
showing large difference in wall thickness. The above mentioned factors can
inﬂuence the effect of HIP, cause incipient melting of low melting point phase, such
as Laves phase, then induce the scrapping of castings eventually. So it is necessary to
conduct homogenization treatment for the castings with large differences in solidi-
ﬁcation conditions before HIP process. In this article, the as-cast microstructures of
IN718C alloy with different solidi ﬁcation cooling rates were studied, including
segregation, phase constitution, etc. Then the microstructures of samples after ho-
mogenization treatment from 1075 –1125 °C were analyzed. The effect of homog-
enization temperature on the elimination of segregation and dissolution behaviour of
different phases were also investigated. Some relationships about homogenization
temperatures, microstructures and solidi ﬁcation cooling rates for IN718C alloy have
been determined. They can be used to choose homogenization temperature for
IN718C investment castings with complex shapes before HIP process.

Introduction
IN718C superalloy is widely used as the structural components due to the superior
castability, mechanical properties and low cost [ 1, 2]. Casting defects, such as
porosity, are normally formed in castings made by IN718C superalloy due to the
structural complexity. Therefore, hot isostatic pressing (HIP) process is conducted
in order to eliminate the porosity and improve the performance stability of castings.
IN718C superalloy presents obvious segregation behavior during solidi ﬁcation,
which is detrimental to the mechanical properties [ 3, 4]. Due to the different so-
lidiﬁcation conditions, the segregation and microstructure present various features
in different positions of castings, especially for castings showing large difference in
wall thickness. The segregation of alloying elements caused incipient melting in
low melting point region during HIP, which reduced fatigue capability of castings,
then induced the scrapping of castings eventually [ 1]. So it is essential to conduct a
homogenization treatment to decrease the segregation degree of castings before HIP
process.
In this paper, four IN718C samples with different thicknesses, corresponding
with various cooling rates during solidi ﬁcation, were chosen to simulate the dif-
ferent positions of castings. The segregation degree of the main alloying elements
as well as the phase constitution in as-cast samples and samples after homoge-
nization treatment from 1075 to 1125 °C for 2 h were characterized systematically.
The effectiveness of homogenization temperature on the elimination of segregation
and dissolution behaviour of different phases were also investigated.
Experimental
As-cast samples of IN718C alloy were prepared by investment cast process at
1430 °C. The measured composition of IN718C alloy used in this study is listed in
Table 1. It was measured by NCS Testing Technology Co., Ltd using quantitative
chemical analysis. Ni and Cr were measured by titration method, C was measured
by infrared absorption method, and other elements were determined by inductively
coupled plasma-atomic emission spectrometry. Figure 1 presents the sketch of the
step block casting used. Samples were named as I, II, III and IV, respectively,
according to the thickness of samples.

To evaluate the microstructural evolution after homogenization treatment, the
as-cast samples were homogenization treated in air at the temperature range of
1075–1125 °C for 2 h, followed by air cooling. To determine the in ﬂuence of the
homogenization treatment on the HIP process, as-cast and homogenized specimens
of sample I were thermally exposed at 1170 °C for 4 h followed by water
quenching.
To observe the microstructures of IN718C alloy, such as Laves phase, MC
carbides and δ phase, samples were electrolytically etched with a solution of 10 ml
nitric acid, 30 ml hydrochloric acid and 50 ml glycerol. The microstructural
examinations were performed using an optical microscope (OM) and a JEOL
JSM-7800F ﬁeld-emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM). Secondary
dendrite arm spacing was measured using Image-Pro Plus software by linear
intercept method. In order to obtain statistically signi ﬁcant results, 20 lines were
measured. To determine the degree of segregation, the contents of the main alloying
elements were tested by JXA-8530F ﬁeld-emission electron microprobe analyzer
(FE-EPMA) with wavelength dispersive spectrometer (WDS), 20 points were
measured in dendritic core and interdendritic regions, respectively, and then seg-
regation coefﬁcients were calculated.

The above results indicate that the segregation of Nb could not been eliminated if

Conclusion
(1) Microstructures of IN718C superalloy were signi ﬁcantly inﬂuenced by cooling
rate. Secondary dendrite arm spacing and segregation degree decreased with
cooling rate increasing. Blocky Laves phase precipitated during solidi ﬁcation at
slow cooling rate (1.73 –2.89 °C/s), eutectic Laves phase precipitated at rela-
tively faster cooling rate (1.73 –5.62 °C/s), but the precipitation of Laves phase
was inhibited at fast cooling rate (22.11 °C/s).

(2) Laves phase and MC carbides didn ’t dissolve into the γ matrix during the
homogenization treatment from 1075 to 1125 °C for 2 h, but the amount of δ
phase decreased gradually with temperature increasing. Moreover, the ho-
mogenization treatment could decrease the segregation degree in IN718C alloy.
(3) The homogenization treatment is very essential before HIP processing in order
to avoid incipient melting. The segregation of Nb could not been eliminated if
incipient melting occurred during thermal exposure. Moreover, cracks were
also induced by incipient melting.
