Grain Re ﬁnement on Microstructure
and Mechanical Properties of IN718
Superalloy
Taiwen Huang, Ziqi Jie, Jun Zhang, Lin Liu and Hengzhi Fu
Abstract The mixed re ﬁner of Co 3FeNb2 and CrFeNb ternary intermetallic
compounds and melt superheating treatment under the modi ﬁed
thermally-controlled solidi ﬁcation (TCS) process have been designed to achieve
grain reﬁnement and further improve mechanical properties of IN718 superalloy. It
is found that the re ﬁnement effect of addition grain re ﬁners under TCS process is
quite superior to that by convention casting (CC) process with re ﬁner, as experi-
ment results show that the grain size is re ﬁned from 3340 to 126 μm and greatly
reduce the amount of porosity, during the re ﬁnement process. In addition, the
applied melt treatment can re ﬁne grain size from 6420 to 89 μm and greatly reduce
the amount of porosity. Meanwhile, after grain re ﬁnement, the stress rupture
property under 650 °C/620 MPa is signi ﬁcantly improved. Grain re ﬁnement
mechanisms are also discussed.
Keywords IN 718 ⋅ Melt superheating treatment ⋅ Grain re ﬁners
Microstructure ⋅ Mechanical properties
Introduction
IN718 superalloy has been widely utilized as a structural material for fabricating
large thin wall parts with complicated shape in aerospace industry, because of its
excellent superior mechanical property, good structural stability, excellent weld-
ability and reasonable cost [ 1, 2]. These components are subjected to complex
in-service stress-temperature-time cycles, high-stress and high-operating tempera-
ture [ 3]. Under such service conditions, uniform and ﬁne-grained microstructure is
desired to obtain good low cycle fatigue resistance and high tensile strength [ 3, 4].

## Page 281

Usually, uniform and ﬁne grained microstructure of casting mainly depends on
the nucleation stage and subsequent growth condition [ 5]. As the classical nucle-
ation theory, more uniform grain structure can be achieved if nucleation rate is
larger than growth rate. During solidi ﬁcation, the methods to raise the nucleation
rate are mainly increasing the effective nucleation of particles or raising nucleation
undercooling by melt superheating treatment [ 3, 6–9]. However, at the condition of
conventional process, the nucleation usually originates at the mold wall, where the
free energy barrier to nucleation is lowered due to the chilling effect of the mold
[10]. So, the effects of grain re ﬁner and melt superheating treatment on grain
reﬁnement have been reduced because of the existence of recalescence. A technique
called thermally controlled solidi ﬁcation (TCS) evolved from directional solidi ﬁ-
cation [ 11]. Its velocity is antiparallel to the one-dimensional heat ﬂow and there
can be reduce recalescence due to sequential solidi ﬁcation. In addition, the mold
temperatures of the in TCS are set between the solidus and liquidus temperature to
ensure the thin-wall castings are completely ﬁlled.
In this work, the TCS process was deliberately modi ﬁed to successfully produce
equiaxed IN718C superalloy with little porosity. Thereafter, the in ﬂuence of melt
superheating temperature and grain re ﬁner on the microstructure and mechanical
properties of IN718C superalloy are investigated.
Materials and Experimental Procedures
The commercial IN718 alloy with the following chemical composition (wt%) of
0.056 C, 0.01 Co, 0.61 Al, 0.94 Ti, 52.54 Ni, 19.15 Cr, 3.11 Mo, 5.03 Nb, 0.0026 B,
0.028 Zr and with the balance being Fe was used for the experiments. A Netzsch
409CD comprehensive differential thermal analysis (DTA) instrument was used to
perform the measurement of the characteristic temperatures. From the differential
thermal analysis (DTA), the equilibrium liquidus and solidus temperatures of the
alloy are 1349 and 1270 °C, respectively.
To ensure that the grain re ﬁner does not introduce inclusions and pose any bad
inﬂuence on the mechanical properties of alloy, two intermetallic compounds of
Co
3FeNb2 and CrFeNb are prepared as re ﬁners, whose constituent elements are the
elements presented in the IN718 superalloy. The mixture of the two re ﬁners was
prepared by physically mixing with the proportion of 1:1 in weight percentage.
They were ground into powders with size of 30 –50 μm and the weight with 0.1% of
the ingot was added into the melt. For melt superheating treatment, the alloy was
melted and superheated to different temperatures (1380 –1680 ºC) for 10 min. After
melt treatment, the liquid melt was maintained at 1380 ºC then poured into the
preheated mold with the inner size of 110 mm long and 30 mm diameter and the
mold was withdrawn from the heating zone at a withdrawal speed of 400 μm/s.
The average grain size at transverse cross-section was determined by a standard
quantitative metallographic technique. The grain size was also estimated using
276 T. Huang et al.

## Page 282

ASTM E112-96. The rupture stress life was measured at 650 °C and 620 MPa
using a SATEC M3 stress life machine.
Results and Discussion
The Modi ﬁcation of TCS Process
Using TCS process, cast macrostructure of alloy by adjusting the ratio of the
temperature gradient (G) to the solidi ﬁcation rate (R) at the solid/liquid interface
front. During solidi ﬁcation, relatively low G/R ratios tend to correlate with
equiaxed macrostructure [ 11]. For extend the range of equiaxed structure, the
thermal insulating layer is set between the mold and water-cooled copper chill plate
to reduce G/R ratios range (Fig. 1). At the condition of TCS, columnar-to-equiaxed
transitions (CET) are observed (Fig. 1). However, all equiaxed grains are found at
the condition of modi ﬁed thermally controlled solidi ﬁcation (MTCS) (Fig. 2).
The Effect of Grain Re ﬁners on Microstructures and Stress
Rupture Properties of IN718
Figure 3 shows the grain structures in the middle area of the sample at different cast
conditions. For convention casting (CC) condition, it consists of columnar grains at
the edge and equiaxed grains in the center (Fig. 3a). The average grain size is about
4560 μm. After adding the re ﬁners, an equiaxed grain is formed and the average
grain size is re ﬁned to 1230 μm, as shown in Fig. 3b. At the condition of TCS,
coarse equiaxed grains are found (Fig. 3c). Moreover, when the re ﬁners are added,
the average grain size is re ﬁned from 3340 to 126 μm, as shown in Fig. 3d.

produce the ﬁner and uniform grain size. Therefore, high re ﬁning effect is obtained
than with the CC process. Moreover, the proportion of equiaxed grain at the TCS
process could be increased obviously comparing with CC process, because the
temperature gradient between mold temperature and melt temperature is decreased.
So, it is helpful to form the equiaxed grain.

of the grain interior should be small which causes low possibility of crack [ 4]. In

The Effect of Melt Superheating Treatment on Microstructure
and Stress Rupture Properties of IN718 Superalloy
Figure 7 shows grain size at different melt superheating temperatures. It can be seen
that the grain size decreases with increasing the melt superheating temperature until
1550 °C. However, grain size increases with increasing the superheating temper-
ature from 1550 to 1600 °C. At the superheating temperature of 1680 °C, the grain
size is re ﬁned remarkably. The grain size decreases from 6420 to 89 μm with
increasing the melt superheating temperature from 1380 to 1680 °C (Fig. 7c, d).
It is well known that the grain size is largely affected by nucleation undercooling
which is associated with melt superheating treatment. In order to understand the
effect of superheating treatment on the nucleation undercooling of IN718 superal-
loy, the solidi ﬁcation process of IN718 superalloy is investigated by DTA.

The effect of nucleation superheating treatment on nucleation undercooling
obtained from DTA is shown in Fig. 8. It can be concluded that the nucleation
undercooling of the alloy increases with increasing the melt superheating temper-

temperature of 1680 °C, which is consistent with the results of Kolotukhin et al.
[14]. The nucleation undercooling variation for the different superheating temper-
ature can be explained by the change of internal melt structure [ 14, 15]. It is
considered that the alloy melt structure is composed of a large number of atomic
clusters, such Ni 3Al-like cluster, residual MC carbide and other high-melting par-
ticle near to the liquidus temperature (1400 –1500 °C) [ 14, 15]. Therefore, nucle-
ation undercooling must be small. With increasing melt superheating temperature,
the size of these clusters and MC carbides become smaller in the heating process,
which causes the increase in nucleation undercooling slightly. When the melt
superheating treatment is higher than 1600 ºC, the clusters are destroyed and the
refractory particles are free to alloy melt, therefore, the nucleation undercooling
decreased. When the superheating temperature increases to1680 °C, the melt will be

According to Eq. ( 1)–(4), the critical nucleating energy ( ΔG*) and critical
nucleus (r
k) can be reduced by increasing the undercooling ( ΔT). Therefore, the
nucleation rate (I) increases and the critical nucleation radius (r k) decrease with the
increase of undercooling, resulting in grain re ﬁnement. Furthermore, under the
large undercooling, the nucleation rate is greater than growth rate. The increased
nucleation rate results in the increased number of grains growing simultaneously.
Therefore, the growth time of solidi ﬁed phase reduces with the increase of melt
superheating and the grain size decreases.
Figure 9 shows melt treatment temperature on the Laves phases and carbides of
IN718 superalloy. The morphology of Laves in the coarse grain samples is coarser
and long chains of interconnected whereas in condition of 1680 °C is ﬁne and
dispersived. The quantity of Laves decreases with increasing of melt treatment
temperature. The quantitative analysis show that the volume fraction of Laves phase
is about 5.44% when the grain size is 6420 μm. It was reduced to 1.33% if the grain
is reﬁned to 89 μm. Moreover, with the increase of melt treatment temperature, the
morphology of carbides changes from big block into dispersively distributed ﬁne
particles.
The stress rupture properties of heat treated alloys tested at 650 ºC and 620 MPa
as a function of the superheating treatment temperature are shown in Fig. 10. The
stress rupture life and elongation of IN718 superalloy are obviously improved with
increasing superheating temperature from 1550 to 1680 ºC (Fig. 10). At the

Conclusions
1. An integrated technique, combining thermally controlled solidi ﬁcation process
with the mixed re ﬁner of Co 3FeNb2 and CrFeNb ternary intermetallic com-
pounds, has been designed to enhance grain re ﬁnement and restrain porosity in
IN718 superalloy. Under the condition of convention casting process, the grain
size is re ﬁned from 4560 to 1230 μm and the stress rupture life increases from
76 to 117.2 h. Moreover, the grain size is re ﬁne from 3340 to 126 μm and the
stress rupture life improve from 89 to 201.5 h during the integrated technique.
The MDS by introducing grain re ﬁners can greatly decrease grain size of the
IN718C superalloy. The grain size has been re ﬁned from 3340 to 126 μm.
2. The thermally controlled solidi ﬁcation technique in association with melt
superheating has been designed to re ﬁne grain. The grain size decreases from
6420 to 89 μm with increasing the melt superheating temperature from 1380 to
1680 °C. At the superheating temperature of 1680 ºC, the stress rupture life
reached 242 h which is three times than that of 1550 ºC.

Melt Parameters and Resulting
Characteristics in Laboratory-Scale
Electroslag Remelting
Martin Detrois and Paul D. Jablonski
Abstract Vacuum induction melting (VIM) and electroslag remelting (ESR) are
techniques used to produce ingots of alloys with complex chemistries while low-
ering the amount of defects, inclusions or extent of elemental segregation. Those
practices are widely employed in aerospace applications and more recently in
fossil-fueled power plant components due to the increasingly demanding operating
conditions. Consequently, research is ongoing to improve and control the melting
of commercially available alloys for optimal performance in service. In this
investigation, a laboratory-scale (200 mm –200 kg) ESR furnace was used to remelt
various alloys with a focus on the ingot quality. Several approaches were consid-
ered to study and improve the melting characteristics. Targeted additions of minor
elements in master alloys were found to improve the melt range which affected the
melt pool volume and subsequently increased the remelting ef ﬁciency. Furthermore,
the melt parameters during ESR of some select alloys were modi ﬁed to improve the
melting characteristics. Finally, the in ﬂuence of the size of the ESR electrode was
observed and provided a better understanding of the mixing mechanisms in the slag
region and their effect on the voltage swing and melt rate. The results are presented
using a combination of experimental and computational (thermodynamic and
CFD-based) data.

Introduction
The use of vacuum induction melting (VIM) and electroslag remelting (ESR) has
become mandatory for numerous applications that require the production of clean
alloys and when powder-processing routes are considered too expensive and
unsuitable [ 1]. For Ni-based superalloys operating in critical sections of turbine
engines or power plants, ESR has become an essential process following VIM [ 2].
Both VIM and ESR are bene ﬁcial to lowering the amount of inclusions and tramp
elements, such as oxygen, nitrogen, and sulfur, present in an alloy [ 3, 4]. Internal
oxides are particularly harmful to the mechanical properties of superalloys as they
are known to accelerate fatigue crack nucleation [ 5]. Furthermore, sulfur has
detrimental effects in Ni-based superalloys as it embrittles interfaces [ 6, 7] and can
form undesirable phases [ 8]. Finally, careful attention must be given to nitrogen
concentrations as it is prone to the formation of inclusions in alloys that contain
nitride formers such as Ti, Nb or Ta [ 9]. The continuous increase in performance
requirements of alloys used in power generation applications requires reducing the
amounts of inclusions and tramp elements tolerable in today ’s commercially
available alloys. While ESR is an effective process in metal re ﬁning, several factors
and parameters can be modi ﬁed to increase its effectiveness.
ESR is a process by which a consumable electrode is placed in a water-cooled
crucible with reactive slag in contact with the bottom of the electrode [ 10]. Joule
heating allows for the slag to melt and form an electrically resistive liquid pool
while current passes from the electrode to the bottom of the crucible. When the
electrode starts to melt, liquid metal droplets travel through the slag from the
bottom of the electrode to the solidifying ingot. The metal drops are superheated in
the slag which enhances reactions such as desulfurization and the removal of
non-metallic inclusions. The electrodes are generally made using VIM by pouring
the liquid metal into a mold with suitable dimensions based on the ESR crucible
size. The weight and ﬁll ratio (cross section of the electrode over cross section of
the crucible) play an important role in the remelting characteristics such as the time
in steady state and mixing in the slag region. The majority of slags (or ﬂuxes)
contain combinations of CaF
2, CaO, Al 2O3 and MgO, with the overall composition
and constituents adjusted depending on the alloy to be remelted. Furthermore, the
slag can be subjected to elemental additions or heat treatments to further enhance
the remelting process.
Depending on the alloy composition and melt stock quality, special procedures
can be considered to approach the melting process. Particularly, the af ﬁnity of Cr
for oxygen and nitrogen can considerably increase the concentration of tramp
elements in the ﬁnal product, especially in Ni-based superalloys. For instance, the
Cr used in this investigation contains 5200 ppm O. This can be addressed by using
master alloys, generally of Ni-Cr or Ni-Co-Cr, in the weight up of the superalloys to
be melted. The master alloys are previously remelted to lower the concentration of
tramp elements. Often, iterations of VIM and ESR are preferred to further improve
288 M. Detrois and P. D. Jablonski

## Page 294

the alloy ’s chemistry. During the ﬁnal weight up of a Ni-based superalloy, the
master alloy can be used to completely avoid having loose Cr in the VIM crucible.
In this investigation, the in ﬂuences of elemental additions on the remelting
characteristics and resulting tramp elements following VIM and ESR of Ni-25Cr
and Ni-30Co-30Cr master alloys are determined. Additionally, the in ﬂuence of the
electrode ﬁll factor during ESR is investigated. In this case, 316 stainless steel is
selected as an analogue to the master alloys since it has similar melting
characteristics.
Procedure
Melting
The various alloys considered in this investigation were vacuum induction melted
from commercial-purity raw starting materials to formulate the Ni-based master
alloys, or commercial-grade melt stock, for the stainless steels. The materials, with
target weights of 45 or 68 kg, were loaded in an alumina crucible. The alloys were
melted under partial argon pressure of 200 Torr to a target temperature of
T
L + 50 °C, where T L is the liquidus temperature. The alloys were then poured into
either 97 mm or 114 mm steel molds, depending on the initial weight, to form ESR
electrodes. The electrodes were then remelted into a 152 mm diameter crucible and
an argon cover gas was used when remelting Ni-based master alloys. The process
was repeated for the melting of master alloys such as Ni-30Co-30Cr or Ni-25Cr, as
represented in Fig. 1. First, layers of raw Ni, Co and Cr with chosen elemental
additions were placed into the crucible and induction melted to form the ESR
electrode. Subsequently, the ESR ingot was cut and remelted in the VIM furnace
along with the electrode top and chemistry slices. The resulting electrode was
remelted using ESR to obtain the ﬁnal ingot. The VIM + ESR process was repeated
twice.
Experimentally optimized parameter pro ﬁles were used during ESR and varied
depending on master alloy or stainless steel. The slag used, however, was identical

started using compacts made of turnings of the VIM material layered with slag.
Additional slag was added in the feeder for startup. More detailed information about

Computational Tools
The software Thermo-Calc [ 12] with the TCNi8 database was used for thermo-
dynamic predictions such as phase diagrams and solubility limit plots. In addition,
JMatPro [ 13] with the TTNi8 database was used to obtain thermo-physical prop-
erties of the alloys for modeling of the ESR process. The slag properties were
obtained from Refs. [ 14, 15] and Thermo-Calc. Modeling of the ESR process was
performed using the computational ﬂuid dynamics (CFD) software MeltFlow-ESR
from Innovative Research, LLC [ 16]. The simulations were run using the dimen-
sions of the electrodes and of the crucible from the experiments. The melting
conditions used in the simulations were extracted from the recorded data of the ESR
runs and consisted of the measured melt rate, the current set point and the voltage
set point over 12.4 min long time intervals. Other properties considered include the
density of the electrode at room temperature, liquidus and solidus, the volume
expansion coef ﬁcient, solidus and liquidus temperatures, latent heat, partitioning
coefﬁcients, and conductivity (electrical and thermal), speci ﬁc heat, viscosity, solid
fraction vs temperature from room temperature to T
L + 50 °C. Inclusions were
added to the simulations with a range of densities and sizes.

Chemical analysis was performed after each melt on ∼10 mm thick slices sectioned
from the bottom of the VIM electrodes and ∼15 mm thick slices from the top of the
ESR ingots. The metal chemistries were obtained by x-ray ﬂuorescence (XRF) us-
ing a Rigaku ZSX Primus II with NIST traceable standards (reported values are
accurate to 0.01 wt%). Carbon and sulfur chemistries were determined with a LECO

Results and Discussion
Part I: Elemental Additions
Solidiﬁcation Range and Ef ﬁciency
Melting of simple alloys such as the subject master alloys can be challenging during
ESR, particularly due to the small melt range associated with simple compositions.
Figure 2 represents the calculated melt range from Thermo-Calc in the
Ni-30Co-30Cr alloy with additions of C or Ti. In the simple ternary alloy, the melt
range only spans 5.9 °C. Additions of 300 ppm C considerably expands the melt
range to 33.8 °C. Similarly, a 1.0 wt% addition of Ti increases the melt range
to 38.8 °C. Consequently, C addition is more effective at increasing the melt range
of the ternary alloy: a factor 5.7 with only 300 ppm C added compared to a factor of
6.6 when 1.0 wt% Ti is added.
The narrow melt range can affect the solidi ﬁcation characteristics of the alloy by
restricting the volume of the mushy zone and associated “excess” enthalpy of
solidiﬁcation [ 11]. The insets of Fig. 2 represent the melt pool during steady state

considerably expands the liquid + solid fraction lines, Fig. 2b. With only 300 ppm

power recorded during ESR of several ∼45 kg Ni-30Co-30Cr electrodes. No
additions to the ternary alloy required ∼105 kW to melt at ∼2.25 lb/min. With Fe
contamination from the crucible during VIM, the electrode melted with a power
of ∼115 kW producing a melt rate of ∼3.75 lb/min. Finally, with targeted C and Ti
additions, the ternary alloy melted using a power of ∼65 kW and a melt rate
of ∼3.25 lb/min. The minor additions of C and Ti expanded the melt range and the
mushy zone volume resulting in better solidi ﬁcation characteristics and providing
an approximately 41% decrease in the power required to melt at a rate around
3 lb/min.
Inﬂuence of Elemental Additions on the Alloy Chemistry
Alloying additions were demonstrated to be bene ﬁcial to ESR of simple alloys in
the previous section, however, as they alter the chemistry of the ﬁnal product,
careful attention needs to be given to the chemistry and phases. The chemistry of
two Ni-25Cr master alloys was measured after each step of the melting process
represented in Fig. 1 and the data is reported in Table 2. The additions investigated
in the previous section were considered here using 1 wt% Ti and 323 ppm C in the
initial chemistry. The two master alloys are referred in this section as MA1 and

the reader is encouraged to refer to Ref. [ 19] for more detailed information.

Part II: Melt Parameters and Geometry
Electrode Geometry
The melt rate and voltage swing are critical to the quality of the ingots produced by
ESR. Those parameters are dependent on the voltage, current, voltage swing and
other terms set on the pro ﬁle used for remelting and controlled throughout the
experiment. These ESR melts were performed using melt rate control (feeding into
the current set point) to attain a target melt rate of 3 lb/min and voltage swing
control (feeding into the voltage set point) to maintain a voltage swing of 0.8 V as
those parameters were shown to produce ingots with clean and smooth sidewalls
[11]. Comparison is made for two electrodes of 42 and 64 kg of 316 stainless steel
as an analogue for the master alloys. Although attention is given to the in ﬂuence of
the electrode weight, a more important factor is the electrode diameter with the
lighter electrode measuring 97 mm in diameter while the heavier was 114 mm in
diameter. This affects the ﬁll ratio ( ﬁll factor) which will be investigated in the next
section. The results are compiled in Figs. 6 and 7 where the data was recorded and
presented every second and the controls were based on a running average of 1 min.
In Fig. 6, the startup occurred at around 5 min into the pro ﬁle for both elec-
trodes. The feeder containing additional slag was then emptied over the next 5 –
8 min until reaching steady state. With different weights but relatively similar
current and voltage set points, remelting of the 42 kg electrode, Fig. 6a, ended after
31 min while the 64 kg end time was recorded at 50 min, Fig. 6b. This resulted in a
considerably shorter time in steady state during ESR of the 42 kg electrode. Fur-
thermore, the decrease in melt rate from ignition to the target value was found to
occur during the ﬁrst 30 min of melt time. Consequently, for the 42 kg electrode
“steady state ” was completed prior to reaching the target melt rate, Fig. 6a, the
target melt rate is reached around the time hot top starts. Conversely, the heavier
electrode melted at the target melt rate value for almost 20 min prior to hot
top. Similar trends were observed on the voltage swing, Fig. 7. The voltage swing
stabilized at about 15 min in for the 42 kg electrode and 20 min in for the 64 kg.
Overall the values were higher than the target swing of 0.8 V. When stable and
prior to hot top, the voltage swing during remelting of the 42 kg electrode was

Fill Ratio and Inclusion Motion
MeltFlow simulations of remelting of the two 316 stainless steel electrodes mea-
suring 97 and 114 mm diameter were ran using the melt parameters of the previous
section. The dimensions of the electrodes correspond to ﬁll ratios of 0.41 and 0.56,
respectively. Figure 8 provides the simulated temperature gradient in the slag
region and top of the forming ingot as well as the liquid velocity ﬁelds during
steady state. The liquid velocity ﬁelds show two ﬂow cells: one underneath the
electrode with counterclockwise ﬂow and the other closer to the crucible wall
showing clockwise ﬂow. Signi ﬁcantly higher velocities are predicted underneath
the electrode and at the slag/liquid interface for both conditions. Furthermore, the
results reveal overall higher temperatures and liquid velocities during remelting of
the smaller diameter electrode, Fig. 8a. This can be attributed to the higher current
density beneath the center of the electrode as the ﬁll ratio decreases [ 23].

The inclusion motion within the slag region was modelled for remelting using
the 0.41 and 0.56 ﬁll ratio electrodes for a range of particle densities and diameters,
Fig. 10. The results better reveal the two ﬂow cells observed in Fig. 8 with the

heat loss from the slag to the bottom of the electrode being greater with higher ﬁll

inclusion motion/travel, Fig. 10a, the lower ﬁll ratio was more prone to produce
low concentrations of oxygen and sulfur, Fig. 9, which can be attributed to greater
mixing and superheat of the liquid metal drops.
Conclusions
Laboratory-scale ESR was performed on a number of alloys to control the efﬁciency of
the process and the amount of inclusions and tramp elements present in the ﬁnal
products. Several conclusions were drawn from the results of this investigation:
Fig. 10 Inclusion motion

## Page 306

1. Minor additions of targeted elements such as C and Ti are bene ﬁcial to the
melting of simple binary or ternary alloys as they extend the melt range and
increase the mushy zone volume which increases the ef ﬁciency of the ESR
process. A 41% reduction in the power required to melt at an approximately
constant melt rate was obtained using minor additions of C and Ti.
2. Al additions from the feeder at the early stage of ESR has negligible effect on
the concentration of tramp elements and inclusions observed. Al pick-up mostly
originates from the Al
2O3 in the slag by reaction with Ti from the metal, as
opposed to pick-up from the raw Al granules.
3. The time at steady state and at targeted values of melt rate and voltage swing,
which is affected by the electrode weight/ ﬁll factor, did not in ﬂuence the quality
of the ESR ingots in terms of sidewalls.
4. A lower ﬁll ratio was responsible for higher liquid velocities and temperature in
the slag and greater travel of inclusions. Experimentally, overall greater
decreases in the oxygen content was measured following ESR using a ﬁll ratio
of 0.41 compared to 0.56. The decrease in sulfur content from VIM to ESR was
relatively independent of the ﬁll ratio.

## Page 308

Production of Nitride-Free 718
by the VIM-VAR Processing Route
Ioná Macedo Leonardo, Cláudio Silva da Hora, Mariana Beatriz dos
Reis Silva and Kleber Sernik
Abstract The current state of the art of superalloys manufacturing process makes
possible to obtain materials substantially clean of oxides associated with a ﬁne grain
structure. However, little progress happened in the elimination of nitrides from the
Cr-Nb-Ti containing superalloys. The nitrogen is mostly carried into the melt by
chromium and niobium master alloys, associate with leaks in the melt chamber. The
present development obtained by CBMM ’s materials and processing research
program provides a process for the manufacturing of material above mentioned in
which the precipitation of nitrides during the solidi ﬁcation can be essentially
eliminated. This is done by a two-step melting process. In the ﬁrst one the nitrogen
is taken out a bath formed with the non-reactive metals (Ni, Fe, Mo) by a controlled
carbon-boil. Subsequently Cr and Nb bearing master alloys with extra-low nitrogen
content (produced by a special smelting process developed by the company) are
added to the bath, together with Ti, Al and B. The VIM furnace utilized is designed
in a way that it is virtually atmospheric leak-free. That will result in an ingot whose
nitrogen content is below the limit for the TiN precipitation during the solidi ﬁcation
of alloy 718.

Introduction
The lifespan of rotating metal parts in aircraft engines is typically determined by
fatigue cracking. In this process, cracks are initiated at certain nucleation sites
within the metal and propagate at a rate related to the material characteristics and
the stress to which the component is subjected. That, in turn, limits the number of
cycles the part will withstand during its service life [ 1, 2].
Clean melting production techniques developed for superalloys have given rise
to the substantial elimination of oxide inclusions in such alloys to the extent that
nowadays, fatigue cracks are mainly originated on structural features, for example,
on grain boundaries or clusters of primary precipitates such as carbides and nitrides
[3].
It has been found that the primary nitride particles formed during the solidi ﬁ-
cation of alloy 718 [ 4, 5]— which is one of the main alloys utilized in the pro-
duction of aircraft engine rotating parts and for oil and gas drilling and production
equipment— are pure TiN (titanium nitride) and that the precipitation of primary
Nb-TiC (niobium-titanium carbide) occurs by heterogeneous nucleation over the
surface of the TiN particles, thereby increasing the precipitate particle size. The
particle size can be decreased by two means: either by lowering the carbon content
as much as possible, or by lowering the nitrogen content [ 6, 7].
Many commercial speci ﬁcations for superalloys, stainless steel, and other spe-
cialty steels, establish minimum carbon content, usually in order to prevent grain
boundary slipping at the service temperature. As a consequence, the only practical
means to decrease particle size compositionally is to reduce the nitrogen content in
the material as extensively as possible. In that way, in as much as the nitrides
precipitate ﬁrst, removing nitrogen supersedes the importance of removing carbon
[6].
However, once the nitride precipitation is suppressed, the carbon content of the
bulk liquid may also be decreased, due to the fact that no carbon will be consumed
by precipitation around the nitride particle. This shall lead to an improvement in
eventual differences of densities between the interdendritic liquid at the solidi ﬁ-
cation front and the bulk liquid. As a consequence, a lesser degree of segregation
should be obtained which may facilitate the production of ingots larger than the
current standards in the industry, while still meeting all the properties and expected
performance criteria in use.
The present development provides processes for manufacturing alloys in which
the precipitation of nitrides during their solidi ﬁcation can be essentially eliminated.
This result is obtained by the two-step melting process of the present innovation, as
described below.
304 I. M. Leonardo et al.

## Page 310

The Manufacturing Process
In the ﬁrst step, elements or alloys of such elements that do not dissolve appreciable
amounts of nitrogen, e.g., cobalt, nickel, iron, molybdenum, tungsten and the like,
are charged to a refractory crucible within a vacuum induction furnace and melted
therein, as shown on Fig. 1.
After melting is completed, a vigorous and controlled heterogeneous bubble
nucleation or carbon boil is effected in order to remove the largest part of the
residual nitrogen carried into the melt by those elements. The carbon boil is initiated
by adding carbon in a controlled manner by means of inserting a graphite electrode
to the melt in order to minimize carbon pick up which could lead to carbide
formation in the solid metal. The Fig. 2 illustrates this procedure. The boiling action
promotes rinsing or scrubbing of the molten liquid through agitation resulting in
diffusion of nitrogen to the gas/liquid interface and absorption of the nitrogen into
the bubbles which rise to the surface of the melt and are removed under the reduced
pressure maintained within the furnace. To illustrate the carbon boil and its effec-
tiveness in the removal of nitrogen, a typical composition of alloy 718 contains
iron, nickel and molybdenum, which together usually comprise about 75% by
weight of the alloy and which together contribute about 20 ppm nitrogen to the
charge. Consequently, this would add about 15 ppm nitrogen to the ﬁnal alloy
composition. However, by employing the carbon boil technique, the original
nitrogen content can be reduced to less than 2 ppm in the ﬁnal alloy composition.
As the oxygen in the system becomes depleted, the carbon boil subsides and is
ultimately completed.

Once the carbon boil is completed, the remaining elements or compounds
necessary for the manufacture of the superalloy can be added to the melt. Con-

available raw materials are totally unsuitable for obtaining low nitrogen chromium/
niobium-containing nickel-based superalloys, since the sum of the chromium and
niobium contents in those speci ﬁcations is above 15%, and about 24% for alloy 718,
in particular. Therefore, the chromium and niobium-bearing raw materials must be
produced in a manner which do not permit the nitrogen present in the atmosphere to
contaminate the metal phase during manufacture because once nitrogen is absorbed,
it will be extremely dif ﬁcult and expensive to remove. Figure 3 shows the addition

## Page 314

The Manufacturing Process of ELN Master Alloys
The goal of obtaining a low nitrogen, essentially nitride-free chromium or chro-
mium plus niobium-containing nickel-based alloy can only be achieved, however,
by adding the chromium and niobium as a low nitrogen master alloy obtained by a
metallothermic reaction conducted under reduced pressure, in which the air is ﬁrst
removed by an evacuation system, the mixture is ignited and the reduction, so-
lidiﬁcation and cooling of the material is effected under reduced pressure, resulting
in a chromium and niobium master alloys containing no more than 5 ppm nitrogen
[8, 9].
Mitchell [ 6] presented a review where it is shown that one of the most effective
means of control of the nitrogen content lies in the choice of raw materials for the
alloy make-up, and that the subsequent nitride formation can be minimized by
correct choice of process routes in VIM, ESR, VAR and EBCHM.
Electron beam melting is a well-known process for producing low nitrogen
nickel-based alloys; however, it is very expensive and extremely slow when
compared to the state-of-the-art vacuum induction melting furnace whose produc-
tivity is at least one order of magnitude greater. For example, the productivity of the
electron beam melting process is about 100 kg/h; whereas, the productivity of a
vacuum induction melting furnace is about 3 –5 metric tons per hour.

## Page 319

Discussion
The results obtained have demonstrated the effectiveness of the processing route
employed.
In a ﬁrst step extra-low nitrogen raw materials containing chromium and nio-
bium were produced with a proprietary technique resulting in unprecedented low
levels of contamination in regard to that element. The experiments resulted in
contents consistently at a 5 ppm maximum level.
In a second step the residual nitrogen contained in the non-reactive elements —
nickel, iron and molybdenum — was ef ﬁciently removed by a carbon boil. The
material was melted at a high pressure highly puri ﬁed argon and had its temperature
adjusted to 1.500 C.
After that the boil was promoted by means of inserting a graphite rod into the
liquid metal bath containing only those three elements. The contents obtained by
this technique were consistently below 1 ppm.
The insertion of a rod was done with two purposes. The ﬁrst one was to promote
de formation of CO bubbles in whose interior the partial pressure of nitrogen was
close to zero, thereby absorbing the nitrogen dissolved in the liquid phase and
rinsing it out. The second is to control the intensity of the reaction, therefore
avoiding liquid metal over ﬂow by a very vigorous reaction in the beginning, or
large carburization of the alloy as it weakens over time due to the lowering of the
dissolved oxygen content. In either case the rod can be lifted out immediately.
The third step consisted in adding the reactive metals produced with extremely
low nitrogen content to the nickel, iron and molybdenum bath after the boiling
subsided. For the successful implementation of this phase, the furnace leaks have to
be minimized by all means, preferably with the combination of high internal
pressure obtained by pure argon back ﬁlling, and double-sealing at the movable
ﬂanges.
In the case of using the double-sealing technique, a dedicated vacuum pump
shall be utilized to constantly maintain a low pressure in the annulus between the
seals. Considering that the pressure inside the melting chamber will be much higher
than the one in the seals, the leaks will happen from inside out.
If the furnace does not have this capability, it is necessary to work at a very high
pressure in the chamber, otherwise considerable leaking from outside will occur.
In any case, the pure argon high pressure inside the furnace will not only
minimize nitrogen coming from outside, but will immediately dilute its partial
pressure if it comes in, thus greatly diminishing its absorption by the liquid alloy.
The limiting factor for how high this pressure can be is the water cooling capacity
of the melting chamber shell.
The virtual absence of nitrogen in the inclusions found in the forged billet
suggests that the content obtained was below the solubility limit for this element in
the alloy.
314 I. M. Leonardo et al.

## Page 320

Conclusion
The present development represents a substantial cost-effective contribution to
enhance the quality of chromium and niobium-bearing superalloys, providing a
reliable processing route to produce low nitrogen, essentially nitride-free chromium
plus niobium-containing nickel based alloys by a VIM/VAR melting route, while
keeping the high quality standards as required by the major end users.

## Page 322

Characterization and Modeling
of Deformation Mechanisms in Ni-Base
Superalloy 718
D. McAllister, D. Lv, L. Feng, H. Deutchman, A. Wessman, Y. Wang
and M. J. Mills
Abstract Although the relationships between processing and the resulting prop-
erties are relatively well known for alloy 718, a better understanding of the
deformation mechanisms activated across its usable temperature range is needed to
create more mechanistically accurate property models. In this work, direct
atomic-scale imaging with high angle annular dark ﬁeld scanning transmission
electron microscopy (STEM) has been complemented by phase ﬁeld modeling
informed by generalized stacking fault surface calculations using density functional
theory. This coupled experiment/modeling approach has shed light on the complex
shearing processes occurring in alloy 718 following a standard commercial heat
treatment, which produces both monolithic γ and γ″ particles, as well as composite
particles. Deformation at room temperature occurs through complex shearing of γ″
into intrinsic stacking fault con ﬁgurations that were restricted to the precipitates.
Exploration of possible shearing sequences with the aide of phase- ﬁeld dislocation
dynamics has revealed that precipitate shearing by motion of coupled 1/2<110>
dislocations of non-parallel Burgers vectors on the {111} glide plane is the dom-
inant deformation mechanism at lower temperature. A “fast-acting” yield strength
model is discussed which takes into account microstructure variations and defor-
mation mechanism transitions. Deformation at higher temperature (427 and 649 °C)
has revealed a distinct transition in deformation modes, including stacking faults
extending into the matrix, as well as microtwinning. The possible origin of the
temperature and rate dependence of the stacking fault and microtwinning modes
and temperature will be discussed.

## Page 323

Introduction
Alloy 718 is a γ″-strengthened Ni-base superalloy. The γ″ phase is a D0 22 ordered
Ni3Nb structure that forms as lenticular particles with minor axis parallel to the
[001]γ″. Three variants form with [001] γ″ parallel to the three <100> γ principle axes
[1]. Though the γ″ often forms as monolithic particles, certain heat treatments and
compositional modiﬁcations lead to the formation of many composite morphologies
where the γ′ and γ″ form as co-precipitates with the phase boundary along the
(001)γ″ and {100}γ′ [2]. The planar phase boundary is visible in high angle annular
dark ﬁeld mode in scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF STEM)
due to its low intensity from the segregation of Al atoms [ 3]. It has been shown
previously that commercial heat treatments produce large numbers of composite
particles [1]. The formation of these composite particles is not well understood, and
so the driving force, as well as the precipitation and growth mechanisms were
investigated.
Previous studies have been performed to determine the deformation mechanisms
in alloy 718. Depending on the heat treatment of the sample, several shearing
mechanisms have been reported. Early sources predicted that dislocations should
move through the cooperative motion of four like-signed 1/2<110> dislocations,
and these mechanisms were con ﬁrmed in underaged samples [ 4]. Simple antiphase
boundary (APB) formation was predicted in certain studies. Other studies showed
stacking fault formation within the γ″ and the matrix, while microtwinning was
reported in overaged particles [ 5]. So, a consistent understanding of the deformation
mechanisms within commercial samples at a variety of temperatures was sought.
Most current attempts at modeling the yield strength of alloy 718 are based upon
the simpliﬁed assumption that only APB shearing mechanisms can be active. It has
been assumed that either single 1/2<110> dislocations shear the γ″ and leave
behind an APB or the dislocation would loop, depending on particle size. This
method fails to take into account multiple mechanisms that have been seen
experimentally in literature, like microtwinning and stacking fault formation. It also
neglects the formation of composite particles. Co-precipitation may make the
likelihood of shearing and looping dependent on the energies of both phases since
they will be either sheared or looped in tandem.
These current limitations in modeling yield in alloy 718 have led to the study of
active mechanisms and their integration into a mechanistically-accurate yield
strength model. Ideally, a model can be developed that would accurately predict the
microstructure resulting from a given heat treatment and tailor the yield strength
prediction to the microstructure from known mechanisms.
320 D. McAllister et al.

## Page 324

Experimental Methods
Microstructural and deformation characterization were performed primarily using
scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM). A FEI probe corrected
Titan3™ 80–300 S/TEM was used to perform atomic resolution HAADF STEM
imaging on dislocation cores. A FEI image corrected Titan3 ™ G2 60 –300 S/TEM
was used to perform high resolution energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS).
Diffraction-based STEM techniques were performed on a FEI Tecnai F20 S/TEM
system.
Heat treated samples were tensile tested at 72, 800 and 1200 °F at strain rates of
5×1 0
−3 min−1 to failure, and also interrupted at a plastic strain of 0.5%. Lon-
gitudinal cuts were extracted from the gauge length and 3 mm disks were produced.
The 3 mm disks were polished incrementally to a ﬁnal thickness of 90 μm.
A Struers dual-jet electropolisher was operated at −40 °C and 10 V with a solution
of 20% HClO 4 and methanol.
Particle analysis was performed on a sample undergoing a standard heat treat-
ment with selected interruption points. Samples were cut to 1 × 5 × 10 mm and
then encapsulated in argon. A solution heat treatment was performed by encapsu-
lating the sample at 1904 °F for 1 h followed by a water quench in which the
capsule was immediately ruptured. The samples were then subjected to a standard
commercial dual-step heat treatment with an 8 h hold at 1324 °F followed by a cool
at 108 °F/hr to 1148 °F where it was held for an additional 8 h. Interruption points
were chosen at the end of the solutionizing and quench, the end of the ﬁrst 8 h hold,
the end of the cool step, and the ﬁnal microstructure. The chosen interruption points
are indicated in Fig. 1.

## Page 325

Precipitate Microstructure Development
Initial investigation of the γ″ morphology in conventionally heat treated samples
revealed that γ″ commonly forms as composite precipitates with γ′ particles. The
mechanism that leads to the formation of composite particles was sought by looking
at a standard heat treatment with multiple interruption points. It is expected that the
composite particle morphology is bene ﬁcial, so it would be ideal to be able to tailor
the microstructure to improve the particle morphology.
Observation of Precipitate Morphology Evolution
The initial solution and quench step showed no signs of precipitate structure.
Parallel beam diffraction of <001> zones showed no superlattice re ﬂections, and
subsequent HAADF STEM imaging failed to produce any contrast consistent with
γ″ precipitates. So, all precipitation of particles happens during the dual-step heat
treatment if alloy 718 is quenched suf ﬁciently quickly following the supersolvus
solutionization step.
The second interruption point, after the isothermal hold at 1324 °F, showed a
complex microstructure. The γ″ precipitates came in monolithic, single-lobed, and
dual-lobed morphologies. The number fraction of each particle type is indicated in
Fig. 2 for each interruption point as well as the average γ″ major diameter. At this
point, 32.8% of the particles were monolithic, 56.9% were single-lobed, and 6.3%
were dual-lobed particles. The average particle size was 16.5 nm in diameter and
4.9 nm in thickness.
Fig. 2 The morphology and average size of γ″ after each interruption point in the representative
heat treatment presented in Fig. 1
322 D. McAllister et al.

## Page 326

The third interruption point, after the cool step, showed small changes in γ″
morphology. The γ″ size did not change signi ﬁcantly. The particle size was found
to be 14.1 nm in diameter, which is likely within experimental error. Interestingly,
the morphology became slightly more complex than the second interruption point.
The number fraction of monolithic and single-lobed particles decreased to 29.1%
and 46.6% respectively. The dual-lobed microstructure increased signi ﬁcantly to
18.6%.
The ﬁnal interruption point at the end of the heat treatment continued the trends
seen earlier. The average diameter was 15.6 nm, so there was no signi ﬁcant dif-
ference in particle size. The monolithic morphology decreased to only 17.2% of the
number fraction, and the single-lobed morphology accounted for 48.4% of the
particles. About 27.4% of the γ″ particles were dual-lobed.
This analysis indicates that the size of the precipitate microstructure is not
increased with the second hold in commercially processed alloy 718. The bene ﬁto f
the dual-step process seems to be in the evolution of particles from simple
monolithic morphology into more complex morphologies. The more complex
morphologies become more prevalent after the second hold. It is possible that the
composite morphologies are preferred for commercial applications.
The mechanisms by which the composite microstructure forms as well as any
beneﬁts they may provide for the yield strength were sought. The γ″ phase has a
larger lattice parameter that γ′, and both are larger than the lattice in the matrix [ 6].
It would stand to reason that the interfacial energy from the mis ﬁt between the γ″
and the matrix would be signi ﬁcantly higher than that of the γ″ and γ′. Thus, the γ′/
γ″ phase boundary is preferred due to its lower strain energy, so composite pre-
cipitates would be likely to form. Phase ﬁeld modeling has shown that the strain
ﬁeld around the composite particles is lower than a single monolithic γ″. Figure 3
shows the strain ﬁeld around particles varying from 100% monolithic γ′ to 100%
monolithic γ″.
If the interfacial energy for γ″ to form is lowered by composite particle for-
mation, it is likely that the overall stability of the particle will be affected in such a
way that the growth kinetics will be more sluggish. The γ′ would be limited by the
size of the adjacent γ′ since the γ″ would increase its energy signi ﬁcantly if it
outgrew the γ
′. The increased energy is due to the formation of a high energy region
of γ″/matrix (001) interface. Additionally, the existence of a γ′ phase on one side of
the γ″ will limit the amount of Nb that can diffuse into the γ″ from that phase
boundary. The γ′ phase has a lower solubility of Nb, so Nb would not easily be able
to enter the γ″ phase through the γ′ side.
Modeling of Elastic Strain Field of Composite Precipitates
Experimental observations of alloy 718 have shown that commercial heat treat-
ments lead to a large number fraction of γ″ in composite particle morphologies [ 1].
The formation of composite particles can be explained by the evolution of total
Characterization and Modeling of Deformation Mechanisms … 323

## Page 327

energy in microstructure. Preliminary simulations of the strain ﬁeld around com-
posite particles were utilized to understand the drive towards co-precipitation of the
γ″ and γ′ phases. The lattice parameters used for the phase ﬁeld simulation are a γ =
3.6Å, a γ′ = 3.49 Å, a γ″ = 3.62 Å, c/2 γ″ = 3.70 Å as presented in literature [ 7].
As is shown in Fig. 3, the stress ﬁeld of the dual-lobed composite particles
provides insight into how the elastic interaction varies locally. The volume ratio is
characterized with the ration of b/a (see Fig. 4), which can be adjusted from 0 to 1,
indicating from pure γ″ to γ′ particle. In Fig. 4, the mis ﬁt stress ﬁelds σ11, σ22 and
σ12 are displayed. In the case of pure γ″ phase, a very high positive stress levels are
obtained near the particle. In the case of pure γ′ phase, a stress ﬁeld with a small
negative value is obtained near the particle. Although the stress ﬁeld for the γ′ phase
is weak, when b/a = 0.5, the stress ﬁeld of γ″ phase is largely suppressed. The
compensation between elastic stress ﬁelds of γ′ and γ″ phases can be demonstrated
by the total elastic energy as a function of b/a ratio [ 1]. In that work, it is found that
the total elastic energy is obviously reduced when elastic interaction between γ′ and
γ phases is considered. Thus, the composite particle is elastically preferred com-
pared with separated particles.
It should be mentioned that the γ″ phase itself prefers to form a disk-like particle
due to the smaller mis ﬁt of the (001) γ″ plane. In order to reduce the elastic energy
to the minimum amount, the optimal morphology is formed when the (001) plane of
γ″ contacts with γ′ particle. When the contacting surface deviates from (001), much
higher energy will be induced. As a result, for each variant of γ″ phase, only one set
of (001) planes is available for co-precipitation. Consistent with this analysis, the
composite morphologies have been viewed experimentally in all three variants
within grains of commercially heat-treated samples.

Phase Field Modeling of Dislocation Interactions
with Precipitates Structures
This understanding of the precipitate morphology and evolution in commercial
samples lends itself to creating more accurate structures within the phase ﬁeld
model. With more accurate phase ﬁeld modeling inputs, it is possible to gain a
greater understanding of the complex interactions of dislocations with different
particle sizes and morphologies.
Generalized Stacking Fault Surface Calculations
In order to accurately model the shearing modes prominent in γ″, the energy
landscape across a single shear plane was sought. A generalized stacking fault
(GSF) [ 8] surface was formed for the (111) plane of the γ″ phase to help predict
shear modes in the hardening precipitates. This was calculated at 0 K using a
density functional theory (DFT) method using the Vienna ab initio simulation
package (VASP) [ 9, 10]. A projected augmented wave (PAW) [ 11, 12] potential
and generalized gradient approximation (GGA [ 13]) were used according to the
methods detailed by McAllister et al. [ 14].
Initial investigation of the GSF surface for γ″ showed that there were signi ﬁcant
differences from those of the γ′ and γ phases. First, the lower symmetry of the γ″
Fig. 4 Color maps of the strain ﬁeld around idealized spherical particles. Particles range from
pure γ″ to pure γ′ by adjusting the b/a ratio from 0 to 1 in a dual-lobed composite particle
morphology
Characterization and Modeling of Deformation Mechanisms … 325

## Page 329

dictates that the GSF surface has a lower symmetry, and because of this, traditional
dislocations with Burgers vectors of the same magnitude but different directions
will lead to varying fault structures. Additionally, γ″ forms as three variants with
[001]
γ″ parallel to the three principle directions in the matrix. So, any dislocation
interacting with a realistic microstructure would be interacting with all three GSF
surfaces with a 120° rotation. The single shear in the three γ″ variants would lead to
multiple fault types being formed.
A closer look at the GSF gives valuable insight into the shear structures that
could be expected in γ″. The fault structures, which have been detailed previously
[14], are shown in Fig. 5. It can be seen that fault structures that can be accessed by
a single 1/6<112> dislocation are either complex stacking faults (CSF) or intrinsic
stacking faults (ISF). The ISF con ﬁguration has a very low energy (close to that of
the perfect crystal), and it is stable since it sits at a minimum in the energy land-
scape. The CSF con ﬁguration sits at a signi ﬁcantly higher energy, but it sits on a
slope in the energy landscape, making it inherently unstable. Similarly, unstable
conﬁgurations occur after translations of 1/2<110> directions. In the γ′ phase, any
1/2<110> would access a stable antiphase boundary (APB) structure, but the γ″
phase allows for both APB and APB-like structures. APBs in γ″ are both stable and
relatively high energy, but the APB-like structure is high energy and unstable. Since
the APB-like con ﬁguration is unstable, it would not naturally occur following any
shearing event. So, the simple APB shearing predicted in literature is not possible in
2/3 of the γ″ precipitates in a given microstructure region during the passage of a
single 1/2<110>.
Fig. 5 Various fault types can be accessed in the γ″ phase can be seen on the GSF surface of the
{111} plane
326 D. McAllister et al.

## Page 330

Another expectation that the GSF surface reveals is the possible spontaneous
degeneration of a fault structure. If the resolved shear stress (RSS) is such that a full
1/2<110> is able to shear through the particle and leave behind an unstable
APB-like structure (e.g. a 1/2[01 ̄1] in Fig. 5), the resulting structure would likely
spontaneously degenerate into the nearest stable, low energy ISF con ﬁguration.
This would be accomplished by the generation of a partial dislocation loop within
the particle itself (e.g. a single 1/6 [2 ̄11] in Fig. 5 after the shear of the previous
example).
The bene ﬁt of the GSF is that it can be used to inform the fault structure in
realistic particles used in phase ﬁeld modeling of shearing mechanisms. The energy
landscape of the GSF is used to describe the γ″ phase in phase ﬁeld modeling efforts
so realistic dislocation/particle interactions.
Phase Field Modeling of Shearing Mechanisms
In order to investigate the dominating deformation mechanism in alloy 718, phase
ﬁeld simulations are performed in a precipitate microstructure with spatial and size
distribution of particles. The ab initio GSF surface is applied to describe the
stacking fault inside the particles.
Several different dislocation con ﬁgurations are initiated to interact with the
microstructure, which in the cases shown contain only monolithic γ″ particles with
all three of its variants. The crystalline energy contours as well as the deformation
pathways inside γ″ particles are shown in Fig. 6. All the simulations are performed
at 500 MPa, and the applied stress is along the net Burgers vector of dislocation
group.
As is shown in the deformation pathways in Fig. 6, in contrast to the classic
understanding, the spontaneous stacking fault transition prevents the deformation
pathway of the AC pair from reaching the APB in 2nd and 3rd variants of γ″.
Instead, the created partial dislocation triggers the formation of a 1/6<112> type
dislocation loop, which cannot move in either matrix or γ″ particle under the
applied stress. In the 2nd variant a B δ +A δ creates a δC loop. In the 3rd variant the
δB+ δC shear forms a A δ loop. Due to the formation of the 1/6<112> type loops,
the movement of an AC dislocation pair reveals decoupling between leading and
trailing ACs. While the leading AC can shear through all the particles, the trailing
AC forms 1/6<112> type dislocation locks which cannot cut into the 2nd and 3rd
variants of γ″ particles. As a result, the trialing AC can only loop around the 2nd
and 3rd variants of γ″ particles. When the average particle size is small and the
interparticle spacing is narrow, this looping can dramatically increase the critical
shear stress for operation of the AC pair.
In contrast to the AC pair, whose trailing AC is forced to loop around particles,
the activation and movement of an AC + AB dislocation group is actually enhanced
by the spontaneous stacking fault degeneration that leads to partial loops around the

γ″. As is shown in Fig. 7, during the particle shearing, an AC + AB shear will

Following the passage of the ﬁnal partial, a spontaneous stacking fault transition
removes an APB-like fault and leaves an ISF whose stacking fault energy is only
∼2 mJ/m 2. In the 3rd variant, AC + AB directly passes over the GSF barrier,
creates an ISF as an intermediate state, and ﬁnally restores perfect crystal. As a
result, the deformation of an AC + AB pair only creates stacking fault ribbons
which are narrow and easy to move. Furthermore, the AC and AB are strongly
coupled, since the SISF formation in the 1st and 2nd variants and ISF formation in
the 3rd variant require a reaction between the AC and AB dislocations at the
interface of the γ″ in order to effectively shear the γ″. In the 1st variant, the AC
dislocation can only shear after the leading partial of the AB dislocation ( δB)
creates an ISF within the particle. In the 2nd variant, the AC dislocation and the
leading partial of the AB dislocation together create a stable SISF. In the 3rd
variant, the full AC dislocation and leading partial of the AB ( δB) together create an
ISF. The operation of a coupled AC + AB group is supported by STEM obser-
vations where diffraction contrast was seen to be inconsistent with <110>
dislocations [ 14].
Activation of the AB + AC dislocation group is easier than the AC pair when the
particle size is still small (15 –30 nm), since percolation of an AB + AC
closely-coupled pair does not require any kind of looping mechanism. Although the
AB + AC pair would be expected to create an APB in the γ′,i n
commercially-processed alloy 718, the γ′ has roughly 1/3 of the volume fraction of
the γ″ phase, so the AB + AC pair should be the dominating deformation mech-
anism in these alloys. Additional simulation results of AC quadruplet deformation
shows similar phenomena as for the AC pair. For the AC quadruplet, 1/6<112>
type dislocation locks are also formed, and each AC is decoupled from each other.
At 500 MPa, only the ﬁrst two AC can shear through the crystal, while the fol-
lowing two ACs are totally arrested due to the abundant dislocation loops formed
by the ﬁrst dislocations of the group.
In summary, initial results from the phase ﬁeld simulations show that there is a
signiﬁcant reduction to the CRSS on a {111} plane when certain dislocation
conﬁgurations are passed through the substructure. The single 1/2<110> disloca-
tion required the greatest CRSS to pass the dislocation through the entire sub-
structure. A slightly lower CRSS was required to move a pair of like-signed
1/2<110> dislocations through the same structure. This indicates that if a single
type of 1/2<110> is activated, the dislocations would likely shear as
closely-coupled pairs. A similar CRSS would be required to move quadruplets of
like-signed 1/2<110> dislocations.
Initial diffraction contrast analysis indicates that simple 1/2<110> motion is not
operative in commercially heat-treated alloy 718, and neither is the coupled motion
of multiple like-signed 1/2<110> dislocations [ 14]. In fact, the contrast of dislo-
cations was consistent with a <112> type dislocation, but there was not the

Simulation of Dislocation Interaction with Composite
Particles
The simulations summarized in Figs. 6 and 7 assume the presence of the three
different variants of γ″ particles. However, as indicated in Fig. 2, in commercially
heat-treated alloy 718, a signi ﬁcant fraction of the strengthening precipitates are in
the composite γ′/γ″ particle con ﬁgurations. Thus, it is important to assess the
interactions of dislocations with the common composite particles encountered in
order to assess any signi ﬁcant differences relative to monolithic particle
interactions.
Phase ﬁeld simulations are therefore conducted to investigate the deformation
pathway of the dual-lobed structure sheared by an AC + AB dislocation group,
which is shown previously to have the lowest CRSS compared to a single <110>/2
dislocation and a pair of like-signed dislocation group. The same GSF energy
surface (GSF-surface for short hereafter) of variant 2 in γ″ phase used above is
applied again in this simulation. The GSF-surface of γ′ phase is obtained by scaling
the GSF-surface of Ni
3Al so that the fault energies agree with experimental results.
Both GSF-surfaces are applied to the dual-lobed microstructure respectively, where
the γ′ phase in the middle and the γ″ phase on the outside. The GSF-surface of γ
matrix is estimated by using the GSF-surface of pure Ni. This approximation should
not change the validity of current qualitative results. All the heterophase interfaces
are assumed sharp. The applied stress is 800 MPa along the total Burgers vector
direction. No coherency stress is considered for now.
Figure 8 displays the interaction between the dual-lobed structure and an AC +
AB dislocation group. For the γ″ phase of the dual-lobed structure, the leading
partial δC of AC dislocation cuts in ﬁrst and creates an ISF while the trailing partial
Aδ of AC stays at γ″/γ interface. Then the AB dislocation follows and cuts into γ″
particle together with the trailing partial A δ of AC, creating an SISF ribbon fol-
lowed by an APB-like fault in the γ″ particles (see Frame 2 and its inset). Since the
APB-like fault is an unstable fault, a Shockley partial δB nucleates and converts the
APB-like fault into an ISF in γ″.
For the γ′ phase, the AC dislocation cuts in as a whole and creates an APB in the
particle. When AB dislocation cuts in, due to the relatively low SISF energy

Characterization of Dislocation Activity
The complexity of diffraction contrast imaging of dislocation groups, as well as the
obscuring effect that the precipitate strain ﬁelds have on contrast are signi ﬁcant
challenges for conventional TEM approaches and characterizing deformation
mechanisms. In this case, atomic-scale imaging using HAADF can provide a more
direct measurement of shear events and the interaction of slip with monolithic and
composite particles. Dislocations and stacking faults viewed along <110> zone
axes can provide valuable information as to their Burgers vectors, and also reveal a
single variant of the γ′/γ″ interface in the edge-on con ﬁguration. The edge-on
conﬁguration of composite particles is invaluable when deducing the shear history
of the particle. The γ″ composite particles have a low intensity plane at the interface
between the two phases (indicated in Fig. 10) which serves as an inert marker that
allows the shear history to be determined on a single {111} shear plane. The low
intensity plane has been attributed to an Al rich layer at the γ′/γ″ interface [ 3].
Analysis of samples deformed at all three temperatures showed clear evidence of
shearing of particles in both monolithic and composite form. Looping by full
1/2<110> dislocations was not observed around any particles. During these
shearing events, the γ″ phase is invariably sheared into a stacking fault con ﬁgu-
ration with partial dislocations bound to the edge of the particles at all temperatures.
The stacking faults in the γ″ phase are typically consistent with the ultra-low-energy
intrinsic stacking fault (ISF) con ﬁguration when viewed from a single <110> zone.
An example of a sheared composite particle after deformation at room temperature
can be seen in Fig. 10, along with a schematic representation of the fault and the
partial dislocations that bound the extremities of the particle and the transition to the
matrix. Note that the matrix does not exhibit any faults; however, it is clear in this
case that the matrix has been sheared by multiple perfect 1/2<110> dislocations
based upon the offset of the LI plane.
In fact, the sheared con ﬁguration appears to be consistent with the result pre-
dicted in the phase ﬁeld simulation presented earlier in Fig. 8, which is for a similar
composite particle morphology with γ′ in the center and γ″ capping both sides. The

passage of an AC + AB unlike pair results in ISFs in both γ″ phases. Here is no

limits de ﬁnitive determination of this fault. The bounding partial dislocation loop
allows the γ″ to attain the low energy ISF con ﬁguration without creating stacking
faults in the matrix.
At elevated temperatures, stacking faults were often seen extending into the
matrix from the γ″ particles. Extended stacking faults were rare at low temperatures
and became more prominent at 800 °F and above. The reason for this transition is
not presently clear. It is possible that a lowering of the intrinsic stacking fault
energy within the matrix at elevated temperatures allows faults isolated to the γ″
particles to break away and extend through the matrix.
Microtwinning was also observed as a prominent deformation mode in alloy 718
at elevated temperatures, while it was never observed after room temperature
deformation. Deformation at 800 °F produced very thin microtwins isolated to γ″
phase regions, as exempli ﬁed in Fig. 11. In this case, a three-layer twin has been

Some general trends predicted by the GSF surface analysis were validated in the
experimental observations of deformation at all temperatures. First, the γ″ phase
was never seen to be faulted to a position consistent with the APB-like con ﬁgu-
ration. Additionally, and most importantly, clear evidence was found for the
shearing of multiple 1/2<110> dislocations on the same slip plane. The fault
structure contained within some particles indicated that it could have only been
created by the passage of two 1/2<110> dislocations with different Burgers vectors.
Multiple 1/2<110> dislocations were typically visible on the same slip system
within individual grains. This result has con ﬁrmed the phase ﬁeld modeling pre-
diction that groups of different 1/2<110> dislocations would be the most ef ﬁcient
method for shearing the composite precipitates involving the γ″ phase present in
commercially heated-treated alloy 718.
Overall, it has been con ﬁrmed that single and multiple 1/2<110> dislocations
were operative across all temperatures. Though this is the case, complex shearing
mechanisms including microtwinning were also observed that were inconsistent
with the simpli ﬁed models used to predict the yield strength in literature, and
require additional study.
Implementation into a Fast-Acting Model
In this work, a fast-acting yield strength model for alloy 718 has been established.
The model predicts the yield strength of alloy 718 as a function of temperature,
average precipitate size, and volume fraction of γ″ phase. Several major strength-
ening mechanisms have been considered in the model, including (a) precipitation
hardening, (b) lattice strengthening (solid solution hardening (SSH) + forest dis-
location hardening) and (c) grain boundary strengthening (Hall-Petch relation). The
focus of our efforts has been on incorporating temperature-dependent fault energies
and precipitate size and volume fractions predicted from CompuTherm ’s precipi-
tation model into the precipitation hardening module of the fast-acting model, while
contributions from the other strengthening mechanisms are calculated according to
models developed in the literature [ 2, 3] and experimental data [ 16]. The only ﬁtting
Characterization and Modeling of Deformation Mechanisms … 335

## Page 339

parameters in this present model are the stacking fault energies for the γ″ phase and
the cut-off size of particle size distribution.
As shown in Fig. 13, the overall framework of the fast-acting yield strength
model consists of four essential parts: (1) microstructure characterization,
(2) shearing versus looping population prediction, (3) superposition of each
mechanism, and (4) parameter ﬁtting and model validation.
In the ﬁrst part of the model, the major microstructural parameters such as
average particle size and volume fraction are obtained from CompuTherm ’s pre-
cipitation model. The particle size distribution is assumed to be log-normal and its
cut-off particle size is one of the ﬁtting parameters. The aspect ratio of γ″ particles is
important for particle shearing versus looping population prediction and is obtained
from phase ﬁeld simulations.
In the second part of the model, populations of sheared versus looped particles
are calculated as an intermediate output. These calculations require detailed
microstructural inputs including average particle size, volume fraction, cut-off
particle size, and aspect ratio. The population is actually a weighting factor of
different hardening mechanisms. These mechanisms include shearing and looping
of each variant of γ″ phase.
In the third part of the model, the yield strength increment from precipitation
hardening is ﬁrst calculated. This part uses inputs from both the 1st and 2nd parts of
the model. Finally, contributions from all strengthening mechanisms, including
lattice stress hardening (SSH + forest dislocation) and grain boundary
Fig. 13 The framework of fast-acting yield strength model
336 D. McAllister et al.

## Page 340

strengthening (Hall-Petch), are added together and the total yield strength of the
alloy is predicted as a function of temperature.
A successful fast acting yield strength model should be able to predict the yield
strength of polycrystalline materials for a range of microstructures and precipitate
morphologies, while being faithful to the underlying deformation mechanisms. The
principal temperature dependence derives from a change in stacking fault energy.
However, the change in mechanism to microtwinning that is clearly operative at
elevated temperature is not incorporated in the present model, and will be con-
sidered in future work.
Conclusions
Development of a mechanistically-accurate yield strength model for alloy 718 has
required the implementation of complex shearing mechanisms due to the low
symmetry of the sheared γ″ phase. Phase ﬁeld modeling, including input for GSF
calculations via DFT, predicts that shearing of the γ″ phase should occur by the
motion of unlike 1/2<110> dislocation groups, where individual partials often lead
to the formation of low energy intrinsic stacking faults. Atomic resolution high
angle annular dark ﬁeld STEM has shown that multiple 1/2<110> are active on a
single slip plane at multiple temperatures. Many faulted γ″ particles sit at faulted
positions consistent with an ISF con ﬁguration. Additionally, microtwinning is
isolated to the γ″ at intermediate temperatures but extends through the matrix and
multiple particles at 1200 °F. With con ﬁrmation of these deformation mechanisms,
phase ﬁeld modeling can be used to inform a fast-acting model to predict yield
strength values after a given heat treatment. Future versions of the fast acting model
will be able to implement high temperature deformation mechanisms, such as
localized and extended microtwinning.

Introduction
The superior mechanical properties of Ni-based superalloys are generally attributed
to microstructural features, i.e. a mis ﬁt between γ and γ′, solution hardening, and
microstructures involving the grain size of the matrix and precipitates [ 1–4].
Therefore several studies have been conducted to characterize such microstructures
using Scanning and Transmission Electron Microscopy (SEM and TEM) [ 1–4].
Those studies have provided much useful information to improve the understanding
of the qualitative relationship between mechanical properties and microstructures,
but a number of issues remain to be explained. For example, while two step aging is
widely known to be bene ﬁcial for modifying the mechanical properties, the
microstructural origins of these changes have not yet been made clear [ 5]. One of
the reasons can be attributed to the presence of complex multi-scale structures
including three different generations of the γ′ phase, usually referred to as primary,
secondary and tertiary γ′ particles, which decrease in size. In addition, when
compared to the single crystal Ni-based superalloys [ 5], the spatial distribution of
microstructures in polycrystalline superalloys are quite different when observed
over the limited area that direct observations can cover [ 6]. Figure 1 shows one
example of a SEM micrograph of the Ni-based polycrystalline superalloys. Large
primary γ′ particles of a few μm in size exist together with a secondary γ′ phase
having a diameter range of 10 < D < 100 nm, and ﬁne tertiary particles with
D < 10 nm. In addition, there are areas where no particles are observed by SEM.
Since the area observed by TEM or Atom Probe Tomography (APT) is much
smaller than that shown in Fig. 1, we need to be be very careful in the choices of
locations for those observations. Also, the effect of the smallest γ′ particles
(D < 10 nm) is often treated as negligible due to their low volume fraction.
However, an understanding of the formation process of these small particles in the
aging process is likely to be useful for the further precise controlling of mi-
crostructures. Therefore, statistically representative values of size and volume
fraction, including the smallest γ′ particles with D < 10 nm, in a much larger
sampling volume that averages out the local heterogeneity of the microstructure, is
required for a better understanding of the formation process of the ﬁnal mi-
crostructure and producing a quantitative relationship between microstructures and
mechanical properties. For this purpose, we applied Small-Angle X-ray Scattering
(SAXS) to quantitatively characterize the average size and volume fraction of
nano-size γ′ phase in a sample volume that is 10
8 times larger than those investi-
gated by TEM and APT.

Experimental Procedure
SAXS is a method used to analyze the peak in scattered X-rays appearing at the
scattering angle 2θ = 0, although the data is usually expressed as a function of the
scattering vector Q,d e ﬁned as | Q|=4 πsinθ/λ. Although the SAXS curve looks
very different from the diffraction peaks seen in powder diffraction patterns, the
basic analysis of SAXS data is the same as that used in line broadening analysis of
diffraction peaks; a wider peak means smaller size and narrower one corresponds to
larger size. One of the differences between SAXS and powder diffraction is that the
width of SAXS is not affected by the existence of dislocations, which is advanta-
geous for the size analysis of precipitates. The SAXS intensity, I(Q) can be
described as follows;

The formation of ﬁne γ′ particles by aging has been widely shown in previous
studies [ 2, 4, 7], but their average features and quantitative evaluation during the
aging process has not been discussed. SAXS analysis, in contrast, clearly shows
that aging produces an average size of D < 10 nm. Increasing aging time and/or
temperature cause the formation of more of these γ′ particles but their size is still
below 10 nm for the samples aged at Low-T and Mid-T. For High-T, coarsening
occurs and therefore, the size distributions widen, as shown in the Fig. 10b. These
changes seem to be typical of most of the precipitation processes seen in many
systems. In contrast, the change in the scale range from 20 to 100 nm is rather
complicated; initially that volume fraction is decreased by aging from 18 to 24 h
but further two step aging increases the volume fraction again. The same tendency
