has been con ﬁrmed for both Low-T and High-T aging. Note that a decrease in the
number density of secondary particles can also be con ﬁrmed from the SEM
micrograph shown in Fig. 3; the changes from (a) to (b) and (c) correspond to the
formation of particles with 20 < D < 100 nm and from (c) to (d) corresponds to
the decrease of the number density, which accords with the results obtained by
USAXS analysis. Meanwhile, the formation of γ′ particles with D <1 0n m
becoming prominent from 16 to 24 h is con ﬁrmed by the SAXS measurements,
indicating that the formation of such small γ′ particles is stimulated by the disap-
pearance of γ′ particles with 20 < D < 100 nm. Combining the results of SAXS
and SEM, we can say that newly formed γ′ particles with D < 10 nm exist in the
grey regions in SEM where the number density of secondary γ′ is low. The part of
the secondary γ′ particles visible in Fig. 3c disappear and the remaining particles
become larger, as seen in (d) indicating that coarsening occurs, just as usual.
However, during this process, the formation of the particles with D < 10 nm occurs
simultaneously. The reason why it happens can be the difference of the formation
temperature of γ′ particles with 20 < D < 100 nm in As-ST and the early stage of
aging. Because they form during cooling, their composition is different from the
equilibrium composition at the aging temperature. The γ′ phase precipitate on the γ′
particles with 20 < D < 100 nm together with newly nucleate the particle with
D < 10 nm during aging. The newly precipitates γ′ phase are stable at the aging
temperature, but the compositional difference occurs inside and outside of γ′ par-
ticles with 20 < D < 100 nm. Of course, diffusion occurs for making uniform
concentration inside γ′ particles and it cause that the total concentration become off
equilibrium at the aging temperature. Consequently, the number density of γ′
particles with 20 < D < 100 nm decrease in the late stage of precipitates. The
disappearance of γ′ particles with 20 < D < 100 nm cause a change in local
composition and stimulates the formation of the particles with D < 10 nm.
The effect of two steps annealing is as follows; the ﬁrst aging step at Mid-T
forms the
γ′ particles of D < 10 nm with high number density. The second step
aging at High-T causes the growth of those particles and the sizes reaches the range
from 20 to 100 nm, which is the optimum size for increasing hardness. Thus, the
microstructure seen after 16 h single-step and two-step aging looks similar but they
are in some way different, probably due to a difference in composition of the γ′
particles with 20 < D < 100 nm. To con ﬁrm those models, the details of the dif-
ferences in γ′ particles during aging, small-angle neutron scattering (SANS) and
atom probe tomography (APT) analysis is now underway.
Summary
Microstructures of the newly developed P/M Ni-based superalloy, HGN 300 have
been studied by using SEM and SAXS techniques. The results obtained are as
follows;
350 M. Ohnuma et al.

## Page 354

1. In addition to γ′ particles with 20 < D < 100 nm, γ′ particles with D <1 0n m
form as a result of the aging.
2. The number density and size of γ′ particles with 20 < D < 100 nm increases on
aging for 8 and 16 h, while they decrease on aging for 24 h at all annealing
temperatures.
3. Those two results suggest that the formation of γ′ particles with D <1 0n mi s
stimulated by the disappearance of γ′ particles with 20 < D < 100 nm in the
single step aging.
4. Two step aging with the combination of Mid-T and High-T causes the maxi-
mum number density of γ′ particles with 20 < D < 100 nm. Those particles are
the result of growth of the γ′ particles with D < 10 nm formed by the ﬁrst aging
step.
The results show that the aging pathway of forming ﬁnal γ′ particles with
20 < D < 100 nm is through their dissolution and the growth of newly formed
particles with D < 10 nm. Additional data are required to understand the details of
the effect of two step aging.

Development of an Automated Property
Simulation Tool for Direct Aged Alloy
718 Engine Disk Forgings
Martin Stockinger, Aleksandar Stanojevic, Volker Wieser
and Peter Raninger
Abstract As the optimization of highly demanding engine parts like engine disks
pushes the materials used to their limits, the estimation of the material properties
becomes increasingly important. The complex interactions of strengthening
mechanisms in direct aged (DA) Alloy 718 forgings demand detailed modeling of
each mechanism. As some strengthening mechanisms are in ﬂuenced during the
billet processing it is essential to consider the forging stock manufacturing in the
design process of forged engine disks. Therefore, a ﬁnite element analysis of the
billet processing was incorporated in an existing simulation chain of the closed die
forging process of engine disks. It includes all thermo-mechanical operations after
vacuum arc remelting, i.e. homogenization, upsetting, drawing and radial forging of
the billet as well as prepressing, forging and heat treatment of a disk. In order to
implement the local variations of microstructure caused by the billet processing a
newly developed grain class model was applied. Furthermore a duplex mi-
crostructure, which is often present in the surface region of the billet, was con-
sidered using the grain class model. For a sound precipitation modeling the local
temperature history of the whole simulation chain was considered in the
thermo-kinetic software tool MatCalc. After parameterization of the MatCalc
model, parameters for the precipitation, solid solution and grain boundary contri-
bution to the total yield strength was calculated. For the determination of the
DA-effect a semi-empirical, deterministic model was developed. The established,

Keywords Alloy 718 ⋅ Microstructure modeling ⋅ Mechanical properties

Introduction
During service life and especially during take-off and landing high and low pressure
turbine disks made of alloy 718 are exposed to high thermal and mechanical loads.
These loads are consequently re ﬂected in quite narrow material and part speci ﬁ-
cations of the engine producers. The challenge for the design of the production
process is therefore focused on reaching the desired properties. In addition, the time
for production process quali ﬁcation and the costs for design and trials have to be
optimized. These requirements led to an increasing application of simulation tools
in the design process in the past two decades, e.g. [ 1].
Usually ﬁnite element codes are used to describe strain, strain rate and tem-
perature development during the closed die forging and heat treatment processes.
Additionally, most FEM codes like DEFORM ™ offer the possibility to include
mean value based semi-empirical microstructure models to describe the develop-
ment of grain size due to recrystallization and grain growth as for instance described
in [ 2–4]. These models are not capable of describing the development of duplex
structures or ALA grains, and thus their in ﬂuence on mechanical properties can ’tb e
considered.
Whereas the full production chain, which affect the microstructure and properties
in the part, consists of melting, re-melting, homogenization annealing, upsetting,
cogging, closed die forging and heat treatment (Fig. 1) the in ﬂuence of the pro-
cesses before closed die forging are in most cases neglected.
Fig. 1 Typical production chain of nickel-based engine disk [ 5, 6]
354 M. Stockinger et al.

## Page 357

Besides the typical radial variation of the microstructure in Alloy 718 triple and
double melt billet material; signi ﬁcant longitudinal and circumferential variations
have also been found in statistical analysis. This leads to non-axisymmetric me-
chanical properties in the ﬁnal part, and therefore neglecting the billet production
processes in the simulation chain may be a risk for the part design.
The goal of the research performed in the last few years was therefore:
• Implementing the in ﬂuence of billet production in the simulation chain
• Improve the microstructure model to consider in-homogeneities
• Include the new models in the prediction of mechanical properties like yield
strength
Billet Processing
The typical steps for the production of billets used for forging engine disks are
shown in Fig. 1. In a cross functional team, between disk manufacturer and billet
manufacture, a root cause analysis to evaluate main in ﬂuences across the production
chain on radial variation of the ﬁnal microstructure was performed. Whereas the last
melting steps and the homogenization cycle were quoted with high severity, but low
probability, the cogging steps (hydraulic drawing and/or radial forging) where rated
with medium severity and medium probability. Therefore the focus was set on
evaluating the later processes using FEM modeling.
Looking at the temperature distribution in the upsetting process it is obvious that
if the process is performed without bowing, tangential variation is negligible; but
signiﬁcant gradients can be seen in radial and longitudinal direction due to die chill,
heat transfer and adiabatic heating, see Fig. 2 left. Evaluating the temperature
distribution of cogging processes, like that demonstrated in Fig. 2 right, tempera-
ture gradients are visual in all directions. As in the upsetting process, die chill and
heat transfer are responsible factors, but due to the constraint of a ﬁnite die bite
width and the rotational and longitudinal movement of the manipulator, additional
variations in the circumferential direction can occur, see Fig. 3. Further, an effect
which results in very localized temperature differences, comes from the contact of
the manipulator grips on top and bottom of the billet.
In addition, the strain introduced in each of the cogging processes varies similar
like the temperature as shown in Fig. 4. Depending on the die size and the forging
process, hydraulic presses or radial forging machine, the strain gradient may look
different.
In order to create a more homogenous microstructure distribution for the billet,
temperature and strain history for all steps have to be balanced carefully. Dynamic
recrystallization should occur in every forging run to re ﬁne the overall structure.
Low strain areas, which may result in abnormal grain growth in subsequent
reheating processes, should be avoided. Using FEM coupled microstructure models

the microstructure can be easier understood as seen in Fig. 5. Due to localized
deformation with different accumulated strains, strain rates, temperatures and dwell
times between bites, evaluation of the implemented model is challenging. Therefore
the microstructure model used for cogging, and in particular for the radial forging
process, needs further evaluation.
In order to consider the above mentioned microstructure variations in the sub-
sequent closed die forging process, the ideal process would be to model each billet
production process according to the actual forging process. Since the billet has to be
sectioned according input weight for the subsequent closed die forging process,
each billet section has to be considered in the simulation chain. This means each

according to the ﬁxed process recipe and to account for the microstructure variation
in the subsequent modeling of the closed die forging into account.
Improvement of the Microstructure Model
The microstructure model currently used in the design of the closed die forging
process, as well as part of the prediction of mechanical properties in the ﬁnal part, is
based on [ 7]. There are two basic physical phenomena, which are described by

The second model set describes all recrystallization effects including dynamic,

deformed structure either during the forming process or during subsequent heating

where X d is the mean recrystallized fraction as a function of strain, φ. The critical
strain for the start of dynamic recrystallization, φc, as well as the strain at 50%

perature and strain rate. The Avrami exponent, a drx, is a material dependent con-
stant. More details can be found in [ 2–4, 6–8].
In order to consider grain size distributions as input quantities in the FEM
models and to describe inhomogeneities, like duplex structures or as-large-as
(ALA) grains after forging and heat treatment, a grain class model has been
developed using the same principle semi-empirical formulations as in the mean
value model. The main problem in such models is the description of the change of
sub-fractions in the sub-routines of the FEM software. Assuming a uniform dis-
tribution of grain fractions in 10 classes at the beginning of a forging step, each
class has a different φ
c and φ0,5 according Eq. 2 and results in a smaller grain size
with fraction X d. This new fraction has to be added to the corresponding grain size
class after the relevant process has been ﬁnished, e.g. the strain rate is zero in case
of dynamic recrystallization. An example is shown in Fig. 6 where a deformation at
a constant temperature with a constant strain rate leads to a reduction of fractions in
the class regime between ASTM 7.5 and 11 as well as in an increase of fraction in
the ﬁne classes ASTM 11.5 and 12. The same process has to be performed for
post-dynamic and static recrystallization. In addition, the physical constraint that
the sum of all fractions must be 1.0 has to be ful ﬁlled in each ﬁnite element at each
time step. This obvious requirement becomes essential if re-meshing steps are
included during the simulation. Dependent on the dimension of the model (2D, 3D)
a FEM software speci ﬁc algorithm is used to transfer all element speci ﬁc values,
like temperature, strain, strain rate but also size fractions from the old to the new
358 M. Stockinger et al.

## Page 361

mesh. For grain class models this frequently leads to a violation of the before
mentioned constraint of the sum of fractions. Furthermore, if a fraction of one or
more elements which take part in the interpolation to a new element is zero the
resulting grain size in this fraction is too small. Therefore it is necessary to apply
sufﬁcient corrections in order to avoid errors in the ﬁnal results.
In case of grain growth, the change from the mean value model to the grain size
class model is straightforward. The main aspect to be considered is the change of
classes for each growing fraction in each element and time step. An example is
shown in Fig. 7, where for instance the grains in class ASTM 12 grow from a mean
diameter of 5.6 µm until they reach the next coarser class. In case the fraction is
attributed to class ASTM 11.5 and class ASTM 12 disappears, the resulting grain
size in class ASTM 11.5 corresponds to the weighted average of the contributing
fractions within the class. The procedure is repeated for every class if the diameter
reaches the limit for the next coarser one.
Despite the fact that the mathematic approach for the grain size model uses only
basic arithmetical operations, the implementation in the FEM code is a challenge.
Whereas the mean value model below has 50 user variables, the grain class model

Comparing the mean value model with the grain class model in a simple pre-

the grain class model show very similar mean grain sizes (Fig. 9). In the subsequent
reheating process, after post dynamic recrystallization and enough time for sig-
niﬁcant grain growth, the two models show a deviation of up to one grain class
(Fig. 10). The deviation can be attributed to the slightly different recrystallization
and growth kinetics of individual grain classes compared to a single average class.
These differences add up and become visible at the end of the simulation.

Prediction of Yield Strength Including Process
Variation In ﬂuences
One of the main parameters for the design of an engine disk is the minimum yield
strength. Therefore, the prediction of this property, and its dependence on the
production process for critical areas of the disk de ﬁned by the engine producer, is
very important. In order to reach this goal, the main strengthening effects, which are
strain hardening, grain boundary strengthening, precipitation strengthening, solid
solution strengthening and the direct age effect, should be taken into account.
Summarizing the main ﬁndings published in [ 10] this means:
(a) The base strength for nickel as well as the strain hardening is currently
implemented as a constant value [ 10].
(b) Prediction of grain boundary strengthening σ
gb according to Hall-Petch (3) with
k the Hall-Petch parameter and the mean grain size d. In this case d is derived
from the FEM coupled microstructure model [ 11, 12]
σgb = k ⋅ 1ﬃﬃﬃ
d
p ð3Þ
(c) Prediction of precipitation effects in case of Alloy 718 on γ′ and γ″ assuming
that the coherency hardening delivers the signi ﬁcant contribution using the
thermos kinetic software MatCalc [ 13]
(d) Solid solution strengthening using the Gypen-Deruyttere model also imple-
mented in MatCalc [ 14]
(e) A phenomenological model based on the forming conditions during the last
forge step, which determines the dislocation arrangement, has been imple-
mented to consider the direct age effect. Since published in [ 10] several further
disks have been used for validation as discussed in [ 15]. This model is also
implemented in the FEM subroutine.
The simulation chain consists of three software packages which are controlled
via an Octave script. The billet and/or disk forging process is simulated with the
commercial FEM package DEFORM ™ delivering temperatures, strains, strain
rates, and grain size classes in each element as an output. The evolution of the
precipitates is calculated for each area of interest in the ﬁnal disk shape using the
thermal history of the FEM simulation as an input in the thermo-kinetic software
MatCalc. As an example, each of the time-temperature histories of four points along
the radius of a rotary forging pass, as shown in Fig. 11, have been used as an input
for the production simulation of a disk. Even though this procedure is of no
practical use, it offers an easy way to investigate the in ﬂuences of the billet pro-
duction process. For further simpli ﬁcation, no variances of processes prior to the

A further step towards an improved design process has been generated by
including an automatic variation of relevant process parameters in the disk pro-
duction like transfer times, furnace temperatures, die speed and ﬁnal die distances.
Of course, a full DOE of all parameters would result in an enormous amount of
simulation time and lengthy analysis. Therefore, only those parameters, which are
also varying in the actual production process, have to be considered in the relevant
range. For instance a Latin hypercube sampling may be chosen to reduce the
number of quasi experiments to a manageable number [ 16], but at least a best, mean
and worst case scenario has to be considered. In any case, if all simulation results
deliver mechanical properties and grain sizes within speci ﬁcation, a robust pro-
duction process can be guaranteed. As an example, in Fig. 14, the in ﬂuence of die
distance variation in a pre-pressing operation on the yield strength at ﬁve different
points shows there is no optimum stroke for any of the points. However, for points
1 and 5 in the rim section, a slight variation of 1 mm results in a reduction
of ∼50 MPa. Another example is shown in Fig. 15. By varying the transfer time
between furnace and forging equipment, a clear optimum in the yield strength can
be identi ﬁed around 35 s for all ﬁve tracked points in the disk.

## Page 368

Conclusions
It has been demonstrated that it is possible to simulate the production chain from
ingot upsetting to ﬁnal heat treatment of an engine disk including microstructure
and yield strength modeling. The in ﬂuence of position dependent variances of the
time-temperature curves in the billet production process can be considered in the
subsequent closed die forging process. Simulating each billet produced, followed
by a part speci ﬁc 3D simulation of the closed die process would be the most
accurate, but due to the lengthy total simulation time, it is economically not pos-
sible. Therefore, simulating a set of worst, mean and best case billet production
processes, in accordance with the ﬁxed method of manufacturing, using a newly
developed grain class model has been proposed.
This also offers the possibility to consider non-uniform microstructures like
bimodal or ALA grains in the disc production process. Currently, more effort is
being put into additional double cone trials to further improve the model parame-
ters, for instance post dynamic recrystallization and abnormal grain growth, as
proposed by Aoki et al. [ 17]. To consider typical variation of a closed die forging
process in the design process, an automatic DOE simulation process including the
modeling of mechanical properties has also been developed. Overall, both models
offer the possibility to evaluate the robustness of the designed closed die forging
process before forging the ﬁrst part and therefore reduce the probability of
non-conforming parts during serial production.

Microstructure Dependence of Dynamic
Impact Behaviour of ATI 718plus ®
Superalloy
G. Asala, J. Andersson and O. A. Ojo
Abstract ATI 718Plus ® is a γ′-strengthened nickel-based superalloy developed to
substitute the widely used Alloy 718 in aero-engine applications. This newer su-
peralloy is a candidate material for aero-engine turbine structures, with the
requirement to withstand impact loading occurring at high strain rates during tur-
bine blade out events. Furthermore, the understanding of the high strain rate
response of ATI 718Plus
® is important in optimising its machinability during
cutting operations. To predict and model the behaviour of ATI 718Plus ® during
these events and in other dynamic impact applications, proper understanding of the
high strain rate behaviour of the alloy is important, but not presently available.
Therefore, in this work, the in ﬂuence of microstructural condition and strain rates
on dynamic impact behaviour of ATI 718Plus
®, using a modi ﬁed version of direct
impact Hopkinson bar, is investigated. It is observed that the age-hardened alloy
exhibits a signi ﬁcantly reduced strain hardening and strain rate hardening capa-
bilities compared to the solution heat treated microstructure. Furthermore,
microstructural examination of the deformed samples shows that the formation of
adiabatic shear bands, which usually serve as damage nucleation site, is substan-
tially suppressed in the solution heat treated microstructure, while the aged mi-
crostructure exhibits high propensity to form localised shear bands.

Introduction
In a bid to economically increase the operating temperature of the extensively used
Ni-Fe based superalloy, Alloy 718, ATI 718Plus ® was developed through some
signiﬁcant compositional variation to its baseline alloy [ 1]. The modi ﬁcation
resulted in the change of the main strengthening phase from the metastable γ″ phase
in Alloy 718 to a more stable γ′ phase in ATI 718Plus ®. This alteration in the
principal strengthening phase has been found to increase the working temperature
of ATI 718Plus
® to about 55 °C over which is normally stipulated for Alloy 718
without signi ﬁcantly affecting its process-ability [ 2].
This recent alloy, is seen as a candidate material for turbine engine containment
system [3] with the requirement to withstand dynamic impact loading, at high strain
rates, in a possible blade-out event. Furthermore, the understanding of the defor-
mation behaviour of the alloy under high strain rate is important to model and
optimise the machinability of ATI 718Plus
®. The dynamic behaviour of materials
and their tendency to adiabatic shear failure, is known to be in ﬂuenced by loading
conditions, some of the material ’s properties and most importantly its microstruc-
ture [ 4].
The effect of microstructure, especially the presence of strengthening precipi-
tates, have been reported to either improve the dynamic fracture resistance of alloys
or to increase their propensity to failure depending on the nature of the precipitates
[5, 6]. Recent dynamic impact study of Alloy 718 has shown that the alloy ’s
microstructure, particularly the presence of γ″ precipitates have a signi ﬁcant effect
on its dynamic failure behaviour [ 7, 8]. Although several works have been carried
out recently in understanding the effect of the change in the principal strengthening
phase, in ATI 718Plus
®, on the mechanical properties, little or no work has been
done in investigating this effect on its dynamic impact behaviour.
Therefore, the aim of this work is to investigate the microstructure dependence
of dynamic impact behaviour of ATI 718Plus ®, in terms of the alloy ’s heat treat-
ment condition.
Materials and Methods
Material
The material investigated in this work is a hot-rolled ATI 718Plus ® plate with
dimension 12.5 × 110 × 45 mm and having a chemical composition as presented
in Table 1. Cylindrical test specimens (9.5 mm dia. × 9.5 mm in length) were
machined using electric discharge machine (EDM) for both the quasi-static and
dynamic tests. The test specimens were subjected to different heat treatment to
produce two microstructures —solution heat treated microstructure and an aged
microstructure. The heat treatment procedures for the two conditions and the

Dynamic Impact Test
The dynamic properties of the alloys, at high strain rates, are investigated using a
direct impact Hopkinson pressure bar (DIHPB). The schematic diagram of the
DIHPB is shown in Fig. 2. The equipment consist of a transmitted bar and a
projectile, both 38 mm in diameter and made of AISI 4340 steel, a gas gun used to
ﬁre the projectile, and a strain gauge attached to the transmitter bar which is
connected to a differential ampli ﬁer and a digital oscilloscope to capture the strain
history during the impact test. The length of the projectile and the transmission bar
are 225 mm and 1.5 m respectively. Deformation tests using this equipment has
been discussed in detail elsewhere [ 9]. To minimise friction, the ends of the bar is
grounded and polished and lubrication is applied at the bar-specimen interface.

Results
Quasi-static Compression Test
The quasi-static compression test results for the two microstructures of ATI
718Plus®, deformed to 400 kN, is presented in Fig. 3a. The solution heat treated
alloy shows a signi ﬁcantly lower yield strength (about 350 MPa) compared to the
aged alloy with yield strength close to 1200 MPa. Despite the signi ﬁcantly high
strength of the aged alloy, strain hardening dominates the deformation of the alloys
in both heat treated conditions. Figure 3b presents the work hardening rate, which is
the slope of the true stress-true strain curve,
dσ
dε, for the alloys in both heat treatment
conditions. From the curves, it can be noted that the strain hardening rate of the
aged alloy decreases rapidly until it saturates to 1750 MPa/unit strain at 0.3 strain.
The strain hardening rate in the solution heat treated specimen, however, initially
decrease rapidly to about 0.05 strain, then saturates temporarily at 2750 MPa,
before decreasing steadily to 1750 MPa/unit strain. A signi ﬁcant decrease in the
strain hardening rate for the aged specimen between 0.65 and 0.7 strain can be

Dynamic Impact Test
The dynamic impact test results for the solution heat treated and aged ATI 718Plus ®
is presented in Fig. 4a. Similar to the observation in the quasi-static test, the aged
alloy shows a superior strength, but strain hardening is more pronounced in the
solution heat treated alloy. In contrast to the behaviour of the alloys under
quasi-static loading, the effect of thermal softening is observed to quickly dominate
the strain hardening response of the alloy under dynamic loading. The inception of
adiabatic heating leading to strain localisation occurs when the strain hardening rate
curve of the material decreases below zero. Figure 4b shows the strain hardening
rate of the alloys under dynamic loading as a function of true strain. It can be
observed that thermal softening is more pronounced in the aged specimen where
strain hardening curve rapidly drops below zero at about 0.155 strain. The solution
heat treated specimen however, shows signi ﬁcant work hardening response to
suppress the strain localisation, caused by thermal softening, until about 0.4 strain.
Table 3 summarise the condition of the specimens after deformation in reference to
the dynamic test in Fig. 4a. It is observed that the propensity to adiabatic shear
failure is higher in the aged alloy as fragmentation of the sample occurred at
3500 s
−1 strain rate. In the solution heat treated alloy, the appearance of adiabatic
shear band and cracking begins to appear at 4600 s −1 strain rate.

strain rates which provides an idea of the strain rate sensitivity of the alloys. ATI
718Plus
®, in both heat treatment conditions, shows a positive strain rate sensitivity

The micrographs of deformed solution heat treated specimen on Fig. 7a shows that
signiﬁcant bulk deformation occurred in the alloy before the onset of shear localisa-

the grains along the shear band and minor bulk deformation of the sample.
Discussion
It can be seen from the results that the heat treatment condition of the ATI 718Plus ®
and the loading rates have great in ﬂuence on its deformation behaviour. The studied
conditions of ATI 718Plus ® in this work, are comparable to those typically
encountered during machining and in the service life of aero-engine structures.
Under both loading conditions, the age-hardened alloys exhibit a greater ﬂow stress,
compared to the solution heat treated alloy, which can be attributed to the stronger
inﬂuence of strengthening precipitates, in the age-hardened alloys, to impede the
movement of dislocation. However, the aged-hardened alloy shows a greater ten-
dency to strain localisation when compared to solution heat treated alloy. In the peak
aged condition, the strengthening of ATI 718Plus
® is believed to be provided by the
anti-phase boundary (APB) effects from dislocation shearing of γ′ precipitates and
coherency strain effects arising from the γ′–γ misﬁt. [12]. Since the alloy deforms by
the shearing of γ′ precipitates, it is proposed that, it is much easier for slip to occur
within existing active planes of the aged alloy, where precipitates had already been
sheared, than on other inactive slip systems [ 8]. This decreases the strain hardening
behaviour of the age-hardened alloy, and tends to promote strain localisation as seen
in the micrograph on Fig. 7b. In the solution heat treated alloys, where the precip-
itates are very ﬁne and easily shearable, slip on hitherto inactive planes can be
activated as the slip on the existing system becomes more dif ﬁcult, which can attest
to the bulk deformation seen in the micrograph of the solution heat treated specimen
in Fig. 7a. Moreover, during dynamic loading of materials, it is known that sig-
niﬁcant rate of strain hardening can aid the suppression of strain localisation that
leads to the formation of detrimental adiabatic shear band. [ 13]. The lower strain
hardening tendency of the age-hardened alloy may promote higher propensity to
adiabatic shear failure, compared to the solution heat treated alloy, which exhibits a
considerable strain hardening capability to suppress shear localisation.
Conclusion
The microstructure dependence of alloy ATI 718Plus ®, in term heat treatment
condition, was investigated under quasi-static and dynamic loading. Deformation
results showed that ATI 718Plus
®, in both the age-hardened and solution heat
treatment, showed increasing ﬂow stress with increase in strain rates.
Microstructure Dependence of Dynamic Impact Behaviour … 377

## Page 379

In contrast to the alloy ’s behaviour under quasi-static loading, where strain
hardening dominates the deformation, ATI 718Plus ® suffers from adiabatic heating
and thermal softening leading to strain localisation and adiabatic shear failure
occurred under dynamic impact loading.
Under the impact loading, age-hardened ATI 718Plus
® showed a greater
propensity to strain localisation and adiabatic shear failure than the solution heat
treated alloy. While the solution heat treated alloy exhibits an extensive bulk
deformation before shear localisation, the age-hardened alloy displays a more
localised deformation with only minor bulk deformation before failure. This sug-
gests that, though the solution heat treated ATI 718Plus
® possesses lower yield and
tensile strengths compared to the age-hardened alloy, it may, however, perform
better than in the aged condition, under ballistic impact deformation, with respect to
resistance to damage.

3D Stochastic Modelling
of Microstructure Evolution During
Solidiﬁcation of Alloy 718
Laurentiu Nastac
Abstract A three-dimensional (3D) stochastic model for simulating the evolution
of dendritic crystals during the solidi ﬁcation of alloys has been developed. The
model includes time-dependent computations for temperature distribution, solute
redistribution in the liquid and solid phases, curvature, and growth anisotropy. The
current 3D simulation software was written in Fortran 90 with threading (shared
memory system with multiple cores) in both native Linux and Windows threads.
This 3D software is highly ef ﬁcient. It can run on PCs with reasonable amount of
RAM and CPU time. 3D stochastic mesoscopic simulations at the dendrite tip
length scale were done to simulate the evolution of the columnar and equiaxed
dendritic microstructures, columnar-to-equiaxed transition and segregation patterns
during solidi ﬁcation of alloy 718.
Keywords Alloy 718
⋅ Solidiﬁcation ⋅ Microstructure evolution
3D modelling
Introduction
A two-dimensional (2D) stochastic model has been proposed for the modelling of
the evolution of dendritic morphologies during solidi ﬁcation [ 1]. The signi ﬁcance
of the stochastic modelling approach is that the evolution of simulated micro-
structures can be directly visualized and compared with the actual microstructures
from experiments at two different scales: dendrite grain characteristics such as grain
size and location and size of the columnar-to-equiaxed transition can be visualized

## Page 381

at the meso-scale, while dendrite morphology (including dendrite tip, various
dendrite arm spacings, microsegregation patterns) can be viewed at the microscale.
One of the challenges associated with stochastic modelling is reduction in mesh
anisotropy. Basically, because of mesh anisotropy, dendrites will grow aligned with
the axis of the mesh or at 45° independently of the initial crystallographic orien-
tation, which can be called anisotropy in growth direction. Furthermore, dendrites
aligned with the axis would have narrower tips than predicted by classic theories,
which can be termed anisotropy in growth kinetics. To reduce the mesh anisotropy,
a formulation to correct the curvature in 2D was proposed and successfully vali-
dated [2]. A detailed discussion about correcting the grid anisotropy using the phase
ﬁeld approach is presented in [ 3].
Detailed comparison of predictions with measured microstructures requires the
2D stochastic model to be extended to 3D. This is why several 3D models for
simulating dendritic growth have been proposed in the literature including phase
ﬁeld approach [ 3, 4] and Lattice Boltzmann and Cellular Automaton approach [ 5].
To be efﬁcient, these models require parallel computations and can be used only for
relatively small domains. A 3D Cellular Automaton approach for modelling the
evolution of dendritic grains has also been developed [ 6]. This 3D dendritic grain
model is relatively fast but it cannot simulate the evolution of dendrites and of
microsegregation patterns at the dendrite tip level.
The main goal of the current contribution is to develop and then utilize an
efﬁcient 3D stochastic mesoscale dendritic nucleation and growth modelling code,
which is based on the recently developed 3D stochastic mesoscale model presented
in [ 7], to predict the formation of 3D microstructures and segregation patterns
including the columnar-to-equiaxed transition in alloy 718. The 3D model includes
computations for convective velocity, temperature, solute, curvature and anisotropy
at the dendrite tip level.
Model Description
The mathematical representation of the dendritic solidi ﬁcation process of a binary
alloy is considered in a restricted 3-D domain ( Ω). A cross section of this 3D
domain is shown in Fig. 1. Here, n⃗is the interface normal vector, K is the mean
curvature of the interface, and the curve Γ represents the solid/liquid (S/L) interface
which evolves in time and has to be found as part of the solution.
The solidi ﬁcation of binary alloys is governed by the evolution of the temper-
ature Tx , y, z, tðÞ and concentration Cx , y, z, tðÞ ﬁelds that have to satisfy several
boundary conditions at the moving S/L interface as well as the imposed initial and
boundary conditions on the computational domain. The equations that describe the
physics of the solidi ﬁcation process in 3-D Cartesian coordinates are as follows (see
the 2D equations in [ 1, 6, 8, 9]).

where TEQ
L is the equilibrium liquidus temperature of the alloy, mL is the liquidus
slope, K is the mean curvature of the S/L interface, Γ is the Gibbs-Thomson
coefﬁcient, and f φ, θðÞ is a coefﬁcient that accounts for growth anisotropy, where φ
is the growth angle ( i.e., the angle between the normal and the growth axis) and θ is

In Eq. ( 6), second term in the right side is the constitutional undercooling and
the last term in the right side is the curvature undercooling. The interface tem-
perature is also affected by the kinetic undercooling. The kinetic undercooling is not
accounted for in this model since its effect becomes signi ﬁcant only at very high
solidiﬁcation velocities (i.e., in the rapid solidi ﬁcation regime). Also, the coef ﬁcient
f φ, θðÞ in Eq. ( 6) assumes an axisymmetric approximation where the anisotropy
and the interface shape are independent of the polar angle ϕ in the x-y plane per-
pendicular to the growth axis [ 2].
The solidiﬁcation process is governed by Eqs. ( 1)–(6) and a stochastic model for
nucleation and growth. In addition, Navier-Stokes equations (continuity and
momentum equations) are solved in 3D to account for natural convection. The
numerical procedures for calculating the nucleation and growth, temperature and
concentration ﬁelds as well as the growth velocity of the S/L interface are described
in detail in [ 10]. It consists of a regular network of cells that resembles the geometry
of interest. The model is characterized by (a) geometry of the cell; (b) state of the
cell; (c) neighborhood con ﬁguration; and (d) several transition rules that determine
the state of the cell. In this work, the geometry of the cell is a cube. Each cell has
three possible states: “liquid”, “interface”,o r “solid”. The selected neighborhood
conﬁguration is based on the cubic von Neumann ’sd eﬁnition of neighborhood, that
is the ﬁrst order con ﬁguration and it contains the ﬁrst six nearest neighbors.
Solidiﬁcation behavior depends to a great extent on the transition rules. In this
model, the change of state of the cells from “liquid” to “interface” to “solid” is
initiated either by nucleation or by growth of the dendrites.
An explicit ﬁnite difference scheme is used for calculating the concentration
ﬁelds in the liquid and solid phases. Zero- ﬂux boundary conditions were used for
cells located at the surface of the geometry. The solution algorithm includes the
“interface” cells by multiplying the concentration in the liquid by the liquid fraction
and the concentration in the solid by the solid fraction of the particular interface
cell. Also, during each time-step calculation and for each “interface” cell, the

Results and Discussion
Thermo-physical properties of the alloys used in simulations are presented in
Table 1. The domain size is 10 mm × 30 mm × 2 mm for the geometry in Fig. 2
and 10 mm × 20 mm × 1 mm for the geometry in Fig. 3. Newton cooling
boundary condition was applied only to the bottom of the computational domain.
All other boundaries were perfectly insulated. The surface heat transfer coef ﬁcient
used in the current simulations is h = 3.0 × 10
3 Wm −2 K−1. Zero- ﬂux solute
boundary conditions were applied at the boundaries of the computational domain
(i.e., a closed system was assumed). The initial melt temperature was 1400 °C.
Also, an initial concentration equal to C
o was assumed everywhere on the com-
putational domain.
In Fig. 2a, c, middle cross sections of 3D simulated microstructures at two
different times during the unidirectional solidi ﬁcation of alloy 718-5 wt% Nb are
presented. The legend in Fig. 2 shows 256 color indexes ( CI) (shown here in 16
classes, where each class contains 16 different colors), which are used for dis-
playing the preferential crystallographic orientation angle. The competition between

The strong growth competition from the sample bottom (>30 dendrites) to 1/4 of
the sample height (24 dendrites) to 1/2 of the sample height (10 dendrites) to 3/4 of
the sample height (7 dendrites) can be observed in Fig. 2. Figure 2 also shows the
formation of the columnar-to-equiaxed transition (CET). The competition between

shown in Fig. 2. In Fig. 2, the equiaxed grain density was 10

Concluding Remarks
A 3D microstructure model was developed and implemented in Fortran 90 with
threading (shared memory system with multiple cores) in both native Linux and
Windows threads. The model was applied to study the formation of CET and
segregation patterns in 3D domains. The model is highly ef ﬁcient. The 3D simu-
lation problems shown in the current study took only a few hours on a Dell XPS
laptop with 4 cores.
The developed 3D model can be applied to study the CET formation during
solidiﬁcation of alloy 718 and other superalloys under different solidi ﬁcation
conditions. Consequently, it can be used to assist in the solidi ﬁcation process
improvements of various cast superalloys.

Analysis of Microporosity-Dependent
Fatigue Crack Behavior in Alloy 718
by Using Synchronic Radiation X-Ray
CT and FEM
Yahui Liu, Maodong Kang, Yun Wu, Mengmeng Wang, Haiyan Gao
and Jun Wang
Abstract Inﬂuence of microporosity on the mechanical properties of superalloy
have been studied by numerical and experimental methods for long time. In this
paper, the real morphology of microporosity in polycrystalline Alloy 718 specimens
was inspected by synchronization radiation X-ray micron computerized tomogra-
phy ( μCT) and 3D model was reconstructed for the numerical simulation based on
ﬁnite element method (FEM). Fatigue testing of the heat treated samples and heat
isostatic pressured samples were conducted to verify the numerical analysis.
Response surface analysis based on FEM was used to establish the linear function
relationship between fatigue life and factors including of porosity, pre-deformation
and residual stress. The simulation results showed that the interdendritic region on
the surface of microporosity was the place of stress concentration in metal and the
crack site of fatigue failure. Experimentally, heat treated sample fractured at mi-
croporosity, while the HIPed samples disrupted due to the matrix ductile fracture.
The good agreement was obtained between the simulation and experimental results.

Introduction
As an excellent instance, Alloy 718 has been utilized in turbine engine for long time to
manufacture the key components including of casing, blade, and so on [ 1]. Con-
ventional investment casting is one of the main processes to form these casting goods.
However, with the development of aircraft, the turbine engine industry is seeking new
route to save cast and improve the service life of product, which transmits the
requirement directly to the parts suppliers. Continuous technical breakthrough inﬁeld
of material development and manufacturing is another threat to the traditional casting
market [2, 3]. In large-scale thin-walled casting market, control of the metallurgical
quality and improvement of product life are two predominant topics where the mi-
croporosity and fatigue life are the important focus in practice [ 4].
Microporosity is one of the most important defects in Alloy 718 made by
investment casting [ 5–9]. The unavoidable micropores can seriously reduce the
fatigue life of superalloy casting [ 10]. Effect of microporosity on the mechanical
properties and cracking behavior of nickel based superalloy has been widely
researched by using experimental method and numerical simulation [ 11–13]. Gen-
erally, the microporosity dominates the crack initiation in superalloy during external
loading. In some large stress amplitude, low-cycle situations, the microporosity-
sensitive cracking has been numerously observed from room temperature to 650 °C.
Hot isostatic pressing is effective way to heal the micropore in superalloy [ 14–16].
Commonly, morphology of microporosity in castings can be observed by met-
allographic picture which can be used to calculate the porosity of casting [ 17].
While new synchrotron radiation X-ray CT technology can be used to generate
high-resolution image of material and the accurate digital model of internal mi-
crostructure can be obtained through 3D reconstruction technology, which provides
an advanced method for the study of casting defects [ 18–21].
In this study, an accurate digital model of microporosity in nickel based su-
peralloy Alloy 718 was obtained by a combination of X-ray scanning experiment
and 3D reconstruction. The numerical simulation based on ﬁnite element method
(FEM) was performed to analyze the effect of microporosity on the fracture life of
superalloy, and the simulation strategy based on response surface model (RSM)
was proposed to control the total number of simulation. Simultaneously, low-cycle
fatigue experiments were carried out with the superalloy samples after heat treat-
ment and hot isostatic pressing.
Materials and Methods
Materials Preparation and Fatigue Experiment
Nickel based superalloy Alloy 718 in the study has the average compositions of
the follows (wt%): 0.05 C-19.00 Cr-53.00 Ni-3.00 Mo-5.00 (Nb + Ta)-0.50
390 Y. Liu et al.

## Page 391

Al-0.90 Ti-rest Fe. The commercial alloy ingot was molten in a vacuum induced
furnace until the temperature reached 1500 °C and poured into ceramic shell which
was preheated to 1000 °C in a muf ﬂe furnace. The investment casting process was
performed in vacuum environment to avoid the gas involving into molten alloy and
oxidation. When the casting produce solidi ﬁed at ambient environment, the ceramic
shell was kicked off to obtain precision casting. Specimen bars removed from the
casting were divided into two groups: one group was subjected to standard heat
treatment (SHT) and another group was subjected for heat isostatic pressing (HIP)
to eliminate microporosity in superalloy. The regime of HIP processing was
designed as 1170 °C × 4 h × 140 MPa. After ﬁnishing the clearance, the two
groups of specimen bars were machined into standard fatigue bars with the gauge
diameter of 6 mm. Low fatigue experiment was performed on a hydraulic experi-
mental platform MTS810, where the strain control condition was applied to every
test. The parameter setting of the fatigue experiment includes: strain amplitude
ε = 0.4%, strain ratio R = −1, triangular frequency f = 0.2 Hz.
The subsequent characterization includes the optical micrograph (OM) with an
Olympus BX51 M optical microscope and the fractography observation with a
RISE Microscopy, (TESCAN-MIRA/WITEC). The OM pictures were processed to
segment the as cast pore from the matrix and to calculate porosity of specimen.
X-Ray μCT and 3D Reconstruction Technique
In order to observe the microporosity in the superalloy casting, industrial X-ray CT
instrument was utilized to scan superalloy casting to obtain the approximate loca-
tion of microporosity and marked carefully. Secondly, the round pin with a size of
Ø 0.5 mm was divided from the marked location of microporosity on the casting by
wire-electrode cutting. The round pins were used for synchrotron radiation X-ray
scanning experiment which was carried out on the beam line BL13W1 of Shanghai
Synchrotron Radiation Light Source (SSRF).
The positions of the scanning experiment apparatus and the sample are shown in
Fig. 1. The x-ray beam has an electron energy of 3.5 GeV. The X-ray beam has
superb penetrating ability and can therefore be used to accurately inspect mi-
crostructure within the dense nickel based superalloy. In this study, the voxel of the
CCD camera has a minimum resolution of 0.65 μm × 0.65 μm × 0.65 μm,
which meets the magnitude of the micropore. During the scanning experiment, the
rotation center of the pin sample was ﬁrst calibrated in the 2 times magni ﬁcation
viewport to keep the rotation center of the pin unchanged during the rotation of
θ = 180°. Then specimen moved vertically to search the location of microporosity.
After locking a microporosity location, a series of vertical projections are taken at
certain exposure time of about 7 s, obtaining a total of 720 projections to ensure the
high precision modeling. Resulting projections will be imported into the P3
Analysis of Microporosity-Dependent Fatigue Crack Behavior … 391

## Page 392

software developed by SSRF to complete the rename and format conversion, where
the picture background can be removed. The formatted CT slice can be used for the
3D reconstruction of the material model. The 3D reconstruction process are pro-
cessed by ImageJ and Amira software in this study. The 3D model can be used for
the micropore statistics and ﬁnite element modeling.
The 3D reconstructive model of microporosity with STL format ﬁle was
imported into Geomagic Control 2015 software for related statistics in terms of
diameter, volume, number, spacing, and real porosity.
FEM Simulation Strategy Based on RSM
With the 3D model of the micropore and alloy, modeling of the tensile testing was
implemented by using ABAQUS software to obtain the stress distribution results in
the model, especially the stress concentration at the internal surface of microp-
orosity. Based on the pre-deformation and stress value, the fatigue analysis was
performed using fe-safe 6.5 software, and then the calculation results of fatigue life
was exported and analyzed in ABAQUS software.
Simulation strategy was applied in the work based on design of experiment
(DOE) which includes the central composite design (CCD) and response surface
analysis (RSA), in order to analyze the effects of important factors on the fatigue
behaviors of the nickel based superalloy. In detail, three factors were selected as
porosity (A, unit: %), pre-deformation (B, unit: Pa), and residual stress (C, unit:
MPa) and the two responses were logarithmic fatigue life (R1, unit: 1) and maxi-
mum fatigue strength (R2, unit: MPa). Reconstructive models of microporosity
with different porosity were utilized in the simulation plan. The three levels of the
porosity was 0, 0.425, and 0.799% which was calculated from the real model of the
Fig. 1 Synchrotron radiation X-ray CT scanning experiment device and sample movement

## Page 393

pin sample. The number of pore model limited the range of porosity. While the
ranges of pre-deformation and residual stress can be continuous in software
ABAQUS and fe-safe, respectively. With the simulation plan table, quantity
function relationship between factors and response can be obtained by regression
analysis and the accuracy of the function can be evaluated by ANOVA.
Results and Discussion
Comparison of Metallography and 3D Reconstructive
Microporosity
In order to determine the porosity of the superalloy, comparison of the metallog-
raphy and 3D reconstructive model was conducted, as shown in Fig. 2. Conven-
tionally, metallography is widely used to obtain the porosity based on a series of
sectional view pictures of material. The pro ﬁle morphology of microporosity can be
observed in the picture with different magni ﬁcation while the details of the internal
Fig. 2 Comparison of the metallography and 3D reconstructive model: a micropore in SHT
superalloy, b dense matrix of HIP superalloy, c pin sample with micropores, d the micropore with
complex structure, and e pin sample without micropore
Analysis of Microporosity-Dependent Fatigue Crack Behavior … 393

## Page 394

surface of microporosity cannot be inspected due to the depth contrast of the optical
microscope. The accuracy of statistic results depends on the quality and quantity of
metallographic pictures. However, during the segmentation of the metallographic
images, systematical error of the 2D statistic method is very high and is unknown
because the operation of continuous cutting work is complicated in practice.
Figure 2a suggests the microporosity in the superalloy casting after standard heat
treatment, reveling that the average size of the microporosity ranges from ∼1t o
∼50 μm. The porosity of the superalloy is 0.96%. However, ﬁnite number of
metallography pictures provide limited information of microporosity with complex
spatial structure. Microstructurally, both MC carbide and acicular δ were observed
in the superalloy, and the acicular δ was formed in the phase transition from Laves.
After HIP processing, no void was observed in the superalloy casting, while a large
number of MC carbide still dispersed in the interdendritic region and grain
boundaries (GBs), see Fig. 2b.
Post-processing 3D reconstruction was performed based on the resulting data
from synchrotron radiation X-ray CT scanning experiment. The reconstructive
model of superalloy with casting microporosity was obtained, as shown in Fig. 2c.
The porosity of the 3D model is 0.799%, which is 16.77% smaller than the results
obtained from 2D metallography. The difference comes from the high resolution of
synchrotron radiation X-ray CT as well as the systematic error of 2D metallogra-
phy. Figure 2d shows a large-scale microporosity in the 3D superalloy model,
revealing the complex spatial structure and internal surface of the casting micro-
pore. As an instance, the superalloy without signi ﬁcant microporosity was shown in
Fig. 2e.
Simulation and Experimental Results of Low-Cycle Fatigue
Implement of fatigue testing modeling required the usage of stress distribution
calculated with the tensile simulation, and ﬁnite element model of fatigue was
inherited from the tensile simulation. Firstly, tensile simulation of the superalloy
was conducted in ABAQUS software, and the simulation parameters were set as
follows: (1) material properties of Alloy 718: density 8220 kg/m
3, Young ’s mod-
ulus 186 GPa, Poisson ’s ratio 0.33; (2) simulation step: general static mechanic;
(3) load and boundary condition: pre-deformation load at top end equals 3 kPa in
+Z direction, full ﬁxed freedom of the element at the bottom end; (4) output the
distribution of stress and displacement in the FE model.
Simulation of fatigue was completed in fe-safe software based on the
stress results in tensile simulation. The whole FE model was used to conduct the
fatigue simulation where the analysis settings included of surface ﬁnish
0.6 < Ra ≤ 1.6 μm, material Alloy 718 SDL, residual stress 200 MPa, and SN
scale 1. The loading settings included the elastic block based on the load scaler
(Fig. 3) and the tensile stress value. The output data was the LOG life and max
yield stress, and max stress.
394 Y. Liu et al.

## Page 395

Figure 4a shows the predicted results of Mises stress contour tensile simulation.
It is clear from the sectional view that the severe stress concentration occurs on the
surface of the casting pores, while the stress value in horizontal direction is much
larger than the value in vertical direction, revealing the close relationship between
pre-deformation direction and stress distribution at microporosity. It ’s interesting to
note that the homogeneity of stress distribution at the pore elongated in vertical
direction (loading direction) is much higher than the pore elongated in horizontal
direction, indicating the in ﬂuence of pore distribution on the stress concentration.
Stress distribution on the surface of microporosity provides in ﬂuence of pore
morphology on the stress distribution. As an instance, the stress output on the
surface of the largest volume microporosity was divided from the FE model.
Almost each micropore was constructed with several concave areas and convex
areas. Actually, the concave area represented the ﬁnal dendritic cap after solidi ﬁ-
cation of metal while the convex area represented the interdendritic region or grain
boundary. It’s not difﬁcult to ﬁnd the fact that stress concentration occurs mostly at
the concave area whose normal vector is vertical to the loading direction. Since, the
brittle TCP phases (e.g. Laves) are prefer to form at the interdendritic region, the
severe stress concentration may cause the cracking of those harmful phases, which
has been observed in physical experiment.
The distribution of the predicted fatigue life was similar to the tensile simulation,
as shown in Fig. 5.I t’s not difﬁcult to ﬁnd that micropore has lower fatigue life than
the matrix (Fig. 5a) and the lowest fatigue life occurs mostly at the concave area
whose normal vector is vertical to the loading direction (Fig. 5b). This indicated
that the micropore was the fatigue crack source in the Alloy 718 casting, and the
interdendritic region on the surface of the micropore was the fatigue crack initiation
sites. Moreover, the predicted max yield stress shows the lowest fatigue strength of
microporosity in the nickel based superalloy (Fig. 6).
Low-cycle fatigue experiment was performed to provide a con ﬁrmation to the
numerical simulation of fatigue. Fractography of the fatigue samples were observed
by scanning microscope, as shown in Fig. 7. Figure 7a suggested that a micropore
in the subsurface layer of the sample after standard heat treatment (SHT) caused the

Conclusions
The inﬂuence of microporosity on the fatigue crack behavior in the superalloy was
studied by ﬁnite element method and experiment. Several conclusions can be
summarized as follows:
1. The morphology of microporosity in polycrystalline nickel based superalloy
Alloy 718 casting was characterized by 2D metallography and 3D reconstruc-
tion. 3D reconstructive model with high dimensional accuracy provides more

strong con ﬁrmation to the fact that microporosity was cracking source in the

2. The simulation results of fatigue suggested that homogeneity of stress distri-

the orientation of largest diameter, and surface curvature of certain micropore.
The convex area on the surface of micropore has lower strength and fatigue life
than the concave area. Low cycle fatigue experiment coincided with the sim-
ulation results.
3. Response surface analysis suggested that linear relationship between fatigue life
and relevant factors including of porosity, pre-deformation and residual stress.
Fatigue life decreased with the increasing of those factors. This method may be
used to optimal design of fatigue life for industrial component made of Alloy
718.

Characterization of the Initial Stages
of Dynamic Recrystallization in ATI
718Plus®
C. Kienl, A. Casanova, O. M. D. M. Messé, C. Argyrakis and C. M. F. Rae
Abstract ATI 718Plus ® is a polycrystalline multi-phase strengthened Ni-base
superalloy suitable for turbine disc applications in aero engines. A typical tur-
bine disc experiences temperatures in the rim up to 650–700
◦C and stresses as
high as 1000 MPa in the cooler parts of the component. The manufacturing pro-
cess, especially forging and heat treatment, plays a pivotal role in achieving the
ﬁnal microstructure and associated mechanical properties needed to withstand this
harsh environment. The microstructural evolution during aforementioned processes
is directly related to dynamic recrystallization. The changes occurring during the
initial stages of deformation are of particular interest as partially recrystallized areas
with a broad range of grain size can be detrimental for the mechanical properties of
the component. ATI 718Plus
® has been used in this work to study grain nucleation
and growth during recrystallization. To evaluate the importance of the deformation
conditions on the outcome of the forging, a set of specimens were produced from a
single billet of ATI 718Plus
®. Hot compression tests were performed on Rastegaev-
samples across a wide range of temperatures, strains and strain rates. In addition, the
characteristics for meta-dynamic recrystallization were evaluated on a samples sub-
set. The evolution of the ﬂow curves as well as the development of the microstructure
will be presented. This study speciﬁcally focuses on the role of deformation param-

Keywords 718plus⋅ Recrystallization⋅ EBSD⋅ TEM
Introduction
Turbine discs in jet engines are categorized as critical components because a failure
will compromise the integrity of the aircraft. Hence, the material and its response to
the manufacturing process needs to be thoroughly understood to prevent failure in
the ﬁnal component.
Inconel 718 (hereafter IN718) is currently the workhorse material for disc appli-
cations due to its strength and low cost. However, the main strengthening phase 𝛾
′′
(tetragonal, Ni3Nb) deﬁnes its maximum operating temperature of 640◦Ca si to v e r -
ages quickly to form 𝛿 [1]. For higher temperatures, Waspaloy is often the alloy
of choice with the disadvantage of poor processability and weldability. The alloy
ATI 718Plus® was developed to ﬁll the gap between the nickel-iron-base IN718
and the nickel-base Waspaloy. ATI 718Plus® (hereafter 718Plus) is a polycrystalline
multi-phase strengthened Ni-base wrought alloy. Based on IN718 it was designed
for operating temperatures of 704, 55 ◦C above IN718 [ 2]. The increased temper-
ature stability in comparison to IN718 was achieved by precipitating the cubic 𝛾′
(Ni3Al[Al,Nb,Ti]). In addition to 𝛾′ 718Plus forms a grain boundary precipitate
deﬁned as hexagonal 𝜂 (Ni6[Al,Ti]Nb) with ﬁne layers of an orthorhombic delta-
phase (Ni3Nb) [3, 4].
To tailor the microstructure the manufacturing process of the component is as
important as the alloy itself. During forging the material undergoes dynamic recrys-
tallization (DRX), characterized by the growth of new grains during continuous
deformation [5]. The recrystallization kinetics of metals and alloys with low stacking
fault energies has been studied extensively and reviewed in [6, 7]. However, little is
known about the recrystallization behavior of 718Plus. A few studies have analyzed
the development of the microstructure of 718Plus during high temperature compres-
sion [8, 9]. Interestingly, these results show an increase of recrystallized fraction
with the rise in strain rate. This contradicts the expected behavior of Ni-base super-
alloys where the measured recrystallized area decreases with an increase in strain
rate [10, 11].
In this study the microstructural evolution of 718Plus during high temperature
compression tests has been characterized with the aim of shedding light on the behav-
ior contained in previous ﬁndings.

Experimental Methods
The 718Plus billet material used for this study was produced by ATI and supplied by
Rolls-Royce Detschland. It was triple melted (vacuum induction melt/VIM, electro
slag remelted/ESR, vacuum arc remelted/VAR) and cogged into billets with a diame-
ter of 220 mm. The chemical composition of the as-received state had been measured
by means of energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) and is listed together with
the nominal values in Table1.
High Temperature Compression Tests
High temperature compression tests were performed to simulate the forging condi-
tions for a turbine disc and trigger DRX.
Prior characterization revealed small amounts of 𝜂 in the billet rim and a gradi-
ent in grain size from bore to rim [ 12]. To avoid the inﬂuence of a heterogeneous
microstructure on the results all the specimens were extracted from the midsection.
Cylindrical samples with the dimensions 10 × 15 mm were machined with shallow
pockets on both ends. During the test, the recesses were ﬁlled with glass lubricant
Delta Glace Fb417 to reduce friction.
Uni-axial compression tests were performed at the Advanced Forming Research
Centre at the University of Strathclyde on a Zwick/Roell Amsler HA 250 servo-
hydraulic machine with temperatures ranging from 850 to 1025
◦C at constant strain
r a t e so f0 . 0 1t o1s−1 to two diﬀerent strains of 0.8 and 1.2. In the testing procedure
the furnace was preheated to 650 ◦C before it was moved in place to enclose the
specimen. The heating rate was set to 12◦Cm i n−1 followed by a 15 min dwell time
at the testing temperature. After the compression the specimens were water quenched
within 5 s. A second batch of samples was kept in the furnace after compression at the
testing temperature for 2 min before quenching in order to investigate meta-dynamic
recrystallization (MDRX) for selected deformation parameters.
Quantitative Metallography
The samples were further analyzed using electron backscatter diﬀraction (EBSD) in
a scanning electron microscope (SEM) and bright-ﬁeld imaging in a transmission
electron microscope (TEM).

For microstructural characterization in the SEM, the compressed specimens were
cut longitudinally and mounted in conducting Bakelite. The grinding and polishing
was ﬁnished oﬀ using an oxide polishing suspension (OPS) with colloidal silica of
0.05 µm for 10 min in order to improve the quality of the electron backscatter pattern
(EBSP).
The EBSD measurements were performed on an FEI Philips XL30 ﬁeld emission
gun SEM. The acceleration voltage was 25 keV with a sample tilt of 70
◦ and working
distances between 10 and 15 mm. The step size for the scans was set to 15µm. Post-
processing of the data was done with Oxford Instruments’ HKL Channel 5 software
as well as the MTEX toolbox for MATLAB. Therefore, the minimum grain size
was set to 10 pixels and the misorientation angle for grain reconstruction of 5
◦. Zero
solutions were adjusted by considering at least ﬁve neighboring pixels for the closest
match.
A JEOL 200CX TEM with an acceleration voltage of 200 keV was used for
detailed characterization of the microstructure. The samples were sliced into 0.15–
0.2 mm thick plates and spark-eroded into 3 mm discs. Subsequently, the discs were
electropolished with a solution of 6 vol% perchloric acid in methanol at −5
◦C and
20 V.
Results
The as-received billet of 718Plus had an average grain size of 26µm with equiaxed
grains and no signs of 𝜂-precipitates.
Flow Curve Analysis
The ﬂow curves obtained from the deformation tests were corrected for machine
compliance, friction and adiabatic heating. The corrected stress-strain curves for 975
and 1000
◦C and strain rates of 0.01, 0.1 and 1 s −1 are presented in Fig. 1.W i t h
increasing strain rate both the peak stress and the ﬂow stress rise. At low strain rates
the yield point is followed by a decrease in stress reaching the lower yield point. Such
a yield point phenomena has been reported frequently for Ni-base superalloys and
is attributed to the pinning and generation of dislocations on solutes until a critical
strain is reached [8, 13, 14].
The yield point phenomena becomes stronger with slower strain rates for constant
temperatures. Considering the inﬂuence of temperature, the maximum yield point
drop is shifted to higher temperatures when the strain rate becomes faster indicating
it is an activated process. Even though the stress-strain curve for the highest strain
rate at 1 s
−1 does not show a yield point drop at the temperatures tested, a noticeable
dent around 400 MPa became gradually stronger at 1000◦C( F i g .1b). After the yield
drop the curves reach the peak stress followed by a gradual fall. This indicates the

Discussion
Within all samples the gradual shift of LAGB towards HAGB with rise in recrys-
tallized fraction is apparent. This is attributed to the nucleation and growth process
of DRX. Nucleation of recrystallized grains occurs preferably at former high angle

## Page 415

Characterization of the Initial Stages of Dynamic Recrystallization . . . 415
Fig. 7 TEM bright ﬁeld images of samples compressed to a strain of 1.2. a T = 975 ◦C, ̇𝜀 =
0.01 s−1; b T = 975 ◦C, ̇𝜀 =1s −1; c T = 950◦C, ̇𝜀 =1s −1, 120 s dwell
boundaries by the formation of cell walls which further develop into SGB. These
SGB generate an imbalance between adjacent grains where one side bulges out [21].
The bulge is closed with a HAGB forming a recrystallized grain [22]. The formation
of subgrains and the migration of HAGB is heavily depended on the deformation
parameters and will be discussed in detail for DRX as well as MDRX.
Eﬀect of Temperature and Strain
The increase of temperature in 718Plus resulted in a larger recrystallized area. As
the grain boundaries become more mobile with temperature, the grains can grow fur-
ther after nucleation. Alongside the faster movement stacking errors at the migrating
grain boundary are more likely to occur which can result in the formation of twin
boundaries [23]. Hence, the higher the grain boundary mobility, the more twins are
generated. This was seen in the the evolution of grain boundary misorientation angle.
The kinetics of MDRX is inﬂuenced by temperature in a similar way.

## Page 416

416 C. Kienl et al.
Deforming the sample to higher strains results in a greater density of dislocations
in the material. The dislocations provide a source of stored energy for nucleation and
growth.
Eﬀect of Strain Rate
The literature describing similar forging simulations on 718Plus demonstrate a
counter-intuitive rise in recrystallized volume fraction with increasing strain rate [8,
9]. It is normally argued, as in case of IN718 [10, 24], that the longer time involved
in slower strain rate tests allows much more recrystallization to occur leading to a
higher recrystallized volume fraction. The forging time for the various strain rates
used in the current experiments deformed to the upper strain of 1.2, vary from 0.7 s
for the 1 s
−1 strain rate to 70 s for the slowest strain rate of 0.01 s−1. The experiments
contain a 5 s transfer time between the compression and the water quench. MDRX
starts immediately after deformation is ﬁnished without any incubation period [ 6].
Figure 8 shows the evolution of DRX and MDRX in IN718 at 980◦C. To investigate
the DRX regime the samples were immediately quenched after deformation at vary-
ing strains up to 0.82. The recrystallized area increases with lowering the strain rate.
However, the dwell time after deformation has a signiﬁcant inﬂuence on recrystal-

lization. After 3 s, the specimens compressed with a strain rate of 1.1 s−1 show the

When the delay of 5 s in removing the sample from the furnace is added, it makes
the meta-dynamic component of the high strain rate tests very signiﬁcant in compar-
ison to the deformation time but contributes relatively little at lower strain rates. In
the TEM images in Fig. 7a we see the eﬀect of the meta-dynamic component in the
recrystallized grains of the slow deformed sample. These contain a signiﬁcant den-
sity of dislocations, albeit rather lower than the unrecrystallized grains, which show
a well-developed sub-grain structure. This is apparent from the large increase in the
fraction of SGBs at lower strain rates, Fig. 5. In the case of the grains illustrated in
Fig. 7a, it can be observed that part of the grain is dislocation free with a distinct
boundary between the two areas. Such observation suggests that the clear part of the
grain recrystallized after the forging has ceased. In the case of the 0.01 s
−1 strain
rate the 5 seconds meta-dynamic component was 7% of the total exposure (dynamic
+ meta-dynamic) but nevertheless makes a signiﬁcant contribution in some grains
which grow the same distance during MDRX and DRX. In the faster strain rate sam-
ple 1 s
−1, the deformed grains, constituting 57% of the sample, show a very high and
relatively homogeneous dislocation density. In contrast, most of the recrystallized
grains are generally clear of dislocations, indicating that they formed during meta-
dynamic period of the deformation; however, some show signiﬁcant densities of dis-
locations indicating that they formed during the 0.7 s of forging time. It is tempting to
assume that the relative size of the meta-dynamic component of the recrystallization
time in the high strain rate samples is the reason for the rise in recrystallized vol-
ume fraction with strain rate; however, two other papers describe the same eﬀect [8,
9]. The compression tests performed by Mitsche et al. [9] contain a transfer time of
less than 0.5 s but the DRX volume fraction also increases with strain rate. Similar
experiments with IN718 have been performed with delays in quenching of up to 3 s
showing the expected behavior of less DRX at lower strain rate [10].
What is clear is that the rate of recrystallization is dramatically increased by
increasing the strain rate—what happens in 70 s at low strain rate happens in 0.7 s
at higher strain rates. Not only is the nucleation very rapid, but the growth is phe-
nomenally fast. Ignoring nucleation time and allowing growth throughout dynamic
and meta-dynamic processing, growth rates are greater than 0.48µms
−1 at 1 s−1 and
0.021 µms−1 at 0.01 s−1 some 23 times faster at the high strain rate. It is hard to jus-
tify this diﬀerence on a simple driving force argument as the dislocation density,
although lower through recovery at the low strain rate, is not 23 times lower. What
is also interesting is that there are many more smaller grains in the lower strain rate,
Fig. 4—the grain coverage is similar with roughly the same number of boundaries
showing no or very few nuclei. This suggests that nucleation at the slow strain rates
happens readily, but that the grains do not grow. A possibility is that the recovery
gives locally high dislocation levels able to initiate the grain bulging but that as the
grains grow they encounter the lower density of subgrain interior and cease to grow.
The observed substructures are commonly used to distinguish between contin-
uous (CDRX) and discontinuous DRX (DDRX) [ 8, 26]. While CDRX contains a
progressive strain-induced subgrain rotation DDRX is referred to the bulging mech-

## Page 418

418 C. Kienl et al.
anism of pre-existing high angle grain boundaries. These two mechanisms are meant
to progress on diﬀerent time-scales explaining the strain rate dependency of the
recrystallized fraction. Even though CDRX is thought to be the rotation of subgrains,
computer simulations as well as experiments were only able to conﬁrm this for a
few well deﬁned grain boundaries [27, 28]. It is more helpful to think of CDRX as a
progressive subgrain growth where a subgrain consumes the adjacent substructures
leading to a continuous increase in grain boundary misorientation angle. However,
the formation of the bulges in DDRX also requires the arrangement of subgrain
boundaries [29] which weakens the assumption that subgrain development causes
the time delay.
The consistent trend in 718Plus to increase the recrystallized fraction with increas-
ing strain rate is opposite to the trend observed in IN718. Yet the ﬂow curves of the
two alloys deformed in the same series of experiments reported by Momeni et al. [8]
are remarkably similar, in particular the rate of softening is much the same. Momeni
et al. interpret this as change from DDRX at high strain rates characterized by high
ﬂow stress and rapid softening from recrystallization to a ﬂatter curve with little soft-
ening characterized by a recovery at a rate able to keep up with the strain rate. They
highlight the potential change in SFE produced by the increase in Co in 718Plus but
there is little evidence of the change in behavior from the ﬂow curves. It could be
possible that 718Plus has a recovery rate fast enough to prevent the rapid recrys-
tallization but not sharp enough to give such well-deﬁned subgrains that produce a
recrystallized structure.
The strain rate also seems to have a distinct inﬂuence on the evolution of twin
boundaries. Samples at slow strain rates develop fewer twins than at faster strain
rates. In line with the observed rise in SGB and LAGB a higher degree of recovery
takes place at low strain rates [30]. The decrease in twin boundaries can be explained
by the growth accident model published by Gleiter [ 23]. This theory assumes that
twins form at migrating boundaries due to a stacking error. The higher the grain
boundary mobility, the more twins are generated. If the microstructure recovers
before the onset of recrystallization the grain boundary migration rate is lower and
therefore fewer twins are formed.
Conclusion
The eﬀect of deformation parameters on the ﬂow curves and the kinetics of DRX in
718Plus has been studied. The yield point phenomena is dependent on temperature
as well as strain rate.
The recrystallized area increases with temperature, strain and strain rate. While
the fraction of twin boundary increases with strain rate, subgrain boundaries are
more prominent at low strain rates. While the former is related to the higher migration
rate of high angle grain boundaries, the latter is explained in terms of dislocation
mobility. Dislocations move easier at low strain rates and subgrains can form. We
could provide evidence of an increase in recovery for low strain rate deformation. In

## Page 419

Characterization of the Initial Stages of Dynamic Recrystallization . . . 419
addition, the DRX and MDRX could clearly be distinguished using TEM bright ﬁeld
imaging. The high recrystallized fraction with strain rate is likely to have resulted
from MDRX occurring during the transfer time between deformation and quench
but we are unable at this stage to explain the necessary high migration rates of the
boundaries.

Compositional Design and Mechanical
Properties of INCONEL ® Alloy 725
Variants
Martin Detrois, Kyle A. Rozman, Paul D. Jablonski
and Jeffrey A. Hawk
Abstract With a combination of high strength, toughness and resistance to
corrosion, INCONEL ® alloy 725 has been widely used in marine, aerospace, and
land-based power industries. Typically, the alloy presents a conventional
precipitate-strengthened γ-γ′/γ″ microstructure when appropriate aging treatments
are employed. Although the corrosion resistance of INCONEL ® alloy 725 is sig-
niﬁcant, its use is limited to relatively low temperatures when compared to other γ′
precipitate-strengthened Ni-based superalloys. This can limit the use of the alloy as
turbine engine components or in other power-generation applications since future
engine designs suggest increases in the operating temperature. This investigation
aims at modifying the composition of the alloy to assess its high-temperature
mechanical properties. Variations to the Ti/Al ratio were considered with respect to
the precipitate phases stability as well as additions of Ta and Nb. Thermodynamic
and kinetic predictions, such as phase fraction/stability and time –temperature–
transformation diagrams, were used to help in the design process and were validated
experimentally. The various compositions and relative aging treatments investi-
gated produced microstructures differing in grain boundary phases and γ′ precipi-
tate sizes and fractions. Tensile and creep testing were performed and the effect of
the various compositions and microstructures on the mechanical performance of the
modiﬁed INCONEL
® 725 alloys was examined.
