Introduction
INCONEL® alloy 725, referred to as IN725, is a precipitate-strengthened Ni-based
superalloy with high strength and corrosion resistance [ 1]. It is a derivative of the
solid-solution strengthened INCONEL ® alloy 625 with added titanium to promote
the formation of γ′ precipitates [ 2]. The composition range of the alloy is listed in
Table 1. Due to its attractive properties, the alloy ﬁnds use in marine applications
where resistance to aqueous corrosion, pitting or stress corrosion cracking in sea
water is essential. The alloy is particularly desirable as it offers relatively compa-
rable strength to INCONEL
® alloy 718 (IN718) [ 3] at low to slightly elevated
temperatures.
The typical microstructure of IN725 consists of a face-centered cubic
(FCC) matrix with γ′/γ″ precipitates embedded within, when appropriate heat
treatments are employed [ 4]. The γ′ precipitates are Ni 3(Al,Ti), ordered FCC L1 2
crystal structure. The γ″ phase is typically Ni 3(Nb,Al,Ti) and has an ordered
tetragonal DO 22 crystal structure. Both precipitates have solubility for elements
such as Co, Cr, Nb and Mo among others [ 5]. Furthermore, η phase has been
reported to precipitate in IN725 when exposed to higher temperatures (approxi-
mately 750 –900 °C) and longer times (10 to 100 h depending on the temperature)
[4]. The η phase is typically Ni
3Ti, ordered hexagonal DO 24 crystal structure and
forms on the grain boundaries in the form of thin plates. Although Mannan et al. [ 4]
did not observe precipitation of δ phase in their time-temperature-transformation
diagram study of IN725, the phase can potentially precipitate especially when
relatively high Nb concentrations are present in the composition of the alloy [ 6].
The δ phase is typically Ni
3 (Nb, Ta), ordered orthorhombic DO a crystal structure.
Furthermore, alloys with excess Nb have been reported to precipitate a second type
of η phase of similar crystal structure but different composition (Ni
6AlNb) [ 7, 8].
Due to relatively high levels of Nb in the composition of IN725, Table 1, all
aforementioned phases can be expected to form. Finally, carbides such as MC (Ti-
and Nb-rich) and M 23C6 (Cr-rich) are known to form in the alloy.
To date, very limited high-temperature mechanical properties are available for
IN725 and most are only assessed up to 550 °C or 650 °C [ 1, 9]. Using the alloy in
high-temperature applications would be very valuable to fully utilize its superior
corrosion resistance. In this investigation, the high-temperature tensile and creep
properties of IN725 variants are studied. Changes from the nominal compositions
were made according to the Ti/Al ratio and additions of Ta and Nb. The rela-
tionships between alloying, thermodynamic predictions, microstructures and me-
chanical properties are presented and discussed.

Procedure
Casting and Thermal Processing
The compositions of the alloys investigated were designed using computational
thermodynamic software Thermo-Calc [ 10] with the TTNi8 and TCNi8 databases.
The Thermo-Calc database TCNi8 was used to obtain properties necessary for
melting and fabrication of the alloys such as the liquidus temperature, T
L. Seven
heats listed in Table 2 were made with changes in compositions from a standard
alloy STD of composition within the range speci ﬁed in Table 1. While the com-
positions of the alloys cannot be provided, only the changes in Ta, Nb and Ti/Al are
necessary for the scope of this investigation. Alloys A, B, C, and D contained a low
addition of Ta. From A to D, the Ti/Al ratio was decreased to obtain values above 1
(A, D), equal to 1 (C), and below 1 (D). Alloys E and F have identical nominal
Ti/Al ratio as Alloy D with added Ta in Alloy E and Nb in F. For each heat, the
melt materials were measured to a target weight of 7000 g using high-purity
industry-grade melt stock. Only Cr was not added loosely due to its 5200 ppm
concentration of oxygen. Therefore, a Ni-25Cr master alloy using vacuum induc-
tion melting (VIM) and electroslag remelting (ESR) was made instead to reduce the
amount of tramp elements [ 11, 12]. Also, 400 ppm carbon and 30 ppm boron were
added to the melts. The alloys were subsequently melted under 200 Torr argon
partial pressure to a superheat temperature of T
L + 50 °C. The heats were poured
into 75 mm diameter graphite molds having non-reactive ceramic wash coat to
form ∼150 mm height cylinders for fabrication.
Slices were cut from the ingots following casting for measurement of compo-
sition using X-ray ﬂuorescence (XRF) with a Rigaku ZSX Primus II utilizing NIST
traceable standards (values are accurate to 0.01 wt%). Tramp element contents were
measured using LECO analysis methods with NIST certi ﬁed standards (values of
carbon and sulfur are accurate to 2 ppm and oxygen and nitrogen to 1 ppm).
Concentrations of nitrogen between 6 and 17 ppm, sulfur between 6 and 9 ppm,
and oxygen between 5 and 20 ppm were measured in the ﬁnal products. The ingots
were homogenized following a computationally optimized homogenization treat-
ment [ 13] consisting of 1 h at 1050 °C + 3 h at 1070 °C + 3 h at 1100 °C + 3 h
at 1120 °C + 10 h at 1140 °C + 30 h at 1160 °C which yielded a predicted

residual inhomogeneity of ±1% of nominal, or better, for each element. Following
homogenization, the ingots were conditioned and fabricated using step forging
operations followed by hot rolling, all at 1100 °C. Alloy fabrication parameters
were identical and the fabrication process resulted in approximately 400 mm by
125 mm plates with a thickness of 10 mm. The plates were solution heat treated
after the last rolling step at 1100 °C and then aged in vacuum under argon partial
pressure using the standard aging treatment for this alloy (from Ref. [ 1]), consisting
of 730 °C for 8 h followed by controlled cooling at 56 °C/h to 620 °C, holding at
this temperature for 8 h, with a ﬁnal argon gas fan cool to room temperature.
Mechanical Testing and Characterization
Blanks measuring 85 mm in length and 10 × 10 mm 2 cross section were cut from
the plates to prepare tensile and creep specimens. The bars were machined into
cylindrical samples of L = 4D geometry with a 32 mm gauge length and 6.3 mm
diameter gauge cross-section. ASTM E-8 [ 14] and ASTM E-139 [ 15] were fol-
lowed in performing tensile and creep tests, respectively. Tensile testing was per-
formed at room temperature (RT) and 750 °C with strain rate of 0.127 mm/min
until yield and 1.27 mm/min thereafter. Creep testing was performed at 700 °C
under a creep screening stress of 483 MPa using a constant load creep frame.
Metallographic samples were prepared at each step of this investigation to
evaluate the microstructures following casting, homogenization, aging and me-
chanical testing. The specimens were ground and polished to 0.05 µm ﬁnish using
colloidal silica. Etching was performed using a γ′ etchant consisting of 1:1:2 HCl –
HNO
3–H2O by volume. The microstructure was observed using a FEI Inspect F
ﬁeld emission scanning electron microscope (SEM). Finally, the digital image
analysis software ImageJ [ 16] was used for various quantitative measurements on
the SEM images.
Results
Computational Assessment
A preliminary computational assessment of the compositions listed in Table 2 was
performed using Thermo-Calc. The phase diagram for Alloy D using the TCNi8
database is represented in Fig. 1a. The predictions reveal stability of M
23C6
(Cr-rich) and MC (Nb-rich) carbides, σ phase, γ, γ′, δ and η. The σ phase is a TCP
phase, rich in Ni, Cr, and Mo, and it is not expected to precipitate unless
424 M. Detrois et al.

## Page 425

signiﬁcantly long exposure at elevated temperatures occurs. Therefore, it is omitted
in the rest of this investigation. Similar phases were predicted using the TTNi8
database. The solvus temperatures of the γ′, δ and η phases are represented for both
databases in Fig. 1b and Table 3 for all of the alloys. The change in Ta content
between STD and A was not predicted to in ﬂuence the phases present, their relative
fractions and solvus temperatures. Decreasing the Ti/Al ratio from Alloys A to D
resulted in an increase in the fraction of the γ′ phase while the fraction of δ phase
decreased. This is consistent with the known composition of the phases, Ni
3Al for
γ′, and from the known partitioning of Ti to the δ phase [ 7]. Finally, higher
concentrations of Ta and Nb in Alloys E and F, respectively, resulted in predictions
similar to Alloy D, Fig. 1b, with increased δ phase fraction and solvus temperature.
While the general trends for γ′ and δ phase stability and evolution of the solvus
temperatures are consistent qualitatively between both databases, signi ﬁcant dif-
ferences were observed in the values obtained, see Fig. 1b. Furthermore, the η
phase was predicted to form using both databases. However, the differences in
solvus temperatures were considerable as was their respective trends. TCNi8 pre-
dicted an increasing solvus temperature of η phase with decreasing Ti/Al ratio for
Alloys A to D, while TTNi8 predicted a decrease in the solvus temperature and
stability only in Alloys STD, A and B. This is attributed to the predicted compo-
sition of the η phase where TCNi8 calculated the major partitioning elements to be
13Ta, 10Al, 2Ti while TTNi8 predicted 20Ti, 4Nb (atomic pct.). Both databases
were, however, in agreement with regards to major partitioning elements in the γʹ
(Ti, Al, Nb) and δ (Nb, Ti) phases.

Microstructural Analysis
Figure 2a is representative of the general grain structure of all of the alloys fol-
lowing rolling and solutioning. The micrograph reveals an equiaxed grain structure
in the longitudinal direction which demonstrates full recrystallization following
fabrication. All alloys presented ASTM 6 grain sizes determined using the linear
intersect technique. A relatively high amount of MC carbides was found in the
samples (see Fig. 2a, b) with a fraction of approximately 0.1% and an average size
of about 1.5 µm. EDS measurements indicated those to be Nb-carbides with par-
titioning of Ti and traces of Ta. While a high proportion of grain boundaries were
free of any precipitate phases, Figure 2c, evidence of ﬁne grain boundary carbides
(most likely M
23C6 Cr-carbides) was observed at higher magni ﬁcation. Those
features were dif ﬁcult to fully resolve using SEM, however, over-etching of the
sample surfaces revealed higher fraction of grain boundary carbides with decreasing
Ti/Al ratio (not shown). The alloys with higher Ta and Nb, Alloys E and F,
respectively, were also shown to contain a bright grain boundary phase, see Fig. 2d,
e. Finally, very ﬁne γ′ precipitates, which can be observed in Fig. 2e, were found in
all specimens. Their size and fraction increased with decreasing Ti/Al ratio.

to conventional IN725 [ 1] and IN718 [ 3]. The data is represented graphically in
Fig. 3 for observation of the various trends with respect to the testing temperature.

Minimal differences in elongation to failure were observed in all samples at RT
while a broader range was recorded at 750 °C; however, no trend can be accurately
deﬁned.
When compared to conventional IN725, Fig. 3, the IN725 variants were found
to have similar UTS and yield stress at room temperature with lower values
associated with the lower Ti/Al ratios in Alloys C and D. The maximum UTS at RT
and 750 °C were measured at 1282 and 806 MPa in Alloy A, respectively. Simi-
larly, the highest yield strength was measured in Alloy A at 861 and 643 MPa at RT
and 750 °C, respectively. The elongation to failure was on average 39% higher in
the IN725 variants as compared to conventional IN725 (Ref. [ 1]). Finally, com-
pared to IN718 the peak aged state in the IN725 variants has lower UTS and yield
stress. However, the IN725 variants did not signi ﬁcantly underperform at 750 °C.
The UTS measured in the IN725 variants was relatively close to that of IN718 and
only 5% lower when comparing with Alloy A. On average, the yield stress was 26%
lower. Finally, greater elongations to failure were measured in the IN725 variants,
and it was on average twice that of IN718.
Results from creep screening tests at 700 °C and 483 MPa are represented in
Fig. 4 from data compiled in Table 5 for the IN725 variants with comparison to
IN718 [17, 18]. Interestingly, decreasing the Ti/Al ratio resulted in a decrease in the
creep strain, time to failure, and Larson-Miller parameter (LMP). The maximum

creep strain, time to failure and LMP were measured at 9%, 217 h, and 39.14 in
Alloy A, respectively. Decreasing the Ti/Al ratio from 5.43 to 0.73 reduced creep
strain by 81%, decreased time to failure by 63%, and changed LMP by 2%
(insigniﬁcant given creep test variability). At a constant Ti/Al ratio ∼0.73,
increasing the Ta or Nb content resulted in a 30% or 114% increase in time to failure
in Alloys E and F as compared to Alloy D, respectively. Furthermore, higher LMP
and lower steady-state creep rates were measured in these alloys. Although the
elongation was relatively unchanged with addition of Nb, it considerably decreased
with Ta additions, going from 1.7 to 0.6% in Alloy D to E.
Comparison to IN718 resulted in a 56% lower steady-state creep rate, on aver-
age, in the IN725 variants with several alloys exhibiting longer failure times,
namely STD and Alloys A, B and F. From the Larson-Miller plot of Fig. 4b and the
calculated LMP of Table 4, the 725 variants perform well in creep when compared
to IN718.
Representative fracture surfaces following tensile and creep testing are shown in
Fig. 5. Room temperature testing resulted in ductile fracture of the specimens,
Fig. 5a, with evidence of secondary cracking. The grain boundary carbide phase
is observed in the magni ﬁed inset of the secondary crack of Fig. 5a. Secondary
cracking and mixed intergranular failure was more pronounced with decreasing
Ti/Al ratio, Fig. 5b.
For specimens tested at 750 °C, at low magni ﬁcations, it was apparent fracture
initiated at thumbnail like features. At higher magni ﬁcations, these thumbnail like
features showed intergranular initiation features followed by mixed intergranular/
ductile rupture. Signi ﬁcant intergranular secondary cracking was observed on the
specimen pro ﬁles, Fig. 5c, except for Alloys A and E, which both had the highest
yield stress. Overall, the IN725 variant creep specimens exhibited intergranular
failure with evidence of secondary cracking, Fig. 5d.

Secondary cracks were observed below the plane of the fracture surface, and they

be noted that a signi ﬁcantly greater density of the δ phase was present in grain

Discussion
Variations in the Ti/Al ratio were considered by decreasing Ti and increasing the Al
content from Alloy A to Alloy D. Following aging treatment, the size and fraction
of the γ′ precipitates increased with decreasing Ti/Al ratio from the added Al in
solution, available for the formation of the Ni 3Al γ′ precipitates. The formation of
M23C6 grain boundary carbides was also promoted by the decrease in Ti/Al ratio
which is likely attributed to less stable MC carbides (Ti-containing) with lower Ti
concentrations. Therefore, carbon is available for precipitation of the M 23C6 car-
bides during aging, Fig. 1a. From the room temperature tensile fractography results
presented in Fig. 5, the increased density of M 23C6 grain boundary carbides is
likely responsible for the decrease in ductility (i.e., increase in intergranular sec-
ondary cracking) from Alloy A to Alloy D. The presence of a dense repartition of
grain boundary carbides can act as crack initiation sites or favor crack propagation
by building up of dislocations or enabling cavitation damage during testing [ 19].
Thus, intergranular fracture and secondary cracking was promoted with decreasing
Ti/Al ratio following tensile testing at room temperature.
Signiﬁcant variations in the creep properties were observed between the alloys as
a function of the Ti/Al ratio as compared to the limited differences in tensile
properties. This can be attributed to the operative deformation mechanisms during
creep. Both the time to failure and elongation decreased with decreasing Ti/Al ratio,
Fig. 4. As previously discussed, a greater fraction of M 23C6 grain boundary car-
bides likely caused increased intergranular failure and secondary cracking follow-
ing tensile testing. Following creep testing, the size and density of grain boundary
carbides continued to increase, Fig. 6a, due to the test temperature falling within the
M23C6 precipitation region, see Fig. 1a. Additionally, the γ′ precipitates are affected
by creep deformation especially from the long hold time at temperature. Evidence
of γ′ coarsening was observed in the specimens following creep testing. While the
size of the precipitate was found to increase from Alloy STD to Alloy F following
aging, Alloy STD showed comparable size of the precipitates than that of Alloy F
after deformation, Fig. 7. This is not attributed to the time at temperature as
Alloy STD had a similar, although slightly longer, time to failure than Alloy F,

194 h compared to 171 h, respectively. Therefore, greater γ′ coarsening occurred
during creep testing of the alloys with higher Ti/Al ratio. γ/γ′ lattice mismatch
(misﬁt) values at the test temperature of 700 °C were obtained from JMatPro [ 22]
and reported in Fig. 8. The lattice mis ﬁt was found to decrease with decreasing Ti/
Al ratio in this set of alloys. Thus, the greater γ′ coarsening in Alloy STD is likely
attributed to the higher lattice mis ﬁt. Although the lattice mis ﬁt decreases with

Alloy D, see Fig. 4a. Therefore, the in ﬂuence of the lattice mis ﬁt may not be as
strong as that of the grain boundary phases; however, this could be valid only for
the demanding creep testing conditions investigated.
Formation of the δ phase was observed following aging in the alloys containing
elevated levels of Ta and/or Nb, i.e., Fig. 2d, e. Composition measurements of the
precipitates indicated elevated levels of Nb which is in agreement with the
Thermo-Calc phase composition predictions of Table 3. According to those pre-
dictions, the solvus temperature of the δ phase is near 900 °C, or 1000 °C,

## Page 434

depending on the database used. Consequently, both the aging treatment and the
creep testing temperature fall within the region of δ phase stability (Fig. 1a).
Observation of the threaded sections of the creep specimens revealed the presence
of the δ phase in all creep specimens. Therefore, the longer hold time at 700 °C as
compared to the aging treatment was suf ﬁcient to form δ precipitates within the
grain boundaries. The precipitates were present as plate or blocky-like precipitates,
Fig. 6c–e, which is consistent with the reported phase morphology [ 7, 20]. Those
were found to grow towards the bulk, away from the grain boundaries. Discrep-
ancies were observed in the grain boundary phases between the threaded and gauge
section of the creep specimens (see Fig. 9 for Alloy D). Overall, and for all
specimens, larger and a denser distribution of the δ phase precipitates were
observed close to the fracture surface as compared to the threaded section. Con-
sequently, the formation of the δ phase is further promoted in the presence of stress
[21].
Although decreases in the Ti/Al ratio resulted in faster times to failure, additions
of Ta and Nb tended to prolong creep life, see Fig. 4a. Furthermore, lower steady
state creep rates were recorded in those alloys (E and F), Table 5. For a similar Ti/
Al ratio, the creep life was extended by 114% from Alloy D to Alloy F with added
Nb, and 30% from Alloy D to Alloy E with the added Ta. This can be attributed to
both the decrease in the lattice mis ﬁt, Fig. 8, and the stronger presence of the δ
phase, Fig. 6d, e, with additions of Ta or Nb. While the lower mis ﬁt increases
strengthening, the δ phase potentially stitches the grains.
The Nb addition was signi ﬁcantly more effective at increasing the time to failure
than Ta as a 32% increase in the Nb content resulted in a 171 h creep life while a
860% increase in Ta content resulted in a 104 h creep life. Because the δ phase is
rich in Nb, its formation was further promoted by addition of Nb than Ta, Table 3.
Furthermore, Nb is known to provide some level of solid solution strengthening to
the matrix [ 22]. Consequently, adding Nb is bene ﬁcial to the creep life and
enhances ductility as compared to Ta, Fig. 4a. The slight increase in the amount of
δ phase in Alloy E with added Ta is attributed to the partitioning of Ta to the MC
carbides, thereby freeing Nb back into the matrix.
The mechanical properties of the IN725 variants investigated were promising
when compared to the commercial alloy from Ref. [ 1] and IN718 from Ref. [ 3, 17,
18]. Although the room temperature UTS and yield stress were overall lower than
the commercial alloy Ref. [ 1], they presented greater elongations during tensile
testing at room temperature and 750 °C, and good UTS values at 750 °C when
compared to IN718, Table 4 and Fig. 3. Furthermore, low steady-state creep rates
were observed while the Larson-Miller parameters on the IN725 variants were close
to that of IN718. Alloy A had the highest LMP of the IN725 variants tested. While
the alloys were designed for use at higher temperatures, the standard aging treat-
ment was considered for comparison to commercial alloys. Further work is ongoing
to target an optimal aging sequence.
During this investigation, the thermodynamic predictions from Thermo-Calc
were obtained using the databases TCNi8 and TTNi8, Fig. 1 and Table
3. Signif-
icant discrepancies were obtained in terms of phase stability, solvus temperatures
434 M. Detrois et al.

## Page 435

and phase compositions. Approximately 100 °C difference in solvus temperatures
was found between the two databases for both the γ′ phase and δ phase. TTNi8
predicted signi ﬁcantly lower solvus temperature of the γ′ phase for the two alloys
with high Ti/Al ratio (STD and A). Aging trials at 650 °C tend to agree with
TTNi8. The η phase predictions were signi ﬁcantly different as TCNi8 predicted
major partitioning of Ta and Al, while TTNi8 predicted a conventional Ni 3Ti phase
with partitioning of Nb. No η phase was observed in the specimens, most likely due
to the short times at temperature during aging or creep testing. Therefore, it is
impossible to conclude on the accuracy of the η phase predicted composition and
validating the thermodynamic predictions is beyond the scope of this investigation.
Conclusions
IN725 variants were designed and their mechanical properties were assessed and
compared to conventional IN725 and IN718. Based on the results from this
investigation, the following conclusions can be reported:
1. Decreases in the Ti/Al ratio resulted in a greater amount of grain boundary
carbides and increased γ′ content due to the reduction of MC (Ti-containing)
carbide content. This freed carbon for the precipitation of M
23C6 carbides. The
increase in the Al concentration partitioned to the γ′ phase.
2. Signi ﬁcant intergranular fracture and secondary cracking were observed in
alloys with low Ti/Al ratio. This behavior was attributed to the growth of the
grain boundary carbides.
3. The formation of δ phase precipitates was enhanced by additions of Nb, and Ta
to a smaller extent. The phase presented as a plate, or blocky-like, morphology,
and its formation was promoted in the presence of strain.
4. Additions of Nb and Ta were bene ﬁcial in increasing the time to failure during
creep due to a reduction in the γ/γ′ lattice mismatch and an increase in the
formation of δ precipitates stitching the grain boundaries. Niobium was more
effective at extending the time to failure in creep as less additions resulted in
longer times as compared to Ta.
5. Signi ﬁcant differences exist between thermodynamic predictions using the
TCNi8 and TTNi8 database.

Constrained Lattice Mis ﬁt Measurement
in Bulk Inconel 718 Using High
Resolution Neutron Diffraction
R. Y. Zhang, Z. N. Bi, H. L. Qin, J. Zhang, A. D. Fortes
and H. B. Dong
Abstract Lattice mis ﬁt is important in Inconel 718 (IN718) as coherency strain
strengthening from γ″ precipitates is the principal source of strengthening in this
alloy. The value of lattice mis ﬁti sd e ﬁned by the difference in lattice parameter
between each phase. In this study, high resolution time-of- ﬂight (TOF) neutron
diffraction has been used to measure the constrained lattice parameters and lattice
misﬁts of a bulk IN718 sample. Thanks to the high resolution of the diffractometer,
overlapped diffraction peaks are successfully deconvoluted, and the lattice param-
eters of different phases and lattice mis ﬁts are determined. The measured con-
strained lattice parameters of γ″ phase are much less than the reported
unconstrained lattice parameters measured from extracted γ″ precipitates. The lat-
tice mis ﬁt between γ″/γ phases along c-axis of γ″ phase is −0.015% indicating the
γ″ precipitates are largely constrained and highly coherent with γ matrix in bulk
IN718.

Introduction
The nickel-iron based superalloy IN718 has been widely used as turbine disc
material in aero engines for decades [ 1–5]. It has superior mechanical properties at
high temperatures not exceeding 650 °C [ 4]. The excellent high-temperature
properties are mainly due to a dispersion of γ′ and γ″ precipitates in γ matrix [5–9].
The intermetallic γ′ phase is L1 2 crystal structure with chemical formula Ni 3Al, γ″
phase is DO 22 crystal structure with chemical formula Ni 3Nb. It is known the main
hardening phase in IN718 is the γ″ phase [ 5–8]. γ″ phase displays a distinct ori-
entation relationship with γ matrix phase as (001) γ″ // {100} γ, and [001] γ″ //
<100>γ [7]. γ″ precipitates are disc-shaped particles, with the thickness about
10 nm and the diameter about 30 nm [ 10]. Lattice parameters of γ″ and γ phases are
very close, leading to a very small lattice mis ﬁt between the precipitates and matrix.
Lattice mis ﬁt is signi ﬁcant in IN718 since it in ﬂuences the coherency strain
strengthening and morphology of precipitates, which contribute to the mi-
crostructure and mechanical properties of IN718 [ 4, 11, 12].
Lattice mis ﬁti sd e ﬁned as δ =2 a
p − am
/C2/C3
̸ ap + am
/C2/C3
, where ap and am are the
lattice parameters of precipitates and matrix, respectively. The lattice parameter can
be measured by various diffraction techniques, e.g. X-ray, neutron or
convergent-beam electron diffraction [13–16]. Lattice parameters of precipitates can
be measured on extracted precipitate powder when matrix is dissolved (uncon-
strained lattice) [ 5, 17, 18], or on bulk sample where precipitates are embedded in
the matrix (constrained lattice) [ 12, 19–23]. Constrained lattice parameters in bulk
γ′ hardened Nickel-based superalloys have been measured using neutron diffraction
[12, 20–23]. These kind of measurements requires a deconvolution approach to
separate the overlapped diffraction peaks from precipitate phase and matrix phase.
Difﬁculties arise when using this method to measure constrained lattice parameters
in γ″ hardened Nickel-based superalloys such as IN718: (i) γ′ and γ″ precipitates
present; (ii) Two precipitate types diffraction peaks overlap with γ matrix peaks;
(iii) Low precipitates volume fraction ( γ′ + γ″ ∼ 20–25%) [ 24]; (iv) Very ﬁne
precipitate particles ( ∼10–30 nm) [ 10].
To address the above challenges, we proposed to use a high resolution neutron
powder diffractometer (HRPD) at the ISIS neutron spallation source; HRPD is one
of the highest resolution neutron powder diffractometers in the world thanks to its
95-meter-long neutron ﬂight path. The HRPD diffractometer consists of a bank of
backscattering detectors (focussed in software to a common scattering angle of
168.33°) and two banks of detectors at 2 θ = 90°. Using the instrument's standard
30–130 ms time-of- ﬂight mode the backscattering detectors cover the d-spacing
range from 0.65 to 2.6 Å with a resolution ≈ 4–5×1 0
−4, while the 90° detectors
cover a larger range of d-spacings from 0.85 to 3.9 Å [ 25]. The high resolution and
complementary detection design make the deconvolution of overlapped peaks from
IN718 feasible. The present study shows the constrained lattice parameter and
lattice misﬁt measurement on a bulk IN718 sample using time-of- ﬂight (TOF) high
resolution neutron diffraction (HRPD) at ISIS.

Material and Experimental Procedure
A cylindrical Inconel 718 specimen was provided by Central Iron and Steel
Research Institute (China). Nominal chemical composition of the sample is given in
Table 1. The specimen with a gauge volume of ϕ 2 mm × 3 mm was extracted out
of a forged IN718 disc then subjected to heat treatment. The heat treatment involved
a solution treatment at 980 °C for 1 h and then water quenched to room temper-
ature, followed by ageing at 720 °C for 8 h. Then it was furnace cooled to 620 °C
for another 8 h ageing for stabilisation of γ′ and γ″ precipitates, with a ﬁnal air cool
to room temperature. γ′ and γ″ precipitates are shown in SEM micrograph in Fig. 1,
the unit cell of γ″ phase can be considered as two face-centred cubes stacking
together as shown in Fig. 1.
The specimen was put into a 3 mm diameter neutron-transparent vanadium can
and placed in the diffractometer ’s evacuated sample tank. The sample was mea-
sured at room temperature and neutron diffraction data acquisition time was about
90 min. Diffracted neutrons were detected by the backscattering detectors and 90°
detectors (Fig. 2).

3. Lattice parameters and lattice mis ﬁts
The constrained lattice parameters for all three phases and lattice mis ﬁts in bulk
IN718 are listed in Table 5 with the reported unconstrained lattice parameters. The
measured lattice parameter of γ phase is in general agreement with those lattice
parameters of γ phase reported in literature [ 5, 17, 18, 29, 30]. Lattice parameter of
γ′ phase is slightly larger than those reported lattice parameters of γ′ phase which
between 3.59 and 3.61 Å [ 5, 17, 18, 29, 30]. The signi ﬁcant difference of lattice
parameters between constrained and unconstrained is found on γ″ phase. The
constrained a
γ00 and cγ00 are about 1 and 2.7% less than the unconstrained aγ00 and cγ00
respectively. The values for γ″ phase were obtained from extracted precipitates,
precipitates extraction from γ matrix will lead to stress relaxation of the precipitates,
this could be the reason that the measured constrained lattice parameters for γ″
phase are signi ﬁcantly smaller than those unconstrained lattice parameters obtained
from extracted precipitates. Differences between lattice mis ﬁts measured at con-

Conclusions
Constrained lattice parameters of strengthening precipitates in a bulk IN718 sample
was measured using high resolution TOF neutron powder diffraction (HRPD).
HRPD shows a high resolution of diffraction pattern which enable the observation
of γ′(100) and γ′(110) diffraction peaks. Overlapped peaks from the coherent γ, γ′
and γ″ phases were separated into individual peaks for four ( hkl)r eﬂections. Lattice
parameters and lattice mis ﬁts were calculated on the basis of peaks deconvolution.
Lattice parameters of γ and γ′ phases are similar to those reported in literature on
matrix and extracted γ′ precipitates, while lattice parameters of γ″ phase exist
signiﬁcantly smaller than the values obtained from extracted γ″ precipitates. Lattice
misﬁts between phases in the bulk sample are compared with earlier measurements
on extracted precipitates and yield signi ﬁcant differences. Magnitude of lattice
misﬁts along c-axis of γ″ phase in bulk sample is much smaller than that measured
on extracted precipitates, indicating the γ″ precipitates are signi ﬁcantly constrained
and coherent with γ matrix.

Dependence of Creep Strength
on Cooling Rate After Subsolvus
Solution Treatment in Wrought Alloy
718
Satoru Kobayashi, Chuuya Aoki, Tomonori Ueno
and Masao Takeyama
Abstract It was recently found that the creep strength and creep life of wrought
alloy 718 samples showed an interesting dependence on the cooling rate in the
standard subsolvus solution temperature: the time to 0.2% creep strain varies from 5
to 400 h depending on the cooling rate between 1 and 199 °C/min with the max-
imum value at an intermediate cooling rate of 51 °C/min under a creep condition of
621 °C/724 MPa. In the present paper, microstructures were observed for samples
after creep deformation to 0.2% creep strain to understand the dependence of the
creep strength on the cooling rate. The microstructural observations using a ﬁeld
emission type scanning electron microscope and transmission electron microscope
showed that the size of coherent γ″/γ′ precipitates in grains decreased and the
number density increased with increasing the cooling rate but they saturated around
the cooling rate at which the creep strength was maximized. A careful observation
on grain boundaries revealed that the precipitation of ﬁne γ″ phase precipitates was
enhanced along grain boundaries and coherent twin boundaries at intermediate
cooling rates and that of δ phase platelets was pronounced along grain boundaries
and incoherent twin boundaries at slower cooling rates. These microstructural
features suggest that the maximized creep strength is related to an enhanced pre-
cipitation of γ″/γ′ particles along grain/twin boundaries as well as a high number
density ( ﬁne size) of ﬁne γ″/γ′ particles in grain interiors.

Introduction
Alloy 718 is the most widely used Ni based wrought superalloy for high temper-
ature components such as aircraft engine and land-base gas turbine disks because of
good mechanical properties and fabricability etc. [ 1, 2]. The microstructure of this
alloy contains several types of second phase s of δ-Ni3Nb (D0 a), γ″-Ni3Nb (D0 22)
and γ′-Ni3(Al,Ti) (L1 2) etc. in the γ-Ni (A1) solid solution matrix, which is con-
trolled to obtain the mechanical properties that are required for particular high
temperature components.
The standard heat treatment adopted for this alloy, the so-called subsolvus heat
treatment, is a solution treatment below the δ solvus temperature above which the
δ-Ni
3Nb (D0 22) phase is completely dissolved, followed by rapid cooling, and a
subsequent two-step aging heat treatment (holding at 718 °C for 8 h, furnace
cooling to 621 °C and holding at the temperature for a total aging time of 18 h
followed by air cooling) [ 3, 4]. This subsolvus solution treatment is intended to
form ﬁne recrystallized grains pinned by residual δ phase precipitates in order to
obtain good fatigue resistance. Rapid cooling from the solution treatment temper-
ature is speculated to cause the precipitation of ﬁne γ″/γ′ phase in the matrix phase
not during the cooling but in the two-step aging heat treatment in order to obtain
high strength. Creep properties might have been of secondary importance for the
conventional use of the alloy treated with the subsolvus heat treatment, but the
relative importance of creep properties to fatigue properties should increase in near
future due to an increased temperature in turbine disks to meet a requirement to
improve the ef ﬁciency of aircraft engines.
Aoki et al. recently found that a wrought alloy 718 sample showed an interesting
dependency of creep properties on the cooling rate after the subsolvus solution
treatment temperature; the time to 0.2% creep strain and the creep life showed a
maximum value at an intermediate cooling rate under a creep condition of 621°C/
724 MPa. The lower creep strength at slower cooling rates allows us to expect that
the dependence is related to the precipitation of coherent γ″/γ′ particles within
grains, but the lower creep strength at higher cooling rates raises a question on what
microstructural factor causes the strength. In the present paper, microstructures
were observed for samples after creep deformation to a creep strain of 0.2% to
understand the dependency of the creep strength on the cooling rate.
Experimental Procedures
The alloy used was a hot-forged and ring-rolled 718 alloy. The chemical compo-
sition, analyzed by ICP-OES, is shown in Table 1. The rolled sample was cut by
electro discharged machining into cylindrical specimens of 14 mm in diameter and
150 mm in length along the circumferential direction of the rolled sample parallel to
450 S. Kobayashi et al.

## Page 450

the length of the cylinders. The specimens were solution treated at a temperature of
982 °C for 1 h, and cooled at different cooling rates between 1 and 199 °C/min to
600 °C by gas quenching , followed by air cooling. The cooling rates were selected
to investigate the effect of cooling rate that can be applicable to real forging parts.
The measurements of cooling rates were made with a thermocouple inserted to a
hole in a dummy sample with the same size. Each cooling rate shown is the
averaged one between 982 and 600 °C. The solution treated specimens were
subsequently aged in the two-step standard condition (holding at 718 °C for 8 h,
furnace cooling to 621 °C and holding at the temperature for a total aging time of
18 h followed by air cooling).
Creep tests were conducted at a temperature of 621°C under a constant load to
have an initial stress of 724 MPa in air to a creep strain of 0.2% and to rupture.
Samples were taken for microstructural observations from the gauge portion of the
creep-interrupted specimens. The observation was performed using a ﬁeld emission
type scanning electron microscope (FESEM) and transmission electron microscope
(TEM). The sample surface was prepared for FESEM observation by mechanical
grinding and polishing down 1 μm sized diamond suspension, followed by
electro-polishing with 10% perchloric acid in acetic acid. The sample for TEM
observation was prepared by a twin-jet method using a solution of 10% perchloric
acid in methanol.
Results and Discussion
Creep Properties
The creep strength and the creep life greatly vary as a function of the cooling rate
from the solution treatment temperature, as shown in Fig. 1. The time to 0.2% creep
strain varied from 5 to 400 h depending on the cooling rate between 1 and 199 °C/
min with a maximum value at an intermediate cooling rate of 50 °C/min under the
creep condition. The creep rupture time also shows a similar dependence on the
cooling rate to the short time creep strength behavior with a maximum rupture time
at somewhat shorter cooling rate. Table 2 summarizes the time to reach 0.2% creep
strain and to rupture of the 718 alloy specimens obtained in the present study.

Microstructural Characterization
FESEM and TEM observations revealed that the microstructures along grain
boundaries as well as in grains in the specimens depend on the cooling rate from the
subsolvus solution treatment, especially in the morphology and distribution of δ and
γ″ phase precipitates.
Figure 2 shows grain structures and distribution of δ phase precipitates in some
of the creep-interrupted specimens at a low magni ﬁcation of backscattered electron
(BSE) imaging. It is seen that the matrix grain sizes are almost equivalent and their
average size was ∼14 μm regardless of the cooling rate. δ phase precipitates,
imaged in bright contrast, are elongated and are 10 μm at maximum in size along
their longitudinal directions, and their size and volume fraction increase slightly
with decreasing the cooling rate. The size of δ phase precipitates and their
dependence on the cooling rate allow us to deduce that the precipitates exist at the
solution temperature and grew during cooling according to the cooling rate.

Figure 3 shows the existence of precipitates at grain boundaries of the specimens
at a high magni ﬁcation of BSE imaging. Fine acicular precipitates as well as coarse
ones are recognized at grain boundaries in the specimens of relatively slow cooling
rates (Fig. 3c, d), while only ﬁne precipitates are seen at grain boundaries in the
specimens of relatively fast cooling rates (Fig. 3a, b). These morphological fea-
tures and the heat treatment pro ﬁles indicate that the ﬁne/acicular precipitates are
δ phase ones that were formed during cooling from the solution treatment tem-
perature. Figure 4 shows the distribution of precipitates in the matrix grains and at
grain/twin boundaries on a high magni ﬁcation secondary electron image on
strongly etched sections. Fine grain-like precipitates are seen not only in grain
interiors but also at grain boundaries and coherent twin boundaries, and the pre-
cipitation at the boundaries becomes more pronounced as the cooling rate
decreases. The ﬁne grain-like precipitates are presumed to be γ′/γ″ phase, according
to their morphology based on a common knowledge in microstructure formation in
alloy 718. Acicular precipitates, identi ﬁed as δ phase, are also recognized at
non-coherent twin boundaries that are twin boundaries, which divide twin-oriented
grains but do not coincide with any crystallographic (111) planes, in the specimens
of slow cooling rates.
TEM observations also revealed a dependence of the distribution of
grain-boundary precipitates on the cooling rate. Figure 5 shows examples of TEM

Dependence of Microstructure on the Cooling Rate
in the Solution Treatment
The observed dependence of microstructure on the cooling rate in the subsolvus
solution treatment is summarized as follows:
(1) The size of γ″/γ′ precipitates in grains decreases with increasing the cooling rate
from 1 to 51 °C/min but saturates above these cooling rate s.

(2) Precipitation of γ″ phase is enhanced on grain boundaries and coherent twin
boundaries at an intermediate cooling rate of 51 °C/min.
(3) δ phase platelets precipitate on grain boundaries and incoherent twin bound-
aries. This precipitation is pronounced as the cooling rate decreases.
The dependence of the precipitation of γ″ and δ phase on the cooling rate
indicate that the precipitations occurred during cooling from the solution treat-
ment. These results are not inconsistent with the results reported by Geng et al. [6].
The dependence of creep strength on the cooling rate is discussed below based
on the microstructural features obtained in the present study. It was con ﬁrmed that
the lower creep strength at slower cooling rates is rationalized by coarser γ″ phase
precipitate size and their smaller number density. Chaturvedi et al. [ 7] prepared
alloy 718 samples with different γ″ phase size in grains by changing the period of
aging at 725 °C and found that the minimum creep rate of the samples shows a
minimum at a γ″ phase size of 20 –30 nm under a test condition at a temperature of
600 °C and various stress levels between 670 and 815 MPa. They explained this
result by an effect of the γ″ size on the ease of dislocation glide and dislocation
climb motions. This explanation is, however, not true for the faster cooling rates of
the present case since the size of γ″ phase saturates at and above the cooling rates at
Fig. 6 Transmission electron images taken from grain interiors in the gauge portion of the alloy
718 specimens after 0.2% creep strain: a–c bright ﬁeld images in the same magni ﬁcation,
d–f selected area diffraction patterns B = 001, a, d 199 °C/min, b, e 51 °C/min, c, f 1 °C/min
Dependence of Creep Strength on Cooling Rate … 457

## Page 457

which the creep strength was maximized. Wisniewski and Beddoes [ 8] reported an
improved creep strength by grain boundary serration in Waspaloy. A signi ﬁcant
grain boundary serration was, however, not observed in the present case. The
observed microstructural features and literature survey lead us to speculate that the
reduced creep strength at higher cooling rates is related to a less enhanced pre-
cipitation of γ″ precipitates on grain/twin boundaries.
A positive effect of grain boundary precipitates on creep rupture strength has
been reported so far under a low stress condition. Takeyama et al. [ 9] reported that
the minimum creep rate decreased with increasing the area fraction of grain
boundaries covered by W phase (A2) precipitates in a Ni-20Cr-20 W alloy, and
called this strengthening effect ‘grain boundary precipitation strengthening
(GBPS)’. Takeyama [10] have recently found grain boundary precipitation inhibits
local deformation around grain boundaries and thereby reducing the acceleration of
creep rate, resulting in the extension of creep life. This GBPS effect has never been
reported in high stress condition, as far as the authors know, and further investi-
gations are therefore needed to conclude the effect of grain boundary precipitates on
creep deformation under a high stress condition.
Summary
The present paper investigates the effect of cooling rate in the standard subsolvus
solution treatment on microstructure in aged 718 alloy specimens after a creep
deformation to 0.2% creep strain, and correlates with a maximized creep strength at
an intermediate cooling rate. The main results are:
(1) The size of γ″/γ′ precipitates in grains decreases with increasing the cooling rate
from 1 to 51 °C/min but saturates above the cooling rate.
(2) Precipitation of γ″ phase is enhanced on grain boundaries and coherent twin
boundaries at an intermediate cooling rate of 51 °C/min.
(3) δ phase platelets precipitate on grain boundaries and incoherent twin bound-
aries. This precipitation is more pronounced as the cooling rate decreases.
(4) The dependence of creep strength on the cooling rate is explained such that the
reduced creep strength at slower cooling rates is due to a coarser γ″ phase
precipitate size and their smaller number density, and the reduced strength at
higher cooling rates is related to a pronounced precipitation of γ″/γ′ precipitate
particles on grain/twin boundaries.

4,000 h in air. Fatigue testing was performed at 840 °C after exposure and the
microstructures and fracture surfaces were characterized. Both grain sizes had
similar amounts of oxide and alloy depletion, but it was found that the ﬁne-grained
material experienced signi ﬁcant depletion induced grain growth in the near-surface
region. While 875 °C is signi ﬁcantly below the temperatures where grain growth is
active for the bulk alloy composition, the depletion of Al, Ti, and Cr in the near
surface region decreased the γ′ solvus and increased grain boundary mobility.
Property testing was performed on the as-oxidized surfaces as well as
post-machined surfaces to study the effect of this microstructural change. The
experimental results show that the coarse-grained material had longer fatigue life
after 4000 h, and that surface degradation had a more signi ﬁcant effect on the life of
the ﬁne-grained material.
Keywords Fatigue
⋅ Superalloy ⋅ 751 ⋅ Oxidation ⋅ Depletion
Introduction
Alloy 751 is a wrought γ′ strengthened superalloy with approximately 22% γ′ phase
fraction at room temperature. It is an alloy that is very similar to the more common
X-750 with the primary difference being that 751 has slightly lower titanium and
higher aluminum than X-750. All other elements are essentially the same. It is also
somewhat similar to alloy 80A in terms of γ′ volume fraction. Despite the presence
of niobium at a 0.95% nominal level, the alloy is not strengthened by γ″ phase due

## Page 460

to the elevated levels of aluminum and titanium that suppress the formation of γ″ in
favor of γ′. It should be noted that all three alloys, 751, X-750, and 80A are all
nominally cobalt free. The alloy compositions are provided in Table 1.
The high cycle fatigue performance of alloy 751 has been studied in some detail
by Yoshiba and Miyagawa [ 1] and Jones [ 2]. In these published studies, the primary
objective was to study the effect of high temperature corrosion, particularly sul ﬁ-
dation corrosion, on the fatigue performance of the alloy. Yoshiba found that the
ﬁne-grained material demonstrated a more signi ﬁcant reduction in fatigue strength
than the coarse-grained material when subjected to a corrosive atmosphere. He
attributed this to the fact that the deleterious effects in the ﬁne-grained material were
twofold, reduced time to crack initiation due to intergranular corrosion plus
increased crack propagation rate due to intergranular corrosive damage, whereas the
coarse-grained material always demonstrated transgranular propagation so therefore
only had a fatigue strength reduction due to enhanced intergranular initiation.
Corrosion of alloy 751 was studied by Clark [ 3]. He found that the failure of and
engine valve was caused by sul ﬁdation attack by CaSO4 and C deposits at 816 °C
and above, and that the intergranular attack played a signi ﬁcant role in the failure
mechanism.
Fatigue is generally divided into initiation and propagation stages, and the
mechanism by which these phenomena occur in relation to the microstructure (i.e.
intergranular or transgranular) contributes signi ﬁcantly to the fatigue strength of the
material. For Nimonic 80A, it was found that over-aging the material led to a
signiﬁcant reduction in fatigue life at 800 °C [ 4] and that as the fracture surfaces
become more intergranular, the fatigue strength drops signi ﬁcantly [ 5]. The cited
studies [ 4, 5] were on material of a single grain size, so the grain size dependence
was not included in that work. Work performed on Waspaloy shows similar
reduction in the low cycle fatigue performance when the crack path became
intergranular [ 6].
In the present study, the long-term stability of the alloy after prolonged high
temperature exposure in air, absent of other corrosive species, is of interest.
Expected lifetimes of components can be in the thousands or even tens of thousands

## Page 461

of hours, and during this time when exposed at elevated temperatures the properties
can be reduced signi ﬁcantly. Acquiring an understanding of the time dependent
degradation is critical to the designer for material selection and life analysis. In
addition, understanding how microstructural features like grain size affect the
degradation is important in selecting not only the right material but also the right
process for a given application.
When aged at 875 °C, the properties are expected to degrade due to the envi-
ronmental surface degradation (oxidation) as well as metallurgical sub-surface
degradation. The γ′ precipitates coarsen, the carbides degenerate, and even the grain
structure itself can be altered. The oxide structure of similar alloy X-750 has been
studied to show that structure is comprised of outer spinel layers and an inner layer
of discontinuous internally oxidized base material [ 7], not a more protective con-
tinuous alumina scale. Gaining an understanding of the effect of the oxide in
concert with subsurface microstructural changes is the goal of this study.
Experimental Procedure
Materials
Alloy 751 was procured in as-hot-rolled bar 25.4 mm diameter. Ingot production
was VIM+ESR method. Chemistry is provided in Table 1. The material was in
conformance with SAE J775. The starting microstructure was equiaxed grains with
an average grain size of 12 μm (ASTM grain size no. 10). Starting hardness was 37
HRC.
To produce the coarse grain size, the material was subjected to a supersolvus
solution treatment followed by water quenching and then a two-stage aging treat-
ment. The ﬁne-grained material was subjected to the same two stage aging treat-
ment without a solution treatment. Details of the heat treatment cycle are provided
in Table 2. The supersolvus treatment served to grow the grains considerably as
shown in the table, while the double aged only cycle did not cause a signi ﬁcant
change in grain size.

Thermal Exposure
Material was exposed at 875 °C in a box furnace without atmospheric control. The
heat was provided by electric heating elements and consequently there were no
products of combustion in the furnace. The furnace was situated on a factory ﬂoor
setting without air conditioning or controlled humidity. Note that the majority of the
fatigue specimens were exposed in the fully machined condition. Some specimens
were tested without oxide, and those specimens were exposed in the rough
machined condition, with care taken to allow suf ﬁcient stock removal so that the
effects of oxidation were separated. Finish machining was performed after the
thermal exposure. For all specimens, care was taken to avoid dimensional distortion
during the furnace exposure, and no observable distortion was observed on the
specimens. If present any distortion would have been readily detectible as the
rotating-bend test has stringent runout requirements for test validity.
Fatigue Testing
Rotating bending fatigue was performed in accordance with ISO 1143 on Fatigue
Dynamics RBF-300HT machines produced by Systems Integrators LLC. This
machine model is a single point bending style where a load is applied to the
specimen end. A clamshell furnace was used to heat the specimen during the test.
An isometric view of the machine model is shown in Fig. 1, with the specimen

Specimens were tested so as to target failure at one million cycles, or one mega-
cycle. Testing was conducted at 80 Hz under fully reversed loading conditions with
R= −1 at a test temperature of 840 °C. For each grain size-exposure time com-
bination 11 to 20 specimens were tested. The total number of fatigue tests con-
ducted in this study was 140. Although longer and shorter times were tested, the
focus of this paper is the one megacycle fatigue strength.
The test specimens used were of the hourglass type. Dimensions are provided in
Fig. 2. The reduced section of the specimen was produced using a low stress
grinding process followed by longitudinal polishing.
Characterization
Post-test characterization of the specimens was performed on a Hitachi S3400
scanning electron microscope and by optical methods. For oxide measurements, the
specimens were all evaluated in the as-polished (unetched) condition. For grain size
and microstructural characterization, the specimens were etched using a modi ﬁed
Marbles reagent. Care was taken to evaluate the microstructure within 3 mm of the
fracture surface.
Results
Fatigue Performance
The fatigue results are shown in Fig. 3 showing strength for one megacycle. Both
grain sizes resulted in similar strength levels in the virgin (unexposed) condition. It
is clear that the thermal exposure reduced the properties considerably for both the
ﬁne-grained and the coarse-grained material, but the time dependence is quite
different. Note that the data is normalized to the highest fatigue strength for one
megacycle, which was demonstrated by the ﬁne-grained material in the virgin
condition, and the same scale is used for both Fig. 3a, b.
In Fig. 3a it can be seen that when oxide was present on the surface, the
ﬁne-grained fatigue strength reduced by approximately 40% after 4000 h of

exposure, and this reduction occurred gradually over time. A similar reduction was
seen for the coarse-grained material, but occurred much more rapidly; the reduction
was observed after only 500 h of exposure. Longer term exposure beyond 500 h
appeared to strengthen the coarse-grained material slightly. Figure 3b shows the
difference in fatigue strength for 4000 h exposed material with different surface
conditions. When the specimens are machined after the thermal exposure and the
oxidized surface layer is not present, the material has higher fatigue strength for
both gran sizes. The difference is more prominent for the ﬁne-grained material.
Microstructural Characterization
The near-surface microstructure of the failed specimens is shown in Fig. 4. For both
grain sizes there is a continuous surface oxide and a subsurface internal oxide. For
the ﬁne-grained material, the subsurface oxide is primarily intergranular, while for
the coarse-grained material it is both intergranular and intragranular. With
increasing exposure times, the continuous oxide thickens and the internal oxide
grows deeper into the base material. The micrographs in Fig. 4 are shown in the
unetched condition so as to not obscure the oxides with etched grain boundaries.
The oxide thickness and the core hardness of these specimens was measured
post-test and those results are shown in Fig. 5. The oxide thickness includes both
the continuous surface oxide thickness as well as the internally affected depth. It can
be seen in Fig. 5a that the ﬁne-grained material exhibited a thicker layer of oxidized
material than the coarse-grained. Figure 5b shows that the hardness for both the ﬁne
and coarse-grained material decreased signi ﬁcantly over the course of the thermal
exposure at 875 °C.
The specimens were subsequently etched to reveal the base material
microstructure. Micrographs of the ﬁne-grained 500 and 2000 h exposed material

The ﬁne-grained 4000 h specimen was examined by SEM-EDS to evaluation the
depletion of elements in the subsurface region. Those results are shown in Fig. 8.I t
can be seen that the surface oxide is chromia and titania rich, whereas the internal
oxide is predominantly alumina. It can also be seen that in the grain growth region,
the aluminum and titanium levels have been reduced to approximately 0.5 and 1.1,
respectively. Chromium has also been depleted but by a lower relative percentage.
The microstructure of select specimens was examined in the SEM to further
characterize the structure to better understand the reduction in properties. Of par-
ticular interest was understanding why the 500 h coarse-grained material exhibited
such a signi ﬁcant reduction in strength, and then showed improved fatigue strength
after additional exposure duration. The results of that investigation are shown in
Fig. 9. At the lower magni ﬁcation images of Fig. 9a, c, no difference is discernible.
However, at higher magni ﬁcation, examination of the grain boundaries shows that
the 500 h material has a near-continuous precipitate ﬁlm. In the 4000 h
coarse-grained material, not only have the intragranular γ′ precipitates coarsened,
but the particles decorating the grain boundaries have also coarsened. The widening
of these grain boundary precipitates has occurred to such an extent that they ceased
to be a continuous network and are now discrete.

Discussion
Fatigue Performance
It is generally understood that ﬁne-grained materials have superior tensile and
fatigue properties, while coarser grained materials will have superior creep prop-
erties at an equivalent γ′ volume fraction [ 8, 9]. This point is illustrated by the
example of dual microstructure disks for gas turbine engines world, engineered to

## Page 470

have ﬁner grains near the center for burst strength and coarser grains near the outer
rim for creep strength where temperatures are higher [ 10].
However, when tensile, fatigue, and creep are all important at high temperatures,
the choice of grain size is not so straightforward. The issue becomes even more
complex when degradation after long term exposure is explored. The current study
shows that even at 840 °C, ﬁne-grained material can perform very well and can
have even greater fatigue strength than coarse-grained under certain conditions. The
fatigue strength in the virgin condition as well as at the 4000 h aged condition is
nearly the same for both grain sizes. The difference is in the exposure time
dependence of the fatigue strength. The coarse-grained material reduces signi ﬁ-
cantly after 500 h but is stable thereafter, even increasing slightly. The ﬁne-grained
material reduces more gradually such that at 500 h the fatigue strength is greater
than the coarse-grained material. Extrapolating to longer times, it appears that
beyond 4000 h the ﬁne-grained material may continue to drop in fatigue strength,
whereas the coarse-grained material is more stable.
Although this study appears to be somewhat counter to conventional wisdom in
terms of grain size dependence, other factors must be considered. For example,
because the fatigue testing was fully reversed, this study does not incorporate mean
stress effects, where it is expected that creep strength will become even more
important and that larger grains may yield better performance. It has been shown
that a cyclic tensile mean stress can be the most damaging to a material at high
temperature [11], and a structure with larger grains is expected to have better creep
resistance [ 9].
Fracture Mechanisms
Initiation and initial propagation is always transgranular for both grain sizes at the
test temperature of 840 °C. For coarse-grained virgin material, the propagation
remains predominantly transgranular until ﬁnal fracture. However, for the same
material in the 500 h aged condition, the propagation mode transitions abruptly
from transgranular to intergranular soon after initiation. This can be seen in Fig. 11.
This is likely due to the signi ﬁcant amount of coarsening of the precipitates on the
grain boundaries as shown in Fig. 9d. With the continuous grain boundary network,
the strength is lower for one megacycle than for 2000 h or even 4000 h exposed
material in the coarse-grained condition.
For the ﬁne-grained material, the propagation always initiated in a stage I
transgranular manner then transitioned to intergranular regardless of the grain size,
though the transition was more gradual than for the 500 h exposed coarse-grained
material. The continuous grain boundary network was not developed on the
ﬁne-grained material, likely due to the signi ﬁcantly larger grain boundary area.
472 M. D. Veliz

## Page 471

Microstructural Evolution
Based on the analysis presented in Fig. 8, it is clear that the grain growth beneath
the oxide in the ﬁne-grained material was depletion induced. An analysis of the
alloy 751 composition using JMatPro yielded the results shown in Fig. 12. The
nominal composition shows a γ′ solvus just over 900 °C, whereas the composition
from the depletion induced grain growth region has a γ′ solvus of just over 700 °C.
At the exposure temperature of 875 °C, the precipitates were no longer present to
impede grain growth, and therefore the result was the observed microstructure.
Regarding the oxidation behavior of alloy 751, it should be noted that the
damage was not extensive in this isothermal study, even after 4000 h. However, in
a thermally cyclic application the alloy may be much more prone to greater oxi-
dation damage depths due to the nature of the chromium and titanium rich oxide,
which can exhibit greater extent of oxidation damage, especially in the presence of
water vapor [ 12, 13].
Although the grain boundary precipitates that caused the 500 h embrittlement
were not fully characterized, it is expected that they are M 23C6 carbides based
information in the literature [ 8]. Figure 12 suggests that M 23C6 would be fully
dissolved at 875 °C and that the mechanism could possibly be different. However,
it has been reported that M 23C6 can be stable up to temperatures of 980 °C [ 14],
particularly as the result of continuous breakdown of MC carbide at high temper-
atures. [ 15]. Continuous carbide at the grain boundary, either as ﬁlm or a “zip-
perlike” structure has been reported in Waspaloy [ 15], among other alloys, to
provide an easy path for crack propagation. It is expected that the phenomenon
observed in the current study of alloy 751 is similar to what has been reported in
Waspaloy.

Conclusions
For the one megacycle fatigue strength of alloy 751 at 840 °C:
• Virgin as-heat treated material with no subsequent exposure had similar strength
in both the ﬁne and coarse-grained conditions.
• After 4000 h of exposure at 875 °C, the strength of both materials was similar,
but reduced by approximately 40% over virgin material.
• The coarse-grained material showed a 40% strength reduction after 500 h
without further decline at 2000 and 4000 h. The fatigue strength increased
slightly from 500 h to 2000 h before a slight decrease from 2000 to 4000 h. The
strength minimum at 500 h corresponds to the most rapid transition from
transgranular to intergranular fatigue crack propagation.
• The ﬁne-grained material showed a more gradual reduction in strength with
exposure time, with a 23% reduction at 500 h, 35% reduction at 2000 h, and
40% reduction at 4000 h. For the long term aged material exhibiting depletion
induced grain growth, the propagation through the large grained zone was
transgranular, then transitioned back to intergranular as the crack grew back into
the ﬁne-grained base material.
• The transition to intergranular fatigue crack propagation resulted in a signi ﬁcant
reduction in fatigue strength in both ﬁne and coarse-grained material.

474 M. D. Veliz

## Page 473

The microstructure of alloy 751 was altered by exposure such that:
• The coarse-grained material exhibited a 40 μm thick oxide affected layer with 75
μm of depleted zone beneath.
• The ﬁne-grained material exhibited a 70 μm thick oxide affected layer with
approximately 100 μm of depleted zone beneath, where extensive grain coars-
ening occurred due to the depletion of precipitates. This depletion induced grain
growth zone had a grain size of 100 μm. Grains size abruptly transitioned back
14 μm below the depleted zone.
• Both ﬁne and coarse-grained materials exhibited signi ﬁcant coarsening of the
precipitates after 4000 h. The coarse-grained material exhibited a 500 h
embrittlement phenomenon where the intergranular particles developed a con-
tinuous network. Longer exposure times of 2000 and 4000 h served to coarsen
the boundary precipitates to the point that they became discrete and fatigue
strength increased slightly.

Abstract Many Ni-base superalloys are susceptible to intergranular brittle fracture
during holding under high stresses at relatively low temperatures, known as
stress-assisted grain boundary oxidation (SAGBO). These superalloys are
strengthened by geometrically close-packed precipitates such as Ni
3Al (L1 2) and
Ni3Nb (D0 22) within grain interiors, whereas role of grain-boundary precipitates in
strengthening of the alloys is limited. It is thus interesting to know how the presence
of grain-boundary precipitates affects the SAGBO behavior. Recently Takeyama
et al. has developed a novel austenitic heat-resistant steel Fe-20Cr-35Ni-2.5Nb
(at.%) strengthened by intermetallic phases of topologically close-packed Fe
2Nb
Laves precipitated at grain boundaries, together with Ni 3Nb within grain interiors.
The creep rupture strength of the steel at 800 °C is comparable to Ni-base alloys,
and the higher the area fraction ρ of the grain boundaries covered by the Laves
phase, the lower the creep rate, thereby leading to the superior strength. This
strengthening mechanism is called “Grain-boundary Precipitation Strengthening
(GBPS)”. In this study, the relationship between the GBPS and SAGBO behavior
has been investigated using the novel steels based on Fe-20Cr-35Ni-2.5Nb. Two
specimens with similar strength but different ρ values were prepared. Constant-load
tests were conducted at 90% of the yield stress and 600 °C in air. Rupture time and
rupture elongation become larger in high ρ specimen. Ductile morphologies were
observed on the fracture surfaces in the high ρ specimen, whereas intergranular

Grain-boundary precipitation strengthening
Introduction
SAGBO is intergranular brittle fracture that occurs during holding under high
stresses at relatively low temperatures. It has been reported that such clean inter-
granular fracture is suppressed by grain-boundary precipitation [ 1], while role of
grain-boundary precipitates on crack has not been clearly understood.
Novel austenitic heat-resistant steel Fe-20Cr-35Ni-2.5Nb (at.%) developed by
Takeyama et al. is strengthened by intermetallic phases of topologically
close-packed Fe
2Nb Laves phase precipitated at grain boundaries, together with
Ni3Nb within grain interiors [ 2, 3], which grain strengthening mechanism is similar
to Ni-base superalloys. Its extensive creep strength obtained by novel mechanism
has been reported [ 4], but another advantage of this steel is that grain strength and ρ
value can be controlled ﬂexibly by aging heat treatment.
This work prepared heat treated material from Fe-20Cr-35Ni-2.5Nb (at.%) that
has similar strength level to Ni-base alloy with different ρ values. Effect of
grain-boundary precipitates on SAGBO behaviors was veri ﬁed.
Experimental
Material
Nominal chemical composition of the material is Fe-20Cr-35Ni-2.5Nb (at.%).
Forged/hot rolled plates with thicknesses about 15 mm were prepared and heat
treated as shown in Table 1. 1,000 °C × 10 h aging treatment and 700 °C × 24 h
aging treatment are for precipitation of Fe 2Nb Laves phase on grain-boundary and
Ni3Nb within grain interior, respectively.
Microstructures of heat treated materials are shown in Fig. 1. Material with
1,000 °C × 10 h (W.C.) –700 °C × 24 h (W.C.) aging (High ρ material) has

Tensile Test
Figure 3 show test results of high ρ material and low ρ material. Ultimate tensile

Summary
The role of the grain-boundary precipitates on SAGBO behavior has been examined
for austenitic heat-resistant steel Fe-20Cr-30Ni-2Nb (at.%). The followings are the
results obtained:
1. With grain-boundary precipitates, susceptibility to SAGBO under high load
condition was effectively suppressed.
2. Rupture time and rupture elongation are greater for grain-boundary precipitation
strengthened material.

Effect of Heat Treatment
on Microstructure and Mechanical
Properties of VDM Alloy 780 Premium
M. Bergner, J. Rösler, B. Gehrmann and J. Klöwer
Abstract VDM Alloy 780 Premium is a new 718-type superalloy recently
developed in a cooperation between Technical University Braunschweig and VDM
Metals GmbH [ 1, 2]. It contains the γ′-phase for strengthening in addition to a
second phase, in the following referred to as δ-phase (Note that determination of the
crystal structure is pending. It may not have the same DO
a structure as the δ-phase
in Alloy 718.). As in Alloy 718, the δ-phase may be used for grain re ﬁnement and
strengthening of grain boundaries at elevated temperatures. Most important dif-
ferences in chemical composition compared to Alloy 718 are the essential
replacement of Fe by about 25% Co and a higher Al-content (about 2%) in com-
bination with a lower Ti-content (about 0.2%). Firstly, these measures stabilize the
strengthening phase and allow for application temperatures of up to 750 °C. Sec-
ondly, the δ-phase is preserved despite the relatively high aluminum content. To
make best use of Alloy 780, the precipitation kinetics of both phases along with the
concurrent evolution of microstructure and mechanical properties must be under-
stood. Consequently, this article deals with the in ﬂuence of heat treatments on the
phase kinetics, microstructure evolution and mechanical properties. Firstly, it will
be demonstrated that proper control of the heat treatment parameters allows for a
distribution of the δ-phase as in Alloy 718. Secondly, Vickers hardness testing
along with creep rupture experiments will be presented, revealing interdependencies
between heat treatment strategies and mechanical properties. At ambient tempera-
ture, the strength of the new alloy meets or exceeds that of Alloy 718 despite
absence of the γ″-phase, while its creep strength is far superior.

Introduction
Ever increasing temperatures in gas turbines not only require new blade alloys but
also disc alloys with improved temperature capability. Currently, Alloy 718 is the
most widely used disc material in aero engines because of its excellent strength and
manufacturability [ 3]. However, its microstructure becomes unstable at about
650 °C and this also limits its application temperature. Therefore, there is demand
for new disc alloys, maintaining the manufacturability of Alloy 718, yet, allowing
for higher service temperatures. VDM Alloy 780 Premium is an alloy which was
recently develop along this line in a cooperation between Technical University
Braunschweig and VDM Metals GmbH [ 1, 2]. As in case of Alloy 718, it relies on a
high temperature phase enabling ﬁne grain forging, in the following referred to as
δ-phase. Note, however, that the determination of its crystal structure is pending. It
may not have the same DO
a structure as the δ-phase in Alloy 718. In contrast to
Alloy 718, the main strengthening phase is γ′, yielding a more stable microstructure
than that of Alloy 718, thus, allowing for higher application temperatures. In terms
of chemical composition, VDM Alloy 780 Premium is distinguished from Alloy
718 by a high cobalt content (25 wt%), replacing iron and nickel. Cobalt is a key
element, stabilizing on the one hand the δ-phase and limiting the solvus temperature
of the γ′-phase on the other hand, despite a relatively high Al-content of the alloy.
Furthermore, as mentioned, the aluminum content is increased while the amount of
titanium is diminished, rendering the strengthening phase more stable. Its
approximate chemical composition in wt% is: Ni-25Co-18Cr-3Mo-2Al-0.2Ti-
5.4Nb.
As mentioned, a ﬁne grain size can be achieved in the course of forging and
recrystallization with the help of the high-temperature phase, as it hinders grain
growth. On the one hand, the ﬁne-grained structure provides high strength at
ambient temperature but, on the other hand, grain boundaries become weak areas at
elevated temperatures. Since turbine disc materials must have high strength at low
and elevated temperatures, the grain boundary behavior must be precisely con-
trolled. Precipitations at the grain boundaries, minor elements or interlocked grain
boundaries are required [ 4–6]. Following [ 4], the high temperature phase may be
used to stabilize the grain boundaries at elevated temperatures. In this context, the
role of the cooling process from the solutioning to the precipitation heat treatment
on the precipitation behavior and the resulting mechanical properties is emphasized
in [4]. Therefore, the precipitation kinetics of the high temperature phase compared
to the strengthening phase has to be analyzed and controlled.
The aim of this paper is to analyze the precipitation kinetics of the high tem-
perature phase and γ′-phase in VDM Alloy 780 Premium. After the investigation of
simple, isothermal heat treatments, the effects of two complex heat treatments on
the microstructure and mechanical properties are studied, focusing particularly on
the role of the cooling rate from solution to precipitation heat treatment.

Experimental Procedures
Microstructure and mechanical properties were investigated on forged pancakes of
VDM Alloy 780 Premium. The forging procedure was identical for all investigated
samples except for the cooling rate, which was either by air cooling or water
quenching. After forging, the material was essentially devoid of secondary phases.
A number of heat treatments were then conducted to study the precipitation kinetics
of the γ′- and δ-phase. Note once again that the crystal structure of the latter phase
may not be identical to that of the δ-phase in Alloy 718. The heat treatment
parameters are shown in Table 1. All samples were cooled by water quenching
(WQ).
For measurement of the Vickers hardness and microstructural analysis all
samples were ground and polished. All samples for morphological investigations
were additionally etched with V2A-stain. They were then investigated by ﬁeld
emission scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (Zeiss LEO 1550 Gemini), using
InLens and Everhart-Thornley detectors.
Finally, two complex heat treatments were selected for characterizing the
mechanical behavior. Both heat treatments are shown in Table 2. For both condi-
tions microstructural analysis, hardness measurements and stress rupture tests at
650 °C/700 °C and 690 MPa load were conducted. The fracture surfaces were
characterized via SEM.
Experimental Results
Figure 1 shows the resulting microstructure of the conducted heat treatments
according to Table 1. It is apparent that precipitation of the δ-phase is sluggish at
850 °C. Only few, relatively small δ-particles are present even after the longest heat
treatment duration of 16 h (see arrows in Fig. 1a). In contrast, a much larger
volume fraction is obtained in the temperature range between 900 and 975 °C
(Fig. 1b–d). The evolution of the δ-phase with time is shown for the temperature of
975 °C in Fig. 2. Already after 1 h, ﬁrst precipitates can be discerned. This also
holds true for the heat treatments at 900, 925 and 950 °C. Their size and volume
fraction increases with the duration of the heat treatment. As expected, there is a

Hardness measurements at room temperature as a function of annealing time and
temperature are shown in Fig. 3. Except for 850 °C, the hardness diminishes with
annealing time at all temperatures, even though this effect is slight. This suggests an
overaged condition with respect to the strengthening γ′-precipitates. Furthermore,
the hardness diminishes steadily from 850 to 975 °C because the γ′-particles
become coarser and, additionally, their volume fraction decreases. Note that heat
treatment at 1000 °C, where the γ′-phase is absent, leads to a hardness of about
200 HV10. Thus, there is still a ﬁnite strengthening contribution by the γ′-particles
at 975 °C.
Based on these results, a more complex heat treatment procedure was established
as mentioned above (Table 2). The objective of the ﬁrst heat treatment step at
900 °C/11 h is to precipitate a substantial amount of the δ-phase along grain
boundaries, thus stabilizing grain boundaries and preventing grain growth on fur-
ther heat treatment. The second step at 955 °C/1 h is meant to essentially dissolve
the γ′-phase, even though a small amount still persists, yet maintaining δ-phase.

Two different cooling rates from 955 °C, namely furnace cooling at 4 K/min and
air cooling, were then selected to study cooling rate effects on microstructure
evolution. The ﬁnal heat treatment steps at 800 and 650 °C are used for precipi-
tation strengthening by further precipitation of the γ′-phase. Given the results
above, no morphological change of the δ-phase is to be expected at these relatively
low temperatures.
Figures 4 and 5 illustrate the microstructure evolution during this heat treatment
procedure. As expected, a signi ﬁcant amount of δ-phase along with some γ′-precip-
itation is present after the second heat treatment step at 955 °C/1 h (Fig. 5a, b). The
distribution of the δ-phase resembles that of Alloy 718. Figures 4 and 5c, d represent
the microstructures after completion of the heat treatment step at 650 °C/8 h. There is
a bimodal size distribution of the γ′-particles with relatively large cube-shaped par-
ticles, having an edge length in the range of 100 nm, in addition to extremelyﬁne ones
(see insert in Figs. 4c, d and 5c, d). While the former ones have formed at 955 °C and
subsequently during cooling to 800 °C, the latter ones are essentially a result of the
heat treatment at 800 °C/8 h. Furnace cooling leads to a larger volume fraction and
size of the cube-shaped particles compared to air cooling. Consequently, air cooling
must lead to a larger volume fraction of the ﬁne precipitates.
A further microstructural difference relates to the shape of the grain boundaries.
They are rather straight after air cooling, but wavy after furnace cooling. Appar-
ently, slow furnace cooling favors heterogeneous nucleation of the γ′-particles
along grain boundaries as supercooling is small. This, in turn, causes bending of the
grain boundaries [ 8]. This mechanism does not occur during air cooling. In fact, the
coarser γ′-precipitates tend to form in the grain interior rather than in the vicinity of
