Summary
In this study, the effect of heat treatment procedure on the microstructure evolution
and mechanical properties of VDM Alloy 780 Premium was investigated. The
results can be summarized as follows:
• In the as-forged state, substantial precipitation of the high temperature phase,
denoted here as δ-phase, occurs within hours in the temperature range between
900 and 975 °C. In contrast, the precipitation was observed to be sluggish at
850 °C. The precipitation is heterogeneous along grain boundaries.
• During isothermal heat treatment, precipitation of the γ′-phase is homogeneous
and fast throughout the investigated temperature range. The γ′-phase is nearly
dissolved at 975 °C.
• A heat treatment procedure consisting of a δ-precipitation heat treatment at
900 °C, a γ′-solution heat treatment at 955 °C followed by controlled cooling to
a γ′-precipitation heat treatment at 800 and 650 °C was investigated. This
results in a distribution of the δ-phase similar to that in Alloy 718 and, within
the limits of the resolution by SEM, a bimodal size distribution of the γ′-
precipitates.
• It was demonstrated that the cooling rate from 955 to 800 °C has a pronounced
effect on microstructure evolution and mechanical properties. Air cooling leads
to a ﬁner γ′-structure and, hence, to higher strength at ambient and elevated
temperatures. In contrast, furnace cooling leads to wavier grain boundaries and
more pronounced coarsening of the γ′-precipitates. This reduces hardness and
creep rupture strength but increases ductility. Thus, control of the cooling rate is
an effective means to adjust the mechanical behavior depending on the appli-
cation requirements.
• Stress rupture testing at 650 °C led to transcrystalline creep failure, while
intercrystalline creep failure along with ﬁnal transcrystalline plastic collapse was
observed at 700 °C.

Effect of Homogenization on Creep
of Additive Manufactured Alloy 718
Tomoki Otsuka, Hideki Wakabayashi, Daisuke Igarashi,
Achmad Ariaseta, Shinya Imano, Yuting Wang, Satoru Kobayashi
and Masao Takeyama
Abstract Creep of additive manufactured (AM) and wrought alloy 718 has been
examined in order to understand the difference in nature between the AM and
wrought alloy. Three types of homogenization (solution) treatments, 982 °C
(subsolvus: SUB), 1060 °C (supersolvus: SUP) and 1200 °C (ultra supersolvus:
USS) for 2 h, were employed, prior to the standard aging treatment (760 °C/10 h +
650 °C/8 h → AC) known as supersolvus aging in the wrought alloy. Note that,
unlike the wrought alloy, ﬁne particles of a few tens of nm in diameter remain with
a high number density even after the USS treatment. All the specimens exhibit a
similar hardness value of 500 Hv after the aging. Creep test was conducted at
650 °C under a constant stress of 630 MPa in air, and the creep rate was monitored
through extensometer by linear valuable differential transducer. The creep rate ( ε̇)i n
the transient stage becomes slower with increasing homogenization temperature;
the minimum creep rate of USS and of SUP at ∼0.5% creep strain is one order of
magnitude slower than that of SUB at 0.8% strain. However, in the accelerating
stage, ε̇ at 2.5% strain becomes the same among the three specimens. Eventually the
rupture time increases with increasing the homogenization temperature, which is
282 h, 822 h and 1006 h for SUB, SUP and USS specimens, respectively. These
values are almost the same as or a little shorter than those of the wrought alloy. The
rupture elongation is, however, limited to less than 5%, which is the highest for the
USS specimen. The difference in creep deformation among the specimens and
between the AM and wrought specimens is discussed in terms of creep rate versus
time(strain) curves in conjunction with the nature of the AM and wrought
microstructures.

Introduction
Alloy 718 is widely used as wrought alloys for high temperature components such
as turbine disks in gas turbine engines of airplanes and power generation due to a
combination of excellent mechanical properties and fabricability of the material
[1, 2]. Two types of heat treatments are adopted to this alloy: the ﬁrst one, which is
more standard and called “subsolvus heat treatment ”, is to obtain ﬁne grain-sized
materials for high strength and good fatigue properties, and the second one, called
“supersolvus heat treatment ”, is to obtain a coarse grain size for good creep
properties [ 3, 4]. In the subsolvus heat treatment, hot-forged ingots are solution
treated below the δ solvus temperature above which the δ-Ni
3Nb phase is com-
pletely dissolved, followed by rapid cooling. This process forms ﬁne recrystallized
grains pinned by residual δ phase precipitates and partially dissolves solute ele-
ments such as Nb and Ti etc. into solid solution in the γ matrix. This solution
treatment process is subsequently followed by a two-step aging heat treatment
(holding at 718 °C for 8 h, furnace cooling to 621 °C and holding at the temper-
ature for a total aging time of 18 h followed by air cooling) to cause the precipi-
tation of ﬁne γ″-Ni
3Nb/γ′-Ni3(Al,Ti) phase in the matrix phase. In the supersolvus
heat treatment, forged ingots are solutionized above the δ solvus temperature,
followed by rapid quenching. This process forms coarse recrystallized grains due to
no residual δ phase and dissolves the solute elements completely. This solution
process is followed by a two-step aging heat treatment (holding at 760 °C for 10 h,
furnace cooling to 649 °C and holding at the temperature for a total aging time of
20 h followed by air cooling) for the precipitation of γ″/γ′ phase in the matrix.
The additive manufacturing (AM) process has been recently used to fabricate
metallic components in the ﬁeld of automotive and medicine and is being used in
airplane engines, combustion and exhaust systems. This process is applied also to
alloy 718 and peculiar microstructures and mechanical properties have been
reported [5–12]. Chlebus et al. [ 5] observed the microstructures of an AM 718 alloy
and found that ﬁne precipitates of the δ, MC carbides and Laves phase were formed
through microsegregation of Nb and Mo during rapid cooling in the process, and
those precipitates pin the subgrains and grain boundaries in the AM structure during
solutionizing treatments, so that completely recrystallized microstructures were not
obtained not only in a subsolvus condition but also in supersolvus conditions.
Similar behaviors are reported by Tucho et al. [ 6] and Kuo et al. [ 7]. Also, an AM
718 alloy was found to show shorter creep rupture life and smaller rupture elon-
gation in a standard heat treatment condition compared with those in conventional
wrought 718 alloys [ 8].
In the present study, creep of AM and wrought 718 has been examined in
different solution treatment conditions plus a standard aging treatment in order to
understand the difference in nature between the AM and wrought alloys.

Experimental Procedures
Cylindrical AM specimens which were 8 mm in diameter and 80 mm in length
were fabricated from 718 powder by a selective laser melting process in an argon
atmosphere with a layer thickness of 25 μm without preheating. Detailed process
conditions cannot be described here because of industrial reasons. The chemical
compositions of the powder, analyzed by inductively coupled plasma (ICP) —op-
tical emission spectroscopy (OES), is listed in Table 1. A cast and hot-forged
(wrought) 718 specimen was used as a reference. The chemical composition of the
wrought alloy is listed in Table 1. Three types of solid solution treatments, 982 °C
(subsolvus: SUB), 1060 °C (supersolvus: SUP) and 1200 °C (ultra supersolvus:
USS) for 2 h, were employed to the AM and wrought specimens, prior to the
standard aging treatment (760 °C/10 h + 650 °C/8 h → AC), known as supersolvus
aging in the alloy. The heat treatment pro ﬁles are illustrated in Fig. 1. These heat
treatments were performed in air in a form of cylindrical pieces with 8 mm in
diameter and 8 mm in length for AM specimens and of rectangular pieces with
10 × 10 × 8 mm
3 for wrought specimens.
The microstructures of the specimens were observed on a cross section 1 mm
inside from the surface of the heat treated samples with ﬁeld emission scanning
electron microscope (FESEM). The cross section was prepared by mechanical
polishing with diamond down to 1 μm, chemical polishing with colloidal SiO 2 and
electro-polishing using the solution of 500 ml H 3PO4 + 80 g CrO 3. The hardness of
the specimens was measured with a microvickers hardness testing machine with a
load of 0.98 N.
Creep testing was conducted at 650 °C under a constant stress of 630 MPa in air.
The creep rate was monitored through extensometer by linear valuable differential
transducer.

Results and Discussion
Initial Microstructure for Creep Tests
AM specimens show a strong resistance against recrystallization during solution
treatment. Figure 2 shows grain structures of AM specimens, together with those of
wrought specimens, after the three types of solution treatments, SUB, SUP and
USS. In the wrought specimen, fully recrystallized grains with a grain size of about
10–15 μm are formed in the SUB condition and extensive grain growth occurs in
the SUP and USS condition, resulting in the grain size of ∼300 μma n d ∼1000 μm,
respectively (Fig. 2d–f). In AM specimens, on the other hand, ﬁne grain structure
remains almost entirely in the imaging, which suggests that only recovery takes
place in the SUB condition (Fig. 2a). Recrystallization just starts in the SUP
condition, as shown in the micrograph (Fig. 2b) where a recrystallized grain is
located in the center. Grain growth takes place in the USS condition although the
grain size is smaller than in the same solution treatment of the wrought specimen
and their grain boundaries are winding (Fig. 2c).
This strong resistance against recrystallization in the AM specimens is caused by
the presence of a high number density of ﬁne particles of a few tens nm in diameter
in the solution heat-treated specimens. The ﬁne particles are shown in Fig. 3 as
bright and dark spots, the latter spots correspond to pits where the particles have
fallen out during surface preparation. These ﬁne particles are not observed in
wrought specimens at all, which is not unreasonable with respect to common
understanding of the wrought alloy [ 13, 14]. The presence of the ﬁne particles in the
AM specimens and higher concentration of Oxygen found in the power used for
AM process by two orders of magnitude than that of the wrought alloy allow us to
speculate the particles are oxides. Needle-like precipitates are present along grain
boundaries in the SUB condition but not in the SUP and USS conditions in AM
specimens. This needle-like precipitates can be identi ﬁed from their morphology
Fig. 1 Heat treatment pro ﬁles conducted for the AM and wrought 718 specimens

are seen to be orthogonally arranged in some matrix grains in the micrographs,
which indicates the particles are of γ″-Ni3Nb phase, typically available in alloy 718.

Creep Behaviors
Figure 9 shows the Larson-Miller Parameter (LMP) plots of the creep rupture lives
for the AM and wrought 718 specimens used in the present study together with
LMP curves for wrought 718 alloys available in public domain [ 1, 13]. The LMPs
of the SUB specimens fall almost on the public data regardless of the processing
route. The creep rupture lives of supersolvus specimens are also in a good agree-
ment with the public domain data while the AM specimens show somewhat shorter
lives than the wrought ones.
Effects of solution treatment temperature on the creep lives of the AM specimens
and differences in creep behaviors between the processing methods, AM or
wrought, are discussed below in terms of creep rate versus time (strain) curves and
limited information on their initial microstructures.
Effects of Solution Heat Treatment Temperature in AM Specimens
The comparison in creep rate versus time (strain) curves (see Fig. 6) allows us to
ﬁnd the following dependence of creep deformation on the solution treatment
temperature; with increasing the temperature, (1) the creep rates in all the regimes
decrease, (2) the time to reach minimum creep rate increases, (3) the strain to reach
minimum creep rate is lowered and (4) the duration of acceleration regime

## Page 506

increases, as schematically illustrated in Fig. 10. This dependence indicates a
decreased dislocation mobility to contribute to creep deformation and an increased
difﬁculty in dynamic recovery/recrystallization to trigger the creep acceleration at
higher solution treatment temperatures, according to a classical understanding of
creep mechanism [ 14]. The higher/lower dislocation mobility might be related the
degree of recovery/recrystallization/grain growth after the solution treatment, i.e.
the higher the temperature, the lower (mobile) dislocation density and the lower
density of sub-boundaries that is related to the velocity of dislocation glide and
climb. Another reason could be the degree of dissolution of Nb during the solution
treatment that could change the distribution of γ″ phase precipitates in the γ phase
after the aging treatment. A small difference between the creep behavior between
the SUP and the USS is due to a longer acceleration regime in the USS specimen
(see Fig. 6c). The longer acceleration regime indicates that a higher resistance
against dynamic recovery/recrystallization during creep. This feature could be
originated by a completely recrystallized microstructure in the USS that has less
mobile dislocation density and sub-boundaries in grain interiors.
Difference Between AM and Wrought Specimens
The comparison in the creep rate versus time (strain) curves (see Figs. 7 and 8)
between the AM and wrought specimens allows us to ﬁnd the following common
tendency regardless of the solution treatment condition; (1) the creep rates in the
transient creep regime are higher in the AM specimens, (2) the strain to reach the
minimum strain rate is larger in the AM specimens, when compared in the same
solution treatment conditions, as illustrated in Fig. 11. This tendency might be due
to a difference in the grain structures, i.e. recovered structures, probably with higher
mobile dislocation density and more recovery sites, in the AM specimens versus

In the SUB condition, even with the easier creep deformation of the AM
specimens than the wrought specimens, acceleration creep rates were slower and
the acceleration creep regime was longer in the AM specimen, which leads to a
longer creep life, as illustrated in Fig. 11. This slower and longer acceleration creep
behavior in the AM specimen should be caused by a slower dynamic recovery/
recrystallization kinetics during the creep regime, which could be caused by a high
density of ﬁne particles. In the SUP condition, the acceleration creep regime is
longer and the creep rate is faster in the AM specimen than the wrought specimen,
as illustrated in Fig. 11. These results suggest that the rate of dynamic recovery/
recrystallization is slow in the wrought specimen than the AM specimen. The
slower dynamic recovery/recrystallization rate could be related to its recrystallized
grain structure in the wrought specimen, compared with a recovered grain structure
in the AM specimen.

## Page 508

Another remarkable difference in creep behaviors between the AM and the
wrought specimens is their creep ductility. One of the reasons for smaller creep
ductility in the AM specimens might be caused by the presence of ﬁne nm sized
particles that may promote stress concentration and crack nucleation. Another
reason could be the presence of voids in the AM specimens. Rationalization of the
creep behaviors needs more detailed and quanti ﬁed microstructure characterization
not only for their initial states but also after creep deformation, and this is a future
work of this study.
Summary
Creep properties of additive manufactured (AM) 718 specimens with different
homogenization (solution) treatments plus a standard supersolvus aging treatment
were compared with wrought 718 specimens with equivalent heat treatment con-
ditions under a creep test condition of 650 °C and 630 MPa. The main results are:
(1) Creep lives of the AM specimens strongly depend on the condition of the
solution treatment: The creep rate ( ε̇) in the transient stage becomes slower with
increasing the solution treatment temperature, and the minimum creep rate of
USS and of SUP at 0.5% creep strain is one order of magnitude smaller than
that of SUB at 0.8% strain. However, in accelerating stage, ε̇ at 2.5% strain
becomes almost the same among the three specimens. Eventually the rupture
time increases with increasing the homogenization temperature, which is 282 h,
822 h and 1006 h for SUB, SUP and USS specimens, respectively.
(2) The creep lives of AM specimens are almost the same as or a little shorter than
those of wrought specimens. However, the rupture elongation of the AM
specimens, limited to less than ∼5% which is the highest for the USS specimen,
is apparently smaller than that of the wrought specimens.
(3) The creep deformation of AM 718 is characterized by a faster transient creep
rate and larger strain to reach minimum strain rate, compared with wrought
alloys with equivalent heat treatments. Their creep lives depend on their
acceleration creep behaviors.

Effects of Post-processing
on Microstructure and Mechanical
Properties of SLM-Processed IN-718
Mohsen Sei ﬁ, Ayman A. Salem, Daniel P. Satko, Richard Grylls
and John J. Lewandowski
Abstract Nickel-based superalloys have been developed extensively and have
proven attractive for various industrial applications over the past four decades, due
to excellent mechanical properties that are maintained at high temperature. This
study investigates selective laser melting (SLM) of the nickel-based superalloy
IN-718 and documents the effects of post-processing treatments on the resulting
microstructure and mechanical properties. Comprehensive microstructural charac-
terization was performed on both as-deposited and post-processed materials using
various techniques (e.g. EBSD, OM, BSE, CT). The as-deposited alloy exhibited
ﬁne and elongated grains that contribute to the mechanical anisotropy presented in a
companion paper while post-processing produced a more equiaxed microstructure
and reduced the mechanical anisotropy. Tensile, fracture toughness, and fatigue
crack growth tests conducted at room temperature are reported in this work while
elevated temperature properties are reported elsewhere. This work revealed the
changes of the microstructure ( γ morphology, γ crystallography, and precipitate
distributions) and hence the mechanical behavior due HIP+HT which resulted in
mechanical properties that approach wrought alloys after comparable heat treat-
ment. The results are discussed in this light and focus on the differences in mi-
crostructure resulting from the AM process.

Introduction
Inconel 718 (IN-718) is a precipitation hardened nickel-based superalloy, which is
strengthened by γ″ (Ni3Nb) and γ′ (Ni3(Al,Ti)) phases in the γ matrix. Due to its
ability to retain mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, excellent resistance
to oxidation and favorable weldability, it has been used extensively in jet engine
applications [1]. Recent work [ 2–4] has documented orientation-dependent fracture
and fatigue properties of as-deposited AM materials prepared by electron beam
melting. While it was also shown that fracture toughness and fatigue crack growth
behavior of the as-deposited AM materials were in the range of those reported for
cast and wrought material [ 2], the presence of unmelted particles, porosity, and
other defects will likely reduce the combination of properties possible. Although
these process-induced defects will be detrimental to some of the mechanical
properties, HIPing can be effectively used for their minimization/removal
depending on their origin [ 4–6]. Other recent works have investigated the effects
of build orientation on fracture and fatigue behavior of these alloys [ 4, 7–11].
Although preliminary work has examined the orientation dependence of me-
chanical properties on bulk samples in various conditions (e.g. as-deposited,
post-processed) at a number of institutions [ 2–4, 12–16], there is also a critical need
to understand the detailed process-microstructure-defect-property relationships that
arise [ 4, 17, 18]. The present work addresses these linkages using SLM-processed
IN-718 while also characterizing the location-dependent mechanical properties.
Materials and Methods
An SLM 280 machine was used to produce 10 mm × 20 mm × 120 mm length
cuboidal bars using SLM pedigree gas-atomized IN-718 spherical powders with an
average particle size of 15 –45 µm. A standard SLM raster strategy was used to
deposit the bars and small turbine blades in the manner shown in Fig. 1. The small
turbine blades are being evaluated for other ongoing work. Details of the tension
samples excised from the bend bars are also shown in Fig. 1. The main SLM
processing parameters included 30 µm layer thickness, 0.12 mm hatch spacing,
200 W laser power, and 900 mm/s scanning velocity.
Post-processing of some specimens involved HIP and then heat treatment
according to ASTM Standard F3055 [ 19]. HIPing was ﬁrst performed at 100 MPa
and 1120 °C, followed by rapid cooling under an inert atmosphere (150 °C/min)
according to ASTM Standard F3055 [ 19]. After HIP, a two-step heat treatment
outlined in the ASTM speci ﬁcation was used (i.e. Step I: Solution Anneal at 980 °C
(1800 °F) for 1 h, air (/argon) cool; Step II: Ageing treatment; hold at 720 °C
(1330 °F) 8 h, furnace cool to 620 °C (1150 °F) in 2 h, hold at 620 °C (1150 °F)
8 h, air (/argon) cool).
516 M. Sei ﬁ et al.

Detailed microstructure characterization (e.g. BSE, large area EBSD) was con-
ducted to analyze the as-deposited and HIP+HT conditions. Metallographic sam-
ples were excised via wire EDM, ground, and electropolished for optimum EBSD
results. Backscatter electron (BSE) imaging was used to reveal precipitates and any
heterogeneity after HIP+HT. For this purpose, samples were electropolished in a
solution of 10 mL perchloric acid and 90 mL methanol at −30 °C using a D.C.
power supply with 13 V. Both vertical and horizontal build directions were
examined. To quantify any microstructure variability along the axis of the excised
tensile samples, Fig. 1, three locations (i.e. center, gauge section, and grip section)
were inspected by BSE at two different magni ﬁcations. This paper only reports
results obtained from the center region. Room temperature tensile testing on the
excised samples, Fig. 1b, was performed on an Instron screw driven machine at a
strain rate of 10
−3 s−1. The 0.2% offset yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and
relative elongation to fracture were determined.
Fracture toughness was determined on both the as-deposited and HIP+HT bend
bars in three point bending using single edge notch (SEN) specimens on a Model
810 MTS servo-hydraulic machine in general accordance with ASTM E399 [ 20]. In
this study, orientation-speci ﬁc fracture properties were determined in the vertical
and horizontal orientation, Fig. 1, as described in previous work [ 2]. The
as-deposited bend bar samples were ﬁrst notched using a slow speed diamond wire
saw to introduce a notch root radius of about 75 –100 μm followed by fatigue
pre-cracking to a crack depth/sample width (i.e. a/w) of 0.45 –0.55, in accordance
with ASTM E399 [ 20]. The Direct Current Potential Drop (DCPD) technique,
based on the procedure outlined in ASTM E647 [ 21], was used to monitor the ΔK
rate in order to adhere to ASTM E399. The fracture toughness experiments were
conducted to failure at a displacement rate of 0.05 mm/min. Fracture Technology
Associates (FTA
TM) software was used to continuously monitor crack growth in
both the fatigue and fracture toughness tests in order to also comply with existing

ASTM requirements. In all cases a 1 –1.5 A current input was used with voltage

Fatigue crack growth tests were performed on these same two orientations,
Fig. 1, at 20 Hz in room temperature air with a relative humidity of 40% in
accordance with ASTM E647 [ 21]. The DCPD technique was again used to
monitor and control crack growth. Fatigue crack growth tests were ﬁrst started at an

establish the true fatigue threshold, ΔKth, as required by ASTM E647. The fatigue
test was then stopped and restarted at a ΔK that was 5% lower than that used
initially (i.e. to obtain enough data overlap) and the test was run under rising ΔK
conditions until catastrophic fracture. The Paris regime exponent, m, and fatigue
overload K
c was calculated for multiple tests conducted in this manner. The fatigue
crack growth experiments were also conducted to determine the presence of any
anisotropy in properties between the horizontal and vertical builds, Fig. 1.
X-ray micro-computed tomography (µ-CT) was carried out using an YXLON
FF35 system at 195 kV and 120 µA with a resolution of about 15 –20 µm.
Three-dimensional defect volumes were determined by rotating the sample 360°,
enabling the detector to capture numerous two-dimensional projected images from
which a three-dimensional data set of volume elements (voxels) was reconstructed
based on appropriate algorithms and high computing power clusters.
Results and Discussion
Figure 2 shows an SEM image of the SLM powder that was used in this study
while Fig. 3 shows BSE images of as-deposited and HIP+HT samples.
The shades of gray shown in Fig. 3 reveal changes in crystallographic orienta-
tion of the IN-718 grains while the BSE images also revealed a heterogeneous and
large γ grain structure. While columnar grains can be expected in the as-deposited
material, the large heterogeneous grains present after HIP+HT suggest partial re-
crystallization during the HIP cycle at 1120 °C since it is above the δ phase solvus
temperature. Although the 980 °C/1 h is above the γ″ and γ″ solvus temperature, it
is estimated to result in δ grain boundary precipitation and hence may hinder
coarsening during subsequent aging steps. Thus, it is estimated that most of the
recrystallization and coarsening occurred during the HIPing or in early stages of
solution treatment before the precipitation of δ grain boundary. It worth noting that
the double aging currently employed is conducted to induce precipitation
strengthening (mainly γ″) (Fig. 3c). More detailed work will be conducted in the
future to focus on examining precipitate characteristics and their effects on
mechanical behavior.
The large area EBSD scans and build direction IPF maps revealed columnar
grains in as-deposited material and recrystallized grains after HIP+HT. Figures 4
and 5 show build direction IPF maps and pole ﬁgures from the large area EBSD
conducted on the as-deposited and HIP+HT conditions. Pole ﬁgures (Fig. 4)
518 M. Sei ﬁ et al.

showed two main cube texture components with [001] aligned along the build
direction (BD) and ±45° to the BD in the as-deposited condition. However, HIP
+HT produced a cube texture with higher intensity of [001] perpendicular to the
build direction. The change of the texture from [001] along the BD (in as built
columnar grains) to lower intensity of the [001] along the BD after HIP+HT that is
associated with equiaxed grains is consistent with the trials of Dehoff et al. [ 22]t o
control the site speci ﬁc microstructure of IN718 by the transition from columnar to
equiaxed grains and the associated texture changes. The driving force for the re-
crystallization into equiaxed grains with [001] away from the BD and toward the
transverse direction requires further work. The black areas present in the IPF maps
are not porosity, but rather are small recrystallized grains with an orientation that is
colored black in the coloring scheme by the large area IPF plotting software.
The tensile behavior shown in Fig. 6 and summarized in Table 1 reveals an
increase in the yield/ultimate tensile strength after HIP+HT and reduced elongation
in comparison to the lower strength as-deposited material. This change in the
mechanical behavior is attributed to the precipitation hardening from the HT.
The yield and ultimate tensile strength slightly exceed wrought/annealed values
[16] while the elongation values are in the same range. However, the wrought
(aged) Inconel 718 strength (yield and UTS) [ 16] exceeds the SLM-fabricated and
HIP+HT material, with signi ﬁcantly lower elongation.
Fracture toughness results for the vertical and horizontal orientations tested are
provided in Table 2. The sample thickness requirement (i.e. >20 mm) for valid K IC
measurements was not met presently, requiring the present fatigue-precracked
fracture toughness data to be reported as K q. Much higher toughness values were
obtained in the as-deposited versus HIP+HT conditions. More detailed information

The source(s) of the defects shown in Fig. 8 are not completely clear at this point.
Optimized processing conditions often continue to produce samples with such de-
fects. Much additional work is needed to determine the regimes and source(s) of
such defects, with a view toward their elimination during the process.
Conclusions
SLM fabrication of cuboidal parts of Inconel 718 in Ar atmosphere using
pre-alloyed powders followed by post-processing have been conducted in order to
determine resulting microstructures and mechanical properties. As-deposited ma-
terial exhibited a columnar microstructure composed primarily of γ grains with
cube texture aligned along the BD and 45° to the BD. HIP+HT under the condi-
tions presently used caused the precipitation of γ′ with γ recrystallization and grain
growth into heterogeneous grain structure with 001 directions mainly perpendicular
to the BD.

524 M. Sei ﬁ et al.

## Page 520

Tensile behavior, fracture toughness and fatigue crack growth behavior of
as-deposited IN-718 has been documented. While the as-deposited properties were
in the range of those reported for wrought IN-718 (annealed) and lower than the
aged condition, the properties were also orientation-dependent between different
build orientations. Preliminary work has also been conducted to identify defect
distributions before and after post-processing. In addition to microstructure
heterogeneity both within and between builds, various defects were present in the
as-deposited materials. These consisted of isolated porosity, lack of fusion, and
unmelted regions. The HIP+HT procedures reduced the defect density while also
changing the microstructure from columnar to equiaxed. This post-processing
produced increases in the tensile properties and reduced ductility due to precipi-
tation hardening, although both orientation- and location-dependent toughness and
fatigue crack growth properties remained, albeit improved. The detailed effects of
such processing/post-processing schemes on the microstructure and properties will
be examined in continuing work. This includes optimization of the initial pro-
cessing conditions (e.g. control of the melt pool size) in an attempt to eliminate such
features. This will enable a more de ﬁnitive examination of microstructure-depen-
dent properties.

Effects of Phosphorus Addition on Creep
Properties of Wrought γ′ Strengthened
Ni-Based Superalloy
Y. Hasebe, M. Yoshida, E. Maeda and S. Ohsaki
Abstract Large and reliable components by wrought γ′ strengthened Ni and Ni-Fe
based superalloy are strongly demanded for advanced ultra-supercritical (A-USC)
power generation, which is one of the most promising and ef ﬁcient technologies
with steam temperature of above 700 °C. In this work, the effect of phosphorus on
the creep properties and microstructure change of wrought γ′ strengthened Ni-based
superalloy (alloy 282), was investigated, focused on the effects of carbides pre-
cipitation. In an alloy with phosphorus content of 8 ppm, precipitation of M
23C6
carbides was observed in both grain boundaries and grain interior prior to the creep
tests. Grain boundary coverage by carbide increased until the phosphorus content
up to about 30 ppm. On the other hand, the amount of M
23C6 in grain interior
decreased with increasing phosphorus content. Results of the creep tests revealed
the relationship between the time to rupture and the grain boundary coverage by
carbide. Microstructure of the crept specimen showed the existence of misorien-
tation at the vicinity of grain boundary without carbides by means of an electron
backscattered diffraction (EBSD) analysis. These results suggest that the
improvement of the time to rupture is due to the grain boundary precipitation
strengthening mechanism by grain boundary carbides and phosphorus content
affects precipitation behavior of M
23C6 carbides in grain interior and grain
boundaries.

Introduction
Huge effort has been continuing for A-USC power generation in order to reduce the
CO2 emission, from the view point of environmental sustainability. In Japan,
development of heat resistant materials for A-USC coal- ﬁred fossil power plant
with the creep rupture strength of 100 MPa for 10 5 h at 973 K has promoted [ 1–3].
Furthermore, another projects aiming to raise the steam temperature about 1023 K
classes has started in several countries [ 4, 5].
Alloy 282, age-hardened Ni-based superalloy [ 6, 7], is considered as one of the
most possible candidates of turbine rotor materials for 1023 K class A-USC power
plant. For the further increase of creep strength, it is effective to improve the
strength of grain boundaries, which act as weak points at elevated temperature
because of faster diffusion.
Although trace elements such as phosphorus (referred as P in below) and sulfur
are usually considered to be eliminated as low as possible in the melting process to
avoid ductility loss in the large components, some previous studies reported that an
adequate amounts of P has bene ﬁcial effects in improving creep properties of Ni-Fe
based superalloys for alloy 718 [ 8–10]. Xie et al. reported that the alloy 718 with
30 ppm of P content showed longer creep life by ductility improvement at
923 K/150 MPa [ 11]. They suggested that the improvement is mainly due to the
effect of interaction between P segregated at grain boundary and other alloying
elements. Cao et al. also reported that P behaves positively for creep property at
922 K/669 MPa of alloy 718 and there is an optimum amounts of P contents [ 12].
They pointed out an interaction of P and B affects on creep properties.
As mentioned above, there are a number of reports about P effects on creep
properties, however, the strengthening mechanism by P addition is not enough clear
yet. Recently, on a modi ﬁed alloy of alloy 706, contains less niobium (referred as
Nb in below) and a large amount of aluminum (referred as Al in below), we have
revealed that P addition promotes grain boundary coverage of Nb-rich compound
and improves creep life [ 13, 14]. We have also claimed that the improvement was
due to the grain boundary precipitation strengthening of a Nb-rich compound that
was reported by Takeyama [ 15]. As same as the modi ﬁed alloy of alloy 706, this
grain boundary precipitation strengthening mechanism by phosphorus addition is
considered to be applicable for also alloy 282. Thus, the aim of this study is to
investigate the effects of P addition on microstructure for alloy 282, especially
focused on the grain boundary precipitation.
Experimental Procedure
The alloys with different P contents are studied, as shown in Table 1. P was added
150 mass ppm (hereinafter, concentration is referred to as mass ppm or %, unless
otherwise stated) in maximum, some alloys also contain Nb for the purpose of
528 Y. Hasebe et al.

## Page 524

promoting the phosphide precipitation. These samples were melted by vacuum
induction melting to 50 kg ingot and wrought to plates with 35 mm in thickness.
Solution heat treatment was conducted at 1373 K for 5 h, followed by two-step
aging of 1323 K for 24 h (1st step) and 1063 K for 8 h (2nd step) before creep test.
To determine the time-temperature precipitation (TTP) diagram of carbides, another
aging was carried out after solution heat treatment of 1373 K at several temperature
between 1073 and 1323 K for up to 40 h.
For microstructural observation, small pieces with the size about 20 mm length
of cube were cut from the plates, polished by abrasive paper up to #1200, ﬁnished
by diamond paste of 3 μm particle, then electrolytic etched. Microstructural
observation was performed by ﬁeld-emission scanning electron microscope
(FE-SEM) and transmission electron microscope (TEM) with energy dispersive
spectrometer (EDS) using JEOL JSM 7100F and JEOL JEM 2100F, respectively.
Creep tests were performed at 1023 K/333 MPa for the samples with heat treated
by two-step aging. Specimens for the creep tests were taken from the plates per-
pendicularly to the forging direction. Dimension of specimen were determined in
accordance with Japan industrial standard (JIS) Z 2201 (accordance with ISO 6892).
The grain boundary coverage ρ was quantitatively evaluated in this work using
the following de ﬁnition; ρ = L/L

Results and Discussion
Effects of P on Creep Properties
Figure 1 shows the creep rate versus time curves of each alloys. In the base alloy
(HP0), creep rate dropped rapidly to 10 −5 order, then gradually increased showing
long acceleration stage. Every alloy with a P addition showed longer rupture life
than HP0. This improvement resulted from the extension of the acceleration stage.
Figure 2 shows the changes in time to rupture and minimum creep rate with P
addition. Time to rupture raised rapidly with increasing P addition until about
30 ppm, slightly decreased with further P addition. On the other hand, minimum
creep rate varied inversely.
Figure 3 shows microstructures after two-step aging. Although no phosphides
were observed, M
23C6 precipitation was observed in grain interior of HP0 (base
alloy). It also precipitated in grain boundaries with the coverage of 65% (shown by
ρ in Fig. 2). HP1 (32 ppm of P), in contrast, had no precipitation in grain interiors.
Grain boundary coverage increased drastically up to almost 100%. Figure 4 shows
SEM secondary electron image (SEI) and GROD map from EBSD measurement of
HP2 crept at 1023 K/333 MPa. Misorientation was observed at the vicinity of grain
boundary with no precipitation, whereas it was suppressed at the vicinity of grain
boundary with M
23C6 precipitation. In other words, grain boundary M 23C6 sup-
presses the deformation around grain boundary. Thus, improvement of creep life
with P addition is assumed to be the result of the enhancement of creep resistance
by increased grain boundary coverage.

Ohishi has reported the change in lattice parameter of γ matrix by P addition in
austenitic heat resistant steel [ 16, 17]. That reason was explained by the difference
in atomic radius between Fe (0.1274 nm) and P (0.1241 nm) that occupy substi-
tutional site of γ-Fe matrix in solid solution [ 18]. In relation to alloy 282, the
difference in atomic radius between Ni (0.1246 nm) and P is quite small. Therefore,
the change in lattice parameter of γ matrix in this study is supposed to be the result
from dissolution of M
23C6 containing Cr that has large atomic radius (0.1282 nm)
compare to the γ-Ni matrix. Based on the classical nucleation theory, driving force
of nucleation ( ΔG*) is described as follows [ 19, 20]:
ΔG* = 16πσ3
3 ΔGv − ΔGsðÞ 2 ð2Þ
r* = 2σ
ΔGv − ΔGs
ð3Þ
Here, σ is interfacial energy between γ and precipitates, ΔGv is free energy
change by transformation per unit volume, ΔGs is misﬁt strain energy, and r* is the
critical radius of nuclei. When mis ﬁt between γ matrix and M 23C6 increases, ΔGs
also increases. Therefore, nucleation of M 23C6 needs higher barrier energy of ΔG*,
is considered to result in the suppression of grain interior precipitation of M 23C6.
Conclusion
In this work, the effect of phosphorus on the creep properties and microstructure
change of wrought γ′ strengthened Ni-based superalloy (alloy 282), was investi-
gated, focused on the effects of carbides. Main results are shown in below:
(1) Creep life increases with increasing P addition. This assumes to be the results
from the enhancement of creep resistance by increasing grain boundary cov-
erage of M
23C6.
(2) Nose temperature of M 23C6 precipitation in grain boundaries was estimated at
around 1123 K for both HP0 and HP1. Upper limit temperature of M 23C6
precipitation in grain boundary was also estimated about 1373 K, whereas it
fell to about 100 K in HP1.

(3) P addition is considered to suppress the precipitation of M 23C6 in grain
boundary at 1st aging temperature due to segregation of P atoms at grain
boundaries. Precipitation of M
23C6 in grain boundaries was enhanced by the
increase of supersaturation of C at 2nd aging temperature.
(4) Lattice parameter of γ matrix was increased in the alloys with high P contents
and both Nb and P addition. The results corresponded with dissolution of
M
23C6 within grain interior.
(5) P is considered to lose mis ﬁt between γ matrix and M 23C6 by increasing elastic
strain energy, resulting in the suppression of grain interior precipitation of

Enhanced Strength of Inconel 718
by High Rate Severe Plastic
Deformation
Prabhat Chand Yadav and Shashank Shekhar
Abstract Inconel 718 is Ni-based superalloy commonly used for manufacturing
engine components in aerospace industry. Nickel-based super-alloys are particu-
larly well suited for service in high temperature environment where resistance to
creep, corrosion, and thermal shock are of primary requirements. Alloy 718 forms
various nano-precipitates which endow higher strength to the material and thermal
stability to the microstructure up to 650 °C due to grain boundary pinning of these
nano-precipitates. In order to further improve the strength of the alloy at elevated
temperatures, we utilized high rate severe plastic deformation (HRSPD). Machining
was used to impose HRSPD on the alloy, and the chip thus formed was used to
study the response of thermomechanical process. Machining led to signi ﬁcant
microstructural transformation and resulted in “bi-modal” grain size distribution.
Grain re ﬁnement led to signi ﬁcant increase in strength. Further improvement in
strength was attained after extended heat-treatment at 600 °C for 10 h. This
increment in strength can be attributed to the formation of nano-precipitates which
results in obstructing dislocations movement and pinning of grain boundaries.
However, it is known that deformed microstructure with very ﬁne grains saturated
with dislocations, results in brittle behaviour of alloy rendering them unusable for
most applications. In order to alleviate this problem, post-process heat-treatment
was designed. Three different temperatures were selected for short heat-treatment at
700, 800, and 900 °C for 15 min. This short heat-treatment resulted in varying
amount of recrystallization of the matrix and precipitation and ripening of γ″ and γ′
phase. Transformation in microstructure and ensuing properties after thermome-
chanical processing are discussed in this paper.

Introduction
Plastic deformation introduces strain in the materials leading to microstructural
changes that provides improved strength to material. Strain introduced in processed
materials depends upon severity of deformation technique. Various high deformation
techniques, called as severe plastic deformation (SPD) techniques are available that
can easily introduce strain of the order of ∼1–10. The focus on obtaining
nano-structured materials, by way of deformation, is to enhance strength multi-fold by
suppressing dislocation mobility. Ultra-re ﬁned nano-structured materials were cre-
ated by imposing severe plastic strain in several bulk materials [1–7]. Microstructural
reﬁnement in deformed materials was studied in a comprehensive way by Embury and
Fisher [4] and Langford and Cohen [5]. Machining is another such technique that can
cause severe plastic deformation in metals and alloys during the formation of chips
from the work-piece. Plane strain machining has been found to be one of the most
effective SPD techniques in recent years to develop ultra-re ﬁned nano-structured
materials, particularly because of the ability to vary strain-rate and temperature
simultaneously [ 8, 9]. Apart from leading to severe deformation in the chips, ma-
chining can also introduce severe deformation at material surface. This results in
graded microstructure near the surface, withﬁne ultra-reﬁned grains at the surface and
large un-deformed grains away from the surface. These nano-grains are responsible
for larger strength while the large grains endow the material with good toughness. The
modiﬁed properties through this technique can effectively be used for applications
where materials start failing from the surface, i.e. fatigue, stress corrosion cracking,
irradiation assisted applications etc.
The origin of increase in strength of materials after creating nano-structured
grains can be attributed to Hall-Petch relation [ 10]. Strength of precipitation
treatable nano-structured materials (e.g. severely deformed Inconel 718) can further
increase after applying heat-treatment to introduce second-phase strengthening
particle. Second phase (precipitates) is signi ﬁcantly hard, which provides not just
higher strength but also provides thermal stability by continuously pinning the
grains boundaries. As pointed out earlier, severe plastic deformation often makes
the material very brittle due to high saturation of dislocation density. This limited
ductility is a major lacuna in nano-structure materials and stumbling block in
making this process useful for commercial applications. Therefore to improve
ductility, some researchers have recommended short time heat-treatment at higher
temperature which makes strain free grains [ 11, 12]. Still others have recommended
obtaining “bi-modal” microstructure by applying post-process heat-treatment to the
deformed samples [ 12–14]. In this work, we have explored application of
post-process short heat-treatment to improve the ductility of the samples. We have
applied short heat-treatment at 700, 800, and 900 °C for 15 min to yield controlled
recovery of microstructure without causing large extent grain coarsening. Such
microstructure is expected to result in improved ductility without causing signi ﬁ-
cant drop in strength of thermal stability.
542 P. C. Yadav and S. Shekhar

Material
Inconel 718 alloy was used to study the effect of intermediate and post
heat-treatment on microstructural evolution. Inconel 718 alloy for present study was
obtained from Katariya Steels Mumbai, India. Nickel based superalloy (Inconel
718) forms various precipitates (i.e. γ′, γ″, δ etc.) in different temperature ranges.
Some of these precipitates viz. γ″ and γ′ appears as nano-precipitates in the matrix.
Formation of these nano-precipitates is known to pin the grain boundaries which
endow higher strength as well as thermal stability to the treated material. Optical
emission spectroscopy (OES) was used to obtain chemical composition of Inconel
718 alloy which is shown in Table 1.
Experimental Procedure
As-received Inconel 718 alloy was solution heat-treated at 1035 °C for 1 h followed
by water quenching. Cylindrical Inconel 718 bar (solution heat-treated) was
plane-strain machined using tungsten carbide tools (P30 Grade) with −20° rake
angle to obtain Inconel 718 chips at constant machining parameters i.e. feed rate
(0.064 mm/rev.), depth of cut (4 mm) and cutting speed (27 m/s) which led to
constant effective strain of ∼5.4 in the chips. Net effective strain in as-machined
(AM) chips was calculated using relation ∈ =
cos αﬃﬃ
3
p
sin ∅ cosðα −∅ Þ where α is rake
angle and ∅ is shear plane angle. AM Inconel 718 chips were intermediate
heat-treated at 600 °C for 10 h (known as H6) to allow the γ″ and γ′ phase to
precipitate and pin the grain boundaries to provide better strength as well as sta-
bility. It is well studied that formation of γ″ and γ′ precipitate leads to many fold
increase in strength of the AM Inconel 718, however it shows extremely brittle
nature. The brittle nature of processed materials makes them unusable for most of
the applications. As discussed earlier, it is expected that heat-treatment at elevated
temperature could relieve the stress introduced in deformed materials. Meanwhile, it
was also kept in mind that strength should not drop signi ﬁcantly while gaining
ductility. Hence, post-process short heat-treatment of intermediate heat-treated
as-deform Inconel 718 was designed. Post short heat-treatment was done at three
different temperatures, viz. 700 °C (SH7), 800 °C (SH8) and 900 °C (SH9) for
15 min followed by water quenching. Heat-treatment at elevated temperature leads
to release of stored energy by dislocation annihilation. Elevated temperature
heat-treatment also introduces recrystallized strain free grains which tend to
improve the ductility of processed materials. Hence, microstructural transformation

during post short heat-treatment was examined in terms of recovery, recrystal-

Inconel 718 chips samples were polished with emery papers up to 2000 grade
followed by ﬁnal polishing using electropolishing technique with Struers standard
A2 electrolyte. Orientation imaging microscopy (OIM) based Electron back scat-
tered diffraction (EBSD) attached to SEM was used to characterize microstructure
for particular processing condition samples. Scan area of 400 × 400 µm and step
size 0.5 µm was used during EBSD. Since EBSD resolution was not suf ﬁcient to
identify the ultra-re ﬁned nano-grains and the precipitates that were smaller than
100 nm, therefore we used transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to get better
understanding of these very ﬁne grained regions as well as nano-precipitates.
Vickers hardness test was also performed on thermo-mechanically processed chips
using 500 gf weights for 10 s dwell time. Average hardness (VHN) with standard
deviation was calculated by taking at least 25 readings at random locations.
Results and Discussion
Microstructural Evolution of Chips
The aim was to understand the kind of grain re ﬁnement and microstructural
transformation taking place in machining followed by heat-treated materials.
Hence, we did microstructural analysis using OIM technique, which is clearly
shown in Fig. 1a–f. After machining, solution treated materials (equiaxed grains)
get converted into severely deformed grains with alternate band of moderately
reﬁned (MZ) and ultra-re ﬁned zone termed as shear zone (SZ), which is obvious
from Fig. 1b. Moderately re ﬁned region consists of grains of the order of few 10 s
of micrometer and can be easily identi ﬁed in the micrographs. On the other hand,
ultra-reﬁned grains are too small to be resolved using OIM and hence appear as
un-indexed points. Therefore based on this fact, we can say that bands seen in
micrographs are alternate layers of MZ and SZ which are inherently ‘bi-modal’ in
nature. It is known that ‘bi-modal’ microstructure leads to improved ductility
compared to materials having shear zone or ultra-re ﬁned grains through out the
microstructure [ 15, 16]. This bi-modality can be seen to be retained up to SH8
sample condition (Fig. 1e). From the micrograph, it is clear that SH9 sample
condition represents the onset of recrystallization. For 700 and 800 °C short
heat-treatment, only recovery takes place and the overall microstructure looks
similar. This is also con ﬁrmed by correlating the microstructure with the
un-indexed points which represent the fraction of shear zone. We found from OIM
micrographs that un-indexed points which are co-related as shear zone remained
approximately constant up to SH8 sample condition.
AM chips were intermediate heat-treated at 600 °C which generates large
fraction of γ″ and γ′ nano-precipitates. These, nano-precipitates are closely spaced

and start pinning the grain boundaries and retain the ‘bi-modal’ microstructure even
after heat-treatment at elevated temperatures. The reason behind retaining
‘bi-modal’ microstructure is reduced grain boundary mobility throughout the
sample. Apart from that we also expect very high strength, good ductility as well as
better thermal stability of these thermally treated severely deformed chips because
of second-phase particle pinning the grain boundary. However, we have shown in
our earlier study that the AM chips are very brittle probably because of saturation of
dislocations [ 17]. Heat-treatment at 600 °C increases the brittleness of chips due to
larger fraction of hard precipitate as well as saturated dislocations in
nano-structured grains in the SZ [ 14, 18]. Second-phase particles and larger strain
in the sample signi ﬁcantly affect the recrystallization behaviour. It increases the
stored energy of the materials which increases the driving force for recrystallization.
Second-phase particles larger in size may also act as site for nucleation of recrys-
tallization. Apart from that, if second-phase particles are closely spaced, they may
exert a substantial pinning force in both MZ as well as SZ. First two effects of
second-phase particles and severe strain promote the recrystallization while last one
suppress the recrystallization [ 19]. It is important to understand the complex
interplay of these behaviour in order to design proper process for obtaining desired
properties.
Since we already performed OIM analysis and have quantitative information of
microstructural transformation and hence, we used it to plot misorientation angle
distribution curves for the various conditions shown in Fig. 2a–c. We observed
from Fig. 2a that SA sample shows a peak at 60° in misorientation plot which
represents presence of large fraction the annealing twin boundaries. Therefore, as
expected, this sample condition represents a completely recrystallized

introducing intermediate heat-treatment at 600 °C for 10 h then post short

OIM micrographs have limited resolution and cannot throw much light on

sample i.e. H6 shows nano-grains with some sub-grain boundaries which can be
directly correlated with the un-indexed zone and recovered zone of the OIM

and the volume fraction of γ″ is ∼15% [20–22]. They have also shown that these γ′
also contributes to the strength of the alloy, although, to a lesser extent, because of
their lower volume fraction.
Grain Boundary Characterization of Chips
Microstructural modi ﬁcation takes place with transformation in nature of grain
boundary which continuously changes with strain and temperature. We wanted to
examine the change in nature of grain boundary with elevated temperature. Hence,
we did grain boundary analysis of processed samples and observed some nominal
change in the microstructure up to SH8 and drastic change in SH9 in terms of
formation of recrystallized strain free grains. Modi ﬁcation in microstructure directly
affects the mechanical properties i.e. strength and ductility. Hence, we ﬁrstly ana-
lyzed the average grain size of processed sample without considering unindexed
regions which represent the nano-structured grains in SZ shown in Fig. 4a.
Figure 4a shows drastic drop in average grain size for AM condition followed by
approximately constant grain size for all the sample condition except SH9, which
shows marginal increase. We see that the grains in the moderately re ﬁned region is
of the order of few micrometers.

sample. Interesting result was obtained in SH8 where slight change in width of
curve was obtained, indicating that sample still have suf ﬁcient strain which is
responsible for higher hardness. After 900 °C short heat-treatment, drastic change
in width of curve was obtained in SH9 which leads to comparatively lower strain

smaller grain size and high strength. So, one can simply say that H6 is better for

SH9 should possess better ductility and toughness.
Mechanical Behaviour of Chips
From above microstructural investigation, we observed marginal change up to SH8
sample condition which indicate microstructural stability in terms of formation of
strain free recrystallized grains. Delay in recrystallization up to SH8 is due to
formation of larger fraction of closely spaced ﬁne precipitates which has already
been discussed above. However, SH9 causes transformation of shear zone into
larger fraction of recrystallized grains. Smaller fraction of shear zone still remains
along with recrystallized grain in SH9. These shear zones strongly affect the
mechanical strength of processed sample which is normally un-indexed region.
Therefore, fraction of shear zone was measured in terms of un-indexed points of
processed sample from OIM data which is shown in Fig. 5. Fraction of un-indexed
point was found approximately constant with marginal change up to SH8 which is
depicted in Fig. 5. This marginal change is due to fractional reduction in disloca-
tions during recovery whereas drastic change was noticed for SH9 due to con-
version of shear zone into larger fraction of recrystallized grains. Approximately
constant fraction of un-indexed point up to SH8 can also be related to the brittle
behaviour of the material. On the other hand, SH9 sample condition has much
lower un-indexed point and hence can be expected to be ductile and tough. This
analysis clearly shows that a multiphase system i.e. Inconel 718 offers us much
better handle at microstructural tuning. By selecting suitable temperature, we can
control the fraction of sheared zone which limits the ductility of the processed
sample.
We have already stated that thermal treatment changes the strength of precipi-
tation treated materials i.e. Inconel 718, and the picture will become clear from
hardness plot which is shown in Fig. 5. We observed higher hardness of AM w.r.t.
SA which is due to formation of very ﬁne nano-grains as well as larger fraction of
dislocations tangles. Further increase in hardness was obtained for H6 sample after
introducing heat-treatment due to formation of larger fraction of closely spaced γ″
and γ′ nano-precipitates which leads to strengthening of the material by continu-
ously pinning the grains boundaries. Marginal drop in hardness of SH7 and SH8
sample was also observed, but was found to be still much higher than SA condition.
The marginal drop in hardness can be attributed to some amount of recovery that
Enhanced Strength of Inconel 718 by High Rate Severe … 549

## Page 545

takes place at elevated temperature. Meanwhile, SH9 sample shows noticiable drop
in hardness, but it is still much higher than SA condition. Drop in hardness up to
SH8 sample was due to reduction in dislocation density (recovery) while drop in
hardness of SH9 was due to recrystallization taking place in SH9.
Conclusions
After performing plane-strain machining of Inconel 718 alloy, AM chips were
intermediately heat-treated at 600 °C for 10 h followed by post short heat-treatment
at 700, 800 and 900 °C for 15 min which gives following pertinent conclusions:
1. Plane strain machining leads to ‘bi-modal’ microstructure with ultra-re ﬁned
sheared zone and moderately re ﬁned zone.
2. The average grain size for AM chips and various heat-treated samples remained
constant. From misorientation plot, it is clear that primarily recovery took place
for SH7 and SH8 sample condition with some indication of start of recrystal-
lization for SH8. Whereas 900 °C post short heat-treated sample showed
appreciable recrystallization. Recrystallization took place mainly in the
ultra-reﬁned zone which becomes clear after co-relating this data with grain size.
3. Average hardness and strength of AM chips increases drastically, which further
increases after intermediate heat-treatment at 600 °C for 10 h. The average
hardness starts decreasing slightly after applying post short heat-treatment for
15 min but was still much higher than bulk Inconel 718 at the end of 900 °C
heat-treatment.
Based on the above results, we conclude that AM chips intermediate heat-treated
at 600 °C result in largest hardness and AM chips heat-treated at 600 °C then again
post short heat-treated at 900 °C results in microstructure with ultra-re ﬁned grains

Evaluation of the Stress-Strain State
in Alloy 718 After Hydrogen Charging
S. Kolesov and E. Alekseeva
Abstract The changes in the stress-strain state as a result of hydrogen saturation of
Alloy 718 produced via traditional and 3D metal printing routes were studied. The
stress-strain state of the material after electrochemical hydrogen charging was
measured by X-ray technique using diffractometers with two power levels to obtain
the information from different depths from the surface. It was found that most of the
hydrogen accumulated in the thin surface layer. It was found that the microstrains
and sub-microstrains changed up to 35% in a depth of ∼5–30 μm as a result of the
electrochemical hydrogen charging. The changes in the residual stress (macrostress)
as a result of cathodic charging were not detected in the studied materials. As a
result of hydrogen desorption at 200 –800 °C, the stress-strain state of the investi-
gated alloy returned to its initial state for traditionally made material. The bulk of
hydrogen after cathodic charging was removed by heating to 300 °C.
Keywords Hydrogen embrittlement
⋅ Hydrogen charging ⋅ Stress-strain
state ⋅ Alloy 718 ⋅ SLM ⋅ X-ray method ⋅ 3D metal printing
Additive manufacturing ⋅ UNS N07718
Introduction
Researches dedicated to hydrogen embrittlement process and related to the
hydrogen material degradation are published every year. Despite numerous studies,
still there is no universally recognized theory of the mechanism of hydrogen
embrittlement, as well as the state and location of hydrogen in the metal [ 1].

## Page 549

Precipitation hardened alloy 718 was chosen as the material for investigation
because it is commonly used in the oil and gas industry and several ﬁeld failures of
Ni-based corrosion-resistant alloys (CRAs) due to hydrogen embrittlement have
occurred [ 2–5].
It is known that hydrogen, despite its small size, is capable of causing signi ﬁcant
strain, accumulating in the crystal lattice, while the type of lattice remains the same,
and there is also a tendency to restore the initial stress-strain state of the metal in
connection with the release of hydrogen in result of desorption.
Hydrogen can be trapped into metal by metal matrix, point defects, dislocations,
grain boundaries, voids, and nonmetallic inclusions, etc. [ 6–9]. Trapped hydrogen
can cause stress-strain state changes at various structure levels. In accordance with
stress classi ﬁcation to the structure scale level there are 3 types of stresses:
(1) macrostress level associated with throughout the part/sample, (2) microstress
level associated with grain boundaries and into grains and (3) sub-microstress —
atomic level [ 10].
Occluded hydrogen could be conditionally divided by trapping/binding energies
into two groups: mobile and ﬁxed (residual) hydrogen [ 7]. Hydrogen with high
binding energies and high temperature of extraction (above 800 °C) accumulated on
nonmetallic inclusions (oxides, sul ﬁdes, carbides) have been grouped together as
residual hydrogen [ 7–9]. All other hydrogen in metal have been grouped as dif-
fusible hydrogen but with different rate of mobility. Both mobile and residual groups
of hydrogen cause negative effects on materials: (1) Mobile hydrogen could cause
accelerated crack growth as a result of diffusion to crack tips [ 11]. (2) Residual
hydrogen could cause the stress to increase around the associated microstructural
defects and create an easier path for crack growth along a chain of local stressed sites
[12]. Hence it is important to study the state and distribution of hydrogen.
The purpose of this paper is to evaluate trapping energies of hydrogen and
stress-strain state changes in the studied materials as a result of hydrogen charging.
Materials and Experiments
Samples of alloy 718 were obtained from production by (1) traditional metallurgical
technology via vacuum-induction melting (VIM) plus vacuum arc-remelting
(VAR) processes then forged and (2) additively manufactured using selective
laser melting (SLM) of powder material.
Selective laser melting was carried out using SLM 280HL machine. The
machine used had two ytterbium single mode continuous lasers (YLR-laser) with
wavelength of 1070 nm and maximum output power of 400 W and 1000 W
respectively. The following parameters were used: laser power −275 W, scanning
speed −805 mm/s, hatch distance −120 µm, layer thickness −50 µm, laser spot
diameter −81 µm, parts were manufactured in argon atmosphere. The samples used
for this investigation were sectioned perpendicular to the printing direction as
presented in Fig. 1.
554 S. Kolesov and E. Alekseeva

## Page 550

After sectioning, the samples were heat treated by solution annealing in the 1870 –
1925 °F (1021 –1052 °C) range for 2 h followed by ageing in the 1425 –1475 °F
(774–802 °C) range for 8 h. The chemical composition of the studied samples met
the requirements of API 6A718 [ 13] standard as presented in Table 1. The surface of
the samples was mechanically ground (120 –1200 grit SiC papers) and polished
(6–0.05 μmA l 2O3 polycrystalline diamond suspension).
Hydrogen was introduced into the specimens, prior to test by cathodic polar-
ization in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution at ambient temperature at the current density of
30 mA/cm 2 for 72 h. The platinum electrode was used as the anode.
The industrial AV-1 mass-spectrometric hydrogen analyzer was used for total
hydrogen content measurement, which is based on the Vacuum Hot Extraction
(VHE) method. The sample preparation system consists of a vacuum extractor and
furnace. The sample inside the quartz glass extractor is heated gradually up to an
extraction temperature of 800 °C. The hydrogen released at heating in vacuum was
analyzed by means of the mass-spectrometer. The time-dependence of the hydrogen
ﬂux registered by means of the data acquisition system yields the extraction curve.
Constant heating ramps were used to assess activation energies of the hydrogen
traps. The analysis method and the analyzer have been described in [ 14, 15]i n
details. The measurement accuracy of method is ±0.05 ppm.
An X-ray method was used to estimate the stress-strain changes resulting from
the hydrogen charging process. Alloy 718 samples were examined before and after
hydrogen charging and after hydrogen desorption. The X-ray diffraction pattern was
recorded at room temperature using a low-power portable diffractometer equipped
with MnK α-radiation in range of Bragg angle 2 θ from 140° to 148° and D8
Advance Bruker diffractometer with CuK α-radiation in a wide range of Bragg angle
2θ from 20° to 148°.
The use of two different power diffractometers (3 and 30 kW) provided for
measurement of the stress-strain state at two different average depths from the
surface. Because the hydrogen was the only variable that changed, the change in the
stress and strain — depth state can be associated with the presence of hydrogen.
Based on the power and wavelength of X-ray and materials density of X-ray D8
Advance Bruker diffractometer obtain information up to a depth of ∼30 μm, and
low-energy portable diffractometer up to a depth of ∼5 μm.

Analysis of the stress-strain state was carried out by evaluating the diffraction
peak intensity and diffraction peak broadening (420) obtained on the samples in the
initial state, after hydrogen charging, and after vacuum desorption of hydrogen. The
degree of broadening of the diffraction peaks is estimated from the integral width of
the pro ﬁle-B, which is de ﬁned as the ratio of the area bounded by the background
lines to the peak height. By decreasing the intensity, an estimate can be obtained
regarding the magnitude of the distortion of the lattice. A decrease in the ratio I
hkl/
Ibackground corresponds to an increase in lattice distortions. Since the change in the
stress-strain state effect is more visible at high angles peaks, the (420) peaks were
analyzed. A more detailed approach to stress-strain evaluation by means of X-ray
method is presented in [ 16–18].
Results
Vacuum Heating Results
The vacuum heating analysis was performed to identify the existing trap states of
hydrogen in the samples and total amount of hydrogen. Figure 2 shows the
hydrogen desorption pro ﬁles in the samples before and after hydrogen charging.
In the 718 samples (traditional and additive) in the initial state before hydrogen
charging, total amount of hydrogen was less than 1 ppm. This hydrogen in initial
state had high binding energies, i.e. desorbed to a greater extent at temperatures of
400–600 °C. The total amount of hydrogen increased by 2 or more times (about
1 ppm) after electrochemical saturation. Hydrogen that entered the samples due to
cathodic charging was found to be associated exclusively with low binding energy
at the 200 –300 °C extraction temperature range.
It was observed that the added hydrogen after the electrochemical charging was
almost completely extracted at temperature lower than 300 °C, Fig. 2. The low
temperature hydrogen after hydrogen charging indicated a weaker binding state of
occluded hydrogen. The total amount of hydrogen and its distribution in the area of
higher binding energies (400 –800 °C) was found to be essentially equal for
non-charged and hydrogen charged samples.
The hydrogen binding energy changes with the various trapping sources, e.g.
matrix, interphases, and dislocations, etc. [ 6–9]. Added hydrogen after cathodic

charging (see Fig. 2) captured probably by matrix, dislocations and grain bound-
aries for both studied materials, based on low level of binding energy or extraction
temperature range 200 –300 °C. The total added hydrogen content after cathodic
charging in the both studied alloy versions (metallurgical made and 3D printed)
measured by the vacuum heating method was ∼1 ppm.
There were no signi ﬁcant differences between natures of desorption curves for
samples produced by different technologies (traditional and additive) before and
after hydrogen charging despite differences in the defect state and potentially dif-
ferent hydrogen traps caused by the technology.
The low binding energy of hydrogen con ﬁrms the fact that there are no hydrides
on the surface, as well as other chemical compounds with hydrogen. This was
because of the higher trapping energies associated with these compounds of
hydrogen [ 7–9].
The results indicated that the electrochemical hydrogen charging lead to an
increase of the amount of low-binding energy hydrogen which is diffusion-mobile.
The hypothesis here is that the main amount of hydrogen after electrochemical
hydrogen saturation was occluded by the matrix, dislocations, and grain boundaries.
The amount of hydrogen with high binding energy did not change signi ﬁcantly after
cathodic charging.
X-Ray Diffraction Results
X-Ray diffraction technique (XRD) was applied to determine stress-strain evolution
at hydrogen charging process. Since Alloy 718 has an austenitic structure, the
overall hydrogen diffusion will be slow while the solubility is high. During cathodic
charging, hydrogen penetrates into the metal and is occluded by it causing an
Fig. 2 Extraction curves
Evaluation of the Stress-Strain State in Alloy 718 … 557

## Page 553

increment in the metal planar spacing. Deviations from the ideal crystalline lattice
propagate in all directions and can be observed in a diffraction pattern.
Deviations can be contingently distinguished by scales to a level that corre-
sponds to a stress-strain level: (1) macro-strain are expressed in the peak shift at
diffraction pattern, (2) micro-strains at crystallite level are expressed as broadening
of XRD peaks (3) sub-microstrains or lattice distortions at the atomic level expands
as the intensity of the peak changings [ 16]. The alternative reason of X-ray peak
broadening could be changes of Coherent Scattering Zones (CSZ) in case of CSZ
variation in the range lower than 1000 Å. CSZ were measured with taking in
account the instrumental peak broadening. It was de ﬁned by method described in
that CSZ signi ﬁcantly higher for both versions of alloy [ 18].
In this study, stress changes due to hydrogen penetration have been detected as
micro-strains and sub-microstrains. Although in the literature stresses causing peak
shifting by hydrogen charging were detected in duplex stainless steels [ 19].
The X-ray diffraction patterns are presented in Fig. 3. It shows a comparison
between non-charged sample, catholically hydrogen charged sample and sample
after hydrogen desorption for two diffractometers, low power — Fig. 3a, higher
power— Fig. 3b. The smoothing of the original peaks was carried out by ﬁtting the
Lorentz function.
After hydrogen charging of traditional samples 718 using low power diffrac-
tometer, it was observed that peaks were broadened and intensity felled down. After
hydrogen desorption in vacuum up to temperature 800 °C it is observed almost full
recovery in the peak parameters, Fig. 3a, b. This behavior evident about hydrogen
dissolution and then hydrogen desorption with the restoration of the lattice
parameter and stress-strain condition in lattice. Excess on desorbed pattern could
cause by the increase in dislocation density due to electrolytic hydrogen charging.
Diffraction pattern of the traditional 718 alloy sample obtained by using higher
power diffractometer show less signi ﬁcant effects of peak broadening and intensity

falling after hydrogen charging. Thus it can be assumed that hydrogen accumulated
in quite thin layer about 5 μm and trapped basically by grain boundaries and matrix.
For the 718 SLM sample, the diffraction pattern showed less signi ﬁcant

contrasting effect of hydrogen charging was observed, i.e. decrease of integral peak

compressing stresses were possibly compensated by tensile stresses resulting from

For the 718 SLM sample, a smaller change in intensity for two depths was
observed. The narrowing of diffraction peaks was detected for both higher and
low-power diffractometers. It is possible to assume that hydrogen accumulated in

The results of estimated microstrains and sub-microstrains for traditional and
additive samples are presented in Tables 2 and 3 respectively. It is shown that in the
traditional 718 sample after hydrogen charging the microstress changes are up to
35% in a layer ∼5 μm and up to 5% in a layer of ∼30 μm. After desorption of
hydrogen, the strains values return to near the initial condition values. The
sub-microstrain changes after hydrogen charging is ∼25%, which indicates the
presence of a signi ﬁcant amount of hydrogen in matrix of the sample.
It should be noted that the level of stresses on the surface of the additive 718
sample was signi ﬁcantly higher compared with the 718 obtained by traditional
technologies. The level of micro-stresses after hydrogen charging changes were
observed using both diffractometers that indicated that the hydrogen effect spreads
down to at least the 30 μm layer. Sub-microstrains slightly change (by 2 –3%) in the
layer to 30 μm. Thus distortions at the atomic level are very small but hydrogen
penetrates deeper than in traditional 718 alloy sample. Taking into account the
results of mass-spectrometry, it can be assumed that the main amount of hydrogen
is concentrated on the grain boundaries.

## Page 556

It was shown that for both 718 traditional and SLM samples after hydrogen
desorption the stress level returns to near the initial state.
Anomalous change in the stress-strain state of the additively manufactured
sample may indicate a state of the material associated with non-equilibrium so-
lidiﬁcation, related to the technology of its production. The statement about com-
pressive stresses along grain boundaries was indirectly con ﬁrmed by a series of
comparative fatigue tests of traditional and additive samples of Alloy 718 [ 22]. The
SLM materials exhibited increased number of fatigue cycles to failure as discovered
in this study. It is hypothesized that higher compressive stresses at the grain
boundaries are the cause which can be a greater barrier to the growth of a fatigue
crack.
The stress-strain state changes as a result of hydrogen charging of the material,
and there are some characteristic differences as a result of the manufacturing route.
The most signi ﬁcant change in stress-strain state occurs at the grain level which is
related to the state of grain boundaries.
Summary and Conclusions
The effect of electrochemical hydrogen charging for 72 h on stress-strain state was
studied by means of X-ray methods on alloy 718 produced by conventional met-
allurgical technology and by selective laser melting of powder. Two different
diffractometers of various powers and mass-spectrometer method were utilized for
understanding the hydrogen concentration and distribution.
The main amount of hydrogen adsorbed during electrochemical hydrogen
charging was found to be associated with a low binding energy and desorbed at a
temperature lower than 300 °C.
After electrochemical hydrogen charging changes were observed in the
stress-strain state. Residual stress (macrostress) changes as a result of hydrogen
charging were not detected. After hydrogen desorption by vacuum heating it was
observed that the stress-strain state returned to near that of the initial state. The
change in the stress-strain state after electrolytic hydrogen charging was inhomo-
geneous with respect to depth.
The increase in microstrain was measured by means of changes in the X-ray
peaks: peak broadening and intensity on the diffraction pattern. In the traditionally
manufactured 718 alloy, the microstrain was found to change by 35% in a depth to
about 5 μm. The total amount of hydrogen which caused the microstrain change
was less than 1 ppm.
The main amount of hydrogen was found to be concentrated in a thin surface
layer more than 30 μm for additively manufactured (SLM) 718 alloy. For the SLM
718 alloy there was no signi ﬁcant increase in microstrain. The SLM 718 material
had an anomalous effect on stress-strain state after hydrogen charging: despite its
dissolution in the lattice, a decrease in the microstrain was observed. It could be
Evaluation of the Stress-Strain State in Alloy 718 … 561

assumed that after hydrogen charging in SLM 718 alloy the bulk of hydrogen
accumulated by grain boundaries and compensate signi ﬁcantly high initial
microstresses.
