M. G. Fahrmann and L. M. Pike
Abstract HAYNES® 282® alloy was developed by Haynes International as an
age-hardenable, yet fabricable, wrought Ni-base superalloy. To date, the alloy has
been speciﬁed for a number of applications, most notably in the hot sections of both
aero- and industrial gas turbines. A Time-Temperature-Transformation (TTT) dia-
gram is a useful guide to assess an alloy ’s behavior during thermo-mechanical
processing and heat treating. Starting with the (commercially relevant) 1149 °C
(2100 °F) mill-annealed condition, a time (0.1 –100 h) —temperature (649–1121 °C
(1200–2050 °F)) exposure matrix was executed. Precipitates, which had formed as
a result of these exposures, were analyzed by light microscopy, scanning electron
microscopy/energy dispersive spectroscopy (SEM/EDS), and, in selected cases, by
x-ray diffraction (XRD). Chie ﬂy, γ′ and two types of carbides, Cr-rich M
23C6 and
Mo-rich M 6C, were found. Approximate C-curves for these phases were con-
structed, and some implications for the alloy ’s processing and properties charac-
teristics are discussed.
Keywords 282 alloy ⋅ TTT diagram ⋅ Gamma-Prime ⋅ Carbides
Introduction
HAYNES® 282® alloy was developed by Haynes International [ 1] as a wrought,
high-creep-strength, yet fabricable alternative to alloys such as Waspaloy. To date,
the alloy has been speci ﬁed for a number of applications, most notably in the hot
gas path sections of both aero- and industrial gas turbines.

## Page 560

In order to understand and control the alloy ’s behavior during
thermo-mechanical processing (e.g., rolling, forging) and heat treating
(solution-annealing and aging), an experimental TTT diagram is a useful guide. No
such diagram has heretofore been generated for this alloy. We stress the emphasis
on experimental since, in principle, TTT diagrams can nowadays also be con-
structed by means of computational thermodynamics and kinetics [ 2–4]. However,
the latter approach still requires the input of crucial experimental parameters, such
as interfacial energies for meaningful predictions.
The presented work follows a rather practical approach: we chose the
mill-annealed condition for a starting point rather than trying to create a hypo-
thetical, single-phase initial condition. In fact, the latter is virtually impossible to
achieve in the presence of strong carbide and nitride formers such as titanium. This
means that certain constituents, notably primary carbides/nitrides, would already be
present prior to thermal exposure. We also note that the construction of the C-curve
for a secondary phase would ideally refer to a certain speci ﬁed volume fraction of
this phase. Such detailed quantitative measurements were beyond the scope of this
study; instead, we focus on the practical aspects of the observed transformations.
For example, we address the implications of these constituents for strength and
ductility.
Material and Experimental Methods
The nominal composition of 282 alloy is shown in Table 1. The material of this
study originated from commercially produced 1.6 mm (0.062 ″) thick sheet stock
that was mill-annealed at 1149 °C (2100 °F). This particular product form was
selected since it represents one of the most chemically homogeneous states on
account of its thermo-mechanical processing history. In addition, lab heat treat-
ments of sheet coupons result in rapid thermal equilibration, thus minimizing
uncertainty, particularly for short exposure times.
The time-temperature exposure matrix covered times of 0.1, 1, 10, and 100 h
and temperatures of 649 (1200), 704 (1300), 760 (1400), 816 (1500), 871 (1600),
927 (1700), 982 (1800), 1038 (1900), 1093 (2000), and 1121 °C (2050 °F). This
matrix was, in part, devised based on the known age-hardening characteristics of
the alloy [ 5]. Temperature in the laboratory box furnace used was controlled to
better than ±5.6 °C (10 °F).
The thermally exposed sheet coupons were cut in half; one half was used for
hardness readings on the Rockwell A scale, the other half was used for

metallographic preparation employing standard metallographic techniques. Two
different electrolytic etching techniques were employed to reveal various phases:
(a) “γ′ etch” using a mixture of 15 g CrO
3 + 150 ml H 3PO4 +1 0m lH 2SO4, and
(b) “carbide-etch” using 5 g oxalic acid dissolved in 95 ml HCl.
SEM/EDS work was performed on a ZEISS SIGMA FEG SEM equipped with a
SDD detector. Secondary, back-scattered, and high-resolution in-lens imaging
modes were employed. The standard-less EDS work was typically done at 10 kV
(thus minimizing the beam-sample interaction volume), utilizing the L peaks for the
heavier elements.
Phase extraction/XRD work was performed on a limited basis, chie ﬂy for 100-h
exposures only. The extraction solution used was 5% HCl + 5% H
3PO4, balance
being methanol. The extracted powders were analyzed in a PANalytical X ’Pert3
powder diffractometer using CuKα radiation. The 2-θ scan range was approximately
20°–90° at a scan rate of 0.020° per step and a dwell time 1 s per step. The
diffraction peaks were indexed using the current database of the International
Centre for Diffraction Data [ 6]. Only the evidence of phases for which multiple
strong diffraction peaks were found, was considered conclusive.
Particle size analysis of γ′ encompassed manual tracing of a suf ﬁcient number of
particles (N > 100) on multiple high-magni ﬁcation, high-resolution SEM in-lens
micrographs. The traced images were subsequently digitized and processed using
the public-domain image processing software Image J [ 7]. Since these samples were
deep-etched, no correction for particle truncation was deemed necessary. Also,
since only particles with well-de ﬁned perimeters (no overlaps) were traced, no
volume fraction measurements were attempted. In order to assess the impact of bias
in the tracing procedure, selected sets of micrographs were traced independently by
two different persons, and then processed and analyzed to the same protocol.
Results and Discussion
Initial Condition
A representative photomicrograph of the initial (mill-annealed) condition is shown
in Fig. 1. The average grain size was rated as ASTM 3. The presence of scattered
particle stringers in the rolling direction is not uncommon to superalloy sheet
products. Notice that the grain boundaries exhibit only a very light, if any deco-
ration. More detail about these particle stringers is shown in the BSE micrograph in
Fig. 2. SEM/EDS analyses indicate that three different types of particles, subse-
quently referred to as primary carbides, are present in the mill-annealed sheet stock:
(a) TiN nitrides, often in a core-rim con ﬁguration with the rim presumably being a
carbide,
(b) Ti- and Mo-rich MC-type carbides,
(c) Mo-rich M
6C-type carbides.

The TiN particles formed presumably during melting and served subsequently as
nucleation sites for carbides during solidi ﬁcation. The MC-type and the M 6C-type
carbides are believed to be solidi ﬁcation products. The combination of size, mor-
phology, location, and stringer-like arrangement of these primary carbides served as
a crucial footprint for their distinction from any secondary carbides that formed
upon thermal exposure.
While not detectable on traditional LM micrographs, high-magni ﬁcation in-lens
imaging in the SEM revealed the presence of what appears to be cooling γ′ (Fig. 3).
These very small, densely packed features tended to be spherical in shape and of a
diameter of roughly 10 nm. The presence of cooling γ′ in this alloy is to be
expected; on a mill-scale, its precipitation cannot realistically be suppressed [ 8].
Nonetheless, hardness is low (roughly 90 HRB) and ductility/formability is high
(tensile elongation in excess of 50%) in this condition.
Thermal Exposures —Gamma-Prime
Since γ′ appeared to be already present in the initial condition, a classical C-curve
could not be generated for this phase. Taking the aforementioned rather practical
approach, the evolution of average γ′ size during aging was tracked instead.
Measuring average γ′ size was meaningful since these particles tended to be

The average γ′ diameter as a function of aging time is plotted in Fig. 5, aging
temperature being the curve parameter. Notice that 982 °C (1800 °F) is the upper
limit in this plot since no γ′ was detected after aging at 1038 °C (1900 °F),
consistent with a γ′ solvus temperature of approximately 1000 °C (1830 °F) [ 5].
The uncertainty in the average diameters is estimated to be on the order of the
symbol size, based on the aforementioned independent measurements by two
persons. This plot is useful since it allows one to correlate heat treat parameters with
the size of the resulting strengthening γ′ precipitates. For example, based on the
generated Time-Temperature-Hardness (TTH) diagram in Fig. 6 (notice the
Rockwell A scale), the optimal aging condition (maximum hardness in minimum
time) appears to be 788 °C (1450 °F)/8 h, as recommended for the alloy [ 5]. Further
discussion of the recommended heat treatment for 282 alloy will follow later in this
manuscript. Referencing Fig. 6, the corresponding mean γ′ diameter after 788 °C
(1450 °F)/8 h would be roughly 30 nm. Conversely, one could estimate the mag-
nitude of the age-hardening effect (and infer its impact on processability) if the
material is held at any of these studied temperatures during manufacturing. We note
that the temperature-dependent γ′ volume fraction needs to be factored in such
estimates as well.

Determination whether a potential secondary carbide particle indeed formed
during thermal exposure or was already present in the initial mill-annealed condi-
tion proved dif ﬁcult at times as illustrated by the BSE image in Fig. 8. Composi-
tionally, the particle with label 3 was clearly identi ﬁed as M 6C. However, the fact
that it did not reside in a grain boundary and that in its vicinity a string of similarly
bright particles were observed in this BSE image, lead to the conclusion that this
particular particle was most likely present in the mill-annealed condition. Another
important criterion for distinction between primary and secondary carbides was
based on the observation that the bulk of the secondary carbides formed in the grain
boundaries. This is quite common in Ni-base superalloys since both types of sec-
ondary carbides feature very large unit cells [ 6] that are dif ﬁcult to nucleate
homogeneously in the bulk of the grain.
Another experimental dif ﬁculty resulted from the small size of the secondary
carbides in certain exposure conditions, and the associated matrix interference in
the EDS analyses. In this case, the results were inconclusive.

analyses and the potential interference by the matrix, it appears that the chemical

## Page 570

(1) The kinetics of precipitation of M 23C6 carbides in the grain boundaries are
approximately two orders of magnitude faster than that of the M 6C carbides.
(2) The solvus temperatures of both secondary carbides appear to be in the vicinity
of 1121 °C (2050 °F).
The former conclusion can be rationalized by the known sluggish diffusivity of
Mo, the key M 6C-forming element, compared to that of Cr, the key M 23C6-forming
element [ 9]. We note that the latter conclusion is quite discrepant from several
CALPHAD-type phase constitution simulations: the presence of M 23C6 carbides at
these high temperatures is not predicted.
Secondary carbides in Ni-base superalloys can affect grain size evolution during
thermo-mechanical processing, and are known to impact key mechanical properties
such as creep resistance and ductility. However, it is not only their nature, but also
their size and distribution in the grain boundaries that determine their impact. It is

576 M. G. Fahrmann and L. M. Pike

## Page 571

generally accepted that discrete grain boundary carbides are bene ﬁcial to creep
strength, while not unduly degrading ductility. Such discrete grain boundary dec-
oration was observed at all exposures above the γ′ solvus. Accordingly, the rec-
ommended two-step aging cycle of 282 alloy encompasses a ﬁrst aging step at
1010 °C (1850 °F) for 2 h. Therefore, the results of this study have con ﬁrmed the
implications of the standard 2-step aging treatment (1010 °C/2 h + 788 °C/8 h) for
282 alloy: the ﬁrst step resulting in discrete M
23C6 carbides at the grain boundary,
and the second step providing the optimal age-hardening.
We note that the presented results are consistent with those published previously
[10] for 1,000-h exposures at similar temperatures, in that the alloy (a) forms
secondary M 23C6 and M6C carbides, and (b) that no additional phases were found.
The latter ﬁnding warrants some discussion. At the typical boron levels in the alloy,
the presence of sub-micron sized Mo-rich M 5B3 boride particles was reported by
Osoba et al. [ 11]. However, these authors performed detailed TEM work to arrive at
this conclusion. The methods employed here (SEM/EDS, phase extraction/XRD)
lead only to a conclusion that the amount of any boride would have been below the
detection limits. Another possibility for the lack of borides is the potential parti-
tioning of B to a M
23(C,B)6 type carbide, as suggested for alloy 617B [ 12]. Lastly,
TCP phases such as μ and σ (both predicted by CALPHAD software) were not
found to have formed even for extended exposure times, presumably on account of
their sluggish precipitation kinetics at T < 816 °C (1500 °F).
Summary and Conclusions
1. Utilizing commercial sheet stock, an approximate TTT diagram of HAYNES
282 alloy was generated.
2. In the initial, mill-annealed condition, primary TiN, (Ti,Mo)C, a few M 6C
carbides, and very ﬁne cooling γ′ were found to be present.
3. Upon exposure at temperatures ranging from 649 to 1093 °C (1200 –2000 °F)
and times up to 100 h, secondary M 23C6 and M6C carbides formed in the grain
boundaries. The kinetics of precipitation of secondary M 23C6 carbides seems to
be roughly two orders of magnitude faster than that of secondary M 6C carbides,
however, the solvus temperatures of both phases appear to be in the vicinity of
1121 °C (2050 °F).
4. Exposures at temperatures ranging from 649 to 982 °C (1200 –1800 °F) pre-
sumably coarsened the pre-existing cooling γ′, and resulted in signi ﬁcant
hardening for certain exposure conditions.
5. By SEM and XRD methods only, borides could not be detected. Deleteri-
ous TCP phases were not found for any of the studied exposure conditions.

## Page 573

Inﬂuence of Residual Stresses on Ageing
Precipitation Behavior of Alloy 718
Hailong Qin, Zhongnan Bi, Ruiyao Zhang, Hongyao Yu, Guang Feng,
Xia Guo, Hai Chi, Jinhui Du and Ji Zhang
Abstract The interior residual stresses, which were generated at previous stages of
forging and water quenching, exist as a pre-condition of γ″ precipitation during the
subsequent thermal ageing. To clarify the issue, a re ﬁne investigation for the
preferentially orientation of γ″ precipitates in Inconel 718 can be achieved by
means of TEM, FE-SEM and small angel neutron scattering. Compared with the
isotropic nucleation in the early stage of ageing, the preferential orientation during
the coarsening process has a speci ﬁc orientation-relationship, due to the volume
diffusion of niobium atoms affected by elastic strain, with the load direction in a
multiple crystal system. The inhomogeneity and anisotropy in microstructure give
rise to a deterioration and anisotropy of mechanical properties.
Keywords Inconel 718
⋅ Residual stress ⋅ Preferential orientation
Volume diffusion ⋅ Mechanical property
Introduction and Motivation
Nickel-base alloys are commonly used in oil and natural gas production. Inconel
718 (hereinafter referred to as alloy 718), a precipitation-strengthened Ni-based
superalloy, has been widely used in aviation, space ﬂight, energy, and chemical

## Page 574

engineering industries [ 1, 2]. The disk-shape intermetallic compound γ″ (Ni3Nb) is
the main strength phase. In order to achieve the speci ﬁc requirements of oil ﬁeld
applications, alloy 718 is usually subjected to a solid solution between 1021 and
1052 °C for 1 –2.5 h before being water quenched. Then, it is usually given a
one-step ageing treatment between 774 and 802 °C for 6 –8h[ 3, 4]. Residual stress
in superalloy ’s components is mainly produced during rapid post-solution cooling
(e.g., quenching in water, oil). In many cases, they are compressive at the rim but
tensile in the center, and the magnitude is about −400 ∼ 400 MPa for alloy 718
[5–7].
Residual stress is that which remains in a body that is stationary and at equi-
librium with its surroundings [ 8]. A sequence of thermo-mechanical process during
the manufacturing of metallic components, such as forging, quenching, and
welding, can produce uneven plastic deformation, and result in the generation of a
high level of residual stress. Residual stress can be very detrimental to the per-
formance of a material or the life of a component [ 9, 10], and even have an
inﬂuence on precipitations. The quenching-induced residual stress may exist as a
pre-condition of γ″ precipitation process. There are three variants of the γ″
(tetragonal) phase lying on {100} matrix (cubic). Oblak et al. [ 11] found that by
ageing an [001] crystal under an elastic tensile load, a microstructure can be pro-
duced where only the variant lying normal to the [001] stress axis is formed.
Nevertheless, there is still a lack of explanation for the missing of other γ″ particle
variants or preferentially orientated coarsening. There are many researches con-
cerning about the in ﬂuence of elastic stress condition on the directional coarsening
of γ′ precipitates in cubic ( γ′-particles)-cubic ( γ-matrix) superalloy systems during
service [12–14]. Directional coarsening of γ′ precipitates, namely rafting, can affect
the mechanical performance lifetime of Ni-based superalloys and lead to aniso-
tropy. The main contribution to rafting of γ′ is the volume diffusion affected by
local internal stress [ 15] and the lattice mis ﬁt between γ′ and γ matrix [14]. Besides,
many studies [ 16–18] have found that external stresses, instead of residual stresses,
can strongly affect the precipitation behavior of strengthening phases in Al alloys
during the ageing treatment (namely, stress ageing).
The uniformity of microstructure is very important for Ni-based superalloy
forging components, such as jet engine turbine disks. The distribution of
quenching-induced residual stresses is commonly gradient and uneven in the
component, which may cause inhomogeneity in microstructure and different mor-
phology of γ″. The strengthening effect of the γ″ precipitates depends largely on
their size and morphology. Therefore, the mechanical property in the rim and center
of the workpiece varies, referring to the uneven distribution of quench-in residual
stress.
Bearing in mind above consideration, this paper investigates quenching-induced
residual stress and its effect on the preferentially orientation of γ″ particle. Factors
which can affect the formation of γ″ phase preferentially orientated coarsening are
also discussed. The effects of preferentially orientated coarsening on the mechanical
properties and anisotropy were studied by hardness and tensile test.

Experimental Procedures
Table 1 gives the chemical composition (wt%) of the alloy 718. The material was
manufactured by the vacuum induction melting (VIM), electro-slag remelting
(ESR), and vacuum arc remelting (VAR) processes. Then, the ingot was forged into
a bar with a diameter of 220 mm. A cylindrical sample with both a diameter and
height of 40 mm was machined from the core of the hot-forged bar to ensure the
microstructure’s uniformity. The sample was subjected to a solid solution at
1030 °C for 1 h followed by water quenching, which developed signi ﬁcant residual
stresses.
The average cooling rate of cylindrical sample is over 100 °C/min, which is fast
enough to avoid precipitation of the γ″ phase, according to Geng ’s research [19]. As
shown in Fig. 1, the microstructure of solution-annealed condition was fcc- γ grains
with the average grain size of about 35 μm. A small quantity of carbide and δ phase
were also observed.
Then the sample was subjected to an ageing treatment at 790 °C for 8 h as one
piece to investigate the effect of quenching-induced residual stress on γ″ precipi-
tation during ageing. Rockwell hardness tests were carried out in a hoop section of
the cylindrical sample. In order to release the residual stresses and minimize their
effects on hardness tests, the specimens were cut into a slice with a thickness of
3 mm. A load of 150 kg was applied for 2 s. The slice was also used for
microstructure observation at different locations: region A, B, and C, as shown in
Fig. 3. Different regions exhibit different stress states. A three-dimensional
axisymmetric ﬁnite-element model of the quenching process was implemented

## Page 576

using DEFORM software [ 5]. The model was based upon a 30,000-element mesh
of the cylindrical geometry and incorporated a fully coupled thermal-mechanical
analysis of elastic-plastic deformation and heat transfer.
In order to simplify the analysis, constant external stress, instead of residual
stress, was applied during the ageing heat treatment. The stress magnitude was
chosen referring to the yield strength and creep data such that plastic deformation
would be minimized or even avoided [ 6]. Rod specimens (12 × 67 mm) for aging
under external stress were subjected to the following treatments: (i) Solid solution
treatment at 1030 °C for 1 h; (ii) Air cooling from 980 to 500 °C (average 80 °C/
min) to minimize the residual stress and avoid precipitation of the γ″ phase [ 19];
(iii) Aging at 790 °C for 8 h under external tensile stress of 300 MPa, which was
controlled by an electromechanical universal testing machine.
For preparing TEM specimens, electropolishing was carried out at about 20 V.
The electrolyte contained 70% butanol, 20% ethanol and 10% perchloric acid. TEM
observation was performed on FEI Tecnai G
2 F20 transmission electron microscope
operated at 200 kV. The samples for the ﬁeld emission scanning electron micro-
scopy (FE-SEM) observations were etched chemically with a mixed solution
composited by 5 g CuCl
2 + 100 ml hydrochloric acid + 100 ml ethanol. The
FE-SEM and electron back scattered diffraction (EBSD) measurements were carried
out on a JSM-7800F (JEOL, Akishima, Japan) FE-SEM equipped with EBSD.
Small angel neutron scattering (SANS) experiments were carried out at the
V4 SANS instrument at Helmholtz Zentrum Berlin (HZB). The wavelength of the
incident neutron was set at 0.60 nm, and the distance from the sample to detector
was set at 8 m. The samples with a diameter of 6 mm and a thickness of 1 mm were
used. The mechanical properties were investigated using tensile tests at room
temperature. The tensile tests were performed according to the ISO 6892-2 2011
standard, and the dimensions of the specimens were chosen according to the ASTM
D3165-1995 standard.
A ﬁrst-principle calculation was performed to determine the in ﬂuence of stress
on diffusion energy barrier for Nb atoms. All these calculations (including the bulk
property optimization, the activity of Nb in Ni under stress/strain were determined
by using DMol3 code [ 20, 21]. The generalized gradient approximation
(GGA) with the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) functional [ 22] and all-electron
double numerical basis set with polarized function (DNP) have been employed. The
convergence tolerance of energy is 1.0 × 10
−5 Ha (1 Ha = 27.21 eV), and that of
maximum force is 2.0 × 10 −3 Ha/Å. Each atom in the storage models is allowed to
relax to the minimum in the enthalpy without any constraints. Exterior strain have
been added in z-direction, and the stress intensities are re ﬂected by changing the
lattice constants in z-direction based on the elasticity modulus of bulk materials [ 23,
24]. The Nb atoms move in the parallel and vertical directions compared the
exterior stress direction, and the energy barriers of them have been calculated by
considering the transition states.

Results and Discussion
Preferentially Orientated Coarsening of γ'' Phase
The stress states in the three regions are different during the ageing treatment.
Figure 2 shows the distribution of quenching-induced residual stresses in different
directions for the cylindrical sample before ageing, calculated by DEFORM soft-
ware. The calculated results by ﬁnite element method (FEM) are very close to the
measured results by the neutron diffraction experiments [ 5, 6]. After quenched, A,
B and C is subjected to tensile stress in three directions (hoop, radial and axial),
compressive stress in two directions (hoop and axial), and compressive stress in one
direction (hoop), respectively. The magnitude of residual stress is from −400 to
400 MPa.
After water quenched, the cylinder sample was subjected to an ageing treatment
at 790 °C for 8 h as one piece to investigate the effect of quenching-induced
residual stress on γ″ precipitation during ageing. The morphology of D0
22 γ″ in
different position of the cylinder sample is shown in Fig. 3. It is easy to observe a
stress-orientation effect on γ″ precipitation in B and C region with one or two
orientated variants of γ″ partially absent. The obvious differences in measured
particle sizes of three regions are not statistically signi ﬁcant. The mean size of the
γ″ precipitates in region B and C are slightly larger than that in A. In all the three
samples, obvious characteristics of coarsening can be observed: the larger precip-
itates increase their size to the expense of the small particles, which disappear.
The excellent high temperature strength of alloy 718 is attributed largely to the
γ″ (Ni
3Nb-type) precipitates, which are coherent and have an ordered
body-centered-tetragonal D0 22 crystal structure. The strengthening of γ″ phase is
due to coherent strains arising from lattice distortion as this precipitate forms.
Employed methods revealed that γ″ precipitates are mainly elongated-disc shaped.
Between γ″ phases and γ matrix, three equivalent orientation relationships are
possible (Hong et al. [ 25]):
(1) (100) γ″ // (100) γ; [001] γ″ // [001] γ,
(2) (100) γ″ // (010) γ; [001] γ″ // [010] γ,
(3) (100) γ″ // (001) γ; [001] γ″ // [001] γ.

Effect of Stress Condition on Diffusion
Diffusion is another major factor affecting coarsening process. The γ′ phase rafting
is basically a diffusion-conditioned process. The recent investigations of rafting [ 14]
showed clearly the importance of stress in determining the pathway of diffusion. The
isotropic coarsening of γ″ phase follows the time-law predictions of
Lifshitz-Slyozov-Wagner (LSW) theory with a volume diffusion-controlled growth.
The activation energy for the coarsening of γ″ precipitates is found to be equal to
272 kJ/mol [ 28]. This value is close to the activation energy for the diffusion of
niobium in nickel, which is 257 kJ/mol. It strongly suggests that the γ″ precipitates
coarsening process is controlled by volume diffusion of niobium in the matrix.
However, the LSW theory neglects the effect of the elastic ﬁeld which can be caused
by external load or internal residual stress. Elastic stress/strain may promote or block
the diffusion for atoms in different directions, due to the diffusion channels may be
strengthened or weakened [ 15]. Elongated lattice or interplanar spacing have a large
diffusion channel. When the sample is loaded in tension, the direction perpendicular
to stress have a low diffusion energy barrier (E
D) so that the γ″ variant, perpendicular
to tensile load, occur growth and coarsening, while the other two variants dissolve.
The ﬁrst principle calculation was applied to verify the diffusion energy barrier.
Figure 8a shows the pattern of atomic migration parallel or vertical to elastic strain.
The diffusion energy barrier in different directions (parallel to strain ED-par or
vertical to strain ED-ver) display a declining trend with the strain increasing from
compressive to tensile when the sample is loaded in z axis (Fig. 8b). The effect of
elastic strain on the diffusion vertical to stress axis is more severe and dramatic.
E
D-par is signi ﬁcantly lower than ED-ver, when the sample is loaded in tension.
Therefore, the diffusion for Nb atoms in vertical directions is promoted, resulting in
the preferential orientation of γ″ precipitates vertical to the stress axis. According to
Figs. 7 and 8, it can be inferred that the diffusion perpendicular to the tensile stress
is facilitated. Effect of stress condition on diffusion can lead to the preferentially
orientated coarsening of γ″ precipitates.
Anisotropy of Microstructure due to the Local Stress
Condition
The grain orientation is isotropic initially and after ageing. The elastic residual
stress cannot cause anisotropy of the grains. However, habit plane of the γ″ phase
has orientation relationship with the grain orientation. Therefore, there may be
macro anisotropy of the texture. SANS measurement, which could analyze size
distribution, volume fraction, morphology and dissolution of γ″ nanoparticles in
Ni-base alloys, was used to investigate the anisotropy of microstructure. The
symmetric and asymmetric circles of SANS data indicate the texture is isotropic or
not.
588 H. Qin et al.

## Page 583

The two-dimensional SANS data from different samples (Fig. 9) clearly show
the orientation-dependent scattering for B and C, while for A, scattering is the same
along various directions. This can be explained by the existence of a preferred
orientation of the γ″ nano-plates in B and C. In other words, the γ″ nano-particles in
B and C tend to align up into some particular direction, while there is no preferred
orientation found in the A. Nevertheless, the FE-SEM results (Fig. 3) also support
this conclusion at the sub-micrometer scale, and the nano-particles tend to align up
into some particular directions in B and C.
Not only the orientation distribution of the nanoparticles but also the preferential
orientation of crystal grains can generate orientation-dependent scattering in SANS.
The pole ﬁgures are used to characterize the preferred orientation of crystal grain.

Effect of Preferentially Orientated Coarsening
on the Mechanical Properties
Figure 11 shows that the hardness distribution of the cut-out slice is non-uniform

easily hardened by quenched, so the hardness of the surface is higher than that of
the core. The strengthening effect of the γ″ precipitates depends largely on their size
and morphology. The results of present study are just the opposite of that phe-
nomenon, indicating that preferentially orientated coarsening of γ″ nano-plates
could result in a deterioration of the mechanical properties.

## Page 586

Conclusion
In the present study, quenching-induced residual stress and its effect on the pref-
erential orientation of γ″ phase during ageing were investigated and analyzed in
detail. The following conclusions can be derived from the study:
(1) The quenching-induced residual stress exists as a pre-condition of γ″ growth
and coarsening process, resulting the preferentially orientation of γ″ precipi-
tates. In the early stage of ageing, the phenomenon is presented for the isotropic
nucleation and growth process, and all of the three variants γ″ precipitates
generate simultaneously. However, the preferential orientation of γ″ occur
during the coarsening process.
(2) The relevant mechanisms are discussed: the volume diffusion of niobium atoms
is the main factors, which can affect the formation of preferentially orientated
coarsening.
(3) Preferentially orientated coarsening cause the inhomogeneity and anisotropy in
microstructure, which lead a deterioration of mechanical properties and ani-
sotropy of material strength.

Machine Learning to Optimize Additive
Manufacturing Parameters for Laser
Powder Bed Fusion of Inconel 718
Branden Kappes, Senthamilaruvi Moorthy, Dana Drake, Henry Geerlings
and Aaron Stebner
Abstract Approximately 3600 samples have been printed to characterize the build
parameters for laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) fabrication of Inconel 718. The
tested samples connect pore formation to part orientation, part location and the use of
recycled powder. These data serve as the basis for development of a Random Forest
Network machine learning (ML) model capable of two-way modeling of process–
property and process–structure relationships. These results show how common pro-
cedural steps in the setup and execution of L-PBF eﬀect porosity, particularly the
formation of keyhole and lack of fusion (LOF) defects, and how data collection, pro-
cessing, and validation can expose even subtle connections between input features
and output parameters using a general ML framework.
Keywords Additive manufacturing
⋅ Laser powder bed fusion⋅ Inconel
Machine learning ⋅ X-ray computed tomography⋅ Porosity⋅ Powder morphology
Introduction
From its ability to construct complex geometries, or as a pathway to functionally
graded materials, additive manufacturing (AM) is a transformative technology for
both the ﬂexibility it provides and the impact it has had on component design, man-

## Page 589

596 B. Kappes et al.
ufacturing, and materials engineering [ 16]. AM largely separates the mechanics of
the build process from component shape, and in so doing, adds the ability to pro-
duce complex internal features to the complex external features currently possible
with subtractive machining. Simultaneous manufacture of the part and the material
during AM inextricably links the properties of the material to the complex thermal
gradients, and corresponding thermal stress, that develop in the part are a function
of source material, part geometry, thermal conductivity, part spacing and position,
and the laser settings: speed, spot size and power. Together, these create microstruc-
tures that are distinctly diﬀerent than traditional materials synthesis routes, such as
forging or castings [8, 12].
As in traditional metallurgy, the microstructure of additively manufactured metal
parts is controlled by composition and thermal history. Some materials, such as
Inconel 718 and Ti-6 Al-4 V, form a strongly textured microstructure in response
to the highly directional heating and cooling of L-PBF [ 4, 14, 16, 21]. High den-
sity cellular dislocation networks also form to accommodate the large thermal gradi-
ents and corresponding thermal stresses that develop during the build process. These
stresses can aﬀect the net shape of the part if the part is not properly supported during
build and the thermal stresses are not relaxed in a post-build anneal.
The laser settings also introduce defects often seen in welding processes. LOF
defects can occur with insuﬃcient power density: when either the laser power is
too low or the laser speed too high. These defects negatively impact mechanical
properties, and should be avoided [ 19]. Keyhole porosity develops when the laser
power density is too high, but unlike LOF defects, these defects tend to be small,
<40 µm sphere-equivalent-radius. The eﬀect of the extensive keyhole pore network
near the surface of L-PBF parts seems to have little eﬀect on the static mechanical
properties [11], but the eﬀect on the dynamic mechanical properties is still unknown
[19, 20].
The dislocation networks that form from thermal stresses provide work hardening
in stainless steel and Inconel, increasing the yield strength, and in the case of Ni-Ti
alloys, suﬃciently to enable superelastic or shape memory behavior without need for
additional area reduction [1, 4, 18]. Large thermal gradients and rapid cooling rates
aﬀect phase formation, grain size and grain morphology; features known to aﬀect
mechanical properties, such as yield stress, toughness and hardness. Controlling
grain size and morphology to tailor materials’ properties is a well-established prac-
tice in metallurgy. Directional solidiﬁcation, recrystallization, precipitation harden-
ing, and devitriﬁcation form the basis for diverse applications: from turbine blades to
transformer cores. And because the processing steps to achieve targeted mechanical
properties require a precise sequence of thermomechanical treatments, development
of appropriate processing conditions required to meet or exceed the performance of
established materials is necessary for the success of AM [5, 9].
This work provides an introduction to a machine learning (ML) and data
informatics framework with the goal of identifying process-structure-property (PSP)
relationships in AM. The focus of this research is to construct an ML frame-
work for identifying process-structure and structure-property correlations from high-

throughput materials characterization data, enabling engineering and design for AM
by predicting structure and variability.
Methods
To isolate the eﬀect of part geometry and powder processing history, all samples
were built using manufacturer-recommended laser settings, laser scan path, purge gas
atmosphere and ﬂow rates, coater blade speeds, layer thickness, and raw feedstock
source. The Inconel 718 powder (−45+10 µm) and recommended build parameter
settings for this powder stock were purchased from Concept Laser, and six builds
produced based on those settings. The design of experiment divides six factors into
(N) levels: coupon position (605), orientation (9), fraction recycled powder (2), and
laser incidence angle (2). These 21,780 combinations are reduced to 3,630 by assum-
ing variations along the blade and transverse directions (Fig.1b) are continuous. This
enabled more coarse sampling along the blade direction and, by repeating each orien-
tation 2–3 times along the transverse direction, coarse sampling along the transverse
direction as well. The laser incidence angle is, by geometric necessity, related to both
the sample position and orientation. Despite this reduction in feature space, without
an ap r i o r iknowledge of variable importance, a technique insensitive to extraneous
features is needed to deconvolve the eﬀects of these variables.
Imaging data were collected and analyzed on approximately 600–2 mm∅× 4m m
compression cylinders. All built with the same laser settings, except laser incidence
angle, these test coupons are positioned and oriented to identify the build variabil-
ity that can be expected across a single build volume. Each build consists of parts
oriented at 0
◦ (vertical), 45◦,o r9 0◦ (horizontal) with respect to the build direction
(polar angle), and at 0◦,4 5◦,9 0◦, and 135◦ with respect to the coater blade direc-
tion (azimuth angle), as shown in Fig.1. In addition to position and orientation, each
build plate introduces a single global parameter change: post-build heat treatment,

Several machine learning techniques are capable of ignoring extraneous variables,
but in general, require a large amount of data. The number of measurements required
to train a machine learning model depends both on the type of model used and the
number and nature of the relationship between the response and model input. A high
throughput characterization workﬂow is set up to observe the microstructural fea-
tures that result from the AM parameters and correlate these to the mechanical prop-
erties of the ﬁnal part.
Imaging and Characterization
Correlation of additive manufacturing build parameters to defect concentration in
additively manufactured parts relies upon a combination of electron microscopy and
X-ray computed tomography (XCT). These are used examine the size and morphol-
ogy of both the source powder and porosity defects.
XCT uses diﬀerences in X-ray absorptivity through each volume element of a
sample to identify the presence of microstructural features based on their mass
absorption coeﬃcients, 𝛼. A series of projections are taken as the sample is rotated
through 360
◦. Together, these projections provide an overdetermined solution to the
Beer-Lambert Law.
Composed predominantly of Ni and Fe, Inconel 718 has a large mass absorption
coeﬃcient and as such, requires high energy X-rays to image samples of any appre-

## Page 592

Machine Learning to Optimize Additive Manufacturing Parameters . . . 599
ciable size. The Zeiss Xradia Versa 520 [22] uses a tungsten target and an adjustable
accelerating voltage of 30–160 kV to generate hard X-rays. At an operating voltage
of 160 kV and current of 62.5 µA (10 W), the spot size for this source is approxi-
mately5 µm and is able to image the cylindrical Inconel 718 test coupons at a spatial
resolution of 4.5 µm. These settings were used to image both the pores in the com-
pression cylinders and the source powder.
The mass absorption coeﬃcient of a material phase is a function of composition
and density, therefore diﬀerentiation of air (porosity) from metal is straightforward.
Both virgin and recycled powder where characterized with XCT to identify particle
size and shape distributions. The powder was dispersed in a quick-set epoxy and
drawn under vacuum into 2mm ∅cylindrical molds and allowed to set. The use of
quick-set epoxy prevented any sedimentation that would complicate segmentation.
Automated tomography data processing pipelines are required to enable the iter-
ative development of analysis techniques capable of processing the 1,000–10,000
defect structures in each of 550 tested sample coupons. This automated analysis
capability is developed for X-ray micro-CT (computed tomography) images using
tracr [7]. In order to reliably diﬀerentiate pores from metal, the image must ﬁrst
be segmented. Several algorithms exist for this task, including Adaptive Threshold,
Yen, Li, and Otsu, but of these, the global Otsu threshold is well suited to the bimodal
distribution present in this high-contrast, two-phase (air + metal) system. The Otsu
segmentation algorithm maximizes interclass variance, or equivalently, minimizes
intraclass variance [10, 13]. Tomography ﬁelds of view were selected to produce an
approximately equal volume of metallic sample (highly absorbing volume) and air
(low absorption).
Once segmented, or “binarized”, the identiﬁcation and characterization of dis-
crete defects is automated using a marching cubes ﬂood-ﬁll algorithm, as imple-
mented in thelabel function in thescipy.ndimage.measurements module
available in the python programming language. This function labels each spatially
distinct, i.e. unconnected, pore, and provides statistics on pore size, shape and orien-
tation: speciﬁcally, volume, maximum pore equivalent diameter (critical ﬂaw size),
mean pore equivalent diameter, median pore equivalent diameter, mean neighbor
center-of-mass distance, median neighbor center-of-mass distance, fraction poros-
ity, and sphericity.
Machine Learning
Machine learning (ML) abstracts data analysis by formalizing the process of identify-
ing correlations between feature variables (inputs) and response variables (outputs).
ML algorithms broadly fall into two categories: supervised learning, which attempt
to make predictive correlations between the feature space and the response space,
and unsupervised learning, which looks for patterns, clusters, or groups. A Random
Forest Network (RFN) is a supervised learning algorithm capable of both classiﬁca-
tion and regression, and was selected to ﬁt coupon position, orientation and recycled

## Page 593

600 B. Kappes et al.
powder content to part porosity. It was selected from among the many other machine
learning algorithms for several reasons. Importantly, RFN are relatively insensitive
to irrelevant features, which is important in AM applications, as the relative impor-
tance of processing conditions is not consistent across all processes and materials
systems.
Originally proposed by Breiman [3], RFN consist of an ensemble of decision trees
that recursively subdivide the data. Each division is chosen to maximize the informa-
tion gained by that division, where the amount of information gain is often quantiﬁed
by the Gini impurity or the entropy gain [2]. This recursive division stops, forming
leaf nodes, once a predeﬁned termination condition is met or the information gain
is zero. Predictions are made from the RFN by following the logic of each deci-
sion tree and combining the results from all trees through an ensemble combination
rule. This combination rule can be algebraic, e.g. min, max or mean (for regression)
or voting based for classiﬁcation using, for example, majority voting ( mode). Each
RFN model used in this study was comprised of 346 estimators (decision trees), a
minimum leaf node size of 1, a maximum tree depth of 30, and an arithmetic mean
ensemble combination rule.
Results and Discussion
Although laser settings are known to have a signiﬁcant eﬀect on the L-PBF process,
several other factors can potentially impact the quality of a ﬁnal build, such as the
location and orientation of each part and the number of times the powder has been
recycled. Recycle count is a practical metric that encompasses the complex relation-
ship between previous build environments, powder contamination, sieve practice and
powder spreading dynamics. This speaks to an outstanding challenge in L-PBF, and
AM generally; identifying which metrics are probative surrogates for the physics that
underlie process mechanisms. What follows is a discussion on the potential surro-
gacy of the easily observable part location, orientation and recycled powder content
to the physics that control the formation of porosity in ﬁnely featured parts.
Recycled and Virgin Powder Diﬀer Most Noticeably
in the Accumulation of Fines
In L-PBF, assessing the quality of the ﬁnal built part begins with the evaluation
of the powder feedstock. While both ASTM and ISO standards exist to characterize
ﬂowability, no standard currently exists to deﬁne the spreadability of the powder, i.e.
a quantitative metric that describes the “goodness” with which powder spreads under
a transverse load, as with L-PBF recoaters. Spreadability aﬀects powder packing and
the ability to form a fully dense AM built part.

Quantifying the inﬂuence of the powder’s properties on ﬁnal build quality requires
a standard array of tests that can provide enough information to accurately predict
how the powder will behave in a given powder bed set up, i.e. provide an assessment
of the quality of the powder. Inconel 718 AM powder feedstock has been examined
using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to identify powder morphology and x-ray
computed tomography (XCT) to identify the particle size and shape distributions.
SEM shows similarities in the powder morphology between virgin and recycled
powders including gross particle size, distribution and the presence of satellites—
small particles fused to larger. This is not entirely surprising, since only a small per-
centage of the spread powder was used to construct the compression cylinders. How-
ever, there are also clear morphology diﬀerences. The recycled powder appears more
ellipsoidal, has more oblique particles, such as platelets and needle-shaped powder,
and the presence of ﬁnes, particles of much smaller diameter, are much more preva-
lent in the recycled mixture. It is unknown if these ﬁnes are formed from cast-oﬀ
during the build process or by mechanical attrition of satellites during powder han-
dling. The powder size distribution in Fig. 2 clearly shows a broad monodispersity
around 25 µm, with few particles below 10 µm or above 45 µm. This is consistent
with the −45+10 µm sieve protocol from the powder supplier. Unlike the virgin
powder, the recycled powder is only sieved to−40 µm, revealing a marked increase
in the concentrations of ﬁnes. This broad distribution of ﬁnes ﬁt into the interstices
of the powder ﬁeld, leading to a higher density powder layer, but negatively impact
the spreadability of the powder [15].

The shapes of the keyhole pores is indicative of the mechanics of their formation.
While spherical voids will tend to form in an unperturbed, single phase liquid, the
elongated shapes of the pores suggest a mechanism that leads to ellipsoidal geome-
tries. Additionally, the porosity is concentrated approximately 100–200µm from the
surface. This is consistent with keyhole porosity during the ﬁnal advanced contour
step, which traces the outline of the part after the interior of each layer is formed.
This presents two interesting observations: (1) the laser settings for the advanced
contour are the same as those used for the skin (these samples use no core build
strategy), so it is expected that this porosity forms throughout the build process and
is healed either as subsequent layers are deposited or as the laser rasters in an area-
ﬁlling operation, and (2) the elongation of the pore is consistent with a pinning event.
A mechanism for keyhole void formation is proposed based on these observations:
A pinning event begins to elongate the keyhole near its base. This leads to an
instability as the laser continues along its path. Models from [ 6]s h o wﬂ o wi n
the direction of the laser travel around the keyhole only at its leading and trailing
surfaces, but elsewhere, including ﬂow at the bottom of the keyhole, is receding.
This leads to the principal elongation observed from Fig. 8 from a pinning event
that may occur at an inclusion or by a brief modulation in the ﬂuid ﬂow that
pinches oﬀ the keyhole to form the pore. The pore then elongates by the continued
pinning at the inclusion and/or the combined subductive ﬂow at the bottom of the
keyhole and obductive ﬂow above the pore.

## Page 600

Machine Learning to Optimize Additive Manufacturing Parameters . . . 607
Pore buoyancy drives the pore upward, but slowly relative to the solidiﬁcation
rate of the melt. The ascending pore impinges on the solidiﬁed surface and ﬂattens
laterally, elongating the pore in all directions perpendicular to the surface normal
until solidiﬁcation locks in the shape of the pore. Alternatively, the pore, still
pinned by an inclusion, elongates toward the surface normal. Further investigation
into the pore eccentricity relative to the build direction is required to clarify the
pore formation mechanism.
Remelting occurs as the laser completes an adjacent track, the next layer, or both.
The newly remolten metal allows the pore to escape at the surface, or the keyhole
present in the second pass simply subsumes the pore. Because the same laser
speed, power, and size is used for the advanced contour and for the skin regions,
the absence of keyhole porosity in the skin and presence in the advanced contour
suggests that the remelting is critical to the annihilation of pores. It is predomi-
nantly this ﬁnal, advanced contour pass, which is never remelted, that results in
the greatest pore concentration. The few pores in the center of the compression
pillars suggest that most pores are eliminated by subsequent laser passes.
RFN Models of Porosity Reveal a Weak Correlation to Part
Position and Orientation
From the morphology of the pore distribution, an RFN is used to predict fraction
porosity, median pore diameter and median pore spacing from sample position and
orientation. The predicted versus actual plots, Fig. 9a, c, e are a concise method to
present the predictive capability of a model; with perfect performance, all predicted
values would lie on the green, 1:1 regression line. Each model is trained using a 3-
fold cross validation scheme. In this approach, the data is randomly shuﬄed, the ﬁrst
one-third reserved for testing and error prediction, and the model is trained on the
remaining two-thirds. This process is repeated with the second third as the test set
and the ﬁrst and last thirds as the training set; and again with the ﬁnal third as the test
data. Each training set creates a domain across the multidimensional input feature
space. If a test point lies inside the shell formed by the training domain on this high
dimensional manifold, then the predicted value for that test point is interpolated.
If, however, the test datum falls outside this shell along any axis, the model must
extrapolate for that test point.
Split locations in the decision tree are deterministic, so each tree must be trained
on a diﬀerent, random subset of the data in a process known as bootstrap aggregat-
ing, or bagging. To reduce overﬁtting, each split in each tree is made on a random
subset of the available features. Because the prediction from the RFN is aggregated
from the results of all decision trees, agreement between trees, which reﬂect logi-
cal connections between features and response, occur more regularly than random
correlations that occur in single trees due to bagging, random feature selection, and
most importantly, noise in the original data.

The predicted versus actual plot of fraction porosity, Fig.9a, shows that this prop-

around the ideal regression line and the low Pearson Correlation Coeﬃcients (PCC)
suggest that, while the transverse direction, blade direction and azimuth angle bias
pore formation, the process is fundamentally stochastic and cannot be eliminated
by part position and orientation. This is consistent with the observation of keyhole
defects and the eﬀect of laser parameter settings, which were not varied in these
experiments, on keyhole pore formation [1, 14, 15, 20].
Conclusions
Investigation into the eﬀects of part position, orientation and fraction recycled pow-
der on part porosity revealed several trends:
∙ Standard practice among users of L-PBF is to sieve powder to a maximum par-
ticle diameter before reuse; however, failure to use a minimum particle diameter
introduces a signiﬁcant contribution of ﬁnes into the particle size distribution.
∙ Although SEM reveals platelet-shaped particles in the recycled powder, particle
sphericity reveals that recycled powders retain a consistent shape proﬁle. There-

## Page 602

Machine Learning to Optimize Additive Manufacturing Parameters . . . 609
fore the presence of ﬁnes, which tend to negatively impact the rheological charac-
teristics of powder, is largely responsible for the change in powder ﬂow dynamics.
∙ Keyhole pore shape suggests a formation mechanism that both elongates and ﬂat-
tens these pores. A pinning mechanism is proposed, but several questions remain,
e.g. whether an inclusion or a keyhole instability is responsible for the initial for-
mation of the pore, and how the major and minor axes of the pore orient relative
to the laser and build directions.
∙ An RFN trained on part position, orientation, and fraction recycled powder reveals
a weak correlation between these input features and the fraction porosity, median
pore diameter and median pore spacing. The orientation of the part has the greatest
eﬀect on the pore population while the position on the plate, transverse to the blade
direction, has the greatest impact on the median pore size and distribution.

Mechanical Performance of Various
INCONEL® 740/740H Alloy
Compositions for Use in A-USC Castings
Kyle A. Rozman, Martin Detrois, Paul D. Jablonski
and Jeffrey A. Hawk
Abstract The use of Ni-based superalloys as structural components of advanced
ultra-supercritical steam and CO 2 turbines is becoming necessary due to the
increasing performance requirements of future power plant designs. Although
numerous Ni-based superalloys can respond to the demanding mechanical perfor-
mance, very few present a combination of high-strength and creep resistance while
maintaining good ductility and weldability. Furthermore, the improved performance
is often associated with wrought alloys while the fabrication of large castings is the
primary target for those applications. With the comparatively lower mechanical
properties of cast alloys, new designs based on compositional changes are neces-
sary to allow for the use of Ni-based superalloys in A-USC castings. This lack of
performance is primarily associated with the large and inhomogeneous grain size as
well as elemental segregation and other casting anomalies. This investigation
presents various alloys with compositions within the range of INCONEL
® 740/
740H designed to overcome the issues associated with the use of Ni-based super-
alloys in A-USC castings. Modi ﬁcations to the chemistry were based on thermo-
dynamic simulations and experimental results. Particular attention was given to
reactive element additions, element partitioning, γʹ precipitate phase promoting
elements and grain boundary carbides. The effects of the various compositional
changes on the tensile and creep properties of INCONEL
® 740/740H will be
discussed.

Introduction
Inconel 740H [UNS N07740] is a recently introduced and boiler certi ﬁed alloy. It is
a derivative of Nimonic 263 alloy, with increased chromium content. Inconel 740H
(IN740H) is γ′ strengthened and has been reported to precipitate η phase at elevated
temperatures at or above 750 °C after 1000 h [ 1–3]. The development of IN740H
was intended for use in boilers for advanced ultra-supercritical steam turbine plants
operating up to 760 °C at 35 MPa. With boiler certi ﬁcation IN740H is an attractive
alloy to transpose into structural parts of turbines. Minimum properties for cast
components in advanced ultra-supercritical steam turbines are, a yield strength of
350 MPa, 100,000 h creep rupture strength of 100 MPa, both at 760 °C and a
fracture toughness of 55 MPa √m at room temperature [ 4]. The National Energy
Technology Laboratory (NETL) is developing and optimizing a cast form of
IN740H for use in structural turbine components.
Cast forms of components are attractive from a manufacturing standpoint.
Casting may enable the use of Ni-based superalloys in complex geometries such as
valve chests where multiple welds in thick materials (>100 mm) would be required
to manufacture. While austenitic stainless steel alloys are currently used for
ultra-supercritical turbines (where temperatures do not exceed 700 °C), casting
Ni-based superalloys presents unique challenges as the microstructure tends to
segregate under casting. Segregation is a particular problem in superalloys where
alloys are composed of ﬁve or more elements [ 5–7]. Elemental segregation is
exacerbated with use of refractories, which are slow to diffuse.
In order to address elemental segregation in cast superalloys, NETL has
developed a computationally based homogenization heat treatment [ 8]. This com-
putationally based heat treatment has shown positive results in reducing refractory
element segregation, such as molybdenum [ 9]. When applied to cast superalloys
such as, Nimonic 105, Haynes 282 and Haynes 263 mechanical performance
approached that of the wrought version [ 10]. However IN740H has signi ﬁcantly
underperformed [11]. This manuscript will outline the alloy design changes made to
IN740H in attempt to increase its mechanical performance.
In brief, the rationale behind each rendition of IN740H casting is as follows. The
ﬁrst attempt to cast IN740H, IN740-A was kept near the nominal composition, see
Table 1. Detrimental carbosul ﬁdes and cellular carbides [ 7] were found in the
microstructure for this heat. It is thought the sulfur is originating from the industry
grade chrome. Vacuum distillation was attempted, however sulfur was unable to be
removed below 40 PPM [ 9]. With the failure of vacuum distillation, reactive

## Page 606

elements were explored to reduce sulfur content. Additions of group IIA and IIIA
elements were selected for computational simulation by Thermo-Calc software
using the TCNi8 database. It was found that lanthanum, yttrium and magnesium
offered the greatest potential for sulfur reduction [ 9, 12]. Experimental results with
a Ni-22Cr experimental alloy showed a reduction of sulfur to 4 PPM with La, 23
PPM with Y and 54 PPM with Mg. Therefore, to mitigate carbosul ﬁde formation,
treatment with lanthanum was used to strip the alloy of sulfur.
To address the cellular carbide formation, molybdenum was increased to the
maximum allowable within UNS N07740. As found by Thermo-Calc software
simulations, Fig. 1, molybdenum will increase the solubility of nickel in M 23C6
carbides, reducing the driving force of the cellular carbide formation in superalloys.
A new heat was poured, IN740-B with these modi ﬁcations. Large lanthanum
precipitates appeared in the matrix and ribboned among grain boundaries in
IN740-B heat.
To remove the lanthanum precipitates, a new heat was poured, IN740-C. Nickel
oxide was mixed to react with the lanthanum and remove it to the slag. Further,
boron was incorporated into IN740-C heat as it is well known boron can increase
the coherency of grain boundary carbides [ 13].
For the ﬁnal heat reported on in this manuscript, the effect of carbon content on
the alloy was investigated. Previous heats showed thick continuous carbides. It was
thought reducing the carbon content would change the grain boundary carbide
morphology from thick and continues to ﬁne and discrete. Research from Li et al.
[14] supports this hypothesis, as their research found carbide morphology changed
from dendritic morphology at high concentrations (320 PPM) to discrete tetrahedral
morphology at low concentrations (40 PPM). Carbon content was reduced by
approximately half, resulting in IN740-CLC heat.

Experimental Methods
Alloy Preparation
The alloys were prepared from high-purity industry-grade melt stock consisting of
Ti, Nb, Al, Mn, C, Mo, Co, B, Si, and Ni, as one of NETL ’s goals is to develop a
technique which is upscaleable to industry use. Only Cr was not added loosely to
the mix due to its high oxygen content. Master alloys consisting of NiCrLa,
Ni-50Cr, Ni-25Cr, and Ni-30Co-30Cr were used instead. Those were products of
vacuum induction melting (VIM) and electroslag remelting (ESR) to control the
amount of impurities [ 15, 16]. All melt materials were measured to reach a ∼7000 g
target weight and melted using VIM under 200 Torr Ar partial pressure to a
superheat temperature of T
L + 50 °C, where T L is the liquidus temperature from
Thermo-Calc (TCNi8). The melts were poured into 100 mm diameter graphite
molds coated with zirconia wash to prevent carbon pickup. The molds were sub-
merged in loose sand to simulate cooling conditions similar to those found in
full-size castings.
To verify the casting meet the IN740H speci ﬁcations, X-ray ﬂorescence
(XRF) was performed in house on samples cut from sections of each heat with a
Rigaku ZSX Primus II utilizing NIST traceable standards (reported values are
accurate to 0.01 wt%). Additionally, impurities were measured by gas analysis
techniques. Oxygen and nitrogen contents were measured by inert gas fusion with a
LECO TC436AR using NIST certi ﬁed standards (reported values are accurate to 1
PPM) while sulfur and carbon were measured by combustion analysis with a LECO
CS4444LS using NIST certi ﬁed standards (reported values are accurate to 2 PPM).
Mechanical Testing and Sample Post Processing
Mechanical testing samples were cut from the columnar zone to avoid mold
shrinkage and porosity. Mechanical testing samples had a cylindrical pro ﬁle with
gauge section 32 mm in height and 6.3 mm in diameter. Tensile testing was done
in accordance to ASTM E8 [ 17] at 20 and 800 °C to screen each heat for perfor-
mance. Strain rates were kept to 0.005%/min until yield were after it increased to
0.50%/min. Creep testing was also performed in accordance to ASTM E139 [ 18]
primarily at 760 °C with 260 MPa applied stress using a dead weight creep frame.
Fractured mechanical testing samples were investigated on a FEI Inspect F ﬁeld
emission scanning electron microscope (SEM) using standard examination tech-
niques. After acquiring images of the fracture plane and pro ﬁles, one of the frac-
tured halves were sectioned for metallographic analysis. Samples were polished and
etched with ASTM etchant #88 [ 19] for 15 s. This provided adequate contrast
between γ′, carbides and other phases present in the microstructure.

Results
Casting Analysis
The 4 in. diameter ingot was subsequently bisected and etched. The macroscopic
grains structure is shown in Fig. 2, showing the columnar grains near the mold wall
and central equiaxed grain structure.
The UNS07740 compositional limits are shown in Table 1. While speci ﬁc
chemistry cannot be disclosed each alloy is within the compositional limits of
UNS07740. The minor chemistry alterations are tabulated in Table 2.
The ﬁrst casting, IN740-A had a composition near the nominal composition. Iron
was picked up as a contaminant from the skull left in the crucible from the prior
melt. For the second heat, IN740-B, Mo and La were increased relative to IN740-A.
A slight reduction in Al was noted, yielding an overall strengthening content of
3.8% rather than 4.0% wt%. As a consequence the Ti:Al ratio was increased to
1.5–1.
For the third heat, IN740-C, a high purity Ni-30Co-30Cr source was utilized
eliminating both S and La. Some Fe was picked up from remelt contamination.
Boron was intentionally added just below the maximum for the case code (60 ppm)
with a boron content in IN740-C heat weighed at approximately 50 PPM. Boron
content was not veri ﬁed, with no in house measurement technique for boron.

The last heat was poured with intention of reducing carbide thickness. Chemistry
of IN740-CLC heat was kept nearly the same at IN740-C heat except with a
reduction of carbon from 325 PPM in IN740-C heat to 176 PPM in the IN740-CLC
heat.
Mechanical Properties
Tensile and creep tests were performed to screen the alloy for its performance,
which is reported in Table 3. At room temperature, compared to the wrought alloy,
yielding occurred at roughly 24% less stress, for all heats. Fracture ductility for
IN740-B, IN740-C and IN740-CLC heats dropped 71%, 86%, and 24%
respectively. Alloy IN740-A is not presented in this manuscript as detrimental
sulfocarbides and cellular carbide formations were present, which can be found in
reference [ 11].
At elevated temperatures yielding occurred at 40% less stress than the wrought
alloy for all heats. Regarding the fracture ductility, IN740-B, IN740-C and
IN740-CLC dropped 45%, 53%, and 93% respectively. While the cast alloy
underperforms the wrought alloy, it is important to note the yield strength still
meets the 350 MPa yield requirement at 760 °C for cast advanced ultra-supercritical
structural components.
The creep results are shown in Fig. 3. For heat IN740-B, which was the only
heat tested above 760 °C (760 –800 °C, denoted on Fig. 3), time to ruptures were
∼23x faster, (94 h at 260 MPa at 760 °C) than the wrought version (2185 h at

## Page 610

265 MPa at 750 °C) [ 20], and ductility at rupture fell nearly 75%, from 11% in the
wrought condition to 2.7% cast. For IN740-C heat, time to ruptures occurred at a
maximum of ∼9x (250 h) and a minimum of ∼2x faster (1070 h). Ductility for
IN740-C heat similarly was reduced by approximately 81% (11% for wrought,
average of 2% for cast). For IN740-CLC heat, the stress rupture time was accel-
erated by 150x, lasting only 15 h and rupture ductility was reduced by approxi-
mately 99% (11% for wrought, 0.04% for cast).
Overall, while the tensile performance exceeded the advanced ultra-supercritical
steam turbine requirement of 350 MPa yield stress at 760 °C, the creep perfor-
mance was not meet. The minimum creep requirement is 100,000 h creep rupture
stress at 100 MPa at 760 °C, this corresponds to a Larson-Miller parameter of 25.8.
Wrought IN740H has been shown to meet, but not exceed a LMP of 25.8 at
100 MPa [ 4]. With all castings falling short of the wrought LMP curve, it is
projected the cast alloy will not meet a LMP of 25.8 at 100 MPa. The large scatter
of stress rupture times, and persistent low ductility in all heats is concerning. Low
ductility may lead to brittle fracture, which would be unacceptable for a structural
component where parts are required to yield before failure.

completely intergranular manor. At higher magni ﬁcations (Fig. 4c) intergranular
secondary cracking is observed. Bright lanthanum precipitates (bright contrast on
backscatter image) are observed on some grain boundaries, typically associated

Discussion
IN740-B Re ﬂections
To review, the ﬁrst heat, IN740-A was cast near nominal composition. Detrimental
features such as cellular carbides and sulfocarbides were detected (not included, see
Reference [ 7, 21]). To mitigate these detrimental microstructural features molyb-
denum was increased to increase the solubility of nickel in the carbides, which
theoretically lowers the driving force for cellular carbide formation. To mitigate the
sulfocarbides, lanthanum was added to chemically bind the sulfur.
The result was a microstructure free of sulfocarbides Fig. 7a. Grain boundary
carbides were continuous in morphology, with backscatter contrast showing mul-
tiple phases, see Fig. 7a. At slightly lower magni ﬁcations than Fig. 7, grain
boundaries appeared to be regularly offset from the primary plane, which suggests
the carbides alternated coherency with the grain above and below the carbide
Fig. 6 Facture surface for IN740-CLC heat pulled in tension at 800 °C. a Low magni ﬁcation
overview, b proﬁle view, c high magniﬁcation of fracture surface, d high magni ﬁcation of pro ﬁle
view
620 K. A. Rozman et al.

## Page 614

boundary. Carbide thickness was measured in ImageJ ( https://imagej.net/), at an
average of 260 nm with a standard deviation of 170 nm, over 45 measured car-
bides. Some local areas of the grain boundary carbides also show γ′ free zones
which may lead to localized enhanced plasticity. These denuded regions are
associated with a blocky like carbide between the grains (See Fig. 7a). While
unknown at the time of writing, it is speculated this feature may be MC type
carbides. Further TEM work may help identify carbides phases.
Some TiN precipitates were detected, primarily in the matrix. The TiN precip-
itates were globular, about 5 × 20 μm in major dimensions. These precipitates
readily oxidized in creep, but were not found to in ﬂuence mechanical properties as
no denuding or corrosion of the matrix was found near TiN precipitates, nor was
there any associated deformation detected near them both on fracture surfaces and
in cross sections.
While there are a lanthanum deposits both on grain boundary triple points and on
the grain facets (Fig. 4c), the lanthanum deposits do not appear to have a primary
inﬂuence on fracture mode. Minimal plastic deformation is detected on the grain
facets. The lanthanum deposit between the grains appears symmetrically cracked
(Fig. 4c), suggesting it was coherent with both grains. Without signs of plastic
deformation associated with the deposits one may conclude they do not play a
primary role in the fracture of the alloy.
From the fractography the pro ﬁle view (Fig. 4d) revealed areas of the ductile
shear deformation, which appeared inclined at an approximate 45° angle from the
loading direction. Further evidence of this is shown in Fig. 8, where ductile cup and
cone fracture occurred. Together, Figs. 4d and 8 show that the grain boundary
carbides are sensitive to local geometry. When grain facets are oriented normal to
the loading direction, grain boundaries appear to rupture, while when grain facets
are inclined, the grain boundaries tend to support ductile plastic ﬂow.
Fig. 7 Microstructure of IN740-B. a High magni ﬁcation showing carbide structure, b high
magniﬁcation, near fracture plane showing cavitation failures leading to secondary cracking

## Page 615

To explain the intergranular failure observed in the alloy, it is apparent that
grains with facets oriented normal to the loading direction are the weakest (Fig. 4d).
Grain boundary failure by rupture is supported by Fig. 7b where a signi ﬁcant
amount of cavities are found near the fracture plane for a boundary normal to the
loading direction. These cavities appear to form on the interface between the grain
and carbide randomly. Cavities were not detected in association with γ′ free zones.
With such dense network of microcavities, one can easily explain the observed
intergranular failure [ 22, 23]. Hence it can be concluded, when grain facets expe-
rience pure tensile forces the response is formation of microcavities which link
together and cause grain facet rupture leading to intergranular failure (Fig. 7b).
IN740-C Re ﬂections
For the IN740-C heat, chemistry was largely the same to the IN740-B heat, with a
few exceptions. A low sulfur base was used, eliminating the need for lanthanum
additions, and the maximum allowable boron was added, calculated at 50 PPM.
Minor changes include the following: cobalt was increased relative to the IN740-B
heat, iron was picked up from the master alloy (0.6 wt%), nitrogen was reduced to
49 PPM and oxygen content increased to 83 PPM.
The microstructure of IN740-C heat is shown in Fig. 9a, b. With the lanthanum
free source all lanthanum deposits were eliminated from the microstructure. Some
TiN precipitates were detected, with similar inert response of the precipitates to that
of IN740-B heat.

Boron was added at 50 PPM to stay within the bounds of Inconel 740 desig-
nation. Kontis et al. [ 13] found for a directionally solidi ﬁed alloy boron suppressed
M23C6 formation in favor of M 5B3 borides with associated growth of γ′ at grain
boundaries. Kontis et al., added boron from 55 to 147 PPM, while this research
only added boron to 50 PPM. No borides or associated γ′ growth was detected in
IN740-C heat, with borides expected to show dark backscatter contrast.
While signi ﬁcant secondary cracking was detected in the pro ﬁle, grain bound-
aries supported less shear than that of IN740-B heat, as shown by the lack of shear
deformation in Fig. 5d. This suggest the grain boundaries were marginally weaker,
however, still capable of transmitting enough stress for secondary cracking. Unlike
IN740-B heat, no ductility was observed on grain facets inclined to the loading axis,
see Fig. 5d.
Grain boundary carbides in IN740-C heat have similar thickness to that of
IN740-B heat, averaging 290 nm in thickness with a standard deviation of 150 nm
over 57 measured carbides. The R value for these populations is 0.34, hence carbide
size is quantitatively the same between IN740-B and C.
While the thickness of the carbides is the same as IN740-B heat, the morphology
of the carbides is different. IN740-C heat shows three distinct grain boundary car-
bides. The ﬁrst districting grain boundary carbide is featured in the lower portion of
Fig. 9a, showing thick carbides with a zig zag geometry between each grain. The zig
zag morphology suggests alternating coherency with the grain above and below the
carbide grain boundary. This carbide morphology is expected to be strong, which is
conﬁrmed in Fig. 9b, showing a large void originating from multiple acicular phases
where the zig zag grain boundary carbide is adhered to both grains above the noted
fracture. The second typical grain boundary appears to multiphase with alternating
backscatter contrast. Energy dispersive spectroscopy suggests this type is composed
of alternating layers of M 23C6 carbide, γ′ phase and γ matrix. This morphology is
expected to be weaker with a γ′ free zone around the boundary which may allow
localized plasticity. The third type of grain boundary consists of an acicular phase,

which energy dispersive spectroscopy suggests are rich in Ti and S. Transmission
electron microscopy would help clarify this phase. If they are sul ﬁde phases it is well
known they act as weak points in superalloys [ 7]. The acicular phases appear par-
ticularly detrimental, as shown in Fig. 9b, where a large cavity was formed by
debonding of acicular phase.
To explain the intergranular failure experience in IN740-C heat, very large
cavities ( ∼10 µm in IN740-C vs. 0.25 µm in IN740-B) initiated at acicular phases.
These large cavities likely caused stress concentrations leading to rupture between
the grain facets.
IN740 CLC Re ﬂections
The chemistry of IN740-CLC and C heats are largely the same, except for inten-
tionally reducing carbon in the CLC heat. Some minor additions of nitrogen and
oxygen were picked up in the melt. Inert round TiN precipitates were detected in
IN740-CLC alloy, about 20 μm in diameter.
The microstructure of IN740-CLC heat is show in Fig. 10. Grain boundary
carbides appeared distinct and unconnected unlike that of previous heats. Average
thickness of the carbides was reduced to 175 nm with a standard deviation of
140 nm over 59 measured carbides. The P value against the IN740-C heat is
0.00003 which is statistically signi ﬁcant. Multiple boundaries were devoid of any
carbide structure whatsoever (Fig. 10a). No γ′ free zones were detected near
boundaries. Acicular type particles were detected in IN740-CLC heat similar in
morphology and size as the IN740-C heat, however, these acicular type particles
were in tack and not the apparent cause of intergranular failure.
