## Page 618

Comparing the fracture surfaces (Fig. 6) to the microstructure (Fig. 10)o f
IN740-CLC heat, again intergranular failure by cavitation along grain boundaries is
observed. Cavitation seems to be initiated at carbides (Fig. 10b) in a similar manor
to that of IN740-B heat where the interface between the matrix and carbides ini-
tiated the cavity. While acicular particles were detected in the grain boundaries,
they appear intact below the primary fracture plane. Very little secondary cracking
was observed in the IN740-CLC heat suggesting the grain boundaries are very
weak with fracture isolated to the primary fracture plane. Hence it can be concluded
for the IN740-CLC heat, intergranular failure is caused by linking of microcavities
caused by debonding of carbides with the matrix. The naked boundaries exacerbate
failure by providing no resistance.
Conclusions
While yield strength for all attempted cast heats of Inconel 740H meet or exceeded
the minimum yielding requirement for cast advanced ultra-supercritical turbines of
350 MPa at 760 °C, the creep requirements of 100,000 h rupture strength at
100 MPa, at 760 °C was not meet or approached. All heats showed intergranular
brittle failure at elevated temperatures, causing concern for yield before failure of
cast turbine parts.
Attempted improvements to the alloy include: lanthanum additions to react with
sulfur, increased molybdenum to mitigate cellular carbide formation, re ﬁned melt
stock free of sulfur, boron additions in attempt to increase carbide coherency and
reduced carbon content to alter the grain boundary carbide morphology. While
mechanical performance increased relative to the original casting, all attempts failed
to achieve adequate mechanical performance. Boron additions were ineffective.
Lowering the carbon content signi ﬁcantly reduced tensile ductility, and creep life
time was reduced to just 15 h.
All heats were observed to show intergranular fracture caused by micro-cavities
forming on grain boundary carbides where signi ﬁcant portions of the facet oriented
normal to the loading direction. Thus, the dense repartition of relatively thick grain
boundary carbides was detrimental to the ductility of the cast alloys. Two of the
heats showed acicular phases which were very weak and formed large
micro-cavities contributing to intergranular failure. Further efforts should be
focused on removing these acicular phases from the microstructure.
The most promising result was found in the Inconel 740-C heat where zig-zag
like carbide morphology was shown to retain coherency with the grains, above a
large micro-void caused by multiple acicular phases. If one could better control the
precipitation of the grain boundary carbides, the authors predict the performance of
cast Inconel 740H may approach that of the wrought form. Further investigation on
the heat treatment of the alloy are planned as well as on the identi ﬁcation and
removal of the acicular phases.

## Page 621

Microstructural Characterization
and Mechanical Properties of Rene 65
Precipitates
C. M. Katsari, H. Che, D. Guye, A. Wessman and S. Yue
Abstract Nickel based superalloys are used in the aerospace industry as turbine
rotor material due to their high strength and excellent fatigue resistance at high
temperature. High strength is required for the high stress and high temperature
environments in which these alloys operate. This is achieved by their microstructure
of gamma matrix/gamma prime precipitates. The latter can cause thermomechanical
processing issues since they can make the material extremely hard. The purpose of
this work is to characterize the gamma prime precipitates which are present in Rene
65, a newly developed cast and wrought nickel-based superalloy by General
Electric and ATI. The main precipitate that was examined was the gamma prime
phase [Ni3 (Al, Ti)], which largely determines the mechanical properties of the
alloy. The gamma prime in this particular alloy was found to form in three different
sizes; primary, secondary and tertiary. After various heat treatments, the differences
in the volume fraction and morphology of each precipitate type is described and the
effect of the precipitates on hardness is determined.

## Page 622

Introduction
The manufacture of single crystal and directional solidi ﬁcation turbine blades
requires a high precision casting technique. For cast and wrought superalloys, a
thermomechanical processing route is required for compressor blades. Nickel based
superalloys consist of a gamma matrix ( γ) and usually gamma prime ( γ′) or gamma
double prime ( γ″) precipitates as strengthening phases. Their mechanical properties
depend mainly on the characteristics of those precipitates (e.g. size, volume frac-
tion, morphology).
Rene 65 (R65) is a newly developed nickel-based superalloy by General Electric
and ATI Allvac. Its microstructure consists of γ matrix and three sizes of γ′ Ni
3(Al,
Ti) precipitates. It can perform at higher temperatures than the commonly used
Inconel 718 and it has lower production cost than the similar chemistry alloy Rene
88DT. More speci ﬁcally, R65 is designed to operate at temperatures up to 700 °C,
whereas IN718 operates at 650 °C. Moreover, R65 is a cast and wrought alloy, so it
is less costly than the powder metallurgy route of R88DT [ 1].
The microstructure of Rene 65 consists of the Ni gamma matrix (FCC) and three
different sizes of gamma prime precipitates: primary, secondary and tertiary. The
primary γ′ serves the purpose of pinning the grain boundaries, which prevents grain
coarsening and thereby increases fatigue resistance, whereas secondary and tertiary
contribute to the strength and creep resistance of the alloy [ 2–4].
In this report, the effect of various heat treatments on the morphology and the
volume fraction of each precipitate as well as the hardness will be presented.
Experimental Procedure
As-extruded cylindrical compression samples (9 mm height and 6 mm diameter) of
Rene 65 were provided by GE Aviation Canada (9 mm height and 6 mm diameter).
The nominal composition can be found in Table 1.
As mentioned before, the objective of this work was to improve the formability
of Rene 65. Therefore, a heat treatment of the superalloy samples was introduced in
order to produce a microstructure that could be easily thermomechanically pro-
cessed to produce blades. The approach for the design of the heat treatment was to
dissolve the majority of precipitates that exist in as-extruded condition. The com-
plete absence of precipitates would lead to grain coarsening, which is not desirable
for fatigue resistance. Therefore, the microstructure should consist of coarse pre-
cipitates that would inhibit grain coarsening, while minimizing the impact on
strength.

## Page 623

The heat treatment design was based on the precipitation data of Ref. [ 5]. It
consisted of ﬁrstly an anneal at 1095 °C which is close to, but below, the solu-
tionizing temperature (1116 °C) for 30 min to ensure homogeneous annealing in an
industrial environment; for the size of the samples given, 10 min should be suf ﬁ-
cient. Following the annealing step, samples were cooled to 954 °C, held for
various times from 0 to 2 h, and either air cooled (AC) or water quenched (WQ) to
room temperature. The temperature of 954 °C was selected because the equilibrium
precipitation quantity at that temperature as predicted by Ref. [ 5] is almost 75% of
the total precipitation available. Since only 25% of precipitates would be available
at that point, the concept was to minimise any further precipitation during air
cooling and coarsen the existing 75%.
For the heat treatments, an infra-red furnace was used in order to achieve the best
temperature control. When compared to the box furnace there is less ﬂuctuation in
the temperature, which is particularly important for the annealing stage, as well as
being able to better specify the cooling rate from annealing to the hold temperature,
as well as the cooling rate to room temperature.
Characterisation by light optical microscopy (LOM) was achieved using a
Nikon EPIPHOT 200 optical microscope coupled with CLEMEX image analysis
software in order to measure the grain size. To etch the grain boundaries and
primary γ′ precipitates, an etchant based on Kalling ’s Reagent was used [ 6].
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was carried out using a Hitachi SU3500
Variable-Pressure microscope at accelerating voltages of 30 and 5 kV. To reveal
the γ′ under SEM conditions electropolishing and electroetching at 20 V and 5 V
were carried out respectively. Image analysis for quantifying microstructural fea-
tures was achieved using ImageJ software. The secondary γ′ precipitates, were
measured manually by Image J software, with a range of 48 –75 representative
precipitate measurements for each mean value.
The effect of heat treatment on Vickers micro-hardness was measured using a
Clark CM-100AT micro-hardness testing machine in conjunction with
CLEMEX CMT indent measurement software. This was done as it is a quick way
to initially evaluate the mechanical properties of the material, as there is a rela-
tionship between hardness and ultimate tensile stress and a rough correlation
between hardness and yield stress. Indents were created with a force of 200 g and
measured at a magni ﬁcation of 500X.
Results and Discussion
Initially, the as received samples from GE Aviation were microstructurally char-
acterized and all hardness results after heat treatment are compared with as received
(extruded) sample hardness, 445HV. In Fig. 1 the equiaxed grain structure of the
superalloy can be observed, with ASTM grain size of 9.5 (11.9 µm). The grain
boundaries are pinned by the primary γ′ precipitates which were 12% of the volume

From the aforementioned observations, there is a notable relationship between
the hardness and the mean secondary precipitate size as can be seen in Fig. 12.
When there is a decrease in the mean secondary precipitate size hardness increases
and when mean secondary precipitate size increases hardness decreases.
The distribution of measured secondary precipitates for the air cooled series
gives an indication of why the mean precipitate size behaves this way. Based on the
literature [7], the length of delay before the cooling and reduced severity of cooling
always increases the size of the secondary γ′ precipitates. Therefore the expectation
is that the mean size of the secondary γ′ precipitates from hold times 0 –120 min
will be increasing. This is not the case, due to what appears to be an increasing
number of ﬁne secondary γ′ precipitates being present in the structure. The sec-
ondary γ′ precipitates, which are measured by Image J software, are considered to

be representative of those which exist throughout the structure. It is clear that large

an increased frequency of small precipitates in the structure for all periods less than

can be made for the water quenched samples.
As secondary precipitates, experience growth beyond 50 nm there is a decrease
in strength of the material with increasing secondary precipitate size. If the mean
secondary γ′ precipitate sizes for hold times from 30 to 120 min are used, due to the
reduction in the evolution of new ﬁne secondary γ′ precipitate, there is a strong
negative linear relationship between the secondary γ′ precipitate size and hardness
of Rene 65, highlighting the difference between air cooled and water quenched
samples, as can be seen in Fig. 11.
Conclusions and Future Work
Microstructural characteristics and their effect of hardness of Rene 65 has been
investigated. As conclusions from the current work, we can observe that the
strength of that Rene 65 is dependent on the size and distribution of secondary γ′
precipitates. Microstructural γ′ precipitate evolution was shown to be in ﬂuenced by
holding at a temperature below the annealing temperature. The mean secondary

precipitate size decreases for short times because of the effect of nucleation new
secondary precipitates being greater than the effect of the growth caused by delayed
cooling of existing precipitates. For longer hold times at 954 °C, the growth
expected is seen because the effect of growth of secondary γ′ precipitates is greater
than the effect of nucleation of new precipitates.
There is a need to quantify the effect of heat treatment on the fraction of sec-
ondary γ′ precipitates. Image analysis of SEM images appears to be a good method
for the quanti ﬁcation of the primary γ′ precipitates, it cannot be employed for
accurate quantiﬁcation of the secondary γ′ precipitates. Although, after etching, the
morphology of the secondary precipitates are revealed well, because of the volume
of precipitates and the interaction of the electron beam with the sample, the area of
the surface covered by secondary γ′ precipitates cannot be determined.
For future work, further investigation of precipitate characterization with EBSD
and STEM will be conducted as well as compression testing to reinforce the
hardness results of the current work.

## Page 634

Microstructure Development
in Track-by-Track Melting
of EBM-Manufactured Alloy 718
Paria Karimi, Dunyong Deng, Esmaeil Sadeghimeresht, Jonas Olsson,
Joakim Ålgårdh and Joel Andersson
Abstract Electron beam melting (EBM) is a powder-bed fusion process within the
group of additive manufacturing (AM) technology that is used to fabricate high
performance metallic parts. Nickel-Iron base superalloys, such as Alloy 718, are
subjected to successive heating and cooling at temperatures in excess of 800 °C
during the EBM process. Characterization of the dendritic structure, carbides, Laves
and δ-phase were of particular interest in this study. These successive thermal
cycles in ﬂuence the microstructure of the material resulting in a heterogeneous
structure, especially in the building direction. Hence, the aim of this study was to
gain increased fundamental understanding of the relationship between the pro-
cessing history and the microstructure formed within a single layer. Different
numbers of tracks with equal heights were for this purpose produced, varying from
one to ten tracks. All tracks used the same process parameters regardless of number
and/or position. Microstructure characteristics (sub-grain structure, grain structure
and phases) were analyzed by optical microscopy, scanning electron microscopy
equipped with energy disperse spectroscopy and electron backscatter diffraction.
The direction of dendrites changed in the overlap zones within the tracks due to
re-melting of material in the overlap zone. The primary dendrite arm spacings
slightly increased along multi-tracks owing to a slight decrease in cooling rate by
addition of the next tracks. Epitaxial growth of grains were observed in all samples
due to partial re-melting of grains in previous layers and surface nucleation was also
found to occur in all tracks.

## Page 635

Introduction
Additive manufacturing (AM) is categorized into a group of manufacturing tech-
nologies in which the parts are fabricated in a layer-by-layer-wise fashion, usually
from a CAD model [ 1]. With the capabilities of AM to produce complex designs,
its applications span into energy, medical, aerospace, automotive and defense
sectors [ 2, 3]. Advantages are the capabilities of AM processes to produce parts
with boundless geometric complexity in a near net shape manner, which is virtually
impossible to be produced by conventional processing [ 3]. Nonetheless, there exists
serious challenges for all AM processes in the form of phase transformations in the
liquid to solid (within molten pool in top layer), and solid to solid (bottom layers
that undergo repeated thermal cycles) due to the complex thermal history that the
material faces during the track-by-track and layer-by-layer manufacturing. The AM
process electron beam melting (EBM) comprises the following physical phenomena
during building of a part: heat transfer, phase transformation, ﬂuid ﬂow within the
melt pool, surface-tension caused by temperature/concentration gradients, evapo-
ration and emission of material, chemical reactions, absorption and scattering of
beam radiation, etc. [ 4]. Moreover, the EBM process involves melting and solidi-
ﬁcation of a small volume of material, initially in the form of track-by-track and
later layer-by-layer. Apparently, the electron beam is able to raster in a line or spot,
and it melts the powder which solidi ﬁes as a thin track or layer of material.
A typical single track deposit is repeated with a well-de ﬁned overlap to construct a
fully dense part. Figure 1 shows a simple schematic of the track-by-track deposition
that occurs during EBM process.
Generally, the fundamental physics of EBM is similar to multi-pass welding, in
which a heat source locally melts the material. As the energy source does multiple
passes, the solidi ﬁed material is partially remelted again by the next pass [ 5].
Hussein et al. carried out a three-dimensional heat transfer model for selective laser
melting (SLM) to understand the effect of scan tracks on the thermal distribution
within a single layer [ 6]. The overlap zones between the scan tracks are exposed in
repeated thermal cycling during melting of the next track [ 6]. Mostafa et al. found
different microstructure in the overlap zone compared to the rest of the track in
Single Track Track-by-Track
Fig. 1 Schematic illustrating of a single track and a track-by-track melting of material in EBM
644 P. Karimi et al.

## Page 636

SLM manufactured Alloy 718 due to different thermal history in those zones [ 7].
Generally, the properties of a part manufactured by EBM processing strongly
depend on the microstructure and the complex thermal history condition. In order to
understand the microstructure evolution in EBM process, an in-depth study of
microstructural feature formation in very ﬁne scale such as building tracks and
layers is highly demanding. The aim of this study is therefore to discuss the op-
portunities and challenges facing EBM from the perspective of solidi ﬁcation phe-
nomena and phase transformations encountered in Alloy 718.
Materials and Experimental Procedure
An Arcam A2X EBM machine (Arcam AB, Sweden) was used to build 10 samples
starting by 1 × 1 (track × layer) to 10 × 1 track-by-track with the track length of
20 mm. The feedstock material was plasma-atomized Alloy 718 powder with a size
distribution of 45 –105 µm and nominal chemical composition given in Table 1,
which was supplied by Arcam AB, Sweden. For the sample builds, the EBM
machine, with software version 4.2.201, used a standard linear melt theme with a
power calculation in off-mode and a unidirectional scan strategy. The build began
once the preheat temperature of 1023 °C was reached. A beam current of 7 mA and
scan speed of 1.25 m/s with a gun-accelerating voltage of 60 kV was used
throughout the tracks. The layer thickness and line offset were constantly held at 75
and 125 µm during whole process, respectively.
As shown in Fig. 2, an additional substrate called a stand, made of the same
material (Alloy 718), was used in this study. The stand was built using Arcam
standard theme before building the tracks on top of it. The main advantages of using
such a design are to avoid dilution effects which contribute to changes in melting
temperature of the powder, to provide a ﬂat surface with correct height for building
of tracks and to save samples during the grit blasting. Ten different numbers of
tracks were designed to be made on these stands. The distance between each stand
was 5 mm and the height of each stand was 8 mm from the build plate.
As shown in Fig. 3d, the samples were cut perpendicular to the scanning
direction and then polished down to a grit size of 1 μm. Finally, the polished
samples were electro-etched using oxalic acid at room temperature with a voltage of
6 V for 5 –10 s. The microstructures of all samples were analyzed by optical
microscope (OM), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy dispersive spec-
trometer (EDS) and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) system from Oxford
Instrument operating at 20 kV of accelerating voltage. Grain orientation mappings

Results and Discussion
Surface Morphology
As seen in Fig. 3, it is clear after three tracks next to each other, a stable, continuous
and uniform solid layer was formed. Figure 3a, b show some gaps in the 1 × 1 and
Fig. 2 Schematic of stand and CAD ﬁle of track-by-tack samples

2×1 , c sample 3 × 1, and d sample 5 × 1
646 P. Karimi et al.

## Page 638

2 × 1 samples which revealed the interior of the melting track onto the surface of
the stand. The absence of a stable melt track was evidence that the beam power used
in this study was insuf ﬁcient, most likely due to a too high of a scan speed which
resulted in a low energy input. Moreover, there were some irregularities, solidi ﬁed
melt pool distortion and ball-shaped drops for the 1 × 1 to 5 × 1 samples,
believed to be caused by ﬂuctuation of the beam movement during melting of
powder.
Microstructural Characterization
The optical micrographs of the etched cross-sections clearly showed morphology i.e.;
molten pool boundaries, melt pool width, penetration depth and microstructure within
the tracks and in the overlap zones, see Fig. 4. There were channel-like features after
etching of material which were tracing the solidi ﬁcation direction in the melt pool,
seen as darker areas in Fig. 4. To better visualize the melt pool boundaries after
etching, white/black dashed lines were drawn in Fig. 4a, b. Figure 4a, b presents the
cross-section of samples 3 × 1 and 5 × 1, respectively, and reveals columnar
cellular/dendritic structure perpendicular to the scan direction of the built samples.
The orientation of dendrites in the overlap zones was different from the orientation of
dendrites in the rest of the track due to the re-melting of the previous track. It was
either parallel to the scanning direction (zone II) or towards the next track (zone I), as
shown in Fig. 4b. It seemed the angle between the orientation of the dendrites in
overlap zone and the rest of the track were around 90°. The possible reason for this
could be explained as the solidi ﬁcation progressed, the temperature gradient and the
solidiﬁcation orientation turned from a direction parallel to the build direction into
scanning direction, mainly transverse (zone I and zone II).
As shown in Fig. 4a, one of the common defects observed in track-by-tracks
samples were clusters of pores located in the bottom of overlap zone due to
un-melted powder particles caused by less heat input or insuf ﬁcient overlap. The
pores could be eliminated by adding layers which leads to re-melting of the pre-
vious layers or increasing the overlap zone for tracks next to each other.
As shown in Fig. 5a, b, the solidi ﬁcation mode in the tracks was predominantly a
dendritic structure with ﬁne secondary arms, however the presence of cellular
structure was also evident due to unsteady state condition within the melt pool in
the EBM process. In general, during solidi ﬁcation within the melt pool, four dif-
ferent regimes of growth conditions such as; planar, cellular, coexistence of cellular
dendrites, columnar dendrites and equiaxed dendrites can be obtained (see Fig. 5c).
In a very high thermal gradient (G) and very low growth rate (R), planar solidi ﬁ-
cation mode can be achieved. By increasing growth rate and lowering thermal
gradient gradually, cells, latter columnar dendrite and eventually equiaxed dendrites
can be seen. Both cells and dendrites would coexist in the intermediate growth
velocity in the microstructure [ 8, 9].
Microstructure Development in Track-by-Track … 647

## Page 639

In the present microstructure, formation of the columnar dendritic structure with
very ﬁne secondary arms can be explained by a change in thermal gradient and
growth rate along the solidi ﬁcation direction [ 7]. The solidi ﬁcation condition is
changing during solidi ﬁcation of the melt pool. As solidi ﬁcation of the melt pool
starts, the growth rate is low and the temperature gradient is steepest along melt
pool boundary, as reported in the literature [ 8, 10]. With continuation of solidi ﬁ-
cation, the growth rate increases and thermal gradient decreases [ 10]. Thus, cellular

grain orientations. Overall, the microstructure exhibited a high degree of texture,
with the ˂001˃ crystallographic orientation parallel to the build direction. This is
typical within AM processed Alloy 718, where the red color corresponds to the

## Page 641

˂001˃ crystallographic grain orientation in the IPF colour legend, Fig. 6c[ 8, 9]. As
shown in Fig. 6a, b by the hatched squares, a part of the track in overlap zone is
partially re-melted, thus solidi ﬁed grains in the overlap zone were re-melted and the
direction of solidi ﬁed grains were changed towards the adjacent track. One possible
reason could be due to the re-melting of the previous layer, the grains grow epi-
taxially towards the centre of the new melt pool, where the thermal gradient is
parallel to the scanning direction, which is always in a same direction for adjacent
tracks. The ﬁnal outcome is that the grain direction rotates to the centre of adjacent
tracks as shown in the white hatched square [ 7]. Vrancken [ 11] reported similar
behaviour in grain orientations for material in the overlap zones for the SLM
process.
Figure 6a, b show some columnar grain growth, initiated from the grains in the
stand. Re-melting of the underlying layer and strong thermal gradients along the build
direction led to formation of the columnar structure. It can also be seen that new
grains nucleated at the surface which can be explained to occur as undercooled
thermal condition resulting from radiation of heat from the surface [8]. The size of the
grains at the surface of the tracks were smaller than the grains in the overlap zone,
(point 1: surface grains, points 2 and 3: overlap grains in Fig. 6). It can be explained
by referring to the cooling rate which was slightly slower in the overlap zone. As
expected, the heat input content in the overlapping zone was higher than that in the
remaining area of the track because overlap zone experienced double pass in the same
layer however the rest of the track only experienced one pass. Hence, the heat
dissipation was expected to be slower in the overlap zone. Consequently, the slower
cooling rate in the overlap zone was probably at the origin of the formation of rotated
columnar grains and a bit larger grains than surface grains [ 7].

Evaluation of Primary Dendrite Arm Spacing (PDAS)
Primary dendrite arm spacing (PDAS) can be used to estimate the cooling rate in
Alloy 718 [ 12, 13]. The average values for PDAS has been measured for each track
in all ten samples to understand the variation of cooling rate during a single layer
formation. Based on PDAS values (about 10 measurements) an average and stan-
dard deviation is calculated for each track shown in Fig. 7. Based on a previous
work [ 14], the cooling rate, Ṫ, during the solidi ﬁcation process of a dendritic
microstructure can be estimated using Eq. ( 1);
λ = A Ṫ
− n
ð1Þ
where λ is the primary dendrite arm spacing, A and n are proportionality coef ﬁ-
cients related to material which for Alloy 718 can be taken to be 122.6 μm and
0.342 (dimensionless), respectively [ 15].
Use of these values are valid for directionally solidi ﬁed (DS) material in high
cooling rate range of 3 × 10 4 to 3 × 10 6 K/s processing, due to the parallel
relationship between the direction of dendrite growth to the direction of the thermal
gradient. In the DS processes, these directions are essentially aligned so that the
dendrite growth rate is maximized [ 14, 16]. As shown in Fig. 7, the average values
of primary dendrite arm spacing was slightly increasing along tracks in the different
samples having 3, 5, 7 and 10 numbers of tracks. It is most likely owing to
decreasing the cooling rate within tracks from the ﬁrst deposited track to the last
deposited one in each sample. Based on the correlation between cooling rate and
PDAS, it can be estimated that the average cooling rate along a single layer was
approximately in the range of 6 × 10
4 to 3 × 10 5 K/s.
Conclusions
The structure, texture, phase evolution and primary dendrite arm spacing of EBM-
built Alloy 718 were investigated and discussed.
• Using the beam and scan parameters in this study, deposited tracks became
continuous solid material after adding three tracks next to each other by using
constant scan speed and current along the track.
• Dendrite direction in the overlap zone changed around 90° from the build
direction towards either the adjacent track or the scanning direction.
• The cross-section of the EBM-manufactured samples showed epitaxial growth
of columnar grains with strong ˂001˃ texture from previous layers and nucle-
ation of ﬁne new elongated grains in the overlap zones. Also, small size
equiaxed grains on the surface of the tracks were observed which are most likely
as result of heat radiation from the surface.

• Coarsened new grains in the overlap zone compared to the new grains on the
surface of the tracks was an indication of slightly slower cooling rate in overlap
zone than the rest of the track, due to double beam exposure and thus slower
heat dissipation.
• Characterization of primary dendritic arm spacing in different tracks for each
sample showed slightly increasing changes of PDAS along a single layer with
20 mm length and subsequently estimation of cooling rate in the range of
6×1 0

## Page 646

Modeling Tensile, Compressive,
and Cyclic Response of Inconel 718
Using a Crystal Plasticity Model
Incorporating the Effects of Precipitates
Marko Knezevic and Saeede Ghorbanpour
Abstract A comprehensive elasto-plastic polycrystal plasticity model is developed
for Ni-based superalloys. To demonstrate the microstructure sensitive predictive
characteristics, the model is applied to an Inconel 718 (IN718) superalloy that was
produced by additive manufacturing (AM). The model with the same set of material
and physical parameters is compared against a suite of compression, tension, and
large strain cyclic mechanical test data applied in different AM build directions. The
model embeds the contributions of solid solution, precipitates shearing, and grain
size and shape effects into the initial slip resistance. The hardening law is based on
the evolution of dislocation density. It is demonstrated that the model is capable of
predicting the particularities of both monotonic and cyclic deformation to large
strains of the alloy including decreasing hardening rate during monotonic loading,
the non-linear unloading upon the load reversal, the Bauschinger effect, the hard-
ening rate change during loading in the reverse direction as well as anisotropy and
concomitant microstructure evolution. The microstructure constituents and behavior
of IN718 under these conditions is similar to other Ni-based superalloys, and
therefore, it is anticipated that the general model developed here can be applied to
other superalloys fabricated using AM and other approaches. Additionally, the
material is tested in fatigue and results are presented and discussed.
Keywords Microstructures
⋅ Crystal plasticity ⋅ Inconel 718
Introduction
Ni-based superalloys are employed for components of jet engines and gas turbines
as well as various components in electric and nuclear power plants [ 1–3]. Most of
these parts are exposed to elevated temperature like 500 °C. The parts often have

## Page 647

complex shapes. Achieving the shapes requires machining. The cost involved in
machining of superalloys is high, since they are very hard materials. An alternative
technique to make the required shapes of superalloys is additive manufacturing
(AM). The advantage of producing end-use parts with complex features is advan-
tageous for many industries [ 4, 5]. Additionally, AM provides an effective way to
restore geometrical featured of damaged components. With the growth of AM as a
ﬁnal-product manufacturing process, the performance of these materials is being
increasingly studied. Inconel 718 (IN718) is a Ni-based superalloy showing a range
of outstanding mechanical properties including high yield strength, toughness, and
corrosion resistance enabling the components made of it to operate under extreme
thermal and mechanical conditions [ 6–8].
Modeling the deformation behavior of IN718, made by any manufacturing
process, is challenging due to its complex microstructure featuring γ′ and γ″ pre-
cipitates within a γ matrix [6, 9, 10]. The chemical composition of the γ′ precipitate
is Ni
3(Al,Ti). This γ′ precipitate is usually spherical in shape with a diameter of 20 –
30 nm when the material is heat treated according to AMS 5663, where the atoms
are arranged in a L1
2 structure [11, 12]. The lattice parameter a for the γ′ compound
face-centered cubic (FCC) crystal structure is 0.3605 nm [ 13]. The alloy retains its
strength at up to 650 °C primarily due to metastable γ″. The chemical composition
of the γ″ precipitate is Ni 3Nb. These precipitates are disk shaped, wherein the atoms
are arranged in a D0 22 structure [ 11, 12]. The diameter of the disks is 20 –30 nm,
while their thickness is 5 –6 nm, when the material is heat treated according to AMS
5663 [ 9, 11, 14, 15]. The values of lattice parameters a and c for the γ″
body-centered tetragonal (BCT) compound are 0.3624 nm and 0.7406 nm,
respectively [12, 16, 17]. Additionally, the alloy typically contains a small, less than
one weight percent, fraction of coherent δ precipitates [18]. The composition of the
δ phase is also Ni
3Nb but the structure is orthorhombic with the following lattice
constants a = 0.5114, b = 0.4244 nm, and c = 0.4538 nm [ 19, 20]. The meta-
stable γ″ decomposes into the stable Ni 3Nb δ phase at very long aging times, which
could be met in service.
The plastic deformation response, including ﬂow stress, hardening rate, tension-
compression asymmetry and temperature dependence of Ni-based superalloys
depends on the precipitate volume fraction and morphologies. Plasticity of the γ
matrix is primarily carried by twelve octahedral 111 fg ⟨1
10⟩ glide systems,
although activity of the six cubic 001fg ⟨110⟩ glide systems has also been reported
[21–23]. Generally, the γ′ and γ″ precipitates are the primary strengtheners. Dis-
locations gliding on octahedral planes shear the γ′ and γ″ precipitates, since they are
very small, nanoparticles, much smaller than the critical radius above which a
dislocation would instead loop around the particle. When a dislocation shears
through an ordered γ′ or γ″ precipitate, it leaves an anti-phase boundary
(APB) behind, which increases the energy of the crystal [ 24–26]. The APB values
can affect the slip system selection. The APB energy for the cubic planes tends to be
lower than that for the octahedral planes [ 27] and hence, screw dislocations would
tend to cross slip onto the 001fg planes. In contrast to γ′ or γ″ strengtheners, the δ
656 M. Knezevic and S. Ghorbanpour

## Page 648

precipitates are known to deteriorate mechanical properties, unless they appear as
spherical δ precipitates at grain boundaries, in which case they can prevent grain
boundary sliding and improve the material ’s creep behavior [ 1, 28].
Linking these mechanisms to mechanical behavior is possible with microstruc-
ture based constitutive laws. We have recently developed a version of the
elasto-plastic self-consistent (EPSC) model called P-EPSC to account for the effects
of precipitates, in particular the APB formation due to precipitate shearing [ 29]. The
model, called P-EPSC, is applied to an IN718 Ni-based superalloy that has been
fabricated using the direct metal laser sintering process (DMLS), which is an
additive manufacturing (AM) process. A summary of the model along with few
example case studies in tension, compression, and large strain tension-compression
are presented in this paper. Additionally, low cyclic fatigue and high cyclic fatigue
behavior of the same material is presented.
Material and Experiments
Figure 1 shows the initial crystallographic texture in the studied material measured
using electron-backscattered diffraction (EBSD). The measurement ﬁnds that the
samples possess a moderately intense <001> texture component along the AM
build direction (BD).

Figure 2 shows the measured compressive and tensile true stress –true strain
responses at room temperature of DMLS heat-treated material for the three loading
directions relative to the BD. The plot also includes the data for wrought material.
All specimens were heat treated (HT) per AMS 5663 after machining. Vacuum
furnace was used for heat treating of the samples. The solution HT was performed
at 954 °C for 1 h, followed by fan cooling in argon to below 120 °C. Then, the
double aging HT was performed, which consisted of holding at 718 °C for 8 h,
followed by furnace cooling at a rate of 50 °C/h to 621 °C and holding at 621 °C
for 8 h, and ﬁnally air cooled to room temperature. We observe that all curves
exhibit a classical decreasing hardening rate throughout, a signature of the
slip-dominated plastic deformation. Samples in all build directions exhibited ten-
sion-compression (T-C) asymmetry.
Next, the DMLS material was tested under large strain cyclic deformation at
room temperature. Figure 3 shows the true stress –true strain curves for the hori-
zontal sample. Upon unloading, the material exhibits an initial linear portion and a
subsequent non-linear portion. The extent of the macroscopically non-linear portion
increases with the level of plastic pre-strain. When the material becomes com-
pressed, it yields at a lower value than yield in the tensile pre-strain. After yielding,
the hardening rate rapidly increases. The lower yield in reverse loading followed by
a rapid hardening rate is characteristic of the Bauschinger effect for many materials [30].
Subsequently we tested strain based low cyclic fatigue behavior of the IN718
materials [ 31, 32]. These tests were performed at room temperature using the
University of New Hampshire MTS Landmark 270 servohydraulic testing system
with Flextest software and controller. The load was recorded using an MTS
661.22H-01 250kN load cell with a maximum error of 0.35%. Specimen elongation
was measured using a MTS 634.12E-24 0.5 ″ extensometer. Strain rates were
approximately 4 × 10
−3 s−1 and frequency approximately 0.15 Hz. The number of
cycles to failure for strain amplitudes ranging from 0.6 to 1.4% is shown in Fig. 4.
As expected, Nf decreases with increase of the strain amplitude for each material

have different initial microstructure [ 31]. The DMLS material contains some
porosity and has a ﬁner grain structure [ 32].

pertaining to the hardening law within P-EPSC, which is speci ﬁc to IN718.

Modeling Results
The initial texture used in the simulation is the measured texture given in Fig. 1 and
the grain shape aspect ratio is set to 5 representing the measured columnar grain
structure [ 32]. Deformation simulations are carried out in simple compression or
tension for the three sample categories. Figure 6 compares the calculated curves
with the measurement for each build direction. As shown, the model captures well
the tension-compression asymmetry and hardening rate in each case.
Figure 7 compares the model and measurement for the large strain cyclic
loading. Clearly the agreement in non-linear unloading, ﬂow stress, hardening rate,
and BE are good. Notably, the model captures the increase BE with larger
pre-strains, the lower yield in reverse loading, the higher hardening rate after yield.
Future work will utilize the model for simulating the fatigue tests.
Due to the moderate texture and elongated grain structure along the BD as
typical for microstructures formed during DMLS, the samples show anisotropy as a
function of BD. We observe that all curves exhibit a classical decreasing hardening
rate throughout, a signature of the slip-dominated plastic deformation [ 58, 59].
Samples in all build directions exhibited signi ﬁcant T-C asymmetry. The T-C
asymmetry did not depend on build direction; the tensile ﬂow stresses are lower
than the compression ﬂow stresses in all cases. Upon unloading, the material
Modeling Tensile, Compressive, and Cyclic Response … 663

exhibits an initial linear portion and a subsequent non-linear portion. The extent of
the macroscopically non-linear portion increases with the level of plastic pre-strain.
When the material becomes compressed, it yields at a lower value than yield in the

## Page 656

tensile pre-strain. After yielding, the hardening rate rapidly increases. The lower
yield in reverse loading followed by a rapid hardening rate is characteristic of the
Bauschinger effect for many materials [ 30]. The lower yield in the reversal com-
pression path than forward tension path can be attributed to the BE rather than the
T-C asymmetry. The BE became more pronounced with higher pre-strain. Since the
model is texture and grain shape sensitive, it successfully captured these charac-
teristics of the behavior of IN718.
Conclusions
This work presented an experimental and modeling study of the room temperature
deformation behavior of a Ni-based superalloy IN718 fabricated by an additive
manufacturing technique called DMLS. The experiments consisted of monotonic
tension and compression, cyclic tension-compression, and fatigue. EPSC poly-
crystalline model, called P-EPSC, was used to simulate the behavior except fatigue.
The material response in monotonic loading, the tension-compression asymmetry,
and the non-linearity during unloading, the BE, and permanent softening associated
with cyclic loading was successfully predicted by the model as a function of loading
directions and level of pre-strain. As many of these features in the behavior of
IN718 are similar to other Ni-based superalloys, the present modeling framework is
expected to be useful for a wider set of materials such as superalloys and other
cubic metals.

Novel Fractgraphy of Ni-Based Alloy
by SEM/EBSD Method
Keiji Kubushiro, Yutaro Ota, Yohei Sakakibara and Hitoshi Okada
Abstract Alloy 718 superalloy has been used for blades of air craft jet engine and
gas turbine. The failures of these parts derive from fatigue and creep, but it is
difﬁcult to estimate applied stress from observation of samples from damaged parts.
Oxidation and crush on fracture surfaces prevent from the estimation by fractgraphy
especially. Therefore, we established the novel observation of the microstructure on
the cross section beneath cracks by using EBSD. Tensile test, fatigue test and creep
test were performed, and the change in dislocation density and the difference of
strain contour of these specimens were speci ﬁed by the new method. Finally the
applied stress could be estimated and the test temperature could be also estimated.
Keywords Alloy 718
⋅ Fractgraphy ⋅ Misorientation ⋅ EBSD
Stress intensity factor
Introduction
Alloy 718 is typical Ni-based superalloy which shows high strength and good
corrosion resistance. This alloy is widely used for rockets, aircrafts, land-based gas
turbine engines, and cryogenic tankage in the world. There has been various
investigations of creep [ 1–3], fatigue [ 4–6], crack propagate property [ 7–13], and
corrosion. In particular, much Alloy 718 is mostly used under fatigue mode in case
of application as a rotator, thus fatigue and crack growth properties are signi ﬁcant.
When some structures fail by fatigue, stress is estimated by the striation on the
fracture surface. However, it is often unable to observe the striation on the fracture
surface because of oxidation or another reason. It was investigated that the plastic
strained area could be estimated by microhardness measurement [ 14, 15], X-ray
[15–17], and chemical etching method [ 18, 19] instead of fractgraphy by the

striation. Clave et al. [ 20] were reported that plastic strain area in the fatigued Alloy
718 could be identi ﬁed to observe β phase because post heat treatment could change
γ″ to β with more than 1% plastic strained area. It is therefore necessary to identify
plastic strained area without the striation.
Recently, Electron Back Scatter Diffraction (EBSD) method plays an important
role in the quanti ﬁcation of plastic strain. This method can quantify the plastic strain
by the misorientation within the grain, hence there are many evaluation report of
creep and fatigue damage [ 21–24], plastic strain [ 25, 26], and residual plastic strain
of bend [ 27] or weld joints [ 28]. It is expected that this method become powerful
technique to identify plastic strain under fatigued specimens. The aim of the present
work has been the development of novel fractgraphy of Alloy 718 by SEM/EBSD
method.
Experimental
The test specimen material in this study was Alloy 718. CT specimen geometry,
shown in Fig. 1, was prepared for crack growth test. All specimens were introduced
pre-cracks which were about 0.01 mm and tested in accordance with ASTM E647
at constant loading level and frequency of 10 Hz. The wave form was sin. and the
stress ratio was R = 0.1. Test temperature was 400, 600, and 750 °C in air. Crack
length was calculated by polynomial method (5 points). After the tests, specimens
were examined by scanning electron microscopy (JEOL, JSM-7100) equipped with
an EBSD pattern detector. The cross section of the fracture was observed.
Backscatter Electron Image (BEI) with an accelerating voltage of 15 kV was
obtained for observations of crack growth passes. Measurement of misorientation at
the fracture was conducted by EBSD method with an accelerating voltage of 20 kV
and 0.2 μm step. Grain Orientation Spread (GOS), which analyzed strains in
individual grains, was calculated by means of EBSD patterns.

Figure 2 shows fatigue crack growth rate curves at a different temperature. Crack
growth rates at 400 and 600 °C under the same stress intensity factor were almost
same, but the rate at 700 °C was higher. The difference in fatigue crack growth rate
strongly depended on tested temperature in 10 –20 MPa √m. These results agreed
with previous reports. Next, the change in plastic strain with the stress intensity
factor was investigated with these tested specimens.
Invers Pole Figure (IPF) maps of fatigue crack growth specimen tested at 400 °C
are shown in Fig. 3. The bottom side corresponds to the fractured area. Color
contrast in the stereographic triangle means the orientation of the measured points,
and grain boundaries are de ﬁned by the rule that the misorientation between two

the difference in the relation between GOS values and stress intensity factor. In

depending on test temperature and dwell time [ 6, 9, 11]. It was reported that this
phenomenon occurred due to bigger creep effect at higher temperature and longer
dwell time. In this study, transgranular fracture occurred under 600 °C because of
weaker creep effect, while intergranular fracture occurred at 750 °C because of
stronger creep effect. It is seemed that this change of fracture mode should result in
the difference in the relation between GOS values and stress intensity factor. In
particular, the striation cannot be observed in the case of intergranular fracture at
high temperature, thus our novel fractgraphy must be effective method.
Conclusion
In order to establish the novel fractgraphy method, we discussed the relation
between GOS values and stress intensity factor by measurement of crystal orien-
tation under fractured area of crack growth specimens with SEM/EBSD method.
The main conclusions are summarized as the follows:
(1) Crack grows through transgranular under 600 °C, while through intergranular
at 750 °C.
(2) The misorientation under fractured area increase with increasing stress intensity
factor at all temperature. At higher temperature, GOS values become higher at
the same stress intensity factor.
(3) According to fracture mode, the relation between GOS values and stress
intensity factor is organized with one line respectively.
From the above, deformed temperature range might be inferred by observation
of crack growth pass. After that, the measurement of GOS values leads to prediction
about stress intensity factor and crack growth rate by means of the relation in this
study. Therefore, fractgraphy by SEM/EBSD method is signi ﬁcantly effective
without fracture by the striation.

On the Effect of Alloying Additions
to the Ni-Cr-Al-Nb Dual-Superlattice
Gamma-Gamma Prime-Gamma Double
Prime Superalloys
P. M. Mignanelli, N. G. Jones, M. C. Hardy and H. J. Stone
Abstract Recent work has identi ﬁed a novel Ni-Cr-Al-Nb alloy capable of gen-
erating a γ-γ′-γ″ dual-superlattice microstructure with excellent microstructural
stability and tensile strength. In this study, we report on the effect of additions of
alloying elements that traditionally partition to the γ matrix. Attention is focussed
on their effects upon the microstructure, hardness and lattice mis ﬁto f
dual-superlattice superalloys. The results obtained from these studies indicate that
judicious alloying may further enhance the properties and stability of these
dual-superlattice superalloys and that they offer the potential of greatly increased
temperature capability compared to other alloys reinforced by γ″ precipitates.
Keywords Nickel alloys
⋅ Superalloys ⋅ Microstructure
Introduction
It is well understood that the temperature capability of Inconel 718, which is
reinforced by metastable γ″ precipitates, is limited to temperatures below 650 °C
by the coarsening of the γ″ precipitates and the transformation to the thermody-
namically stable δ phase [1]. Historical efforts to increase the temperature capability
have included minor chemical modi ﬁcations and alterations to heat treatments to
produce compact morphology precipitates [ 2]. Whilst such approaches have led to
improved thermal stability, the bene ﬁts are relatively modest. Recent research has
identiﬁed alloy compositions that generate a three phase γ-γ′-γ″ dual-superlattice
microstructure with excellent microstructural thermal stability, with respect to other
γ″ containing alloys, and greatly increased tensile strength over most superalloys,

## Page 671

achieved with a Ni-Cr-Al-Nb composition with minor additions of C, B and Zr
[3–5].
In order to develop nickel-base superalloys to meet the large range of property
requirements, consideration must be made of alloying additions beyond that of the
Ni-Cr-Al-Nb quaternary system used to demonstrate the viability of the γ-γ′-γ″
microstructure [ 6]. The correlation between solid solution strengthening of the γ
matrix and the creep strength of nickel-base superalloys has been well established,
with improved properties being obtained with greater alloying concentrations,
provided the formation of secondary phases can be avoided [ 7–9]. This is crucial as
over-alloying of the γ matrix can lead to the precipitation of topologically close
packed phases, such as sigma and mu, which are detrimental to the alloys properties
[10, 11]. The use of Mo and W to increase the solid solution strengthening of the γ
matrix is the most common method of improving the mechanical properties of
polycrystalline nickel-base superalloys, given the very high levels of strengthening
conferred by each of these elements on a per atomic percent basis [ 12, 13].
In addition to Mo and W, Fe and Co are also commonly added to nickel-base
superalloys and are added in considerably greater quantities to ful ﬁl their different
roles. Additions of Fe convey two primary bene ﬁts to nickel-base superalloys.
Firstly, the very low cost of Fe relative to other alloying elements helps to reduce
the overall cost of the alloy. Secondly, by introducing Fe to an alloy it increases the
processability of the alloy. However, care must be taken with Fe additions to avoid
the formation of Laves phases [ 14, 15]. Co on the other hand is introduced to reduce
the stacking fault energy, which can lead to increased strength through a greater
extent of twinning [ 16]. Alloying with Co has also been recently applied to the
development of an Inconel 718 type alloy, where the Co is used to stabilise the δ
phase, leading to an alloy with a large forging window, despite an increased pre-
cipitate volume fraction, compared to Inconel 718 [ 17].
In order to optimise the performance of the γ-γ′-γ″ superalloys, increased
compositional complexity is required to deliver the range of properties needed,
beyond tensile strength, for structural components in high temperature applications.
To investigate the development of more advanced alloys we have studied additions
of Mo, W, Fe and Co to the base Ni-15Cr-4Al-6Nb at.% alloy of 1 and 2 at.%
(Mo and W) or 4 and 8 at.% (Fe and Co).
Experimental
To investigate the effect of alloying on the microstructure of γ-γ′-γ″ superalloys a
series of nine alloys with composition Ni-15Cr-4Al-6Nb-X (at.%), where X = Mo,
W, Co or Fe were manufactured. The material was produced as ∼50 g bars by
vacuum arc melting, using elements with more than 99.9% purity, and a procedure
of 5 inversion and melting steps to ensure homogeneity. The alloys were then
homogenised at 1200 °C for 4 h under vacuum to minimise micro segregation.
The composition of each alloy was determined using energy dispersive X-ray
680 P. M. Mignanelli et al.

## Page 672

measurements across 5 large areas of each sample, encompassing ∼0.5 mm 2.
Following homogenisation, the alloys were sectioned into ∼1c m 3 pieces for
encapsulation in Ar back ﬁlled quartz ampoules and subsequent thermal exposure at
800 °C for 10 or 100 h. Metallographic preparation of the samples was completed
by mechanical grinding up to 2500 grit paper followed by diamond polishing to a
0.25 µm ﬁnish. The polished samples were subsequently electrolytically etched
using 10 vol.% phosphoric acid solution at ∼3 V. Scanning electron images were
obtained using a FEI Nova NanoSEM 450 in secondary electron mode. Values of
the material hardness were obtained as a proxy for strength using a Vickers hard-
ness indenter with a 20 kg mass and a dwell time of 30 s. Measurements of the
lattice parameter were obtained by synchrotron X-ray diffraction using the I12
beamline at the Diamond Light Source, Didcot, UK. The incident beam had an
energy of 79.98 keV and dimensions of 0.5 × 0.5 mm. Fitting of the experimental
data and derivation of the lattice mis ﬁt was completed using a Pawley re ﬁnement in
the TOPAS diffraction software package [ 18]. Thermodynamic calculations were
completed using Thermo-Calc with the Thermotech nickel database TTNi8.
Results and Discussion
The nominal and experimentally determined compositions of each alloy, along with
the alloy designation that will be used throughout this manuscript, are shown in
Table 1 in atomic percent. All of the experimentally determined values were within
15% of the nominal, target composition, with the exception of the 2 at.% Mo
addition and both of the W additions, which varied by 18, 19 and 28.5% respec-
tively but represent small variations in at.% terms.
To investigate the microstructural stability of the γ-γ′-γ″ microstructure with
alloying additions, two heat treatments of 10 and 100 h at 800 °C were completed.

## Page 673

The heat treatment for 10 h was chosen to represent an aging heat treatment, shown
to generate a γ-γ′-γ″ microstructure in the base alloy, with a high hardness [ 4].
Similarly, 100 h at 800 °C was chosen to maintain the same exposure temperature
as the short treatment, whilst producing an accelerated assessment of the mi-
crostructural evolution, given the likely service window of these alloys would be
close to 700 °C. Previous work [ 4], has shown the coarsening after 100 h at 800 °C
to be comparable or greater than the coarsening observed for longer durations at
both 700 and 750 °C for the base alloy. These previous results indicate the con-
servative nature of this higher temperature exposure given that the greater coars-
ening of the γ′ and γ″ precipitates at 800 °C will lead to deterioration in the
mechanical properties, which would be expected to be overestimated by this higher
temperature exposure.
The microstructures of the base alloy and the alloys with γ partitioning additions
following heat treatment for 10 h at 800 °C are shown in Fig. 1. A comparison of
the nine alloys reveals that the alloys appear broadly similar, with both γ′ and γ″
precipitates present in the microstructure, and the alloying with Mo or Fe has had
the smallest effect. However, further small variations with composition can be
observed across the two other alloying systems. Alloying with W, and especially
the greater addition of 2 at.% W, lead to agglomeration of the precipitate phases,
and a conjoined γ′-γ″ precipitate network, as opposed to distinct boundaries
between the two phases. Conversely, alloying with Co has reduced the precipitation
of γ″ in the microstructure compared with the base alloy, and has thereby reduced
the connected nature of the precipitate phases.
In order to further assess the microstructural variations produced by the alloying
additions, following 10 h at 800 °C, X-ray diffraction experiments were completed
at the Diamond Light Source, seeking to measure the lattice parameter of the
precipitates and hence derive the lattice mis ﬁt between the constituent phases. The
results of the diffraction data analysis are presented in Fig. 2. The addition of Mo,
Fig. 2a, can be seen to have little effect upon the lattice parameter of the γ′ pre-
cipitates. However, it can be seen to increase the lattice parameter of both the γ
matrix and the a-axis of the γ″, whilst the c-axis of the γ″ can be seen to decrease. In
contrast, the addition of W, Fig. 2b, shows an increase followed by a decrease in
the lattice parameter of the γ matrix and the a-axis of the γ″, whilst the lattice
parameter of the γ′ and the c-axis of the γ″ are increasing and decreasing respec-
tively. The addition of Fe, Fig. 2c, to the base alloy shows a consistent trend across
all three phases (and by extension all four measured lattice parameters) as the lattice
parameters all increase with increasing Fe content. The addition of Co, Fig. 2d, is
similarly complex as that of W, as the γ matrix and γ′ lattice parameter decrease and
subsequently increase, whilst the a- and c-axes of the γ″ both increase with Co
content, albeit only by small amounts.
The variation in the lattice mis ﬁt, presented in Fig. 2e–g can be seen to exhibit
similar trends across the four alloy systems. The γ-γ′ lattice mis ﬁt, Fig. 2e, is
observed to decrease with increasing content of both Mo and Fe, whilst W increases
the lattice mis ﬁt and Co decreases before increasing, such that the values are quite
similar. The lattice mis ﬁto ft h e γ matrix and the γ″ a-axis, Fig. 2f, shows similar
682 P. M. Mignanelli et al.

## Page 674

behaviour for all alloying additions except for the addition of 8 at.% Fe. In all cases
the lattice mis ﬁt increases from a negative value to a value approaching zero, and
this value is approximately constant when moving from either 1 to 2 at.% in the
case of Mo and W or from 4 to 8 at.% in the case of Co, whereas the addition of 8
at.% Fe leads to a decrease in the lattice mis ﬁt. The ﬁrst point that should be made
about the lattice mis ﬁt between the γ matrix and the γ″ c-axis, Fig. 2g, is that the
value of the lattice mis ﬁt is approximately ﬁve times that of the γ-γ′ lattice mis ﬁt.
Analyses of the results show that the behaviour of Co and Fe are similar, and that
the lattice mis ﬁt increases with increasing content of these elements. However, the
addition of Mo reduced the lattice mis ﬁt and the addition of W led to an increase
followed by a decrease.

that the Mo partitions primarily to the γ matrix and the γ″, resulting in an increase to
the γ lattice parameter and the γ″ a-axis, whilst shortening the γ″ c-axis. By con-
trast, a 1 at.% addition of W seems to partition equally between all three phases,

further in the case of γ-γ′, and levelling off or decreasing in the case of γ-γ″ (a-axis)

and the γ-γ″ (c-axis) respectively. The addition of Fe led to an increase in the lattice
parameter across all three phases, suggesting that it partitioned approximately
evenly across the three phases. However, this led to con ﬂicting variations in the
lattice misﬁt between the phases as the change in lattice parameter across the phases
occurred at different rates. The effect of Co additions on the lattice parameter and
lattice mis ﬁt was subtler than the other alloying elements. The variation in the
lattice parameter of each phase was small by comparison and led to small variations
in the lattice mis ﬁt, as the Co did not appear to have a preference for partitioning to
any one of the constituent phases.
In order to better understand the results obtained from the microstructural
analyses, thermodynamic calculations were completed to investigate the predicted
partitioning of the alloying elements between the γ, γ′ and γ″ phases, Fig. 3.B y ﬁrst
considering the change in Ni content of the three phases, Fig. 3a–c, it can be seen
that the Ni decreases in concentration in all three phases, with increasing amounts
of the alloying additions. This result is unsurprising, as Ni is used as the balance
element in these alloys and hence all of the alloying additions are added at the
expense of the Ni. However, it should be noted that of the alloying elements added
to the base alloy, the Co addition is the most effective at reducing the Ni con-
centration in the γ′ and γ″ phases, Fig. 3b and c, both by raw amount and on a per
atomic percent basis. In contrast to the Ni concentration in the γ, the Cr concen-
tration in the γ, Fig. 3d, is increased by the addition of all of the alloying elements,
with only W producing a weak change, and it would be hoped that this increase
would lead to a greater resistance to oxidation and corrosion damage. This result
can be correlated with the Cr concentration in the γ′ phase, Fig. 3e, which is shown
to decrease with the increase in alloying additions, again with the exception of W,
whilst the γ″, Fig. 3f, contains very little Cr (<0.5 at.%) in all nine alloying
variations.
Consideration of the Al concentration, Fig. 3g–i, in all three phases reveals that
there is very little change in the Al content across the complete range of alloys
studied. By contrast, the Nb content, Fig. 3j–l, changes considerably across the nine

To assess the preliminary mechanical properties of the alloys, hardness mea-

presented in Fig. 5. Comparison of the data for each alloy revealed that there was
little variation in the hardness between the 10 h and 100 h heat treatments, indi-
cating the good thermal stability of these alloys. It can also be seen that the alloying
with Mo, W and Fe all led to increases in the alloy hardness, which increased with
larger additions of the alloying element. Conversely, the addition of Co produced a
decrease in the alloy hardness. Comparison of the rates of change in hardness, per
atomic percent, revealed that W was the most effective element at strengthening the
γ-γ′-γ″ alloy, whilst the addition of Mo was next most effective, followed by Fe and
the addition of Co leading to a decrease in hardness. However, the increase in
hardness conveyed by W additions comes at the expense of the morphological
stability of the γ′ and γ″ precipitates in the alloy, which is thought to be undesirable.
Similarly, the increased coarsening of the γ″ precipitates, brought about by addi-
tions of Co, is a likely cause of the observed decrease in hardness.

## Page 680

Conclusions
This work has shown that the γ-γ′-γ″ forming superalloys exhibit good solubility
for alloying elements, critical to improving the overall mechanical properties of this
new class of alloys. The addition of Mo and W led to substantial hardening of the
alloy, potentially leading to improved mechanical properties. However, for the
addition of W, this comes at the expense of the morphology of the precipitates
formed in the alloy and may have to be traded off against the potentially deleterious
precipitate network that is formed in alloys that contain an excess of W. The
addition of Fe and Co provided a small hardening increase in the case of Fe, but in
the case of Co, led to a deterioration in the γ-γ′-γ″ microstructure after exposure for
100 h at 800 °C and a consequent decrease in the alloy hardness.

Optimization of the Forging Process
Window in Respect of AGG, IGG
and Direct Age Effect in Alloy 718
Engine Disks
Aleksandar Stanojevic, Christian Bucher, Markus Gruber,
Bernd Oberwinkler and Martin Stockinger
Abstract Alloy 718 is commonly used for turbine disks in aircraft engines. The
very demanding loading conditions require top notch mechanical properties of the
material. In order to maximize the mechanical properties a perfect use of the direct
age (DA) effect is necessary. An optimal DA effect contributes approximately
150 MPa to the total yield strength. However, the effect is only present in a certain,
narrow process window. It was observed that small deformations at speci ﬁc local
temperatures during the last forging step lead to an ideal DA-effect. As the ideal
process window in respect to the DA-effect can hardly be maintained in the whole
forging, regions with a decreased DA-effect occur. A connection between the
regions with decreased DA-effect and abnormal respectively irregular grain growth
(AGG and IGG) was analyzed based on forging simulations. Therefore, the
meta-dynamic recrystallization velocity parameter v
mrx was developed for indica-
tion of AGG and IGG. A correlation of the introduced parameter and the DA-effect
was found. In addition, v
mrx was used for the design of solution annealed forgings
containing coarse grain regions. Those forgings were manufactured and analyzed
using laser ultrasonic testing (LUS) and metallography on cut-ups. The occurrence
of ALA grains was identi ﬁed but no white spots (light etch indications) were found.

Introduction
Engine disks for jet turbines are critical parts due to high rotation speeds and
operating temperatures that require excellent mechanical properties. To meet those
demanding requirements, superalloy forgings are used. The most commonly uti-
lized alloy for turbine disks is alloy 718.
The yield strength of forged alloy 718 engine disks can be greatly in ﬂuenced by
the heat treatment after forging. The conventional heat treatment route of alloy 718
consists of solution annealing and duplex aging (SA). The direct age (DA) process
skips the solution annealing, thus the aging treatment takes place directly after the
forging process [ 1] (see Fig. 1). With this method, the process costs can be
decreased and more importantly the strength properties of alloy 718 can be further
improved.
Furthermore, alloy 718 forgings show different microstructure anomalies based
on the processing route. Direct age forgings tend to exhibit coarse grain regions and
a decreased direct age effect in a certain processing window whereas solution
annealed and aged forgings tend to show white spots (light etch indications).
Strengthening Mechanisms
The total yield strength can be divided into different strength contributions. The
precipitation strengthening shows the highest contribution to the total yield-strength

## Page 684

where the coherency strain ﬁelds of the γ″ precipitates is the dominant strength-
ening effect [ 2]. The solid solution strengthening depends on the alloying elements
and their relative size difference in comparison to the matrix. This strengthening
effect is highly inﬂuenced by the chromium and molybdenum content [ 3]. The grain
boundary strengthening is controlled by the grain size and follows the Hall-Petch
relation [ 4, 5]. Other strength contributions are the basic and the dislocation
strengthening (strain-hardening) effect. All those strength contributions are dis-
played in Table 1 [6]. A model for all these strengthening contributions – beside the
direct age effect —are implemented in the thermo-kinetic simulation tool MatCalc.
The simulation approach proposed by Oberwinkler [ 6] is based on the exact
implementation of local temperature histories into MatCalc. The direct age effect is
considered as an additional strengthening contribution and is described in the fol-
lowing section “Direct Age Effect ”.
Direct Age Effect
The demanding strength requirements of forged disks can only be ful ﬁlled by
incorporating the full direct age effect. The strengthening effect due to the direct
aging is not fully understood yet. However, there are a number of theories about
possible strengthening mechanisms responsible for the DA-effect. Most of the
theories describe the DA strengthening effect through a different precipitation
pattern and an increased amount of warm work.
Horvath et al. [ 7] stated that the key to a pronounced DA-effect is the remaining
amount of dislocation due to warm work in the microstructure after the last blow.
After heat treatment the dislocations are greatly diminished due to recovery effects
so that the increased dislocation effect is not available after solution annealing. The
aging temperature however is not suf ﬁcient for a noteworthy dislocation recovery,
hence, providing enough dislocations for a pronounced DA-effect. This theory can
be supported by the ﬁnding of Jin et al. [ 8]. They found that direct age samples
show distinct dislocation structures contrary to solution annealed and aged
(CHT) samples.

## Page 685

Another difference between the CHT and DA condition is the fraction and
morphology of the strength-contributing precipitates γ′ and γ″. According to Miller
[9] the nano-precipitates nucleate and grow in a speci ﬁc relation. The γ″ precipitate
nucleates ﬁrst engul ﬁng Nb for coarsening and rejecting Al in that process. This
leads to an oversaturation of Al causing a γ′-nucleation and coarsening. Hence, the
precipitates coexist as γ′-γ″ duplets and even as γ′-γ″-γ′ triplets. Slama et al. [ 10]
compared the precipitations between the CHT and DA condition showing a pro-
nounced occurrence of γ′-γ″-γ′ triplets in the CHT condition. The DA samples
however, showed γ″-γ′-γ″ triplets. The strength contribution was explained through
the interface mismatch of the precipitates. The mismatch between the γ″ phase and
the matrix phase is clearly higher than the γ′-γ″ or the γ′-matrix interface, hence,
responsible for a higher strength due to γ″-γ′-γ″ triplets.
Description of the Direct Age Effect
The strength contribution with the highest variation is by far the DA-effect (see
Table 1). In order to describe the DA-effect, despite the not fully understood
mechanism, Oberwinkler [ 6] developed a statistical model. Due to the high amount
of available test data based on serial disks the statistical model was calibrated and
validated by speci ﬁc forgings. The statistical model expresses the connection
between temperature and strain through the introduction of a new parameter,
namely the Oberwinkler-ratio O (see Eqs. ( 1)–(3)).

The necessary parameters for the Oberwinkler-ratio Tmax and Tmin are dependent
on the imposed local strain φ. Together with the local temperature T the Ober-
winkler ratio can be calculated. All other parameters are material constants.
The analysis of the total yield strength in dependence of the Oberwinkler-ratio
shows distinct regions of a pronounced DA-effect. Small deformations and low
temperatures during the last deformation operation lead to a pronounced DA-effect
with a relatively small scatter. With increasing deformation and temperature, the
expected average DA-effect decreases while the scatter band increases. Hence, three
different regions along the Oberwinkler-ratio axis can be de ﬁned. Oberwinkler ratio
−1.5 ≪ O < 0.3 shows a pronounced DA-effect, 0.3 ≤ O < 1.5 shows a continuous
transition to a decreased DA-effect and −1.5 < O > 1.5 shows no DA-effect [ 6]
(Fig. 2).

## Page 686

Abnormal and Irregular Grain Growth
In addition to the processing window for distinct strengthening a concurrent pro-
cessing window for abnormal grain growth (AGG) exists. This phenomenon is not
speciﬁc to alloy 718 as it occurs on other materials as well [ 11, 12]. The upsetting
investigations on alloy 718 double cones performed by Aoki et al. [ 13] showed
distinct strain and strain rate domains where AGG is active. Furthermore, Aoki
found an additional grain growth mechanism after a partial recrystallization. This
phenomenon was de ﬁned as irregular grain growth (IGG) in accordance to Bhowal
and Schirra [ 14]. Both effects are illustrated in Fig. 3. This effect is only visible by
metallographic analysis after solution annealing.
Furthermore, the underlying effect behind AGG and IGG is believed to be
responsible for the increased scatter of the yield strength in DA forged engine disks.
Solution annealing after the last deformation during the CHT processing route will
cause coarsening due to AGG and IGG in certain regions of the forging that showed
speciﬁc deformation and strain rates. AGG and IGG coupled with local inhomo-
geneities of the δ-phase will cause strongly localized coarsening, referred to as light
etch indications (see Fig. 4).
By skipping the solution annealing and imposing the ageing temperature on the
as-forged condition, the aging temperature is not suf ﬁcient for AGG and IGG to
occur. Nonetheless, partially recrystallized grains or grains with increased dislo-
cation density can still be present after aging but disguised as “normal” grains. Due
to the inability to discover dislocation density by usual light optical microscopy, the
strength of the material appears different dependent on the position of the sample
without any detectable differences in grain size. The similarities between grain

Laser Ultrasonic Testing
Laser ultrasonic is a remote and contactless measurement technique for materials
inspection and characterization [ 15, 16] which was used in this research for
non-destructive detection of coarse grain regions in Alloy 718 forgings. Dur-
ing LUS a short pulse laser beam is focused on the sample surface to generate
ultrasonic waves in all directions on the sample surface and bulk. The waves can be
remotely detected either at the front or opposite surface of the sample by LUS
interferometers. This method has many advantages over conventional techniques
based on contact and noncontact piezoelectrics as described in [ 15]. For laser based
detection of ultrasonic waves, several different interferometers such as confocal
Fabry-Perot, Michelson, long path difference [ 15] and photorefractive (PR) inter-
ferometers [ 17], with different frequency responses and sensitivities are used.
However, most of them are applicable just for samples with high re ﬂective surfaces
[15, 17]. For samples with rough surfaces, LUS receivers (Fig. 5a) based on
two-wave mixing (TWM) in an adaptive PR material exhibit high sensitivity
[17, 18]. The measurements were performed in transmission mode (Fig. 5b).

Investigation Approach
To predict potentially coarse grain regions in alloy 718 forgings, an indication
parameter was de ﬁned based on simulation and experimental results of a direct age
engine disk that showed coarse grain regions. This coarsening parameter was used
to develop a speci ﬁc forging procedure for pancakes exhibiting coarse grains.
Those forgings were manufactured and non-destructive tested using the laser
ultrasonic (LUS) method. After LUS testing the forgings were metallographically
investigated to validate the LUS measurements.
The coarsening parameter was also analyzed based on DA disk forgings dedi-
cated to investigate the DA-effect (cf. Fig. 2) but also on additional disk geometries.
This additional data helped to con ﬁrm the Oberwinkler model as well.
Development of an Indicating Parameter for AGG and IGG
During the development process of a speci ﬁc engine disk the ﬁrst design iteration
led to coarse grain regions. Hence, investigations of the responsible effect behind
the abnormal coarsening were initiated. The disk was forged in four forging steps
with a subsequent duplex ageing. The preforming steps were performed with a low
strain rate on a hydraulic press. The ﬁnal pressing and the DA blow were performed
with a relatively high strain rate on a screw press (see Fig. 6). The microstructure
investigation of the disk after forging and heat treatment showed regions with
coarse grains but also bimodal microstructures and ALA (As Large As) grains (see
Fig. 7).
The processing parameters for the disk with coarse grain regions were imple-
mented into DEFORM ™. The forging simulation contained the whole forging and
heat treatment process. Furthermore, a constitutive recrystallization model was
applied that is capable of simulating dynamic (DRx), meta-dynamic (MRx) and
static recrystallization (SRx) as well as the effective, recrystallization-corrected
strain accumulation. The recrystallization model utilizes different empirical equa-
tions, where the model parameters were optimized for forging of alloy 718 [ 19].
During deformation, dynamic recrystallization is active. Immediately after each
deformation process, the meta-dynamic recrystallization becomes active for a short
time period (usually up to 15 s after the deformation process, depending on the
process parameters). Due to the processing window during closed die forging the
static recrystallization is of minor importance. After recrystallization, grain growth
takes place. The applied model is capable of the simulation of mean grain sizes but
is not capable of predicting AGG and IGG. Therefore, a further parameter was
developed that indicates regions where AGG and IGG are likely to occur.
The meta-dynamic recrystallization takes place immediately after the deforma-
tion but only if the dynamic recrystallization was active during deformation. Fur-
thermore, if the microstructure is completely recrystallized through dynamic
698 A. Stanojevic et al.

## Page 690

recrystallization the meta-dynamic recrystallization won ’t initiate. Therefore, the
meta-dynamic recrystallization after deformation is a reliable indicator for an
incomplete recrystallization.
The driving force for grain growth due to meta-dynamic recrystallization is the
local dislocation density gradient between a critically work-hardened region and the
nuclei caused by a previous dynamic recrystallization. According to Zhou and
Baker [ 20] the strain rate in the previous deformation process de ﬁnes the extent as
well as the velocity of the meta-dynamic recrystallization.
