The fraction of meta-dynamic recrystallization over time Xmrx tðÞ is de ﬁned by
the sum of all temperature corrected time steps WtðÞ and the temperature corrected
time at 50% of the meta-dynamic recrystallization W0.5 that de ﬁnes the kinetics of
the recrystallization process. The kinetics is mainly in ﬂuenced by the effective
strain φm and the Zener-Holomon parameter Z that again is dependent on the
effective strain rate φ̇ and the temperature T. All other parameters are material based
constants. The meta-dynamic recrystallization velocity is the temporal derivation of
the meta-dynamic recrystallization fraction and is described by Eq. ( 10). The
meta-dynamic recrystallization can also be described by discrete time steps sub-
stituting the integrals with sums.
A very low v
mrx parameter signalizes an already completed or almost completed
dynamic recrystallization. A high vmrx signalizes enough energy in form of dynamic
recrystallization induced nuclei that will lead to a complete recrystallization through
meta-dynamic recrystallization. Both cases are not critical in respect to residual
un-recrystallized grains. However, as meta-dynamic recrystallization can also lead
to grain coarsening, a high v
mrx coupled with a high temperature for a suf ﬁcient time
period will cause coarse grain regions. A high vmrx immediately after the defor-
mation process also signalizes a high dislocation density that is responsible for
AGG. If v
mrx remains in a certain range it signalizes an incomplete recrystallization
causing IGG. As coarsening needs time to take place, vmrx is evaluated at a certain
time after the deformation. Hence, following relationship was established:

If the temperature in the forging exceeds the δ-solvus temperature Tδ, and vmrx
after a certain meta-dynamic recrystallization time tmrx (usually ﬁve seconds after
the deformation) is high enough, AGG will occur as a coarse grain region.

δ (but higher than a necessary temperature TIGGÞ coupled
with a vmrx in a speci ﬁc scale (see Eq. ( 11)) will cause IGG in form of bimodal
microstructure or ALA-grains. This relationship was derived based on the results

Most grain coarsening investigations are performed by cooling immediately after
forging and a subsequent solution annealing (e.g. [ 13]). The same effect causing
grain growth during solution annealing also applies if the forging temperature
remains high for a suf ﬁcient amount of time. Hence, the coarsening can be
explained due to the high and lasting temperature immediately after forging, just
like shown in Fig. 7.
Similarities Between AGG, IGG and the Increased
Scatter Band
If the temperature is lower than TIGG no abnormal or irregular grain growth will
take place. However, the responsible mechanisms for AGG and IGG can still be
initiated but not detected by standard investigation methods. To analyze the simi-
larities between the AGG and IGG mechanism and the increased scatter band of DA
forged engine disks, an existing automated simulation chain at voestalpine BÖH-
LER Aerospace GmbH & Co KG was used for the simulation of multiple serial
disks, including the AGG and IGG indication parameter. As a byproduct of the
simulations, more yield strength values for the Oberwinkler model were generated
increasing the statistical signi ﬁcance of the model (see Fig. 8). Furthermore, Fig. 8
shows a connection of the region with increased scatter band and the AGG and IGG
indication parameter v
mrx. The simulation results showed that a critical vmrx is
occurring after an Oberwinkler-ratio of 0.375, hence, proving the connection
between AGG, IGG and the variation of the DA-effect.
Validation of the Indicating AGG and IGG Parameter
Dedicated pancake forgings were designed to investigate the effect of the
meta-dynamic recrystallization velocity v
mrx based on a solution annealed material
condition. Two different designs with multiple strokes were created: one with a vmrx

Summary and Outlook
In this paper, the connection between the abnormal, irregular grain growth and the
meta-dynamic recrystallization was investigated. Following ﬁndings can be
summarized:
1. Multiple serial disks incorporating the direct age effect were simulated
according to the Oberwinkler-model [ 6]. The simulation results con ﬁrmed this
approach. Hence, the Oberwinkler-model is capable to predict the yield strength
of direct age forgings.
2. The meta-dynamic recrystallization parameter v
mrx was introduced. A correla-
tion between vmrx and microstructure irregularities expressed by bimodal mi-
crostructure, ALA grains and coarse grain regions was found.
3. Furthermore, the parameter vmrx was applied on the simulations of direct aged
serial disks. A connection between the increased scatter of the direct age effect
and the meta-dynamic recrystallization velocity was found. Hence, the increased
scatter can be explained through AGG and IGG to a certain degree.

4. Speci ﬁc pancake forgings based on vmrx were designed and manufactured to
investigate the AGG and IGG behavior due to solution annealing. For the
identiﬁcation of critical regions in terms of increased coarsening, laser ultrasonic
testing was applied and investigated by metallography. Instead of the anticipated
white spots, several ALA grains were found, hence, partially validating the
meta-dynamic recrystallization induced coarsening.
As the presented results are based on work still in progress, the following
investigations will be carried out in the near future:
• Detailed investigation of the pancake forgings in terms of bimodal mi-
crostructures, ALA grains, coarse grain regions and white spots.
• Enhancement of the meta-dynamic recrystallization velocity parameter for a
more speci ﬁc prediction of the different AGG and IGG morphologies for the
solution annealing condition.

Oxidation-Assisted Cracking at 650 °C
in Superalloy 718 Manufactured
by Laser Beam Melting: Effect
of Temperature and Strain Rate
Alexandre Pancou, Eric Andrieu and Arnaud Votié
Abstract Additive manufacturing of complex parts in superalloy 718 by Laser
Beam Melting (LBM, also referred to Selective Laser Melting, SLM) is currently
under the evaluation by the aerospace industry, due to the opportunity to combine
alloy 718 excellent properties and versatility of use, with the bene ﬁts and increasing
maturity of LBM technology. In this work, the interactions between fracture modes
and deformation modes for LBM-manufactured 718 were studied at 20, 450 and
650 °C. Vertical and horizontal tensile specimens were fabricated, then heat-treated
with two sets of standard solution-aging treatments, before being tested in air over a
range of strain rate from 8 × 10
–5 to 3 × 10 −2 s−1. Results of these tests showed
evidence of a coupling effect between oxidation and mechanical loading, resulting
in oxidation-assisted cracking of LBM 718 alloy for the same temperature and
strain rate conditions than conventionally-manufactured alloy 718. Also, in spite of
consisting of fundamentally different microstructures, relationships between frac-
ture modes and deformation modes for laser beam melted 718 were found to be
surprisingly consistent with the ones previously established for conventional 718.
These results suggests that microstructure parameters such as grain size and mor-
phology, or phase distribution are not involved at the ﬁrst order in the mechanisms
controlling these interactions. To further describe these phenomena, the interactions
between solute elements, mobile dislocations and interfaces must be considered.

Introduction
Among emerging metal additive manufacturing processes, Laser Beam Melting
(LBM, also known as Selective Laser Melting and as Direct Metal Laser Melting),
is at this point one of the most promising: the manufacturing technique demon-
strates high technology readiness, and its main bene ﬁts—namely weight savings,
products cycle time cuts and cost reductions through functional integration —lead to
an open range of perspectives for the aerospace industry (LBM process is described
elsewhere [ 1]). Due to its good weldability, superalloy 718 is eligible for LBM
process. In addition, its excellent corrosion and mechanical properties at high
temperatures, combined with alloy 718 adaptable, versatile microstructure make it a
relevant choice for many LBM-targeted applications, such as aircraft engine parts.
Still, several barriers are to be overcome for LBM full-scale industrialization to
begin. While most effort is currently put into LBM parts quali ﬁcation, under-
standing process-microstructure-properties relationships with regard to oxidation-
assisted failure at high temperature is of prime interest for lifetime assessment of
these parts. Indeed, in spite of stringent control on its elaboration and transfor-
mation parameters, alloy 718 is known to be sensitive to oxidation-assisted inter-
granular cracking (OAIC) under mechanical loading in its usual service
temperature range. This behavior is closely related to the alloy deformation mode,
as the apparition of plastic ﬂow instabilities —serrated yielding —systematically
triggers a change of fracture mode, from intergranular to transgranular. These
fracture-deformation modes interactions were consistently evidenced for rolled, cast
and wrought 718 in previous studies [ 2–7], in which the role of the local
mechanical state at grain boundaries, as well as alloy content in interstitial species,
were highlighted. Still, the mechanisms involved are not well understood. Specif-
ically, the relative contributions of metallurgical, mechanical and environmental
parameters must be clari ﬁed, because the mechanisms proposed so far are neither
explaining why these interactions are constantly observed in alloy 718 regardless of
its metallurgical state, nor fully satisfying regarding some physical metallurgy
aspects.
The fact that LBM microstructures show fundamental scale differences from
their conventionally-manufactured counterparts naturally leads to wonder if the
LBM-manufactured 718 exhibits the same susceptibility to OAIC. Most studies
conducted on laser beam melted alloy 718 focus on the mechanical properties at
ambient temperature; some authors carried out tensile tests at different temperatures
[1, 8] but neither of these works discuss the occurrence (or absence) of oxidation-
assisted failure at elevated temperature. In Trosch et al. study [ 1], intergranular
fracture was observed at 450 and 650 °C, but was attributed to plate-like inter-
granular precipitation of δ phase. To the author ’s knowledge, there is no published
information available on the effect of tensile strain rate and deformation mode (in
particular serrated yielding) on the rupture mode of laser beam melted alloy 718.
This work primarily aims to address the aforementioned point by studying defor-
mation modes —fracture modes interactions for LBM manufactured 718 tensile
712 A. Pancou et al.

## Page 703

specimens at 650 °C, as it may provide valuable information to understand the
mechanisms involved in oxidation-assisted intergranular cracking of this alloy.
Materials and Methods
Material
For this purpose, specimen for tensile tests and microstructural characterizations
were fabricated in an EOS M280 Laser Beam Melting system. Three batches were
produced with the same set of manufacturing parameters, provided by EOS GmbH.
Samples were melted under protective Argon atmosphere using 400 W Ytterbium
laser ﬁber with wavelength of 1060 –1100 µm. Scanning strategy consisted of stripe
pattern with contouring, the scanning direction being rotated of 30° on each con-
secutive layer; powder layer thickness was set to 40 µm. Batch 1 was produced
using alloy 718 powder from supplier A, while batched 2 and 3 were manufactured
using powder from supplier B. Powders chemical compositions, in agreement with
AMS 5662, were provided by materials suppliers (Table 1). Both powders were
produced by gas atomization in argon. Sieve analysis, coupled with metallographic
observations, showed that most particles are spherical, with particles size distri-
bution between 15 –53 µm.
Batch 1 was composed of vertical bars only; it was heat treated after laser beam
melting using HSA2 solution-ageing treatment (Table 2). Vertical tensile speci-
mens (i.e. tension axis parallel to vertical building direction, Z) were CNC
machined from the heat treated bars as follows: 7 vertical, round tensile specimens
with a gage length of 30 mm and a diameter of 5.00 mm; and 6 vertical, ﬂat tensile
specimens with a gage length of 15 mm and a gage section of 3.00 × 1.00 mm.
Flat tensile specimens were used to extend fracture analysis capabilities. Batch 2
was only used for microstructural characterizations on the as-fabricated (AF) met-
allurgical state. Batch 3 was composed of both vertical and horizontal bars. It was
heat treated using HSA1 solution-ageing treatment (Table 2) then vertical and
horizontal round tensile specimens with a gage length of 28 mm and a diameter of
5.00 mm were machined from those bars.
Mechanical Testing
Tensile specimen surface was kept as-machined (Ra 1.6 µm), except for ﬂat
specimens from batch 1, which were mechanically polished using SiC grit paper up
to grade 2400, then diamond suspension up to 1 µm grade, to facilitate SEM
observations of crack initiation on these specimens. All tensile specimens were
cleaned with ethanol in ultrasonic bath for 3 min before testing. Gage sections were

Microstructural Characterizations
Microstructural characterizations were carried out on the three metallurgical states:
as-fabricated, HSA1 and HSA2. Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements
were achieved on 1200 SiC grit polished samples in the XY manufacturing plan
using a Bruker D8 system. A Bragg-Brentano θ-2θ conﬁguration was used with
angular range of 20° –80°, step of 0.03°/2 s and sample spinning. Sample for
metallographic observations were mechanically polished up to 1 µm diamond
suspension, and ﬁnished with 0.05 µm alumina suspension. As-fabricated and
HSA2 samples were chemically etched 30 s in 32 wt% hydrochloric acid, then
4 min in Kalling solution. HSA1 samples were electrochemically etched 5 s in 1:1
hydrochloric acid —acetic acid solution, at 5 V. Electrolytic extraction of the pre-
cipitates was also performed on HSA2 metallurgical state, using a solution of 10
vol.% of hydrochloric acid in ethanol, and a current density of 70 mA/cm
2,a t
ambient temperature. After 9 h of dissolution, the solution was ﬁltrated and the
obtained powder residue was analyzed by XRD, using angular range of 20° –120°,
step of 0.02°/2 s and sample spinning. Microstructures were observed using a
Nikon Optical Microscope (OM) and a Leo 435-VP Scanning Electron Microscope
(SEM), with an accelerating voltage of a 15 kV. Energy Dispersive Spectroscopy
(EDS) was used for qualitative elementary analysis. Electron Back-Scatter
Diffraction (EBSD) was performed on 800 × 600 µm maps with step size of
1 µm on a JEOL JSM 7100F FEG-SEM for HSA2 metallurgical state to investigate
microstructural texture and grain morphology. Vickers hardness was measured on
(XY) surface for each metallurgical state from a minimum of 10 indentation, using
a 30 kg load for 10 s holding time. Fracture surfaces of the tensile specimens were
observed using binocular magni ﬁers and SEM.
Results and Discussion
Microstructural Characterizations
Microstructural Scales
The ﬁrst major difference between laser beam melted and conventionally manu-
factured alloy 718 microstructures is the scale at which they are formed during the
solidiﬁcation stage. As it may be seen from observations of the etched mi-
crostructure, the as-fabricated LBM microstructure is textured by the laser scanning
pattern, with laser path visible in horizontal plane (Fig. 1a), and corresponding melt
pools in vertical plane (Fig. 1b).
Melt pool size was estimated by image analysis in the (YZ) plane. The average
width is approximately 120 µm (value is only indicative because laser scanning
tracks overlap). The average melt pool depth was measured for the last-melted layer
716 A. Pancou et al.

## Page 707

to be an average value of (72 ± 16) µm. From these values, and approximating the
melt pool by a cylindrical shape, the elementary solidi ﬁcation volume may be
estimated to 1.10 −3 mm3 for these LBM parameters. By comparison to the values
commonly encountered in casting (from 1 cm 3 to 1.10 −2 m3 during ingot solidi-
ﬁcation [ 9]), it is shown that the solidi ﬁcation volume in laser beam melting is
lower by at least 6 orders of magnitude than those encountered in casting. Focusing
on that LBM elementary solidi ﬁcation volume, it may be seen from Fig. 2a that
solidiﬁcation inside the melt pool mainly occurs in a cellular/dendritic regime,
sometimes with secondary dendritic arms located at melt pool interfaces where
solidiﬁcation conditions seem to be slower. Primary Dendrite Arm Spacing (PDAS)
was measured for the as-fabricated state by image analysis by the intercept method.
The average value obtained from (XY) plane and (YZ) plane measurements is
(0.66 ± 0.21) µm. This value is in good agreement with the ones reported for LBM
alloy 718, such as by [ 8] (0.500 µm) and [ 10] (0.689 µm). From these measure-
ments, the corresponding solidi ﬁcation rate for as-fabricated LBM microstructure
may be estimated using the following expression, primarily proposed by Hunt [ 11]
for cellular or dendritic solidi ﬁcation, and later assessed by Quested and McLean
[12] for directionally solidi ﬁed nickel-based superalloys:

cess, which are typically of the order of magnitude of 10 5–106 Ks −1 [14, 15]. For
comparison, in cast alloy 718 microstructures, typical values of PDAS range from
40 µm to more than 200 µm (Fig. 2b): using values of G reported in [ 12], the
corresponding cooling rates calculated with Eq. ( 2) range from 9 × 10 −2 to
6×1 0 1 Ks −1. The main conclusion of these calculations is that alloy 718 cooling
rate in LBM is at least 4 orders of magnitude higher than in conventional casting.
These two major differences, in time and space scales, regarding solidi ﬁcation
phenomena encountered in conventional manufacturing (casting) and additive
manufacturing (LBM) are fundamental to understand the other LBM microstruc-
tural speci ﬁcities presented below.

Texture
As mentioned above, the as-fabricated alloy 718 presents a macroscopic texture
induced by laser scanning pattern. This texture, referred as fabrication texture in the
following (visible in Fig. 1), is a general feature of this manufacturing process, and
is susceptible to affect mechanical properties; this last point is discussed in sec-
tion “Tensile Tests”. The second level of texture investigated in this study is found
at the polycrystal scale, and results from two contributions: morphological texture ,
i.e. preferential shape orientation of non-equiaxed grains, and crystallographic
texture, i.e. preferential crystalline orientation of the grains. With respect to mor-
phological texture, it may be seen from Fig. 1 that the as-fabricated, as well as heat
treated metallurgical states are characterized by columnar grains, preferentially
oriented in the building direction, Z. This texture was commonly reported in lit-
erature, and results from the directional nature of the LBM process, with heat ﬂuxes
(input and output) mainly oriented along the vertical Z axis, leading to local so-
lidiﬁcation conditions close to those encountered, for instance, in directional cast-
ing. This aspect, coupled with the layer-by-layer fabrication pattern which
emphasize dendrite nucleation at the bottom of the melt pools, lead to a preferential
dendritic growth along the Z axis during solidi ﬁcation (Fig. 3a). It is interesting to
notice that a same grain may grow through several melt pools. As illustrated by
Fig. 3b, dendrite growth orientation mainly depends on which point they nucleate
on the melt pool interface, along with the orientation of the solidi ﬁed dendrite tips
on which they may nucleate. If the dendrites at the solid —melt pool interface are
oriented parallel to the interface normal direction, new dendrites in the melt may
nucleate on the tips of the former ones and grow in the same direction. As a result,
Fig. 3 Solidiﬁcation texture in the LBM as-fabricated state that shows the a dendrite orientations

(black arrows), the dendrite growth perpendicular to the orientation of the melt pool interface

It is worth noticing that the morphological texture is mostly conserved after heat
treatments (HSA1 or HSA2). EBSD analysis was carried out on the HSA2

edges were excluded): an average elliptical aspect ratio of (2.9 ± 1.7) was calcu-

EBSD results for the as-fabricated and HSA1 states were not available, but it may at
least qualitatively be concluded that the heat treatments applied on LBM alloy 718
does not erase the microstructural texture (fabrication texture or morphological
texture). In fact, the effect of those heat treatments on the two levels of textures
seems moderate when comparing the microstructures presented in Fig. 1. These
results are in general agreement with the literature on laser beam melting of alloy
718: see for instance [ 8, 17–19].
Phase Identi ﬁcation
XRD measurements were not really conclusive regarding phase identi ﬁcations: for
all 3 metallurgical states, FCC matrix γ was the only phase identi ﬁed (no other
diffraction peaks). Similar results for LBM alloy 718 have been reported for this
technique [ 8, 10, 19], which may seem surprising with regard to the effect of
standard heat treatment HSA1 on conventionally manufactured alloy 718. An
electrolytic extraction of the precipitates was therefore performed on an HSA2
sample, and the powder residue obtained analyzed by XRD, where γ″ and NbC
(Fm
3m) phases were unambiguously identi ﬁed, each contributing to a strong
diffraction signal for this analysis. The γ matrix (dissolved by the extraction pro-
cess), γ′ or δ phase were absent from the XRD spectrum.
Further phase identi ﬁcation was carried out on etched samples by SEM analyses.
As shown in Fig. 5, several phases may be found in the as-fabricated state: they are
mostly segregated in interdendritic regions or at grain boundaries, where they form
an almost continuous precipitation ﬁlm. EDS analyses shows that interdendritic and

Structural and Chemical Heterogeneities —Effect of Heat Treatments
As described in section “Microstructural Scales”, LBM as-fabricated microstructure
is structured at 3 different scales: the fabrication texture scale (melt pools), the
polycrystalline structure scale (grains), and the solidi ﬁcation scale (dendrites). Each
scale contribute to the structural heterogeneity of the laser beam melted alloy,
which is only partially reduced by the application of heat treatments (Fig. 1).
Regarding structural periodicity induced by scanning parameters (i.e. melt pools
size and spacing), as shown in Fig. 6a and Fig. 1 the melt pools and laser scanning
pattern persists after heat treatments, either in the form of grain morphology texture

## Page 713

or precipitation, depending on the level of element segregation at melt pool inter-
faces. At intermediate scales, grain size distribution is also a source of structural
heterogeneity. Comparison of LBM and cold-rolled 718 microstructures on Fig. 4
(both being heat treated with similar heat treatments) lead to an average grain size
of (18 ± 25) µm for HSA2 LBM alloy, and 25 µm for the cold-rolled alloy. In spite
of these relatively close values, grain size distribution ranges are very different:
(3–290) µm for LBM alloy 718, compared to (5 –40) µm for cold-rolled alloy 718.
Grain size distribution is therefore much more heterogeneous in LBM mi-
crostructure compared to cold rolled products. This heterogeneity is correlated with
the presence of large grains for both heat-treated states. Grain recovery was con-
ﬁrmed by EBSD analysis on HSA2 state, as shown by local misorientation map in
Fig. 4b.
Similarly to structural heterogeneity, chemical heterogeneity may be described at
different microstructural scales: chemical segregation in interdendritic spaces (i.e.
minor segregation), chemical segregation between dendrite packs (i.e. intergranular
segregation) and difference in segregation intensity between zones of different
cooling rates (e.g. melt pool interfaces). These segregations, illustrated on Fig. 5a,
inﬂuence phase distribution in the microstructure, depending on the heat treatment
applied on the as-fabricated state. One of the key feature of LBM microstructure is
that the chemical gradient spatial periodicity (primarily dendrite arm spacing) is,
compared with casting, orders of magnitude lower in LBM alloy 718. This simple
fact has direct consequences on all diffusion-based phenomena in LBM mi-
crostructure, as well as on the maximum size of precipitates that may be formed
from these interdendritic segregations (Fig. 5b), thus impacting mechanical prop-
erties and heat treatments de ﬁnitions. Put differently, the formation of large carbides
or Laves phases, often referred as detrimental in conventionally cast alloy 718
(ingots), is prevented in LBM alloy 718 by the small size of PDAS in its
microstructure.

Tensile Tests
Effect of the Manufacturing Orientation at 20 °C
The results of tensile test performed at 20 °C and 8.0 × 10 −5 s−1 on vertical
(Z) and horizontal (X) tensile specimens for HSA1 state, and vertical (Z) specimens
for HSA2 are presented in Fig. 8. In the stress-strain curves presented below,
circular end point is used for vertical (Z) tensile specimens, square end point is used
for horizontal (X) specimens and dashed line is used for cold-rolled and aged 718.
At room temperature of 20 °C, the HSA1 and HSA2 states exhibit almost
identical tensile properties and mechanical behavior in the vertical (Z) direction.
This observation is consistent with microstructural similarities identi ﬁed in section
“Microstructural Characterizations” between these states. For HSA1 state, results of
tensile tests performed on vertical (Z) and horizontal (X) directions demonstrate
moderate anisotropy of the mechanical properties: yield and tensile strengths are 4%
higher, and elongation to failure is 11% lower for horizontal (X) direction than for
vertical (Z) direction. This anisotropy is a consequence of the microstructural
texture evidence in section “Texture”, where morphological texture is likely to be
main contribution. These results are consistent with those reported by [ 8, 18], who
also found mechanical anisotropy of the same order of magnitude on LBM 718
alloy heat treated with similar conditions as HSA1. As shown in Fig. 8, the fracture
surfaces were transgranular ductile for all tested specimens. A closer observation

## Page 716

Regarding the effect of the manufacturing direction on tensile behavior evolution
with temperature, it is observed that the trend at 450 °C is the same as at 20 °C for
the yield and tensile strengths, but is inversed for the elongation to failure, which is
higher for horizontal (X) specimens than vertical (Z) ones at 450 °C. At 650 °C, the
effect of the manufacturing orientation on yield and tensile strengths is almost
non-existent, but the effect is dramatically increased for elongation to failure
compared with 20 °C. The augmented anisotropy of elongation to failure at 650 °C
may be related with differences in crack propagation modes between these two
orientations, as it may be seen from fracture surfaces observations in Fig. 9. These
anisotropy effects will be discussed in a future publication.
Regarding deformation modes evolution with temperature, it worth noticing that
specimens tested at 450 °C exhibit PLC effect ( Portevin Le Chatelier , also known
as serrated yielding), while tests performed at 650 °C stay in the continuous plastic
ﬂow regime, called DSA ( Dynamic Strain Aging ) due to the dynamic interactions
between diffusing elements and mobile dislocations occurring with plastic defor-
mation. In fact, PLC effect is a speci ﬁc manifestation of the DSA phenomenon, but
these domains will be distinguished here for simpli ﬁcation purpose. Another
interesting observation is that the fracture mode is different between these two
temperatures. Fracture surfaces are transgranular ductile for tensile tests performed
at 450 °C, while intergranular fracture is observed at 650 °C. In addition, fracture
surfaces at 650 °C exhibit clear signs of oxidation on the crack initiation and stable
propagation zones, indicating that intergranular fracture is, in this case, correlated
with the effect of oxidation (tensile test in vacuum are scheduled to con ﬁrm this
coupling effect).
Effect of Strain Rate on HSA2 Tensile Behavior
In order to study the effect of strain rate on mechanical behavior of LBM 718 alloy,
tensile tests were performed on vertical (Z) HSA2 tensile specimens at 650 °C in air
for 3 values of initial strain rate: 8.0 × 10
−5, 1.0 × 10 −3 and 3.0 × 10 −2 s−1.
These values were purposely chosen to correspond to each domain of deformation
mode—fracture mode interactions reported in previous studies for cold rolled alloy
718 [ 5].
As shown in Fig. 10, the evolution of tensile properties at 650 °C with strain rate
may be described as follows: at low strain rate (8.0 × 10
−5 s−1), plastic ﬂow is
continuous and elongation to failure is moderate, while at intermediate strain rate
(1.0 × 10 −3 s−1), plastic ﬂow is also continuous, and elongation to failure is com-
parable to the value obtain at 20 °C; lastly, at high strain rate (3.0 × 10 −2 s−1),
plastic ﬂow is serrated and elongation to failure is decreased by half of its value at
20 °C. Yield and tensile strengths were weakly dependent on strain rate, while
elongation to failure was strongly dependent. When comparing the fracture surfaces
of these tests, it may be seen that tensile test performed at low strain rate is associated
with intergranular fracture, similar to the results obtained for HSA1 at 650 °C. For
intermediate strain rate, both intergranular and transgranular zones were observed;

alloy 718 manufactured by Laser Beam Melting. However, as reviewed in the
introduction, these interactions have been extensively studied for conventionally
manufactured alloy 718. The test performed on LBM 718 alloy are plotted on the

• For the tests carried out in the DSA, propagation controlled regime (650 °C,

## Page 721

Two major phenomena arise from these experimental observations: ﬁrst, there
are strong experimental facts that showed a coupling effect between the mechanical
load and the oxidizing environment in the laser beam melted 718 alloy, leading to
oxidation-assisted intergranular cracking (OAIC) damage. This coupling effect
occurs, for LBM alloy 718, under the same temperature and strain rate conditions as
established for OAIC in a conventionally manufactured alloy 718 produced by
cold-rolling. In addition, these similarities of behavior between conventional and
LBM alloy 718 are not limited to the OAIC fracture mode, and also apply to the
deformation modes. As mentioned above, a transition from DSA (continuous
plastic ﬂow) to PLC (serrated plastic ﬂow) is observed for LBM 718 alloy when
increasing the strain rate at constant temperature, or increasing the temperature at a
given strain rate. It should be emphasized that, similar to the fracture mode, the
deformation mode transition observed for LBM alloy 718 occurs under similar
experimental conditions as the ones established for conventional alloy 718.
To summarize, the experimental work carried out in this study examines de-
formation mode—fracture mode interactions in laser beam melted alloy 718. In the
DSA domain, LBM alloy 718 exhibits sensitivity to oxidation-assisted intergranular
cracking. When approaching the DSA-PLC transition zone, the sensitivity to OAIC
is progressively reduced, resulting in inhibited intergranular crack propagation and
moderate crack initiation. The occurrence of PLC effect completely suppresses the
intergranular damage, leading to a fully transgranular ductile failure. It is striking
that these deformation mode —fracture mode interactions are consistent for both
LBM and conventionally manufactured alloy 718, in spite of the numerous dif-
ferences in microstructure. This last point may indicate that microstructural
parameters such as grain size, texture, or even phase distribution are not, in this
case, involved to a ﬁrst order in the mechanisms controlling these two phenomena,
namely fracture mode —deformation mode interactions, and OAIC. Although the
effect of texture and precipitation state are not negligible (as it will be shown in a
future paper), the present study emphasizes the importance of studying ﬁner mi-
crostructural scales in order to provide a complete description of the mechanisms
involved in the two aforementioned phenomena: crossed interactions between
solute elements, mobile dislocations and interfaces networks.
Conclusion and Perspectives
In this paper, the microstructural speci ﬁcities of laser beam melted alloy 718 were
investigated for 3 metallurgical states: as-fabricated, HAS1 (solutioned at 1095 °C/
2 h (AC) and double-aged at 720 °C/8 h, (FC) at 55 °C/h, then 620 °C/8 h (AC))
and HSA2 (solutioned at 1095 °C/3 h (AC) and double-aged at 760 °C/5 h, (FC) at
55 °C/h, then 650 °C/1 h, (AC)). Tensile behavior under several temperature and
strain rate conditions was examined for HSA1 and HSA2 states. Main results are
summarized as follows:

• Laser Beam Melted alloy 718 exhibit pronounced microstructural differences
compared with conventionally manufactured (e.g. cold-rolled) alloy 718: the
LBM microstructure is ﬁner, more textured and heterogeneous than its con-
ventional counterpart.
• Application of standard heat treatments on the LBM as-fabricated material lead
to moderate microstructural modi ﬁcations: hardening precipitation is similar to
conventional 718, but homogenization is very limited regarding structural
heterogeneity.
• Tensile behavior of LBM alloy 718 at 20 °C is very similar to cold-rolled and
aged 718, and exhibit a slight degree of anisotropy, commonly expected for this
additive manufacturing technique.
• A coupling effect between oxidation and mechanical loading, resulting in oxi-
dation-assisted intergranular cracking, was evidenced for laser beam melted 718
alloy; furthermore, the OAIC was observed in similar temperature and strain rate
conditions as for conventional 718.
• Relationships between fracture modes and deformation modes for laser beam
melted 718 are consistent with the ones previously established for conven-
tionally manufactured 718, in spite of fundamentally different microstructures. It
may thus be concluded that typical microstructure parameters —such as grain
size, morphology, phase distribution, etc. —are unlikely involved in these
interactions, at least not at the ﬁrst order.
These results may be used to narrow down the list of metallurgical factors
controlling these interactions to lower scales. In other words, microstructural
speciﬁcities of LBM could be used as an opportunity to enhance our current
understanding of deformation mode —fracture mode interactions in alloy 718.

## Page 724

Precipitation Behavior and Mechanism
of Sigma Phase in Alloy 925
Zhaoxia Shi, Xiaofeng Yan and Chunhua Duan
Abstract The aim of the present work was to investigate the precipitation behavior
and mechanism of the sigma ( σ) phase in Alloy 925 by employing several com-
plementary techniques of microstructural analysis and thermodynamic calculations.
The thermal exposures were performed at 650, 750 and 850 °C for different times,
after which the thermally exposed specimens were studied and compared in terms
of their microstructure and the micro-hardness of γ matrix. It was found that the
chemical composition of σ phase in Alloy 925 could be represented as (Cr,Mo)
6(Ni,
Fe)5 with the lattice parameters a = 0.878 nm and c = 0.457 nm. Higher local
concentrations of Cr and Mo in the γ matrix caused by the formation of γ′ phase
and η phase resulted in the formation of σ phase along the grain boundaries and in
the vicinity of η phase. Higher contents of Cr, Mo, Al, Ti and Nb in the alloy could
accelerate the formation of σ phase. The increase in C content could inhibit the
precipitation of σ phase. The formation of σ phase most likely occurred during the
thermal exposure at 750 °C. The amount of σ phase was remarkably increased with
the thermal exposure time increasing, which led to the softening of γ matrix.
Keywords Precipitation behavior ⋅ Precipitation mechanism ⋅ Sigma phase
Alloy 925 ⋅ Thermal exposure

Introduction
Alloy 925 is widely used in applications that require high strength and excellent
corrosion resistance such as oil and natural gas production, marine and energy
industries. [ 1, 2]. However, the relatively high contents of chromium and molyb-
denum make the alloy unstable because of the formation of sigma ( σ) phase, which
becomes a severe problem when the heat treatment, welding or hot working process
is inappropriate or the alloy is used for a long duration at elevated temperature.
Once formed, σ phase is known to severely deteriorate the mechanical and
anti-corrosion properties of the alloy, which can shorten the service life of structural
components [ 3–5].
σ phase is a topologically closed-packed (TCP) phase that can form in
nickel-based alloys, which has the tetragonal crystal structure with a c/a ratio of
0.52 [ 6, 7]. It contains 30 atoms in the repeat cell and belongs to the D
14
4h space
group, with a composition range of AB 7 to A7B, where A and B commonly are Cr
and Mo and/or Ni and Co in nickel-based superalloys [ 8–10]. For instance, the
formula of σ phase in U720 and U720Li can be given as (Cr 0.5,M o 0.1), (Ni 0.2,
Co0.2)[ 4]. So far, the knowledge about the precipitation behavior and mechanism of
σ phase in nickel-based alloy with high content of Fe are rarely reported, resulting
in the lack of theoretical basis for improving the performance of Alloy 925 by
controlling the formation of σ phase.
The aim of the present work was therefore to investigate the precipitation
behavior of σ phase in Alloy 925 during thermal exposure and elucidate its pre-
cipitation mechanism. Finally, the suggestions for avoiding the σ phase formation
were proposed.
Materials and Methods
The chemical composition of the material used in this research is given in Table 1.
The alloy was manufactured using a 25 kg vacuum induction furnace and then hot
forged into bars with diameter of about 16 mm. Then the hot forged bars were cut
into samples with the dimension of Φ10 mm × 10 mm. Subsequently, the samples
were solution treated at 980 °C for 1 h and quenched in water to obtain approxi-
mately single-phase of austenite ( γ) except for MC-type carbide. Heat treatments
for acquiring precipitation were performed at 650, 750 and 850 °C for different time
ranging from 1 h up to 2025 h, followed by water quenching.

A phase extraction technique combined with X-ray diffraction (XRD) was used for

Results
Initial Microstructure and Equilibrium Phases
The microstructure in initial condition after solution treatment is presented in
Fig. 1. As indicated in Fig. 1, austenitic equiaxed grains are shown after solution
treatment. The visible particles are identi ﬁed as the MC-type carbide that cannot be
eliminated by solution treatment. The intermetallic phase cannot be detected in the
initial microstructure.
Thermodynamic database models such as JMatPro software can be adopted to
predict the equilibrium phases formed in the alloy system. Figure 2 shows the
equilibrium phase diagram calculated by using JMatPro software for the experi-
mental Alloy 925, which indicates the formation of η phase, MC-type and M 23C6-
type carbide and σ phase. The initial precipitation temperature of σ phase is cal-
culated to be 872 °C. In addition, the composition of σ phase can also be

Effect of Alloying Element Content on the Formation
of σ Phase
To systematically investigate the precipitation behavior of σ phase, the effect of
alloying element content on the initial precipitation temperature and the maximum
precipitation amount of σ phase were calculated by JMatPro, as shown in Fig. 5.I t
can be seen that with the content of alloying element such as Cr, Mo, Al, Ti and Nb
increasing within the speci ﬁed limits, both the initial precipitation temperature and
the maximum precipitation amount of σ phase increase. The acceleration of Cr and
Mo on the formation of σ phase is more signi ﬁcant than that of Ti, Al and Nb.
Conversely, as C content rises, the formation of σ phase is decreased.

## Page 729

Figure 6 shows the effect of alloying element content on the TTT curve for the
precipitation of σ phase. It can be seen that with the increase in Cr and Mo content,
the nose temperature for the formation of σ phase is remarkably increased and its
formation incubation period is signi ﬁcantly decreased, which is identical with that
reported in hyper duplex stainless steel [ 11]. The increase in Al and Ti content also
can facilitate the rapid precipitation of σ phase at high temperature. Nb content
has no apparent impact on the TTT curve of σ phase. However, the increase of C
content has the opposite effect on the σ phase formation. That is, the elevated C
content could retard the precipitation of σ phase. It follows that the medium level of
alloying element is favorable to minimize the formation of σ phase while main-
taining the excellent performance. Therefore, the chemical composition of Alloy
925 used in this study is designed according to the medium level of speci ﬁed limits.
Precipitation Characteristics of σ Phase
According to the calculated equilibrium precipitation temperature and the TTT
diagram nose temperature of σ phase, the thermal exposures at 650, 750 and 850 °C
for different times were carried out. With the specimen exposed at 750 °C for 225 h
as the representative, the precipitation characteristics of σ phase in Alloy 925 was
investigated. Figure 7 shows the microstructure of Alloy 925 exposed at 750 °C for
225 h. The microstructure consisted of a large number of precipitate phases which
appeared as block and needle shapes along the grain boundaries (Fig. 7a). Globular
γ′ particles are distributed in the γ matrix, as shown in Fig. 7b. The γ′

Discussion
Under the exposure conditions studied in the present work, the precipitation
behavior of σ phase can be summarized as follows: Firstly, the thermal exposure at
750 °C will result in the maximum precipitation amount of σ phase for the same
exposure time. Secondly, the amount of σ phase has been increased signi ﬁcantly
with the prolonging of exposure time at 750 °C. Previous researches have shown
that it is unfavorable for the long-range diffusion of the σ phase-forming elements
such as Cr and Mo at low temperature, which will result in the insuf ﬁcient growth
driving force for the formation of σ phase [7, 14]. Therefore, when the specimen is
exposed at 650 °C, the precipitation of γ′ phase from γ matrix is the main form of
microstructural evolution, which will cause the the micro-hardness of γ matrix to
gradually increase with exposure time. At the beginning of exposure at 750 °C, the
micro-hardness of the matrix will be increased due to the precipitation of γ′ phase.
The precipitation of σ phase at 750 °C can be attributed to the enhanced diffusion of
Cr and Mo at high temperature and the consequent elevated growth dynamic of σ
phase. However, the formation of σ phase will inevitably deplete the strong solution
strengtheners such as Cr and Mo in the γ matrix during thermal exposure and then
weaken the solid-solution strengthening effect, which is the main reason for the
matrix softening with the further exposure time at 750 °C [ 4, 7]. The decrease in the
micro-hardness of the γ matrix may be considered as an indicator of σ phase
formation, which will be studied in the future. Furthermore, the micro-hardness of
the γ matrix continually decreases at 750 °C after about 25 h, and that probably
means the amount of σ phase continues to increase. When the alloy is exposed at
850 °C, needle-like η phase is directly precipitated from γ matrix along grain
boundaries. In addition, some precipitated γ′ phase tend to get converted to η phase.
With the exposure time increasing, η phase signi ﬁcantly precipitates along grain
boundaries and extends into the grains, resulting in the large γ′ phase-depleted
zone. Therefore, the micro-hardness of γ matrix will be decreased rather than
increased with the increase in exposure time at 850 °C.
The JMatPro software predicted 0.01% σ phase formation in 4.4 h (Fig. 4) while
the precipitation of σ phase has been quantitatively identi ﬁed by XRD after 27 h of
thermal exposure at 750 °C. However, the initial precipitation time has not been
determined by experiments in the present work. Based on the microstructural
evolution during thermal exposure, the precipitation mechanism of σ phase in Alloy
925 can be summarized schematically in Fig. 14, in which grain boundary is a long
line, γ matrix is white, γ′ phase is a dot, η phase is a short line and σ phase is a
sector. Prior to thermal exposure (t
0 = 0), the microstructure is single-phase of
austenite. After t1 (t1 >t 0) time exposure, the ﬁrst observation is the precipitation of
γ′ phase from the γ matrix, which will lead to the early increase of micro-hardness.
With the further increase of exposure time (t 2 >t 1), η phase begins to form along
the grain boundaries. The precipitations of γ′ phase and η phase will result in the
local accumulation of Cr and Mo in the γ matrix and around the η phase. As Cr and
Mo are major formers of σ phase, the concentration of these solutes in the γ matrix
Precipitation Behavior and Mechanism of Sigma Phase in Alloy 925 745

## Page 735

likely serve as the primary driving force for the nucleation of σ phase [ 9, 15, 16].
t3 (t3 >t 2) time after, when the concentration of the γ matrix is enriched suf ﬁciently
in Cr and Mo, σ phase nucleates and grows, occurring both along the grain
boundaries and in adjacent to the η phase.
On one hand, the high content of Cr and Mo in the alloy will promote the
precipitation of σ phase. On the other hand, the high content of Al, Ti and Nb will
facilitate the formation of γ′ phase and η phase, causing the higher local concen-
tration of Cr and Mo in the γ matrix and the consequent easy precipitation of σ
phase. However, higher C content in the alloy will promote the formation of M 23C6,
which consumes the concentration of Cr in the γ matrix and then inhibits the
formation of σ phase. Therefore, it is advisable to control the content of Cr and Mo
at low level of speci ﬁed limits to decrease the susceptibility to the precipitation of σ
phase. High content of C is desirable for reducing σ phase formation. The content
of Al, Ti and Nb should be controlled at medium level within the speci ﬁed limits to
avoid the formation of σ phase while retaining adequate mechanical performance.
Furthermore, the thermal exposure at 750 °C longer than 25 h should be avoided to
reduce susceptibility to the formation of σ phase and that at 850 °C should also be
averted to retain the performance of the alloy.

746 Z. Shi et al.

## Page 736

Conclusions
Based on the observations and results obtained in this work, the following con-
clusions can be reported:
(1) When Alloy 925 was thermally exposed at 750 °C, σ phase formation occurred
both along the grain boundary and in the vicinity of the η phase, having typical
chemical composition given by (Cr,Mo) 6(Ni,Fe)5, lattice parameters
a = 0.878 nm and c = 0.457 nm. The formation of σ phase was not detected in
Alloy 925 thermally exposed at 650 and 850 °C, at least for the exposure times
studied here.
(2) The precipitation of σ phase during the thermal exposure at 750 °C could be
attributed to the intensi ﬁed diffusion of Cr and Mo at high temperature and the
locally elevated concentrations of Cr and Mo in the γ matrix due to the for-
mation of γ′ phase and η phase, which provided a higher driving force for phase
formation. The amount of σ phase formed at 750 °C increased with thermal
exposure time prolonging, which was the main reason for the softening of γ
matrix.
(3) For Alloy 925, a low level of Cr and Mo, medium level of Al, Ti and Nb as well
as high level of C within the speci ﬁed limits is bene ﬁcial to alleviate the
formation of σ phase and maintain the ideal performance. Furthermore, it is not
recommended to conduct heat treatment at the temperature close to or higher
than 750 °C.

Jian Liu, Qian Chen, Yunhao Zhao, Wei Xiong and Albert To
Abstract The lack of a reliable theoretical model of the processing-microstructure
relationship of AM (Additive Manufacturing) material is preventing AM technol-
ogy from being widely adopted by the manufacturing community. The goal of this
work is to establish the link between the microstructure (texture) and the process
parameters of metal AM processes. A quantitative method based on the epitaxial
growth of columnar grains within and across melt pools is proposed to predict the
texture formation during a metal AM process. The state-of-the-art
CALPHAD-informed FEM ( ﬁnite element method) simulation has been used to
predict the geometry and thermal pro ﬁle of the quasi-steady melt pool. The thermal
gradient distribution within the 3D melt pool determines the crystallography
direction and growth direction of the columnar grains within each deposited single
tracks. The single tracks with the predicted geometry are amalgamated together to
represent the bulk part, and the epitaxial growth of grains across the boundary of
neighboring tracks are quantitatively modeled. The proposed method is calibrated
and validated by experimental studies of metal AM processed Alloy 718.
Keywords Additive manufacturing
⋅ Inconel 718 ⋅ Microstructure
Introduction
The objective of this research is to develop a part-scale process-microstructure
simulation tool to predict the microstructure evolution of Alloy 718 processed by
powder bed laser fusion process integrating FEM thermal analysis and grain texture
modeling. A great research interest of additive manufactured Alloy 718 is
improving the performance of structural components for high temperature appli-
cations such as jet engine parts, where both creep and strength are critical and need
to be designed for. The methodology developed in the proposed research will

our columnar grain growth model is applicable. The columnar dendrite mode is also

Columnar Grain Growth Model for Texture Prediction
A new Lagrangian approach for simulating columnar grain growth is proposed
based on solidi ﬁcation theory. The solidi ﬁcation morphology of metals depending
on the thermal gradient and solidi ﬁcation rate values at the solid-liquid interface [ 3].
In the case of columnar dendrite mode solidi ﬁcation in AM, dendrite arms will
grow epitaxially from the seed crystal provided by the base metal, since the solid
(base) metal and the liquid metal have similar chemical composition and the same
crystal structure. Each dendrite arm will have the same crystallographic orientation
as its seed crystal. The polycrystal base provides different seed crystals of different
orientations at different locations. Within a small element surface around a point,
the crystallographic orientation of the dendrite arm grow from this location can be
determined if we know the 3D microstructure of the substrate. The growing
direction of the dendrite will be along one of the <001> axis of its crystallographic
orientation (the one that is most closely aligned with the local thermal gradient
vector) [ 4]. In the proposed grain growth model, the dendrite arms were simpli ﬁed
as line segments and the growth of the arms will be simpli ﬁed as the tracking of
moving front point of each dendrite arm line. Such a Lagrangian approach is
expected to be much more computationally ef ﬁcient than the Eulerian approach
such as cellular automaton [ 5–8]. At each step in the proposed approach, the growth
direction of each dendrite arm line needs to be evaluated, since the local thermal
gradient is changing, and hence the growth direction could change from one crystal
<001> axis direction to another. While the dendrite arms grow from the same seed
crystal are mostly parallel to each other, dendrite arms from different neighboring
seed crystals will be either converging or diverging. For the converging case, the
competition of dendrites and the growth of more preferred dendrites over the less
preferred arms need to be incorporated into the model. For the diverging case, the
branching mechanism needs to be incorporated to generate new dendrite arms to ﬁll
the gap between diverging primary dendrites. A 2D case demonstration of the grain
growth model is shown in Fig. 2. After the growth, the dendrite arms grown from
the same seed crystal will have identical crystallographic orientation and can be
grouped into one columnar grain that has a 3D shape and volume. The resulting
overall texture of one scan track can be obtained by adding each columnar grain
orientation and its associated weight (volume) into a collection. An ideal shallow
melt pool (W/D = 3) is employed as input to predict the grain growth and the
resulting texture of a single track scan (Fig. 3). The computation time for such as a
simulation was about 10 min on the desktop computer.

## Page 743

Conclusions
In this research, FEM thermal analysis of melt pool geometry and thermal pro ﬁles
in single track depositions is performed and employed as input for texture pre-
diction. An ef ﬁcient epitaxial columnar grain growth model is developed to predict
grain growth and resulting texture. EBSD measurement of the transverse (Y-Z
plane) cross-section is then used to validate the grain growth model. A good match
between prediction and experiments has been observed. The columnar grain growth
model will be extended from single track to multiple tracks and multiple layers to
study effects of processing parameters (hatching space, layer thickness and scan-
ning strategy, etc.) on the texture evolution in 3D bulk part additive manufacturing.

Cracking the 718 Alloy Using In-Situ
Observation
Lu Xudong, Du Jinhui, Deng Qun, Wang Minqing, Bi Zhongnan
and Zhang Yuchun
Abstract The 718 alloy possesses excellent mechanical properties at high tem-
peratures, good process ability, therefore, it has been widely used in aero engine
turbine disks, compressor disks, and power turbine shafts (i.e., rotating compo-
nents). The fatigue properties of the 718 alloy are a key factor that determines the
safety and reliability of the engine. In this paper, the fatigue properties of the 718
alloy are investigated under high temperature conditions at 455 and 600 °C. The
initiation of fatigue cracks, and the relationship between fatigue life and grain size
are discussed. The results show that the twin boundaries in large grains and carbides
are acting as a crack initiation site for plate specimens, and string-type or heap-type
carbides distribution promotes crack propagation and shortens fatigue life. Carbides
respond as a crack initiation site for cylindrical specimens. The grain size is smaller,
and the low cycle fatigue properties of the alloy are improved.
Keywords In-situ
⋅ Low cycle fatigue ⋅ Crack propagation ⋅ Slip bands
Introduction
Polycrystalline nickel-based superalloys are widely used to manufacture turbine
disks in aerospace and power generation industries because of their excellent bal-
ance of mechanical and chemical properties at elevated temperature [ 1, 2]. Among
the Ni-base superalloys, 718 is predominantly used in high-temperature applica-

## Page 746

tions due to its highly satisfactory price/overall performance ratio, good corrosion
resistance and mechanical properties with excellent weldability. The major appli-
cations of this alloy are turbine discs in gas turbine engines [ 3–5]. The operational
lifetimes of rotating components comprising 718 alloy are determined by me-
chanical properties, especially the creep and fatigue properties [ 6–8]. 718 alloy
components were used in service experience in monotonic, cyclic and sustained
static loading in an oxidising environment under elevated temperatures. Once a
crack has initiated, it may grow as a result of further cyclic loading. The grain
boundaries may, on the one hand, assist crack channeling as surfaces of reduced
cohesion; or may, on the other hand, appear as barriers for microcrack growth in
polycrystalline materials. The micro-mechanisms of crack growth vary signi ﬁcantly
with temperature, environment, type of loading, microstructure and their conjoined
effects [ 9]. Cyclic plastic strain localization and the formation of persistent slip
bands are the primary mechanisms responsible for microstructural fatigue crack
initiation, and their formation is dependent on both intrinsic factors, such as mi-
crostructure and deformation mechanisms, and on experimentally imposed condi-
tion such as cyclic stress levels. Cyclic plastic strain localization is often associated
with local stress concentrations that arise from microstructure heterogeneities and
fatigue cracks have been found to initiate from large grains [ 10]. Statistical analysis
also shows that large grain size on the high end of the grain size distribution has
important effects on fatigue crack initiation [ 11]. Twin boundaries have also been
reported as sources for fatigue crack initiation in nickel-based superalloys [ 12].
However, the contributions of microstructure features, such as grain orientation and
twin boundaries, to cyclic strain localization still remain unclear. The variation in
these microstructural heterogeneities and synergistic combinations of these
microstructural features may also in ﬂuence fatigue crack initiation life, thus con-
tributing to the variability of fatigue life [ 13].
Numerous studies have demonstrated that in situ fatigue in scanning electron
microscopy (SEM), is an effective tool to investigate of the microstructural effects
of alloy on the development of slip features [ 14–16] and on crack initiation [ 17, 18].
In addition, the analysis of the mechanisms of crack growth and the quantitative
determination of small crack growth rates [ 19, 20], related research about crack and
crack tip opening displacements [ 21, 22], and further examination of interactions
between fatigue crack growth with the microstructure as well as for the inspection
of crack closure have been carried out recently [ 23].
In this paper, the main purpose is to study low cyclic fatigue behavior at various
temperatures. In the current study, the fatigue crack initiation behavior of a poly-
crystalline nickel-based superalloy 718 was examined in the fatigue lifetime region
from 10
4 to 106 cycles at 455 and 600 °C using an in situ fatigue test machine and
an MTS. Based on experimental observation, micromechanics of fatigue crack
nucleation in this alloy at 455 and 600 °C are analyzed.

Experimental Procedures
A forging bar of 718 alloy with a diameter of 80 mm, which was produced from
double vacuum melt (VIM/VAR) ingots, was used in the experiments. The
chemical composition (in wt%) was: Ni, 53.44; Cr, 18.56; Mo, 3.02; Nb, 5.3; Al,
0.44; Ti, 1.04; C, 0.026; P, 0.005; S, 0.001; B, 0.002; and Fe bal. It is typically
subjected to a solution and aging treatment, the exact temperature, time, and cooling
rate, depend on the needs of the speci ﬁc application. Engine parts, require high
tensile and fatigue strengths, and good stress-rupture properties; thus a solution
treatment below delta-solvus and a two-step aging treatment are needed. In this
study, the alloy was heat treated as follows in accordance with the AMS 5596
standard: solution annealing at 960 °C for 1 h; rapid cooling in water; precipitation
hardening at 720 °C for 8 h; furnace cooling to 620 °C; aging at 620 °C for 8 h;
and air cooling.
Cylindrical low-cycle fatigue (LCF) specimens were machined from the
heat-treated blanks with threaded ends (length, 30 mm; diameter, 12 mm; gage
section diameter, 5.5 mm; and shoulder radii, 25 mm). The gage sections of the
LCF specimens were mechanically polished by emery papers (3/0 and 4/0 grades).
Sylvet cloth with alumina powder was then used to remove machining marks to
produce a smooth surface. Low-cycle fatigue tests were carried out on a fully
computer-controlled servo hydraulic MTS testing machine with a capacity of 100
KN capacity and Teststar ’s interface. The frequency of the fatigue test was 10 Hz.
Fully reversed low-frequency fatigue tests were performed in air under total axial
stress control, until fracture occurred.
High-temperature in situ fatigue studies were conducted using scanning electron
microscopy (SEM). The characteristics of the specimen cross sections for SEM are
important and should be speci ﬁcally addressed. First, the specimens should have a
thin gauge section in order to minimize the temperature gradient. The heating
system employed in this study allows specimen temperature up to 800 °C. For
specimens with a gauge thickness of 1 mm, a maximum temperature gradient of
less than 10 °C can be obtained within the gauge length. Similarly, a thin sample
with a small surface area in the gauge length is optimum; meanwhile, the heat and

The geometries of the plate low-cycle fatigue specimens are shown in Fig. 1.
In situ fatigue tests were performed using a Shimadzo Servopulser controlled

to 10 Hz. To obtain images, the test rig was stopped at minimum load, and the load
was then increased in a stepwise manner. Images were taken at each step for further
analysis.
Disk samples for TEM studies were sectioned perpendicular to the loading axis
from the gauge section of the failed fatigue specimens. The samples were ﬁrst
mechanically processed to a thickness of about 100 μm. Discs were subsequently
punched from these ground samples, and these discs were thinned by dual jet
electropolishing at about 20 V. The electrolyte contained 70% butanol, 20% ethanol
and 10% perchloric acid. TEM analysis was performed using a JEOL JEM-2010
high-resolution transmission electron microscope to con ﬁrm the deformation
mechanisms.
Results and Discussion
The time-independent crack growth mode depends on three main parameters,
namely, frequency, load ratio and maximum load, and temperature. Since 718
superalloy is heavily used for high-temperature applications, its fatigue crack
growth behavior has been studied widely in order to understand the effects of
different parameters, such as temperature, environment and the microstructure. It is
understood that the variation of frequency affects the fracture mode of this material.
At higher frequencies transgranular failure occurs, as fatigue dominates, while at
lower frequencies creep/oxidation exert greater in ﬂuence. Experimental observa-
tions demonstrate that the fatigue crack growth rate (FCGR) in air increases with
decreasing loading frequency and is usually several orders of magnitude higher than
that in vacuum, as has been reported for other superalloys [ 24–26]. Furthermore,
the mode of fracture is transgranular in vacuum and, at relatively high frequency of
loading, also in air, while it is predominantly intergranular in an oxidizing envi-
ronment at intermediate frequencies.

In-Situ Observation High-Temperature Tension
High temperature tension of 718 alloy at 455 °C, is shown in the true stress-true
strain curve in Fig. 2. It can be found that yield strength and ultimate tensile
strength of alloy at 455 °C are 980 MPa and 1060 MPa, respectively. In the high
temperature tension process, when the stress exceeds that of the yield strength of
materials, slip bands are clearly visible, showing that the slip of dislocations is main
deformation method, as shown in Fig. 3. Figure 3a–c correspond to the ﬁrst, second
and third point in the stress-strain curve. At the ﬁrst point, the following features are
observed: dislocations gathered around carbides, harmonious plastic deformation
and a stress concentration exceeding the strength of the carbide, which leads to the
formation of microcrack. At the second point, several adjacent carbides crack. At
the third point, string carbides crack and the initial microcrack is open. Therefore,
the carbide is crack source of high temperature tension for 718 alloy.

## Page 750

In-Situ Observation of Low-Cycle Fatigue of Plate Specimens
For the ﬁne grained materials with carbides, and uniform distribution, there are no
string-type and heap-type arrangements. under the low cycle fatigue test conditions
with maximum stress of 905 MPa, stress ratio of 0.1, frequency of 10 Hz, and
temperature of 455 °C, for the grain sizes in ASTM 8 level, ASTM 9 level or
ASTM 10 lever, the primary fatigue microcrack initiates in twin boundary of the
large grain, as indicated in Fig. 4a–c. A low-stress state is not suf ﬁcient to actuate
the slip system in 718 alloy, and the main mode of plastic deformation is twining.
The uniform deformation reduces the local stress concentration, and minimizes
intergranular cracking, and decreases the stress concentration at grain boundaries.
With increasing numbers of cycles, deformation increases further, and the stress
concentration of the twins cannot be released. When the stress concentration
exceeds the interfacial strength, microcracks initiate in twin boundaries, eventually
leading to fracture.
Mismatch of coef ﬁcient of thermal expansion and elastic modulus between
carbides and the matrix lead to local stress concentration of high temperature plastic
deformation, and other forms of residual stress interaction around carbide cause the
larger stress concentration. Effect of external load leading to slip in the matrix, the
dislocations tangle around carbides, and the pile-up causes greater stress concen-
tration. The external load and larger stress concentration effect lead to fracture of
carbides or the interface between carbide and matrix, then forms a microcrack.
In the experiment performed at 455 °C, σmax = 850 MPa, R = 0.1 and 10 Hz,
the fatigue life of the specimen without string-type and heap-type carbides is
106,219 cycles, far higher than that of the specimen with string-type and heap-type
carbides (65,622 cycles). Therefore, string-type and heap-type carbides promote
crack propagation and shorten fatigue life. Figure 5 demonstrates that the micro-
cracks link with string-type carbides.

Effect of Grain Size
The relation between fatigue life and grain size, was studied at 455 °C, σmax =
850 MPa, R = 0.1 and 10 Hz. The average grain sizes of the 718 alloy specimens
were about 50, 20, 15, 10 and 5 μm, as shown in Fig. 6. The grain sizes were
measured according to ASTM E112-96 (Table 1).
As shown in Fig. 7, as grain size increases from 5 to 20 μm, the fatigue life of
718 alloy rapidly decreases from 378,706 cycles to 95,402 cycles. When grain size
further increases to 50 μm, fatigue life slowly decreases to 61,363 cycles. Figure 7
indicates the variation of the low cycle fatigue life versus the grain size of 718 alloy,
and it is shown that the low cycle fatigue life of 718 alloy increases with the
decreasing of grain size. Figure 7 shows for grain sizes ranging from 5 to 20 μm.
The slope of the grain size versus fatigue life curve is −1.89 × 10 4, for grain sizes
from 20 to 50 μm, the slope of the curve is −1.13 × 10 3.
The in ﬂection point of fatigue life curve corresponding to the grain size is 20
microns, which is about ASTM 8 level [ 12]. Therefore, for the 718 alloy, the ﬁne
grained materials with higher ASTM 8 grain size have excellent low cycle fatigue
properties. In polycrystalline materials, the fatigue crack growth mainly is

represented through dislocation slip realization. With the grains being further ﬁner,
grain boundary density become larger, which leads to dislocation slip encountering
more obstacles. As a result the fatigue crack growth rate reduced and low cycle
fatigue life is extended.
Under low cycle fatigue alternative load conditions, different grains have dif-
ferent slip system orientations, where the slip cannot continuously move from one
grain to another grain. The dislocations at grain boundaries are present in a pile-up,
which leads to a great concentration of stress [ 27, 28]. The dislocations of adjacent
grain moving and the occurrence of the corresponding slip dislocations are pro-
duced by external force, and stress concentration is released. Dislocation slip
occurred before restarts, then dislocations move from the grain and the crack
extends from one grain to another grain. The typical characteristic at this stage is
cleavage fracture facet, as shown in Fig. 8a.
As the stress intensity factor increases, cracks propagate along two slip systems,
either simultaneously or alternately. A double sliding mechanism is observed in the
second stage of fatigue crack growth. The most important microscopic characteristic
in this stage is fatigue striation, as shown in Fig. 8b. The fatigue facet is focus of
normal lines of fatigue striations. Therefore, the fatigue faces are the fatigue crack
initiation sites.
During the ﬁrst stage of fatigue crack propagation, dislocations are not easily
actuated since the dislocation density is large, and the pinning effect is strong; thus,
slip speed is slow. During the fast propagation stage, the pinning effect of dislo-
cations is small, and a large amount of extra stress is present; thus, slip speed
becomes fast. During the crack growth process, the stress state at the crack tip and

## Page 754

Low-Cycle Fatigue of Cylindrical Specimens
The fatigue fracture (obtained in the experiment performed at 600 °C, σmax =
1100 MPa, R = 0.1, and 10 Hz) show cleavage facets features, indicating obvious
oxidation (Fig. 10). Energy disperse spectroscopy (EDS) analysis further con ﬁrms
that the oxidation zone comprises clusters of NbC. Under low cycle fatigue con-
ditions, large alternating loads promote plastic deformation in the-matrix.
The mismatches in thermal expansion coef ﬁcient and elastic modulus between
carbides and the matrix lead to local stress concentrations. The dislocations tangle is
around carbides, and its pile-up causes a greater stress concentration. The external
load and larger stress concentration lead to cracking in the internal or interface of
carbides. The microcracks initiate in the internal or interface of carbides, and the
nearby cracks are interconnected (Fig. 5), the fatigue cracks expand further until
ﬁnal fracture.
Under low-cycle fatigue alternating loads, stress concentrates at carbides
(NbC) and cannot be released. Cracks initiate at the interface of carbides, and with
further crack propagation. Interior oxidation occurs via grain boundary diffusion at
the fatigue crack initiation site, where it is exposed at 600 °C in an air environment.
The formation of oxides promotes intergranular crack propagation. This experi-
mental phenomenon is in accord with literature [ 28]. Many experimental studies
show that the process of embrittlement during fatigue crack propagation occurs at
the crack tip. Both strain rate and stress and strain ﬁelds within the plastic zone
ahead of the crack tip play a signi ﬁcant role in the mechanism of oxygen-induced
intergranular fracture. The abrupt change in fracture mode con ﬁrms that the role of
oxygen is simply to reduce the grain boundary energy in such a way that the crack
growth path becomes intergranular. In this case, plastic deformation can still take
place within the grain, while slip bands serve as diffusion paths for oxygen to reach
the grain boundaries. When the crack front intercepts the grain boundaries, inter-
granular diffusion of oxygen takes place.
Nevertheless different crack growth mechanisms were identi ﬁed in this analysis,
such as microcracking followed by subsequent linking, and pure shearing. Grain

Conclusions
The fatigue crack initiation and propagation behavior of 718 alloy under low cycle
fatigue conditions at 455 and 600 °C have been investigated, and conclusions are as
follows:
(1) The twin boundaries in large grains or carbides act as a crack initiation sites for
plate LCF specimens. The carbides respond as a crack initiation site on
cylindrical LCF specimens. The string-type or heap-type carbides promote
crack propagation and shorten fatigue life.
(2) LCF life of 718 alloy increases with the decrease in grain size. For grain sizes
ranging from 5 to 20 μm, the slope of the grain size versus fatigue life curve is

Shear Spinning of Nickelbased
Super-Alloy 718
Fredrik Niklasson
Abstract Manufacturing of aerospace engine components by very high straining
methods require knowledge of the material response to solution heat treatment. This
paper presents evaluation of the shear-spinning forming process by experimenting,
with different heat treatment temperatures and time at temperature, to increase
knowledge of re-crystallisation of the strained grains. Spinning and shear-spinning
has the potential to replace conventional sheet metal forming methods for small to
medium volumes by reducing cost, increase ﬂexibility, lower forming forces and
reduced development time. The shear spinning performed resulted in an engi-
neering strain of 176% in the axial direction and −55% in the sheet thickness
direction. The hardness increased from HV
1.0 kg 228 to HV 1.0 kg 446. The heat
treatment experiments showed that the lower end solution treatment is suf ﬁcient to
reach full re-crystallisation in Alloy 718 even at a time as low as 20 min. Low to
medium temperatures resulted in signi ﬁcant grain size reduction due to
re-crystallisation. Using the higher end of the temperature range the original grain
size and hardness could be re-established. Low solution temperature resulted in an
increase of delta phase in the grain boundaries and inside the grains which was not
found at the higher temperatures.

Hardness
Introduction
Fabrication of aero components offers the potential to reduce weight (reduced CO 2
emission) and product cost. The concept of fabrication involves welding sheet metal
parts, castings and forgings together to utilise the unique characteristics of each
material condition. Spinning of sheet metal offers the potential to produce products

## Page 758

which are difﬁcult to produce by other sheet metal processes. It can reduce the total
cost due to less expensive tooling and as plasticity is localised to a small volume at
the point of forming, lower deformation forces are necessary [ 1]. Due to a longer
cycle time required, the process competes with, for example, deep drawing at low to
medium volumes.
Spinning is de ﬁned as a forming process that produces axial symmetric hollow
parts. Spinning is done by clamping a sheet metal blank onto a tool/mandrel and the
sheet is formed onto the tool surface with a roller. This can either be done by one or
several passes with the roller as described in Fig. 1. Metal spinning is often divided
into three groups: conventional spinning, shear spinning and tube spinning. Con-
ventional spinning is done in several passes with the roller and resulting in close to
zero reduction in sheet thickness. Shear spinning and tube spinning on the other
hand results in sheet thinning [ 1].
Shear spinning is typically achieved in one pass with the roller tool that results in
very high strain hardening [ 1, 2]. The relationship to predict the ﬁnal part thickness
is given by t1 = t0 sin α where t0 is the starting thickness, t 1 is the ﬁnal thickness and
α, the tool angle.
This paper presents an evaluation of shear formed Alloy 718 which has been
subjected to very high straining. High straining has to be taken into account during
further processing such as welding and heat treatment processes such as aging. The
effect of different solution heat treatment conditions and time at temperature has
been investigated to reduce the cold work and hardness by recrystallization before
further processing.

Materials and Experimental
The material used for this investigation was Alloy 718 (AMS5596) [ 3]. Alloy 718 is
a nickel base gamma super alloy, primarily double prime strengthened with a
contribution from gamma prime [ 4]. The main chemical composition of the tested
material in weight percent is presented in Table 1.
All shear spinning experiments were performed with the material in the solution
heat treated condition (solution heat treat in a continuous furnace at 982 °C for 2.6
min, air cooled) and an initial sheet thickness of 2.55 mm. The starting mi-
crostructure is presented in Figs. 2a, b, average grain size is 12.3 µm with hardness
of HV 1kg228.

presented in Fig. 3.
The test samples were cut out from the shear spun sheet in the axial/tangential
direction, Fig. 3, prior to heat treatment. Heat treatment was done in a pre-heated air
furnace (Nabertherm) with a tolerance of ±8 °C. Temperatures investigated were
954, 982 and 996 °C for times of 20, 40 and 60 min. The solution treated

Conclusions
In the presented work, heat treatments were performed on shear spun Alloy 718 to
re-establish original microstructure by re-crystallisation. The conclusions are:
 The material can withstand a very high amount of strain without fracturing. The
engineering strain was measured to 176% which is signi ﬁcant higher compared
to a tensile test. Due to severe straining the hardness increased with 96% after
shear spinning.
 All solution temperatures evaluated showed full re-crystallisation after 20 min.
 Lower solution temperatures resulted in a very ﬁne microstructure and was not
affected by time in furnace up to 60 min. The lower solution temperature
evaluated showed an increase of delta-phase and MC-carbides. Also,
delta-phase was observed inside the grains.
 The higher solution temperature resulted in a grain growth after 20 min at
temperature compared with the original grain size. Some indications was seen of
continuing grain growth for a longer period of time in the furnace due to loss of
delta phase pinning the grains.
 The hardness was reduced for all temperatures and was not effected by time at
temperature.
 The two lower solution temperatures did not fully restore the hardness due to a
very ﬁne microstructure and precipitations. The higher temperature restored the
hardness below the original hardness.
