Strain Controlled Low Cycle Fatigue
Behavior of U720Li Disk Superalloy
Above 700 °C
Fei Sun, Yuefeng Gu, Kyoko Kawagishi, Hideyuki Murakami
and Yoko Yamabe-Mitarai
Abstract The low cycle fatigue behaviors of Udimet 720Li (U720Li) and the
related microstructure evolution have been investigated at 725 °C under strain
control tests. The interrelationships between microstructure factors and properties
were analyzed using transmission electron backscatter diffraction (t-EBSD) in
scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM).
For comparison, LCF behaviors at 650 °C were also presented to ﬁnd the inferior
aspects of U720Li alloy at relatively higher service temperatures. The results show
that recrystallization occurs during the LCF testing at 725 °C. The extent of re-
crystallization increases with the strain. The LCF property at 725 °C is weakened to
a large extent after recrystallization, which could be the signi ﬁcant factor that
causes LCF degradation. Combination t-EBSD and TEM are bene ﬁcial for char-
acterizing and analyzing the microstructure evolution in terms of primary γ′ pre-
cipitates and dislocations, proposing that gliding dislocations could concentrate into
walls to form sub-grain boundaries, with the combination of primary γ′ precipitates
to form sub-grains.
Keywords U720Li
⋅ Disk superalloy ⋅ Low cycle fatigue ⋅ Microstructure
Transmission-EBSD ⋅ TEM
Introduction
Turbine engines create harsh environments for structural materials due to the high
operating temperatures and stress levels [ 1]. Continuous effort has been made to
develop new structural materials with excellent mechanical properties at elevated
temperatures for the structural components applications in turbine engines, such as
blades and disks. In view of the high speed of rotation and associated centrifugal

stresses experienced by disks, disk alloys should possess excellent properties in
fracture toughness, creep, and fatigue resistance. The chemistry of alloy 720Li
evolved from that of alloy 720, originally developed for blade application in
land-based gas turbines [ 2]. However, the high strength, excellent hot corrosion
resistance and particularly the excellent workability made the nickel-base superal-
loy U720Li interesting for turbine disk application [ 2, 3]. U720Li alloy is an
advanced commercial cast and wrought disk superalloy, which can be used to
around 675 °C.
Given the thermal cycling and stress state imposed on a turbine disk, low cycle
fatigue (LCF) properties are an important consideration in design of engines, and
thus must be understood [ 4]. However, the low cycle fatigue (LCF) behaviors and
related microstructural factors affecting fatigue performance of U720Li alloy at
temperatures above 700 °C has not been well documented. Therefore, to ﬁnd the
inferior aspects of U720Li alloy at relatively higher service temperatures is bene-
ﬁcial to develop new advanced disk superalloys.
Strain controlled LCF behavior and microstructure evolution in terms of basic
deformation microstructure, γ′ precipitates, dislocation con ﬁgurations and their
interactions with γ′ precipitates, as well as the interrelationships were analyzed
using transmission electron backscatter diffraction (t-EBSD) in scanning electron
microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to better under-
stand the microstructure effect on properties.
Materials and Experimental Procedure
The nominal chemical compositions of U720Li alloy are given in Table 1. The
specimens were heat treated under standard heat-treated condition: 1100 °C/4 h
followed by oil quenching and then aging at 650 °C/24 h/air cooling +760 °C/
16 h/air cooling. The LCF tests were performed on smooth cylindrical specimens
(gauge diameter of 6.35 mm and gauge length of 19.0 mm) in a closed-loop ser-
vohydraulic testing machine with computer-controlled loading spectra programmed
as speci ﬁed by ASTM E606 standard test method at 650 and 725 °C, covering a
wide range of total strain amplitude (0.8, 1.0 and 1.2%), in fully reversed (R = –1)
condition, using triangular waveform at a frequency of 0.5 Hz.
Microstructure characterization and analysis were conducted by SEM and TEM
in the following aspects: grain size, grain boundary misorientation, γ′ precipitates,
dislocation con ﬁgurations and interactions with γ′ precipitates, and the fatigue
fracture behaviors. In addition to conventional microstructures assessment after
fatigue fracture, structures were also observed using t-EBSD in SEM. This is a new

Results and Discussion
LCF Behavior and Microstructure of Fatigue Ruptured
Specimens
Figure 1 shows the numbers of cycles to failure as a function of total strain ranges.
It can be seen clearly that the LCF property of U720Li drops with the increasing
temperature and decreases slowly with the increasing total strain. To better
understand the basic microstructure evolution with increasing temperature, t-EBSD
analyses were performed to get the basis microstructure in terms of grain size and
grain boundary misorientations, etc. Figure 2 shows the t-EBSD patterns obtained
from various temperatures and stains, as noted at the upper regions of each t-EBSD
image. Figure 3 shows the t-EBSD results of number fraction of grain size and
misorientation angle distribution behaviors. Clearly, the microstructure consists of a
mixture of coarse and ﬁne grains. As shown in Fig. 3a, there is more small grains
(150–210 nm) formation at 725 °C, indicated by a black dot rectangle, which
maybe results from recrystallization. In addition, it is also found that there are many
small-angle grain boundaries appeared in the 725 °C samples with the strain from
0.8 to 1.2%, especially in some coarse grains. It seems that the number fraction of
misorientation angles increases with strain at 725° C, as indicted by a black dot
ellipse in Fig. 3b. Small grains or sub grains with small grain boundary rotation
angles seem to be formed and even the number of small or sub grains increase with
strain.

Dislocation Con ﬁgurations and Interactions
with γ′ Precipitates
Figure 6 shows the dislocations interactions with γ′ precipitates. It can be seen
clearly that dislocations bypass γ′ precipitates through Orowan bowing processes.
Dislocation loops encircle the γ′ precipitates after the bypass operation, and then, a
subsequent dislocation would have to be extruded between the loops. That is to say,
the secondary γ′ precipitates play a key role in impeding the dislocation movement.
Actually, dislocation con ﬁgurations and interactions with γ′ precipitates depend on
the size, distribution, and mean distance between γ′ precipitates, etc. As mentioned
above, the volume fractions of γ′ precipitates have no obvious change during the
LCF deformation at 650 and 725 °C. So, it does not affect the interactions between
dislocations and secondary γ′ precipitates. So, these similar conditions provide
enough possibilities for Orowan looping around secondary γ′ precipitates, the
predominant strengthening mechanism.
The primary γ′ precipitates that were not fully dissolved during the solid solution
treatment process pins at the grain boundaries. So the dislocation gliding along
grain boundary may have interactions with those primary γ′ precipitates. Figure 7
shows the dislocations interactions with the primary γ′ precipitates at/near grain
boundaries. The primary γ′ precipitates act as barrier for dislocation movement,
difﬁcult to overcome through by-passing mechanism. So, dislocations are prone to
accumulate at the interface between primary γ′ precipitate and matrix. That is the
reason why high density of dislocations surrounding the primary γ′ precipitates, as
shown in Fig. 7. If the dislocation accumulates to a certain extent, the dislocation
pile-up could create a stress concentration which may activate dislocation gliding
into the primary γ′ precipitates. That could be con ﬁrmed by the gliding dislocations
in the primary γ′ precipitates at 650 and 725 °C as the strain varies from 0.8 to
1.2%, as shown in Fig. 7. The high density dislocation surrounding the large-size
primary γ′ precipitates could also make them non-coherent with the matrix. In
addition, these large-size primary γ′ precipitates shearing by the dislocations could
not act as effective strengthening particles in the alloy. Therefore, the secondary γ′
precipitates are the signi ﬁcant strengthening particle in U720Li.

to a large extent at 725 °C, as well as the extent of recrystallization increasing with

Summary and Conclusions
This paper evaluates the strain controlled LCF behaviors of U720Li alloy and
related microstructure evolution at 725 °C, to explore the inferior aspects of U720Li
alloy above its typical maximum service temperature, which is of bene ﬁtt o
development of new advanced disk superalloys. During the LCF deformation,
gliding dislocations have a tendency to surround the separate primary γ′ precipitate
or concentrate into dislocation walls to associate several primary γ′ precipitates to
form sub-grains at nano-, submicro-, micro-scales. Dynamic recrystallization that
occurred to a large extent in local regions at 725 °C could be the signi ﬁcant factor
that caused LCF property degradation.

## Page 777

Stress Relaxation Behavior Comparison
of Typical Nickel-Base Superalloys
for Fasteners
He Jiang, Jing Yang, Jianxin Dong, Maicang Zhang, Zhihao Yao
and Xishan Xie
Abstract In the present work, stress relaxation behavior of three typical
nickel-base Superalloys: Alloy 718, Waspaloy and AEREX 350, were investigated
in a temperature range of 600 –800 °C for up to 10 h. The effects of stress relaxation
parameters on behavior were analyzed and stress relaxation characteristics of the
three superalloys are compared and mechanisms revealed by FESEM and TEM
observation. The study results show that the stress relaxation property of Alloy 718
is very sensitive to temperature. It is very stable at 650 °C, but decreases extremely
with temperature increasing to 750 °C as a result of serious microstructure
degeneration. Moreover, stress relaxation stability is related with initial stress, and
appropriate increase of initial stress under normal service temperature can increase
the stress relaxation limit of Alloy 718. The stress relaxation resistance of Waspaloy
decreases with increasing temperature. The increase of initial stress and initial strain
is beneﬁcial for stress relaxation resistance of Waspaloy, but the in ﬂuencing degree
is related with temperature. Furthermore, Waspaloy with heat treatment A (1020
°C × 4 h/AC + 845 °C × 4 h/AC + 760 °C × 16 h/AC) shows better stress
relaxation resistance than that with heat treatment B (1080 °C × 4 h/AC + 845
°C × 24 h/AC + 760 °C × 16 h/AC). In addition, stress relaxation stability of
AEREX 350 is the best among the three superalloys in the temperature range of
600–800 °C on the whole. The combined effect of γ′ phase and η phase guarantee
the stress relaxation property of AEREX 350.

## Page 778

Introduction
Loosening of connection is a major failure model for fasteners, hence, the stress
relaxation property can better re ﬂect the characteristics of fastener materials than
durable strength. Nickel-base superalloy is frequently used for fasteners due to the
excellent high temperature properties. The investigation of stress relaxation prop-
erty seems to be more and more important, since superalloys are more and more
widely used in long term service conditions, such as nuclear power stations and
ultra-supercritical power plants, in which any tiny failure may lead to catastrophic
results.
AEREX 350 is a newly developed Ni-Co base superalloy recently commer-
cialized for high temperature applications [ 1]. The excellent high temperature
mechanical property and microstructure stability make it suitable for fastener ap-
plications [ 2]. This alloy is mainly strengthened by γ′ phase and intergranular η
phase precipitates [ 3, 4].
Waspaloy is a γ′ precipitation hardened superalloy widely used in blades, disks,
fasteners and other aero-engine applications in the temperature range 700 –750 °C
and even above [ 5, 6]. For example, it is equipped on an engine as bolt because of
its satisfactory stress relaxation property.
Alloy 718 is widely used for the outstanding corrosion resistance and me-
chanical properties at temperatures up to 650 °C [ 7]. The alloy is mainly
strengthened by metastable body centered tetragonal γ″ in accompany with a small
amount of γ′ phase [ 8]. Fasteners manufactured with Alloy 718 alloy have been
widely used in offshore and subsea applications due to the high strength and
excellent corrosion resistance [ 9].
During the service of fasteners, stress relaxation takes place and may result in the
loosening of connection. Hence, the research of stress relaxation property is more
necessary than ductile property for fastener materials. Generally, the stress relax-
ation behavior depends highly on temperature, initial stress and initial strain, and
microstructural evolution [ 10]. The effect of experimental parameters on stress
relaxation behavior is complicated and can be investigated by stress relaxation test.
Liu and Jonas [ 11] ﬁrst applied the stress relaxation method in 1980s to follow the
kinetics of strain induced precipitation of carbonitrides in austenite. Since then, the
method has been widely employed for studying not only the precipitation kinetics
but also the recovery and recrystallization processes in steels and other alloys [ 12].
Up to now, much work has been done about the stress relaxation behavior of
copper and aluminum alloys. However, when it comes to nickel-base superalloy,
previous studies mainly used stress relaxation as a method to measure the residual
stress left by manufacture process [ 13, 14]. Collins et al. [ 15] carried out more
detailed research by stress relaxation accompanied by in situ neutron diffraction to
detect the mismatch between γ′ phase and γ matrix caused by heat treatment.
Monajati et al. [ 16] used stress relaxation method to investigate the strain induced
precipitation of γ′ in Udimet 720. Woodford et al. [ 17, 18] demonstrated the
possibility of stress relaxation method as a quick way to attain the design stress
790 H. Jiang et al.

## Page 779

level instead of creep test in superalloys for turbines. Generally, stress relaxation is
applied as an assistant method to study the properties of superalloys. Little attention
is paid on the stress relaxation of superalloy itself, such as the behavior, mechanism,
related microstructure evolution, comparison between different alloys and so on.
Recently some investigations have been made about the stress relaxation of single
crystal superalloy [ 15, 19]. However, hardly any paper has been published on stress
relaxation behavior of wrought nickel-base superalloy, especially the related
mechanism. The investigation of stress relaxation behavior can help recognize and
understand the stress relaxation property of fastener materials, and avoid potential
loosening failure of fasteners. Hence, it is of vital necessary to carry out in detail
investigation and get a thorough understanding of stress relaxation behavior and
mechanism of superalloy for fasteners.
For the above reasons, the aim of present work is to investigate the stress
relaxation behavior and mechanism of typical wrought nickel-base superalloys for
fasteners: Alloy 718, Waspaloy and AEREX350, hoping to provide some theo-
retical guidance on stress relaxation characteristics of superalloy fastener materials.
Materials and Experiments
Nickel-base Superalloys, Alloy 718, Waspaloy and AEREX 350 are used for
investigation. The chemical compositions are listed in Table 1. Each material was
manufactured by vacuum induction melting (VIM) and vacuum arc remelting
(VAR), and then experienced different deformation process. The ﬁnal heat treat-
ment was 870 °C × 4 h + 740 °C × 4 h for AEREX 350 and 980 °C × 1 h/
AC + 720 °C × 8 h/FC + 620 °C × 8 h/AC for Alloy 718. To investigate the
effect of heat treatment on Waspaloy stress relaxation behavior, two heat treatments
were used: heat treatment A is 1020 °C × 4 h/AC + 845 °C × 4 h/AC + 760
°C × 16 h/AC, and heat treatment B is 1080 °C × 4 h/AC + 845 °C × 24 h/
AC + 760 °C × 16 h/AC.
The as-heat treated microstructures of each alloy are shown in Fig. 1. The mi-
crostructure of AEREX 350 (Fig. 1a) exhibits a ﬁne, homogeneous dispersion of γ′
particles, short rod-like η phase on grain boundary and needle-like η phase within
the grains. The microstructure of Waspaloy with heat treatment A is composed of
spherical primary γ′ phase with average diameter of 260 nm and secondary γ′ phase
with average diameter of 45 nm in the matrix, and carbides on grain boundary as

Processing
A typical σ-t (stress—time) curve for stress relaxation test with some characteristic
parameter is demonstrated in Fig. 2a. Here, σ0 is the initial stress. Generally, the
stress relaxation curves can be divided into two stages: in the ﬁrst stage the stress
decreases rapidly and the stress decreases more and more slowly to a stable value in
the second stage [ 21]. This stable value is determined by the asymptote line of the
stress relaxation curve along t axis, and this value is called the stress relaxation limit
σ

and can be determined by cubic exponential function ﬁt of stress relaxation curve as

The above analysis shows that there are many characteristic parameters to
describe the stress relaxation behavior, and every parameter gets its own meaning
and feature. To compare the stress relaxation behavior, a relaxation stability
coefﬁcient S0 is proposed based on comprehensive consideration of all the factors
as: S0 = σ′

Stress Relaxation Characteristics of Alloy 718
The stress relaxation behavior can be affected by a number of factors, such as
temperature, initial stress, initial strain and so on. The effect of stress relaxation
parameters on Alloy 718 is demonstrated in Fig. 3. Each curve shows a similar
behavior: the stress decreases rapidly in the initial stage and then gradually reaches
a steady state (i.e. the stress relaxation limit). The stress relaxation resistance of
Alloy 718 is extremely good at 650 °C, since the stress does not show much
decrease during the stress relaxation. However, the stress relaxation resistance of
Alloy 718 drops dramatically when the temperature increases to 750 °C. Similar
phenomenon can be both detected with an initial stress of 510 MPa and 380 MPa as
shown in Fig. 3a, b. It is found that besides temperature, initial stress plays an
important role in stress relaxation. The effect of initial stress on 650 °C Alloy 718
stress relaxation behavior is compared in Fig. 3c. The result indicates that stress
relaxation limit increases with increasing initial stress.

## Page 783

As discussed, dramatic degeneration of stress relaxation resistance is detected
with the increase of temperature in Alloy 718. The morphology in Fig. 4a indicates
that the microstructure after stress relaxation test at 650 °C does not change much
compared with original microstructure (Fig. 1d), with short rod-like δ phase on
grain boundary and disc-like γ″ phase and spherical γ′ phase in grain. The good
morphology stability can explain the excellent stress relaxation resistance at 650 °C
[7]. However, when the temperature increases to 750 °C, morphology change takes
place with γ″ coarsening (Fig. 4b). More δ particles can be detected both on grain
boundaries and intragranular with obvious coarsening. Many previous studies have
reported that the precipitation and coarsening of δ phase consumes metastable γ″
phase [ 24], however, δ phase does not contribute to the strengthening of the alloy
beyond grain boundary pinning. Hence, the γ″ and δ phase at 750 °C will certainly
degenerate the mechanical properties of Alloy 718 for a given grain size.
To further uncover the microstructure evolution during stress relaxation test,
TEM observation is employed. Figure 5a shows that ﬁne disc-like γ″ distributes
homogeneously after 650 °C stress relaxation test and shows good coherency with
the γ matrix. Very abundant precipitation and apparent coarsening of γ″ phase is
observed after 750 °C stress relaxation test as shown in Fig. 5b. It has been reported
that apparent softening can take place as the result of considerable coarsening of γ″
phase when exposed at 750 °C for 100 h [ 8]. The fringe contrast associated with the
planar defects within γ″ particles suggests that these are stacking faults [ 25]. Fur-
thermore, it can also be detected that γ″ particle is cut by dislocation during 750 °C
stress relaxation test as shown in Fig. 5b. The leading dislocation cutting through
will result in the following cutting by trailing dislocations [ 26, 27]. The repeated
dislocation shear can lead to reduced resistance to dislocation movement [ 28].
Hence, the resistance to stress relaxation degenerates apparently at 750 °C.
It can be concluded from above analyses that the stress relaxation behavior of
Alloy 718 is closely related with temperature. It shows good stress relaxation
resistance at 650 °C, and a dramatic decrease of at 750 °C, which can be attributed
to the serious phase coarsening and microstructure degeneration. Furthermore,

Waspaloy can provide strong blocks to the movement of dislocations. However,
there are only ﬁne γ′ particles in Waspaloy with heat treatment B, which cannot
inhibit the movement of dislocations effectively. Hence, the stress relaxation
resistance of Waspaloy with heat treatment A is higher. As a result, the heat
treatment of 1020 °C × 4 h/AC + 845 °C × 24 h/AC + 760 °C × 16 h/AC is
recommended for Waspaloy to get higher stress relaxation resistance.
Stress Relaxation Characteristics of AEREX 350
AEREX 350 is a common used superalloy for fasteners and the effect of temper-
ature on stress relaxation behavior of AEREX 350 is shown in Fig. 8. The stress
relaxation resistance decreases with increasing temperature. Apparent degeneration
of stress relaxation resistance can be detected at 780 °C. The stress relaxation
behavior is related to microstructure evolution during thermal exposure.
Microstructure observation coarsening of intragranular η phase and an increased
amount of η phase after test (Fig. 9) compared with as-heat treated morphology

This phenomenon signiﬁes that η phase also participates in the deformation. Serious
distortion takes place in the surrounding strain ﬁeld of γ′ phase and more dislo-

severe at 800 °C. At the same time, the deformation of η phase is more apparent
with more dislocations as demonstrated in Fig. 10f.
Comparison Between Different Alloys
The stress relaxation limits of Alloy 718, Waspaloy and AEREX 350 with an initial
stress of 510 MPa are compared in Fig. 11a. Generally, the stress relaxation limit
decreases with increasing temperature. To get more intuitionistic comparison of
stress relaxation behaviors of the three alloys, calculated stress relaxation charac-
teristics are compared in Fig. 11b–d by the method introduced in section “Char-
acteristics of Stress Relaxation Curve and Data Processing ”. Generally, AEREX350
is considered as a good material for fastener [ 29], however, the stress relaxation
limit is lower than that of Waspaloy at 600 °C (Fig. 11a). The stress relaxation
resistance of AEREX 350 is better in higher temperature condition, and the

Conclusion
In this work, the stress relaxation behavior and mechanism of AEREX 350,
Waspaloy and Alloy 718 were investigated in the 600 –800 °C temperature range by
stress relaxation curve analysis, FESEM and TEM observation. The following
conclusion can be derived from the investigation and discussion:
(1) Alloy 718 stress relaxation property is very sensitive to temperature. It shows
excellent stress relaxation resistance at 650 °C, but degenerates signi ﬁcantly at
750 °C. The dramatic decrease of stress relaxation resistance can be attributed
to coarsening and degeneration of strengthening precipitates. Appropriate
increase of initial stress under normal service temperature can increase the
stress relaxation limit of Alloy 718.
(2) The stress relaxation resistance of Waspaloy decreases with increasing tem-
perature. The increase of initial stress and initial strain is bene ﬁcial for the stress
relaxation resistance for Waspaloy, but the in ﬂuencing degree is related with
temperature. Waspaloy with heat treatment A (1020 °C × 4 h/AC + 845
°C × 4 h/AC + 760 °C × 16 h/AC) shows better stress relaxation resistance
than that with heat treatment B (1080 °C × 4 h/AC + 845 °C × 24 h/
AC + 760 °C × 16 h/AC).
(3) AEREX 350 shows the best stress relaxation stability among the three alloys in
the temperature range of 600 –800 °C. As with 718 and Waspaloy, increasing
temperature resulted in decreased stress relaxation resistance. Both γ′ phase and
η phase contribute to stress relaxation resistance in AEREX 350.

Study of the Oxidation Assisted
Intergranular Cracking Mechanism
on a Ni-Base Superalloy
J. Milanese, E. Andrieu, J. B. Osio, J. Alexis and D. Bardel
Abstract In order to collect accurate information about the widely reported Oxi-
dation Assisted Intergranular Cracking (OAIC) mechanism of the superalloy 718 at
650 °C in air environment, we investigated a new tensile test procedure which
enables to have access to a quantitative semi-continuous assessment of the dam-
aging process of the alloy 718 during a standard tensile test. Tensile tests were
carried out on a solutionized and aged alloy 718 by varying the deformation mode
of the alloy during the ongoing experiment. The semi-continuous quanti ﬁcation of
the intergranular damage was performed after a fracture surface analysis of samples
tested in both Dynamic Strain Ageing (DSA) domain and DSA-subdomain where
Portevin-Le Chatelier (PLC) effect occurs. This innovative testing method allows to
characterize the intergranular damage that occurs when the material is stressed with
an unserrated DSA deformation mode as the alloy 718 is only sensitive to OAIC in
this domain. In these conditions, the onset of the intergranular cracking process was
found to be around 10% of total strain. An increase in the cracking kinetic when
necking occurs was also noticed. A close connection between the intensity of the
intergranular damage and the cumulated strain in DSA deformation mode before
the onset of the damaging process was found. The gathered information represents a
signiﬁcant improvement in the understanding of still debated OAIC or Stress
Corrosion Cracking (SCC) mechanisms.

Introduction
The superalloy 718 is well known for possessing good mechanical properties and
corrosion/oxidation resistance over a wide range of temperatures [ 1–3]. However,
the alloy 718 is widely reported to be subject to an intergranular brittle fracture
when loaded in particularly harsh environments [ 4–6]. The effect of the environ-
ment is essential in the damaging process of the superalloy as no intergranular
brittle fracture was observed on samples tested under vacuum or inert gas [ 7, 8].
Whether in the water of Pressurized Water Reactors (PWRs) or in air at 650 °C, the
resulting intergranular damage of the alloy (assimilated to an InterGranular Stress
Corrosion Cracking “IGSCC” mechanism on one side and to an Oxidation Assisted
Intergranular Cracking “OAIC” mechanism on the other side) depends on the de-
formation mode of the alloy. The transition from an unserrated ﬂow typically
observed in the Dynamic Strain Aging (DSA) domain to a serrated ﬂow observed
when the Portevin-Le Chatelier (PLC) effect occurs in a DSA subdomain lead to a
transition in the fracture mode from intergranular fragile to fully transgranular
ductile [ 7–9]. Even if several still-debated mechanisms for the IGSCC or OAIC of
the alloy 718 have been reported in literature [ 10–18], the particular ﬂow induced
by the plastic instabilities and the resultant modi ﬁcation of the interaction between
dislocations and solutes inhibits the damaging mechanisms of the alloy in which a
preferential loading of grain boundaries or segregating elements at grain boundaries
are possibly involved [ 7–9, 19].
The analysis of fractured samples after conventional tensile tests at high tem-
perature in air environment is used to characterized and quantify the intergranular
damage of the superalloy 718. However, only one information about the total
intergranular damage at the breakage of the material can be deducted from this
assessment. No information on the damaging process, as its onset or its develop-
ment during the mechanical test, is available.
The objective of this study was to determine the occurrence and the evolution of the
intergranular cracking of a superalloy 718 due to an OAIC mechanism during a tensile
test at 650 °C in air environment by means of an innovative method. Tensile tests
during which the deformation mode of the superalloy 718 is modi ﬁed from a DSA
mode to a PLC mode at a given strain level and vice versa were carried out. The
intergranular damage which exclusively occurs over the section of the tensile curve
performed in DSA can be therefore determined by a standard fractography analysis of
the tensile samples. Thus, a semi-continuous assessment of the intergranular dam-
aging process of the superalloy 718 at 650 °C in air environment was achieved.
806 J. Milanese et al.

## Page 795

Experimental Procedure
The material used for this research was a 0.260 mm thick nickel base superalloy
718 strip whose chemical composition is given in Table 1.
The alloy was fully solutionized at 1080 °C during 48 s and conventionally aged
as follows: 720 °C for 8 h, cooled to 620 °C at 50 °C/h, 620 °C for 8 h then
furnace cooled. From the manufacturing route described above, only remains a
δ-free γ′/γ″-hardened fully recrystallized solid solution with an average grain size of
about 13 µm. As shown in Fig. 1, carbides alignments in the rolling direction and
dispersed isolated primary carbides which cannot be redissolved at these temper-
atures are still observed in the proportions of ∼0.46 surf.%.
Tensile tests were realized under laboratory air testing conditions at a temper-
ature of 650 °C with a strain rate controlled by the travel speed of the testing
device. The mechanical testing procedure is automatically de ﬁned and allows to
change the strain rate at a given deformation level during the ongoing test. Strain
rates of 1.10
−3 s−1 and 1.10 −2 s−1 were used as they respectively result in a
conventional DSA deformation mode and in a PLC deformation mode for the used
material at 650 °C. Immediately prior to the test, samples were hold at 650 °C for
10 min in order to homogenize the sample temperature and allow oxidation phe-
nomena to occur. An exhaustive list of the carried out tests is given in Table 2.
Fractured tensile samples were then observed by secondary electron microscopy
using a FEI INSPECT S50 microscope.
Results
Constant Strain Rate Tensile Tests
Stress-strain curves performed at a constant strain rate during the whole test are
provided in Fig. 2. As expected, the selected strain rates of 1.10 −3 s−1 and 1.10 −2
s−1 lead respectively to a continuous and serrated ﬂow of the material. A decrease
of about 20 MPa in the tensile strength and of 3% in the ultimate strain is observed
when the PLC effect occurs.
A mixed transgranular ductile and intergranular fragile rupture mode is observed
on the samples strained at 1.10
−3 s−1 (Fig. 3b, c) while the fracture mode of the
tensile samples strained at 1.10 −2 s−1 in the PLC subdomain is fully transgranular
ductile (Fig. 3a). As reported in literature [ 7–9], the effects of the combined
environment and mechanical load on the damaging process of the superalloy 718
are enabled when the ﬂow is unserrated whereas they are suppressed when the
plastic instabilities related to the PLC effect occur.

Two Strain Rate Tensile Tests
Curves of tensile tests realized by switching from DSA to PLC deformation modes
and vice versa during the ongoing test are presented in Fig. 4. It is important to note
that the second part of the two strain rate test curves (black curves in Fig. 4) ﬁts
well with the standard tensile test curves (grey curves in Fig. 4). Despite an

Quantiﬁcation of the Intergranular Damage
The intensity of the damage was evaluated by means of a fractograph analysis. As
detailed in Fig. 5, an Oxidation Assisted Intergranular Cracking Index (OAICI) is
calculated as the ratio of the sum of the edging lengths of the intergranular fracture
zones by the total perimeter of the analyzed specimen. Only is taken into account
the intergranular fracture zones whose depth is strictly greater than one grain.
The Table 3 shows the results of the OAICI determinations. Whatever the test
sequence was, the intensity of the intergranular damage seems to be directly related
to the deformation cumulated with an unserrated ﬂow of the material (i.e. DSA
deformation mode).
From DSA to PLC tests, an increase from 0 to 16.5% of the total strain
cumulated in DSA mode leads to an increase in the intergranular sensitivity of the
material from 0 to 9.0%. The same conclusion can be drawn from PLC to DSA tests
as an increase from 0 to 12.5% in the cumulated strain in PLC mode (i.e. a decrease

Discussion
The Fig. 6a shows the evolution of the intergranular damage intensity calculated
from the DSA to PLC tensile tests as a function of the total strain. Values are
replaced over the standard DSA stress/strain curve of the studied alloy 718 at
650 °C in air environment. The onset of the intergranular damage occurs between
10 and 12.5% of total strain. It also corresponds to the strain when the material
strength is maximal. The perceived maximal strength and necking on the stress/
strain curve of the material at 650 °C in air environment seems to be directly related
to the appearance of the intergranular damage. It can potentially be considered that
the decrease in the load-bearing cross section which occurs when intergranular
cracks form is accountable to the perceived ﬂow of the material. As they are widely
inﬂuenced by the damaging effect of the environment, the noted material strength
and elongation from a tensile test carried out at 650 °C in air environment do not
correspond to the inherent mechanical properties of the alloy 718 but only re ﬂect
the particular behavior of the material in a particular environment.
An explosion of the OAICI at the very end of the tensile test/necking is also
observed. The OAICI increases from 1% to around 8.5% as the total strain goes
from 15% to 18.5%. The intergranular cracking of the alloy 718 is a very rapid

mechanism as the majority of the intergranular damage is generated in about 35 s.
The average intergranular cracking propagation speed was calculated at 0.5 µm/s.
The Fig. 6b shows the evolution of the OAICI as a function of the cumulated
strain in DSA mode calculated from the PLC to DSA tensile tests. As mentioned
before, the intensity of the intergranular damage increase with the cumulated strain
in DSA mode.
The Fig. 7 shows a standard DSA mode tensile test curve and several tensile
tests carried out with a transition from a PLC deformation mode to a DSA defor-
mation mode at various total strains. It was observed before that the intergranular
damage occurs and develop after 10% of total strain. However, in the case of PLC
to DSA tensile tests, no differences from one test curve to another is noticeable
beyond 10% of total strain whereas the intensity of the intergranular damage
generated during the same period decreases. This change in the intergranular
damaging process can therefore be attributed to the quantity of deformation
cumulated in DSA mode before 10% of total strain as longer this part of the curve
is, greater the OAICI values are. During this period, deformation induced solute
segregation and preferential loading of grain boundaries whose intensities depend
on the deformation cumulated in DSA mode can potentially be implemented. Once
the cohesion stress of grain boundaries is reached intergranular cracking occurs and
only loaded and segregated grain boundary interfaces fail. Thus, the greater the
strain cumulated before the onset of the intergranular cracking, the larger the
weakened grain boundaries and the OAICI value. The time spent in DSA defor-
mation mode before the onset of intergranular cracks can be assimilated to the
“incubation period ” of the intergranular cracking mechanism during which solute
segregation or preferential loading at grain boundaries may potentially occur and
express on the fracture surface of the material.

## Page 802

Conclusions
In order to completely grasp the intergranular cracking process of the alloy 718
during a tensile test at 650 °C in air environment, the following conclusions can be
gleaned from this work:
(1) A certain amount of deformation cumulated in the material in DSA deformation
mode is needed for the intergranular damage of the superalloy 718 at 650 °C in
air environment to occur. In this study, the onset of the intergranular cracking
was found to be around 10% of total strain and affects the mechanical properties
of the alloy.
(2) The intergranular cracking process of the alloy 718 is accelerating at the end of
the tensile test and leads to the breakage of the material.
(3) The intensity of the intergranular damage is directly correlated to the cumulated
strain in DSA mode before the onset of the material cracking during which
preferential loading or solute segregation at grain boundaries can express their
negative effect. However, additional work on this speci ﬁc point needs to be
carried out in order to con ﬁrm these assumptions.

## Page 804

The Effect of Grain Size on the Dwell
Fatigue Crack Growth Rate of Alloy
ATI 718Plus ®
Minqing Wang, Jinhui Du, Qun Deng, Xudong Lv, Chengbin Yang
and Jianxin Dong
Abstract Grain size optimization is an important method to improve the fatigue
crack growth resistance of superalloys. For ATI 718Plus ® alloy, the effect of grain
size on the fatigue crack growth rate (FCGR) is more complex, because of the
complex effects of η-Ni3Al0.5Nb0.5 precipitated at the grain boundaries. In the past,
the ﬁne-grain ATI 718Plus ® alloy was found to exhibit better dwell fatigue crack
growth rate (DFCGR) resistance than that of the coarse-grain alloy at high tem-
perature. An attempt to explain this phenomenon was based on the grain boundary
oxygen diffusion/oxidation viewpoint; however, the mechanism remained unclear
until now. Based on this, we investigated the relationship between the grain size
and the DFCGR of ATI 718Plus
® alloy. The DFCGR of ATI 718Plus ® alloys with
different grain sizes were tested in air at 704 °C. Furthermore, the microstructures
and crack growth paths were analyzed, and the plastic zone near the crack tip was
calculated for specimens with different grain sizes. The better effect ﬁne grain ATI
718Plus® has on DFCGR is related to more η-Ni3Al0.5Nb0.5 phase precipitation and
reduced oxygen diffusion along grain boundaries, as well as the reduction of the
plastic zone near the crack tip and the increase in secondary cracking with
decreasing grain size.
Keywords Grain size
⋅ Fatigue crack growth rate ⋅ Oxygen diffusion
Grain boundary phase ⋅ Plastic zone

## Page 805

Introduction
ATI 718Plus ® (hereafter 718Plus) is a novel turbine disk wrought superalloy ma-
terial with the working temperature of 700 °C and is considered as a good candidate
for important components such as turbine disk, compressor disk, casing and fas-
tener for advanced aero engines [ 1, 2]. As a turbine disk material, 718Plus should
withstand the complex interaction of fatigue, creep and oxidation at the tempera-
tures from 400 to 700 °C under alternate loading and high temperature corrosion
environments [ 1–3]. Study on the mechanisms of crack growth rate under the
fatigue-creep-environment interaction is of signi ﬁcant importance for the long-term
reliability of 718Plus components and the security of an aero engine.
As we know, grain size can signi ﬁcantly affect the FCGR and DFCGR of a
superalloy, and a lot of experimental results indicate that the FCGR and DFCGR of
coarse-grain alloys are usually relatively slower than that of ﬁne-grain alloys.
However, oversize grains are easier to result in intergranular fracture, which reduce
the fatigue crack growth resistance of the material. In addition, the existence of the
precipitated phase at the grain boundaries of 718Plus complicates the effect of grain
size on the DFCGR of the alloy. Therefore, an important method to improve the
fatigue crack growth resistance is through a systematic study on the effect of grain
size on DFCGR for 718Plus alloy.
Liu et al. [ 4] compared the fatigue crack growth rates of 718Plus with different
microstructures and heat treatment. It was found that the performances of DFCGR
with ﬁne-grains were better than that with coarse-grains. From the viewpoint of
grain boundary oxidation, the increase in the grain size can decrease the total grain
boundaries, which would decrease the DFCGR; however, the experimental results
observed were opposite. Therefore, it was thought the grain size effect cannot
explain this phenomenon, and it might be related to the morphology and amount of
δ-phase. Kearsey et al. [ 5] studied the effects of environment and holding time on
718Plus alloy, and the results showed that the DFCGR of 718Plus with two types of
thermal treatments were similar under vacuum condition, but different in air.
Investigation of the fractural surfaces showed that under vacuum condition, the
DFCGR fractural surface was transgranular fracture, whereas the DFCGR fractural
surface was intergranular fracture in the air environment. They thought the main
mechanism of intergranular fracture was an oxygen-induced dynamic fracture.
Nevertheless, the mechanism for why ﬁne-grain 718Plus shows better DFCGR
resistance is still unclear.
Based on above, the DFCGR properties of 718Plus alloy with different grain
sizes was systematically investigated. By observing the microstructure, analyzing
the secondary crack path, and calculating the plastic zone size near the crack tip of
different grain sizes, the effect of grain size on the DFCGR of 718Plus alloy is
discussed in this paper.

Experiments
Materials
The as-received 718Plus alloy was prepared by vacuum induction melting
(VIM) and vacuum arc remelting (VAR). Then, the 50 kg ingot was homogenized,
rolled into bars with a diameter of 40 mm and test samples were cut from the bars
(sample condition A). The chemical composition of the as-received alloy is listed in
Table 1. Some test samples were subjected to a pre-solution heat treatment at 1000
°C for 1 h (sample condition B) and 1020 °C for 1 h (sample condition C). Then all
the samples were subjected to solution heat treatment at 954 °C for 1 h, air cooled,
and then aged at 788 °C for 8 h, furnace cooled at 56 °C/h to 704 °C, held for
another 8 h, and air cooled.
The microstructure of the alloy samples was ﬁrst analyzed by optical microscopy
(OM), and then studied in detail by scanning electron microscopy (SEM, JEOL
JSM-6480LV, Japan) and FESEM (ZEISS SUPRA 55, Germany).
Fatigue Crack Growth Test
The specimen used for crack growth test is the standard compact tension
(CT) specimen con ﬁguration is shown in Fig. 1. The crack plane is parallel to the
hot working direction and the crack grew in the radial direction. The specimens

The microstructure of the three 718Plus samples were observed by OM, and results
shown in Fig. 2. The grain size of the as-received samples, Condition A, illustrated

about 50 µm. Further observation indicated that the morphologies of the precipitated
phases of Condition A were different from those of Condition B and C. Conditions B
and C exhibited two types of η-Ni3Al0.5Nb0.5 morphology precipitated at the grain
boundaries: particle-shape morphology and needle-shape (or lath-shape) morphol-
ogy. Condition A η-Ni3Al0.5Nb0.5 exhibited a short rod-shape morphology. The
amount of η-Ni3Al0.5Nb0.5 precipitated at the grain boundaries of Condition C was

Tensile Properties
After pre-solution and standard heat treatment, tensile properties were tested at 704 °C
for the three conditions and are presented in Table 2, where every result is an average
of three tensile samples. With decreasing grain size, the tensile strength of 718Plus
increases from 1120 to 1170 MPa, and yield strength increases from 875 to 995 MPa.
The elongation and reduction in area of Condition B is similar to that of Condition C;
however, for Condition A, the elongation and reduction in area are greatly increased.
Dwell Fatigue Crack Growth Rate
The DFCGR of 718Plus for the three conditions were then determined at 704 °C,
and the loading process was a trapezoidal wave represented by 15s-90s-15s-2s.
Figure 3 shows the DFCGR curves of 718Plus with three types of grain sizes.
The DFCGR of Condition A (ASTM 10) is approximately two orders of magnitude
smaller than that of Condition C (ASTM 5.5) and Condition B (ASTM 8), so with
decreasing grain size, the fatigue crack growth resistance of 718Plus increases.
Figure 4 shows the fractural morphologies of the fatigue crack growth region of
718Plus with three different grain sizes. Figure 4a of Condition A does shows a
layer of oxide on the fracture surface, though because the fatigue crack growth
resistance is excellent for 718Plus with this microstructure, the crack growth region
withstood the heavy oxidation; however, the fracture surface does show inter-
granular characteristics. Condition B with ASTM 8 grain size shows intergranular
characteristics as well; however, distinct fatigue striations were observed. With the
ASTM 5.5 grain size of Condition C, rock candy shape intergranular morphology
was observed on the fracture surface. The grain boundaries are very smooth, and a
few fatigue striations were observed. Moreover, there is little oxidation evident on
the fractural surface of Condition B and C samples.

Discussion
It is generally assumed that the crack growth rate of coarse-grain superalloys is
lower than that of ﬁne-grain superalloys, and fatigue crack growth resistance can be
improved by increasing grain size [ 7]. This reasoning can be concluded by the
following three aspects [ 8, 9]: (1) Grain boundaries are weakened under high
temperature, and cracks normally grow along the grain boundaries.
High-temperature deformation also normally takes place by grain boundary sliding.
Therefore, larger grain size with less grain boundaries, has less opportunities for
crack growth and grain boundary sliding, thus lower crack growth rate. (2) As
deformation near the crack tip becomes smaller, the coarse-grain structure reduces
the accumulation rate of damage. (3) For a high-temperature fatigue test in air, the
exposed grain boundary area of ﬁne-grain alloys are relatively large, leading to
more serious grain boundary oxidation, thus the higher crack growth. However, the
experimental results in this study indicate that with decreasing grain size, the
DFCGR of 718Plus becomes smaller. Therefore, the fatigue crack growth resistance

between η-phase and substrate (corresponding to rectangle) and b fourier ﬁltered image of ( a) and
c circle indicates the center of dislocation
824 M. Wang et al.

## Page 812

increases with decreasing grain size. This is opposite to the prevailing effect of
grain size on fatigue crack growth rate.
Kearsey et al. [ 5] found the DFCGR of 718Plus under two types of thermal
treatments were similar under vacuum conditions, and very different in an air
environment. Investigations of the DFCGR fracture surfaces showed that under
vacuum, the fracture surface showed transgranular fracture, whereas in air, the
fracture surface had intergranular fracture. The results showed that oxygen was the
main factor of intergranular facture and DFCGR difference, and the different mi-
crostructures, especially grain boundary structure and phases, can affect grain
boundary oxidation. Two main mechanisms, the stress accelerated grain boundary
oxidation (SAGBO) model and the dynamic embrittlement (DE) model are usually
used to express the effect of oxygen on the fatigue crack growth rate of superalloys.
The SAGBO model was initially proposed to clarify the low expansion superalloy
IN903 [ 10]. This indicated that the time-dependent crack propagation is ordinarily
caused by oxidation of the crack tip under stress. Oxygen can diffuse to the crack
surface by short-range diffusion and to the inner material by long-range diffusion,
forming oxides at the grain boundaries with active elements, such as chromium
(Cr), aluminum (Al) [ 11]. These oxides initiate voids under tensile loading and
further accelerate crack propagation. The theoretical model is illustrated in Fig. 7.
Liu and White [ 12] proposed the Dynamic Embrittlement model (DE model),
also illustrated in Fig. 7, to describe the oxygen-induced cracking in Ni
3Al alloy. It
was demonstrated that crack propagation is time-dependent and irrelevant to the
number of cycles [ 13]. The crack propagation rate increases by (a) decreasing cyclic
frequency, (b) increasing temperature and (c) raising oxygen concentration.
Cracking increased by extending the hold time under tensile loading; for a turbine
disk, this phenomenon is called “hold-time” crack growth. Furthermore, Bika et al.
[14] applied the DE model to clarify sulfur- or oxygen-induced crack propagation;
with the stress distribution on the crack tip obtained under alternating load. Under
the stress promotion effect, the sulfur or oxygen will diffuse to the crack surface or
grain boundary, which further reduces the interface bonding force. The crack can
Mechanisms of SAGBO model Mechanisms of DE model
Fig. 7 SAGBO and DE models for oxygen induced crack propagation
The Effect of Grain Size on the Dwell Fatigue Crack … 825

## Page 813

propagate and a step-wise crack propagation formed when the critical value is
reached. Elements leading to dynamic embrittlement can be divided into two types
according to their in ﬂuence mechanisms. The ﬁrst corresponds to grain boundary
segregation elements from the alloy itself, such as the sulfur-induced cracking in
steel and the tin-induced cracking in Cu-Sn alloy [ 15–17]. The second concerns
grain boundary embrittlement elements coming from the environment. Currently,
most of the research studies have focused on oxygen that induces cracking in nickel
base alloys [ 18–21], and in Cu-0.25Be alloy [ 22]. Currently, it is dif ﬁcult to dis-
tinguish the SAGBO or DE mechanism affecting the FCGR property of superalloys.
This has been investigated and will be presented in a future study.
From the discussion about the oxygen diffusion model and microstructure dif-
ferences, the effect of grain size on the DFCGR of 718Plus alloy can be concluded
as follows. First, previous experimental results indicate that the amount of η-
Ni
3Al0.5Nb0.5 phase can signi ﬁcantly affect the DFCGR property of 718Plus alloy.
The η-Ni3Al0.5Nb0.5 phase mainly plays a role of pinning grain boundaries and
reducing the diffusion of oxygen. Thus, the crack growth at the grain boundaries
can be slowed, and the notch sensitivity of the alloy avoided. Therefore, the more η-
Ni
3Al0.5Nb0.5 phase, the more the DFCGR of the alloy can be reduced. Figure 2
shows the amount and morphology of η-Ni3Al0.5Nb0.5 phase precipitated from
718Plus alloy with different grain sizes are different under the same ﬁnal heat
treatments. With decreasing grain size, both the grain boundary area of the alloy
and the amount of η-Ni3Al0.5Nb0.5 phase increase, and the ability of grain boundary
pinning and reduced oxygen diffusion are signi ﬁcantly enhanced, thus the DFCGR
will reduce correspondingly. The DFCGR of ASTM 5.5 grain structure is partic-
ularly fast, because the amount of η-Ni
3Al0.5Nb0.5 phase is relatively low, and notch
sensitivity conﬁrmed by the presence of the rock candy shape smooth intergranular
fracture in the test samples.
Secondly, it was thought that the different fatigue crack growth resistance for the
three specimen conditions originates from the different sizes of plastic zone under
fatigue-creep stress. Rice [ 23] ﬁrst reported that the size of the plastic zone under
creep stress was 4 times that under fatigue conditions using a theoretical calcula-
tion. Subsequently, Irwin et al. [ 24] established equations for estimating the plastic
zone size under creep and fatigue, and Eqs. ( 1) and ( 2) show that the size of plastic
zone will reduce with increasing yield strength.

Equations ( 1) and ( 2) indicate that the size of plastic zone decreases with
increasing yield strength σy. The experimental results con ﬁrm the yield strength of
718Plus alloy increases signi ﬁcantly with decreasing grain size, and the yield
826 M. Wang et al.

## Page 814

strength of ASTM 10 grain structure (Condition A) is 120 MPa higher than that of
ASTM 5.5 grain structure (Condition C). Substituting the yield strength values into
Eqs. ( 1) and ( 2), it can be estimated that the plastic zone sizes of Conditions C and
B are 1.30 and 1.13 times higher, respectively, than that of Condition A under the
same ΔK, indicating that the plastic zone size decreases signi ﬁcantly with
decreasing grain size. From the SAGBO and DE models, the decrease in the plastic
zone reduces the amount of plastic deformation near the crack tip which can reduce
the depth of oxidation and decrease the fatigue crack growth rate.
Thirdly, from the viewpoint of grain boundary oxidation, although the total grain
boundary area of the alloy increases with decreasing grain size, only the grain
boundary near the crack tip is impacted. The smaller the grain size, the more
tortuous the oxygen diffusion path and the more intersections encountered as the
crack grows along the grain boundary, which leads to more secondary cracks,
which can be veri ﬁed from Fig. 5. The formation of secondary cracks consume
large amounts of energy during the fatigue fracture, which disperse the stress and
reduce the stress concentration at the crack front, decreasing the growth rate. The
same experimental result was also found in IN718. Song [ 6] found several inter-
granular secondary cracks in the crack growth region of ﬁne-grain IN718 with a
relatively slow crack growth rate. This was also attributed to more secondary cracks
that appeared with the smaller grain size. It was illustrated in Fig. 6 that a lot of
dislocations are generated near the η-phase, and thus the movement of dislocations
can be effectively slowed by η-phase. So with decreasing grain size, the amount of
η-Ni
3Al0.5Nb0.5 phase increases and this also facilitates more secondary cracks.
Conclusions
In this paper, the effect of grain size on the DFCGR of 718Plus was systematically
investigated. The results of this study indicate that the DFCGR decreases with
reducing grain size in the range of ASTM 5.5 to ASTM 10. This is opposite to the
prevailing effect of grain size on fatigue crack growth rate. The bene ﬁcial effect for
DFCGR for ﬁne grain 718Plus alloy is attributed to the increase in η-Ni
3Al0.5Nb0.5
phase precipitation at the grain boundaries reducing grain boundary oxygen dif-
fusion, increased amounts of secondary cracking, and the higher yield strength
reducing the plastic zone size.

Thermal Processing Design of Cast
INCONEL® Alloy 740H for Improved
Mechanical Performance
Martin Detrois, Kyle A. Rozman, Paul D. Jablonski
and Jeffrey A. Hawk
Abstract The increasing operating temperatures of turbine designs for power
generation applications present challenges in selecting materials. With steam tem-
peratures approaching 700 °C, and beyond, ferritic or martensitic steels are inad-
equate. Ni-based superalloys perform much better under these conditions and
possess mechanical properties suitable for turbine and boiler applications. However,
only limited Ni-based superalloys are available for large turbine castings where a
combination of high-temperature strength (in particular, yield stress), long-term
creep resistance, toughness, and weldability are essential properties. Research was
undertaken at the National Energy Technology Laboratory to produce a cast
INCONEL
® 740H alloy with mechanical properties comparable to those of the
wrought product. Since thermo-mechanical processing is not an option in castings,
aging trials were performed to alter the grain boundary morphology after a com-
putationally designed homogenization heat treatment. Thermodynamic simulations
were used throughout to produce various grain boundary microstructures. Early
investigations on cast INCONEL
® 740/740H revealed less than desirable ductility.
The modi ﬁed microstructures altered the tensile and creep properties, and rein-
forced the possible use of cast INCONEL ® 740H in power plants. The bene ﬁts
associated with the alternate heat treatments were found to originate from the grain
boundary phases present in the alloy controlled through the targeted aging treat-
ments. Those results and the relations between thermal processing, microstructure,
mechanical properties and failure mechanisms of cast INCONEL
® 740H will be
discussed.

## Page 817

Introduction
Fossil fuel power generation applications are facing a rising number of challenges
with today ’s need for cleaner energy. Among them, supercritical coal- ﬁred power
plants typically operate at low ef ﬁciencies between 35 and 37% without carbon
capture. Increasing the ef ﬁciency of the power plants would result in less CO 2
produced for a given amount of usable energy [ 1]. Consequently, efforts are needed
to improve the ef ﬁciency of current coal- ﬁred power plants and reduce
greenhouse-gas emissions. The US Department of Energy has been investigating
solutions in Advanced Ultra Supercritical (A-USC) power generation applications
to achieve ef ﬁciencies above 45%. To attain this goal, operating temperatures and
pressures of components in steam boilers and turbines approach 760 °C and
35 MPa [ 1, 2]. This obviates the use of conventional ferritic-martensitic
high-strength steels, and consequently, Ni-based superalloys are needed to meet
the long-term, high-temperature creep strength requirements.
INCONEL
® Alloy 740H (IN740H) is a commercial Ni-based superalloy of
composition listed in Table 1. Research has shown that the alloy can be used in
A-USC power plants [ 3]. This age-hardenable, γ′ precipitate-strengthened, alloy
demonstrates strength and corrosion resistance necessary to operate under
demanding fossil energy environments [ 4]. The alloy contains a conventional γ-γ′
microstructure where the ordered Ni
3Al γ′ precipitates of L1 2 crystal structure are
embedded within the disordered FCC γ (Ni) matrix. In addition to the γ-γ′ phases,
carbides are also present in the form of MC (Ti- and Nb-rich) and M 23C6 (Cr-rich)
[5, 6]. Additionally, the often undesirable DO 24-ordered Ni3Ti η phase of hexagonal
crystal structure has been reported to precipitate when the alloy is subjected to long
exposure at elevated temperature, with or without the presence of an applied stress
[7–9].
IN740H satisﬁes the performance requirements of A-USC designs in its wrought
version, however, using the alloy in cast form would be very valuable in terms of
cost and range of component sizes and geometries [ 10, 11]. With the increasing
performance requirements of next-generation power plant designs, a target mini-
mum creep strength requirement of 100 MPa at 100,000 h at 760 °C and 35 MPa is
needed [ 2]. Additionally, room temperature and 760 °C requirements of yield
strength for cast products are 550 MPa and 350 MPa, respectively [ 11]. Efforts
were made at the National Energy Technology Laboratory to cast IN740H with
properties meeting the aforementioned requirements [ 12]. However, the various
castings, obtained using chemistries within the allowable range for IN740H,

## Page 818

showed a loss of ductility in creep, which seems to be attributed to the strong
presence of grain boundary carbides. While M 23C6 carbides can thwart grain
boundary sliding by restricting deformation processes at the boundary, excessive
presence of the precipitates at the boundary can alter the local chemistry of the
boundary on the one hand while providing a variety of fracture initiation sites
during long-term creep on the other [ 13]. MC carbides can also act as crack
nucleation sites because of their morphology. In this investigation, the presence of
the grain boundary carbides was investigated using various aging treatments to
observe their in ﬂuence on the alloy ’s mechanical properties.
Procedure
Casting and Thermal Processing
Computational thermodynamic tools, namely Thermo-Calc [ 14] with the TTNI8
database [ 15] and JMatPro [ 16], were ﬁrst used to target down select chemistries,
leading to the desired characteristics of the alloys necessary for melting. More
details on the different alloys can be found in Ref. [ 12]. Two IN740H compositions
Alloy 1 and Alloy 2, within the range set in Table 1, were considered for this
investigation, with Alloy 2 containing less carbon than Alloy 1. Melt materials were
measured accordingly using high-purity industry-grade melt stock, resulting in a
target weight of ∼7000 g. Only Cr was not added loosely due to relatively high
concentrations of oxygen ( ∼5000 ppm), consequently, master alloys of Ni-Cr
produced using vacuum-induction melting (VIM) and electroslag remelting (ESR)
were used [ 17, 18]. This reduced the fraction of tramp elements in the alloy. The
alloys were melted under 200 Torr Ar partial pressure to a superheat temperature of
T
L + 50 °C, where T L is the liquidus temperature calculated using Thermo-Calc.
The melts were poured into 100 mm diameter graphite molds coated with zirconia
wash to prevent carbon pickup. The molds were submerged in loose sand to sim-
ulate cooling conditions of full-size castings. For more information about the
casting process please refer to Refs. [ 2, 11].
Following alloy casting, the ingots were analyzed, computationally, to optimize
the homogenization heat treatment [ 19]. The ﬂexibility of this approach allows a
homogenization heat treatment to be speci ﬁed that limits speci ﬁc element segre-
gation to below ±1% variation from nominal throughout the ingot, and which is
essential for achieving consistency in mechanical properties in cast alloys. The heat
treatment consisted of 1 h at 1075 °C, 3 h at 1125 °C, 8 h at 1200 °C, and 8 h at
1250 °C. Argon gas fan cooling was utilized in the furnace at the end of the
homogenization cycle. Subsequently, the alloys were solutionized at a temperature
of 1150 °C for 4 h followed by air cooling. Then, the standard aging process for
this alloy was used to develop peak strength through γ′ precipitation (i.e., 16 h at
Thermal Processing Design of Cast INCONEL ® Alloy 740H … 831

## Page 819

800 °C). Two other aging treatments were considered to modify the grain boundary
precipitates based on thermodynamic predictions.
Mechanical Testing and Characterization
Blanks measuring 85 mm in length and 10 × 10 mm 2 cross section were cut from
the billets to prepare tensile and creep specimens. The bars were machined into
cylindrical geometry (Length = 4 × Diameter) with a gauge length measuring
32 mm and a gauge cross-section measuring 6.3 mm in diameter. Tensile and creep
testing were performed using the ASTM E-8 [ 20] and E-139 [ 21] standard test
methods, respectively. Tensile testing was performed at room temperature (RT) and
800 °C, while creep testing was performed at 760 °C under a creep screening stress
of 259 MPa using a constant load creep frame.
Various specimens were considered for observation under a FEI Inspect F ﬁeld
emission scanning electron microscope (SEM). Microstructural evaluation was
performed on samples sectioned parallel to the loading axis. The specimens were
ground and polished to 0.05 μm ﬁnish using colloidal silica. A chemical etch was
performed to remove the γ′ precipitates for better observation in the SEM. ASTM
standard etchant 88 was used for 15 s [ 22]. Both secondary-electron (SE) and
backscatter-electron (BE) modes were considered for observation of the various
phases present. Finally, ImageJ software [ 23] was used for making various quan-
titative measurements on the SEM images.
Results
Thermal Processing and Aging Treatments
The phase diagram of Fig. 1 predicts a conventional γ-γ′ microstructure with sta-
bility ranges for the σ phase, M 23C6 and MC carbides, and η phase. The γ′ solvus
temperatures were predicted as 953 °C and 937 °C in Alloys 1 and 2, respectively.
Similarly, the M 23C6 solvus/MC precipitation temperatures were calculated as
approximately 846 °C and 830 °C, respectively. The temperature ranges of η phase
formation were predicted to be from 824 to 987 °C and 777 to 997 °C in Alloys 1
and 2, respectively. According to Fig. 1, the standard aging treatment at 800 °C
should result in a γ-γ′ microstructure with stable M
23C6 carbides. In the authors ’
experience, the standard aging treatment resulted in poor creep properties in cast
IN740H due to the strong presence of the M
23C6 at the grain boundaries that
resulted in failure along those boundaries. Therefore, aging the alloys at higher
temperatures can potentially alter the precipitates present at the grain boundaries by
changing the sequence of carbide precipitation. Based on the Thermo-Calc
832 M. Detrois et al.

## Page 820

predictions, aging at 950 °C should result in the dissolution of M 23C6 carbides,
leaving the more refractory MC carbides. Finally, aging at 850 °C should result in a
compromise between both heat treatments and resulting microstructures. It is worth
mentioning that η is predicted to form at those temperatures.
The time-temperature-transformation (TTT) diagram of Alloy 1 is presented in
Fig. 2 using JMatPro simulations. The γ′ phase was predicted to precipitate rapidly
after approximately 5.4, 1.9, and 0.8 min at 800, 850, and 950 °C, respectively. The
η phase is expected to form after longer exposure to the aging temperatures, for
example, after 2.9, 1.1, and 0.5 h, respectively. Finally, the σ phase forms after low
temperature exposure for considerably longer times. Zhao et al. [ 24] produced a
TTT diagram with experimental data revealing longer times for the η phase to form
as compared to the prediction of Fig. 2. At 800 and 950 °C Zhao et al. showed η
phase formation after 100 and 26 h exposure at these temperatures, respectively.
Furthermore, the TTT diagram of Fig. 2 was calculated for a 0.5% amount trans-
formed. Consequently, aging times past the predicted η phase formation were
chosen, and careful attention was given to the precipitation of the η phase using
microstructural characterization in the SEM. Finally, the γ′ solvus temperatures
from JMatPro were calculated as 994 and 987 °C for Alloy 1 and 2, respectively.
Thus, in addition to the standard aging treatment of 800 °C for 16 h, aging treat-
ments at 950 °C for 2 h followed by 8 h at 800 °C and also 850 °C for 4 h
followed by 8 h at 800 °C were investigated. The second heat treatment step of
800 °C was considered to obtain a stable microstructure with a ﬁnal temperature
close to the target operating conditions.

testing are shown in Figs. 3, 4 and 5 for both alloys. The standard aging treatment,

those specimens, and overall more boundaries or segments were free of precipitates
than in the standard age specimen, Figs. 4c, d and 5. In addition, MC carbides were

Discussion
The grain boundary carbides were ﬁrst investigated in cast IN740H using a com-
bination of thermodynamic predictions and microstructural evaluations. The grain
boundary precipitates observed following the standard aging treatment were pri-
marily M 23C6 carbides, which correlated well with the predictions of Fig. 1 at
800 °C. High-angle grain boundaries were saturated in carbides with the exception
of twin boundaries. There was little to no γ′ free zones around them, Fig. 3.
Conversely, the two step aging treatments of 850 °C/800 °C and 950 °C/800 °C
resulted in more diverse precipitation at the grain boundaries with M 23C6 and MC
carbides as well as sections free of any precipitates, Figs. 4 and 5. For these heat
treatments, γ′ free zones were observed around the MC carbides and sul ﬁdes from
the depletion of γ′ forming elements such as Ti and Nb in the adjacent matrix [ 6].
This is also in agreement with the Thermo-Calc predictions of Fig. 1 where MC
carbides precipitate at 850 and 950 °C. The remainder of the M 23C6 carbides is
attributed to the second aging step of 800 °C, which was used to “stabilize” the
microstructure to a state close to the operating conditions. Further aging trials were
performed and revealed the partial dissolution of the M 23C6 carbides during the ﬁrst
aging step, Fig. 11a in the magni ﬁed inset. Consequently, the partial dissolution of
the M 23C6 carbides and precipitation of MC carbides during aging at higher tem-
peratures resulted in a disruption of the continuity of the M 23C6 grain boundary
carbides and the grain boundaries were overall less saturated with carbide when
exposed to the ﬁnal 800 °C aging temperature.
Mechanical testing was performed at temperatures up to 800 °C in tension and
760 °C in creep. Both temperatures are within the M 23C6 precipitation region of the
phase diagram of Fig. 1. Thus, microstructural changes are expected to occur
during at the higher temperatures. The majority of the creep specimens were
exposed at 760 °C for times from ∼100 h to times close to 1000 h. This resulted in
signiﬁcant precipitation of the M 23C6 carbides, leading to saturation of the grain
boundaries for all aging treatments. Therefore, while grain boundary segments were
free of precipitates in the two step aging treatments prior to testing, long high

temperature exposure complicated by stress resulted in a microstructure close to
that of the standard aging treatment, Fig. 10. Furthermore, the MC carbides were
found to dissolve at the test temperature, subsequently acting as a carbon source for
additional M
23C6 precipitation and subsequent coarsening [ 5]. In addition, grain
boundary γ′ precipitated around the M 23C6 carbides, Fig. 10b–f from the break-
down of the MC carbides: MC + γ → M23C6 + γ′ [25]. Finally, cellular and
lamellar carbides, see Fig. 11b, were observed following creep testing of the
specimens, particularly in Alloy 2, which contained less carbon. Those carbides
commonly form from a supersaturated matrix and are a result of the supersaturated
species partitioning between two or more phases [ 26–28].
Resistance to high-temperature creep deformation is essential for A-USC cast-
ings. Although, the IN740H castings in this study met the tensile property
requirements, they had minimal ductility in creep failing at about 2% elongation.
Fracture of the specimens primarily occurred intergranularly (see Fig. 9) along the
carbides and surrounding phase, Fig. 10f. While discrete M
23C6 grain boundary
carbides are usually bene ﬁcial to the mechanical properties by restricting grain
boundary sliding, saturation of the grain boundaries by blocky or lamellar carbides
can adversely affect ductility of the alloy [ 13]. Consequently, cracks propagate at
the grain boundaries following the debonding of the carbides as observed in
Fig. 12. This can be interpreted using the tensile data of Fig. 6 where RT defor-
mation showed greater elongation of the 950 °C/800 °C aged specimens while
deformation at 800 °C resulted is signi ﬁcantly less ductility with a measured
elongation of ∼4.9%, While RT deformation does not trigger the precipitation of
M
23C6 carbides, testing at 800 °C corresponds to the standard aging temperature
within the M 23C6 precipitation region, Fig. 1. Therefore, the carbide-free grain
boundary segments are likely responsible for the added ductility at room temper-
ature. Furthermore, no γ′ free zones were observed around them and the
precipitate-strengthening of the surrounding matrix is conserved. During creep
deformation, the extended exposure at 760 °C further facilitates formation of
M
23C6 carbides, which continuously affects ductility of the alloy and resulted in
times to failure below 1000 h. The increases in time to failure in the 850 °C/800 °C
and 950 °C/800 °C aged specimens are likely attributed to the more diverse
repartition of carbides and precipitate free segments at the beginning of creep
deformation sequence, which reduces the creep rate, Table 3. Once the boundaries
become saturated with M
23C6 carbides, debonding of the carbides from the matrix
along the boundary occurs due to localized crystallographic stresses from the creep
load. Thus, cracks propagate in an intergranular manner throughout the cross
section of the specimens. Overall, it was observed that secondary cracks were
arrested by carbide-free segments and stopped around the last carbide. Finally, the
overall lower mechanical properties of Alloy 2 were attributed to the precipitation
of cellular carbides which is known to considerably reduce ductility in alloys of this
type [ 29].
The microstructure of all specimens investigated were characterized under the
SEM and no η phase precipitation was observed. Long term η phase precipitation in
Thermal Processing Design of Cast INCONEL ® Alloy 740H … 843

## Page 831

the cast alloys has yet to be investigated. From the results of this investigation,
precipitation of the η phase could be delayed by the high density of grain boundary
carbides as compared to wrought alloys. Furthermore, the larger grains in the cast
version in ﬂuence diffusion mechanisms. Shingledecker et al. [ 30] reported η pre-
cipitation after 1000 h in some of their wrought alloys, depending on the Ti/Al
ratio. Given that none of the creep tests reached 1000 h, there is no basis for
evaluating η formation based on previous studies of wrought alloys.
Conclusions
Different aging treatments were investigated for their effect on the mechanical
properties of cast IN740H, primarily the change in elongation to failure in creep.
The following conclusions are reported based on the results presented in this
investigation:
1. Cast versions of IN740H meet the yield strength property requirements for
A-USC power plants. However, poor elongation in creep was found in all
specimens due to the extensive precipitation of M 23C6 grain boundary carbides
that facilitate stress concentrations during creep at the boundary leading to crack
propagation from debonding of the precipitates from the matrix.
2. Aging temperatures above 800 °C resulted in precipitation of MC carbides and
grain boundary segments free of precipitate phases. The phases that were
observed and the estimated solvus temperatures were in agreement with ther-
modynamic predictions with the exception of the η phase.
3. Longer times to failure and lower secondary creep rates were recorded in the
850 °C/800 °C and 950 °C/800 °C specimens compared to the standard age.
This was attributed to the cleaner grain boundaries at the early stages of creep
deformation and the ability of the carbide-free grain boundary segments to arrest
cracks.
4. Deformation processes due to creep testing and the time spent at the operating
conditions for IN740H contribute to the formation and coarsening of M 23C6
carbides, which is problematic in castings due to the large grain size and

P. Alvarez, L. Vázquez, P. M. García-Riesco, P. P. Rodríguez,
A. Magaña and F. Santos
Abstract High temperature Ni-based superalloys are largely used in components
of aircraft engines which are subjected to high thermal (above 700 °C) and struc-
tural loads. Investment casting has been traditionally implemented for the manu-
facturing of these components with different levels of complexity and size.
However, investment casting of large and complex parts can entail some dif ﬁculties
which lead to higher casting defect ratios and the need of repairing. Therefore, it is
essential to develop easy to repair Ni-based superalloys castings, i.e., castings with
an enhanced weldability or reduced weld cracking susceptibility. Improvement of
weldability will also enable the combination of small size castings with forged and
rolled components in welded structures reducing overall manufacturing costs and
foundry capacity requirements. Cracking susceptibility of Ni-based superalloy
castings is much greater in comparison with equivalent wrought components due to
coarser and non-homogeneous microstructures, grain boundary segregations and
particular chemistry which promote several cracking mechanisms during welding.
A methodology based on Varestraint test (hot cracking test) is introduced to
