Introduction
Ni-based superalloys were developed with the purpose to work in corrosive envi-
ronments and high temperature conditions maintaining their tensile, fatigue and
creep properties [ 1, 2]. The ﬁrst precipitation-strengthened Ni-based superalloys
were strengthened by precipitation of γ′ (Ni
3(Ti, Al)) but they underwent severe
strain age cracking (SAC) after welding and post weld heat treatment. In order to
avoid SAC, in 1963, Inconel 718 alloy was developed with outstanding mechanical
properties thanks to the excess of Nb in the matrix which forms the metastable γ″
precipitates of Ni
3Nb. The precipitation kinetics of γ″ is slower compared to γ′
which contributes to the improvement of weldability and resistance to SAC [ 2]. The
suitable properties of this alloy made possible to employ it in the manufacturing gas
turbines and aero-engine components [ 1, 2].
Precipitation-strengthened Ni-based alloys are composed by an austenite matrix
with secondary and intermetallic phases such as NbC and Laves phases. These last
two phases are present in IN718 as a result of segregation in castings and welds [ 3].
Due to the metastable nature of γ″ precipitate, IN718 alloy is used for temperature
service until 650 °C. Above this temperature γ″ phase is replaced by δ phase which
reduces creep resistance, ductility and weldability.
Wrought and rolled IN718 are considered weldable alloys, however severe
cracking can be obtained when working with equivalent casting parts. The cracking
mechanisms frequently observed in welds in IN718 alloy, are the heat affected zone
(HAZ) liquation cracking [ 4–9] and solidi ﬁcation cracking in the fusion zone
(FZ) [1]. HAZ liquation cracking is caused primarily by the constitutional liquation
of NbC, melting of Laves phase in the grain boundaries, liquation of δ phase and by
coarse microstructures in the HAZ [ 5, 10–12]. Some studies revealed that the
solution annealing reduces the susceptibility to this kind of cracking in IN718 while
ageing heat treatments promotes it [ 6, 7, 13–17]. Moreover solidi ﬁcation cracking
occurs due to the formation of γ/NbC and γ/Laves constituents in the interdendritic
zones as a result of segregation of chemical elements. This segregation occurs due
the presence of residual elements like B, C and Zr or impurities (P and S which
850 P. Alvarez et al.

## Page 837

must be kept as low as possible), low interstitial element like Si, or combinations of
Nb and C. Residual stresses, solidi ﬁcation shrinkage and weld pool size also
inﬂuences the susceptibility to this cracking mechanism [ 18].
The authors of this paper are currently involved in a research project trying to
improve the weldability of IN718 investment castings [ 19]. For that reason it is
important to settle a hot cracking susceptibility assessment trial which can evaluate
weldability improvements and conclude on signi ﬁcant weldability differences
between castings with different chemical compositions, casting conditions or heat
treatments.
Weldability is usually de ﬁned as the material ’s resistance to cracking during
fabrication. Thus, a material that has good weldability will be resistant to various
forms of cracking during welding. Different tests have been previously developed to
compare and quantify weldability. In this context, Varestraint test was designed in
1960s by Savage and Lundin in order to evaluate hot cracking susceptibility due to
metallurgical variables of a material [ 1, 20–22]. The basic test is the longitudinal
one which consists in the application of a bending deformation along the length of
the weld (Fig. 1). It uses several interchangeable die blocks to produce speci ﬁc
augmented strains that lead to different amount of cracking in both FZ and HAZ.
Cracks are measured and the sum of all them gives the total crack length (TCL),
forming a curve that quantitatively represents the weldability for a material.
Nowadays there are several modi ﬁcations of the original test. Despite there is an
international standard covering the application of this test, there are many testing
conditions which are not fully imposed [ 23]. Test results can be used to compare
and rank alloys in the same machine, but trends may not be fully reproducible in
different ones. Also, the measurement procedure is performed in a different ways in
different labs [ 21].
Moreover, this test has an inherent variability which is particularly high for
castings due to their inhomogeneous microstructure. Selected welding (heat input)
and testing parameters (stroke rate, mandrel radius) and the TCL measurement
procedure itself also contribute to result variability. In a recent paper this was nicely
investigated [ 21].
In this work, an evaluation of a testing procedure for studying the weldability of
Ni superalloys is provided. The reliability of this assessment methodology is tested

Experimental Procedure
In this study plates of wrought IN718 alloy were used for testing weldability
assessment methodology. Chemical composition of tested alloy is included in
Table 1. Rolled material ful ﬁlled the standard AMS 5596 and it was in the solution
annealed condition (995 ± 10 °C).
The metallographic preparation for the microstructure analysis of base material
and welds, consisted of polishing the previously mounted sample with diamond
suspension up to 1 µm particle size. After that the samples were chemically etched
with Kalling ’s reagent. The microstructure was observed in the Field emission gun
scanning electron microscope (FEG-SEM) (ZEISS Ultra Plus Field Emission) and
in the light optical microscope (Olympus GX 51).
The weldability of this material was tested in a recently made Varestraint testing
device at IK4-LORTEK facilities (Fig. 2). The test bench was designed and
manufactured by IK4-LORTEK and it complies with the general requirements set
by ISO/TR 17641-3 “Destructive tests on welds in metallic materials-Hot cracking
tests for weldments-Arc welding processes-Part 3: Externally loaded tests ”. The
system is designed to work both with arc welding and laser beam welding equip-
ment as well as different testing parameters (i.e. stroke rate, welding rate, syn-
chronization set-ups).
The Varestraint system integrates a compact tooling for application of bending
deformation during test. It is composed by a mandrel and two rolls which rotate
without restraint (Fig. 2).
The Varestraint test bench at IK4-LORTEK is also composed by a hydraulic
system of a maximum load of 80 KN controlled by a high precision servovalve to
perform an accurate movement of the cylinder. The response time at the highest
stroke rate of 150 mm/s is only 0.03 s which is equivalent to 4.5 mm. This is
observed in Fig. 3, where commanded stroke during deformation time is compared
with real signal from servovalve.
In conventional Varestraint test different augmented strains are applied using
different mandrel radii according to the following equation.

Results
Characterization of the Base Material
An equiaxed microstructure is observed in the base metal, wrought IN718 alloy.
There is a signi ﬁcant presence of twins, which is a common feature in this type of
austenitic superalloys [ 24]. The presence of Nb carbides was detected by
Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) microanalysis (Fig. 4).
The grain size measured is 30 ± 2 µm, corresponding to a grade G7 ASTM.
A representative micrograph is shown in Fig. 5.
The autogenous weld bead achieved with selected welding parameters is shown
in Fig. 6. The width of the fusion zone at the face was approximately 8 mm and full
penetration was obtained with minimum reinforcement in the root.

Discussion
As explained in the introduction, Varestraint tests has been traditionally applied to
study hot cracking susceptibility of Ni-based superalloy [ 21]. This is a well-known
test method to analyze solidi ﬁcation and HAZ liquation cracking in these alloys.
However, a great scattering in the TCL is usually observed in the results obtained
by this test which makes dif ﬁcult to rank alloys and batches.
At the beginning of this work, the standard deviation obtained from 3 samples
tested in the same condition was 36.6% of the mean value for the worst case (i.e.,
2% augmented strain and up to 50X magni ﬁcation for TCL measurement). For the
same testing condition, but increasing the magni ﬁcation, the standard deviation on
the results for the same samples was reduced to 11.7%. The same great reduction on
scattering was observed for samples tested at 4% and 8% when using this mea-
surement procedure (procedure B) leading to TCL standard deviations of 9.1% and

## Page 847

12.3%, respectively (Table 4). Therefore, the TCL measurement procedure and the
magniﬁcation employed are of great importance for the reliability of the results. It is
worth noting that ISO/TR 17641-3:2005 standard suggest to examine cracks at a
magniﬁcation of 25X which in the current study led to an enhanced variability on
TCL [ 23]. According to current work, this magni ﬁcation should be increased at
least to 150X in order to reduce result variability and one should not adhere strictly
to the standard. Next ﬁgure compares the cracks detected and measured in the same
sample when completing the inspection of cracks at 50X and 150X, respectively. It
can be observed that the greatest difference relies in the number of cracks inter-
preted in the FZ. No differences in the number of cracks detected in the HAZ were
observed.
At 50X, 21 cracks were measured in total whereas at 150X this number was
reduced to 18, with MCL of 2.74 mm and 1.68 mm respectively. Therefore, MCL
can be more precisely determined at higher magni ﬁcation since the operator can
decide better on the real starting and ﬁnishing points of cracks. As a consequence
the TCL measured at the lowest magni ﬁcation was comparatively much higher.
This increase on TCL which is consistently observed in current work is also due to
the misinterpretation of marks in the FZ which are not really open cracks if ana-
lyzed at high magni ﬁcation (Fig. 10). Therefore, the operator is able to distinguish
more clearly real cracks from other solidi ﬁcation marks (crests) in the weld bead
when increasing magni ﬁcation.
The increase of the inspection magni ﬁcation ensures also the highest repeata-
bility. This was demonstrated by measuring the same sample 5 times by the same
operator (Table 3). The resulting ratio between Avg. TCL and StDev. TCL was 4.4
and 7.3% for the two samples (2 and 4% augmented strain, respectively) which can
be considered as the minimum error introduced due to the measurement with this
procedure (Procedure B).
Besides the measurement procedure, the synchronization has demonstrated to
directly in ﬂuence Varestraint test results. As shown above (Table 6), much higher

## Page 848

TCL was observed when the deformation was fully completed exactly when the
TIG welding torch surpasses the center point of the specimen. The difference with
the case at which the deformation starts just while welding the central point is huge,
particularly for the case of 4% augmented strain. In this case, the Avg. TCL rises
twofold and this is clearly observed just looking at the surface of tested samples
(Fig. 11). Note that in this analysis, the Procedure B was applied and therefore a
minimum scattering on the measurement of TCL was ensured for samples tested in
each condition. Reduced scattering in the measured average values from 3 tested
samples also supports the robust and repetitive behavior of the Varestraint test
system and con ﬁrms the important effect of synchronization. Fast, accurate and
repetitive synchronization between welding run and deformation is usually con-
sidered as an important requirement of Varestraint test systems [ 20], but to the
author’s best knowledge there is not any relevant deep analysis on this matter.
Concerning speed and accuracy, the Varestraint system used in this study is
equipped with a fast servovalve, advanced control system and pressure accumulator
which provides a response time of 0.03 s to reach the required stroke rate since the
triggering signal is received from the control system.

862 P. Alvarez et al.

## Page 849

As it is shown in Fig. 11, there were clearly larger cracks in the FZ of samples
tested with anticipated synchronization. i.e., when deformation ﬁnishes exactly
while the TIG torch goes by the central point of the testing sample. Note that this
central point is highlighted on the pictures of tested samples in Fig. 11. For the
anticipated condition, total crack length rises to 30.8 mm whereas for the defor-
mation in the center point the TCL is 15.1 mm (Table 6). Moreover average
maximum crack length (Avg. MCL) was much longer (2.6 mm) in comparison with
the other synchronization setup (1.8 mm) (Table 7).
Both higher Avg. TCL and Avg. MCL for the anticipated synchronization can be
explained as follows. Considering that melt pool has a given size which is
dependent on heat input resulting from welding parameters (current, voltage and
welding speed), the relative positioning of melt pool while applying the deforma-
tion (stroke) will affect the induced FZ cracking. This is because the application of
the augmented strain in the sample is not instantaneous and requires some time to
reach to value de ﬁned by Eq. 1. Looking at Fig. 3, 225 ms are required to reach
35 mm stroke required for 8% augmented strain. If the stroke rate is reduced to
10 mm/s, the time to reach 8% augment strain increases to 3.37 s.
If the melt pool is mainly before the contact point to the die mandrel (central
point), it means that the material within this testing area (between the start of
deformation and the central point) will be in the liquid state. Therefore, solidi ﬁ-
cation in this area will be coincident with application of full deformation and
solidiﬁcation cracking will be enhanced in the FZ.
On the contrary, if the melt pool is exactly at the central point or contact pint to
the die mandrel, there will be a lower amount of material in the same so-called
testing area in liquid state. This is because the material in this area will have been
solidiﬁed by the time the deformation reaches the augmented strain value de ﬁned
by Eq. 1. Therefore, FZ cracking will not be so critical even if the same defor-
mation is induced during Varestraint test.
This effect of synchronization is critical at low stroke rates and high augmented
strain levels because the time required to reach augmented strain is longer. It must
be highlighted that due to the nature of Varestraint test. FZ cracks only appear at the
rear of the welding run. Therefore the temperature and physical state (liquid or
solid) of the material placed before the central point during the application of
deformation will be critical. In fact, the sample surface at this central point is the
point where induced longitudinal deformations reach top value.
This effect of synchronization is not observed for the HAZ cracking phenomena
since these cracks are mostly perpendicular to weld bead. In this case a comparable
number of cracks and crack length were observed in the HAZ irrespectively of
synchronization setup.
Finally, since different synchronization criteria induce different cracking in the
FZ, the same one must be implemented if a comparable weldability assessment and
hot cracking susceptibility analysis of Ni-based superalloys is intended. This is
particularly important for castings. Otherwise, there is the risk to draw different
conclusions and observe extremely different FZ cracking behavior.
A Simpli ﬁed Varestraint Test for Analyzing Weldability … 863

## Page 850

Conclusions
The following conclusions are drawn for current work:
• The magni ﬁcation of the microscope is an important factor for an accurate
determination of the cracks, especially in the FZ. A magni ﬁcation of 150X,
which is much higher than the value suggested by current testing standard lead
to reduced standard deviations and lower errors as well as scattering induced by
the measurement.
• Synchronization between welding run and deformation is also a critical testing
parameter which has a direct and huge impact on TCL and MCL. Enhanced
solidiﬁcation cracking in the FZ is induced if bending deformation is introduced
slightly before the central line. This is observed by longer cracks in FZ. Syn-
chronization requirements are not fully de ﬁned by the testing standard and they
must be known when comparing results from different machines.
• This work has enabled to de ﬁne a testing and measuring procedure to reduce
scatter and improve reliability on the investigation of hot cracking susceptibility
of Inco 718 Ni-Fe based superalloy. This methodology reduces test and TCL
measurement related scattering and set the conditions to compare weldability of
different Inco 718 batches (differences in chemical composition and residual
elements, grain size, …) and manufacturing conditions (wrought versus cast).

employing SMAW (Shielded metal arc welding) as well as GMAW (gas metal arc
welding) process. Fatigue crack growth and fracture toughness characteristics of
SMA weld Inconel 625 compact tension specimens of thickness 25 mm in as
welded and after post weld thermal aging treatments(temperatures ranging from 650

plotted between crack length and number of cycles. Fatigue crack growth rate was
examined in delta k range of 21 –39 MPa √m. Varying degree of precipitation in
these welds was observed due to thermal aging which in ﬂuenced their fracture
toughness signi ﬁcantly. The fracture toughness values for SMA weld Inconel 625
specimens in as welded condition was found to be J

crack growth during the J-integral test and J max increased to (221.58 kJ/m 2) and J Q
(12.56 kJ/m 2).

## Page 853

Introduction
Nickel based superalloy Inconel 625 is often used in corrosive environments at very
high temperatures that results in gradual degradation of the overlay in the form of
corrosion leading to stress concentration zones and hence has a tendency of
cracking. Since Inconel 625 is an expensive superalloy, repair is often a more
economic choice then the replacement of the components. For example, ﬂow cells
are used in onshore and offshore re ﬁneries for the measurement of crucial param-
eters ( ﬂow rate, temperature and condition) of the crude oil which is ﬂowing
through the pipes of nuclear power plants, oil and gas re ﬁneries. The temperature of
bad crude oil is high and it carries impurities along with it which is the cause of
pitting corrosion and pits formed thereafter act as crack initiation sites.
Welding/surfacing of low alloyed stainless steel with expensive superalloys
Inconel 625 to enhance the performance of components at relatively low cost has
been investigated by many scholars [ 1–3]. The metallurgical, mechanical and
corrosion resistance properties of Inconel 625 clads/welds using different tech-
niques like laser [ 4–17] and HVOF [ 9, 14, 18–23] have been studied by different
researchers. Further, the properties of this alloy when subjected to different aging
conditions have also been investigated by few researchers [ 9, 24–29]. For instance,
Verdi et al. [ 10] coated Inconel 625 on ferritic and stainless steel substrate using
laser thereafter treated the coatings at 520 and 800 °C for variable exposure times.
They concluded that treating the alloy at 520 °C increased the carbides and sec-
ondary phase formation which resulted in higher hardness and elastic modulus of
300 GPa on the contrary treatment at 800 °C decreased the hardness and elastic
modulus. Mittra et al. [ 27] concluded that treatment of Inconel 625 at 540 °C
resulted in formation of γ phase and Ni
2 (Cr, Mo) and consequently increase in
yield and tensile strength and decrease in ductility. Borowski et al. [ 28] reported
that glow discharged assisted nitriding treatment of Inconel 625 resulted in increase
in hardness from 380 to 1480 HV0.05 and further nitride layer formation increased
the corrosion resistance and fatigue strength.
So based upon the literature reviewed, it is observed that work reported on
Inconel 625 processed using SMAW and GMAW processes is scant. In view of the
industrial importance as well as the potential capabilities of these conventional
processes it seems that if welding/cladding procedures are established and com-
parisons are made on the basis of fracture toughness and fatigue behaviour of these
clads, the data thus generated would be bene ﬁcial for the welding industry involved
in Inconel 625 fabrications. Besides the cladding procedures for fresh overlays, the
data can be extended for repair and reclamation work also, as both these welding
processes possess all positional capability, the potential that can be utilized at site
where repair work may be required to be carried out on structures/fabrications
serving in actual environment. This research gap led to formulating the present
study where investigations were planned to compare the fracture toughness and
fatigue behaviour of Inconel 625 clads overlaid using two welding processes viz.
SMAW and GMAW process and subjecting these clads so made to different post
868 S. S. Sandhu and A. S. Shahi

## Page 854

weld thermal aging treatments (650 °C/10 h, 650 °C/100 h, 850 °C/10 h and 850
°C/100 h). One of the typical nuclear industrial applications that intend to bene ﬁt
from the data generated on the basis of this work is the ﬂow cells of the nuclear
plants which are subjected to high temperature fatigue.
Experimental Details
Material Combination Used
Nickel based superalloy Inconel 625 was used as the ﬁller material to clad 25 mm
thick rolled plates of AISI 304L stainless steel using SMAW and GMAW process.
The chemical composition of the substrate as well as the ﬁller is shown in Table 1.
Welding Procedure and Thermal Aging Treatments
Different welds were fabricated using a single V groove con ﬁguration with a grove
angle of 60° machined in the substrate up to 20 mm thickness. For ﬁlling the
groove volume multipass multilayer technique was adopted which has been detailed
schematically in Fig. 1, using suitable welding conditions as mentioned in Table 2.
Prior to welding, the AISI 304L plates were cleaned mechanically and chemically
so as to avoid any source of dirt, oil, rust, scale etc. which could interact with the
welding arc and result in weld defects. The SMAW electrodes were baked at 300 °C
for 1 h to remove moisture. The overlays of Inconel 625 were subjected to ultra-
sonic testing to ensure that the welds were free from defects like blow holes,
porosity, surface cracks etc. As shown in Fig. 2, for CTOD studies of these welds
suitable number of specimens were extracted from each welded plate. These
specimens were further subjected to four PWTA treatments viz. 650 °C/10 h, 650
°C/100 h, 850 °C/10 h and 850 °C/100 h followed by furnace cooling in each case.

CTOD Testing of Inconel 625 Welds
Fatigue and fracture toughness of the Inconel 625 weld metal was evaluated using
CTOD testing technique. These CTOD test specimens were extracted using a wire
cut EDM from the AISI 304L substrate welded using Inconel 625 as shown in
Fig. 2. The dimensions of the CT specimen are shown in Fig. 3 in accordance with
ASTM standard E 647 and E 1820. The specimens were pre-cracked to 5.5 mm
length, perpendicular direction to welding, with a width (W) of 25 mm and a
0/W
ratio of 0.416 were subjected to CTOD testing. Fatigue crack growth rate test was
conducted at a stress ratio of R = 0.2, where R represents the ratio of P min/Pmax
(with P min of 1.2 kN and P max of 6 kN) and 20 Hz frequency. The dedicated
software was used to plot graphs between crack propagation and the number of
cycles. The testing conditions were kept constant and crack extension from 5.5 to
11.25 mm was analysed for studying fatigue behavior of the clad specimens. The
specimens were pulled apart up to the point of fracture on the same machine to
study the nature of the fracture modes (Fig. 4).

Results and Discussion
Fatigue and Fracture Toughness Performance of Inconel
625 Welds
Different specimens extracted from SMA as well as GMA welded joints were
subjected to CTOD testing as well as J-integral testing for studying their fatigue and
fracture behavior. Based upon the CTOD results, the curves between crack length
(a) versus no. of cycles (N) were generated by the dedicated software and few of
these results are presented in Fig. 5. One CTOD specimen each was tested corre-
sponding to the as cladded condition as well as each post weld thermal aging

extension of the pre-machined crack from 5.5 to 11.25 mm, keeping all other
testing conditions same, total number of cycles withstood by the GMA specimen
(38,766 cycles) were more as compared to the SMA specimen (30,081 cycles).

Under aging condition of 650 °C/10 h and 100 h a signi ﬁcant rise in the fatigue
performance of SMA as well as GMA welds could be attributed probably to the
formation of different precipitates like, Laves phase, γ′ and γ″ besides the possi-

impede the movement of dislocations by creating a sort of pinning effect due to
which fatigue crack resistance of these welds improved signi ﬁcantly. However,
aging condition, of 850 °C/10 h and 100 h, can probably lead to the formation of

(CTOD) of the GMAW weld joint has been reported to be signi ﬁcantly more than
SMAW joints due to presence of ﬁne slag inclusions from the coated electrode in
the resulted dissimilar weld between SA508Gr.3Cl.1 and SS304LN [ 30].
SEM Fractography of CTOD Tested Inconel 625 Welds
All the CTOD specimens of Inconel 625 welds, after attaining the required crack
extension of around 11.25 mm, were fractured by using the machine setting which
facilitated movement of the lower jaw in such a way that the uncracked ligament of
the specimen fractured under gradual tensile loading. The fractured ends of these
specimens were then subjected to SEM examination for studying their fracture
behavior and the fractographs so obtained are presented in Fig. 7a–j. As seen from
Fig. 7a, b, in the as welded condition, GMA weld showed closely spaced striations
as compared to the SMA weld which accounted for its higher fatigue strength.
Figure 7c–f, showed that aging conditions of 650 °C/10 and 100 h, owing to the
presence of different precipitates, resulted into closely spaced and high density
fatigue striations that were observed on the fractured surfaces of these specimens,
which accounted for signi ﬁcant improvement in their respective fatigue perfor-
mances. Corresponding to aging condition of 850 °C/10 h and 100 h, as seen from
Fig. 7g–j, voids as well as cracks of varying sizes, besides the presence of few ﬂat
and featureless regions, showed a drastic loss of fatigue strength in all the
specimens.

## Page 865

Pitting Behavior of Thermally Aged
Inconel 625 Weld Claddings Made
Using SMAW and GMAW Process
A. S. Shahi and Sandeep Singh Sandhu
Abstract Comparative investigations were carried out where multipass
multi-layers of Inconel 625 (UNS N06625) weld claddings were overlaid on
12 mm thick austenitic stainless steel plates (AISI 304L) using SMAW (shielded
metal arc welding process) and GMAW (gas metal arc welding) process. The
specimens extracted from the cladded plates were subjected to four different post
weld thermal aging treatments (650 °C/10 h, 650 °C/100 h, 850 °C/10 h and 850
°C/100 h). The pitting corrosion of Inconel 625 clads was evaluated using PAP
(Potentiodynamic anodic polarization) technique and the results were generated as
pitting curves which depicted their behavior. Pitting potential (E
pitt) for these welds
varied from 31.77 to 922.7 mV. Under all conditions, the GMA welds showed
better pitting performance than the SMA welds. Aging treatment of 650 °C/10 h
improved the pitting resistance of both the welds, as pitting potential of 922.7 mV
(which was recorded as the highest value of E
pitt among all the welds) was observed
in case of GMA weld and 384 mV for the SMA weld. Precipitation strengthening
occurred under this aging condition which was attributable to the presence of Laves
phase, γ′ and γ″-phase, besides carbides in Inconel 625 weld/clad metal. However,
a loss of pitting resistance was observed under aging conditions 850 °C/10 h and
100 h, which could be attributed to the segregation behavior of alloying elements as
well as the formation of delta phase which promoted the tendencies for pit nucle-
ation and their subsequent growth in the matrix of the weld metal.
Keywords SMAW process
⋅ GMAW process ⋅ Inconel 625 weld claddings
Pitting corrosion ⋅ PAP (Potentiodynamic anodic polarization) technique

Introduction
Weld surfacing is de ﬁned as the application by welding, brazing or thermal
spraying of a layer or layers of material to a surface to obtain desired properties or
dimensions as opposed to making a joint. Surfacing is a well-established, proven,
convenient and economical alternative to the use of the solid alloys. Additionally,
surfacing is also used for repair and reclamation of the worn out critical components
for improving their life. Critical components used in harsh and high temperature
environmental conditions need to be built of materials that have appropriate
mechanical strength besides corrosion resistance and wear resistance properties.
Superalloys with high anti corrosion and wear resistance properties are expensive as
these are rich in nickel, chromium and molybdenum. As a result, extensive uti-
lization of wrought superalloys is an expensive proposition. Moreover, superalloys
might not meet strength requirements for the structure components. Thus a pro-
tective layer of superalloy on low alloyed material is designed for strength and
protection against wear and corrosion. Various processes that are known to be used
industrially for cladding of low alloyed metals are shielded metal arc welding
(SMAW), gas metal arc welding (GMAW), submerged arc welding (SAW).
Mendez et al. [ 1] gas tungsten arc welding (GTA) [ 2] plasma arc welding
(PAW) [ 3] laser [ 4, 5] and explosive welding [ 6]. Among the various welding
processes, SMAW and GMAW processes are relatively cost effective. Welding
machine related to these two processes can be easily moved to the repair site and
repairs can be easily done in all positions i.e. ﬂat position(1G), horizontal position
(2G), vertical position (3G) and overhead (4G) [ 1]. These processes cover the range
from manual and semiautomatic to automatic welding.Welding offers several
advantages over other coating techniques such as laser cladding, HVOF coating etc.
Firstly, the metallurgical bond between the overlay and substrate is not susceptible
to spallation. Secondly, the overlays can easily be applied free of porosity and other
defects. Thirdly, weld overlays are very versatile as a large number of commercially
available alloys can be selected to provide protection from a wide range of envi-
ronmental degradation mechanisms. The effectiveness of weld overlays depends
mainly on two factors: (l) the welding process and (2) the overlay alloy compo-
sition. The welding process must be selected to apply protective overlays at high
deposition rates and thermal ef ﬁciency with good control over overlay-substrate
dilution and overlay thickness.
A clad metal is a composite comprising of two or more layers that have been
bonded to each other. The bonding may have been accomplished by rolling,
extrusion, welding, diffusion bonding, casting, heavy chemical deposition or heavy
electroplating. Among all the cladding methods, weld cladding is commonly used
to ensure adequate bond integrity between the clad metal and substrate. Further, the
effect of post weld thermal aging treatments on the precipitation phases that form
during solidiﬁcation of the weld metal and their growth in the matrix also affects its
service performance characteristics. For instance, corrosion rate and hardness
decrease with an increase in heat treatment temperatures/soaking periods which can
882 A. S. Shahi and S. S. Sandhu

## Page 867

be due to the increase in the volume fraction and stability of the austenitic matrix
and favorable morphology of the second phase (carbides) [ 7]. Performance of the
claddings is directly related to the material characteristics.
The superalloy term usually refers to high performing materials which combine
high strength with corrosion resistance at high temperatures ranging between 650
°C and higher. Superalloys are divided into three categories i.e. Nickel based,
Nickel and Iron based and Cobalt based super alloys. Since the inception,
researchers have worked on various ways to improve the usability of the superal-
loys in terms of corrosion resistance, wear resistance and mechanical properties in
extreme environments [ 8]. Nickel based superalloys contain signi ﬁcant alloying
additions of various elements in solid solution. As these superalloys have FCC (face
centered cubic) structure, the structure allows addition of other elements into the
substitutional solid solution which further increases the volume fraction of γ phase.
Additionally, grain boundaries are strengthened by precipitation of metallic car-
bides. In order to increase the strength of Ni-Cr-Al-Ti alloys, many researchers have
worked on addition of various elements (chromium, cobalt, molybdenum, alu-
minum and titanium) to promote solid solution strengthening in order to increase
volume fraction of strengthening phases.
Lately many researchers have worked on precipitation hardening of superalloys
by aging it at different temperatures and exposure times which lead to formation of
complex phases like γ′ phase [Ni
3 (Al, Ti,Nb)], γ″ phase (Ni 3Nb), blocky MC (M
denotes Nb, Ti), M 6C (M denotes Si, Ni, Cr) and M 23C6 (M denotes Cr) carbides
[9–16] revealed that internal strain generated due to addition of particles or solute
atoms in the matrix leads to solid solution strengthening and precipitation
strengthening of superalloys. Also if nickel base alloy and austenitic stainless steel
combinations are to be used, AISI 304H is reported to be extensively used in the
super heater tubes of power boiler due to its superior mechanical properties at
elevated temperatures [ 17].
Inconel 625 has a face centered cubic crystal structure. This alloy is solid
solution strengthened by chromium, molybdenum and tungsten. Their strengthen-
ing effect is proportional to difference in atomic size of these strengthening ele-
ments and nickel. Besides solid solution strengthening, many phases and carbides
precipitate in Inconel 625 alloy depending upon chemical composition and aging
treatments, which makes this alloy precipitation hardened [ 18–20]. The
time-temperature-transformation diagram by [ 10] as shown in Fig. 1.
As can be seen from this TTT diagram number of carbides appear depending
upon solidi ﬁcation rate, carbon content in the alloy, time and temperature of the
holding, such as MC (M rich in Ti and Nb), M
23C (M rich in Cr), M 6C (M rich in
Ni, Mo and Nb). Besides carbides as per the TTT diagram, several ordered phases
precipitate such as γ′, γ″, δ-phase and laves phases in the γ matrix of Inconel 625.
Ni
2 (Cr, Mo) phase is also formed on aging below 873 K and dissolves above this
temperature [11, 21]. As per the TTT diagram, the γ″ phase and δ-phase precipitate
approximately in the range of 570 –820 °C and 650 –1000 °C respectively. Nucle-
ation of δ-phase takes place on the grain boundaries at 700 °C [ 10]. Only δ-phase
forms above 750 °C. The formation of different carbides depends upon the
Pitting Behavior of Thermally Aged Inconel 625 Weld Claddings … 883

## Page 868

temperature and duration of heat treatment the alloy is subjected. MC and M 6C
types of carbides precipitate in the temperature range of 870 –1040 °C. M 23C6
precipitates in the temperature range of 700 –870 °C [ 22].
The critical components which are used in harsh, high temperature and in cor-
rosive environments are cladded with superalloys. They are expected to retain the
designed strength and corrosion resistance during their service life. However,
superalloys also react with the corrosive environment and corrode slowly as their
passive ﬁlm undergoes deterioration. Such destructions in the passive ﬁlm are due
to formation of localized pits. Pitting corrosion is a major problem associated with
the applications where superalloys are used in industries as cladding materials.
These pits act as stress concentration factors which provide sites for cracks to
initiate and propagate and thus leading to failure of engineering components in
service. Welding processes are often used for weld overlaying of different com-
ponents that are meant for being used under severe conditions of high temperature,
corrosion and wear in various critical industrial applications. Among various
welding processes SMAW and GMAW process is extensively used for fresh weld
overlays as well as repair and reclamation purposes so as to restore back the original
engineering functionalities of critical components.
So in view of the industrial importance of Inconel 625 alloy the present work
was carried out to investigate the in ﬂuence of two welding process viz. SMAW and
GMAW process on the metallurgical and pitting behavior of Inconel 625 weld
claddings such that the data generated on the basis of this piece of research could
highlight in comparative terms the productivity of each of these processes as well as
this alloy behavior under different thermal aging conditions.

Experimental Details
Materials Combination Used
Nickel based superalloy Inconel 625 was used as the ﬁller material for overlaying
25 mm thick rolled plates of AISI 304L stainless steel using SMAW and GMAW
process. The chemical composition of the substrate as well as the ﬁller is shown in
Table 1.
Weld Overlaying of Inconel 625
The choice of selection of the parametric combinations was based upon the trial
runs conducted using bead-on-plate experimentation i.e. corresponding to each
combination, clad beads were overlaid on the surface of the substrate plates. These
clad beads were then inspected using dye penetrant test for the presence of any
defect, which could occur in the form of blow holes, porosity, spatters, surface
cracks etc. This helped in selecting suitable parametric combinations that resulted

Pitting Behavior of Thermally Aged Inconel 625 Weld Claddings … 885

## Page 870

Before overlaying the clad beads, the surface of the substrate material was
thoroughly cleaned mechanically and chemically in order to avoid any source of
contamination like oil, dust, grease, rust etc. that could mix with the weld metal and
later on could become a source of major weld defect. For removing moisture, the
ﬂux coated electrodes used in SMAW process were baked by heating to 150 °C for
2 h. Inconel 625 clad beads were overlaid in ﬂat position within a current range of
80–105 A for SMAW and 90 –110 A for GMAW process, such that clad thickness
of around 25 mm could be built up on the substrate. Adequate weld bead contact
angle with the base material was ensured to have uniform bead shape deposition
without occurrence of any defect like voids between successive cladding weld pass
[23]. Dye penetrant test was performed on all the clad layers in order to check the
presence of possible macroscopic external defects such as surface porosity, surface
cracks, blow holes and spatters etc. Ultrasonic testing was carried out for identi-
ﬁcation of sub surface defects. Clad beads were found to be defect free and hence of
sound quality.
Post Weld Thermal Aging Treatments of Clads
As per the Time-Temperature-Transformation (TTT) diagram of Inconel 625, four
treatments (650 °C/10 h, 650 °C/100 h, 850 °C/10 h and 850 °C/100 h), were
chosen for inducing precipitation of ordered phases such as, Ni
2(Cr, Mo), γ′ [Ni3
(Al, Ti, Nb)] phase, γ″ (Ni3Nb) phase and δ-phase Ni (Nb, Mo). Post weld thermal
aging treatments were carried out in a digitally controlled muf ﬂe furnace where the
atmosphere was still air only.
Metallurgical Studies of Clads
Metallurgical characterization was carried out to reveal the microstructure of the
clad/weld metal and to diagnose the fundamental defects such as cracks, pores,
voids and inclusions etc. in the weld metal. Each specimen was extracted from the
weld pads across the welds (i.e. direction transverse to welding) and was cut to the
size of 50 mm × 25 mm × 5 mm. Largely these weld pads contained Inconel 625
clad metal, but the weld volume near to the base plate did contain 304 L base metal
also due to the dilution effect that occurs due to base metal melting which con-
tributes to the weld metal. The samples were ground to smooth the edges and to get
an even surface for the microhardness as well as precipitation studies. Standard
polishing procedures were used for general microstructural observations as per
ASTM E407-07 standard [ 24]. The specimens were polished on a polishing
machine using polishing papers of grit size 100, 200, 400, 600, 800 and 1000. Both
alumina powder and diamond paste were used for lapping using velvet cloth for
smooth ﬁnish. After the specimens achieved the desired ﬁnish, these surfaces were
886 A. S. Shahi and S. S. Sandhu

## Page 871

subjected to electrolytic etching on electrolytic etching machine by using electrolyte
comprising of oxalic acid (10 g) + distilled water (100 ml), and using the param-
eters viz. cell voltage of 6 V and etching time of 1 min, to reveal different phases
that were captured suitably using SEM and were further examined using EDS.
Pitting Corrosion Evaluation of Inconel 625 Welds
PAP (Potentiodynamic anodic polarization) technique as recommended by ASTM
standard [ 25] was used for evaluating clad/weld metal for measuring their pitting
corrosion resistance using a potentiostat (Make: Gamry instruments, USA; Model:
Potentiostat 600). Potentiodynamic scan was carried out to evaluate polarization
characteristics. Each specimen having cross sectional area of 0.441 cm
2 was
exposed directly to the test solution in this polarization test. Testing conditions
included electrolyte comprising of 0.5 M H
2SO4 + 0.1 M NaCl solution and the
electrode combination used comprised of graphite as the counter electrode, satu-
rated calomel electrode as the reference and the surface of the test specimen as the
working electrode. The scan rate of 1.67 mV/s and an initial delay for time period
of 200 s was used. The experimental procedure used for testing these specimens at
room temperature comprised of (i) 5 min delay at open circuit potential (Voc) and
(ii) anodic potentiodynamic scan starts at 50 mV below Voc to 1500 mV (SCE) at a
potential scan rate of 100 mV/min. Based upon the data acquisition during testing,
real time scan plots between potential and current density were generated with the
help of the dedicated software.
Results and Discussion
Microhardness Results
As shown in Table 3, it is seen that in the as welded condition GMA weld pos-
sessed relatively higher microhardness (peak value of 288HV 0.2), as compared to
the SMA weld (251HV 0.2). This difference may be attributed to the welding pro-
cess’s inherent nature by which weld metal cooling occurs i.e. in case of SMAW
process coating of the electrode burns and provides shielding to the weld pool,
while leaving a slag covering on the weld bead which reduces/retards the cooling
rate of the weld. This slower cooling rate in turn leads to coarse microstructure i.e.
in the present case for the weld/clad metal it refers to formation of long dendrites
with larger inter-dendritic spacing which results into lower hardness of the weld
metal. However in case of GMAW process, gas shielding envelope, although
protects adequate shielding to the weld pool, but does not leave any slag shield due
to which relatively higher cooling rates are experienced by the weld metal which
Pitting Behavior of Thermally Aged Inconel 625 Weld Claddings … 887

## Page 872

results into higher hardness of the weld metal. Further, when subjected to aging
treatments the peak hardness of the weld metal increased from 251 VHN to 298
VHN (when subjected to 650 °C/10 h) and further to 315 VHN (when subjected to
650 °C/100 h) in case of SMA clads. Improvement in the hardness was also
observed for the GMA weld metal with the difference that relatively higher
microhardness (increase from 288VHN to 336 VHN and then to 349 VHN) was
observed for the aged specimens, which however corresponding to 850 °C tem-
perature aging treatments showed a decreasing trend of microhardness for both
SMAas wellas GMA clads. Such rise and fall in the hardness of the clad/weld metal
may be attributed to a varying degree of precipitation.
Microstructural Characterization of Inconel 625 Welds
Using SEM and EDS

7, 8, 9, 10 and 11, which show the presence of different precipitates that occurred
due to aging in the as-welded as well as under different post weld thermal aging
conditions.

ðL → L+ γ → L+ γ + NbC → L+ γ + NbC + Laves → γ + NbC + LavesÞ
When subjected to different thermal aging treatments, different transformations
in terms of precipitation were observedin theweld metal microstructure for SMA
and GMA weld metal. The presence of Laves phase in Ni-based weld overlays has
been reported to be in a close range as found in the present work [ 29]. Further, the
segregation as found in the present work, where it was observed that Mo and Nb
showed a tendency to segregate in the interdendritic regions, may be attributed to
their low segregation coef ﬁcient (k), which as reported in the literature is 0.55 and
0.88 for Nb and Mo respectively [ 29]. When these clads were subjected to PWTA
(post weld thermal aging) treatment at 650 °C/10 h, γ′ phase appeared along with
Laves phase which is shown in Figs. 3 and 8 for respective welds. However, when
subjected to 650 °C/100 h, the dissolution of the Laves phase occurred and γ″ along
with carbides appeared (Figs. 4 and 9), which were identi ﬁed through SEM and
EDS examination of these welds.
Further, when subjected to PWTA at 850 °C/10 h and 100 h, it is seen from
Figs. 5, 6, 10 and 11 for respective Inconel-625 welds, that the dissolution of γ′ and
γ″ phase occurred, which resulted into the formation of δ-phase along with for-
mation of different types of carbides like MC and M
6C phases, the presence of
which was con ﬁrmed from the EDS results of these welds. Different precipitates
that were formed in case of SMA and GMA Inconel 625 clad/weld were found to be
in close agreement with the reported results in literature. For instance, the results
matched with the microstructural observations reported for service exposed alloy
625 ammonia cracker tubes subjected to ≈60,000 h at 873 K/600 °C [ 11] where it
is stated that longer aging of this alloy promoted coarsening of γ″ precipitates
besides resulting in precipitation of the δ-phase. δ-phase formation in Inconel-625
has also been reported to occur in approximate temperature range of 1023 –1223 K/
750–1000 °C, and its precipitation is preceded by γ″ precipitation below 1073 K/
800 °C [ 30]. Similarly, segregation behavior of alloying elements like Nb and Mo
have been reported to be segregated in case of additive layer manufactured
(ALM) Inconel-625 using GTAW process which has been found to result into
mechanical heterogeneity and hence its tensile properties [ 31]. From these results it
could be concluded that any welding or manufacturing process used for deposition
of Inconel 625 via its inherent cooling rate characteristics creates a strong in ﬂuence
on its microstructural development, thus leading to formation of different precipi-
tates of varying degree which consequentially can affect its mechanical properties.
Pitting Corrosion Performance of Inconel 625 GMA
and SMA Welds
The pitting corrosion evaluation of Inconel 625 welds using PAP (Potentiodynamic
anodic polarization) technique was carried out and the results so obtained in the
894 A. S. Shahi and S. S. Sandhu

## Page 879

form of pitting curves are shown in Fig. 12, and the pitting potential of each
specimen so tested is shown in Table 3. These values correspond to average of two
readings taken using fresh solution for each experiment. The range of pitting
potential (E pitt) in these welds varied from 31.77 to 922.7 mV, thus indicating a
strong variation of pitting resistance among these welds. In the as welded condition
GMA weld showed E
pitt of 149.2 mV as compared to SMA weld with E pitt value of
31.77 mV, thus indicating better pitting resistance possessed by the GMA welds as
compared to the SMA welds. Under all conditions, the GMA welds performed
better in terms of pitting behavior than the SMA welds which could be attributed to
Fig. 12 Pitting curves for different Inconel 625 clads/welds
Pitting Behavior of Thermally Aged Inconel 625 Weld Claddings … 895

## Page 880

the fact that GMA welds/clads owing to lesser base metal dilution adhered closely
to the ﬁller chemistry of the ﬁller Inconel 625, thus making them rich in Ni as
compared to SMA welds, which accounted for their better pitting performance.
Aging treatment of 650 °C/10 h improved the pitting resistance of both the welds,
however, a signi ﬁcant increase in pitting potential was observed for aging condi-
tion 650 °C/100 h where pitting potential of 922.7 mV (which was recorded as the
highest value of E
pitt among all the welds) was observed in case of GMA weld and
384 mV corresponding to the SMA weld. Such high pitting performance of this
alloy has also been reported by [ 32]. In general, it was observed that aging con-
dition of 650 °C/10 h and 100 h improved the pitting performance of all the welds
which could be attributed to precipitation strengthening that occurred under these
aging conditions. It could be concluded from these observations that the presence of
Laves phase, γ′ and γ″-phase, besides carbides in Inconel 625 weld metal due to
thermal aging improved its microhardness which consequentially improved its
pitting corrosion resistance also. However, a loss of pitting resistance observed
under aging condition 850 °C/10 h and 100 h could be attributed to the segregation
behavior of alloying elements as well as formation of delta phase due to which pit
nucleation and its subsequent growth became easier in the matrix of this weld metal.
Conclusions
Based upon the present work the following conclusions were drawn:
1. GMA Inconel 625 clads possessed higher microhardness as compared to SMA
clads in the as-welded as well as under different post weld thermal aging con-
ditions owing to relatively higher cooling rate experienced in case of GMAW
process.
2. In the as welded condition Laves phase formation in the austenite matrix of the
clads was observed for which compositional differences were indicated by the
EDS examination.
3. Post weld thermal aging condition of 650 °C/10 h and 650 °C/100 h resulted
into the formation of γ′ and γ″ besides the formation of different carbides which
showed proportionately compositional variations for the SMA and GMA
Inconel 625 clads/welds. Further, an aging condition of 850 °C/100 h resulted
into intergranular precipitation of δ-phase along with carbides precipitation.
4. Pitting corrosion resistance as shown by potentiodynamic anodic polarization
(PAP) test results show that in the as-welded condition, GMA weld metal
possessed higher pitting potential (E
pitt = 149.2 mV) as compared to SMA weld
metal (E pitt = 31.77 mV).
5. Among all the clads, the most superior pitting performance (E pitt = 922.7 mV)
was shown by GMA weld subjected to an aging condition of 650/100 h,
whereas high temperature exposure of 850 °C/10 h and 100 h decreased the
pitting performance of both SMA and GMA clads.

Abstract Fabrication and welding of structural components for the hot section of
aero-engines continues to be of high importance to the manufacturing industry of
aero-engines. This paper discusses and reviews the literature on hot cracking and
strain age cracking, cracking phenomena that can occur during welding or subse-
quent heat treatment of precipitation hardened Ni- and Fe-Ni-based superalloys.
The in ﬂuence of chemical composition in terms of i.e. hardening elements and
impurities, microstructure of base material and weld zone, together with welding
processes and corresponding parameters and heat input are discussed and related to
the cracking susceptibility of different nickel based superalloys.
Keywords Hot cracking
⋅ Strain age cracking ⋅ Superalloys
Introduction
The aero-engine and speci ﬁcally the hot section is one of the most demanding
application for materials. It is therefore of utmost importance that the welds used in
the design are of suitable quality to account for the demanding environment.
Despite these challenges, fabrication in which welding is commonly utilized is
being more and more employed to tailor structural fabrications in an improved
manner to reduce weight as well as to increase performance of aero-engines. The
trend of increased share of fabrication emphasizes the importance of understanding
welding and the associated metallurgy. The importance of weld associated concerns
can be furthered coupled with a tremendous boost in interest of additive manu-
facturing (AM) which is very linked to welding and where the lessons learned in
welding can and should be used for AM. Looking at the number of publications that
has developed during the years it can be clearly seen that both welding as well as
AM of superalloys are still increasing [ 1, 2], Fig. 1.

Considering some of the challenges being faced in the fabrication of hot
structural components, one can address weld associated defects wherein there are
two types of categories in general:
1. Geometrical defects associated to the welding operation, the material being
welded and the corresponding ﬁller could be: undercut, porosity, slag inclusions,
lack of fusion, and insuf ﬁcient penetration.
2. Metallurgical associated defects such as: hot cracking and strain age cracking
(SAC).
The second factor is generally the most challenging one from a metallurgical
point of view. As can be seen in Fig. 2, most of the research with regard to cracking
has been related to the hot cracking type whereas SAC has been quite steady
throughout the years [ 3, 4].
In view of the aforementioned paragraph a review on hot cracking and SAC of
precipitation hardened Ni- and Fe-Ni based superalloys is presented.
Superalloys Used in Aero Engines
Weight reduction of mechanical components is becoming increasingly important as
a way to provide more friendly production environment and operation of different
equipment. This is true in almost any manufacturing industry, but is especially
important to the aerospace industry. In hot structural components of aero engines,
an example given in Fig. 3, cast parts are used to comply with complex geometry
and moderate strength requirements, while forged and wrought parts are used where
geometry is less complex but strength requirements are higher [ 5]. AM now also

serves as an additional toolbox apart from cast, wrought and forged material forms
to fabricate these structures. As AM is a new and unique type of material form it is
important to investigate and understand how it behaves in welding to be able to

As for alloy development, both Alloy 718 as well as ATI
®718PlusTM were ﬁrst
available in the wrought form then later also in cast versions. Waspaloy was
developed a few years ahead of Alloy 718 and presented some challenges with
regard to SAC which paved the way for development of Alloy 718. The industry
demanded an alloy that does not possess high risk of SAC which became a major
driver for the development of Alloy 718 which is more or less immune to SAC. The
low susceptibility towards SAC is of course very bene ﬁcial, however, the high Nb
content raised issues with hot cracking instead. It also came with another major
drawback, that is, from a performance point of view. Its main strengthening phase,
the γ″ (Ni
3Nb), is not stable above ∼650 °C and as a consequence the alloy will not
maintain its strength above this temperature. Above ∼650 °C another precipitation
hardening phase named γ′ (Ni3Al, Ti) is stable and thus useful. The γ′ phase is
commonly found in superalloys containing Al and/or Ti and is the main hardening
constituent in alloys as Waspaloy, ATI
®718PlusTM and Haynes® 282®. The volume
fraction of the γ′ phase and temperature capability increases with Al and Ti.
However, the total sum of Al and Ti contents above 4 wt% are seldom seen in some
structural parts, such as the one shown in Fig. 3, due to the fact that they are very
difﬁcult to weld from a SAC perspective.
Producing the Weld
The weld geometry is crucial to produce a defect-free weld, however, even if the
weld is properly made, residual stresses from the welding operation can still cause
signiﬁcant problems i.e. cracking or distortion. The in ﬂuence of welding on the
material is also of signi ﬁcance, not at least with the precipitation hardened Ni- and
Fe-Ni-based superalloys being used in aero engines as well as gas turbines. Various
post weld heat treatments (PWHT) are normally carried out to account for some of
the aforementioned issues, however, the PWHT can cause additional problems on
its own (i.e. distortion, SAC).
The welding process and associated control have improved quite signi ﬁcantly in
the last decades and now allow for good control and ability to use very low heat
input during welding, being necessary when joining sophisticated materials i.e.
superalloys. More recent techniques such as cold metal transfer (CMT), pulsed
mode of gas metal arc welding (GMAW) and various modes of gas tungsten arc
welding (GTAW) such as Force GTAW and high frequency (HF) GTAW.
902 J. Andersson

## Page 887

However, the GTAW, laser beam welding (LBW), plasma arc welding (PAW), and
electron beam welding (EBW) still seem to be the most frequently applied methods
in welding of structural components for aerospace. The methods of LBW and EBM
are quite attractive when it comes to their abilities to make narrow and
deep-penetration welds while also maintaining high production rates. These
methods also provide very low heat input per unit length for a given depth of
penetration. However, there is still a signi ﬁcant amount of challenges not at least
with respect to micro ﬁssuring in coarse grain materials, despite the low heat input
by using EBW or LBW. Since the abilities to make narrow and deep-penetration
welds increases when using EBW and LBW it should also be stressed that the
restraint factor increases as well, which goes hand in hand with increased sensitivity
towards cracking.
The shape of the weld pool is dependent on the welding process and techniques
and is apart from the thickness and geometry of the part being welded also of
signiﬁcant importance when it comes to cracking. High heat input welds are more
prone to hot cracking than low heat input welds but the weld pool shape should not
be neglected. A tear-drop shaped weld pool, which is usually obtained in automated
and robotic welding, is more susceptible to hot cracking due to the orientation of the
solidifying grains than the more desirable elliptical shaped weld pool [ 7]. One
reason for the tear-drop shaped weld pool being more susceptible lies in the fact that
it results in centerline segregation and as such accumulating high amounts of
melting point depressant elements which reduces the hot ductility of the material.
The more elliptical shaped weld pool will on the other hand have a larger distri-
bution of these melting point depressant elements and as such a better hot ductility
in comparison. As mentioned above, the weld pool shape is dependent on the
welding process and conditions, where the welding speed stands out as a very
inﬂuential parameter in controlling the shape of the weld pool. A high welding
speed together with high heat input promote a tear-drop shape weld pool whereas a
reduced travel speed and as such a higher heat input results in a more elliptical
shaped weld pool. In addition to the discussed weld pool shape it has also been seen
that the contour of the weld cross-section can be of importance to account for hot
cracking. A convex shaped contour is generally seen to be more bene ﬁcial in
comparison to a concave contour which can easily crack despite having an elliptical
shaped weld pool. So, to provide the most suitable conditions for a successful weld
it seem like the trailing edge of the weld pool should be elliptical together with a
convex weld contour.
Hot Cracking
Superalloys and some other austenitic materials are susceptible to the so-called “hot
cracking” phenomena, that is, cracking that takes place during welding and involves
liquid phase. It occurs due to complex reactions in the microstructure in
Review of Weldability of Precipitation Hardening … 903

## Page 888

combination with stresses/strains developed by the thermal gradients during
welding and by any additional external restraint from i.e. ﬁxturing. Hot cracking
can be divided into different categories depending on how they form, solidi ﬁcation
or heat affected zone (HAZ) liquation cracking. Solidi ﬁcation cracking can be the
worse type since it can basically grow until the weld stops. It forms in the last
remaining liquid in between growing dendrites or cells during solidi ﬁcation. The
solidiﬁcation range or brittle temperature range (BTR) are usually pointed out to be
closely connected to the susceptibility towards cracking. The second group of hot
cracks is the HAZ liquation cracks where secondary phases close to the fusion
boundary aid liquation of the grain boundaries.
Theories with regard to explaining the cause for these cracks originate back to
dedicated research on hot tearing during casting in the 1950s. Theories such as the
“Strain theory of hot tears ” [8] and the “Shrinkage-Brittleness theory” [9] ﬁrst came
along and were later combined into Borland ’s combined theory known as the
“Generalized theory ” [10]. Many other theories exist as well [ 11–14] where seg-
regation phenomena often is a key to the understanding. Elements such as S, O, B,
P, C, Ti, N, H and most importantly Nb partitions into the interdendritic regions
during solidiﬁcation and as a consequence suppress the melting point. The presence
of these elements is also important in eutectic phase reactions both during heating
and cooling [ 15]. As a result of low melting impurities or constituents, so-called
wetting ﬁlms are created which signi ﬁcantly reduces grain boundary ductility [ 16].
Solidiﬁcation Cracking
The “Shrinkage Brittleness Theory ” was developed by Pumphrey et al. [ 9]t o
explain hot cracking in aluminium casting as well as welding. It was from this
theory where the BTR was postulated and in which a material possesses an
increased risk of cracking due to an intrinsically low ductility. The BTR range is
primarily in ﬂuenced by the composition of the alloy, however, it was postulated
that the BTR had an upper limit called the coherent temperature, the temperature at
which the growing dendrites come into mutual contact by forming a solid-coherent
network. The lower end of BTR was de ﬁned by the solidus temperature.
Pellini, on the other hand, formulated the “Strain theory ” [8] based on the
research performed to investigate hot tearing in castings and adapted the same
theory to welding. The strain theory relies on the presence of liquid ﬁlms close to
the solidus temperature. The liquid ﬁlm at the grain boundaries is the main cause of
reduced ductility due to the low stress required for ﬁlm separation. According to the
strain theory, hot cracks cannot form in the so-called mushy zone, because of the
ability of the liquid to ﬂow and heal the cracks.
Borland developed the “Generalized theory ” [10], which combines the
“Shrinkage Brittleness Theory ” and the “Strain theory ” but with some modi ﬁca-
tions. The solidi ﬁcation range was divided into four stages:
904 J. Andersson

## Page 889

Stage 1, the primary dendrites form as the temperature drops below the liquidus.
Stage 2, the dendrites interlock by forming a solid network and it is only the liquid
which is capable of movement between the dendrites.
Stage 3, grain development takes place and the liquid is not capable of free
movement due to the continuous network.
Stage 4, complete solidi ﬁcation.
Borland postulated that cracking can only occur during stage 2 as soon as an
“almost continuous ” network of dendrites has formed. Crack healing is possible at
this stage since there is suf ﬁcient amount of liquid to back ﬁll the incipient cracks.
Borland also argued for the so called “critical solidi ﬁcation range ” (CSR) being
associated with stage 3. Stage 3 is where signi ﬁcant amount of cracking can occur,
as the liquid is con ﬁned the interdendritic areas inhibiting the free liquid movement
and as such crack healing. The wider CSR, the larger temperature range over which
liquid is present, and hence an increased susceptibility towards cracking. In stage 4,
cracking is no longer possible as the material is fully solidi ﬁed.
There have been a number of modi ﬁed concepts with regard to the previously
mentioned theories whereas Matsuda et al. [ 17] suggested a modi ﬁed concept of
solidiﬁcation cracking to the “Generalized theory ”. The theory was developed by
studying and analyzing the solidi ﬁcation front using a high speed camera mounted
on a microscope placed in the proximity of a weld torch. The set-up and equipment
allowed for movement of the plate being welded, while the weld torch and the
microscope were ﬁxed. Based on their observations, it was concluded that stage 1
(where primary dendrites form as the temperature drops below the liquidus) and
stage 2 (where the dendrites interlock by forming a solid network) should be shifted
towards the liquidus temperature. Furthermore, stage 3 (where the grain develop-
ment occurs) was divided into several stages (the liquid mass stage, liquid ﬁlm stage
and liquid droplet stage). In the modi ﬁed concept, the liquid mass stage forms
during the earliest phase of the solidi ﬁcation process. The critical temperature
where CSR starts as de ﬁned by Borland, is at the transition between the liquid mass
and the liquid ﬁlm stage. Solidi ﬁcation cracks form in the liquid mass stage and can
propagate both towards the liquid mass stage and liquid droplet stage. The prop-
agation of cracks in the liquid mass stage would be slower because of the high
amount of liquid that heals them, in comparison to the droplet stage. However, new
cracks cannot form in the liquid droplet stage, which is characterized by presence of
liquid droplets, making crack initiation dif ﬁcult to occur. In Alloy 718 and
ATI
®718PlusTM it is known that Nb, which is present in both these alloys, pro-
motes the formation of NbC and Laves eutectic products. The latter is more
detrimental since it solidi ﬁes at a lower temperature and thus extends the solidi ﬁ-
cation interval [ 18–26]. The chemical composition in general and the presence of
Nb and C in particular is important in this context [ 18, 27, 28]. However, it has
been concluded that a eutectic liquid is not always detrimental for the hot cracking
since in some cases it has been shown to heal cracks by back ﬁlling [29–32]. Some
researchers have monitored the grain structure of the weld deposit through variation
Review of Weldability of Precipitation Hardening … 905

## Page 890

of the weld process parameters in order to optimize the weldability. It is generally
concluded that an equiaxed grain structure in the weld deposit is less susceptible
compared to a columnar structure [ 33]. This is due to better accommodation of
strain, liquid feeding and lower concentration of impurity elements [ 33, 34].
Heat Affected Zone Liquation Cracking
HAZ liquation cracks forms mainly due to two reasons, constitutional liquation of
secondary phases and grain boundary liquation caused by segregated melting point
depressant elements. Rapid heating is required in both cases to cause liquation
based on large temperature and compositional gradients leading to crack formation
if the stresses involved are suf ﬁciently high. Slow heating, on the other hand, lead to
solid state dissolution of secondary phase constituents by diffusion into the matrix
wherein the material will be more homogenized. As a general assumption, the HAZ
does not experience temperatures above the matrix solidus, liquid can only form if
the melting point is locally suppressed by solute segregation or by the presence of
second phase particles. The formation of liquid ﬁlms at grain boundaries lowers the
ductility, thus, increases the susceptibility towards cracking when a critical strain is
exceeded. The phases or segregating elements responsible for crack formation vary
from alloy to alloy. The formation of the grain boundary liquation can be due to
different mechanisms which have been reviewed by i.e. Robinson and Scott [ 35] for
austenitic stainless steels and nickel alloys. In general, liquation can occur in dif-
ferent ways, i.e. preferential grain boundary melting, segregation of impurities and
by the so-called “Rehbinder-Medovar” effect which involves migration of surface
active elements to the HAZ and constitutional liquation.
Constitutional liquation was originally proposed for maraging steel weldments
by Pepe and Savage [ 36]. It involves melting of a secondary phase particle present
in the HAZ of the material being welded. The melting can occur at any temperature
between the eutectic and the equilibrium solidus of the alloy, see the pseudo binary
phase diagram of ATI
®718PlusTM in Fig. 4 [37].
The liquid formed through constitutional liquation is a result of the interaction of
the intermetallic compound with the surrounding matrix to form a low melting
phase, i.e. Laves phase in ATI
®718PlusTM and Alloy 718. The heating rate need to
be rapid to achieve liquid phase below the equilibrium solidus of the alloy.
Assuming a spherical precipitate together with fast a heating rate to avoid equi-
librium conditions, the phenomenon can be explained by considering Fig. 4. Below
temperature TEUT, the precipitate does not experience any phase transformation. As
the temperature reaches T EUT, a eutectic liquid ﬁlm, γ-Laves, forms at the interface
between the particle and the matrix. As the temperature is increased above the
eutectic point, the amount of melting will increase. Apart from constitutional
liquation, Pepe and Savage [ 37] also proposed the “grain boundary mechanism ”,
explaining how the grain boundary gets covered by liquid which has been formed
around a particle. During welding and due to the very high heating rate, grain
906 J. Andersson

## Page 891

boundary migration can occur. These moving grain boundaries could come into
contact with such a particle, leading to the distribution of the liquid onto the grain
boundary. This will have a pinning effect on the grain boundary movement and
further growth will be impeded. Basically, the liquation of grain boundaries
determines how susceptible an alloy is to hot cracking [ 27]. The liquation in
superalloys is most often associated with melting point depressant elements like B
[38–41] and S [ 42, 43] and secondary phase constituents though the mechanism of
constitutional liquation as discussed above [ 38–41]. Segregation induced liquation
is another mechanism being connected to the “grain boundary mechanism ” sug-
gested by Pepe and Savage which can take place during grain boundary migration,
sweeping impurity elements along causing solute accumulation in these boundaries
[33, 36]. The pre-weld microstructure in ﬂuences the material response due to the
above liquation mechanisms. However, it is not uncommon to ﬁnd contradicting
results in the literature on what material condition is the most favorable. It is
generally believed that the softest possible solution heat treated condition together
with a ﬁne grain structure is preferable compared to the material in the aged and
hard condition with a coarse microstructure [ 27, 34]. This is attributed to the better
ability of small grains to accommodate straining and to a lower concentration of
impurity elements at the grain boundaries due to a larger grain surface area of
material in the ﬁne grain state compared with the same material in the coarse grain
state [ 33].

et al. [ 44] on wrought, selective laser manufactured and cast Alloy 718 in various
conditions it can clearly be seen that the hot cracking response differs signi ﬁcantly,
Fig. 5.
It seems like the difference disclosed in Fig. 5 can be related to the grain size.
The cast condition revealed a signi ﬁcantly larger grain size of ∼1720 μm followed
by ∼25 µm in grain size for the SLM manufactured and wrought Alloy 718

Apart from grain size it is also important to consider the secondary phases
present. In Alloy 718, secondary phases and their in ﬂuence on liquation cracking
has been shown to be attributed to the constitutional liquation of NbC in the
wrought form and to NbC together with Laves in the cast form [ 48, 49]. The
presence of the δ phase (Ni
3Nb) has been claimed to improve the cracking resis-
tance through a “solute blocking mechanism ” [50] (reducing the amount of free Nb)
or by grain boundary pinning [ 51] while others have claimed that the δ phase will
increase the susceptibility to liquation cracking by assisting liquation [ 39, 52]. This
issue is still to be resolved but by judging of the Varestraint test result performed by
Singh et al. [ 53] for ATI
®718PlusTM it can clearly be seen that the η phase (similar
composition to the δ phase in Alloy 718) in ATI ®718PlusTM increased suscepti-
bility towards hot cracking.

Grain boundary segregation of minor elements can also play a very important
