However, it seems likely that large grain size [ 49], amount of secondary phases [ 57]
and high B and P levels in a modi ﬁed ATI®718PlusTM alloy. It has also been seen
that an increased amount of η phase in ATI ®718PlusTM increase weld cracking as
well [ 32, 53].
Strain Age Cracking
SAC is a type of cracking that occurs in the solid state due to hardening in the
material. The phenomenon was initially recognized and investigated in the early
1960s and led to the development of Alloy 718 [ 58], which is resistant to SAC due
to its sluggish hardening response. Cracking takes place when weld stresses are
high at the same time as hardening occurs in precipitation hardened superalloys and
in γ′ hardened alloys in particular. SAC generally occurs during the post weld heat
treatment (PWHT) and is consequently sometimes referred to as “PWHT cracking”
or “Reheat cracking”. The crack formation during PWHT is related to low ductility
in the HAZ combined inadequate stress relaxation. The localization of stress to the
HAZ is related to a lower strength as compared to the base material. It is thus
reasonable that a softer base material lowers the susceptibility to SAC which has
been conﬁrmed by several investigations [ 59–63]. Fully age hardened base material
leds to most severe cracking in the HAZ. Over-aged material on the other hand has
been found to have a bene ﬁcial in ﬂuence, as the lower strength of such a mi-
crostructure results in stress relaxation in the base material [ 61]. An important
feature in the context of what type of cracking takes place during welding is that
SAC may actually also occur during welding, e.g. during multipass repair welding
[64]. SAC is more or less only a problem for γ′ hardened superalloys and is one of
the major reasons why Alloy 718 had such a success since there was a large demand
for a high temperature capable alloy which was readily weldable. The reason is that
Alloy 718 is more or less immune to SAC due to its sluggish hardening response of
γ″ phase. The so called PWHT is carried out to restore strength of the fusion zone
(FZ) as well as the heat affected zone (HAZ) through a full solution and hardening
processing cycle that at the same time relieves stresses that are always introduced
by the welding. This stress relief is unfortunately concomitant with uncontrolled
hardening during the heating cycle of the heat treatment which imposes high strain
on the grain boundaries. In addition, hardening of the alloy generally leads to a
reduced overall ductility [ 59]. This loss of ductility may on its own lead to
Review of Weldability of Precipitation Hardening … 909

## Page 894

something known as ductility dip cracking (DDC), another type of cracking more
commonly encountered in solid solution hardening alloys, where it is not related to
precipitation hardening.
Chemical Composition and Microstructure
A relation between Al and Ti was suggested by Prager and Shira, who proposed a
strong in ﬂuence on the precipitation characteristics of the γ′ phase exists [ 59]. The
higher the content of these hardening elements, the more susceptible towards SAC
since a higher volume fraction of the γ′ phase is present [ 65]. The elements forming
the hardening phase have the largest in ﬂuence on the cracking susceptibility. In
general, a combined Al + Ti content above 6 at.% leads to severe problems with
regard to SAC. This is evident when comparing the highly susceptibility René 41
[66] with that of Alloy 718. The latter was developed with a low amount of γ′
forming elements to achieve a better weldability [ 58]. The more sluggish precipi-
tation of its main hardening phase ( γ″) enables stress relaxation to occur in advance
of any hardening reactions [ 67]. Elements such as Nb and its role on SAC has not
been speci ﬁcally investigated, most likely due to the high SAC resistance of Alloy
718. Alloy 718 contains a quite high amount of up to 5.5 wt% Nb. Hughes and
Berry reported a detrimental effect of C, with a sparse carbide distribution for low-C
heats as the major bene ﬁt[ 66]. Other studies suggest a bene ﬁcial effect of C, since it
limits grain growth and inhibits grain boundary sliding [ 68, 69]. Thamburaj et al.
[70] also found a positive in ﬂuence of C by analyzing data from Carlton and Prager
[71] using regression analysis, but, as pointed out by Prager and Sines [ 69], this
effect is mainly attributed to grain size control and high C content has to be
considered as well for overall susceptibility towards hot cracking [ 51, 72–76].
Another element of high importance is B which also has been reported to have a
positive effect on creep and stress rupture life and as such often intentionally added
as an alloying element [ 77]. However, an increased creep resistance could also lead
to a lower susceptibility towards SAC. The in ﬂuence of other minor and trace
elements like Fe, Mn and S on SAC has been reported not to be signi ﬁcant within
the usual composition range whereas Si has been found to have a negative effect
[70]. The effect of furnace atmosphere during PWHT has been studied by Carlton
and Prager who reported a strong in ﬂuence of O, as they found that SAC could be
completely eliminated for René 41 heat treated in Ar, 0.5 vol.% O and vacuum
atmospheres [ 71]. Udimet 500, on the other hand, did show cracks in all tested
atmospheres, indicating that the O content is only a contributing factor and not
necessary the primary cause for SAC (note that Udimet 500 has a nominal Al + Ti
content larger than 10 at.%, whereas René 41 is in the range of 7 at.%). This can be
further supported by the ﬁndings of d’Annessa and Owens, where a bene ﬁcial effect
of low-O atmospheres could be seen, but no complete elimination of cracking [ 78].
The generally adverse effect of O has also been con ﬁrmed by the ﬁndings of Nakao,
910 J. Andersson

## Page 895

where a decrease in ductility of Waspaloy if the testing atmosphere contained
oxygen was observed [ 79]. Further investigations report a negative effect of the
co-existence of oxide ﬁlms at the grain boundaries and the presence of ﬁnely
dispersed γ′ particles in the grain interior [ 80, 81].
In terms of microstructure, it can be divided into grain size and homogeneity
where the former has been found to have a positive effect if kept small [ 61, 71]. The
rationale here is the distribution of the overall strain to a larger grain boundary area
and hence lower stresses acting on the grain boundaries which basically has the
same validity also for hot cracking (Fig. 5)[ 71]. The drop in ductility in areas
where SAC takes place is presumably associated with severe strain concentrations
at grain boundary triple points due to grain boundary sliding. Bene ﬁcial effects have
been pointed out for carbide precipitation (e.g. M
23C6 and MC) in resisting grain
boundary sliding and decohesion at elevated temperatures. MC type carbides are
believed to have a bene ﬁcial in ﬂuence in restricting grain boundary migration, by
creating tortuous grain boundaries by pinning [ 82]. Microstructural inhomo-
geneities are mainly a concern when it comes to hot cracking [ 83] but the occur-
rence of hot cracking during welding can facilitate further cracking in a subsequent
PWHT.
Precipitation-Induced Stress Development
An effect of mismatch on the development of contraction stresses, that is, the
susceptibility towards SAC has been proposed in several studies [ 59, 84, 85] and
more recent material modelling by Andersson indicate a positive correlation of
negative lattice mismatch on the cracking resistance [ 65]. The change of lattice
parameter of the γ phase as a function of δ, γ′ and γ″ has been investigated for
Alloy 718 by Liu et al. [ 86] who reported a decrease for higher precipitate contents.
However, no information is available about the mis ﬁt created by the precipitation
reactions. Tiley et al. investigated René 88DT by means of synchrotron X-ray and
neutron diffraction and reported increasing lattice mismatch with aging time while
initially decreasing as a function of temperature [ 87]. Whitmore et al. studied
ATI
®718PlusTM and were able to disclose a small positive lattice mismatch
between γ and γ′ after aging following on a HAZ simulation with deformation [ 88].
Dirand et al. measured the lattice mismatch during creep in a single crystal nickel
based superalloy and were able to conclude that the mis ﬁt is strongly dependent on
temperature, stress and previous plastic deformation [ 89]. Available data indicates a
strong relationship between lattice parameter mis ﬁt and SAC, however, quanti ﬁable
data from the time-temperature range where SAC occurs is yet to be obtained.
Review of Weldability of Precipitation Hardening … 911

## Page 896

Conclusions
Hot cracking and SAC is a major concern when welding precipitation hardening Ni-
and Ni-Fe-based superalloys. There are different cracking theories providing a
general explanation of the mechanisms involved, however, there is a large gap
between the theoretical explanations and the “practical” aspects. The general beliefs
with regard to hot cracking can be summarized as follows:
• Cracking occurs when a liquid ﬁlm is present in combination with a critical
strain from the thermal gradient in the weld or from mechanical restraint.
• The wider the solidi ﬁcation range, the wider the temperature at which liquid
ﬁlms exist and therefore, a greater susceptibility towards cracking of the weld
metal.
• The level of impurities is important and should be kept as low possible.
• It is evident that the segregation plays an important role, as it is one of the
prerequisites for liquation to occur since it extends the BTR. Elements such as
Nb contribute to it.
• Fine grain size seem to have a bene ﬁcial impact.
• Increasing heat input results in increased hot cracking.
With regard to SAC, obvious challenges becomes more vital when welding high
temperature resistant nickel based superalloys. The mechanism and its main
inﬂuencing factors can be summarized as follows:
• Increasing strain in terms of weld restraint or precipitation-induced stress have
an impact on SAC as well as the ability of the material to relax residual stresses.
• The kinetics of the hardening phase is in ﬂuenced by the chemical composition
as well as the dislocation density which in turn in ﬂuence the susceptibility
towards SAC.
• Fine grain size together with grain boundary precipitates seem to be bene ﬁcial
since it inhibits grain boundary sliding.

## Page 901

The In ﬂuence of Base Metal
Microstructure on Weld Cracking
in Manually GTA Repair Welded
Cast ATI 718Plus ®
Fabian Hanning and Joel Andersson
Abstract The effect of base metal conditions on the weld cracking response of cast
ATI 718Plus® was investigated in this study, comparing as cast microstructure with
pseudo hot isostatic pressing (HIP) heat treatments at 1120, 1160 and 1190 °C for
dwell times of 4 and 24 h. Linear grooves have been ﬁlled using multipass manual
gas tungsten arc welding (GTAW) to simulate repair welding conditions. Metal-
lographic investigation revealed cracks in both base metal heat affected zone and
fusion zone layers. The heat treatment temperatures chosen below, at and above
incipient laves melting temperature of ATI 718Plus
® were found to have an effect
on weld cracking behaviour, with an increased average total crack length in the base
metal heat affected zone for both 1160 and 1190 °C as compared to the as cast
condition and the 1120 °C homogenization treatment. The increase in cracking
susceptibility shows a correlation with the amount of Nb-rich secondary phases,
with lower amounts leading to crack concentration to solidi ﬁcation grain bound-
aries present from the casting process, increasing the average crack length.
Keywords Nickel alloys
⋅ Weldability ⋅ Repair ⋅ GTA welding
Cracking
Introduction
The application of nickel-based superalloys in hot sections of aircraft engines relies
strongly on the ability of the material to be welded. This is especially important if
the so-called assembly approach is followed, where large structural components are

## Page 902

manufactured from small wrought and cast parts that are then joined together by
welding [ 1]. Furthermore, repair welding operations are often carried out on large
cast parts, which is despite the complexity and dif ﬁculty, economically more fea-
sible than replacement. Besides requiring highly skilled welders, profound
knowledge and understanding of ongoing mechanisms is needed to successfully use
repair welding in practice.
Since its introduction in the early 1960s, Alloy 718 has been the standard grade
for hot structural parts in the aerospace industry [ 2]. Its limited high temperature
stability has more recently however led to the development of derivative grades
such as ATI 718Plus
® [3]. The modi ﬁed chemical composition enables a ∼50 °C
higher maximum service temperature, which is achieved by making ATI 718Plus ®
a gamma prime hardening alloy in contrast to gamma double prime as in Alloy 718.
While originally introduced as wrought material, cast versions are now available
[4], widening the ﬁeld of application of this alloy.
Castings are generally less weldable than the wrought grades which is mainly
due to their highly segregated microstructure. Cast parts are hence usually put
through a homogenisation treatment in advance of any machining and welding. For
Nb-bearing superalloys such as Alloy 718 and ATI 718Plus
® the main concern is
the presence of the Nb-rich, brittle laves phase in interdendritic areas. Due to its low
incipient melting point the presence of residual eutectics can cause heat affected
zone (HAZ) liquation cracking [ 5]. A previous study investigated the effect of
homogenization treatment on the repair weldability of cast ATI 718Plus
® and
disclosed a positive correlation of laves phase content and weldability [ 6]. A more
recent alloy composition with increased Nb content is being focused on in the
present investigation aiming to provide more data on weld cracking behaviour and
further insight into the ongoing mechanisms.
Experimental
Material and Heat Treatments
Investment cast plates of ATI 718Plus ® with the dimensions 150 × 60
× 62.7 mm have been investigated in this study, with the chemical composition
given in Table 1. The as cast condition had a dendritic, segregated microstructure
containing blocky Nb-rich precipitates as shown in Fig. 1a–b, with an average grain
size of 1300 ± 200 µm. The hardness has been measured as 415 ± 5 HV0.5.
Besides the as-cast condition as a baseline, plates have been put through a ho-
mogenization heat treatment. The homogenisation temperature for cast parts can be
Table 1 Chemical composition in weight percentage of cast ATI 718Plus ®
Ni Cr Co Mo Ti Al Fe Mn Si C B Nb W
Bal 20.72 8.34 2.71 0.75 1.50 9.31 0.01 0.04 0.05 0.005 6.02 1.00
918 F. Hanning and J. Andersson

## Page 903

chosen signi ﬁcantly higher (above the dissolution temperature of secondary car-
bides) than for wrought alloys, since grain growth is usually not a concern. The
main goal of such a heat treatment in Nb-bearing alloys is the dissolution of the
brittle laves phase, which forms from residual eutectic liquid during the solidi ﬁ-
cation process. This Nb-rich phase is not stable at the nominal chemical compo-
sition of the alloy, and will hence be dissolved given enough exposure time at high
temperature. Three temperatures were used in this study, 1120, 1160 and 1190 °C,
respectively, with dwell times of 4 and 24 h. The temperatures were chosen below,
at and above the incipient laves phase melting temperature of 1160 °C [ 7].
Homogenization heat treatments of cast material are typically applied in conjunc-
tion with hot isostatic pressing (HIP). In this study they have however been carried
out in a small lab furnace at ambient pressure, followed by machining the plates to
the desired shape.
Repair Welding
Four linear grooves with the dimensions 30 × 10 × 10 mm and a side radius of
5 mm have been machined into the plates, as shown in Fig. 2. The repair welding
has been carried out manually by experienced welders, using manual gas tungsten
arc welding with a tungsten-2% thorium (WT-20) electrode. The welds were
shielded by argon, with a nozzle gas ﬂow of 8 –15 l/min. ATI 718Plus ® wire with
1.14 mm diameter has been used as ﬁller material. A wide nozzle has been used to
create a diffuse gas ﬂow, enabling a large electrode stick-out to reach the bottom of
the grooves. Welding current has been set to 140 A with an inter-pass temperature
of approximately 50 °C.
Fig. 1 Base metal microstructure of the cast plates before heat treatments, a macro image
showing general solidi ﬁcation structure, b SEM micrograph with typical segregation of Nb-rich
phases visible in interdendritic areas
The In ﬂuence of Base Metal Microstructure … 919

## Page 904

Weld Examination and Microstructural Analysis
From each weld 6 cross sections have been cut out along the ﬁlled grooves and
mounted in hot mounting resin for automated metallographic preparation. All
samples have been electrolytically etched with 10 wt% oxalic acid at 3 V DC for 3 –
5 s, followed by visual inspection using a light optical microscope at 200 ×
magniﬁcation. The location of imperfections has been recorded and the crack length
been measured along the centre line of the crack. The data is presented as total crack
length (TCL) averaged over 4 grooves. Microhardness has been measured on
representative samples with an applied force of 0.5 kgf (HV0.5), for which a
Shimadzu HMV-2 microhardness tester has been used. Electron microscopy has
been used for phase identi ﬁcation and high resolution image acquisition. A Leo
1550 FEG SEM has been used in conjunction with an Oxford Instruments EDS
detector. Grain size has been measured on two cross sections per condition on base
metal microstructure using three circles superimposed over recorded images. Unlike
for general microstructural characterisation the samples were etched with 10 wt%
nitric acid at 1.7 V versus stainless steel electrode for 20 s, based on the approach
described in [ 8]. Images were taken at 12.5 × magni ﬁcation such that a total area of
at least 1 cm 2 was covered and subsequently stitched together using Photo-
shop CC 2015. The amount of Nb-rich secondary phases (laves and carbides) has
been quantiﬁed with image analysis using ImageJ on 5 SEM images per condition.
Atomic number contrast visualised by backscattered electrons (BSE) has been used
Fig. 2 Dimensions and location of the weld grooves on the plates

## Page 905

to distinguish between matrix and secondary phases. Thermodynamic calculations
to identify equilibrium phases have been performed using JMatPro. All measure-
ments are presented including their respective standard deviation as a measure for
the error.
Results
Microstructure After Heat Treatment
The heat treatments did not lead to a signi ﬁcant change in grain size, while longer
exposure times led to a decrease in hardness, summarised in Table 2. The base
material microstructure of the heat treated samples is presented in Fig. 3a–f.
A change from the highly segregated microstructure of the as cast condition (cf.
Fig. 1b) can be seen for all heat treated samples, with the homogenization treatment
at 1120 °C for 4 h being visibly less effective in dissolving the Nb-rich secondary
phases. Microstructural characterization of the base metal led to the results pre-
sented in Fig. 4, showing a clear decrease in the amount of secondary phases for all
conditions except 1120 °C 4 h. The remaining ∼0.5% Nb-rich phases match well
with the equilibrium MC carbide phase fraction predicted by JMatPro, which lies
between 0.47 and 0.49 wt%. Gamma- laves eutectics have been found in all con-
ditions heat treated for 4 h and after 24 h at 1190 °C though. Albeit being very few
in all cases this indicates that the equilibrium conditions predicted by JMatPro have
not yet been reached.

quantiﬁed results having a large margin of error. While lack of fusion and pores
have been found in the fusion zone, these imperfections have not been further

Discussion
The heat treatments did not lead to a signi ﬁcant difference in grain size, albeit some
ﬂuctuation being present. The main difference in heat treatments was the amount of
secondary phases present in the material, where all homogenization heat treatments
except 1120 °C 4 h reduced the secondary phase fraction to about 0.5%. The good
match with the equilibrium phase fraction of MC carbides in the material suggests
that most laves phase has been dissolved. Without the possibility to clearly identify
laves phase via the eutectic structure that it forms together with the gamma phase
during terminal solidi ﬁcation, it is still possible that some laves phase is present in
the material in blocky form. The results of the weld examination indicate that FZ
cracking is not clearly affected by the base material condition. Longer exposure
time and higher homogenization temperature however increased the HAZ cracking
susceptibility. This is in contrast to the general belief that large amounts of laves
phase should negatively affect the cracking response.
The difference in TCL goes along with a change of the location where cracks
form within the HAZ. As Fig. 8a–b indicates, there is a transition from small, not
connected cracks in interdendritic areas towards fewer and longer cracks running
along solidi ﬁcation grain boundaries. This general observation is also re ﬂected by
the average single crack length (ACL) shown in Fig. 9, where the material con-
ditions with higher amount of Nb-rich phases (as-cast and 1120 °C 4 h) show
signiﬁcantly reduced values as compared to conditions with low secondary phase
content (cf. Fig. 4). The presence of Nb-rich phases in the interdendritic areas leads
to the formation of liquid, which during subsequent cooling leads to crack for-
mation. The reduced amount of those phases for plates homogenization heat treated
Fig. 8 HAZ liquation cracks in heat treated base material, showing a transition of crack location
from interdendritic areas to solidi ﬁcation grain boundaries present from the casting process, as
indicated by arrows: a 1120 °C 4 h, b 1190 °C 24 h. Note the difference in scale and crack length
The In ﬂuence of Base Metal Microstructure … 925

## Page 910

at 1120 24 h, 1160 and 1190 °C (both 4 and 24 h), combined with concentration of
remaining Nb-rich precipitates to solidi ﬁcation grain boundaries present from the
casting process led to a longer average crack length, cf. Fig. 9. If liquid forms on
those grain boundaries it can spread over a comparatively longer distance.
There was no signi ﬁcant change in grain size after the homogenization treat-
ments (cf. Table 2), indicating that the formation of cracks is further enhanced by
the concentration of stresses to the few available grain boundaries instead of dis-
tributing them also over interdendritic areas. The availability of low melting con-
stituents within the grains shifts the balance towards the formation of smaller,
unconnected cracks. To rule out the effect of concentration gradients that could
locally suppress the melting temperature, EDS line scans were measured across a
grain boundary in 1120 4 h, 24 h and 1190 °C 24 h samples. No difference in
distribution of Nb and Mo has been found for all investigated material conditions,
except for the case where Nb-rich particles were present close to the grain
boundary, as indicated in Fig. 10. Due to the limited capability of SEM mounted
EDS to detect light elements, the segregation of boron and its effect on liquid ﬁlm
formation could not be ruled out during this investigation. A study of Huang et al.
on cast Alloy 718 found boron to segregate on grain boundaries and cause liquation
[10], which could also be the case in the cast ATI 718Plus
® investigated in the
present study. Further analysis would be required to con ﬁrm the validity of this
hypothesis for ATI 718Plus ®.
Based on the HAZ cracking response, the different treatments can be ranked
regarding their susceptibility towards HAZ liquation cracking. The as cast condition
and 1120 °C 4 h homogenization treatment performed best, followed by 1120 °C
24 h and the treatments carried out at 1160 and 1190 °C. This indicates that for the
Fig. 9 Average crack length of HAZ cracks as a function of base material condition, showing
distinctly lower values for materials with high amount of Nb-rich phases
926 F. Hanning and J. Andersson

## Page 911

highest weld cracking resistance it would be possible to use the as cast condition
without any further heat treatments. Cast material does however have a rather
non-uniform distribution of alloying elements which requires a homogenization
heat treatment, usually in conjunction with hot isostatic pressing to reduce porosity.
Since all parts also have to be put through an age hardening treatment after welding
to obtain uniform mechanical properties, combining such a treatment with a ho-
mogenization treatment would enable welding of the material in the as cast con-
dition. This in turn could reduce weld cracking while still obtaining the desired
microstructural properties in both base material and fusion zone. A requirement for
carrying out a homogenization treatment after welding is however that the whole
structure is made out of cast material, since the high temperatures during such a
treatment would lead to extensive grain growth in wrought material. The assembly
approach, where cast and wrought parts are joined together depending on local
geometry and strength requirements consequently makes it impracticable to weld
cast material without prior homogenization treatment. While not being usable for
joining parts together, the approach described here is however still useful for
repairing parts that developed cracks during the casting process.
Conclusions
The effect of homogenization conditions on the repair weldability of cast
ATI 718Plus
® has been investigated. While FZ cracking did not show a clear
inﬂuence of the base material condition, the HAZ cracking response has been found
to be linked to the amount of Nb-rich phases. Large amounts of low melting phases
reduced the average single crack length, while long cracks were present along grain
boundaries in conditions with low secondary phase content. The as cast material
ranks best in terms of HAZ cracking resistance together with the 1120 °C 4 h

condition. This indicates that carrying out homogenization treatments after the weld
operation (and hence welding the material in as cast condition) could reduce
cracking in the HAZ.

## Page 913

Varestraint Weldability Testing of ATI
718Plus®—Inﬂuence of Eta Phase
Sukhdeep Singh, William Fransson, Joel Andersson,
Anssi Brederholm and Hannu Hänninen
Abstract This study investigates the effect of eta phase on hot cracking suscepti-
bility of ATI 718Plus®. Two heat treatment conditions of 950 °C/1 h and 950 °C/15 h
having different amounts of eta phase were tested by longitudinal Varestraint testing
method. The heat treatment at 950 °C/15 h exhibited the highest amount of
cracking. This was related to the higher amount of eta phase precipitation during the
long dwell heat treatment which aided to extensive liquation during welding.
Keywords ATI 718plus
®
⋅ Eta phase ⋅ Varestraint testing ⋅ Hot cracking
Introduction
The Ni-base superalloy ATI 718Plus ® has generated interest among researchers as
its area of applications is intended for those components where the maximum
operating temperature exceeds the temperature capability of Alloy 718. Despite its
name which may suggest similarity to Alloy 718, the main strengthening mecha-
nism is gamma prime ( γ′) instead of gamma double prime ( γ″), which is obtained
through carefully controlling the composition of, i.e., Al, Ti and Nb. This gives a
55 °C higher temperature advantage over Alloy 718 [ 1, 2]. Another microstructural
difference is the formation of a secondary phase, eta ( η-NiAl
6Nb), which in earlier
studies was assumed to be delta phase ( δ-Ni3Nb) [ 3, 4]. These precipitates are
known to be important for grain size control [ 5].

## Page 914

The role of delta phase on weldability of Alloy 718 has generated a debate: some
studies claim its presence to aid liquation cracking [ 6, 7], while others have shown
that delta phase inhibits cracking [ 8]. However, very limited information is avail-
able regarding the effect of eta phase on the weldability of ATI 718Plus ®.
Andersson et al. [ 4] have investigated hot ductility by Gleeble thermomechanical
testing of two conditions having different amounts of eta phase. However, no
signiﬁcant differences between the two conditions were observed.
In this study, the effect of two heat treatments, 950 °C/1 h and 950 °C/15 h, on
hot cracking susceptibility of ATI 718Plus
® by Varestraint (Variable Restraint)
testing method is investigated. The cracking data relative to the 950 °C/1 h con-
dition is taken from a previous study by Jacobsson and Andersson [ 9]. The heat
treatment temperature of 950 °C is the lower limit of the recommended solution
heat treatment by ATI [ 10]. The purpose of the long dwell heat treatment for 15 h is
to have an extensive amount of eta phase precipitation.
Experimental
Composition of the wrought ATI 718Plus ® used in the current study is presented in
Table 1.
The welding and testing parameters for longitudinal Varestraint testing are
shown in Table 2. Augmented strain levels for the test were between 2.1 and 4.3%.
Support plates were tack-welded on the backside of the test plates to avoid hinging
during bending.
After testing, plate surfaces were cleaned to remove any oxide layer and crack
measurements were conducted by using a stereo microscope. Conventional met-
allographic procedures followed to prepare the samples and etching was carried out
electrolytically by using oxalic acid as well as Kalling ’s No. 2 etchant for micro-
scopic evaluation. Grain size measurements were conducted according to ASTM
E112 standard [ 11] and micro-Vickers test (0.5 kgf/HV 0.5) for hardness mea-
surements was used. High resolution characterization was conducted by the use of a
LEO 1550 ﬁeld-emission gun scanning electron microscope (FEG-SEM) equipped
with Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS).

Results
Base Metal Microstructure
The representative base metal microstructure of the 950 °C/15 h heat-treated ma-
terial is shown in Fig. 1. Signi ﬁcant amounts of eta phase in the form of long and
thick plate-like precipitates are present both inter- and intragranularly in Fig. 2b. On
the other hand, the short dwell heat treatment at 950 °C/1 h produced a small
amount of precipitates mainly along the grain boundaries, Fig. 2a.
Varestraint Testing
Crack measurements after longitudinal Varestraint testing of the 950 °C/15 h
condition are presented in Fig. 3. These measurements include both cracking
occurring in the fusion zone (FZ) and heat-affected zone (HAZ) and are compared
to the data relative to 950 °C/1 h condition, obtained from a previous study con-
ducted by Jacobsson and Andersson [ 9]. The comparison in Fig. 3 clearly discloses
an increased cracking susceptibility for 950 °C/15 h condition over 950 °C/1 h
condition.

## Page 920

Discussion
The main effect of the longer dwell time heat treatment of 950 °C/15 h seems to
provide more extensive amounts of precipitation with regard to eta phase in the
microstructure as shown in Fig. 2. The base metal hardness values suggest that the
γ′/γ″ precipitates are not fully dissolved [ 12]. The longer heat treatment for 15 h
leading to coarsening of the γ′ may be an explanation to the reduced hardness of
about 340 HV, in comparison to about 380 HV for the 950 °C/1 h condition.
However, it is dif ﬁcult to say whether eta phase precipitation has any effect on
hardness or not. Base metal grain size of 8.3 µm (950 °C/1 h) and 7.8 µm (950 °C/
15 h) indicates that the longer heat-treatment time did not result in grain growth.
However, comparison of Figs. 5 and 7 and results from Table 3 shows that the
larger fraction of eta phase precipitates is effective in pinning the grain boundaries
in the HAZ of 950 °C/15 h. Average grain size in the HAZ resulted to be about
9.6 µm in comparison to 950 °C/1 h condition, which exhibited signi ﬁcant grain
growth, about 30 µm in average grain size.
Two main liquation mechanisms were seen to occur: grain boundary liquation and
constitutional liquation of NbC. Cracking connected to the highly liquated regions
was associated with constituents having eutectic morphology, often associated with
Nb-rich γ/Laves eutectic. The delta/eta phase is generally known to aid liquation by
two mechanisms, constitutional liquation [ 13, 14] and Nb enrichment on grain
boundaries through solid state dissolution [ 6, 15, 16]. However, it is dif ﬁcult to
conclude about the governing mechanism in the current study, since the characteri-
zation would require the use of more advanced analysis techniques. Moreover, in
950 °C/15 h condition (Fig. 8), further away from the fusion line, cracks were free
from any visible liquation products. EDS linescan analyses did not reveal any Nb
enrichment in this area. Cracks were surrounded by thick and round edged eta pre-
cipitates, which is indication of the initial steps of dissolution [ 6]. Precipitates with
similar characteristics are reported to have a dual role in regards to grain boundary
properties: grain boundary pinning and embrittlement effect. Andersson et al. [4] have
reported a higher hardness of 50 HV for 950 °C/15 h than 950 °C/1 h condition after
on-heating quenching tests conducted by Gleeble testing at temperatures up to
1150 °C. A shift of ductility curve to lower values was observed for the 950 °C/15 h
condition in the same temperature range, below the nil-ductility temperature. Keeping
the above considerations in mind, grain boundary embrittlement may explain the
cracking occurring in the region where partial dissolution of eta phase occurs.
Conclusions
Findings related to the effect of the long dwell time heat treatment at 950 °C/15 h of
wrought ATI 718Plus
® were shown. The important effect of the higher amount of
eta phase precipitation can be summarized as follows:
936 S. Singh et al.

## Page 921

• it limits the grain growth by grain boundary pinning in the HAZ;
• it contributes to extensive liquation;
• it increases hot cracking susceptibility.

## Page 923

The Case for Physical Experiments
in a Digital Age
Erin McDevitt, Ramesh Minisandram and Matias Garcia-Avila
Abstract Casting and solidi ﬁcation simulations, heat transfer models, hot isostatic
press consolidation simulations, hot working simulations, phase equilibrium cal-
culations… the list is quite long of digital technologies embraced by ATI and other
producers of specialty materials and components. Through virtual experimentation,
product development cycle time and cost is reduced, the potential impact of process
upsets can be determined without testing, and sensitivity to process variation can be
assessed prior to ever making any metal, among other ef ﬁciency and cost bene ﬁts.
Nevertheless, effective, ef ﬁcient development of superalloys manufacturing pro-
cesses requires that these digital experiments are complemented by careful physical
experiments at the pilot scale in order to manage risk and expense of scale-up. Pilot
scale development provides critical insight into factors not easily computed, such as
the integrity of a VIM cast electrode, the variation in segregation during VAR
melting, and cracking due to grain structure or surface condition during hot
working. ATI integrates use of physical experiments conducted in pilot research
facilities and computational methods to facilitate both new product development
and development of the manufacturing method. Such an approach has been
instrumental in the development of ATI 718Plus
® alloy and René 65 alloy and an
array of new products including cast-and-wrought, powder, and titanium alloys and
components. This paper will discuss the advantages of using physical experiments
to streamline the development of new products and manufacturing methods and
some of the ways ATI capitalizes on the combined approach.

Background
During the past three decades, the ﬁeld of superalloy metallurgy and more gener-
ally, the ﬁeld of structural materials development and manufacturing, has bene ﬁtted
greatly from the development and application of computational methods in mate-
rials engineering and application [for example 1–5]. CALPHAD methods have
paved the way for understanding multicomponent alloys, like superalloys, without
the requiring manufacture of tens or hundreds of physical samples to experimen-
tally characterize the phase equilibrium [ 6]. Industry consortia like the Specialty
Metals Processing Consortium (SMPC) and Metals Affordability Initiative
(MAI) have developed and validated models that are useful in simulating superalloy
melt processes vacuum arc remelting and electroslag remelting [ 7, 8]. Finite ele-
ment methods and software codes like DEFORM
® and FORGE® are routinely used
for simulating hot working processes, thereby reducing experimental processing in
identifying suitable ingot conversion and part forging practices [ 9, 10].
The Materials Genome Initiative launched in 2011 [ 11] provides funding and
collaboration to build upon a foundation of computational materials science with
the objective of signi ﬁcantly reducing the cycle time for materials insertion. Major
efforts are underway to improve and expand the applicability and use of compu-
tational tools in superalloys and the future holds promise for widespread
application.
Despite the fast pace of development of the Integrated Computational Materials
Engineering (ICME) approach in materials applications, these techniques have been
unable to keep up with the need for vastly reduced design cycle times for new
aircraft and engines. Thus, the reality today for ATI, a developer and supplier of
superalloy mill products, forgings, and components, is that it is essential to maintain
and continually improve capabilities in physical experiments in order that the
timing and performance requirements demanded by engine and airframe OEM ’s are
met. A judicious use of physical experiments coupled with computer simulations
has been key to the recent successes achieved by ATI in meeting the materials
needs of today ’s aerospace industry.
Reducing risk is the primary driver for maintaining pilot scale physical exper-
imentation capabilities. For aerospace alloys (superalloys and titanium alloys pro-
duced via cast and wrought or powder metallurgy routes, the cost of production
scale trials can be one or two orders of magnitude greater than well planned and
executed pilot scale experiments while producing less actionable information.
Therefore, advancing directly from calculations to full-scale production comes with
unacceptable ﬁnancial risks that most aerospace material producers cannot support
even when process and alloy simulation capabilities are mature enough to inform
the outcome of a scale-up trial. Further, those materials producer scale-up and
manufacturability assessment risks are small when compared to risk for an OEM or
airline associated with grounding of an aircraft ﬂeet. So today, the combined risk of
relying exclusively or in large part on modeling and simulation results to assess the

## Page 925

behavior and performance of a material during manufacturing or in service is not
practical for new alloy development and introduction.
A second critical reason for maintaining physical experiment capabilities is that
most material models in use and in development rely on combined physics-based
and empirical descriptions of material behavior, and physical experiments are often
required to generate data necessary to ﬁt physical coef ﬁcients required by the
models. For example, mesoscale modeling of microstructure evolution requires
empirically determined recrystallization information about the alloy being modeled
[12]. Thermodynamics databases are another example where physical observations
are the foundation of the predictive technology. While ﬁrst principles’ methods are
rapidly developing the ability to calculate phase diagrams, databases used in
CALPHAD methods continue to be built largely from data obtained through
carefully executed physical experiments. This paper will describe how a model for
powder consolidation in hot isostatic pressing required pilot scale resources to
generate necessary materials models.
Beyond the need for physical experiment capabilities for developing materials
models, pilot scale physical experiments are a resource ef ﬁcient means to conduct
model validation activities. There is often more capability and ﬂexibility to control
a process and collect clean data when performing pilot scale experiments. ATI is
validating gamma-prime coarsening predictions through a series of controlled pilot
scale thermal-mechanical processing experiments on powder alloys.
Physical experiments also offer a fast method to capture the sources of variation
one may encounter during the manufacturing process. Consider an alloy 718 billet
made from a VIM plus VAR melted ingot. Sources of variation include, for
example, raw materials, composition, cleanliness, ingot microstructure, billet
forging reductions, press time, transfer times, die wear, etc. For established prod-
ucts, these sources of variation are suitably controlled through customer speci ﬁ-
cations and ﬁxed manufacturing practices. When developing new alloys or
materials, the degree of variation due to manufacturing is not known, even though
potential sources of variation are known. Process simulations are routinely used to
identify which sources of variation signi ﬁcantly in ﬂuence material behavior.
However, these models are not suf ﬁciently accurate in predicting all aspects of
component manufacturing to be practical for assessing routine manufacturing
variation. Producing a small number of pilot scale parts is an effective means to
create natural variation, which in turn readily provides information on the impact of
such variation on materials performance.
At ATI, we effectively utilize a development approach that is up to the challenge
of meeting today ’s needs for materials development needs. The ATI approach
combines process modeling with diverse pilot scale manufacturing capabilities. The
development of ATI 718Plus alloy [ 13], RR1000 press billetized powder billet [ 14],
and René 65 [ 15] are examples of superalloy successes resulting from the approach.
This paper describes a few examples where physical experiments have been
instrumental in developing information necessary for successful manufacturing of

ATI maintains a dedicated pilot plant for melting and conversion of specialty
metals at both our Monroe East Operations and Millersburg Operations. Addi-
tionally, there are pilot scale facilities for powder making and hot isostatic pressing
at the Robinson Operations, and isothermal forging capabilities at the Cudahy
Operations. Pilot manufacturing capabilities in Monroe East Operations include:
vacuum induction melting (VIM), vacuum arc remelting (VAR), and electroslag
remelting (ESR) furnaces; press forge, rolling mill, and heat treatment furnaces
(Fig. 1). Equipment is instrumented and controlled suitably to generate controlled
and reproducible experimental conditions along with automated collection of
detailed process data.
ATI also develops and maintains process modeling capability of varying degrees
of maturity to simulate most manufacturing practices in the production of specialty
materials mill products and closed die forgings. A combination of commercial
codes and internally developed software provide a powerful complementary tool to
physical experiments for product and process development.

Integrity of Cast Electrodes
One example where process simulation today is a very powerful tool in under-
standing the macro behavior of a process, but it does not yet deliver microscale
information required to take action, is the process of casting electrodes. A sound
electrode input into the VAR process is important in producing a superalloy ingot
of satisfactory quality for conversion to billet and forgings. Cracks in the electrode
can cause disruption to steady state conditions or electrode fall-in during remelting
and result in melt defects unacceptable for the ﬁnal part. These are not detected until
billet conversion is complete and must be cut out and discarded. Therefore,
developing a robust electrode casting process is critical to producing high quality
superalloy billet.
ATI investigated the effects of casting variables on the soundness of alloy 718
electrodes static cast from VIM. The computational ﬂuid dynamics (CFD) software
package Procast
® was used to simulate the process and calculate information such
as pipe geometry, cooling rates, and probability of porosity. The simulations
qualitatively agreed with experimental results (Figs. 2 and 3) for electrode features,
such as pipe geometry and the probability of porosity, to an extent that the model
proved useful for assessing potential process changes through simulation rather
than by experimental process. Modeling was used to understand how top pipe and
the centerline porosity through the length of the electrode could be reduced.
While modeling those macro features of the electrode structure were useful, the
simulation could not precisely predict what was observed in the electrode. The
amount of electrode porosity is directly related to the probability of electrode
cracking, so while the simulation was useful in understanding how to move the
process to reduce porosity, a quantitative impact on the risk of electrode cracking
and resulting melt defects for a speci ﬁc electrode could not be obtained. Further, the
geometry of the pores was not calculated in the bulk model so that the stress
intensity factor associated with porosity, also a contributor to the probability of
fracture, could not be obtained through these routine casting simulations. Physical
experiments provided material for direct measurement of the amount of porosity
and the size and shape of the pores so that stress intensity factors could be
calculated.
Variability in Delta Solvus in ATI 718Plus Alloy
Thermodynamic calculations were used extensively to support the development of
ATI 718Plus alloy composition and processing parameters [ 16]. These calculations
were instrumental in reducing development time and cost by providing information
regarding microstructural design considerations such as the volume fractions and
stability of the gamma-prime, gamma-double-prime, and delta phases.

During commercialization, an accurate measure of the delta solvus was needed
to engineer forging practices and obtain the required microstructure for desired
alloy performance. The thermodynamic software package JMatPro
® was used to
calculate the delta solvus for multiple heats with results ranging from 1850 to
1856 °F (1010–1013 °C). These calculated values were always higher than the delta
solvus determined through heat treatment and microscopy (Fig. 4).
There are several factors that could have contributed to the differences between
the calculated and measured results. One, there is a minimum volume fraction of
delta phase that must be present before it is observed using optical or scanning
electron microscopy. That volume fraction of delta phase corresponds to a lower
temperature than the thermodynamic equilibrium for the solvus. Second, it has been
reported that the nucleation behavior of ATI 718Plus alloy can be signi ﬁcantly
affected by hot working history and retained strain in the material [ 17]. The effect of

Assessing Risk of Cracking in Billet Conversion
Assessing the risk of cracking during billet conversion as a function of hot working
process remains a challenge using process simulation alone; physical experiments
provide insight regarding risk of cracking and incorporate many real physical
factors that are dif ﬁcult or time consuming to capture in simulations. Figure 6
shows an example of the use of relatively straightforward forge operations to
understand the cracking propensity of a crack-sensitive alloy. In this case, the alloy
selected was a high γ′ alloy, which tends to be crack-prone due to the high volume
fraction of the second phase. In this trial, 3 cylinders (75 mm dia. × 150 mm tall)
were ﬁrst heat-treated in the super-solvus range (to simulate coarse grain structure
typically seen early in the conversion process). They were then upset from a
sub-solvus temperature between ﬂat dies in the open-die press at the Monroe East
Operations Pilot Plant. The goal was to study the effect of two key process
parameters, viz., transfer time and amount of hot work (as measured by reduction in
height) on surface cracking. The ﬁrst of 3 pieces was transferred with typical
transfer time (on the order of a few seconds) and upset to 50% of its original height
(50% RH). The second cylinder was transferred with typical transfer time and given
a 75% RH. The third piece was given a longer hold time between the dies (10 times
the typical) prior to forging and 50% RH.
There are several phenomena of interest in deformation processing that can be
studied in this simple experiment. The ﬁrst occurs in the bulged surface at the
equatorial plane, which is in a complex tri-axial state of stress (typical of more
complex forging operations). The occurrence of large tensile hoop stresses in this
region results in vertical cracks that initiate at this point of maximum hoop stress
(Fig. 7). With the ﬁrst cylinder (50% RH), there were only 1 –2 hairline cracks of
this nature, implying that this process represents the material limit for the con ﬁg-
uration. In the second cylinder (75%RH), this limit was clearly exceeded, with
several prominent cracks developing as a result. By simulating this process, one can
then infer cracking propensity in more complex forging operations.

A second region of interest is the die-workpiece interface. The upset trial can be
used to characterize effect of die temperature and friction on deformation. This
physical experiment then provides boundary conditions that can be utilized in
simulation of more complex forge operations. In the third compact in Fig. 6,i ti s
seen that due to the long hold time, the surface in contact with the top die has
cooled suf ﬁciently to where it locks up completely, and the surrounding material
separates away from the face, leaving a circular crack at the interface. This type of
cracking is also noticed in full-scale upset operations, where it could result in
signiﬁcant material yield loss. Again, ﬁnite element simulations combined with the
sub-scale physical experiments and experience with full-scale processes, help
improve understanding and provide solutions to minimizing this kind of yield loss.
Assessing Feasibility of Billet Conversion
The traditional process for producing superalloy billet from powder metallurgy is
via extrusion of the compact. ATI has developed a new and unique billetizing
process by converting hot isostatic pressed (HIP ’d) compacts with the upset and
draw practice traditionally used for cast-wrought superalloys [ 14]. Figure 8 illus-
trates that it is feasible to use a combination of pilot plant forge operations and ﬁnite
element simulations of this process to infer a priori the material response in a
full-size workpiece. The example being illustrated is that of a subscale HIP ’d
powder compact that was subject to an upset and draw process in the pilot plant
press. The resulting predicted ﬁnal effective strain in the material was shown to be
in the same range as in a typical full-scale conversion process. We therefore infer
that the microstructure resulting from the pilot scale billetizing process should be
representative of what can be expected in the full scale compact. This was validated
when the microstructures from the sub-scale and full-scale compacts were com-
pared (Fig. 9) and shown to have very similar grain size and gamma-prime
distributions.

Hot Isostatic Press Model and Near Net Shape Parts
The powder metallurgy method to produce near net shape parts provides manu-
facturing advantages for high value added parts in low buy-to- ﬂy ratio and reduced
machining compared to forgings. However, this technique has disadvantages: the
can design and manufacturing process for a near net shape container can be costly
and add signi ﬁcantly to the lead time for such parts; the inability to accurately
predict distortions and compaction in the part during the hot isostatic press (HIP)
process can lead to overly conservative can designs with waste in can and powder

materials; much of the HIP part market is composed of specially designed parts that
will be produced in low production runs. To compete in this market, the engi-
neering effort prior to winning the business must be ef ﬁcient and effective.
There is value in having the ability to simulate the part consolidation during HIP
in order to calculate an accurate ﬁnal part shape and predict secondary issues such
as distortion or insuf ﬁcient consolidation in the ﬁnal part. Over the past three
decades, work has been done in developing physics based models of the HIP
process of powder metals [ 19–26]. Typically, extensive material model develop-
ment and validation by experimentation is required to have a model with suf ﬁcent
accuracy that it can be used for part design. ATI has been developing a model to
predict the behavior of near net shape parts during the HIP process for the purpose
of designing the part can and ﬁxturing. ATI has unique pilot plant capabilities with
small scale atomization of powders and HIP capabilities to develop novel metallic
powders and innovative HIP processes at the Robinson Operations. These pilot
plant capabilities allow for design of experiments to develop accurate material
models for metallic powders under compaction processes. Combining modeling
and pilot plant experiments results in simultaneous model development and model
validation of material properties and process parameters and is expected to sig-
niﬁcantly reduce time-to-insertion and cost in the development phase of process
models for HIP ’d parts.
Physics-based models of powder compaction processes rely on non-traditional
plasticity theories. Conventional plastic theory requires constancy of volume of the
deformed material under load. In powder compaction processes, the powder ma-
terial contains porosity, which is eliminated during the compaction process as the
density increases and the volume decreases. For this reason, viscoelastic defor-
mation of powder materials rely on an extension of the Von Mises theory for porous
materials [ 19]. The evolution of the stress of the continuum powder media obeys
the equation proposed by Shima and Oyane [ 19]:

changes during compaction, F approaches the value of 1, and C approaches 0. This
expression can be used to calculate the equivalent stress and includes the effect of
relative density on the stress of the material.

In order to obtain an accurate de ﬁnition of the powder material behavior under
physical perturbations, a material constitutive model must be developed using a
series of controlled experiments. Since all properties depend on the relative density
of the powder material, the initial step in the material model development is to
generate powder material with different levels of densi ﬁcation by using “incom-
plete” or “interrupted” HIP cycles. By performing HIP cycles at different temper-
atures and pressures, a range of densities can be achieved. Figure 10 shows an
example of 5 different titanium cans ﬁlled with Ti-6Al-4V powder and sealed
before HIP processing at different parameters to obtain a range of relative densities
in the powder material. After these interrupted HIP cycles, the powder material
inside the can is characterized for relative density by the use of imaging techniques
on the microstructure, and ﬂow stress and other density-dependent physical prop-
erties such as elastic modulus, Poisson ratio, coef ﬁcient of thermal expansion, and
thermal conductivity can be calculated from dilatometry experiments [ 26]. From
these experiments, the values of F and C in Eq. ( 1) can be ﬁtted and calculated as a
function of relative density.
Once material constitutive model have been de ﬁned as a function of density, it
can be used in conjunction with a ﬁnite element method to simulate the behavior of
a near net shape part under the HIP process. The changes in pressure and tem-
perature during the HIP process model translate into changes in equivalent stress,

Figure 11a shows an example of a NNS part assembly of a turbine blade, where
the inside is loose powder (blue) and the can (grey) is bulk sheet material. During a
HIP process, the powder material densi ﬁes resulting in subsequent deformation and
distortion of the part (Fig. 11b). After the HIP cycle is completed, the relative
density in the powder reaches a value of 1, and all the porosity is eliminated giving
a fully dense part (Fig. 11c).
Conclusion
Physical experiments, especially when coupled with process simulation methods,
play a critical part in the development and application of new aerospace materials
today. Process simulation and materials ’ behavior models are not yet mature
enough to completely eliminate risk in a new alloy insertion in an aerospace
application. ATI is successfully coupling physical experiments and materials sim-
ulation methods to reduce the risk and the time for materials development [ 5, 7, 8,
14–17]. Over the next decade, ATI will continue to innovate in the integration of
process simulation and physical experiments further reducing the risk and cycle
time for alloy introduction. It is unlikely, in that timeframe, that computational
methods alone will be mature enough that those methods alone will be suf ﬁcient for
alloy development and assessment. ATI will continue to participate in the devel-
opment of materials computational tools while understanding and supporting, and
using, physical experiments to bring value to our customers.

The High-Temperature Bauschinger
Effect in Alloy 718
S. L. Semiatin, P. N. Fagin, B. Streich, R. L. Goetz and V. Venkatesh
Abstract The ﬁnal heat treatment of large aerospace components of alloy 718
typically comprises solution treatment followed by oil quenching and aging. Such
operations give rise to small, but non-uniform, plastic strains that can produce sig-
niﬁcant levels of residual stress. During oil quenching, in particular, material elements
may undergo not only concurrent cooling and straining, but also reversed-plastic
ﬂow. Therefore, constitutive relations for the simulation of residual-stress evolution
should include a description of such transient phenomena. To meet this need, a series
of experiments involving reversed straining of short-gage-length samples of 718 was
performed at temperatures between 427 and 871 °C and strain rates of 0.0001 or
0.003 s
−1. These experiments revealed a measurable Bauschinger Effect (BE) over a
range of temperatures. The temperature at which the BE disappeared was a function
of the applied strain rate. A similar BE was also observed in experiments involving
both reversed straining and continuous cooling.

## Page 940

Introduction
Quantitative descriptions of the state of residual stress which evolves during ﬁnal
heat treatment and machining operations are very important in the formulation and
utilization of advanced service-life models for aerospace alloy 718 components. For
heat-treatment operations, such stresses are developed as a result of non-uniform
cooling during quenching that gives rise to small, spatially- and temporally-varying,
plastic strains. Among other input data, the simulation of residual-stress evolution
in such instances typically requires accurate descriptions of interface heat-transfer
coefﬁcients (IHTCs) and the plastic- ﬂow response of the workpiece material.
IHTCs are often taken to be a function of instantaneous surface temperature, and are
typically inferred by an inverse heat transfer analysis of temperature transients
measured using thermocoupled samples.
Plastic-ﬂow properties at the small strains ( ∼0 to 0.02) and low strain rates
(∼10
−5 to 10 −3 s−1) experienced during quenching are often determined by one of
several different techniques. Perhaps the most common is the so-called
“on-cooling” test in which a tension sample is preheated at a high (solution)
temperature, cooled at a prescribed rate to the deformation temperature, held for a
short period (to equilibrate the temperature), and then pulled at speci ﬁed strain rate
[1–7]. The stress-strain data thus obtained are usually ﬁt to an engineering
stress-strain law for ease of application in numerical calculations. With such an
approach, the effect of the retention of a high-temperature, metastable microstruc-
ture on plastic ﬂow and fracture at a lower temperature is quanti ﬁed. A modiﬁcation
of the on-cooling tension test comprises identical preheating and cooling, but a
stress-relaxation experiment (comprising pre-straining followed by load relaxation)
is performed at the deformation temperature. By this means, additional information
regarding the rate-sensitivity of the ﬂow stress is obtained using a single specimen.
A third, somewhat novel, test technique utilizes concurrent cooling and straining to
simulate the actual thermal and deformation transients that pertain to the formation
of residual stress [ 8]. To obtain a nominally-constant plastic strain rate during such
tests, several experiments are required for each set of conditions: one to quantify the
approximate stress-versus-temperature behavior (and thus the variation of elastic
strain with temperature) and a second test in which the total strain rate is gradually
increased during cooling to account for the variation in elastic strain rate.
Computer simulation of the quenching process often reveals that the spatial
variation of cooling rate gives rise not only to small non-uniform plastic strains, but
can also produce reversals in the strain path in a number of locations in
complex-geometry components. Such reversals in straining direction may give rise
to a Bauschinger Effect (BE) in which the yield strength and subsequent ﬂow stress
on loading in the reversed direction is substantially lower than that just prior to
unloading in the forward direction [ 9]. For most engineering alloys, BE measure-
ments have been made at room or only slightly-elevated temperatures, largely
because the phenomenon tends to decrease with increasing temperatures. The
objective of the present work, therefore, was to quantify the high-temperature
958 S. L. Semiatin et al.

## Page 941

Bauschinger Effect (BE) in alloy 718. This work complements that done by Skelton
[10] whose attention was largely focused on the hysteresis behavior in fatigue at
service temperatures of various nickel-base alloys. In the present work, the in ﬂuence
of temperature and strain rate on the magnitude and persistence with strain of the BE
is examined. For this purpose, a number of samples with a short gage length were
extracted from a subscale alloy 718 forging, solution treated, cooled to a prescribed
test temperature between 427 and 871 °C, and deformed via tension → compression
or compression → tension loading. Limited testing involving reversed straining and
cooling was also conducted to assess the presence of a BE under conditions which
mimic those during quenching following solution treatment.
Materials and Procedures
The program material was received in the form of a subscale forging of alloy 718
produced under the US Air Force Metals Affordability Initiative (MAI) program
referred to as the Foundational Engineering Problem on Residual Stress Evolution
in Nickel-Base Superalloys [ 11]. The microstructure of the forging consisted of
equiaxed gamma grains whose average size was approximately 10 μm (Fig. 1).
A number of the gamma grains contained annealing twins. Furthermore, the gamma
grain boundaries were partially decorated with (lenticular) delta-phase particles
(Fig. 1b).
Test blanks comprising right-circular cylinders, each measuring 19.1-mm
diameter × 127-mm length and lying along the direction of primary metal ﬂow
in the forging (i.e., radial direction), were extracted via electric-discharge ma-
chining (EDM). Following EDM, each blank was machined by lathe turning to
produce a centrally-located reduced section 9.5-mm long × 9.5-mm diameter that
was blended to each shoulder using a 5.1-mm ﬁllet radius. This geometry was
chosen to (1) enable reversed deformation to ﬁnite strains without sample buckling
and (2) minimize plastic deformation in the shoulders with their fourfold larger
cross-sectional area. A ﬂat section measuring 25.4-mm length × 19.1-mm width ×
6.4-mm thickness was also milled into the ends of each specimen for gripping.
The BE experiments were performed in a 89-kN MTS servo-hydraulic test frame
outﬁtted with hydraulic grips. The reduced section and a portion of each shoulder
were heated using a multi-turn helical coil (Fig. 2) and a 50 –150 kHz solid-state
induction power supply. Because of the very short length of the gage section and
concomitant challenges with induction-coil design, sample extension was measured
and controlled using a high-temperature extensometer whose probes were initially
44 mm apart, i.e., outside the reduced section (Fig. 2).
Three types of BE experiments were performed: (1) tension followed by
compression (T → C) at a ﬁxed temperature, (b) compression followed by tension
(C → T) at a ﬁxed temperature, and (3) tension followed by concurrent com-
pression and cooling (T → CC). For all tests, the sample was initially solution
treated at 982 °C for 60 min followed by cooling at a constant rate of 195 °C/min.

plastic strain increment of ∼0.015 in both the forward- and reversed-strain direc-
tions without an interruption while the crosshead motion was reversed . To establish
the effect of the level of prestrain on the BE, one 649 °C experiment in which the
forward strain was ∼+0.005 and the reversed strain was ∼−0.015 was also con-
ducted. For the T → CC experiment, the forward (tension) strain of ∼+0.015 was

For the T → C and C → T experiments, deformation was imposed using a

To achieve the prescribed strain rate, each test was performed using the exten-
someter readout as the control signal for the MTS. To this end, it was assumed that
the shoulder regions spanned by the extensometer probes deformed elastically. The

and (ii) the Young ’s modulus at a temperature ∼110 °C below that experienced in
the reduced section, per estimates of the axial temperature gradient.
The load-extension data from each experiment were converted to true axial
stress-true axial strain in the reduced section using standard relationships. For this
purpose, the elastic extension suffered in the shoulders was subtracted from the total
extension, and it was assumed that the deformation in the reduced section was
uniform. Similarly, the imposed strain rate at the end of the forward-strain

During the reduction of load-extension data, it was noticed that the Young ’s
moduli at the beginning of forward deformation were lower than expected; i.e.,
approximately 20 –40% lower than handbook values. However, the corresponding
moduli during unloading from the forward straining as well as during loading in the

small plastic straining in the shoulders, or the presence of constraints due to the
short gage length of the test samples. Despite such a shortcoming, the broad
insights into plastic- ﬂow behavior described below are still thought to be valid.
Results
The principal results of the present investigation consisted of true stress-true strain
curves and quantitative measurements of the ﬂow stress developed during forward
and reverse straining.
T → C Behavior
Typical results for T → C experiments performed with a strain rate of ∼0.003 s −1
are summarized in Fig. 3. For test temperatures of 427, 649 and 760 °C
(Figs. 3a–c), the ﬂow behavior comprised an initial elastic loading, mild strain
hardening to an almost steady-state regime at the end of tension straining, elastic
unloading, yielding at a substantially-lower stress during the compression portion of
the deformation, and, last, a regime that appeared to involve a broad
strain-hardening transient. Such a behavior is typical of a noticeable Bauschinger
Effect (BE), or yielding at a reduced stress (relative to that at the end of the forward
straining) during reversed loading. The magnitude of the BE was quanti ﬁed in
terms of the ratio of the proportional limit during reloading to the ﬂow stress at the
end of the forward straining, BR = ∣σ
r/σf ∣ (Table 1, sample IDs 6a, 3b, 2b, 4). At
the two lower temperatures, BR was of the order of 0.2. BR increased substantially
with increasing temperature, viz., ∼ 0.6 at 760 °C, and ∼0.9 at 871 °C. The tem-
perature dependence of BR tended to show an inverse correlation with the variation
of ﬂow stress with temperature at 0.003 s
−1 (Table 1). The values of σf at the two
lower temperatures were essentially identical, decreased a small amount at 760 °C
and then exhibited a much larger decrease when the temperature was raised to
871 °C. In addition, the stress-strain behavior at 871 °C showed what appeared to
be ﬂow softening (in both the forward and reversed directions) suggestive of

Effect of Loading Path and Prestrain on BE
The present investigation also provided insight into the effect of the loading path
and magnitude of the forward strain on the BE. For example, the stress-strain curves
for T → C and C → T behaviors at 649 °C/0.003 s
−1 are shown in Figs. 3b and 4.
These results (and those in Table 1, sample IDs 3b, 5a) showed a similar BE; the
BR was ∼0.15 for T → C and ∼0.3 for C → T. Similarly, DSA was observed
during the forward loading but not during the reversed straining in the C → T
experiment as it was for the corresponding T → C observation; i.e., there were
distinct stress drops during the initial compression straining but not during the
subsequent tension deformation.
The level of plastic prestrain appeared to have a moderate in ﬂuence on the
magnitude of the BE (Table 1, sample IDs 3b, 12a). In particular, when the pre-
strain was reduced from 1.5 pct. (sample 3b) to 0.5 pct. (sample 12a), the value of
BR increased from 0.15 to ∼0.4.
BE During Concurrent Cooling/Straining
The T → CC test revealed that the magnitude of the BE was similar under both
isothermal (constant temperature) and continuous-cooling conditions (Fig. 5).
Despite some noise in the forward (tension) portion of the T → CC test and the
slightly different strain rates in the two types of tests (i.e., 0.0001 vs 0.00022 s −1),
the elastic limits and the subsequent strain-hardening behaviors during the reversed
loading portion of the experiment were similar to those found for isothermal
T → C BE experiments at 427 and 649 °C. Furthermore, the continuous cooling
experiment revealed DSA behavior during the forward, but not the reverse,
straining increments. However, DSA appeared to be somewhat greater in magni-
tude in the T → CC experiment.

Discussion
Two approaches are commonly used to describe and interpret the BE [ 12]. One is
based on the concepts of continuum/macroscopic plasticity and the other on a
microscopic/mechanistic interpretation.
The ﬁrst (continuum) description typically seeks to ﬁt the stress-strain curves in
forward and reversed uniaxial deformation to engineering stress-strain curves. For
more complex strain paths, the yield locus is typically assumed to translate in stress
space along the initial direction of loading without a change in shape or orientation;
such behavior is referred to as kinematic hardening. More advanced continuum
models may also allow expansion and distortion of the yield locus in addition to
translation.
Microscopic models seek to quantify the effect of the inhomogeneity of plastic
ﬂow associated with grains, second-phase particles, etc. on the evolution of internal,
long-range “back” stresses. For a polycrystalline aggregate, the back stress is

associated with anisotropic yielding from one grain to another during straining in a
“forward” direction such that non-uniform/different states of residual (micro) stress
are developed within individual crystallites. When the straining direction is
reversed, some grains possess microscale residual stresses that promote early
yielding. Alternatively, short-range dislocation interactions within given crystallites
may lead to non-uniform microscale residual stresses that promote a BE during
reversed straining.
In the sections below, several aspects of the BE observations from the present
work are discussed.
Flow Behavior During Reversed Loading
As mentioned in the Introduction, the preponderance of information on the BE in
the literature deals with behavior under ambient- or slightly-elevated-temperature
conditions. This is not surprising in view of the fact that elevated-temperature
deformation tends to promote dislocation climb and recovery and thus the elimi-
nation of the grain-scale stresses responsible for the BE.
One of the few literature reports of the BE in metallic materials at relatively-high
temperatures is that of Skelton [ 10]. His work dealt with a variety of superalloys
and focused primarily on hysteresis effects during fatigue loading involving rela-
tively small strain amplitudes. For alloy 718, for example, Skelton reported results
for temperatures between 550 and 700 °C and plastic-strain amplitudes between
approximately 0.2 and 0.4 pct., i.e., deformations substantially lower than those in
the present work. The shape of the hysteresis loops in Ref. [ 10] and thus the
magnitude of the BE were quanti ﬁed using a Ramberg-Osgood power-law con-
stitutive formulation:
Δσ =A Δε
β
p, ð1Þ
in which Δσ and Δεp denote the stress range and plastic strain range, and A and β
are ﬁtting constants representing the “plastic strength ” and the strain-hardening
coefﬁcient, respectively. Two de ﬁnitions of Δσ are commonly found in the litera-
ture (Fig. 6). For the ﬁrst deﬁnition (that used by Skelton [ 10]), Δσ during reversed
loading is measured from the ﬁnal stress experienced during the forward portion of
the straining process, i.e., ΔσTC. For the other de ﬁnition, denoted as ΔσC, the stress
range is based solely on the compression portion of the ﬂow curve. Obviously,
these two de ﬁnitions give rise to differences in the material coef ﬁcients A and β.
The values of these parameters are summarized in Table 2 for the test conducted at
649 °C/0.003 s −1 in the present work and a fatigue test performed by Skelton on
alloy 718 at 650 °C. Using the ΔσTC deﬁnition of the stress range, the ﬁt from
the present work and that from Skelton [ 10] showed reasonably good agreement
despite the uncertainty with regard to the strain rate used in the earlier research.

This agreement may be fortuitous in view of (i) the limited rate sensitivity of the
ﬂow stress at 650 °C and (ii) the use of a method based on ΔσTC, which tends to
bias the ﬁt to the ﬂow behavior during the forward (unloading) part of the straining
process.
Because of the high temperatures utilized in the present work, it is also of
interest to examine the persistence of the BE with increasing strain in the reverse
direction. For a variety of metals deformed at room temperature, a measurable (or
even constant) stress difference between the ﬂow behaviors in the forward and
reverse directions is often retained to strains of the order of 0.03 –0.06 and, in some
cases, to even 0.10 [ 12]. For the present work, the possible retention of a stress
difference as a function of temperature and strain rate was examined by replotting
the reversed (compression) portions of the stress-strain curves as positive quantities
(Figs. 7 and 8). Because of DSA, the extrapolation of the forward portion of the
ﬂow curves was confounded, but the resulting comparison appeared to still provide
useful, although qualitative, insight. For the T → C results obtained at a strain rate

(Fig. 7a, b). By contrast, the comparison at 760 °C suggested that the reversed,
compression ﬂow curve reached the extrapolated tension- ﬂow-curve stress by a
reverse strain of slightly less than 0.01 (Fig. 7c). A similar trend was observed for
the tests conducted at 0.0001 s
−1 (Fig. 8). However, the loss of relative softening
occurred at lower temperatures. Speci ﬁcally, the compression ﬂow curves appeared
