of Q is typical of the diffusion of interstitial solutes such as carbon in nickel solid
solutions, but considerably less than that for the diffusion of substitutional elements
(i.e., 250 –300 kJ/mol) [ 13].
Dynamic Strain Aging
The DSA phenomena observed in the present work were similar to prior obser-
vations in the literature for alloy 718 [ 13, 14]. Typically, DSA is associated with the
interaction between mobile dislocations and diffusing solutes or point defects that
lead to yield-point phenomena, serrated ﬂow curves, and negative strain-rate sen-
sitivities (m values). A comparison of the forward ﬂow curves in the present work
(Fig. 3) revealed negative m values of various magnitudes at test temperatures of
427, 649, and 760 °C. Similarly, DSA was noted at the two lower temperatures for
both strain rates (0.0001 s
−1 and 0.003 s −1), but only at the higher strain rate at
760 °C. Hence, it appears that the micro-mechanism responsible for DSA may have
undergone a transition between 649 and 760 °C for the strain rates imposed in the
present work. Such a transition in DSA behavior and the accompanying change in
the strain rate sensitivity were similar to prior measurements of m based on
stress-relaxation (SR) tests [ 15]. As in the present work, these measurements were
performed on alloy 718 samples which were solution treated at 982 °C, cooled
rapidly to and equilibrated for 30 s at a test temperature of 704 °C, prestrained 0.02,
and then relaxed. Typical results (Fig. 10) indicated an m of 0.02 –0.035 for strain
rates less than 0.0001 s
−1. The observed negative rate sensitivities based on
The High-Temperature Bauschinger Effect in Alloy 718 971

## Page 954

continuous ﬂow curves in the present work and the relatively small positive rate
sensitivity from the SR test thus ﬁt in with the common trend for m to decrease with
decreasing temperature and increasing strain rate.
The very small/negligible rate sensitivity in the temperature range between 427
and 649 °C can be concluded to be the source of the similarity in BE and DSA
behaviors for the isothermal (T → C) and cooling-straining (T → CC) experiments
(Figs. 3a, b and 5b).
As in previous work in the literature involving forward straining alone, the form
of the serrations observed in the present ﬂow curves showed a noticeable depen-
dence on strain rate and temperature. Typically, such serrations are one of three
types [13, 16]: A (periodic, widely-spaced, associated with dislocation locking that
leads to an abrupt rise followed by a load drop below the general level of the ﬂow
curve), B (oscillations about the ﬂow curve that occur in quick succession), and C
(stress drops below the ﬂow curve associated with the unlocking of dislocations
from solutes/solute atmospheres).
The present observations for forward deformation at the lower strain rate
(0.0001 s
−1) and temperatures of 427 and 649 °C (Fig. 3a, b) indicated type C DSA
serrations. The levels of the load drops here (50 –200 MPa) were somewhat greater
than in prior work (50 –100 MPa) [ 13, 14], however. Such a behavior may be due to
differences in preheat procedures (i.e., direct heating to test temperature versus
solution treatment and cooling to test temperature), the type of test machine (e.g.,
screw driven versus servo-hydraulic), etc. In contrast to the DSA for the forward
deformation, reverse loading showed no or very negligible serrations, at least for
the magnitude of the reverse strains used in the present work. In future work, it
would be useful to determine if larger reverse strains lead to DSA, therefore.
For forward deformation at the higher strain rate (0.003 s
−1), oscillations that
appeared to be between types A and B were noted at 427 and 649 °C; type C DSA
was found at 760 °C (Fig. 3). Unlike deformation at the lower strain rate, notice-
able DSA was also observed during the reverse loading at 0.003 s −1 for the lowest
and highest test temperatures. In these cases, the serrations were similar in type to
those found during the forward deformation.
The dependence of DSA and serration type on strain rate and temperature in the
present effort was somewhat similar to the observations of Hale, et al. [ 13].

In particular, when the present data were inserted onto their Arrhenius plot
(Fig. 11), the serration types for the forward deformation lay close to the corre-
sponding regimes noted previously, except for the experiment at 0.003 s −1/649 °C.
Moreover, as described by Hale, et al., the activation energies deduced from
boundaries delimiting different types of serrations suggest the rate-controlling
mechanisms for plastic ﬂow. For type A/B behavior, for example, the activation
energy was 134 kJ/mol, a value typical of interstitial carbon diffusion in nickel. For
type C serrations, it was 272 kJ/mol, which is representative of substitutional Cr
diffusion in nickel.
In contrast to the work of Hale, et al. [ 13], Prasad, et al. [ 14] have suggested that
DSA at 650 °C may be due to the interaction of dislocations and a precipitate
phase. Isothermal transformation [IT] data for alloy 718 in the literature [ 17, 18]
have shown that the pertinent phase is likely γ′′. Speci ﬁcally, the IT diagram
(Fig. 12) reveals that the γ′′ nose lies at ∼800 °C. At 649 °C and 760 °C, static
precipitation of γ′′ begins at ∼3600 or 430 s (1 or 0.12 h), respectively. These times
are substantially longer than the presoak time used for temperature equilibration in
the present work (30 s) as well as the time for the forward strain increment ( ∼5 and
150 s for tests at 0.003 and 0.0001 s
−1, respectively). However, concurrent
straining likely would have accelerated the aging process by approximately two
orders of magnitude, based on precipitation observations for steels [ 19]. With this
assumption, the time to initiate the formation of γ′′ (which could have triggered
DSA) would have been 36 or 4.3 s at 649 °C and 760 °C, respectively. These times
are comparable to or less than the duration of the forward strain increment for both
strain rates at 760 °C and the slower strain rate at 649 °C. Furthermore, the longer
time within the range of dynamic precipitation for the slower strain rate may be
surmised to be the source of the higher yield strength and ﬂow-hardening rate for
deformation at 0.0001 s
−1 at 760 °C relative to the corresponding behavior at
0.003 s −1 (Fig. 3c).

The High-Temperature Bauschinger Effect in Alloy 718 973

## Page 956

Summary and Conclusions
A number of reversed-loading mechanical tests were performed to characterize the
extent of the Bauschinger-Effect (BE) in alloy 718 samples over a wide range of
temperatures. The following conclusions were drawn from this work:
1. A measurable BE occurs for temperatures between approximately 427 and
760 °C and strain rates typical of those experienced during the formation of
residual stress during quenching following solution heat treatment, i.e., 10 −4 to
3×1 0 −3 s−1. The magnitude of the BE, as quanti ﬁed by the BR parameter,
appears to be controlled by a thermally-activated process with an activation
energy of approximately 140 kJ/mol.
2. The BE appears to be similar irrespective of whether the strain path involves
tension followed by compression or vice versa as well as whether the strain
reversal occurs isothermally or concurrently with decreasing temperature.
3. Dynamic strain aging (DSA) accompanies the BE, especially during forward
straining. As in previous work in the literature on DSA, the form of serrations
observed during forward deformation (and when observed in reverse deforma-
tion) depends on strain rate and temperature and can be ascribed to the inter-
action of dislocations with carbon or chromium solutes. However, the
interaction of dislocations with precipitates formed during deformation may also
be a source of DSA.

Inﬂuence of Temperature and Strain
Rate During Rolling of René 65 Bar
Oscar R. Terrazas, Mark E. Zaun, Ramesh S. Minisandram
and Michael L. Lasonde
Abstract The requirements for rotating jet engine components have placed
increasing demands on materials suppliers in the aerospace industry. Higher tem-
perature demands of blade and rotor disk applications in the compressor section
have led to a need for alloys with properties superior to ATI 718Plus
®™ while
retaining the ability to be processed by the conventional cast plus wrought process.
René 65 was developed for rotor disk applications. The alloy ’s property capability
also makes it an excellent candidate for compressor blade applications. Processing
parameters become critical throughout different stages for this alloy. This study is
focused on the hot rolling process of René 65 for blade applications, with rolling
temperature and strain rate as the parameters of interest. The results show the
signiﬁcant in ﬂuence of starting temperature and strain rate for hot rolling of
René 65 bar when processing through a continuous rolling mill. Slight changes in
rolling temperature and strain rate could ultimately have a major impact on resulting
microstructure and mechanical properties.

Higher gas turbine engine operating temperatures, for enhanced engine perfor-
mance, has led to increased use of powder metallurgy (PM) alloys for critical
rotating components [ 1]. As a result of these higher operating temperatures, there

## Page 959

has also been an increase in the use of higher temperature alloys in the compressor
blade and disk applications beyond the capabilities of ATI 718Plus ®™ such as
ATI 720 ™ and Nimonic 1 105 (N105), which are cast and wrought (C&W) alloys.
While these alloys provide the required properties at elevated temperatures, their
application comes at a high cost due to the expensive processing route required to
produce them [ 2]. This led to the development of René 65 (R65), a derivative of
René 88DT (R88DT), which was developed in collaboration between General
Electric Aviation and ATI Specialty Materials as part of the effort to close the gap
of cost and performance that exists between PM and traditional C&W nickel-base
superalloys. The chemical composition has been modi ﬁed from R88DT to enhance
processing by a C&W route. The nominal composition of R65 is shown in Table 1,
along with the nominal compositions of the other high temperature alloys men-
tioned previously. Since its inception in 2007, R65 has been widely utilized in a
variety of both turbine and compressor disk applications on multiple engine plat-
forms. R65 ’s excellent balance of strength, creep, and fatigue properties for disk
applications also make the alloy well suited for latter stage compressor blades as
compressor discharge temperatures continue to increase.
R65 is a gamma prime (Ni
3Al) strengthened nickel-base superalloy produced by
a triple melt practice that consists of Vacuum Induction Melting (VIM), followed
by Electroslag Remelting (ESR) and ﬁnal Vacuum Arc Remelting (VAR) opera-
tion. The resulting ingot goes through a homogenization treatment to mitigate
chemical segregation prior to thermomechanical processing. The ingot is then
hot-worked through a two-step forge procedure that starts with open-die hydraulic
press forging followed by radial forging. For the present study, the VAR ingot was
508 mm in diameter and was forged down to a 137 mm diameter billet. While there
has been a fair amount of work performed in investigating and understanding R65
processing down to billet [ 3, 4], there is minimal work on further processing. The
present study focuses on the thermomechanical processing performed on the forged
billet by continuous rolling down to 35 mm bar, the differences in gamma prime
morphology as a result of different rolling parameters and their corresponding
impact on mechanical properties. The interest that lies behind processing in a
continuous rolling mill is in increasing production ef ﬁciency by producing a single,
long bar in one heating cycle as compared to the alternate merchant mill method of
rolling multiple short length bars that go through numerous re-heats.

Experimental Rolling Parameters
Multiple conditions, that represent the combined effect between initial rolling
temperature and strain rate, were determined based on modeling and prior expe-
rience with other nickel-base superalloys. The modeling results were generated
using a proprietary in-house ﬁnite element code that simulates the rolling process
using a steady-state formulation to generate thermo-mechanical history of the bar
through multiple stands [ 5]. While the focus of the study was to evaluate the impact
of rolling temperature and strain rate on mechanical properties, certain combina-
tions of such were identi ﬁed as undesirable for various reasons (excessive cracking,
high ﬂow stress, excessive grain growth, etc.). This was supported by modeling
work shown in Figs. 1 and 2. Figure 1 illustrates a typical contour plot of tem-
perature for the cross-section after the ﬁnal stand for the rolling simulation. Figure 2
shows the simulation results for various combinations of rolling temperature and
strain rate which provided process extremes and a possible optimal process. Table 2
shows the different conditions of combined initial rolling temperature and strain rate
selected based on these results. Initial rolling temperatures will be discussed in a
relative scale (baseline and 14 °C offsets) for the rest of the article. Strain rates have
been normalized for the present discussion and are therefore unitless.
Billets were initially heated up to temperature followed by a short soak at
temperature, which helps achieve temperature uniformity throughout the entire
billet. Rolling was performed using a traditional two-high roll mill (alternating
horizontal/vertical) con ﬁguration initially and followed by a three-roll mill con-
ﬁguration in which the rolls are set at 120° angles from each other, alternating
orientation from stand to stand by inverting the rolls. Bars were air cooled once they

The as-rolled microstructure consists of an equiaxed gamma matrix and a high
volume fraction of gamma prime precipitates dispersed uniformly throughout.
Figure 3 shows the microstructures for the different rolling conditions from the low
temperature/low strain rate combination (Fig. 3a) to the high temperature/high
strain rate combination (Fig. 3h). Initial rolling temperature was set below the
gamma prime solvus temperature for all rolling conditions. However, there were
signiﬁcant losses in primary gamma prime that occurred during the rolling process
at the higher temperature/strain rate conditions. This can be observed through the
progression of Fig. 3, where there is a major difference in grain size and amount of
gamma prime. This is a result of adiabatic heating during rolling that is driving the
core temperature near or above the gamma prime solvus temperature for short
periods of time. The microstructures observed in Fig. 3f–h are ﬁner than would be
expected when processing above the gamma prime solvus temperature and this is
caused by the recrystallization kinetics associated with the short exposure time near
or above the gamma prime solvus based on those rolling conditions. The structure
in Fig. 3a, which was processed at the lowest temperature/strain rate condition, has
a greater occurrence of twinning along with a ﬁner grain size. This is believed to be
a result of the rolling temperature being too low to allow for dynamic
recrystallization.
As mentioned previously, it can be observed from the progression through the
rolling conditions in Fig. 3 that the grain size becomes larger with increasing rolling
temperature and strain rate, from an ASTM 9.5-11 to an ASTM 8. Figure 4 shows a
strong correlation between grain size and rolling conditions. Grain size increases
with increasing rolling temperature and strain rate. The ﬁner grain size is a result of
an increased amount of primary gamma prime remaining in the microstructure to
assist in grain boundary pinning. Mitigating primary gamma prime dissolution
during the rolling process is essential in achieving a ﬁne grain microstructure.

Inﬂuence of Rolling Parameters on René 65 Mechanical
Properties
The mechanical properties of R65 were evaluated for each rolling condition by
performing elevated temperature tensile (ETT) tests at two temperatures, 400 and
650 °C on heat treated samples. The heat treatment consisted of a solution step at
1065 °C for 1 h followed by air cool and an age step at 760 °C for 8 h followed by
air cool. These tensile tests were performed in the longitudinal orientation. Strength
and ductility measurements were the results used to evaluate mechanical properties
of R65.
The lower starting temperatures and strain rates already associated with ﬁner
grain sizes also increase the tensile and yield strengths as shown in Figs. 6a and 7a.
While it would be expected to see ductility increase with increasing combinations
of strain rate and temperature, the ductility at 400 °C does not follow this trend with

Conclusions
Although René 65 was developed for rotating disk applications, some of its
properties drove the development and implementation for compressor blade ap-
plications. It has been shown that it is possible to manufacture this alloy without the
need of the expensive processing methods common for other alloys such as PM
and/or merchant mill routes that meet high temperature requirements for similar
applications. A process has been established to produce forging stock for com-
pressor blade applications.
 Hot rolling of René 65 bar through a continuous rolling mill was proven suc-
cessful as a processing route and being more ef ﬁcient than the alternate mer-
chant mill rolling route.
 A strong correlation was established between grain size and both rolling tem-
perature and strain rate with a linear regression model that predicts grain size
within ±0.5 ASTM number of the actual results.
 Although limited, it was demonstrated that there is a processing window that
results in optimal properties for the smaller cross sections of René 65.
 Evaluation of microstructure and mechanical properties proved that minor
changes in temperature and strain rate have a signi ﬁcant in ﬂuence on the
mechanical behavior of the alloy.
 Based on ﬁnite element simulations, the 0.48 strain rate and T
−14 temperature
condition was selected as the ideal combination of processing parameters. This
was further con ﬁrmed to be correct based on the gamma prime and grain size
response observed and the resulting mechanical properties.

Microstructure Controlling
of U720-Typed Superalloys to Improve
a Hot and Cold Workability by Using
Incoherent Gamma Prime
A. Ota, N. Ueshima, K. Oikawa and S. Imano
Abstract For high performance air craft engine disks, high-performance Ni-based
wrought superalloys (e.g. U720Li TM, AD730 TM) with over 40vol% of the γ′ phase
at 600 –700 °C have been developed. Applying them to gas turbines is expected to
improve the efﬁciency. However, due to their low workability, it is dif ﬁcult to make
large size components. We have developed a new innovative process (the MH
process) to improve the workability of high-performance Ni-based wrought
superalloys. The strengthening mechanism of these γ′ precipitation-typed superal-
loys is widely known to be enhanced by the coherent interface between the γ phase
and γ′ phase. We focused on the incoherent γ′ phase that precipitated on the γ phase
grain boundary during forging and it was found that the incoherent boundary shows
no strengthening effect. Formation of γ/incoherent γ′ two-phase microstructure
would dramatically improve their workability. Cold working was achieved by
applying the MH process to the U720-type alloy AD730. The MH process made it
possible to fabricate cold rolled sheets, cold drawn wires and the forged turbine
blades. It also exhibited excellent ductility at high temperature; we obtained 99%
reduction of area at over 920 °C and 500% elongation at 950 °C by applying the
MH process. It was demonstrated that U720Li can be processed by die forging at
low temperature and high strain rate without using superplastic forming. In this
study, we investigated how the heat treatment condition affects the formation of
unique microstructures with good hot and cold workability.

## Page 969

Introduction
Along with the technological innovations in alloy and processing,shown in Fig. 1,
Ni-based wrought superalloys with higher strength than conventional forged
materials, such as IN 718, have been developed for aircraft turbine disks in recent
years and are being promoted for practical use [ 1–5]. These high-performance
Ni-based wrought superalloys have the same level of creep strength are at worst the
same and at best more than 1.5 times higher than precision casting alloys for the gas
turbine blades. Therefore, applying the new alloys to gas turbine blades or disks
makes it possible to expand the blade length, reduce the amount of cooling air
needed, and reduce the thickness. These changes contribute to improved gas turbine
efﬁciency. In addition, since they have higher strength than conventional forged
materials, applying them to a combustor is expected to improve heat resistance at
the operating temperature and thereby extend life. However, these alloys don ’t have
good workability and their use is limited to the production of components such as
aircraft disks.
Generally, as shown in the left side of Fig. 2, in the Ni-based superalloys of γ′
phase precipitation strengthening type, the γ′ phase coherently precipitates in the γ
phase of the matrix, and the interface between the γ phase and the γ′ phase con-
tributes to strengthening (this type of γ′ phase is de ﬁned as “coherent γ′ phase”).
However, we noticed that the γ′ phase precipitated on the grain boundaries of the γ
phase during hot forging at temperatures below that of the γ′ phase solvus does not
achieve lattice matching with the γ phase (this type of γ′ phase is de ﬁned as
“incoherent γ′ phase”). Therefore the incoherent γ′ phase has no strengthening
effect. We found that by applying heat treatment after hot forging, as shown on the
right side of Fig. 2, the workability could be greatly improved by forming a
two-phase structure consisting of a γ phase and an incoherent γ′ phase. Alloys that
have such a two-phase structure can be worked more easily into the desired shape.

Heat Treatment and Evaluation Method
The MH material softening heat treatment process is explained as follows. As
mentioned above, the materials are heated to the forging temperature and the
coherent γ′ phase is dissolved. In this example the AD730 to a forging temperature
of 1070 °C and maintained it at that temperature for 1 h. The material was then
gradually cooled at a controlled rate to the set temperatures shown in Fig. 5 and
then water quenching (WQ).
AD 730 that received the standard solution and aging heat treatment (STAG),
described below, is used for comparison.

Results and Discussion
Relationship Between Formation of Two-Phase Structure
of γ/γ′ich and Workability
It was interpreted that the dynamic recrystallized γ phase precipitates to cover the
boundary of the coherent γ′ phase, so that the interface between the coherent γ′
phase and the newly formed γ phase becomes incoherent. As shown in Fig. 3, with
AD730 it is possible to precipitate an incoherent γ′ phase of about 10% by forging
at 1050 to 1070 °C. In the MH process, this incoherent γ′ phase is grown by
controlled cooling shown in Fig. 5 to form a two-phase structure consisting of an
incoherent γ′ phase and a γ phase.
The microstructures from selected AD730 heat treated specimens were evaluated
by SEM microscopy. Figure 7a shows SEM image of AD730 specimen after
1070 °C/1 h/WQ. Figure 7b, c show AD730 specimens cooled from 1070 °C to
1020 °C and 400 °C respectively at a controlled cooling rate. Figure 7d shows
AD730 after receiving a 1070 °C/1 h/FC (FC: Furnace Cooling) heat treatment.
The cooling rates are described below.
Figure 7a (WQ) > Fig. 7d (FC) > Fig. 7b, c (Controlled Cooling). In the case
of WQ and FC, incoherent γ′ phases and coherent γ′ phases were observed on the
grain boundary and in the grain. Compared with WQ sample, the fraction of
incoherent γ′ phase was increased by FC, but it is not noticeable. Coherent γ′
phases were precipitated during cooling from 1070 °C. In the case of controlled
cooling, where the cooling rate was slower than that of FC, the precipitation of
coherent γ′ phase was not observed in the sample cooled to 1020 °C and it was
conﬁrmed that incoherent γ′ phase increased. It is considered that incoherent γ′
phase tends to increase because the crystal grain size is ﬁne and the precipitation
distance of incoherent γ′ phase is suf ﬁciently short compared to the diffusion dis-
tance of the γ′ phase former.

Conclusions
We investigated the effect of the lattice matching between the γ phase and γ′ phases
on the workability of γ′ phase precipitation strengthened high-performance
Ni-based wrought AD730 and obtained the following conclusions.
(1) We found that the incoherent γ′ phase increased by controlling cooling from the
forging temperature after hot forging of AD730 under the γ′ phase solvus.
(2) We con ﬁrmed that the incoherent γ′ phase did not contribute to strengthening
because the hardness was not increased as the incoherent γ′ phase was
increased.
(3) The results of a high temperature tensile test of AD730 with the MH-process
showed a reduction area of over 50% at 800 °C or higher and nearly 100% at
920 °C. At 950 °C, the elongation of nearly 500% was obtained. In addition,
the 0.2% yield strength at high temperature was lower than that of IN718, and
this can be expected to produce a large forged products.
(4) MH processed AD730 demonstrated improvement in cold, machining and also
hot workability were obtained.
• Rolled thin sheet (Thickness 1.8 mm) and drawn wire ( ϕ5 mm) of AD730 were
obtained at RT demonstrates improved cold workability.
• A turbine blade machining from forged bar shows the machinability is equiv-
alent to that of IN718.
• Die forging is demonstrated at low temperature and high strain rate outside
typical superplastic forming parameters.

## Page 981

Ring Rolling of IN 718 for Critical
Engine Applications
M. Büscher and T. Witulski
Abstract Critical engine disks are typically die forged products due to the high
demand on quality and reproducibility. Therefore, it is state of the art that the die
forging process is well controlled by a closed loop controlled hydraulic press
combined with a tight monitoring of process parameters, e.g. deformation velocity,
press load, transfer time etc. Based on the geometry of the disk, for example, in the
case of low pressure turbine disks that have a large inner diameter, die forging is not
always the most cost ef ﬁcient process. In these circumstances, ring rolling of a
pre-shape for ﬁnal die forging or direct ring rolling of the disk by using contoured
rolls can result in a much higher material yield and reduced production cost and
time. For critical components, that require a ﬁne and homogeneous microstructure
to ful ﬁll the required mechanical properties, ring rolling has not been used due to
the lack of process control and the dif ﬁculties to simulate the process. By using an
improved process control of the ring rolling mill, in combination of an enhanced
process monitoring, a suitable microstructure can be achieved during ring rolling.
Results of rolled rings with rectangular and shaped contours made from IN 718 will
be presented and the necessary process control and process monitoring will be
described. In addition, microstructure results of rolled rings will be compared with
simulation results.
Keywords Ring rolling
⋅ Microstructure simulation ⋅ Contoured rings
Introduction
The alloy IN 718 is broadly used for critical engine applications like high /low
pressure turbine disks or high pressure compressor disks. They are typically die
forged using hammers, screw presses or hydraulic presses. The latter has the
advantage of a precise control of the microstructure by adjusting the forging speed

## Page 982

(i.e. the strain rate) and temperature in a way that a ﬁne and homogeneous mi-
crostructure can be achieved. As standard speci ﬁcations request a grain size of
ASTM 4 and ﬁner, today a minimum grain size of ASTM 8 or in some cases ASTM
10 is required to achieve the optimum static and dynamic properties [ 1].
A robust process and a tight process control are keys for achieving a repro-
ducible and ﬁne microstructure in the forged engine disk. Therefore, it is state of the
art to simulate the forging process to predict temperature, strain, strain rate and the
ﬁnal microstructure (grain size and degree of recrystallization) for each forging
step. In addition, during production all relevant forging parameters are measured
and controlled for each individual disk forging. Only this combination of prediction
and veri ﬁcation during production allows the extension of the prior process
boundaries from standard grain size (ASTM 4) to ﬁne grain (ASTM 10). As a
consequence, ﬁne grain disks have to be die forged with well controlled hydraulic
presses.
Incremental forging operations, like ring rolling, have not been used in the past
based on the absence of simulation tools and lack of process control. From a
commercial point of view, ring rolling could offer a bene ﬁt by reducing the material
input in case of ring shaped discs with large inner diameters, which are typical for
low pressure turbine discs. In addition, contoured rings have the potential to create
undercuts in the radial direction, which cannot be realized by conventional die
forgings. In case of the above mentioned requirement to predict microstructure in
rolled rings by simulation and to monitor and control the ring rolling process, this
would lead to an interesting alternative to the die forging process.
Simulation
Based on recent improvements of commercial available forging simulation tools in
terms of process de ﬁnition and computation power, it is now possible to simulate an
axial-radial ring rolling process as a full 3D simulation within a reasonable time.
The software package Simufact has been used, which has the ability to simulate the
complete rolling operation. For a successful simulation, it is essential to simulate
the control mode of the rolling mill, which either can be implemented into the
simulation software or can be respected by a preprocessor, which transfers the
kinetics of the rolls (main roll, axial rolls and guide rolls) into the simulation tool
(Fig. 1).
At the same time, a microstructure model for the relevant alloy is needed to
combine it with the simulation software to calculate the average grain size and the
degree of recrystallization. The model used in this study is a
Zehner-Hollomon-Type approach [ 2], in which the coef ﬁcients of the relevant
equations were determined by isothermal upsetting tests combined with mi-
crostructure investigations of the upset samples:

## Page 984

The rolling load, as well as the microstructure, could be accurately predicted by
the simulation tool. Therefore, a major step in using ring rolling for critical engine
parts is achieved due to the possibility to simulate the forming process.
Ring Rolling
The ring rolling mill used for the production of engine disks is specially designed to
roll high temperature materials like Titanium alloys or Ni-based Superalloys.
Compared to conventional mills, it utilizes larger axial and radial loads and the
bearing of the mandrel is specially designed to withstand the high bending stresses
during rolling caused by the high ﬂow stress of the alloys, especially that of IN 718
rings. Additionally, compared to conventional rolling mills, used for example for
steel rings, the mill is able to roll rings with a very small initial diameter, as the size
of the hole of the punched disk should be as small as possible to optimize the
material yield.
With a standard closed loop control of the mill, after a ﬁrst initial phase I, which
is necessary to grow the inner diameter of the preform, the ring growth velocity
Fig. 2 Comparison of simulation and process (grain size and rolling loads)
1004 M. Büscher and T. Witulski

## Page 985

(RGV) slowly increases in the main rolling phase II. In many cases the ring growth
velocity overshoots beyond the set value and then slowly decreases until it is
ramped down in phase III of the rolling process to ensure the ﬁnal geometry of the
ring. Not controlling this behavior can lead to an inhomogeneous strain distribution
over the cross section of the ring and therefore can lead to an inhomogeneous grain
size distribution. Due to this, the close loop control had to be modi ﬁed to achieve a
fast increase of the RGV and constant value during phase II (Fig. 3).
Process Monitoring
The key element while producing critical rotating engine parts is reproducibility.
Therefore, the ring rolling process, as well as all other metal forming processes,
needs to be fully automated without the interference of a human being. In addition
to this, process parameter monitoring is necessary to verify that all parts are pro-
duced in the same way. The surveillance approach needs to be capable of moni-
toring process parameters that are changing with time for a highly variable process
like ring rolling. It is based on so called “envelope curves ” deﬁning a corridor of
process variation still leading to conforming properties of the produced part. Parts
produced outside these envelope curves do not necessarily lead to non-conforming
parts but are subject to further investigations. Details of this surveillance approach
are described in [ 3].
The development of the envelope curves is based on process data leading to
conforming parts proven by quali ﬁcation cut-up testing. Based on the process data
of the quali ﬁcation batch, an average curve, the so called master curve, is calcu-
lated. The shape of this master curve is shifted slightly to higher and lower values
deﬁning a corridor of process variability for future batches (Fig. 4). The width of
Fig. 3 Effect of closed loop control on ring growth velocity curve

designed to check the in ﬂuence of process variations (e.g. transfer time, shape
variations of the preform, temperature tolerances of the furnace etc.) on the process
parameter monitoring curves and proven by additional cut up testing. By using this
approach, it is ensured that the corridor de ﬁned by the envelope curves will de ﬁ-
nitely lead to conforming parts.

Envelope curves are typically de ﬁned for process parameters like radial load,
axial load, temperature and ring growth velocity (RGV) (Fig. 5).
All of these measures, the closed loop computer control of the ring mill as well
as the tight process monitoring, result in a very low variation of the process
observable in the ring rolling time, another important process parameter. For
example, the statistical evaluation of the ring rolling time of more than 930 pro-
duced parts showed that 99,73% of the parts only had a variation of ±4,66% from
the average rolling time (Fig. 6).
Results
The standard ring rolling geometry has a rectangular cross section. This can easily
be achieved by the standard set of tools, the main roll and the axial rolls. This
geometry often is used as a pre-shape for subsequent forging operations but it also
could be used to directly machine a component from. By the use of contoured tools,
it is possible to shape the ring rolled part both either on the inner diameter (ID) as
well as on the outer diameter (OD). The use of contoured rings helps to improve the
yield of input material and the necessary tools to produce a contoured ring are much
less expensive compared to the dies necessary to produce a comparable die forged
part. In Fig. 7, an example for a heavily contoured ring rolled parts is presented.
For this study, two geometries were produced, on the one hand a simple ring
with a rectangular cross section and on the other hand an ID-contoured ring
(Fig. 8). Both geometries were manufactured from IN 718.
The standard ring was ring rolled in one reheat while the contoured ring had to
be ring rolled in two reheats. For both variants, the ring rolling process leads to a
ﬁne and homogeneous microstructure (Fig. 9). The achieved grain sizes easily
satisfy the typical grain size requirement for critical rotating engine applications.
Fig. 6 Example for
reproducibility of the process

## Page 988

The ring rolled part with the rectangular cross section made from IN 718 reveals
a homogeneous grain size of ASTM 10 surrounded by a zone with ﬁner mi-
crostructure of ASTM 11. In contrast to this, the center of the contoured ring made
from IN 718 consists of a zone with a grain size of ASTM 9. Also in this case, some
near-surface zones are visible with ﬁner grain sizes up to ASTM 12 in the contoured
area of the part. Most likely, the differences in the grain size mappings are due to
the different process methods used. The splitting of the process into two reheats for
the contoured ring rolling effectively results in a lower amount of strain put into the
center of the part and by this, a coarser microstructure. In contrast, the contoured
area locally gains more strain resulting in a locally ﬁner microstructure.
As an example, in Fig. 10 some light optical photographs of the microstructure
in the center of the parts of both variants are presented. Besides the already

## Page 991

The elevated tensile properties of the two parts made from IN 718 are very
consistent, with no large variation over the different specimen locations and testing
directions observed. It is obvious that the results for yield strength as well as
ultimate tensile strength are slightly higher for the rectangular shaped part com-
pared to the contoured part. The difference is similar for all positions, with an
average value of 20 MPa higher for yield strength and an average value of 10 MPa
higher for ultimate tensile strength. This difference might be explained by the
difference in grain size as previously described. The elongation values for both
variants were very similar at about 25%.
Other mechanical tests like creep, fatigue and crack propagation will be tested on
these parts and will be presented elsewhere.
Conclusion
Ring rolling of rectangular or contoured cross section rings is an ef ﬁcient way to
produce IN 718 engine disks for critical applications. Based on the available
simulation tools and optimized control of the rolling mill, it is possible to produce
ring shaped engine disks without the need of further die forging operations.
Together with a control tool, which allows an online monitoring of the process, the
ring rolling process can be run in very tight boundaries leading to consistent process
parameters and properties in the ring. This successful process can also be expanded
to other Ni-based superalloys.

The Abnormal Dynamic
Recrystallization Behavior
of a Large Alloy 706 Disc
Shuo Huang, Beijiang Zhang, Wenyun Zhang, Guangpu Zhao
and Zhanfu Qi
Abstract The development of equipment and technology makes it possible to
manufacture a Ø2000 mm Alloy 706 disc 800 MN hydraulic press in China.
Generally, high temperature or low strain rate is needed during the closed-die
forging process to lower the requirement for press capacity; however, it will result
in coarse unrecrystallized grains which are not bene ﬁcial for mechanical properties.
In the investigation of hot deformation behavior by thermo-simulation compression
tests in Alloy 706, it is found that abnormal dynamic recrystallization (DRX) be-
havior occurs in a high temperature and low strain rate condition. Electron
backscatter diffraction (EBSD) investigation indicates that the fraction of twin
boundaries in the abnormal microstructure is 80% lower than that in the normal
microstructure, and apparent texture can be detected. Subscale disc forging
experiments were carried out to investigate the effects of abnormal microstructure
on mechanical properties of Alloy 706. The microstructure evolution mechanism of
abnormal DRX is validated and the in ﬂuence on mechanical properties is discussed.
Keywords Alloy 706
⋅ Turbine disc ⋅ Abnormal dynamic recrystallization
Mechanical property

As one of the most important hot section components, the selection of turbine disc
material changes from Cr-Mo-W low-alloying steel to superalloy for higher oper-
ating temperatures. Alloy 706, a derivative of Alloy 718, is used for the large
turbine disc of industrial gas turbines (IGT) due to the good mechanical properties,

ease of fabrication and good machinability [ 1, 2]. The large size and high-quality

[3]. In recent years, China has made progress in the ﬁeld of large superalloy disc
manufacture. As shown in Fig. 1, a Ø2000 mm Alloy 706 turbine disc was integral
die forged successfully by the world largest 800 MN hydraulic press in China.
A triple melting process was used to produce a sound Alloy 706 ingot with a
diameter of 920 mm. Ingot to billet conversion was achieved by a multiple upset
and draw cogging process by an 8000-ton high speed forging hydraulic press.
In order to manufacture an Alloy 706 turbine disc with a diameter larger than
2000 mm, a higher tonnage press is needed. Generally, high temperature or low
strain rate is needed for a forging process to lower the requirement for press
capacity, however, it will result in microstructure with large grains which is not
beneﬁcial for properties [ 3]. In the investigation of hot deformation behavior of
Alloy 706, it is found that high temperature and low strain rate deformation will
result in not only large grains but also grains with abnormal appearance, which is
characterized by the abnormal grain is characterized by texture and curving grain
boundaries [ 4]. It is widely accepted that mechanical properties depend on mi-
crostructure, however, the formation reason for the abnormal microstructure in
Alloy 706 and related effect on mechanical properties are not clear at present.
In present work, the formation mechanism of abnormal grains in Alloy 706 is
investigated by thermo-simulation compression experiment, and the relationship
between the Zener-Hollomon ( Z) parameter and the abnormal microstructure is
established. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) is used to identify grain
boundary character, Taylor factor and texture. Furthermore, the effects of the

abnormal grain on mechanical properties of Alloy 706 are investigated by a sub-
scale forging experiment, which simulates the large turbine disc forging process.
Tensile, rupture and fatigue crack samples were manufactured from the subscale
forging disc to further investigate the effect of abnormal grains on mechanical
properties of Alloy 706. By illustrating the abnormal dynamic recrystallization
mechanism in Alloy 706 and its effects on mechanical properties, guidance can be
given for microstructure control in the manufacture of Alloy 706.
Experimental Procedures
The chemical composition (wt%) of Alloy 706 used in the investigation is as
following: C, 0.02; Ni, 41.0; Cr, 16.0; Al, 0.2; Ti, 1.8; Nb, 2.9; B, 0.004; P, 0.006;
Fe, balance. The processing history consists of vacuum induction melting (VIM),
vacuum arc remelting (VAR), homogenization, cogging to obtain billets with a
diameter of 250 mm for the subscale forging experiment, and hot rolling to obtain
bars with a diameter of 20 mm for the thermo-simulation compression experiment.
The average grain size was measured using the line intercept method and deter-
mined by standard ASTM E112. The grain size of the as-received billet was ASTM
4.0 and the hot rolled bar was ASTM 5.0.
The thermo-simulation compression experiment was conducted on a
Gleeble-3800 thermo-mechanical simulator in a temperature range of 950 –1150 °C
with a strain rate from 0.001 to 1 s
−1. The cylindrical specimens of 10 mm in
diameter and 15 mm in height were deformed to a 60% reduction in height, fol-
lowed by immediate water quenching. Specimens were cut parallel to the com-
pression axis for microstructure observation. EBSD investigation was performed on
JEOL JSM-7800F scanning electron microscope equipped with an Oxford HKL
Nordlys detector.
The subscale disc forging experiment was conducted on a 2000-ton hot die
forging press, with ﬂat dies heated to a temperature of 1000 °C. Cylindrical
specimens with a diameter of 100 and 250 mm in height were forged to a disc with
a diameter of 230 mm and 60 mm in height by two-step upset. The ﬁrst upset was
carried out at temperature of 1100 °C with forging velocity of 20 mm/s and a 50%
reduction in height. The ﬁnal upset forging parameters of the four specimens are
different and summarized in Table 1, followed by immediate oil quenching.

Results and Discussion
Abnormal Dynamic Recrystallization Behavior
Typical normal and abnormal dynamic recrystallization (DRX) microstructure of
Alloy 706 deformed at 1100 °C to a height reduction of 60% with strain rates of 1
and 0.01 s
−1 are shown in Fig. 2, and apparent differences can be detected.
Figure 2a is the microstructure of normal DRX. It is characterized by equiaxed
grains with no preferred orientation. Figure 2b is a typical abnormal DRX mi-
crostructure. The orientation of DRX grains tends to be uniform and texture can be
detected in the 〈001〉 orientation. The maximum value of 〈001〉 texture in abnor-
mal DRX microstructure is double that in the normal DRX microstructure. Ori-
entation imaging microscopy (OIM) in Fig. 2c and d indicates that the fraction of
twin boundaries in abnormal DRX microstructure is much lower than that in normal
DRX microstructure. The twin boundary fraction in normal microstructure is
11.0%, while it is only 2.2% in the abnormal microstructure. Curved grain
boundaries can be detected in abnormal microstructure (Fig. 2d), while in the
normal microstructure the grain boundaries are straight (Fig. 2c). Figure 2e, f are
the Taylor factor distribution maps. The Taylor factor of normal microstructure is
3.01, while the value for abnormal microstructure is relatively lower. Figure 3ai s
the grain boundary misorientation distribution of Alloy 706 deformed at 1100 °C
with strain rate of 0.01 and 0.1 s
−1. It can be found that the fraction of low angle
gain boundaries (<10 °) in sample with a strain rate of 0.01 s −1 is higher than that
with strain rate of 0.1 s −1. Figure 3b is the Taylor factor distribution map for
Fig. 2e, f. The fraction of grains with Taylor factor lower than 3.0 in sample with
strain rate of 0.01 s −1 is apparently higher than that with strain rate of 0.1 s −1.
The formation mechanism of the abnormal DRX microstructure was analyzed by
EBSD. Figure 4 shows the 3D crystal orientation schematic of Alloy 706 deformed
at 1100 °C with a strain rate of 0.01 s −1 to a height reduction of 60%. It can be seen
in Fig. 4b that new grains form by subgrain rotation with a gradual increase of
subgrain misorientation. This phenomenon indicates that subgrain rotation takes
place in the DRX process of Alloy 706 deformed at a high temperature and low strain
rate, which is a typical characteristic of continuous dynamic recrystallization (CDRX).
1016 S. Huang et al.

shown that CDRX occurs in Alloy 718 deformed at 1100 °C with strain rate of
0.1 s
−1, and the CDRX is attributed to re-arrangement of dislocations [ 6, 7].

## Page 997

Generally, the major DRX mechanism in a superalloy is DDRX, which is
characterized with DRX grain nucleation and growth [ 8]. The migration force of a
grain boundary is the dislocation density difference on both sides of the grain
boundary, and a straight grain boundary is the result of minimum surface energy.
However, in high temperature and low strain rate condition, the characteristics of
CDRX can be detected in Alloy 706 as demonstrated in Fig. 4. The nucleation and
growth of DRX grains can occur by subgrain rotation and their new grain
boundaries form by the combination of different grains. As a result, curved grain
boundaries can be detected in the abnormal DRX grains. Curved grain boundaries
are also detected in alloy 617B during low strain rate deformation, and this phe-
nomenon is attributed to the high speed migration of twin boundaries [ 9, 10].
Furthermore, Fig. 2f shows that the fraction of grains with M

Previous study indicates that the DRX behavior of nickel-base superalloys is
inﬂuenced by deformation temperature and strain rate. The in ﬂuence can be well
characterized by the Zener-Hollomon parameter ( Z)[ 6, 8, 13]. The Zener-Hollomon
parameter is the temperature compensated strain rate factor, expressed as Eq. ( 1)
[14]. The value of ln Z can be used to describe the effect of deformation temperature
and strain rate on Alloy 706.

Abnormal DRX in the Subscale Disc Forgings
Based on the result of simulated hot compression tests, subscale disc forgings were
used to con ﬁrm the results of simulated hot compression tests and detect the effect
of abnormal DRX microstructure on mechanical properties. The subscale disc
forgings were carried out using the deformation parameters marked by a rhombus in
Fig. 5 (detail parameter refers to Table 1). Figure 6 is the typical as-forged and
as-heat treated (as-HT) optical microscope (OM) microstructure of the Alloy 706
subscale discs. Figures 7 and 8 are the EBSD microstructure of typical as-forged
and as-HT samples, respectively. The quantitative statistical results of OM and
EBSD are summarized in Table 2. Texture can be detected in the Alloy 706 disc
deformed at 1100 °C with a strain rate of 0.008 s
−1 as shown in Fig. 7a. As
discussed in Fig. 2b, f, apparent recrystallization texture and lower M T can be
found in Alloy 706 deformed with similar conditions in the compression test;
however, the texture is not very apparent in the subscale disc compared with the
compression samples. This is mainly due to the lower cooling speed and larger size
of the subscale disc, hence, metadynamic recrystallization can take place in the
cooling process [ 8, 13]. Furthermore, texture is not found in the subscale disc
deformed at the higher strain rate (0.17 s
−1) as shown in Fig. 7b. The comparison
of Fig. 7e, f shows that the M T value of Alloy 706 disc forged with a strain rate of
0.008 s −1 is lower than that forged with a strain of 0.17 s −1. Although the abnormal
DRX microstructure in the subscale disc is not as apparent as that in simulated hot
compression tests, the microstructure evolution trend is similar.
Figure 6 shows that for subscale disc deformed at 1100 °C the DRX fraction and
DRX grain size decrease with decreasing strain rate. The average grain size and
fraction of twin boundaries decreases with decreasing strain rate after heat treatment
as demonstrated in Table 2, but coarse unrecrystallized (unRX) grains can be
detected in the high temperature and low strain rate condition, and the as large as
(ALA) grain size increases with decreasing strain rate. Hence, it can be concluded
that the abnormal microstructure left by deformation can transfer into coarse grain
structure during heat treatment. The as-forged DRX grain size in samples 12 and 22
are comparable, but the as-HT grain size of the former one is slightly smaller than
the latter one. This can be attributed to the difference in the DRX mechanism. The
nucleation and growth force of DDRX is the difference of dislocation density on
both sides of grain boundaries, while the force of CDRX is the misorientation on
both sides for dislocation cells [ 7]. In high temperature and low strain rate defor-
mation, the CDRX mechanism is more active and the driving force for grain
boundary migration is lower than that of DDRX. Previous study shows that twin
boundaries mainly come into formation by grain boundary migration during hot
deformation in nickel-base superalloys [ 15]. The fraction of twin boundaries in

Effects of Abnormal DRX Microstructure on Mechanical
Properties
In order to determine the effects of abnormal DRX microstructure on the me-
chanical properties of Alloy 706 and provide reference for microstructure and
mechanical property control of large gas turbine discs, tensile, rupture and FCGR
properties of subscale disc forgings after heat treatment were investigated. There is
no apparent difference in RT tensile property of Alloy 706 forged by different strain
rates, but strain rate does show some differences in the 650 °C tensile strengths. The
650 °C tensile strength increases ﬁrst and then decreases with increasing strain rate,
and the variation in yield strength is even more apparent. The yield strength of the
disc deformed with a strain rate of 0.008 s
−1 is 50 MPa lower than that deformed
with a strain rate of 0.04 s −1. In addition, the tensile strength for the disc forged at
1050 °C with a strain rate of 0.04 s −1 is slightly lower than that forged at 1100 °C,
especially the yield strength. This is related to the difference in grain size after heat
treatment. According to the Hall-Petch relationship, the smaller the grain size, the
higher the strength [ 17]. The average grain size of sample 12 characterized with
abnormal DRX microstructure is slightly smaller, hence the tensile strength is
higher. However, the 650 °C yield strength of sample 13 deformed at 1100 °C with
a strain rate of 0.008 s
−1 is apparently low, which is related with the coarse unRX
grains.
Figure 9c, d shows the rupture life and ductility of Alloy 706 tested at 650 °C at
690 MPa. The rupture life and ductility of discs forged at 1100 °C decrease slightly
with increasing strain rate. For discs forged with a strain rate of 0.04 s −1, the
rupture life and ductility for the one forged at 1050 °C is slightly lower than that at
1100 °C. However, it should be pointed out that there is a great amount of variation
in rupture life and ductility for the disc forged at 1100 °C with a strain rate of
0.008 s
−1. The rupture fracture morphology shows that cracks propagate along
grain boundaries for Alloy 706 under constant stress as reported before [ 18]. Fig-
ure 8 is the typical rupture fracture morphology. Apparent coarse unRX grains can
be detected in the fracture surface on samples forged at 1100 °C with a strain rate of
0.008 s −1 as shown in Fig. 10a. The primary and secondary cracks both propagate
along grain boundaries (Fig. 10c). Hence, coarse unRX grains are bene ﬁcial for
rupture life, since there are less grain boundaries to serve as propagation paths for
cracks; however, the appearance of coarse unRX grains during the propagation of
cracks is random, causing variation in rupture properties at high temperature and
low strain rate conditions. The comparison in Fig. 11 further con ﬁrms that

Previous study shows that coarse grains can provide a long slip length for cyclic
strain localization, resulting in a large initial crack that can more easily propagate to
failure [24]. In present work, in high ΔK condition ( ≥ 40), cracks tend to propagate
transgranularly through coarse unRX grains in Alloy 706 (Fig. 13a). This results in
the increase of FCGR in Fig. 12a. Substructures are still left in such coarse unRX
grains after heat treatment with higher M
T value as shown in Fig. 8c. The coor-
dinate deformation ability of such grains are poor and secondary cracks can easily
form. The initiation of secondary cracks can eliminate stress concentrations and
lower the propagation rate of the main crack. Hence, the variation highlighted in
Fig. 12a.
It can be concluded from the above results and discussion that abnormal DRX
grains can be detected in Alloy 706 forged in high temperature and low strain rate
conditions. Such DRX grains are characterized by curved grain boundaries and
texture, which will lead to increased variation in mechanical properties. This
variation is not bene ﬁcial for the manufacture of high quality Alloy 706 discs.
Conclusions
Thermal simulation tests were carried out to study the microstructure characteris-
tics, mechanism and formation of abnormal grain structure in Alloy 706. Further-
more, subscale discs were manufactured to investigate the effect of forging
conditions on mechanical properties. The main conclusions based on these exper-
iments and analyses can be summarized as follows:
(1) Abnormal DRX of Alloy 706 mainly occurs in high temperature and low strain
rate conditions, at which the CDRX mechanism is more active. The fraction of
twin boundaries and the Taylor factor of abnormal DRX are lower than those of
normal DRX. Texture comes into formation under such deformation conditions
by subgrain rotation along the preferential orientation.
(2) Coarse unRX grains cannot be eliminated suf ﬁciently after heat treatment of
abnormal DRX microstructures. Such microstructure is not bene ﬁcial for
650 °C tensile strength and FCGR properties, and can lead to increased vari-
ation in mechanical properties.

Introduction
Superalloys are commonly used in jet engines due to their high temperature stability
of the microstructure and good mechanical properties [ 1]. Like others superalloys,
the processing of Allvac
® 718Plus™ alloy (herein referred as 718Plus), either hot
working and heat treatment of a wrought product, or solidi ﬁcation and heat treat-
ment of the cast product, has to be carefully controlled in order to generate a
required microstructure and therefore the expected mechanical properties. 718Plus
is a nickel-based superalloy developed in the late 1990s with aim to increase
temperature capability over the popular alloy 718. It is a high strength, corrosion
resistant alloy with a 55 °C temperature advantage over alloy 718, while retaining
the excellent weldability and processing characteristics of this alloy. During the
design of a new 718Plus superalloy, ATI Allvac ( Allegheny Technologies Incor-
porated Allvac, Monroe, NC, USA ) made signi ﬁcant changes to the chemistry of
718 to eliminate the unstable γ″-phase (Ni
3Nb, D022 tetragonal) [2–5] and promote
the formation of a more stable γ′-phase (Ni 3Al/Ti, L 12 cubic) [ 6–8]. The main
differences in chemistry between 718 and 718Plus are the addition of Co, lower
concentration of Fe, and decreased Ti to Al ratio. The combination of different
chemistry and heat treatment resulted in elimination of the γ″-phase and instead
precipitation of the γ′ and δ or η phases. The 718Plus microstructure consists of a γ
matrix (Ni-based solid solution) with ordered face centred cubic γ′-Ni
3(Al,Ti)
(Ni3Al/Ti, L 12, cubic, Pm3m) strengthening precipitates, and orthorhombic δ-
Ni3Nb (Ni 3Nb, D0a, orthorhombic, Pmmn) and hexagonal η-Ni3Ti, η*-Ni6AlNb or
Ni6(Al,Ti)Nb (Ni3Nb0.5(Al/Ti)0.5,D 024, hexagonal, P63/mmc) particles precipitated
at the grain boundaries and in the interdendritic regions [ 9–12].
The development of 718Plus started with development of the wrought form of
the alloy, and several years later the development of the cast version of the alloy
was initiated. The grain boundary precipitation of η-phase is critical for effective
1036 A. Kruk et al.

## Page 1014

grain boundary pinning in subsolvus forging, and is essential to improve alloy ’s
resistance to intergranular failure. The η population initially forms during the ﬁrst
stages of the manufacturing process, either solidi ﬁcation or forging, and subse-
quently evolves during heat treatment. The precipitates often occur in plate colonies
in a Blackburn orientation relationship {111} γ || {001} η with one of the adjacent
grains, and then grow in a disc-like morphology on the {111} γ matrix planes
towards the grain interior [ 9, 13] (references 9 and 13 listed are Rolls-Royce/
Cambridge efforts). The control of the η-phase content and structure during forging
deﬁnes the customization of the ﬁnal microstructure. The Laves phase, on the other
hand, may form in the interdendritic regions during solidi ﬁcation, welding, or after
high temperature exposure for long periods of time. This phase, and other topo-
logically close-packed phases, are potentially detrimental and can lead to premature
failure of critical components if they occur in signi ﬁcant volume fractions such as to
cause the depletion of solute atoms which otherwise aid solid solution strengthening
[14–18]. Therefore processing of 718Plus has to be carefully controlled to generate
a desirable microstructure and therefore the required mechanical properties.
Concurrently, the development of high ﬁdelity material property requires
application of innovative methods and advanced characterization techniques to
accurately evaluate the microstructure, and lately the three-dimensional information
on the distribution of phases, grains or extrinsic defects is of a greater interest.
Modern and relatively new in material science imaging techniques such electron
tomography (in SEM and TEM) allow today for acquisition of this information in
appropriate three-dimensional representative volume elements [ 19, 20], and further
augment a 3D polycrystalline modeling such as crystal plasticity. The TEM electron
tomography reconstruction involves four steps [ 21]:
(1) Recording: A specimen is systematically tilted in the microscope to different
angles in the range of ±75° using a special tomographic holder and series of 2D
projections (images) of the specimen are semi-automatically recorded using
dedicated software (e.g. Explore 3D software, FEI). The registered image
contrast must be a projection of some physical characteristic of the sample, e.g.
its mass/electron density (Z-contrast). One of the newer imaging methods is
STEM X-ray spectroscopic imaging (STEM-EDX), that enables the mapping of
local concentrations of selected chemical elements.
(2) Registering: Individual images are aligned using Inspect 3D (FEI) software
(off-line processing) to a common tilt axis origin.
(3) Reconstruction: The Fourier slice theorem is the basic underlying principle of
3D tomographic reconstruction; some methods used for reconstructions are:
Back Projected method (BP), Direct Fourier method (DF) and the Filtered Back
Projection method (WBP), the last two are two of the most used heuristics for
tomographic reconstruction.
(4) Viewing: 3D visualization and metrology of reconstructed volume of the
sample.
Application of Analytical Electron Microscopy … 1037

## Page 1015

The Focused Ion Beam (FIB) in conjunction with SEM has become an important
tool in materials science for studying structure of materials at the micro- and
nanometer scale. FIB-SEM tomography is based on a serial slicing and imaging
technique employing a FIB-SEM dual beam workstation. Dual-beam SEM enables
the acquisition of serial images with small (few nanometers) and reproducible
spacing between the single imaging planes. In many FIB-SEM devices no
mechanical stage tilting is necessary between the FIB milling and the electron beam
(SEM) imaging steps. Application of computer software for experimental raw data
stack processing (e.g. ImageJ 1.45b [ 22]) and graphics packages (e.g. Amira 5.4.1)
for 3D visualization allows for obtaining both qualitative and quantitative infor-
mation about reconstructed volume. It is possible to study features at spatial res-
olutions at the level of tens of nanometers and volumes up to tens of cube microns.
The detailed 3D visualization of 718Plus has not been reported yet. The
objective of this study was to apply electron STEM-EDX and FIB-SEM tomog-
raphy techniques to perform 3D imaging and metrology of the strengthening par-
ticles in 718Plus superalloy in the wrought and cast condition. Electron microscopy
(SEM, TEM, STEM) and EDX spectroscopy were used to reveal details of the
superalloy micro- and nanostructure as well as chemical composition of phases.
Experimental Procedure
Material
The wrought 718Plus was a commercial stock with standard chemical composition
of Ni-18Cr-10Fe-9Co-5.5(Nb+Ta)-1W-2.7Mo-0.7Ti-1.5Al-0.02C (nominal, wt%)
produced by means of vacuum induction melting and vacuum arc remelting fol-
lowed by GFM rotary forging and ring rolling. The stock was subject to a standard
heat treatment after ring rolling: solution at 968 °C for 1 h followed by two-step
ageing 788 °C/8 h + 704 °C/8 h.
The cast version of the alloy has been cast and heat treated in the lab-scale
furnaces. The chemical composition of the cast version of the alloy was the typical
tuned-up composition of Ni-18Cr-9Fe-9Co-6.5Nb(0Ta)-1W-2.7Mo-0.7Ti-
1.5Al-0.2C (nominal, wt%). Heat treatment included homogenization at 1120 °C
for 4 h, followed by an extensive solution cycle at 968 °C for 10 h.
Microstructural Characterization Methods
Microstructural investigation utilized a two-step approach: (1) a conventional light
microscopy (LM) as well as scanning- and transmission electron microscopy (SEM,
TEM, respectively) imaging and energy dispersive X-ray (EDX) spectroscopy.
1038 A. Kruk et al.

## Page 1016

TEM analyses included bright- and dark- ﬁeld imaging (BF, DF, respectively),
selected area electron diffraction (SAED) and high resolution TEM (HRTEM) and
(2) a novel tomography technique to obtain 3D imaging of precipitates in 718Plus
microstructure utilizing TEM and FIB-SEM tomography.
SEM images were acquired using Merlin Gemini II (ZEISS) microscope. The
TEM study was conducted on the lamella prepared by FIB (NEON CrossBeam
40EsB) using a probe Cs-corrected Titan
3 G2 60-300 with ChemiSTEM ™ system
with Super-X EDX detector. This EDX detection system, which was also used in
electron tomography, allowed to achieve high level of X-ray signal over a large tilt
angle of sample and collect series of 2D elemental maps in the angular range from
−60° to +60° with a step of 4°. Pre-processing and alignment of image tilt series
were performed using TomoJ 2.12 software. Tomographic reconstruction of a tilt
series of 31 images (elemental maps) was performed using Simultaneous Iterative
Reconstruction Technique (SIRT) method with number of iteration equal 12, which
allowed visualizing the three-dimensional distribution of selected elements (Al, Cr)
in the analysed volume. Identi ﬁcations of phases were performed using TEM-
SAED method assisted by JEMS computer software [ 23].
The specimens for the FIB-SEM 3D tomography were prepared by FIB (NEON
CrossBeam 40EsB) with Ga-ion beam at parameters: 30 kV, 1 nA, aperture of
30 µm and 54° angle between the electron and the ion beam. The region of interest
(ROI) of the sample ’s surface was selected by SEM imaging. The Pt protective
layer was deposited on the sample top surface, in order to prevent the occurrence of
the curtaining effect, i.e., the irregular removal of material.
Consequently, the acquired stack of images (typical parameters: image size
1024 × 768 pixels, 599 images in 8-bit grayscale, stack size 462 MB) was
transformed directly into a 3D data volume with a voxel size of 18 × 18 × 36
nm. Repeated removal of layers as thin as a 36 nm allowed exploring a total volume
of 10.5 × 9.5 × 5.9 μm (V = 588.5 μm
3). Few reconstructions were acquired
with different parameters and these are provided when discussing the results of the
study. The shift in lateral direction between consecutive recording images due to
mechanical drift of the specimen was calculated and subsequently corrected with
the ImageJA 1.45b software, the 3D reconstruction was performed by Avizo Fire
6.3 software. In order to object segmentation “labelling by reconstruction ” tech-
nique based on the “neighbourhood-algorithm” was used. Voxels with the same and
similar grey level were attributed to one object, so as the result different objects
were marked with different colors. It has to be noted that each viewing can be
accompanied with a 3D movie, which for obvious reasons cannot be presented in
the paper.

Results and Discussion
Wrought 718Plus
A typical microstructure of the wrought 718Plus is shown in Fig. 1. It may be
observed in Fig. 1a, b that the alloy ’s γ matrix is heavily decorated with
non-uniformly distributed precipitates of η-like platelets. The γ matrix contains
uniformly distributed, nearly spherical γ′-phase precipitates (Fig. 1c, d). The TEM
analysis veri ﬁed that the strengthening precipitates are ordered face centred cubic
γ′-phase precipitates, and that the η-like platelets are η-phase particles of hexagonal
crystal structure (Fig. 2). The lamellar η-phase precipitated were recorded inside the
γ grain (Fig. 2a) and along the γ grain boundary (Fig. 2b). Further, the complex
nature of lamellar η-phase precipitates manifested by contrast difference can be
clearly seen in Fig. 2c, d. It is likely the η-phase precipitates have embedded
thin-plates of another phase within individual parent particle.

## Page 1024

Conclusions
Conventional (LM, SEM, TEM) and novel characterization techniques such (TEM
and FIB-SEM tomography) were used for characterization in detail of wrought and
cast 718Plus superalloy down to the atomic scale. The major conclusions of this
study are:
• γ′-phase and η-phase precipitates are present in both wrought and cast version of
the alloy. The as-cast alloy in addition contains Laves phase eutectics as well as
(Nb,Ti) carbides and/or carbonitrides.
• η-phase morphology in the wrought alloy exhibits a complex geometry of
particles aligned along the grain boundaries and as lamellar precipitates inside
Fig. 8 Results of the analysis of η-phase precipitate by electron diffraction: a η-phase lamellar
precipitates in the γ matrix, circle indicates the area subject to further analysis, TEM-BF, b SAED
pattern taken from the circled area in ( a), c, d the experimental SAED patterns with superimposed
diffraction patterns calculated for γ and η phases, respectively
Application of Analytical Electron Microscopy … 1047

## Page 1025

the γ grains. Plate-shaped precipitates were identi ﬁed as Ni 3Ti D0 24 with
chemical composition similar to Ni 6(AlTi)Nb. Some of them were composed of
nano-size thin plates of δ-phase interchangeably inserted into the parent plate.
• 3D reconstruction of γ′-phase using STEM-EDX or FIB-SEM tomography
techniques resulted of similar measurements of volume fraction (V v)o f γ′ phase
in wrought alloy: 12.5% and 11.9%, respectively.
• η-phase particles present in the interdendritic areas in as-cast 718Plus are
composed of a single η-phase. These ﬂat surface plate-like particles are stacked
in colonies in three orientations. Their precipitation is often initiated at the
interface of the Laves phase with the γ matrix.
• In comparison to conventional electron microscopy, electron tomography
techniques permit to obtain complementary information about precipitates size,
shape and 3D distribution in the reconstructed volume with resolution of tens of
nanometers.

Computed Tomography
as an Alternative Method to Measure
Crack Growth in Non-conventional
Geometries
Adrian Loghin, Vipul Gupta, Anjali Singhal and Al Cerrone
Abstract The computed tomography (CT) application presented herein aims at
measuring cracks three dimensionally in a non-traditional fracture mechanics
Superalloy 718 specimen exposed to supercritical CO
2 (sCO2). Superalloy 718 is
one material of choice for manufacturing components for Concentrated Solar Plant
(CSP) units using sCO 2 power cycle. To quantify the low cycle fatigue (LCF) ca-
pability of the Superalloy 718 material exposed to sCO 2, at 550 °C, 200 bar internal
pressure, hollow tensile specimens were designed and LCF experiments at different
loading levels were conducted. The same hollow specimen was considered to
monitor fatigue crack growth (FCG) while the crack surface is exposed to sCO
2
environment. By interrupting the LCF test procedure and conducting ex situ vol-
umetric CT scans, the location, size and shape of several cracks were identi ﬁed and,
incremental crack advancement was measured.
Keywords Crack growth
⋅ Fracture ⋅ Supercritical CO 2 ⋅ Computed
tomography ⋅ Superalloy 718 ⋅ Unconventional specimen ⋅ LCF
Introduction
From early 1960s [ 1] fatigue crack growth rate was measured on different materials,
using different specimen geometries, in various test conditions (loading levels,
temperature, exposure to different environments or in vacuum etc.), in the purpose
to provide supporting material data for component life assessment using damage
tolerant design framework [ 2]. A very recent review on fatigue crack growth rate
measurement provided by McKeight [ 3], covers fatigue crack growth measurement
techniques across 50 years of development. Along with fatigue crack growth

## Page 1029

measurement standardized into ASTM 647 [ 4], modeling techniques and software
packages were developed to support damage tolerant design at component level
[5–7].
In this study a non-typical specimen geometry, hollow round bar, was used to
study fatigue crack growth behavior in Superalloy 718 at 550 °C and exposed along
the inner bore to sCO
2 at 20 MPa. The specimen was adopted from a study [ 8]
where low cycle capability of Superalloy 718 was quanti ﬁed. It is typical in FCG
measurements to machine notches [ 9] in the specimen that can serve as crack
initiation sites. Once initiated, these cracks are monitored using different methods
(optical, direct current potential drop, compliance change) [ 1] to establish material
properties (FCGR) necessary for design purposes. Similar to [ 9] where micro
notches were machined using EDM (Electro-discharge machining) on the specimen
outer surface, in our study the micro notches were machined along the inner bore of
the specimen to further expose nucleated cracks to sCO
2 environment. Tradition-
ally, to quantify crack size during test procedure [ 4, 10], direct current potential
drop (DCPD) technique is used as long there is access to the crack location. Due to
lack of access along the inner bore of the specimen to the micro notch site, DCPD
technique could not be used for the hollow specimen and therefore an alternative
technique was considered, volumetric Computed Tomography, to measure
non-destructively crack size and shape during an interrupted test procedure.
In the past, Computed Tomography has been used to quantify damage size on
composite specimens [ 11]. More recently, using similar equipment with the one
reported in this study, in situ CT was developed to measure delaminations and crack
occurrence in textile composites [ 12] followed by 3D reconstruction. Performing
volumetric CT measurement on metallic materials is a more dif ﬁcult task due to
higher density of the material (in comparison to composite materials). CT technique
was applied to assess crack size and orientation in steel rail heads [ 13] and, in
powder metallurgy Ni base superalloys, to quantify discontinuity content [ 14] and
to study the effects of oxidation on fatigue crack propagation rate [ 15].
Experimental Procedure
For fatigue testing in controlled environment relevant to component-level test
conditions (e.g., high temperature and high pressure), a hollow round bar and
ﬁxture-design were employed [ 8]. This specimen geometry allows exposure of
supercritical CO 2 (sCO2) environment, at 20 MPa pressure, to the internal passage
of the specimen, while permitting induction heating of the outer diameter (OD) of
the specimen, at 550 °C. Note that, given the elevated pressures required to simulate
service conditions, the proposed test cannot be considered uniaxial. The same
specimen geometry was reused for fatigue crack growth measurements by forcing
the crack initiation along the inner bore using EDM micro notches.
Fatigue crack growth tests were conducted in a 20-kip servo-hydraulic test
frame, equipped with an induction heating unit for specimen temperature control,
1052 A. Loghin et al.

## Page 1030

and a pressure vessel capable of converting liquid CO 2 to sCO 2. Supercritical CO 2
is delivered to the internal cavity of the specimen at the desired pressure. A high
temperature capable extensometer, consisting of two alumina rods, was used to
measure the displacement change across the specimen ’s gauge, which also reported
the strain in the gauge section. The loading procedure was accommodated to use
different stress ratios, frequencies and maximum loads during the experiment to
imprint different morphologies on the crack surface and use post-mortem fractog-
raphy to assess crack size during the testing process. In parallel to post-mortem
fractography analysis, volumetric CT was considered to measure crack size and
shape by interrupting the test procedure.
In the preliminary work to evaluate the application of CT technique on the
Superalloy 718 LCF un-notched hollow bar, a benchmark study was performed at
the European Synchrotron Research Facility (ESRF). The ﬁrst ex situ CT mea-
surement at ESRF was conducted on a specimen that sustained 15,000 LCF cycles
at sCO
2 exposure of 200 bar, 550 °C and strain range of 0.7%. The CT scan
conducted with a ﬁeld of view (FOV) of 12.9 × 3.5 mm and resolution of 3.4 μm
in the specimen ’s gage section. The initial conclusion was that no damage was
identiﬁed in this measurement. Additional testing was performed to reach a total of
23,000 cycles and, this time, CT measurement indicated presence of a crack.
Location (outer bore) and shape of the crack in the gage section observed optically
after 23,000 cycles is shown in Fig. 1 along with the similar view of the X-ray
tomography volume reconstruction.
Performing ex situ CT measurement for several specimens at ESRF is not
realistic due to the associated cost and duration. In-house CT machine (V|tome|x
M300) was considered to pursue further this novel alternative way to measure three

To address feasibility of using lab equipment to identify cracks in the Superalloy

Having the crack initiated at the outer bore of the specimen helped validating the

2 environment.
Electro-discharge machining was considered to create micro notches along the inner
bore of the hollow specimen. The notches act as stress concentrators and increase
the probability of crack nucleation (followed by the crack propagation process) at
these speci ﬁc sites which are exposed to sCO
2. Also, damage monitoring (crack
size and shape) is more ef ﬁcient since the location is known apriori to the test
procedure.
Five specimens (718-14, 718-32, 718-23, 718-33 and 718-24) were considered
to undergo the EDM procedure and have micro notches along the inner bore of the
gage section. Due to space limitation, only three specimens are discussed herein:
718-32, 718-23 and 718-24.
A special electrode was manufactured to remove a low volume of material at one
or more locations and create the notches along the inner bore of each specimen. The
designed locations are shown in Fig. 3. For three specimens, 718-14, 718-32,
718-23 (10.16 mm outer diameter, 4.06 mm inner diameter gauge section) four
notches were machined along the inner bore of the specimen, 90° apart. The intent
