Computed Tomography Measurement and Segmentation
All specimens (gauge section only) were imaged using the microfocus tube of the
V|tome|x M 300, made by GE Inspection Technologies [ 16]. The samples were
imaged using an accelerating voltage of 250 kV and ﬁlament current of 180 μA.
The sample was exposed for 0.3 s for each 2D frame; a total of 7 frames were
acquired for each angular projection, equaling an exposure of 2.3 s for a 2D pro-
jection. The total time taken to image one sample was 45 min, for a full 360°
rotation. The images were reconstructed with GE ’s proprietary software Datos [ 17]
with a beam hardening correction factor of 7 and inline median ﬁlter.
Segmentation of cracks from the matrix was conducted with a trainable random
forest classi ﬁer from the Waikato Environment for Knowledge Analysis (WEKA)
exposed in the image processing environment Fiji (Fiji is just ImageJ) [ 18]. This
segmentation technique is particularly adept at discriminating noise from salient
features. Moreover, given that the classi ﬁer operates on the full 3D stack and not on
individual slices, persistence of salient features across adjacent slices is maintained.
In the CT image slices, air (including space between crack faces) presents as
relatively dark clusters of pixels emanating from the notches, Fig. 2. The matrix
presents as considerably lighter clusters of pixels. The segmentation process begins
with training— pixels belonging to both air and matrix were input into the classi ﬁer.
The classi ﬁer was then applied to stacks of images containing the notches. The
Fig. 4 Pictorial representation of the sample set up in front of the X-ray tube

result was a binary classi ﬁcation of the region surrounding each notch. Thereafter,
each classi ﬁed stack that contained pixels classi ﬁed as air was converted into a
VTK rectilinear grid and subsequently visualized in ParaView [ 19] (Fig. 4).
Discussion: Specimen 718-32
Specimen 718-32 was tested initially for 13,800 cycles, at 20 MPa internal pressure,
550 °C, frequency of 10 Hz, load controlled conditions at 64.5 kN maximum load (R
ratio = 0.05). Figure 5 provides images from the CT scan prior to the test procedure
to conﬁrm existence of the notch along the inner bore on 718-32. It is worthwhile to
mention that the images in Fig. 5 are typical to all the notches machined in the
specimens under this development and all specimens underwent CT scanning to
conﬁrm existence on the notches along with size and location measurement. After
13,800 cycles, the test procedure was interrupted and the scan identi ﬁed four cracks,
one at each of the four micro notch locations. Figure 6 provides cross-sections
through gage section volume at the notch locations where cracking occurs. This data
shows that the proposed procedure can be used to measure non-destructively crack
sizes in Ni base alloys using lab equipment. After ﬁrst test procedure, the specimen
was tested for two more sequences (1500 followed by 1000 additional cycles) at a
lower maximum load of 22.24 kN (5000 lbf). Very limited additional growth was
observed in the CT measurement (Fig. 7) which can be related to crack closure due
to modifying maximum load from 64.5 kN (14,500 lbf) to 22.24 kN. The fourth and
the last test sequence of 898 cycles was conducted at a max load of 64.5 kN and a
stress R ratio of 0.5. The fourth cycle block breaks the specimen.
As shown in Figs. 6 and 7, all the four cracks initiated at the notches were
identiﬁed by the Computed Tomography scan. This was a very important accom-
plishment because it provided the opportunity to attempt measuring the crack
growth (consecutive crack increments) under a given load while having the crack
exposed to sCO
2. The specimen failed from the largest crack (based on CT mea-
surement) as expected, since it should carry the largest stress intensity factor range.
Post failure fractography of 718-32 indicates similar beach marks as the crack
measured by the volumetric CT technique. A comparison between the CT slice at
notch #4 and crack surface is provided in Fig. 8. The optical image validates that
CT captures correctly the crack shape and location. First visible beach mark (dis-
cussed below) corresponds well with crack front imaged by CT method. The limit
of crack advancement for rest of the stable fatigue life is highlighted with dashed
line, after which fast fracture occurred.
The characteristic features seen on the fracture surface (in Fig. 8b, c),
thumbnail-shaped curved lines, are known as beach marks or arrest lines. These
beach marks can be related in their density and width to the applied stress level and
number of cycles, and should not be confused with striations. Thus, each beach
mark denotes a single or more blocks of cycles, not a single cycle, and marks
progressive stages of crack propagation. Also, note that beach marks are

macroscopic fatigue features that can be seen on low magni ﬁcation optical image
(Fig. 8b), while striations are microscopic in nature and can be seen only at high
magniﬁcations with the aid of high-resolution scanning electron microscopy
(SEM). In the current work, the beach marks are produced by changes in crack
growth rates when fatigue is applied in blocks of cycles (i.e. test interruptions).
Each loading block produced a total fatigue crack extension that can be seen in
optical and SEM images above. It was also expected that the beach marks will be
produced by other factors than simple changes in crack growth rates during
propagation, such as by oxidation of the free surface depending on time of expo-
sure, sCO
2 temperature, and loads spectra (R-ratio, frequency, etc.). This is evident
as darker area in back scatter SEM image in Fig. 8c, where crack growth appeared
to be slower (i.e. more time for oxidation), compared to brighter area where crack
might have grown at faster rates leading to ﬁnal fracture. In some of the tests and
loading blocks, it was observed that many fatigue fractures produced under con-

The crack surface was further analyzed to identify all eventual beach marks.
A depth measurement for a total of six indications was carried out (Fig. 11). To
understand the relationship between beach mark indications and test procedure, a

Recorded beach mark measurements and the assumed corresponding cycles were
collected to evaluate the fatigue crack growth rate under sCO
2, at 550 °C. To

(considering the depth notch) was propagated to a size of 2.42 mm using 3DFAS

ratio of 0.5. Calibrated 3D model prediction (crack depth vs. cycles) along with
beach mark data is provided in Fig. 15.

Summary
In this study, a non-traditional fracture mechanics specimen was used to evaluate
fatigue crack growth of alloy 718 exposed to sCO
2. A hollow bar used previously in
LCF testing was adapted to a fatigue crack growth experiment by introducing
electro-discharge notches along the inner bore of the specimen to control crack
initiation process and expose eventual cracks to sCO 2 environment. Volumetric

Development of New Alloy 718
with Super Machinability
Chihiro Furusho, Yuya Kousai, Mototsugu Osaki and Koichi Uno
Abstract Alloy 718 has been applied in a lot of applications such as aerospace,
power generation plant, automobile and Oil & Gas. Most products of Alloy 718 are
ﬁnally produced by machining process because there are a lot of complex product
shapes. Therefore, improvement of the machinability can contribute to the manu-
facturability. One of the important factors for the machinability is large carbide
because carbide has very high hardness. Distribution and size of carbides strongly
inﬂuence on cutting tool life. New developed Alloy 718 has low carbon content to
suppress the formation of NbC type carbides. Developed alloy extremely improves
turning tool life in comparison with conventional Alloy 718. Moreover, developed
alloy satis ﬁes chemical compositions and mechanical properties of AMS 5663N
and API 6ACRA.
Keywords Nickel-iron alloy
⋅ Machinability ⋅ Cutting ⋅ Carbide
Abrasive wear
Introduction
Alloy 718 is one of the most popular nickel based super alloys and is an essential
material in many industries such as aerospace, power generation, automobile and
oil & gas because of its great high temperature strength and high corrosion resis-
tance properties. That ’s why various shaped Alloy 718 products have been required
all over the world. In general, Alloy 718 is subjected to a predetermined heat
treatment and then processed into a required shape by cutting. Hence, machinability
of Alloy 718 is an important factor for low cost processing.

## Page 1051

However, cutting property of Alloy 718 is much poorer than that of most carbon
steels because of its high strength, low thermal conductivity and some other reasons
as shown in Fig. 1 [1]. The poverty of machinability can cause degrading pre-
ciseness and productivity, so that improvement of machining process for Alloy 718
has been attempted by various approaches. For examples, Itakura et al. [ 2] and
Sugino et al. [ 3] reported high pressure coolant can extend tool life owing to forced
cooling cutting temperature. Takeyama et al. [ 4] reported adaptability of tool
materials; CBN tools are well applicable to machining Alloy 718 because of its high
heat resistance and high wear resistance property. Ezugwu et al. [ 5] introduced the
prediction technology of relationship between cutting condition and process
parameter by using arti ﬁcial neural network, in order to optimise cutting process.
On the other hand, introduction of metallurgical modi ﬁcation for good machin-
ability has not been performed suf ﬁciently. Alloy 718 contains MC type carbide
which has high hardness as shown in Fig. 2 [6], so that the carbides can be abrasive
particles and can degrade machinability of Alloy 718. In this study, improvement
effect on cutting property of Alloy 718 owing to the reduction of carbides was
veriﬁed from microstructural point of view, and we introduce our new Alloy 718
with super machinability.
Experimental Procedure
Two kinds of Alloy 718 which contain different amount of carbon respectively were
used in this study. The chemical compositions of both alloys are listed in Table 1.
Alloy A is conventional Alloy 718 and Alloy B is developed Alloy 718 with super
machinability. At ﬁrst, 2.2 tons of ingots were prepared by double melting. The ﬁrst
melting was conducted by Vacuum Induction Melting (VIM), and the second one
was done by Vacuum Arc Remelting (VAR). After that, these ingots were
homogenized and hot forged into columnar bars with a diameter of 100 mm, fol-
lowed by the solution treatment and the two-step aging treatment were performed.
The solution treatment condition is at 1248 K for 7200 s then water cooled to room

Discussion
Figure 10 shows the relationship between cutting temperature and factors of tool
wear. Tool wear pattern changes as raising cutting temperature and total amount of
tool wear drastically increases above the temperature at which diffusive wear
becomes dominant [ 1, 10]. Thermal conductivity value of Ni based super alloys is
notably lower than that of carbon steels, so that temperature during cutting Ni based
super alloys rises easily. Therefore high speed cutting process cause severe tool
wear in short span, as shown in Figs. 7b and 9. It is dif ﬁcult to change the value of
thermal conductivity of Alloy 718 by adjusting its minor components or controlling
its micro structure because thermal conductivity value mainly depends on its
principal components such as Fe and Ni. Consequently, reducing the cutting
temperature has been attempted from processing point of view represented by high

## Page 1063

Development of Ni-Base Disk Alloy
for Large-Size Gas Turbines
by Improving Macrosegregation
Property of Alloy 718
T. Shibayama, J. Sato, N. Sato, T. Nonomura, E. Shimohira,
T. Uehara and S. Imano
Abstract Alloy 718, a high-strength Ni-base superalloy, is used for the gas turbine
disks of aircraft engines and thermal power generation plants. However,
macrosegregation defects often form in larger ingots, making it dif ﬁcult to apply
Alloy 718 to large-size industrial gas turbine disks. In order to improve the
macrosegregation properties of Alloy 718, the chemical composition was modi ﬁed
using calculated phase diagrams. The macrosegregation defect type of Alloy 718 is
a sinking type. According to the difference in density, Δρ, calculated using the
Scheil-Gulliver equation, it is found that W, which contributes to the same solid
solution strengthening as Mo, could strongly enhance ﬂoating-type macrosegre-
gation defects. Therefore, it is possible to suppress sinking-type macrosegregation
defects by W addition. A new high-strength Ni-base superalloy (named FX550) for
large-size gas turbine disks has been developed by substituting W for Mo on the
basis of Alloy 718. The microstructure, mechanical properties, and macrosegre-
gation properties of a forging were investigated. According to the experimental
results, the microstructure, microstructure stability, and tensile strength of FX550
were con ﬁrmed as being the same as those of Alloy 718. The macrosegregation
properties of FX550 were also similar to those of Alloy 706, which is used for
large-size gas turbine disks. This paper presents an alloy design method for
improving the macrosegregation properties of Alloy 718. In addition, the trial status
of a large-size disk is described.

## Page 1064

Introduction
Heat-resistant steel with excellent castability is used for the turbine disks of con-
ventional industrial gas turbines. However, high-strength Ni-based wrought alloys
such as Alloy 706 and Alloy 718 have recently been used for the turbine disks of
high ef ﬁciency gas turbines in Europe and America [ 1]. Strengthening elements
such as Al, Ti, Nb, Mo, and W with a different density than that of Ni often cause
macrosegregation. Thereby, it is dif ﬁcult to cast large ingots made from Ni-based
alloys containing a large amount of these strengthening elements. The development
of a Ni-based alloy that enables the production of large ingots has thus become a
critical issue.
Alloy 706 utilizes a strengthening mechanism by the precipitation of γ″ phase
(Ni
3Nb) and shows relatively good castability. Large ingots more than 1000 mm in
diameter made from Alloy 706 can be obtained through a triple melt process
consisting of vacuum induction melting (VIM), electroslag remelting (ESR), and
vacuum arc remelting (VAR).
Alloy 718 is also a γ″ phase strengthened Ni-base alloy and contains a larger
amount of Ni and Nb than Alloy 706. Thus, Alloy 718 has an increased amount of
γ″ phase and exhibits high-temperature strength. Moreover, Alloy 718 can obtain a
ﬁner austenitic grain structure which results in lower noise levels during ultrasonic
testing, allowing a more sensitive inspection than Alloy 706 [ 2].
Strengthening elements such as Nb and Mo tend to concentrate in molten metal
and lead to the formation of sinking-type segregation. As a result, it is dif ﬁcult to
obtain large ingots made from Alloy 718. For these reasons, the applications of
Alloy 718 are limited to small industrial gas turbines and jet engine disks [ 3].

Alloy Design Method
The high strength of Ni-base alloys is achieved by precipitating the γ′ phase (L1 2
structure) and γ″ phase (D0 22 structure), which have a small lattice mismatch with
the matrix γ phase (FCC structure). The amount of γ′ phase and γ″ phase deter-
mines the strength of Ni-base alloys; therefore, to predict strength, the total amount
of precipitation strengthening phase was estimated by phase calculation on the basis
of a thermodynamic equilibrium database using Thermo-Calc ( “Thermo-Calc” is a
trade mark of Stiftelsen for Tillampad Termodynamik registered in Sweden) and
JMatPro ( “JMatPro” is a trade mark of Sente Software Ltd. registered in UK, EU,
USA, China, Japan).
Figure 2 shows the mechanism of forming macrosegregation. Added elements in
the molten alloy are partitioned into either liquid or solid phase at the different ratios
depending on the element type. That leads to microsegregation. Nb is partitioned
more into the liquid phase during solidi ﬁcation (a). In the melting process such as
VAR (b), a difference in density of molten metal near the solidi ﬁcation interface is
generated because of the condensation of alloying elements corresponding to the
solid-liquid partition. Equation ( 1) shows the difference in density Δρ.

Δρ = ρ0 − ρ ð1Þ
Both ρ0 and ρ denote the density of the original molten metal and molten metal
near the solidi ﬁcation interface. Macrosegregation such as freckle defects are
apparently formed by a molten metal ﬂow driven by the difference in density (c).
The density of molten metal is calculated from temperature and alloy compo-
sition, and the density of concentrated liquid phase near the solid-liquid interface is
estimated by calculating the concentration of solute elements during solidi ﬁcation.
The density calculation takes into account the effect of lower temperature until the
ﬂow of liquid phase stops. The partition coef ﬁcient, k, of alloying elements, which
is not de ﬁned in the Ni database, was determined experimentally. The developed
chemical composition was determined from the results of phase calculation and
density calculation. The macrosegregation properties of designed alloys were
evaluated using equipment simulating the solidi ﬁed microstructure of a large ingot.
The difference in density Δρ for Alloy 718 was less than 0, leading to the formation
of sinking-type macrosegregation. Figure 3 shows the calculated composition of
Alloy 718 in the liquid phase using the Scheil module with Ni-data. As solidi ﬁ-
cation progressed, Ti, Nb, and Mo were concentrated in the liquid phase.
The further the atomic weight of alloying elements is different from that of Ni,
the more signi ﬁcant the changes in density become when enriched. Therefore,
increasing the amount of Nb and Mo enhances the formation of sinking-type
macrosegregation, and an increase in Ti has an adverse effect. In order to make the
difference in density close to 0 without lowering the mechanical strength, it is
preferable to substitute Nb with Ti, which stabilizes the precipitation-strengthening
phase (i.e., γ′ phase, γ″ phase). Also, it is thought that solution strengthening
element Mo could be substituted by W (Fig. 4).

Experimental Procedure
Experimental Determination of Partition Coef ﬁcients
In order to accurately calculate the difference in density, the partition coef ﬁcient
was measured by the following method. As macrosegregation is likely to form
when the fraction solid reaches 35%, the temperature corresponding to the fraction
solid of 35% is de ﬁned as the non- ﬂow temperature [ 4]. A test sample was heated to
the temperature calculated fraction solid of 35% using the Scheil-Gulliver equation
and was rapidly cooled to room temperature after being held over 30 min in a
vacuum. Then, the chemical compositions of the solidi ﬁed solid phase part and
liquid phase part were measured by using an electron probe microanalyzer (EPMA).
Solidiﬁcation Simulation
Macrosegregation properties were investigated using a solidi ﬁcation simulator
(Fig. 5) with some compositions that are promising candidates for a large ingot. By
using the simulator, a solidi ﬁed structure of a large ingot exceeding 10 tons can be
simulated with a 10-kg laboratory scale ingot [ 5]. The lab-scale ingot was produced
by remelting the test blocks (200 × 50 × 120 mm in size) in a vacuum or Ar
atmosphere to prevent oxidation. Then the blocks were remelted under the solidi-
ﬁcation conditions of the larger ingot (0.8 –1.0 m in diameter) by cooling from the
chill while controlling both the solidi ﬁcation rate R and cooling rate ε. From the
relationship between the position of the formed macrosegregation and the segre-
gation index SI shown in Eq. ( 2), the critical value of segregation index SI
C, which
is an indicator of the ingot manufacturability, was evaluated [ 6, 7]. The smaller the
value of SI C is, the better the manufacturability.

Mechanical Properties
Mechanical property tests were carried out by forging round bars (14 mm in
diameter) from the 10-kg VIM ingots (Fig. 6). The forging temperature range was
900–1200 °C. The microstructure and tensile strength of Alloy 718 and the can-
didate material were then compared. In order to predict the strength of a large
product with a developed chemical composition, a round bar was made from the
material simulating the microstructure of large ingots, and the strength was
evaluated.
Experimental Results
Solid-liquid partition coefﬁcients of Ti, Nb, and Mo in Alloy 718 were measured to
accurately calculate the density. Since W is not contained in Alloy 718, it was
measured using a composition in which Mo was fully substituted with W. The
results of the partition coef ﬁcient measurement and the Ni-data calculation are
shown in Fig. 7. The measured values of the partition coef ﬁcients of Ti, Nb, and
Mo were virtually the same as the calculated ones. On the other hand, the partition
coefﬁcient of W differs between the calculated and the measured value. Unlike Ti,

phase and the γ″ phase was at the same level, the model A alloy showed an increase
in the γ′ phase and a decrease in the γ″ phase since Nb was replaced with Ti.
Because the γ″ phase, which has a lattice mis ﬁt with the γ phase larger than the γ′
phase, contributes signi ﬁcantly to precipitation strengthening, there is a possibility
that the strength of the model A alloy has decreased. Since the coarsening of the
grain structure greatly affects not only the strength but also the ultrasonic
inspectability, improvement of the composition by replacing Mo with W was
considered to be effective.
Figure 13 shows the fraction solid dependency of the density in the difference
obtained by changing the amount of W added within the range of 2 –6 mass%.
A better chemical composition is W: 4%, Mo: 0, and its Δρ is closer to 0 than that
of Alloy 706. Therefore, the developed model B alloy ’s composition was named
FX550.

The macrosegregation properties of FX550 are quantitatively discussed from the
results of the solidi ﬁcation simulation. The relationship between the distance from
the chill end and the curve of segregation index SI under the solidi ﬁcation condi-
tions of the 10-ton class ingot is shown in Fig. 15. It is known that the critical value
of the segregation index of Alloy 718 and Alloy 706 are 9 and 2, respectively [ 6].
When both of the ingots are manufactured with the same solidi ﬁcation conditions as
these, macrosegregation forms at about 20 and 80 mm from the chill end. The
critical value of the segregation index of FX550 is concluded to be less than 0.7
because there is no sign of macrosegregation in the solidi ﬁcation conditions with a
segregation index of 0.7. From the viewpoint of macrosegregation characteristics,
there is a possibility that an ingot larger than Alloy 706 can be produced with
FX550.

## Page 1074

Trial Production
Figure 17 shows the trial products of FX550 [ 8]. This Ø900-mm ingot was pro-
duced by a VIM-ESR-VAR triple melt process. After that, a billet with a diameter
of about 720 mm was forged from the ingot. Finally, the billet was forged to a disk
with a diameter of 1900 mm or larger by upsetting. No visible cracks were
observed on the surface of the ingot. Figure 18 shows the billet cross-section of the
top position. There was no macrosegregation or detectable cracks, and the billet
passed a UT inspection to AMS-STD-2154 Class A. Figure 19 shows the mi-
crostructure of the disk. In the rim of the disk, the grain size was ASTM 11.5. In the
bore of disk, the grain size was ASTM 10.5. The disk passed AMS-STD-2154
Class AA.
Figures 20, 21 and 22 show the mechanical properties of the Ø1900-mm trial
disk. A tensile test, creep test, and fatigue test were performed for comparison with
the Ø1500-mm FX550 disk [ 9]. All mechanical properties of the Ø1900-mm disk
were equal to those of the Ø1500-mm disk except for ductility. The slight difference

Conclusions
Improvement of Alloy 718 for large-size gas turbine disks was attempted by uti-
lizing the alloy design method considering the formation of macrosegregation. The
results obtained can be summarized as follows:
• As W in Alloy 718 is concentrated in the solid side during solidi ﬁcation, the
addition of W can suppress the formation of sinking-type macrosegregation.
• Decreasing Nb in Alloy 718 prevents the formation of sinking-type
macrosegregation, but the strength also decreased because of the coarsening
of the grains and the reduction of the γ′ and γ″ phase.
• By substituting Mo in Alloy 718 with W, FX550 with improved large-size ingot
manufacturability was developed without lowering the mechanical properties.
• A Ø900-mm VAR ingot using FX550 was manufactured without macrosegre-
gation. A Ø1900-mm class FX550 disk was produced with mechanical prop-
erties that satis ﬁed AMS5663 for Alloy 718.
